en: The Source of the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* School:
In the past, the Master Zhiyi of Tiantai, who was my teacher, the Great Dhyāna Master Si of Nanyue, attained realization of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*.

He beheld the assembly on Vulture Peak as if it were still present, never having dispersed. From that time forward, as he read through various scriptures, his doubts were completely resolved like ice melting away. Upon his awakening...
He pondered for a long time on the meaning of the "Purity of the Six Sense Organs" in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
A monk from the Western Regions said to him, "Only the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* clearly elucidates the merits of the six sense organs; it is sufficient to serve as a corroboration.

Zhizhe thereafter yearned for it with thirst-like longing, bowing toward the west every morning and evening. He continued in this manner for sixteen years. To the left of Mount Nanyue, at Tiantai Temple, there was...
Regarding the ruins of the Scripture-Chanting Terrace: more than a hundred years after Zhiyi’s passing, the *Śūraṃgama Sūtra* first entered China.
The text was transcribed by Fang Xiang (Li Hua), whose phrasing was elegant and refined; consequently, many scholars and gentlemen throughout the realm recited it.

Whenever I have visited the Scripture-Chanting Terrace three times, I would linger there, unable to bear leaving. I inwardly sighed at how the ancients were so deeply devoted to the sacred scriptures, accumulating [their merit] through such practice.
For over ten years, I had not seen it. Now that the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* fills the bookstalls, I have abandoned it and no longer look upon it. Why is this?

Consequently, I resolved to transcribe the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* upon stone, commissioning artisans to engrave it and constructing a stone chamber by laying the slabs in sequence, so that those who come to the Scripture Terrace may read it as they circumambulate.
May all say, "The scripture has arrived," and thus serve as a supplement for the wise.
While I was in the midst of taking up my brush to write, this thought suddenly occurred to me: "What I am writing are merely characters;
they are not the meaning itself. That the wise desire this sutra to come forth is nothing other than their desire for every person to know the meaning of this sutra."
For example, when the ascetic Xuansha Shibei was reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, he clarified the essential point of the mind; he was one who had plumbed its profound meaning.
Furthermore, masters such as Lingyan An, Changshui Xuan, Zhuan’an Gui, Huanglong Nan, as well as Shaolun, Anmin, and others, all attained enlightenment through the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
These various patriarchs did not come in vain; this scripture’s arrival was not for nothing. If...

To understand the meaning through the text and explain the principles by analyzing the characters, one gradually becomes more distant and eventually more superficial; even after passing through dozens of schools, the meaning of the sutra becomes ever more remote.
This is the fault of not seeking it within the mind. Therefore, if one can attain it within the mind, although this sutra has not yet arrived, [its essence is already present].
Yet when the wise establish their doctrines based on the teachings, they often accord with the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.

Failing to grasp the various states of mind, one may face the *Śūraṅgama* daily, yet this scripture remains as if still in the Western Regions. Even if it fills the halls and chambers, what benefit is there?

It is for this reason that the masters of our school regard the elimination of textual interpretations as a primary task, considering them unworthy of esteem; there is indeed a profound reason for this. Nevertheless, these various masters emerged...
The phrasing and diction breathe forth the spirit [of the teachings]. In guiding beginners, the words and meanings are for the most part similar to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
When it comes to revealing the ultimate direction and realizing entry into Bodhi, it is no different from the机缘 (kaiyuan—opportunities for practice) of the twenty-five perfect penetrations.
Thus, even if one does not recite the *Śūraṅgama*, the *Śūraṅgama* is fully present; even if the *Śūraṅgama* had not reached this land, this land has never been without the *Śūraṅgama*. I...
Without measuring my own abilities, I have extensively gathered the words of the patriarchs to pair them with the scriptural texts.

At times they correspond in obscurity; at times they appear in mutual resonance; at times I extrapolate their meaning; and at times I reveal what has not yet been revealed. Wherever my thoughts reached, I took what was needed and found fulfillment.
I myself did not know how my compositions had come to such a state of convergence. Could there truly be such a kind of discourse within heaven and earth?
I have deliberated on this, for throughout many lifetimes I have harbored a long-standing vow, firmly desiring to rely upon this [text] to proclaim the meaning of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.

This is to clarify the scripture by means of the various venerable masters, rather than clarifying the scripture through myself; furthermore, it is to clarify the scripture by means of the essential principle (*zong*), rather than clarifying the scripture through mere textual interpretations.

Thus, I have named this "the Penetration of the Essential Principle" (*zongtong*). Regarding both the Penetration of the Essential Principle and the Penetration of the Teaching (*shetong*), they should...

Is there anyone who has attained realization within their own mind? When the various elder masters open their chests to meet one another, it is as if the single assembly at the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* has not yet dispersed;
and even Zhiyi remains present to this day. Inscribed by Jinjian Zeng Fengyi Shunzheng, Chief of Mount Nanyue.
The Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause for Cultivating and Realizing Enlightenment of the Tathāgata’s Great Uṣṇīṣa and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas, Scroll One.
Translated by the Indian Bhikṣu Paramiti of the Tang Dynasty.
Translated by the śramaṇa Meghaśīla of the kingdom of Ujjayinī;
the oral interpretation provided by the Bodhisattva precept disciple, former Minister of Justice, concurrently Chief Counselor of the Secretariat and Chancellery,
Fang Rong of Qinghe, who recorded the text in writing.
The Bodhisattva Precept Disciple, Formerly the Court Gentleman for Rites and Sacrifices in the Ministry of Rites,
Nanyue Zeng Fengyi, styled Zongtong, said:
"For what reason is this sutra titled *The Great Buddha-Crown Tathāgata’s Secret Cause, Cultivation, Realization, and Definitive Meaning*?"
The myriad practices of the Bodhisattvas are the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
At that time, the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, rising from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and addressed the Buddha, saying: "What should this sutra be named?"

"How shall I and all sentient beings uphold it? The Buddha told Mañjuśrī, "This sutra is named 'The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Śītata-Pāṇḍarā Unsurpassed Jewel Seal,' the pure ocean-eye of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions."

It is also called the "Savior Who Rescues His Own Kin," for it delivers Ānanda and the bhikṣuṇī of this assembly by nature, enabling them to attain the bodhicitta and enter the ocean of universal knowledge.
It is also called the "Tathāgata’s Secret Cause: The Definitive Meaning of Cultivation and Realization.
It is also called the "Great Vaipulya King of the Wondrous Lotus," the "Dhāraṇī Mantra of the Mother of the Buddhas of the Ten Directions," and the "Consecration."
"O Bodhisattvas, you should uphold these chapters and verses of the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, the foremost of all practices.

Although the original text contains many meanings, here it is summarized by the term 'Great Buddha-Crown. This Buddha-Crown Divine Mantra is the *dhāraṇī* mantra that is the mother of the Buddhas of the ten directions;
it is the chapter and verse for consecration (*abhiṣeka*); it is that which delivers Ānanda and the bhikṣu Śubhavyūha."
As for the term "Nī" (nun), it is not repeated here. The mantra says: *Mahā-sitātapatra*. This means "Great White Parasol.
Because it is purely white and clean, and because it covers all things, it is called "Great. This Great Uṣṇīṣa Divine Mantra is inconceivable;
it is the secret cause of the Tathāgata and the definitive meaning of cultivation and realization. All Bodhisattvas...
All myriad practices are herein fully possessed, and thus all are ultimately firm and solid.
Now, that which can proceed gradually but not suddenly cannot be called "Great"; that which can proceed suddenly but not perfectly cannot be called "Great.

What is here termed "Esoteric" and "Perfect" already encompasses the meaning of the sudden; what is termed "Cultivation" and "Realization," as well as the "Myriad Practices," already encompasses the perfect.
In meaning, this uniquely perfect and sudden Dharma-gate is no different from the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

For the stages of faith, abiding, practice, transference, the grounds, and up to the wondrous enlightenment already encompass the *Avataṃsaka*, while the "Perfect Penetration of the Ear-organ" is fully interwoven with the "Universal Gate" chapter;
thus it simultaneously possesses the essential purports of both sutras. Its greatness...
How is this? For one who has not yet awakened, to transform the non-arising and non-ceasing into arising and ceasing is not the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
For one who has awakened, to transform arising and ceasing into the non-arising and non-ceasing is the ultimate, all-pervading solidity.

Therefore, regarding the path that transcends [the mundane], it cannot be realized without awakening. Now, in that case, what connection does mantra have to awakening? And what connection does awakening have to mantra? They are equal.
Why is it called by the name "Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa"? Because the mantra is inconceivable, and awakening is also inconceivable.
The mantra is the realm of awakening; awakening is the realm of the mantra. The path of language is cut off, and the sphere of mental activity is transcended. Even seeing is detached from seeing.
It cannot be reached by ordinary vision; therefore, it is taken from the Buddha’s crown (uṣṇīṣa). This is because it is free from the characteristics of one's own [limited] vision.

Furthermore, the Uṣṇīṣa family of all Buddhas is the most transcendent and direct path for those who are supreme and most noble among the Dharma gates. For this reason, the title of the treatise is called *Zūndǐng* (The Honored Crown).
A monk asked Huangbo, "Why does the Bodhisattva Anantagātra not see the crown-mark of the Tathāgata?
Huangbo said, "In truth, there is nothing to be seen. Why? Because the Bodhisattva Anantagātra is himself the Tathāgata;
he should not see anything further. I merely teach you not to form the view of a Buddha, so as not to fall on the side of Buddhahood, and not to form the view of a sentient being."

They do not fall into the extreme of sentient beings; they do not form a view of existence, nor fall into the extreme of existence, nor form a view of non-existence, nor fall into the extreme of non-existence.
They do not form the views of ordinary people, nor fall into the extreme of ordinary people; they do not form the views of sages, nor fall into the extreme of sages.
To be without all such views is precisely to be the Boundless Body (*anantakāya*). If there is a place for views, one is called a non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*). As for non-Buddhists, they delight in...
Regarding all views, the Bodhisattva remains unmoved by them. The Tathāgata is the meaning of the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena.
Therefore it is said that Maitreya is also suchness. Suchness is non-arising; suchness is non-ceasing;

suchness is without seeing; suchness is without hearing. "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) signifies perfection, yet there is no view of perfection; thus one does not fall into the extreme of perfection. Therefore...

The Buddha-body is unconditioned and does not fall into any numerical categories. It is provisionally compared to empty space; it is perfectly identical to the great void, without deficiency and without excess.
It is naturally at ease and without affairs—do not force yourself to debate other realms. To engage in debate is to become attached, which constitutes consciousness.
Furthermore, a monk asked Baizhang, "Why is it that the Bodhisattva Anantakāya cannot see the crown of the Tathāgata’s head? Baizhang said, "Because..."
One forms views of finitude and views of infinity; for this reason, one does not see the Tathāgata’s crown-mark (*uṣṇīṣa*).
Only when, right now, there is a total absence of all views such as existence and non-existence, and even no view of "non-viewing," is this called seeing the crown-mark.

Regarding the two venerable masters’ explanation of the meaning of the Buddha’s crown, it is like a pearl rolling on a tray: if you know where it lands, you may say that the crown-opening is fully possessed.

The Single Eye. Since it is called "the secret cause of the Tathāgata," it does not depend upon cultivation or realization. Yet, it is also called "the definitive meaning of cultivation and realization";
how then is this distinguished from that which is non-definitive? This is because "Tathāgata" is a name for the fruition. As the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says:
"If someone were to say that the Tathāgata comes or goes, sits or lies down, that person does not understand."
This is the meaning of what I have taught. Why is this? The Tathāgata comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; therefore, he is called the Tathāgata.
Since he comes from nowhere and goes nowhere, what thing could he possibly be? This may be called profound.
The Buddha-śikhara-dhāraṇī is the secret speech of the Tathāgata; its secrecy is non-dual. Taking this secrecy as the cause—

One immediately attains the fruit through this very mystery, just as the core of a lotus [is present within the flower]. Because cause and effect are simultaneously complete, one takes this as cultivation—yet there is no cultivation;
one takes this as realization—yet there is no realization. As the Sūtra says: "What need is there for the toil of cultivating and realizing through the knotty parts of practice?
This is the purport of the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). Were it otherwise, it would still be considered non-definitive (*neyārtha*).
In the past, Huiming pursued and caught up with the Sixth Patriarch.
The Patriarch said, "Since you have come for the sake of the Dharma, you should set aside all conditions and do not give rise to a single thought; I shall speak for you.

After a long silence, the Patriarch said, "When you are neither thinking of good nor thinking of evil—at that very moment—what is the original face of Elder Huiming? At these words, Huiming attained great awakening.
Wu attained enlightenment. He asked again, "Beyond the secret words and secret meanings mentioned above, is there yet another secret meaning? The Patriarch said, "What I have told you is not secret.
If you turn back and reflect, the secret is right with you. Ming said, "Although I was at Huangmei, I truly did not realize my own face.
Now that I have received your instruction, it is like a person drinking water [who knows for themselves whether it is cold or warm]."
Water—its coldness or warmth is known by oneself. Now, the practitioner is none other than this very teacher.
The Patriarch said, "If you are thus, I and you shall share the same teacher at Huangmei; guard and uphold this well.
Furthermore, when Huairang first visited Master An of Mount Song, he asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? An replied, "Why do you not ask about your own mind?"
Rang asked, "What is one's own original intent? Shanshan said, "You must observe the secret function. Rang asked, "What is the secret function?
Shanshan indicated it by opening and closing his eyes. Rang did not understand. Shanshan pointed him toward the Sixth Patriarch.
The Patriarch asked, "Where have you come from? Huairang replied, "Mount Song. The Patriarch asked, "What thing comes like this?
Huairang was unable to answer. After eight years had passed, he finally said to the Patriarch, "I have reached a point of understanding. The Patriarch asked, "How so?"
He replied, "To describe it as being like a single thing is immediately incorrect. The Patriarch asked, "Can it still be cultivated and realized?
He replied, "Cultivation and realization are not non-existent; however, it cannot be defiled. The Patriarch said, "Excellent!
This very state of being undefiled is that which all Buddhas protect and keep in mind. Since you are thus, I am also thus. These two venerable elders were indeed profound.

One realizes the profound intent and attains the definitive meaning through cultivation and realization. Later, a monk asked Baizhang, "The ancestral patriarchs of old all possessed secret words that were transmitted from one to another;
what do you say to this? Baizhang replied, "There are no secret words. The Tathāgata has no hidden treasury.
It is simply the present mirror-like awareness and speech, which are clear and distinct; yet if one seeks their form or characteristics, they are utterly unfindable."

This is the secret language. From the stage of *srotāpanna* upward, all the way to the tenth ground (*daśabhūmi*), whatever words and phrases exist are entirely categorized as the dust and grime of phenomena (*dharmarajas*).
Whatever words and phrases exist are entirely subsumed under the side of afflictions (*kleśapakṣa*).

Whatever words and phrases exist are entirely of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*). No words and phrases whatsoever are permitted; even the teachings of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) are both [excluded].
What further secret words need to be sought? According to Baizhang’s realization, even the single character "secret" must be spat out;
even the teachings of definitive meaning are not established. This can be called walking upon the crowns of the thousand Buddhas and the myriad practices of all Bodhisattvas.
Regarding "not yet having departed from cultivation and realization," what is meant by "all that is ultimately firm and solid"?

It is because all Bodhisattvas, prior to reaching the stage of consecration (*abhiṣeka*), possess both cultivation and realization; once they have reached the stage of consecration, they transcend directly into Equal and Wondrous Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
What cultivation or realization could there be then? Although all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent, everything nevertheless flows forth from within this Wondrous Enlightenment.
The Dharma is quiescent in its own place; therefore, it is called the ultimate and firm. A sutra says:
"There is a samādhi named the Great Buddha-Crown Śūraṅgama King, which fully encompasses the myriad practices and through which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions transcend by a single gate."
The "Path of Sublime Adornment. This samādhi is precisely the Great Samādhi of Śūraṅgama; it is the path of sublime adornment that fully embodies the myriad practices.
It is not a state of concentration that exists apart from the myriad practices as something distinct.
Since everything is concentration, it is said that "all matters are ultimately firm and solid. Master Fu constantly engaged in manual labor by day, and at night...
While practicing the Way, he beheld the three Tathāgatas—Śākyamuni, Suvarṇapuṣpa, and Dīpaṃkara—who emitted light that enveloped his body.
The Great Being then said, "I have attained the Śūraṅgama Samādhi; yet this sutra has not yet arrived, though its name has already been inscribed [upon my brow].

How extraordinary! The Fourth Patriarch spoke to the Chan Master Niu-tou Rong, saying: "The hundreds of thousands of dharma-gates all return to the single square inch of the mind. As numerous as the sands of the Ganges..."

Wondrous Virtue, all is fundamentally within the source of the mind. All gates of precepts, gates of concentration, and gates of wisdom, as well as spiritual powers and transformations, are entirely and spontaneously complete;
they do not depart from your own mind. All afflictions and karmic obstructions are originally empty and quiescent.
All causes and effects are like dreams and illusions. There is no triple world to escape, and there is no Bodhi to seek. Humans and non-humans...
The nature and characteristics of persons are equal. The Great Way is vast and empty, transcending thought and deliberation.

Such a Dharma you have now attained; there is nothing lacking. How is this different from that of the Buddha? There is no other dharma. You need only allow your mind to be free and at ease. Do not perform contemplative practices;
do not attempt to clarify the mind. Do not give rise to greed or anger; do not harbor sorrow or anxiety. Be vast and open.

Unobstructed, moving freely in all directions, neither performing any good nor committing any evil—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, whatever meets the eye or encounters the conditions—is entirely the wondrous function of the Buddha.
Joyful and free from sorrow, he is therefore called a Buddha.
Upon hearing this, Chan Master Rong produced a "sideways branch" of the Buddha-dharma, namely the *Guanding Zhangju* (The Chapter on Consecration). How could anything surpass it? This is the Dharma.

Master Yan said: "To practice for three lifetimes across sixty kalpas, or four lifetimes across one hundred kalpas, and thus proceed until the fruit of the three asaṃkhyeya-kalpas is fulfilled—even the ancients said this is not as good as a single thought-moment of non-arising dependent origination, which transcends the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles. Therefore it is said:
'In a snap of the fingers, the eighty thousand gates are perfectly accomplished; in a kṣaṇa, the three asaṃkhyeya-kalpas are extinguished. —The School (Zong).
Within this very gate there has always existed such a marvelous phenomenon. How could it be said that the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* can only be attained after the fulfillment of the myriad practices?
"Sūtra" (Jing) means the eternal Way. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "In weaving, there is the warp and there is the woof;
the warp is constant while the woof changes. This sūtra was brought forth by Nāgārjuna from the Dragon Palace through silent recitation, and was received by the sovereigns of the Five Indias.
It has been kept secret and not transmitted; how could one know that this sutra is possessed by every person and is lacking in no one, being indeed the eternal Way?
Why, then, must it be kept secret? A monk asked Shoushan, "All Buddhas emerge from this sutra."
"What is this sutra? Yunyan said, "Lower your voice, lower your voice. The monk asked, "How does one uphold it? Yunyan said, "Without defilement. Touzi’s verse says:
Water flows from Mount Kunlun, clouds arise; The fisherman and the woodcutter are ignorant of the cause.
They know only that the surging waves and rocky peaks are vast, Yet they refuse to cast their lines or lay down their axes. Yunyan sought [the Way].
He never permitted others to read the scriptures. On one occasion, while he was reading them himself, a monk asked, "Master, you usually do not allow others to read the scriptures;
why then do you read them yourself? The mountain master replied, "I only wish to shield my eyes. The monk asked, "May I learn this from you, Master?
The mountain master said, "If you were to read them, even ox-hide would have to be pierced through. Thus, one knows that [the practice of] shielding the eyes is a matter of spiritual capacity.

[The text] is complete. This constitutes the excellence of receiving and upholding [the Dharma]. If one does not penetrate the "ox-hide" (i.e., the subtlest obscurations), how could one avoid falling into defilement?

Thus have I heard: at one time, the Buddha was staying in the city of Śrāvastī (translated here as "Abundant Virtue"), in the Jetavana Monastery (that is, the Anāthapiṇḍika Park), together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus, all of whom were great Arhats free from outflows.

The Arhat replied: "Thus have I heard at one time. All sūtras are headed by these words. When Ānanda, following the Buddha’s final instructions, compiled the various sūtras and uttered these six characters, all doubts were instantly dispelled. As for the phrase "Thus, thus": it means that the Tathāgata spoke in accordance with reality, and Ānanda recorded them exactly as they were spoken. It signifies that what was taught is not false, but is precisely as it is. Furthermore, "Thus" refers to the Dharma; "I" refers to the person; "heard" refers to the auditory faculty; "at one time" indicates that the teaching occurred on a single occasion. This establishes the four reliances: relying on the Dharma and not on the person, relying on the meaning and not on the letter, relying on the definitive meaning and not on the interpretable meaning, and relying on direct knowledge and not on discursive consciousness. Thus, the four reliances are established through these six characters. Moreover, "Thus" is the beginning of the sūtra; "I" is the speaker; "heard" is the act of hearing; "at one time" is the time of the teaching; "Buddha" is the teacher; "in Śrāvastī" is the location; "with a great assembly of bhikṣus" is the retinue; "the World-Honored One" is the title of honor; "dwelling" is the state of abiding; "at Jeta Grove" is the specific site; "in the Garden of Anāthapiṇḍada" is the name of the grove; "there" is the place; "together with" is the gathering; "five hundred bhikṣus" is the number; "all of whom were arhats" describes their realization; "free from outflows" means they had severed the afflictions; "with taints exhausted" means they had ended birth and death; "attaining liberation" means they had attained the fruit of nirvāṇa; "their minds well-liberated" means they were liberated from the hindrance of afflictions; "wisdom well-liberated" means they were liberated from the hindrance of the knowable; "having fully exhausted the outflows" means they had no further rebirth; "with the burden laid down" means they had abandoned the five aggregates; "attaining their own benefit" means they had realized the fruit of arhatship; "completely extinguishing all fetters" means they had severed the bonds of existence; "being liberated according to their wish" means they could manifest births at will; "their minds being unshakable" means they were free from the eight worldly winds; "having attained mastery over their minds" means they were unimpeded in the three knowledges; "having fulfilled their duties" means they had completed the work of the Three Jewels; "having cast off the body" means they had transcended the physical form; "having reached the end of the path" means they had attained the ultimate fruit; "having exhausted birth and death" means they would not be born again; "reaching the shore of nirvāṇa" means they had crossed the ocean of suffering; "having accomplished all that was to be done" means they had perfected the path of cultivation; "having laid down the heavy burden" means they had abandoned the burden of the aggregates; "attaining the supreme goal" means they had realized the fruit of arhatship; "completely exhausting the outflows" means they had severed the bonds of existence; "with pure conduct" means they were free from the stains of transgression; "pure in body" means they were free from the defilement of the physical form; "pure in speech" means they were free from the defilement of verbal expression; "pure in mind" means they were free from the defilement of mental activity; "pure in view" means they were free from the defilement of wrong views; "pure in conduct" means they were free from the defilement of improper behavior; "pure in livelihood" means they were free from the defilement of wrong livelihood; "pure in the three karmas" means they were free from the defilement of the three types of action; "pure in the two gates" means they were free from the defilement of the two obstacles; "pure in the two truths" means they were free from the defilement of the two extremes; "pure in the two vehicles" means they were free from the defilement of the two paths; "pure in the two fruits" means they were free from the defilement of the two results; "pure in the two bodies" means they were free from the defilement of the two forms; "pure in the two realms" means they were free from the defilement of the two worlds; "pure in the two liberations" means they were free from the defilement of the two obstacles; "pure in the two knowledges" means they were free from the defilement of the two ignorances; "pure in the two wisdoms" means they were free from the defilement of the two delusions; "pure in the two insights" means they were free from the defilement of the two obstructions; "pure in the two practices" means they were free from the defilement of the two deviations; "pure in the two virtues" means they were free from the defilement of the two faults; "pure in the two merits" means they were free from the defilement of the two evils; "pure in the two blessings" means they were free from the defilement of the two calamities; "pure in the two fortunes" means they were free from the defilement of the two misfortunes; "pure in the two joys" means they were free from the defilement of the two sorrows; "pure in the two delights" means they were free from the defilement of the two anxieties; "pure in the two pleasures" means they were free from the defilement of the two pains; "pure in the two comforts" means they were free from the defilement of the two distresses; "pure in the two ease" means they were free from the defilement of the two hardships; "pure in the two tranquility" means they were free from the defilement of the two agitations; "pure in the two peace" means they were free from the defilement of the two disturbances; "pure in the two bliss" means they were free from the defilement of the two sufferings; "pure in the two happiness" means they were free from the defilement of the two miseries; "pure in the two joy" means they were free from the defilement of the two griefs; "pure in the two delight" means they were free from the defilement of the two lamentations; "pure in the two gladness" means they were free from the defilement of the two despair; "pure in the two contentment" means they were free from the defilement of the two discontent; "pure in the two satisfaction" means they were free from the defilement of the two dissatisfaction; "pure in the two fulfillment" means they were free from the defilement of the two non-fulfillment; "pure in the two completion" means they were free from the defilement of the two incompleteness; "pure in the two perfection" means they were free from the defilement of the two imperfection; "pure in the two excellence" means they were free from the defilement of the two inferiority; One may simply have confidence; there is no room for verbal explanation. If one realizes this Dharma, which was secretly transmitted by the Buddhas and Patriarchs, then all subsequent complications will be nothing more than its footnotes.
A monk visited National Teacher Nanyang Zhong; the Master asked, "What practice do you engage in?
The monk replied, "I lecture on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. The Master said, "What are the first two characters? The monk replied:
"So it is. The Master said, "What is this? The monk had no reply. "Alas! What kind of sutra lecture is this?
Furthermore, Chan Master Xuefeng Cun asked a Dharma Master, "Regarding these two words, 'So it is' (*evam*), they are entirely part of the commentary.
What is the original text? The Master had no reply. Wuyun spoke on his behalf, saying, "One must further divide it into three sections. Now tell me, what did Wuyun bring forth?
"Discourse. This is the topical outline; this is the root text. A bhikṣu possesses three meanings: he is called a "mendicant" (bhikṣu), a "destroyer of evil," and a "terror to Māra.
An arhat also possesses three meanings: he is called a "worthy of offerings" (arhat), a "slayer of thieves," and one who is "without rebirth" (anupapatti).
The beginning cause and the final fruit correspond to one another. They are all termed "Great" to distinguish them from minor works, indicating the source from which they derive.
As for "the matter" (事), it refers to the "Great" of the Great Buddha-Crown; therefore, both are designated by the name "Great. There are likewise three kinds of outflows (*āsrava*):
namely, ignorance (*avidyā*), desire (*kāma*), and existence (*bhava*). As the Sūtra says: "You have often heard me, within the Vinaya, proclaim the three definitive principles of practice:
that is to say, collecting the mind constitutes morality (*śīla*); from morality arises concentration (*samādhi*); and from concentration issues forth..."
Wisdom. These are called the three untainted trainings (*anāsrava-śikṣā*). Precept is freedom from the outflow of desire; concentration is freedom from the outflow of existence;
wisdom is freedom from the outflow of ignorance. These three untainted states are termed the "definitive meaning.
It appears that wisdom is taken as the ultimate standard; yet Dongshan said to Caoshan: "In the age of the Dharma’s decline, many people possess only dry wisdom. If one wishes to discern..."
To verify the true and the false, there are three kinds of leakage: first, leakage of view, wherein the faculty does not leave its station and falls into a sea of poison;
second, leakage of emotion, wherein one stagnates in preference and aversion, and the locus of vision becomes partial and withered;

third, leakage of speech, wherein one pursues the subtle while losing the source, the faculty being muddled regarding the beginning and the end, and turbid wisdom circulating. Regarding these three kinds, you should [be cautious].

This is understood. Within the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*), these three types are further distinguished; without the eye of the discernment of dharmas (*dharmapravicaya-cakṣus*), one cannot penetrate and shatter them.
Therefore, regarding the Arhat who dedicates [his merit] toward the Mahāyāna, one must examine this in conjunction with the words of Dongshan;
only then will the meaning of "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*) be fully realized.

The Buddha’s disciples abide in the maintenance of the teachings and skillfully transcend all realms of existence. They are able to manifest majestic deportment within the lands, turning the wheel of the Dharma following the Buddha and being worthy of his sublime entrustment.
They strictly purify the *vinaya*—here translated as "precepts and discipline"—and establish a grand model for the three worlds.
Their response-bodies are infinite as they deliver and liberate sentient beings, rescuing those of the future and transcending the burdens of worldly dust.
Tong said: "That which is called 'abiding and maintaining' (zhuchi) refers to the ever-abiding enlightened nature, which is able to sustain all phenomena.
These few words provide a general summary that truly encompasses the great purport of the entire sutra.

To say it 'skillfully transcends all realms of existence' means that it cannot be obstructed by the seven inquiries and eight returns, the five aggregates, the six sense bases, the twelve entrances, the eighteen elements, or even the seven great elements. [He] broke [the silence].

The meaning of "delusion" is fully established. What is called "accomplishing dignified deportment" refers to the establishment of the *bodhimaṇḍa*, the three gradual stages, and the fifty-five ranks of the path to Bodhi.
The meaning of "revealing the truth" is fully established.

What is called "wondrously worthy of the final instruction" refers to the twenty-five perfect modes of penetration (*vimalā-prativedha*), each of which realizes its own intrinsic nature and is equally worthy of receiving the prediction of Buddhahood.
The fundamental tenet of seeing one's nature exists inherently; it is said that it establishes a grand model for the three realms.

This sutra upholds the Vinaya, repeatedly emphasizing the four prohibitions, the ten wholesome actions, and the nine successive stages of concentration, thereby extensively manifesting the rules and regulations for the three realms.

When Ānanda requested instruction, he took the severance of lust as his primary task—this is precisely what is present here. It is said that the response-body is immeasurable; thus, [the Buddha] commanded all...
It is said that Bodhisattvas and Arhats manifest transformation bodies within the age of the Dharma-ending period, assuming various forms to deliver those wandering in saṃsāra.
This is precisely for the purpose of protecting sentient beings of the Dharma-ending age from demonic activities, transcending all worldly entanglements, and realizing perfect penetration.
This is truly the ultimate intention of the Tathāgata’s final instructions. These are the words left behind by Chan Master Fengxue Zhao.
He said: "If one speck of dust is established, the state and its families flourish, yet the village elders frown.

If not even one speck of dust is established, the state and its families perish, yet the village elders sing for joy. Xuedou took up his staff and asked, "Is there any monk who shares the same life and death [as all things]?
His intention lay in the place where the speck of dust is established. He then offered this verse: "Let the village elder be taught not to knit his brows; For now, let us strive..."
The house and the state are established upon the foundation; where now are the strategists and the fierce generals? The pure breeze from ten thousand *li* is known only to oneself.
Xuedou does not abandon a single dharma within the gate of Buddhist practice; Tiandong, moreover, does not admit a single speck of dust upon the ground of ultimate reality.
These two dharmas are practiced in tandem and presented together in this verse: "White-haired, he rose by the waters of the Wei to cast his line..."
Lun: "How is he like that man who starved to death on Mount Shouyang? It is merely a matter of how a single speck of dust manifests different transformations;
his lofty reputation and meritorious achievements are both difficult to erase. Furthermore, Changqing said: "If everyone were like today, the old barbarian would have hope. Baofu said:
"If everyone were like today, the old barbarian would have no hope. Tiandong took up the case and said: "The wealthy loathe having too few mouths to feed; the poor lament having even one too many."
There are many such instances. When observing how various senior masters have transmitted and upheld the Great Teaching, they all attained the same realization as the Buddhas and Patriarchs;
their resolve to deliver future generations was indistinguishable from theirs. Therefore, I have recorded these accounts as the law for those who serve as abbots.
Their names were Mahāmati Śāriputra (translated here as "Son of Śāri"), Mahāmaudgalyāyana (translated here as "Great Mung-bean Clan"), Mahākauṣṭhila (translated here as "Great Knees"),
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra (translated here as "Son of Maitrāyaṇī the Full"), Subhūti (translated here as "Empty Birth"), Upānanda (translated here as "Dust-Nature-Empty"),
and others who served as the leaders. Furthermore, there were immeasurable pratyekabuddhas and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Together with his original aspiration, he came to the Buddha’s presence.

At the time when the bhikṣus were observing the *pravāraṇā* at the end of the summer retreat, the bodhisattvas from the ten directions—these sentient beings awakened to reality—sought to resolve their doubts and, out of reverence for the Compassionate and Venerable One, requested the profound meaning.

Thereupon, the Tathāgata spread his seat and sat in peaceful repose, proclaiming the deep and abstruse teachings to the assembly. The pure multitude at the Dharma feast attained what they had never experienced before.
Tong said: "This is the beginning of the sutra's narrative. It states that the various bodhisattvas were about to seek the esoteric meaning, yet it does not say what constitutes the 'esoteric.
It states that the World-Honored One proclaimed the profound, yet it does not say what constitutes the 'profound.
Why was it that the pure assembly at the Dharma feast attained what they had never experienced before? Once, when the World-Honored One ascended the seat, Mañjuśrī struck the gavel."
He said: "Observe closely the Dharma reaching the Dharma; such is the Dharma of the Dharma King. Thereupon, the World-Honored One descended from his seat.
The Celestial Youth (Tiantong) composed a verse: Do you see this single piece of true wind? The subtle Mother of Transformation employs the shuttle of principle.

She weaves an ancient brocade containing the image of spring; Alas, what can be done about the Lord of the East leaking it out? Xuedou composed a verse: Amidst the assembly of the successive sages, he acts...

This is how one knows. The Dharma-king’s teaching does not proceed in such a manner. If there were a *śrāmaṇera* guest within this assembly, why would it necessarily require Mañjuśrī to strike a single blow?

If one could obtain a message while the World-Honored One sat at ease upon his prepared seat, that would be a truly wondrous accord with the profound mystery, one that does not depend on the proliferation of words and explanations. Even for a *pratyekabuddha*, there is the initial arousal of the mind.

He was indeed a follower of the Pratyekabuddhas. At the conclusion of the summer retreat (*pravāraṇā*), the Vinaya permits a period of three days—namely, the fourteenth, fifteenth, and sixteenth of the seventh month.

Then, with a voice like that of the kalaviṅka bird, he caused his sound to pervade the ten directions; Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges gathered at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), along with Mañjuśrī.
He served as their leader.
It was explained that the kalaviṅka bird possesses a beautiful voice even while still in its egg, such that no other birds can rival it;

this is a metaphor for the sudden teaching entering the lineage of the Tathāgata, which does not require gradual cultivation and is beyond the reach of the three vehicles. This voice of the Tathāgata is manifested in response [to beings].
This is because of those with sudden capacity (*tongji*). Formerly, Maudgalyāyana wished to exhaustively fathom the Buddha’s voice;

exerting all his supernatural powers, he traversed worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges until he reached a certain buddha-land. There, the *saṃbhogakāya* was exceedingly vast, and the rice in his bowl surrounded him like a great road.
As Maudgalyāyana shook his mendicant’s staff and walked upon it, the disciples of that buddha asked their master, "What kind of insects are there? and so forth.
The person who appeared there was that Buddha’s voice. He was Maudgalyāyana, a disciple of Śākyamuni Buddha in this Sahā world.
One must not underestimate him because of his small stature. When asked why he had come to this place, Maudgalyāyana replied that he had exhausted the Buddha’s sounds.
That Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana, "The Buddha’s sounds are inexhaustible; they cannot be exhausted by you. Thereupon, Maudgalyāyana...
Thus it is returned. That which is called "pervading the worlds of the ten directions" indeed has its evidence.
Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges each have their own dwelling places, as recorded in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*: Potalaka, Cīrakūṭa, Wutai, Emei, and the Nārāyaṇa Cave.

These monasteries stand in rows facing one another, with followers crowding shoulder to shoulder. As the universe is infinite, what place is there that is not a dwelling for bodhisattvas? So it is heard.
The Buddha’s voice. They gathered at the Buddha’s dwelling; even the sands of the Ganges would not suffice to describe their vast number.

Mañjuśrī—here translated as "Wondrous Virtue" (Miaode)—symbolizes ultimate wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*). Since he proclaims the sudden teaching (*tun-jiao*), Mañjuśrī is the primary recipient of the teaching and thus serves as the leader.
Formerly, the Chan Master Wuzhuo Wenxi once traveled to the Vajra Cave on Mount Wutai to pay his respects to Mañjuśrī.
He encountered an old man leading an ox who invited the Master into a temple. The old man called out, "Junti! and a boy responded by coming out to welcome them.
The old man released the ox and led the Master up into the hall; the entire building was radiant with golden light.
The old man sat upon the couch and pointed to an embroidered seat, commanding him to sit. The old man asked, "From where have you recently come? Huixi replied, "From the South. The old man said:
"How is the Buddha-dharma maintained in the south? Baizhang asked. Huiji replied, "In the age of the Dharma's decline, few bhikṣus uphold the precepts.
Baizhang asked, "How large is the assembly? Huiji replied, "It is either three hundred or five hundred. Huiji then asked in turn about the Buddha-dharma in this region.
"How do you maintain the monastery? the old man asked. Xuanze said, "Dragons and snakes are intermingled; ordinary people and sages dwell together.
The old man asked, "How many followers do you have? Xuanze said, "Three times three before, and three times three after. The old man called for a lad to serve tea, along with some whey and curd.
Xuanze tasted them, and his mind was suddenly enlightened. The old man picked up a crystal cup and asked, "Is there anything like this in the South?"
“Is this it? Xì said, “No. The old man asked, “What do you usually use to drink tea? Xì was speechless. What a pity!
At that moment, he should have simply smashed the glass cup. Seeing that the sun was already low, Xì then asked the old man, “May I stay for one night?
The old man said, “You still harbor a mind of attachment; you may not stay. Xì said:
"Venerable sir, I have no mind of attachment. The old man asked, "Have you ever received the precepts? Huixi replied, "I have received them long ago.
The old man said, "If you have no mind of attachment, what use is there for receiving the precepts? Huixi took his leave and departed; the old man ordered a youth to escort him.
The boy asked, "What is the total of three times three before and three times three after? He called out, "Venerable One! and Hui responded, "Yes.
The boy asked, "How much is that? Hui asked again, "Where is this place? The boy replied, "This is the Vajra Cave Prajñā Monastery.
Hui was moved to sorrowful realization that the old man was none other than Mañjuśrī himself; he could not bear to see him again.
Upon seeing him, he prostrated to the youth and requested, "I pray you, grant me a word as a parting gift. The youth spoke a verse, saying: "No anger on the face is the offering;
No anger in the mouth emits wondrous fragrance; No anger in the heart is the true treasure; Stainless and untainted is the eternal reality.
Having finished speaking, Junti vanished along with the temple. Later, Huiji went to visit Yangshan.
Wenxi suddenly attained realization and entered into spiritual accord with him. Wenxi was appointed as the head cook (*dianzuo*).
Manjusri constantly appeared above the rice-pot, and Wenxi, using his rice-stirring paddle, struck him and said, "Manjusri is Manjusri; Wenxi is Wenxi. Thereupon, Manjusri spoke this verse:
"The bitter gourd is bitter from root to tip; The sweet melon is sweet from stem to end. Having practiced for three great eons, I have instead been struck by an old..."
The monks were dissatisfied. When it comes to this point, do you still say there is a mind of attachment? Xuedou’s verse says: "A thousand bees coil together, their color like indigo;
Who would say that Manjushri is in dialogue with them? How laughable, the vast assembly at Qingliang— Three times three before, and three times three after.
If one can penetrate and be liberated here, I grant that they have met Manjushri face-to-face.

At that time, King Prasenajit (whose name means "Victorious Army") was observing a fast on the anniversary of his father’s death. He invited the Buddha to the inner palace and personally went out to welcome the Tathāgata.
He prepared an extensive array of rare delicacies and unsurpassed, exquisite flavors, and also personally extended invitations to the great bodhisattvas.

Within the city, there were also elders and lay devotees who were simultaneously providing meals for the Saṃgha, waiting for the Buddha to come and respond to their offerings. The Buddha then commanded Mañjuśrī to distribute [the offerings].

Accompanying the Bodhisattvas and Arhats, he was to attend to the various hosts of donors; however, Ānanda (here translated as "Qingxi," meaning Joy)—having previously accepted a private invitation—had traveled far and had not yet returned.
Thus, he was unable to join the assembly in the proper order. Since there was neither a *sthavira* (Elder) nor an *ācārya* (here, a Master of Discipline) present, he returned alone from the road.
On that day, there were no offerings provided for him. At once, Ānanda took up his *pātra* (alms bowl) and proceeded through the city where he was traveling.
He proceeded to beg for alms, first seeking out the final donor (*dānapati*—here translated as "the giver") to serve as the host of the feast.

Without distinguishing between the pure and the impure, whether they were of the *kṣatriya* caste (here translated as "royal lineage") or the *caṇḍāla* (here translated as "butcher"), he practiced equal compassion toward all, making no selection among the lowly or humble.
He resolved to bring to full completion the immeasurable merit of all sentient beings. Ānanda already knew that the Tathāgata, in this world...
The World-Honored One rebuked Subhūti and Mahākāśyapa (here translated as "Drinking Light"), who, though Arhats, were not yet equanimous in mind.

Out of deep reverence for the Tathāgata, he sought to expound the unobstructed Dharma and deliver those subject to doubt and slander. Passing through the city moat, he walked slowly toward the city gate, his deportment solemn and orderly, strictly observing the rules of pure discipline.
Tong said: "King Prasenajit and the elder householder were both feeding the Sangha at the same time;
why was it so grand? It is because the merit of feeding the Sangha is the most beneficial.

The Buddha once explained the retribution for giving to Sudatta, saying that much may be given with little reward, while little may be given with great reward. To make offerings to hundreds of thousands of Buddhas is not as [meritorious as...]"

To support a single practitioner of pure conduct—even to the extent of making offerings to hundreds of thousands of Buddhas—is not as meritorious as making an offering to a single mindless Way-person (*amūḍha-vihārin*).
Furthermore, the *Sūtra of Forty-two Sections* states: The Buddha said, "To feed a hundred evil people is not as good as feeding one virtuous person;
to feed a thousand virtuous people is not as good as feeding one who upholds the five precepts; to feed one who upholds the five precepts..."
Ten thousand [meals] are not equal to feeding one *srotāpanna*. Feeding a million *srotāpannas* is not equal to feeding one *sakṛdāgāmin*.
Feeding ten million *sakṛdāgāmins* is not equal to feeding one *anāgāmin*.
Feeding one hundred million *anāgāmins* is not equal to feeding one *arhat*. Feeding ten billion *arhats* is not equal to feeding one...
Feeding ten billion pratyekabuddhas is not as good as feeding one Buddha of the three periods of time.
Feeding a thousand billion Buddhas of the three periods of time is not as good as feeding one who is without thought, without dwelling, without cultivation, and without realization.
The general meaning is the same. A monk asked Luopu: "It is said that making offerings to hundreds of thousands of Buddhas is not as good as making offerings to a single mindless man of the Way.
What fault do the hundreds of thousands of Buddhas have, and what virtue does the mindless man of the Way possess?"
Puyun said: "A single sheet of white cloud spans the mouth of the valley; how many returning birds are utterly lost as to their nests.
Danxia’s verse says: "Shide is negligent and does not realize dawn; Hanshan is indolent and knows not when to return. Before the sound, a single phrase of perfect resonance;
Beyond all things, the crescent moon shines upon the three peaks. This is a verse solely for the sake of the mindless man of the Way. It is sweet.
A monastery attendant entered Nanquan’s quarters one day to arrange a vegetarian feast. Huangbo was serving as the head seat (*śrāmaṇera*). The attendant requested that alms be given.
Huangbo said, “Between the two gifts of wealth and Dharma, there is no difference. The attendant replied, “If you speak thus, how can you deserve my offering? He then took his leave and departed.
A short while later, he re-entered and said, “Please grant me the gift of wealth. Huangbo said, “Wealth and Dharma... [The text ends here].

The two patrons, Gan and Nai, were equal and made no distinction between them. Gan then proceeded to distribute alms. On another day, he entered the temple to provide gruel and invited Nanquan to recite the scriptures.
Nanquan struck the gavel and said, "I request the assembly to recite the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* for the sake of the marten and the white ox.
Gan brushed out his sleeves and departed. After the gruel meal, Nanquan asked the steward about the lay practitioner.
"Where was he? He replied, "He left right then. Quan then smashed the pot. Shushan commented with a verse:
"Came specifically to serve congee and boast of his refinement; Who knew that Old Wang would be even more elegant?
Smashing the congee pot to expose his own clumsiness— The wildcat and the white ox are both gathered in. If one can grasp this, it may be called true making offerings.

This is the path of the mindless practitioner. There are five meanings to the practice of begging for alms: first, because one has internally realized the principle of equality and thus does not perceive external distinctions between the poor and the wealthy;
second, because one is free from a mind of greed or pride that seeks partial benefit; third, because one possesses great power of meditative concentration.
First, it is because one does not fear evil elephants or the houses of courtesans. Second, it is because one is free from the suspicions and prejudices of ordinary people.

Third, it is because it shatters the conceptual distinctions of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). As Vimalakīrti said: "Those who are equal regarding food are also equal regarding the Dharma;
regardless of whether things are noble or base, pure or impure, all equally realize Bodhi. This constitutes the perfect fulfillment of the immeasurable merits of all sentient beings. Subhūti...
Tiṣya abandoned the poor for the wealthy, while Mahākāśyapa abandoned the wealthy for the poor; thus, their compassion was not impartial and did not constitute equal compassion.
Ānanda conceived such thoughts in his mind, which immediately fell into the discrimination of the conscious intellect (*manovijñāna*) and became the livelihood of the realm of ghosts.
This is why Māra found an opportunity to exploit him. How does this compare to the practice of begging as practiced by Xiqici? He always...
Carrying a staff and a single cloth bag, along with a tattered mat, he stored all his personal requisites within the bag.

Entering markets and villages, he would beg for whatever he saw; even when receiving items such as vinegar, pickled meat, fish, or pickles, he would take only a small portion into his mouth before casting the remainder into the bag.
At that time, he was called "The Man of the Long Embankment. One day, a monk walked ahead of him, whereupon [the Master] patted him on the back.
The monk turned his head back. The Master said, "I beg of you a single coin. The monk said, "If you can speak, I will give you a single coin.
The Master dropped his cloth bag and stood with his hands clasped. On another day, while standing in the marketplace, a monk asked, "What are you doing here, Master?
The Master said, "I am waiting for someone. The monk said, "He has come! He has come!"
The Master said, "You are not this person. The monk asked, "What is this person? The Master said, "Beg me for a single coin.
He once had a verse that says: "One bowl, a thousand households' rice; A solitary body, ten thousand miles of travel.
With green eyes, seeing few people; Asking the way at the head of white clouds. One who accords with this may truly be said to have attained the deportment of all Buddhas.
Thus it was. One day the World-Honored One commanded Ānanda: "The time for the meal is approaching; you shall enter the city carrying the alms bowl.
Ānanda responded with assent. The World-Honored One said: "Since you are carrying the bowl, you must follow the ritual protocol of the seven Buddhas of the past."
Ānanda then asked, "What is the ritual of the seven Buddhas of the past? The World-Honored One called out, "Ānanda!
Ānanda responded, "Yes. The World-Honored One said, "Take this bowl and go. *Heh!* If Ānanda had understood this earlier, how could there have been the matter of Mādrī?
At that time, while Ānanda was on his alms-round, he passed by a brothel and encountered the great sorceress Maṭaṅgī (translated here as "Original Nature").
Using the *pūrva-brahma-mantra* of the Śāvikāra (translated here as the "Yellow-haired Heretic"), she drew him into her bedchamber.

She embraced and caressed him with lustful intent, nearly destroying his precept-body. The Tathāgata, knowing that she had employed such lustful arts, returned immediately after finishing his midday meal. The King and...

The ministers, elders, and householders all came following the Buddha, wishing to hear the essential points of the Dharma. At that time, the World-Honored One emitted from the crown of his head a hundred-jeweled light of fearlessness.
From within this light, thousand-petaled jeweled lotuses emerged, upon which were manifested transformation Buddhas sitting in the full-lotus posture, proclaiming divine mantras.
He commanded Mañjuśrī to take these mantras and go forth to protect [the land], so that evil spells might be extinguished. Thus it was said: "Ti..."
He exhorted Ānanda and Mātaṅgī to return to the Buddha’s presence.
The *Comprehensive Commentary* (*Heshuolun*) states: "The World-Honored One took pity on sentient beings wandering through the three realms, all of whom do so because of attachment to desire.
Among all desires, sexual lust is the most grave; therefore, the sūtra introduces Mātaṅgī at its outset to specifically explain this reason, namely, that [sentient beings] are submerged in it."
This constitutes a great affliction; to sever it is a great benefit. It is like herding sheep: one must strike them on their hindquarters.
Therefore, at the critical juncture of opportunity, one must certainly apply oneself with intense diligence. The Bhikṣuṇī Bāoliánxiāng upheld the Bodhisattva precepts.

If one personally engages in sexual misconduct and falsely claims that lust is neither killing nor stealing and carries no karmic retribution, a great, fierce fire will immediately arise from the female organ;
thereafter, his body will be consumed by fierce flames joint by joint, and he shall fall into the Avīci Hell.
Thus, when Ucchuṣma heard the Buddha say that those who indulge excessively in lust become a mass of fierce fire, he [visualized] the light of fire in three ways.
He attained Arhatship. It is said that once all outflows (*āsrava*) have been extinguished, one gives rise to the great jewel-flame and ascends to unsurpassed enlightenment.
Unsurpassed enlightenment is the stage of the Buddha; yet by contemplating the nature of lust, one is able to ascend to it. The Avīci Hell is an evil realm;
yet by following the affairs of lust, one is immediately cast down into it. Furthermore, when discussing the ten kinds of habitual causes, it is listed first.
Describing the habit of lust, it is said: First, the habit of lustful intercourse arises from mutual friction;
through ceaseless rubbing and grinding, a great and fierce flame is thereby ignited within. For this reason, the Tathāgata characterizes the practice of lust as such.
It is called by the same name as "the fire of desire. Only then does it enumerate greed, pride, and so forth. Furthermore, the *Vinaya* proclaims the practice of the three definitive principles:
namely, "restraining the mind constitutes morality; from morality arises concentration; from concentration arises wisdom.

These are known as the three trainings in the outflow-free (*anāsrava*). Now, although killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying are abandoned [in the precepts], this sutra lists sexual misconduct before...
Furthermore, when Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva described his thirty-two manifestations for preaching the Dharma,
the Brahma King attained clear awakening through his desire-mind and thus became identical in name with the Buddha, bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, and śrāvakas regarding liberation.

The remaining twenty-eight types are merely designated as "accomplishment. Furthermore, because the five pungent roots incite lust and increase anger, one is instructed to establish three gradual stages to sever them;
this is called the first stage of advancement. Moreover, one contemplates sexual desire.
Transgressions are like venomous snakes; the perfection of the prohibitive precepts allows even the fleshly eyes of parents to perceive the ten directions.
All of these are points where one must focus their intent with great urgency.

This treatise summarizes the structural threads of this sutra, repeatedly and earnestly emphasizing that the initiation of the teaching in this scripture must take the severance of lust as its primary concern, striving to cause people to feel such trepidation that their hair stands on end.
I am struck with awe. Nevertheless, one who has realized the truth perceives all sounds and forms as being like illusions or dreams;
how then could evil be sufficient to disturb their inner composure? The Sutra in Forty-two Sections states: The Buddha said, "As for those who are possessed by craving and desire..."
It is like holding a torch while walking against the wind; one’s hand will surely be burned.

A celestial deity presented a jade maiden to the Buddha, wishing to test him and observe his resolve for the Way to determine its depth. The Buddha said, "A leather bag filled with various impurities—what have you come here for?
Begone! I have no need for you. The deity’s reverence increased all the more, and he consequently asked about the meaning of the Way. The Buddha explained it for him.
...he spoke, and immediately attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*. Furthermore, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:
Śāriputra asked the goddess, "Why do you not transform this female body? The goddess replied, "For twelve years now, I have sought the mark of a woman, yet it is utterly unfindable.
How then could there be anything to transform? It is like a magician who conjures an illusory woman; if someone were to ask..."
"Why do you not transform your female body? Is this a correct question? Śāriputra replied, "No.
An illusion has no fixed characteristics; what is there to transform? The goddess said, "All Buddhas are likewise without fixed characteristics.
Why then do you ask why I do not transform my female body? At that moment, the goddess used her supernatural powers to transform—
Śāriputra caused the goddess to become like himself, and the goddess transformed herself into the likeness of Śāriputra and asked him, "Why do you not transform this female body?
Śāriputra, appearing in the form of the goddess, replied, "I do not know by what means I might transform myself back from this female body.
The goddess said, "If Śāriputra were able to transform this female body..."
All women, too, should likewise be able to transform. Just as Śāriputra was not a woman yet manifested in a female body, so it is with all women:
though they manifest in female bodies, they are not women. Therefore, the Buddha taught that all phenomena are neither male nor female.
At that moment, the goddess withdrew her supernatural power, and Śāriputra—
Her body returned to its former state. The goddess asked Śāriputra, "Where now is the physical form and appearance of the woman?
Śāriputra replied, "The physical form and appearance of the woman neither exists nor does not exist. The goddess said, "All dharmas are likewise thus;
they neither exist nor do not exist. Indeed, by the supernatural power of this goddess, you were able to transform Śāriputra from his former [state]."
The Brahma-mantra was unable to destroy Ānanda’s precept-body. These two sections of the sūtra’s meaning may be said to be "two colors in one match.

When Ānanda saw the Buddha, he prostrated himself and wept with grief, lamenting that from time immemorial he had been devoted solely to extensive learning, yet had not fully perfected his power of the Way.

With earnest and respectful solicitation, he requested the Buddhas of the ten directions for the initial expedient means of the wondrous *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna* by which they attained Bodhi.
At that time, there were also Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, along with the great Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas of the ten directions, all of whom likewise desired to hear this;
they withdrew to their seats and remained silent, awaiting the holy instruction.
Tong said: "This question posed by Ānanda is the leader of this entire scripture. From beginning to end, the World-Honored One’s responses are exhaustive.
What is called *śamatha* is translated as 'Ultimate Stillness'; it corresponds to the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). *Samāpatti* is translated as 'The Power of Transformation';
it corresponds to the contemplation of the provisional (*parikalpita-vipaśyanā*). *Dhyāna* is translated as 'Quiescence'; it does not grasp at illusions."
The transformations and all tranquil characteristics are centered in the Middle Way. The *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*) states:

"Quiescent *śamatha* is like a mirror facing various images; Illusory *samādhi* is like a sprout gradually growing; *Dhyāna* (meditative concentration) is solely quiescence, like the resonance within a bell.
These three wondrous gateways of Dharma are all in accord with awakening. All Tathāgatas of the ten directions [attain it through them]."
As well as the great Bodhisattvas, they have attained the realization of the Way because of these three matters being perfectly realized; therefore, it is called ultimate Nirvana.
Ānanda has been exclusively devoted to extensive learning (*bahuśruta*), and since he has long practiced this very path, what need is there to ask him?

However, because I am currently under the influence of illusory arts, the contemplative practices I have long cultivated and the meditative concentrations I have developed have both failed to yield their power.
I privately reckon that the Tathāgatas of the ten directions must surely possess something more wondrous than this.

Upon contemplating the single character "wondrous" (miao), it seems I can vaguely discern the principle of realization through diligent effort and the refinement of the subtlest points; yet I do not know [how to attain it].

As for the initial expedient means, by what means does one awaken and enter? The *Complete Enlightenment Sutra* (*Yuánjué jīng*) also says: "Except for those who have sudden awakening, and those whose nature is not in accord with the Dharma.
Originally there was a "Sudden Gate" (*dùn mén*), which takes the realization of the nature (*jiàn xìng*) as its primary tenet.

Therefore, once one realizes the nature, there is no deliberate effort toward cessation and contemplation (*zhǐguān*), yet cessation and contemplation are spontaneously possessed. If one cannot realize the nature, then even if one practices day after day...
In practicing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, it is difficult to resist demonic realms; only by seeing one's nature does one attain the wondrous.

As for what was said previously regarding the "wondrously luminous true mind," the "wondrous ocean of sublime adornment," and "wondrously luminous, wondrously luminous, wondrous"—these instances are more than sufficient to fulfill the meaning of that character "wondrous" (*miao*).
He concludes with a verse: "This is called the Wondrous Lotus, the Vajra..."
The King of Precious Enlightenment, through the illusory-like samādhi, transcends the stage of no-more-learning in the snap of a finger.
This is the Abhidharma, the single path to nirvāṇa for the Bhagavans of the ten directions; this is the sudden gate.

Therefore, it is not something that can be reached by ordinary śamatha-vipaśyanā or meditative concentration. In the past, Xuefeng went to Touzi three times and to Dongshan nine times; thus, he was one of great learning.
Having succeeded to Deshan, Yunfeng and Yantou went to Aoshan Town in Lishui. They were detained there by snow.
Throughout the day, Yantou did nothing but sleep, while Yunfeng sat continuously in meditation. One day, he called out, “Elder brother! Elder brother! Please arise. Yantou said, “For what?
Yunfeng replied, “This life will not yield its secrets; I am traveling with this fellow Wensui.”
His feet have been dragged about by others everywhere until he has arrived here today, yet he does nothing but sleep. Master Tou shouted, "Go eat and sleep!
You sit on your bed every day like a village tutelary deity in a remote hamlet. In the future, on some later day..."
"Māra has bewitched the men and women of this household; they have gone away. Feng patted his own chest and said, "I am not yet settled here;

I do not dare to deceive myself. Tou said, "I thought you would one day, atop a solitary peak, construct a thatched hut and propagate the Great Teaching, yet you still speak such words. Feng replied, "In truth, I am not yet settled."

Yangshan Tou said, "If it is truly so, then explain your realization point by point; where you are correct, I shall provide you with verification, and where you are not, I shall clear it away for you.
Feng said, "When I first arrived at Yanguan, I heard him ascend the hall and cite the meaning of form and emptiness, and I attained a point of entry.
Yangshan Tou said, "For thirty years from now, you must absolutely avoid mentioning this."
Furthermore, he saw a verse by Dongshan that says: "Above all, do not seek from others; to do so is to distance yourself from me.
He is now precisely I; I am now not he. Tou said, "If it is like this, you have not even mastered your own salvation yet.
Feng then asked Deshan, "Regarding the matter of the ancestral Dharma-lineage, does a student still have a share in it or not?"
Deshan struck him once and asked, "What do you say? At that moment, it was as if the bottom had fallen out of my bucket.
Tou shouted, "Have you not heard it said: 'That which enters through the gate is not the family treasure'? Feng asked, "How should it be after this?
Tou replied, "If, in the future, you wish to propagate the Great Teaching, everything must proceed from within your own breast."
The hem of his robe slipped out. [Feng] took it and said, "I shall bring this to cover heaven and earth. At these words, Feng attained great enlightenment.
He immediately prostrated himself, then rose and cried out repeatedly, "Elder brother, today at last the Dragon Mountain has achieved the Way!
How marvelous, how marvelous! How could such a teaching have been obtained by merely sitting in meditation all along?"
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "You and I share the same spiritual essence; our feelings are equal to those of siblings.
When you first resolved to seek enlightenment within my Dharma, what superior signs did you perceive that caused you to suddenly renounce the deep and heavy affection for the world?

Ānanda replied to the Buddha, "I saw that the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks were supremely wonderful and extraordinary; his physical form was translucent, like lapis lazuli. I constantly reflected upon this."
This mark is not produced by sensual desire. Why is this? The breath of desire is coarse and turbid; it is characterized by the mingling of stench and the confusion of pus and blood.

It cannot give rise to the supreme, pure, wondrously bright mass of purple-gold light. For this reason, out of longing and reverence, he followed the Buddha to shave his head and leave the household life.

Tong said: "Ānanda was fortunate to have this capacity for reflection, which served as a foundation for his initial resolve. Consequently, when he encountered the illusory arts, he was not greatly deluded;

though he entered the chamber of lust, he did not destroy his precept-body. Yet, by contemplating the Tathāgata solely through the thirty-two marks, he could not avoid viewing him through form or seeking him through sound;
thus, erroneous interpretations still remained, and he stayed far removed from the Buddha’s true Dharma-body."
Far-reaching. Chan Master Fawei of Suizhou ascended the hall and said: "The Dharma-body is formless; it cannot be sought through sound.
The wondrous Way is beyond words; how could it be understood through texts? Even if one surpasses the Buddhas and patriarchs, one still falls within the rungs of a ladder.

Even if one speaks of the wondrous and discourses on the profound, one will ultimately be caught by one's own lips and teeth. One must ensure that one’s cultivation is free from transgression, like a shadow [following the form]."
When traces remain no more—like withered trees and cold crags where moisture is gone;

like illusory men and wooden horses whose consciousnesses are all empty—only then can one extend a hand to enter the marketplace and turn the body into other forms. It is said that in the realm of outflows, one cannot remain;
yet returning to the misty groves, one lies amidst the cold sands. If one understands this clearly, what need is there for "supreme purity, wondrous clarity, and brightness"? Purple...
Only after [manifesting] a mass of golden light is one called a Tathāgata.

The Buddha said, "Excellent, Ānanda! You all should know that all sentient beings, from time immemorial, have had their births and deaths continue in succession solely because they do not know the eternally abiding true mind, the essence of pure and luminous nature. They employ various deluded thoughts; these thoughts..."
Because it is not true, there is cyclic existence.

Ānanda said in general: "I have earnestly requested the Tathāgatas of the ten directions for the initial expedient means of the wondrous *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna* by which they attained Bodhi;
my purpose is precisely to recognize and know the eternally abiding true mind and its intrinsically pure nature."
The luminous essence does not enter the cycle of transmigration; it is a single great matter. Furthermore, it is said: "This mark is not produced by desire and attachment.
One has already fully understood that desire and attachment are foul and corrupt, and that confused, deluded thoughts are the root of birth and death since time immemorial.
Therefore, the Buddha sighed in praise, saying: "Excellent! The true mind is eternally abiding; fundamentally, it is without arising or ceasing. [Yet] a flicker arises...

It is because of deluded thoughts that one enters the cycle of saṃsāra. Whether it be coarse and turbid sensual desires or evil karma that is not true, even the attachment of Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas who have not yet transformed their emotional clinging is likewise entirely deluded.
When deluded thoughts are completely purified and the essence of one's nature becomes luminously transparent, it is inherently unborn from the beginning;
how then could there be any further wandering in saṃsāra? This entire sutra is nothing other than an elucidation of this very meaning.
Therefore, know that the eternally abiding true mind is precisely what is called "seeing one's nature. Once one sees one's nature, there is nothing more to be done.
Lingyun addressed the assembly, saying: "Virtuous ones, all that is long or short is entirely impermanent. Observe, for instance, the plants and trees of the four seasons."
Leaves fall and flowers bloom; how much more so over the course of kalpas of dust?

Amidst the seven cycles of heaven and humanity, and the formation and destruction of earth, water, fire, and wind, when causes and effects are about to exhaust themselves, the suffering of the three evil realms has never added or subtracted even a hair’s breadth.
Only the fundamental consciousness remains ever-present. Those of superior capacity, upon meeting a virtuous friend who extends illumination, attain liberation in that very place—this is the Way.
[This is] the site. Those of middling and lower capacities, being dull and ignorant, are unable to awaken or perceive; they are mired in the three realms and wander through birth and death.
For their sake, the World-Honored One established teachings and provided proof throughout the heavens and among humans, manifesting the Ultimate Way.
Do you all understand? A monk asked: "How can one escape from birth, old age, sickness, and death? Yun said: "The green mountains have never moved; the floating clouds..."
"Clouds come and go as they please"—these few words may serve as a commentary on this passage of the sutra; not a single character may be added or subtracted.
If you now wish to investigate the true nature of enlightenment and bring forth its luminous essence, you should respond to my questions with a straightforward mind.
Because the Tathāgatas of the ten directions share one and the same path, they all transcend birth and death by means of a straightforward mind.
Because their minds and words are straightforward, from the beginning stages through to the final positions, there is never any trace of crookedness or deviousness in between.
The Synthesized Treatise says: "Regarding this, it specifically mentions the nature of true illumination. Does there also exist a nature of deluded illumination?
It replies: 'There is. It asks: 'How is this distinguished? It replies: 'That which knows universally and spontaneously, being fundamentally wondrous and eternally quiescent.'"

This is what is called truly illuminating one's nature. It is as it is said: "Because the Tathāgatas of the ten directions follow the same path, they all transcend birth and death by means of a straightforward mind.
This is it. To act out of season and lose the proper timing, or to falsely awaken and force knowledge, is to falsely illuminate one's nature.

This refers to the statement: "It is because one employs various false conceptions; since these conceptions are not true, there is cyclic existence. This is indeed so. [The mind] is fundamentally a single essence.

Because it is without intrinsic nature and without temporal distinction, it merely appears different according to how it is employed. If one knows it through its spontaneous, quiescent, and eternal nature, one accords with the fundamental wondrousness.
