If one perceives it by violating the proper time and missing the opportune moment, one accords with delusive objects. As Aśvaghoṣa said: "The fundamental..."
The nature is pure. Through the non-awakening of ignorance, the characteristics of the defiled mind appear. Although the defiled mind exists, its nature is eternally luminous and clean.

The characteristic of the defiled mind is precisely the active manifestation of ignorance (*sammudhā-pravṛtti-avidyā*); the luminous and clean nature is precisely the essence of the immovable wisdom (*acala-jñāna*).
A monk asked Yun’an: "The *Avataṃsaka-śāstra* states that the active manifestation of ignorance is none other than the Tathāgata’s immovable wisdom."
"This is truly difficult to believe. How can one understand it? At that time, there was a youth who happened to be sweeping the ground. Yun'an called out to him.
The youth turned his head back, and Yun'an said, "Is this not the Immovable Wisdom (acala-jñāna)? He asked again, "What is your Buddha-nature?
The youth looked to the left and right, departed in bewilderment, and Yun'an said, "Is this not active ignorance (pravṛtti-avidyā)?"
The true manifestation of the nature is like the light of a bright pearl, which constantly illuminates the pearl itself from within. Confucius said, "Let there be no deviance in thought";
this comes close to it. The delusory manifestation of the nature is like the east before dawn, when a subtle radiance already appears amidst the clarity and turbidity of the waters.
The *I Ching* says, "In the state of ignorance, the various elements are manifest"; this comes close to it.
Ānanda, I now ask you: when you first resolved upon the path, taking the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks as your object, what did you see, and who was it that felt such love and delight?
Tong said: "This was the World-Honored One’s foremost method of gradual guidance.

How could the World-Honored One not know that 'seeing' belongs to the eye and 'loving' belongs to the mind? Yet there is one who sees and there is that which is seen; there is one who loves and there is that which is loved.
Therefore, he asked, 'Who is it that sees? Who is it that loves? His purpose was to have Ānanda immediately recognize the fundamental."
It is simply the coming of the person. If one can turn the light back upon itself and reflect, seeking to see it, it cannot be found;
all loves and delights are originally without root or stem. To enter suddenly into the Śūraṅgama Samādhi—how joyful this would be!
Later generations of monks frequently employed this pivot. A monk asked Baizhang, "What is the Buddha? Baizhang said, "Who are you?"
The monk said, "So-and-so. The Master asked, "Do you recognize So-and-so? The monk replied, "I see him clearly. The Master then raised his whisk and asked, "Do you see this?
The monk said, "I see it. The Master remained silent. What the monk had asked was about the Buddha;

the Master ultimately did not speak of the Buddha, but instead used the very point where the monk’s vision was established to provoke his realization. This single case is entirely and perfectly entrusted to us.
The *Lengyan zhangzi*.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, it is because of this love and delight that I employ my mind and eyes;
through the eyes I behold the sublime marks of the Tathāgata, and in my heart arises love and delight. Therefore, I have resolved to cast off birth and death. The Buddha told Ānanda: "As for..."
What you have said is truly what you cherish and delight in, for it concerns the mind and the eyes.
If you do not know where the mind and the eyes reside, you will be unable to subdue the afflictions of the dust. It is like a king who, when invaded by bandits, dispatches troops to eliminate them;
those troops must first know the location of the bandits. That which causes you to wander in saṃsāra is the fault of the mind and the eyes. I now ask you: only...
"Where are the mind and the eyes now?
Tong said, "The place where the World-Honored One asked was solely to clarify the single path that points upward. [The Master] asked, "What do you see?
[Tong] replied, "Who would cherish it? This clearly uses a pointing finger to indicate the moon. Ānanda’s response remained within ordinary sentiment; he only knew—
It unites with the objects of the senses but does not realize it is uniting with the perceptions; it turns its back on awakening and unites with the dust. Whose fault is this?

With the six thieves acting as intermediaries, it plunders its own family treasure. Thus, what Ānanda calls "the mind and the eyes" are merely the faculties and consciousnesses that drag one into worldly toil and cause one to transmigrate through birth and death.
The eternally abiding true mind is like a king whose realm is daily invaded by these [defilements]; the pure [mind]...
The sun becomes turbid; that which is bright becomes dark. This mind and these eyes are the thieves of one's nature. One must exhaustively track down their lairs and sweep them away.
When the flow returns to its entirety as one, the six faculties cease their activity. Only then can the fundamental radiance be manifested.
When the six sense organs function interchangeably, and the physical eyes born of one's parents see through to the ten directions, how could the cycle of transmigration be considered a fault?
Once, Chan Master Chong of Zihu shouted loudly in the night, "Thieves! Thieves!
His disciples scrambled up to pursue them. Chong seized one person and said, "I have caught one. His disciples...
[The Master] said, "It is not so. It is I myself. Cong then pushed him away and said, "It is indeed so, yet you simply refuse to accept it.
Because you can accept it, the thief is yourself; because you cannot accept it, you yourself become the thief.
To speak in such a manner is like seeking out a thief for a sovereign—it is another kind of manipulation. Those with discerning eyes distinguish this.
Ānanda said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, all ten types of ordinary beings in the world alike maintain that the consciousness-mind resides within the body.
Even when one gazes at the Tathāgata’s blue-lotus eyes, they are seen to be upon the Buddha’s face;

yet when I now observe these four dusts of the floating roots [the sense organs], they are seen only upon my own face. Thus, this consciousness-mind truly must reside within the body. The Buddha told Ānanda, “You...”
"Now you are currently seated in the Tathāgata’s lecture hall. Looking at the Jeta Grove, where is it now located?
"World-Honored One, this great multi-storied pavilion, this pure lecture hall, is within Anāthapiṇḍada’s Garden; the Jeta Grove is actually outside the hall.
"Ānanda, what do you see first when you are inside this hall now? "World-Honored One, while I am inside the hall, I first see the Tathāgata, and next I observe the great [pavilion]."
"O Assembly, looking outward in this manner, one can finally behold the groves and gardens. Ānanda, by what cause do you behold the groves and gardens?
World-Honored One, because the doors and windows of this great lecture hall are wide open, I am able to gaze afar from within the hall."
Tong said: "The ten kinds of ordinary beings are as listed below among the twelve classes of birth: those born from womb, egg, moisture, or transformation;

those with form and those without form; those with perception and those without perception; those who are neither with form nor without form, and those who are neither with perception nor without perception.
Excluding the two categories of 'void-dissipation-extinction' and 'earth-wood-metal-stone,' these do not belong to the realm of the mind’s eye."
It is said there are ten kinds. Zhang Wujin [Zongze] assigns these to the six ordinary beings and the four noble ones; this is incorrect.

While the four sensory objects—form, sound, smell, and taste—are associated with the "floating roots," all six faculties are likewise so. This passage, however, refers specifically to the eye faculty.
Earth, water, fire, and wind are pure by nature, yet the manifestations of earth, water, fire, and wind each vibrate like dust. The accomplishment of the six faculties depends upon these four.
The six sense organs are submerged within, while the four elements float without; hence they are called the "floating roots" and the "four objects.
The ten types of consciousness and mind reside within. That the eyes are on the face is self-evident and requires no further mention.

Yet, although the Tathāgata’s eyes are on his face, he does not dare to point definitively to the location where the consciousness-mind resides. This is because the Tathāgata has already transcended consciousness; his Dharma-body is perfectly complete.
Because there is neither internal nor external. Ānanda spoke with firm deliberation, and the translator likewise was not careless.
When the World-Honored One wished to refute the notion that the mind resides within, he first employed the metaphors of the lecture hall, the grove, and the windows and doors.
The lecture hall represents the interior of the body; the grove represents external objects; and the windows and doors represent the six sense faculties. Thus, Ānanda clearly understood.
This is one who has attained realization. If you see Ānanda in his true essence, he originally belongs neither to the lecture hall, nor to the grove, nor to the windows and doors;
yet Ānanda comes and goes with ease, such that no "inside" or "outside" can be pointed out.
If you cling to this mind as being fixed within the physical body—taking the internal organs as its inner sanctum and the six sense-gates as its doors—you are deluded.
The windows grasp external objects as gardens and groves; without these, there would be no place for the body to find rest.
Once the hall collapses and the windows break, the objects vanish and the faculty of seeing perishes—where then will that which is called "clarity" abide?

Although the World-Honored One, in accordance with common worldly understanding, clarified the sequence of the internal and external, he also vividly demonstrated that the physical body is like an illusion and is not [ultimately real].
"You should take hold of it. It is like the doors and windows of a lecture hall; they have no connection whatsoever with me," he said.
When Chan Master Zhihui was about to depart, he spoke this verse: "I have a single room, which my parents built for me. For eighty years, I have come and gone within it."
Lately, he perceived that [the dwelling] was decaying and had intended to move elsewhere early on.

He thought, "Since this matter involves likes and dislikes, it would be best to wait until others have demolished it; then there will be no hindrance for either side. Thereupon, he passed away while sitting in the lotus posture.
This is the forgetting of both hatred and love, where coming and going are unimpeded. Since he has forgotten even the capacity for perception itself, how can one speak of "internal" and "external"?
At that time, the World-Honored One, amidst the great assembly, extended his golden arm and stroked Ānanda’s head. He announced to Ānanda and the entire multitude:
"There is a samādhi (this is the concentration that engenders transformations) named the Great Buddha-Crown Sovereign King of Adornments.

It is fully endowed with the myriad practices; it is the wondrously adorned path by which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions transcend through a single gate. You should now listen attentively. Ānanda...
"Difficult to pay homage to! I humbly receive your compassionate instruction.
He replied in general: "This single gate transcends all others; it clearly points out the path of sudden enlightenment. It lies solely in the transformation of consciousness into wisdom.
Only when one is purely endowed with adamantine dry-wisdom (*vimalā-prajñā*) can one speak of the true path to Bodhi. At the end he said: "Thus..."
This wondrous Dharma. In the past, throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, countless Tathāgatas, by relying on the opening of this mind, attained the Unsurpassed Way.
If the aggregate of consciousness is exhausted, then your present faculties will function interchangeably; from within this mutual functioning, [you shall attain liberation].

One is able to enter the Bodhisattva’s adamantine *śuklavipaśyanā* (dry wisdom). With a perfectly luminous and refined mind, one brings forth transformation therein, like pure lapis lazuli containing a precious moon within.
In this way, one transcends the ten faiths, the ten abidings, the ten practices, the ten transferences, and the four stages of preparatory application (*prayoga-citta*).
One proceeds through the Bodhisattva’s practice of the ten adamantine grounds (*bhūmi*) until the perfect luminosity of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), entering the state of the Tathāgata.
The ocean of wondrous adornment brings the perfection of Bodhi to the point of non-attainment.

From beginning to end, the text echoes this theme, establishing that transcending the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate) must be taken as the ultimate goal. The World-Honored One has thoroughly penetrated the continuity of birth and death in the world, seeing it as nothing but various forms of deluded thought that lead one astray without returning.
Once the *vijñāna-skandha* is exhausted, the eternally abiding true mind is finally attained.

Manifest before you is the essence of intrinsic purity and luminosity, which is no different from that of the Buddhas; therefore, one is able to shatter the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) and immediately enter the gate of sudden enlightenment.
Although Ānanda is wise and erudite, he does not transcend the conceptual discrimination of conscious emotion; as long as this conscious emotion is not eliminated, [one remains bound].
Realization depends solely on "attainment," yet the one who realizes Bodhi depends solely on "non-attainment.

Therefore, in the subsequent section where the mind is investigated through seven locations, Ānanda is frequently bound by the notion of attainment, while the World-Honored One eliminates it point by point through non-attainment.
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "The characteristic of attainment is consciousness; the characteristic of non-attainment is wisdom. This is the true and swift realization.
This is the sudden gate of Bodhi. The Second Patriarch, Shen Guang, severed his arm before the First Patriarch, Bodhidharma, requesting the Dharma-gate of "pacifying the mind.
The Patriarch said, "Bring forth your mind, and I shall pacify it for you. Shen Guang replied, "I have searched for my mind, but it is utterly unobtainable.
The Patriarch said, "I have finished pacifying your mind for you. [He further taught that] even if Ānanda were able to believe in the "seven locations where the mind was sought,"...
"It cannot be obtained. Thus, how could the golden brocade *kāṣāya* robe have been bestowed upon Kāśyapa alone?
The Buddha told Ānanda, "As you say, though the body is in the lecture hall, the doors and windows are wide open, allowing one to gaze afar at the groves and gardens."
"Furthermore, there may be sentient beings within this hall who do not see the Tathāgata, yet see those outside the hall.
Ānanda replied, "World-Honored One, it is impossible for one who is inside the hall not to see the Tathāgata while being able to see the groves and springs.
"Ānanda, you are just like that. Your spiritual mind is all-encompassing and clearly aware. If the mind that is clearly aware before you were truly..."
Within the body. At that time, one should first thoroughly understand the internal body. Is there any sentient being who first perceives within the body and only later observes external objects?
Even if they cannot see the heart, liver, spleen, or stomach, they certainly ought to clearly perceive the growth of nails and hair, the shifting of tendons, and the throbbing of pulses.
How could they not know this? If they do not know what is within, how can they know what is without? Therefore, you should understand that your statement [is incorrect].
"That the mind capable of awakening and knowing dwells within the body—this is impossible.
He replied, "The eyes see and the mind knows; this does not depart from the sense organs and their objects. It is from within that it reaches outward; this is simply my common view.
The World-Honored One then refuted his common view: "Since you do not know what is within, how can you say it is within? Even if one possesses wisdom," [it would still be so].
One cannot help but yield to their argument. In reality, the heart, liver, spleen, and stomach are all instances of cognition (*jñāna*);
the nails, hair, tendons, and veins are all instances of sensation (*vedanā*). If these were not cognition and sensation, would they not be nothing more than a mere inert mass?
Master Fu’s verse says: "Night after night, one embraces the Buddha in sleep; morning after morning, one rises together with him. Whether rising or sitting, they are always in each other's company;
whether speaking or remaining silent, they dwell together. Not even a hair's breadth separates them, like the relationship between a body and its shadow.
If you wish to know where the Buddha goes, it is simply this sound of speech. From this it may be said that the mind capable of awakening and knowing abides...
Within the body, there is likewise nothing that is not its proper place. Yunmen, citing the *Pao-tsang lun*, said:

"Within heaven and earth, between the universe and all things, there is a single treasure, hidden within the mountain of form. He then took the lantern and placed it inside the Buddha Hall, and brought the triple-gate entrance onto the lantern.
[The Master asked: "How is this? [Yunmen] answered on his behalf: "The mind shifts as one pursues external objects. Furthermore—
It is said: "Clouds arise and thunder rolls. Xuedou’s verse says: "Look, look! On the ancient shore, who is holding the fishing rod?
Clouds drift slowly; the waters stretch vast and wide. The bright moon and reeds—look for yourself!
This kōan concerns the ease with which the "awakened capacity for knowing" and "original enlightenment's perfect luminosity" may be confused, much like the bright moon and the reeds. One must...

One must exercise discernment. If one can attain such discernment, then not only will lanterns and pillars suddenly penetrate the heart-essence of Yunmen, but the treasure within one's own body will also accord with that of Sengzhao.
This is not something for those who merely dally with their spirits to use as an excuse.
Ānanda bowed his head to the ground and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Having heard such a Dharma-sound from the Tathāgata, I have realized that my mind truly resides outside the body. Why is this? It is like a lamp burning within a room;
that lamp must first illuminate the interior of the room, and only after passing through its door does it reach the courtyard. Yet all sentient beings do not see [the mind] within their own bodies."
To perceive only what is outside the body is like a lamp placed outside a room; it cannot illuminate the interior. This principle must be clear so that there shall be no confusion.
It accords with the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) of the Buddha; could it be false? The Buddha addressed Ānanda and the bhikṣus:
"Just now, after begging for alms in the city of Śrāvastī, I returned to the Jeta Grove and have already finished my meal.
Observe, Ānanda, when one bhikṣu eats, are all the others satiated? Ānanda replied, "No, World-Honored One."
"Why is this? Although these bhikṣus are all arhats, their physical bodies and lives are distinct. How could one person cause the multitude to be satiated?

The Buddha told Ānanda: "If you perceive that the mind which knows, perceives, and sees actually exists outside the body, such that the body and mind are external to one another and do not interact, then what the mind knows, the body would not be able to perceive. Perception would reside at the boundary of the body, while the mind..."

"I cannot know it. I shall now show you my tūla-cotton hand (which in this language means 'fine fragrant cotton' and is white like frost). When you see it with your eyes, does your mind not discern it?
Ānanda replied, "It is so, World-Honored One. The Buddha told Ānanda, "If they are mutually cognizant, why would it be said to be outside?
Therefore, you should know that your statement—that the mind which perceives and knows resides outside the body—is without basis."
"There is such a possibility.

Tong said, "Ānanda’s perspective is not yet true; he cannot avoid generating interpretations based on words. To generate interpretations based on words is precisely where the functioning of consciousness resides.
The World-Honored One wished to uproot the very root of consciousness, and therefore he eliminated each and every [interpretation], causing..."
Ānanda has no place where he can lodge. This is like a king of True Suchness (tathatā) who, knowing the location of the rebels, goes forth to suppress them.
Ānanda’s claim that the mind resides outside the body is consistent with the Buddha’s definitive teaching (nītārtha); it is not a case of having no view at all.

Now, as for the mind: it merges with heaven when latent in heaven, and merges with earth when latent in earth. At times its spirit wanders to the eight extremities of the universe; at other times it dreams through successive lifetimes.
How could it ever be confined within the narrow confines of a single physical shell? Thus it is said: "To realize that my mind truly dwells outside the body. It is further said:

"This principle must be clearly understood so that one will have no more delusions. The World-Honored One established a metaphor for this: what another person eats can certainly not be [the food] of oneself.
"I am full. But with a mind that is detached from conditions, what concern is there for my body? The body is the physical form;
thus, food cannot be made to communicate with it. Consciousness is the spirit; how could it be separated by internal or external boundaries?

It is only because Ānanda clings to the notion that [consciousness] is fixed outside, like some material object, that it can only illuminate the external and cannot illuminate the internal. Thus, that which is outside the body—
The mind is within the body, not outside it. If the mind were outside the body, the body would be unable to perceive it, just as when another person eats, I cannot be satiated.
Yet, that which the eyes see, the mind is able to discern; how, then, could this mind ever be outside?
Therefore, the claim that it is outside is incorrect. Long ago, when Cao Shan heard the sound of a bell, he said: "A-he, a-he."
[The Master] said, "Ye. A monk asked the Master, "What are you doing? The Master replied, "It strikes at my heart. The monk was speechless.
Wuzu Jie spoke on his behalf, saying, "The mind of a thief is always suspicious. Furthermore, the Great Master Fu (Dashi) said in a verse: "The villages of all Buddhas exist within the world;
the mountains and fields of the four seas are filled with them. The Buddha and sentient beings are of one single essence; sentient beings are..."
These are the provisional names for the Buddha. If one wishes to see the Buddha, look at the three prefectures. Fields, houses, gardens, and groves are situated everywhere;
some fly through the empty void with a tumultuous clamor, others dash over mountains and waters with a thunderous roar.
Some form groups and travel back and forth, while others wander alone and solitary. Some cause them to run east and west during the day, and others during the dark night.
They circled through the five watches of the night; some were black, some red, and some white; some purple, some black, and some yellowish-green;
some large and some small, some newly hatched, some old, some young, and some born long ago; some even had lamps and fires upon their bodies and waists.
Some have lutes and zithers upon their wings; some roam through the void, ascending and descending in disorder; some grow among grasses and trees, spreading out in a chaotic jumble;
some leave their dwellings without speech or action; some enter earthen pits to take temporary birth; some bore holes in wood as their native home;
some weave grasses and wood to construct nests and fortresses; some turn nets and meshes into villages and alleys; or...
He lies upon earth and stones, making them his steps and hall; all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do exactly the same.

This is what is called the city of Śrāvastī. Realizing and verifying it within this context means that the mind capable of awakening and knowing dwells outside the body, yet there is no place where it is not present.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the Buddha has said, because it does not see within, it does not abide inside the body;
because the body and mind know one another and are not separate, it is not outside the body. As I now reflect, I know it must reside in a single location.
The Buddha asked: "Where, then, is that location? Ānanda replied: "This cognizant mind, which does not know what is within yet is able to see what is without..."
As I reflect upon it, [the faculty] lies latent within the sense organ. It is like a person who takes a crystal bowl and covers both eyes with it;
although there is something covering them, it does not obstruct vision. That faculty perceives according to what is seen and immediately discriminates it.

As for my conscious mind that is capable of knowing, its failure to see the interior is because it resides within the organ; its ability to gaze clearly at external objects without obstruction is likewise so.
Because the faculties are submerged within. The Buddha said to Ānanda: "As you have said, 'the faculties are submerged within,' it is like crystal.
Suppose that person were to cover their eyes with a crystal casing; would they see the mountains and rivers, yet not see the crystal? [Ānanda replied: "So it is, World-Honored One."
This person would see the lapis lazuli cage as being truly lapis lazuli. The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If your mind were united with the lapis lazuli, you should see the mountains and rivers; why do you not see the eye? If you were to see the eye, then the eye would be identical to its objects."
It cannot be established as a concomitant. If you cannot perceive it, how can you say that this cognizing mind is latent within the sense organs like glass?
Therefore, you should know that your claim—that the mind capable of conscious awareness is hidden within the roots like glass—is untenable.

Tong said: "The *Eight Consciousnesses’ Rules* states: 'The ignorant find it difficult to distinguish consciousness from the faculties. Indeed, the difficulty in discerning the faculties and consciousness has long been known.

If one were to claim that the faculties are not consciousness, then the faculties would be the faculties and consciousness would be consciousness; in that case, consciousness ought to see the faculties."
If one were to claim that the sense organ (*indriya*) is identical to consciousness (*vijñāna*), then why does a dead person, whose eye-organ still exists, not see?

Therefore, we know that the five organs are merely pure, translucent matter (*rūpa-prasāda*) that illuminates objects; it is consciousness that must perform clear and distinct discernment. Thus, the seeds and manifestations (*bīja* and *vṛtti*) of these two categories differ in their perfuming (*vāsanā*).
The five organs are material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) and constitute the direct objective aspect (*sākṣāt-nimitta-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness, which possesses grasping (*grāhaka*).

The two types of objects of cognition are of a pure-neutral nature (*avyākṛta*). The five consciousnesses are mental factors; specifically, they are the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness. They possess all three natures (*tri-svabhāva*), yet they can only perceive them with clarity;

thus, they are termed "objective objects" (*svabhāva-viṣaya*) and belong to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Therefore, it is said: "Objective objects and direct perception pertain to all three natures.
It is only upon reaching the sixth consciousness that there is conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*), which belongs to inference (*anumāna*) and non-valid cognition (*ayathārtha*). This...
This is the distinction between the faculty and consciousness. Ānanda’s claim that the faculty follows the seeing and immediately performs discrimination is correct;
his claim that it lies hidden within the faculty like glass covering it is incorrect. If it were indeed like glass covering it, [consciousness would not arise].
When one sees mountains and rivers with the eyes, and also sees lapis lazuli, the mind that perceives the mountains and rivers should likewise perceive the eyes.

Since the eyes are not seen, it is clear that [the mind] does not reside hidden within the sense organs. This analogy is an incorrect inference; it properly belongs to the category of non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*).
According to what Ānanda has pointed out, the mind capable of awareness and cognition is merely the discrimination of the six consciousnesses. This...
From what does consciousness arise? It is because the seven consciousnesses serve as its conveyance, and the eighth consciousness serves as its repository.
Even if the discernment [of the sixth consciousness] is easily dissolved, the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) is difficult to eliminate.
Even if the aggregate of formations is easily dissolved, the seeds are difficult to transform. Now, Ānanda, you still do not understand the discernment of the six consciousnesses.
As for the point of their falling away—how much less could one know what are called the seventh and eighth consciousnesses?

If one does not even know the point of their falling away, how could one mobilize troops to suppress and eliminate them? This sutra first breaks the nesting place of the six consciousnesses, hence the "seven locations where the mind is sought";

it finally strikes the pivotal hole of the eighth consciousness, aiming for the total exhaustion of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). This is the transformation of consciousness into wisdom (*jñāna*).
This is the general outline. Later in the text it says: "Though one may attain the dissolution of the six, one has not yet lost the one;
only when both the one and the six have dissolved together is there nowhere left to rely upon.

Looking back at this passage, where [the root] lies latent within like glass encasing [a gem], would one not burst into a great laugh? Nevertheless, for those skilled in parables, nothing is impossible. Long ago, Master Hong of Zhongyi...
After Master Yangshan had gone to offer his thanks for the precepts, he asked, "What is the meaning of Buddha-nature? Daoyi said, "I will give you a simile.
Suppose there is a room with six windows, and a monkey is placed inside. Outside, a monkey calls out, 'Singing-sing! and the monkey inside responds.
In this way, if someone calls from all six windows, it responds to each. Yangshan then bowed in gratitude.
Dongqi said, "I have just received the Master's parables and there is nothing I do not understand. However, there is one further matter:
suppose the inner monkey has fallen asleep while the outer monkey wishes to meet him; how would that be?
Yunmen took Yangshan’s hand from the meditation bench and danced, saying, "The *xingxing* [monkeys] have already met you. It is like the *jiaoming* insect."
He built his nest upon the eyelashes of a mosquito and cried out at the crossroads: "The land is vast and the people few;
those who meet one another are rare. Yunju Xi said, "If Zhongyi had not received this single word from Yangshan at that time, how could there have been a Zhongyi?
Choushou Chou said, "Is there anyone who can definitively settle this principle?"
If you cannot definitively grasp it, it is merely a matter of playing with one's vital spirit; where, then, does the meaning of Buddha-nature reside?
Xuangjue said, "Were it not for Yangshan, how could one have seen Zhongyi? Now tell me, where was it that Yangshan attained the vision of Zhongyi?
Tiantong’s verse says: "Sleeping frozen in a snow-covered hut, the years pass in decay."
The secluded vine-covered gate does not open at night; one observes the shifting transformations within the withered gardens. The spring breeze stirs the ashes from the ritual tubes.
This verse clearly praises Yangshan’s place of sleep, which does not fall into desiccation;
it is precisely the point where Zhongyi meets him. Just so, both "one" and "six" are simultaneously dissolved within the realm, yet the gardens continue to transform.
Its appearance is like the ashes in a bamboo tube; it is fundamentally and utterly distinct from the spirit, the soul, the hands, and the feet.
Ānanda said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, I have now further reflected thus: this body of a sentient being has its internal organs within and its orifices on the outside.
Where there are internal organs, there is darkness; where there are orifices, there is light. Now, as I face the Buddha, I open [my eyes]..."
Seeing light with the eyes is called seeing the external; closing the eyes and seeing darkness is called seeing the internal.
What is the meaning of this? The Buddha told Ānanda: "When you close your eyes and see darkness, does this realm of darkness face the eye or not face the eye?
If it faces the eye, then the darkness is in front of the eyes; how can it be considered internal? If it were internal, it would reside..."
In a dark room, there are no sun, moon, or lamps. Within this dark room, everything is your own internal organs.

If it does not correspond to external objects, how can it constitute seeing? If it were established through an internal correspondence apart from external seeing, then when you close your eyes and see darkness, it would be called "within the body";
but when you open your eyes and see light, why do you not see your own face? If you do not see your face, then internal correspondence is not established. If seeing your face were established...
If you understand that the mind and the eye-faculty are actually in empty space, how can they be said to be "within"? If they were in empty space, they would not be your own substance;
in that case, when the Tathāgata now looks upon your face, it would also be your body. If your eyes already possess cognition, then your body ought to be devoid of sensation.
If you insist that both body and eyes possess cognition, there should then be two distinct cognitions; thus, within your single body, there would have to be...
This results in two Buddhas. Therefore, you should know that your claim—that seeing darkness is called "seeing within"—is impossible.
Ānanda replied: "I was merely stuck on the single phrase 'unable to see within,' which gave rise to all these various calculations."
If the latent root is already non-existent, is it not the case that seeing darkness is precisely that [root]? This seeing of darkness involves even more conceptual proliferation.

Although Ānanda did not state this explicitly, the World-Honored One pointed each instance out one by one to refute it. First, he examined whether the darkness being seen constitutes a correspondence or not.
If it corresponds, it becomes an objective realm; if it does not correspond, it is not "seeing. Thus, this darkness is certainly...

It cannot be called "internal. Since the seeing that is capable of seeing arises solely from turning the gaze back upon itself rather than relying on the physical eyes, if one could see darkness by turning the gaze back while the eyes are open, then one should likewise be able to see one's own face by turning the gaze back with the eyes open.
The face cannot be seen; how could darkness possibly know it? This seeing must necessarily be unable to see the interior.
If you were instead to silently confront it with the mind-consciousness, identifying "this is the internal organs" and "this is the face," then this could indeed be called seeing.
But would not this mind-eye, in that case, reside in empty space? Since the mind-eye fundamentally resides in empty space, it is like one who has awakened from a nightmare. Can one...
If you see your own true face, then the body of the Tathāgata is indeed your own body.
Since the vision of the Tathāgata is your own vision, and the body of the Tathāgata is your own body, would not Ānanda’s single body then constitute two Buddhas?
These are many shifting arguments derived from internal oppositions. Internal Opposition.
If seeing-in-darkness cannot be established, then it is impossible to say that one sees within.
Nevertheless, that which is capable of seeing is fundamentally darkness itself; who, then, is it that sees? Yunmen gave this teaching:
"Everyone possesses luminosity, yet when looked for, it is dark and murky. What is this luminosity of yours? From where does it come?
The ancients said, "The kitchen, the storehouse, and the three gates. They also said, "Better not to do good than to do it poorly.
Xuedou’s verse says: "Self-illumination reveals solitary clarity; for your sake, I open a single thread. When the flowers fall, the tree has no shadow; when looking, who does not see?
See or not see—riding a cow backward, one enters the Buddha hall. If you can understand this 'riding a cow backward into the Buddha hall'..."
As for the principle that seeing darkness is called "seeing within," there is indeed nothing incorrect about this.
Ānanda said: "I have often heard the Buddha instruct the fourfold assembly that because the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise;
and because phenomena arise, all manner of minds arise. As I now reflect, the very essence of this reflection is truly my own mind-nature. Following [this thought]...
Wherever there is a conjunction, the mind exists accordingly; yet it does not exist within, without, or in between these three locations. The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Since you now say that various minds arise because of dharmas, and that the mind exists wherever there is a conjunction, this mind has no substance.
If it has no substance, there can be no conjunction. If that which lacks substance could still conjoin, then there would be a nineteenth realm."

"Seven atoms combine. This argument is not tenable. If they possess substantiality, then as you strike your own body with your hand, does the mind that perceives this emerge from within, or does it enter from without?
If it emerges from within, it should see what is inside the body; if it comes from without, it should first see your face.
Ānanda said: "Seeing is the function of the eyes; it is the mind that knows, not the eyes. It is for the sake of seeing..."
This is not correct. The Buddha said: "If the eye were able to see, then when you are inside a room, would the door be able to see?
Furthermore, all those who have already died still possess their eyes; they should all be able to see objects. If they could see objects, how could they be called dead?
Ānanda, moreover, as for this mind of yours that perceives and knows: if it must have a substance, does it consist of a single substance or many substances? At present, while it is here..."
Is your body pervasive throughout its entirety, or is it not pervasive? If it were a single entity, then when you prick one limb with your hand, the other four limbs should feel it;
if all were to feel it, there would be no specific location for the prick. If the prick occurs at a specific location, then your being a single entity cannot be established.
If it were multiple entities, then you would become many people; which of these entities would be "you"? Furthermore, if it were pervasive...
As for its substance, it is the same as what was previously pointed out. If it were not pervasive, then when you touch your head, you would also be touching your feet;

the head would have sensation while the feet would be devoid of consciousness. But this is not the case for you. Therefore, you should know that wherever there is contact, the mind must be present accordingly.
It is impossible for it to be otherwise.
The Master said: "When the head is touched, the head knows; when the foot is touched, the foot knows. Is this not the case that where the mind meets with something, it arises accordingly?
Yet, where the mind meets with something, it arises accordingly, while where it does not meet with anything, the mind is entirely absent.
Is this not the view of annihilationism or eternalism? For now, let us set aside the charge of these views; we shall simply address their meeting."

Regarding this single character "one" (*eka*), its incorrectness is analyzed in detail. A combination must necessarily have a substance; if there were no substance, the meaning of "combination" would not be established.
For example, if the seven objects did not exist, then the nineteen elements (*dhātus*) would not exist. If, however, there is a substance, since this substance does not come from without...
Furthermore, it does not emerge from within. If we discuss the substance of the mind, is it a single entity or multiple entities?

Within the human body, does it pervade the entire body or not pervade it? If one uses a finger to press upon a single limb and the sensation arises precisely where it is pressed, then if this sensation were a single entity, it should be present everywhere.
If this sensation were multiple entities, there should be as many people as there are sensations.

If this awareness were an all-pervading entity, then there would be no location where it is not present. If this awareness were a non-pervading entity, then there would be places where it does not know.
Since all four of these cases are untenable, it possesses no fixed essence; how, then, could it possibly unite with anything?
Regarding that which accords with [the conditions]: does it accord with its single essence? Does it accord with its manifold essence?
Does it accord with its pervasive essence? Or does it accord with its non-pervasive essence? To accord with that is to neglect this; to accord with this is to neglect that.
Furthermore, it is neither one nor many, neither pervasive nor non-pervasive, and ultimately cannot be made to accord. Since it cannot be made to accord, how can there be...?

One sees that it follows after existence. Although the World-Honored One uses this to clarify the error of following what is conjoined, he also clearly demonstrates the wondrous nature of the true mind’s lack of substantiality.
Where there is no substance, there is no conjunction; the mind and its objects do not reach one another.
Liberation occurs right where one is; fundamentally, there has never been arising. Why, then, do you say that when dharmas arise, various kinds of mind arise?
That "the mind arises and various dharmas arise" is no different from the principle that the triple world is mind-only; therefore, there is no need for further discrimination.
Phenomena give rise to various kinds of mind; yet because the mind is fundamentally unborn, when one contemplates it through the medium of objects, it is likewise inherently free from affliction.

However, Ānanda cited this as proof that wherever the mind encounters conditions, it arises accordingly. This is the mind that follows the waves and pursues the ripples, rather than the mind that repeatedly arises in response to objects.
Therefore, upon awakening to the fact that the mind has no substantial essence, one immediately transcends the various [mental states].

Arising does not constitute an obstruction, because conditioned origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is non-arising. A monk asked Jia Shan: "What is it like when one brushes away the dust to see the Buddha?
Shan replied: "You must brandish the sword. If you do not brandish the sword, the fisherman will nest in his hut.
The monk raised this question with Shi Sang: "What is it like when one brushes away the dust to see the Buddha? Sang said: "He has no land; where would he meet [the Buddha]?"
The monk returned and related this to Jia Shan. Jia Shan ascended the hall and said, "In the establishment of the gate and the courtyard, he is not my equal;
yet in the profound discourse on entering into principle, he still falls short of Shi Shang by a hundred paces. Tiantong’s verse says: "The sword’s spirit brushes the oxen;
the military might washes away the dust. Who else could achieve such merit in pacifying the chaos? Once the miasma is cleared from the four seas, the Emperor hangs his robes [in non-action]."
Transformation arises from the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Danxia’s verse says: "A single phrase for the occasion, jade-like and resonant;
inside and out it is transparent, a chill overflowing the eyes. One cannot remain within the realm of no-outflows; it will be difficult to encounter it within the shadows of the moonlight.

This very case shows that even when one brushes away the dust to see the Buddha, one still does not meet him; how much more so when one seeks awakening by conforming to the dust? That too is a delusion.
How great is this perversion! Nevertheless, the single moon universally appears in all waters, and the moons in all waters are subsumed within that one moon.
Wherever conditions meet, what cause for concern is there that it should not be present?

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, when I heard the Buddha conversing with Mañjuśrī and the other Dharma-princes regarding the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*), the World-Honored One also said that the mind is neither within nor without.

As I reflect upon this, there is nothing perceived within, and there is no mutual cognition between the internal and external. Because there is no cognition within, its existence within is not established. [Yet] body and mind do cognize one another; therefore, it exists..."
"It is not outside, for we can perceive it there. Furthermore, since there is no vision within, it must be in between. The Buddha said, "Regarding what you call 'in between':
that which is in between cannot be confused; it must have a specific location. Now, as you investigate this 'middle,' where does it reside? Does it reside in space, or does it reside in the body?
If it resides in the body, then if it is at the periphery it is not the middle, and if it is in the center it is the same as being inside. If it resides in space..."

Does this [direction] have something that indicates it, or does it have nothing that indicates it? If there were no indication, it would be the same as non-existence; if there were an indication, it would lack fixity. Why is this so?

For example, when a person uses a marker to indicate the center, looking from the east it is west, and observing from the south it becomes north. Since the substance of the marker is thus confused, [the direction lacks fixity].
"The mind would then be in a state of confusion. Ānanda said, "What I have spoken of is neither of these two. As the World-Honored One has said:

'With the eye and forms as conditions, eye-consciousness arises. The eye possesses discrimination; the object of form is without cognition. When consciousness arises between them, that is where the mind resides.
The Buddha said, "If your mind were located between the faculty and the object, then as for the substance of this mind, would it be both..."

Second: It cannot be both simultaneously. If it were both, the substance of the object would be confused; the object and its essence-cognition would stand as two opposing entities. How could this be the Middle?
Since it cannot be both, it is neither cognition nor non-cognition, and thus lacks any essential nature. What characteristic, then, could the Middle possess?
Therefore, you should know that to claim the Middle exists in between these two is impossible.
Tong said: "Only upon reaching this point does Ānanda clearly understand that consciousness arises 'in between.

He refers to the six consciousnesses making distinctions between the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*). This is even more substantiated than the previous theory of consciousness being latent within the organs.
However, as for what is called 'in between,' since it is neither inside nor outside, it exists solely from the intersection of the organ and the object."

The consciousness that possesses discrimination is designated as the "mind. One fails to realize that the three—sense organ, object, and consciousness—stand in mutual dependence like bundles of reeds;
they are fundamentally devoid of self-nature. Now, you definitively claim it resides "in between.

If it were truly situated in such a location, does it encompass both [organ and object], or does it not encompass both? If it encompasses both, then one part would know while the other part would not know. This is like the horns [of an animal].
If established, it does not constitute the Middle; if it does not encompass both, it is neither knowledge nor non-knowledge.

If it lacks substance, it does not constitute the Middle. Thus, where would the Middle reside? Therefore, the claim that it must reside "in between" is incorrect. This is when discussing the True Mind.

It both encompasses the two and does not encompass the two. What is meant by "encompassing the two"? Within the Tathāgatagarbha, the two divisions of the seeing and the seen are inherently present from the beginning.
As will be stated later: "The nature of form is true emptiness; the nature of emptiness is true form. How could there be any confusion or disorder here? What is meant by "not encompassing the two"?
The numinous light shines alone, utterly transcending the sense organs and their objects. As will be stated later: "Since the dust [of objects] is no longer conditioned..."
The faculties have nothing with which they can pair; how could they ever lack an essential nature?

If one can believe that this mind is neither knowing nor not-knowing, that it fundamentally lacks self-nature, and that it likewise lacks any characteristic of being "within," then one has profoundly clarified the meaning of the Middle Way.
Once, while the King of East India was inviting the twenty-seventh patriarch, Prajñātāra, for a meal, the King asked him:
Everyone was reciting the sutras, yet only the Master did not recite at all. The Patriarch said, "This poor monk, when inhaling, does not dwell within the realms of the five aggregates;
when exhaling, does not involve himself with external conditions. He constantly recites this very sutra hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of times—far more than just one or two scrolls.
The King then prostrated himself. A Celestial Child (Tiantong) composed a verse on this: "The cloud-rhinoceros gazes at the moon, its brilliance shining forth."
A wooden horse roams the spring, its spirit unrestrained; beneath the brows, a pair of cold, azure eyes. How could one who studies the sutras ever penetrate the ox-hide?
With a mind of clarity that transcends vast kalpas, heroic power breaks through the heavy encirclement.
The wondrous, perfect pivot turns the divine mechanism; Hanshan forgets the path he came, and Shide leads him home, hand in hand. This is the Patriarch.

As for the tradition of our school: neither of the two extremes is established, nor is the Middle Way settled upon. This Great Way of Vacuity and Mystery, the True Doctrine of Non-attachment, is the foremost.
Therefore, it is beyond the reach of the six consciousnesses, the sense organs, and their objects. As for Hanshan and Shide, they come and go with sovereign ease;
not even the slightest trace of conscious emotion hangs within their chests. They are fully capable of meeting with the twenty-seventh patriarch.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, in the past I saw the Buddha together with his four great disciples—Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Subhūti, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, and Śāriputra—as they turned the wheel of Dharma. They constantly spoke of awakening to and discerning the nature of the mind."
Since it is neither within, nor without, nor in between—having no location at all—and is entirely unattached, this is called "mind.
Is it then not the case that my own lack of attachment is what is called "mind"? The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"Regarding your statement that the nature of the mind which perceives and discriminates has no location whatsoever: consider the world, space, water, land, flying creatures, and all such objects and phenomena."
That which is called "all" is what you do not cling to. Does this non-clinging exist or does it not exist? If it does not exist, it is the same as the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit;

how then can there be non-clinging? If it exists, that which does not cling cannot be called non-existent. That which lacks characteristics is non-existent; that which is not non-existent possesses characteristics.

If characteristics exist, then there is existence. How, then, can there be non-attachment? Therefore, one should know that it is impossible for the awakened mind to perceive all things as being characterized by non-attachment.
[The opponent] replies: What Ānanda has cited regarding non-attachment is not incorrect; it is simply that he has added the two characters "all" (yīqiè) too frequently.
This is non-attachment with respect to objects. Where the object exists, non-attachment exists.
To say that both are without location is close to nihilism; such a statement is contradictory. If all objective phenomena were entirely non-existent, where could non-attachment possibly reside?
Since there is non-attachment, one cannot claim that objective phenomena do not exist. If there were no non-attachment...
Regarding the characteristic of attachment: it may be said that there is no place where it resides, yet it is not the case that there is no attachment. Non-attachment itself is the characteristic.
Since there exists the characteristic of non-attachment, this is precisely where the mind resides. The mind truly resides in non-attachment; why then do you say that both are without location?
Since the mind already has a location, how can you further claim that it is without attachment? First...

Thus, that which is capable of illuminating cannot be called "non-existent. Next, because that which is illuminated exists as a characteristic, the principle of non-attachment (*anāsaṅga*) is not established.
Formerly, Venerable Yan-yang asked Zhaozhou, "What is it like when one brings nothing at all?
Zhaozhou said, "Put it down. Yan-yang said, "I am bringing nothing at all; what is there to put down?"
"What is it? the Governor asked. Yunyan said, "If that is so, then take it away. At these words, the Governor attained great enlightenment. Huanglong’s verse says:
Not bringing a single thing, The two shoulders cannot bear it up. In an instant, beneath his words, he knew his error; Within his heart, there was boundless joy.
Poisonous malice forgotten, Snakes and tigers became his intimates. Through the vastness of a thousand years, A pure breeze remains.
It was still not yet finished. A Celestial Youth composed a verse: "The subtle movement of the wheel is already at hand; / Self-awareness of the coarse mind brings shame for the head’s collision.
/ The frame is broken and the axe-handle at the waist has rotted; / Cleansing the mundane bones, one wanders with the immortals.
This verse is neither attached nor unattached; thus, one attains mastery. Generally, those who see non-attachment within objects remain [bound] when separated from objects.
There is no such thing as non-attachment. To perceive non-attachment from the standpoint of inherent nature is to realize that non-attachment is itself the self-nature.
However, it is not permissible to merely maintain a conceptual intention of non-attachment.

At that time, Ānanda rose from his seat amidst the great assembly; he bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I am the youngest brother of the Tathāgata, having received the compassionate love of the Buddha."

Although he has now left the household life, he still relies on pride and self-indulgence; thus, despite his great learning, he has not attained the outflows-free state and cannot subdue the *śāpīra* spells.
He is turned about by them and sinks into brothels, all because he does not know the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) toward which one should proceed.

"We only pray that the World-Honored One, out of great compassion and pity, will reveal to us the path of *śamatha* (here translated as 'quiescence'), so that those who lack faith (*icchantika*, here translated as 'those devoid of faith') may destroy their *mleccha* views (here translated as 'evil views'). Having spoken these words, they prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground;
the entire great assembly likewise waited expectantly with thirsty longing, reverently awaiting his instructions.
Tong said: "According to Ānanda’s realization at this stage, he was still unable to subdue his conscious mind even when reaching the state of profound stillness and immovability;
therefore, he had not yet attained the state of outflowlessness (anāsrava). He initially regarded the capacity for cognitive awareness as a substantial entity.
Thus it was said that [the self] is within, without, or in the sense organs. Once he knew it was not a substance, he nevertheless still believed that consciousness existed."
Therefore it is said that consciousness arises within them as they combine according to conditions. Only when both consciousness and its objects have subsided can one truly believe in non-attachment.
Yet, to have an intention toward non-attachment is itself a form of attachment. Thus, to be entirely without attachment merely severs the seven consciousnesses;
one has not yet reached the state of profound stillness. Even if one reaches such stillness, one remains seated within the nest of the eighth consciousness.
This is what non-Buddhists call the *tattva* (the ultimate principle). If it pertains to the path of *śamatha*, it is a matter of transforming consciousness into wisdom (*jñāna*).
Even for the understanding of the sages, it does not admit of deliberate mental application; how much less could it be led by the ordinary sentiments of commoners?

Therefore, when the sentiments of both the ordinary and the sage are exhausted, the essence of true permanence is revealed; only then is it called the destination reached at the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Once the limit of reality is known, [one no longer...]
Driven by the arts of lust, one does not merely realize tranquility for oneself, but also causes all ordinary people who lack faith to shatter their evil views.
When Master Duan read the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, he composed a verse which says: "The mind was sought in seven locations but was not found;
Ānanda was bewildered and failed to glimpse the ground. Even if one were to seek until seeing that there is no mind, it would still be..."
This is like washing a clod of earth in mud; one might call such a person "one who possesses eyes.
At that time, the World-Honored One emitted various kinds of light from his face; those rays shone brilliantly, like a hundred thousand suns.
The entire Buddha-world shook in six ways. Thus, the lands of the ten directions, as numerous as motes of dust, were all revealed at once.
Through the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha, these worlds were merged into a single realm.
All the great bodhisattvas within those worlds remained in their respective lands, joining their palms in reverent attention.
Tong said: "The emission of light and the shaking of the earth have traditionally been regarded as inconceivable realms; yet they can also be understood through the mind.
In the practice of nourishing life, when the spirit is complete and firm, one’s eyes shine brightly even in the darkness of night, seeing all things without exception."
How much more so for the World-Honored One, who has attained perfection through many kalpas—could his radiance fail to blaze forth?
When one prays and moves the primal qi of the household, it can cause clouds to rise and rain to fall;

how much more so for the World-Honored One’s pure Dharma-body, which is unfathomable—could there be any part of the Buddha-world that does not tremble? When the World-Honored One erects the great banner of the Dharma, he must first...
There is a symbolic meaning here. What is called "causing all worlds to merge into a single realm" implicitly contains the intention that delusions are concealed and return to the Truth.

If one possesses superior faculties and sharp wisdom, upon seeing such light and witnessing such an event, they will immediately realize their original mind and attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Chan Master Yuanzhao said in his discourse on ascending the hall: "Look, look! A brilliant, auspicious radiance!"

It illuminates the great trichiliocosm: ten billion lands as numerous as motes of dust, ten billion oceans, ten billion Mount Sumerus, ten billion suns and moons, ten billion sets of four continents, and even down to lands as minute as motes of dust—all appear simultaneously within the light.
Do you all see them? If you can see them, I grant that you are truly present.
Auspicious Light. If you do not see it, do not say that the Auspicious Light does not shine. Everyone possesses this light;
why then does one who attains perfect illumination see it, while the multitude do not? It is simply a matter of awakening or non-awakening.
The Dharma-nature is omnipresent; delusive objects do not separate it. The realm of wisdom is inherently perfect; emotional measurements do not obstruct it. If you awaken to your own mind, then...
"Know that all these matters are like affairs within a house.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "All sentient beings, from time immemorial, have been subject to various inversions; the seeds of karma arise spontaneously."
Like a cluster of akṣa fruits (where three seeds share a single stalk and none grow in isolation), those who practice cannot achieve unexcelled bodhi;
they may instead become śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or even non-Buddhists, devas, māras, or the retinues of māras—
all because they do not know the two kinds of fundamental roots and thus practice in a confused manner, like boiling sand in the hope of producing fine rice.
Even if one were to pass through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, one would ultimately never obtain it. What are these two kinds?
Ānanda, the first is the root of birth and death from time immemorial—namely, that which you and all sentient beings now take to be your own nature: the mind of grasping at objects.
The second is the fundamentally pure essence of bodhi and nirvana from time immemorial—namely, that which is now your essential clarity of consciousness, capable of...

The conditions for birth arise. As for that which is neglected by these conditions: because sentient beings neglect this fundamental luminosity (*mūla-vidyā*), even though they act throughout their entire lives, they remain unaware of it and thus enter the various realms of existence in vain.

The Master said: "In the 'Investigation of the Mind in Seven Locations,' I pointed out that each was not [the true mind] because you take the攀緣心 (pān-yuán-xīn, the攀緣心, or 'object-seeking mind') as your self-nature.
Ānanda, you also know that this mind has not yet attained the untainted state (anāsrava) and is thus unable to subdue the Śābala spell."

Being turned by those [conditions], one fails to know the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) toward which one is heading; yet, one still dimly perceives the essence of original purity that constitutes bodhi and nirvāṇa.
Therefore, I pray that the Buddha will reveal and instruct us. Thus, the World-Honored One analyzed and spoke to them clearly:

"As previously stated, because one employs various false conceptions (*vikalpa*), and these conceptions are not true, there is cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). This refers precisely to employing such grasping.
That which takes the conditioned mind as its own nature is the very root of birth and death from time immemorial. As stated previously:
"It is all because of not knowing the eternally abiding true mind, the essence of pure and luminous nature.

This is precisely the Bodhi and Nirvana, the primordially pure essence, which is the root of non-arising and non-ceasing from time immemorial. [Sentient beings] revolve through birth and death due to delusion.
The three—karma, suffering, and birth—necessarily coalesce; therefore, they are like the *akṣa* berry cluster.
Not only do celestial Māras and non-Buddhists inevitably enter saṃsāra, but even śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who practice erroneously are collectively termed "inverted. Why is this?

Because it takes arising and ceasing as its cause. If the fundamental clarity of the essence of consciousness can give rise to various conditions, that which is left behind by those conditions is fundamentally neither born nor extinguished.
This is identical in intent to what is said later: "When original clarity shines and produces the objective world, once the object is established, the nature of the shining is lost.
This is precisely the source from which deluded thought arises; having fallen into deluded thought, one consequently leaves [the truth] behind.
The fundamental nature: because one neglects this original luminosity (*mūla-prakāśa*), one enters the various realms of existence and is unable to achieve unsurpassed *bodhi*.

A guest came to visit Changsha; Changsha called out, "Attendant Secretary! The man responded, "Yes. Changsha said, "That is not your original name. [The man] said, "One cannot depart from this very moment of responding;
there is no second master apart from this. Changsha [said]: *Note: The text provided ends abruptly with "沙" (Changsha). The translation reflects the fragmentary nature of the source.*
[The Master] said, "Can you call the Minister 'Supreme Honored One'? [The Disciple] said, "When one does not respond at all in this manner, are you perhaps the master to your disciple?
The Monk said, "It is not only when responding or not responding;
from beginningless kalpas, this has been the very root of birth and death. There is a verse that says: "The student of the Way does not recognize the Real, Precisely because..."
One has recognized the Buddha from the beginning. Since beginningless kalpas, this has been the root of birth and death;
the deluded call it the "original person. But by what means can this original person be known? The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, in the "Appearance of the Tathāgata" chapter, states:
"O Son of the Buddha, there is not a single sentient being who does not possess the wisdom of the Tathāgata. It is only because of delusive thoughts, inversion, and attachment..."
It is not realized. If one is free from deluded conceptualization, then all-knowledge, spontaneous knowledge, and unimpeded knowledge will manifest before one.
A Celestial Child (Tiantong) composed a verse saying: "Heaven covers and earth sustains; they form a single mass and a solid lump, pervading the Dharma-realm without limit."
When analyzed down to the limit of atoms (*paramāṇu*), there is no interior; when one reaches the ultimate subtlety, who can distinguish between front and back?
The Buddhas and Patriarchs have come to repay their karmic debts of speech—go ask the old teacher Nanquan. "Every person eats but a single stalk of vegetable.
Since this principle is possessed by every person, why is it that they cannot all together realize *bodhi*, and instead end up forming separate schools?

Regarding the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Ārya-Avalokiteśvara-Bodhisattva-Paripṛcchā-Sarvabuddha-viṣaya-samantabhadra-bodhicitta-uttaratantra-nāma*) states: "All sentient beings falsely perceive the cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra*).
Those who loathe this transmigration falsely perceive nirvana. Because of this, they are unable to enter pure enlightenment. It is not that enlightenment rejects those who seek to enter it;
rather, there are those who seek to enter, but it is not enlightenment that enters them. Thus, the root of the non-arising and non-ceasing grasping of consciousness is established.
Fundamentally, this cannot be achieved without a great and thorough awakening.
Ānanda, if you now wish to know the path of śamatha and desire to transcend birth and death, I shall now question you further.
At that moment, the Tathāgata raised his golden arm and bent his five fingers, saying to Ānanda: "Do you see this now? Ānanda replied, "I do."

[Ananda] spoke of "seeing. The Buddha asked, "What do you see? Ananda replied, "I see the Tathagata raising his arm and bending his fingers into a fist of radiance, which illuminates my mind and eyes.
The Buddha asked, "By what means do you see? Ananda replied, "Together with the great assembly."
[Ananda] replied, "I shall see it with my own eyes. The Buddha said to Ananda, "Answer me now:
when the Tathagata bends his fingers into a radiant fist to shine upon your eyes and mind, your eyes can see it; but what constitutes the mind when my fist shines?
Ananda said, "The Tathagata is currently investigating the location of the mind, and I am using my mind to investigate and pursue it. That which is capable of this investigation is my mind."
[Ānanda] was about to take this as his mind. The Buddha said, "Ho! Ānanda, this is not your mind. Ānanda was startled and left his seat;
with palms joined, he stood up and addressed the Buddha, saying, "This is not my mind. What should it be called?

The Buddha told Ānanda, "This is a false appearance and conceptualization of the external objects before you, which deludes your true nature. From your beginningless past until your present life, you have mistaken a thief for your own son."
"You have lost your original permanence; therefore, you undergo the cycle of rebirth.
Ānanda said, "I see it. This, it is generally said, was the World-Honored One’s second gradual induction. "Do you see it now? Ānanda replied, "I see it."

Simply awaken to this with vigorous introspection, and you will immediately perceive the original luminosity of the essence of consciousness; it admits of no deliberation and admits of no contrivance.

Bodhi and Nirvana are spontaneously and fully sufficient within it. As soon as one engages in conceptual analysis, one enters the realm of inference (*anumāna*), which is the functioning of the six consciousnesses.
When the stillness (*dhāraṇī*) becomes adhered to and cognition is triggered, one is far removed from true nature. Therefore, the Buddha rebuked him, saying: "This is not [it]."
If your mind, at a moment of sudden panic or confusion, were to suddenly turn its light back within, you would find that original enlightenment (mūla-bodhi) is sovereign.
Why say that apart from this awareness there is nothing else? This so-called "awareness" arises through discrimination in response to external objects (*viṣaya*);
when the objects depart, it ceases to exist, and is therefore called a false thought attached to signs. If it is original enlightenment, it does not depend [on objects].
Because it possesses arising and ceasing amidst the dust of phenomena, it is called "true nature. Yet, awakening is but one.
For this very faculty of cognitive awareness obscures the face of original awakening; thus, this cognitive awareness is truly a thief of original awakening.
If one mistakes cognitive awareness for one's own mind, it is like mistaking a thief for one's son—discarding the non-arising and non-ceasing while guarding that which arises and ceases. Its...
How could there be any doubt regarding this cycle of transmigration? Nevertheless, to seek a separate "original enlightenment" apart from this very awareness is likewise impossible.
As Tiantong briefly stated: "If you can trace the bottom [of this] and realize it is your own mind, then you are mistaking a thief for your son."
Xiu Shan’s Master said: "If you can push [the mind] to its bottom and find it is not your own mind, then you are recognizing your son as a thief.
Tiantong took up this point and said: "Now, even as you push it, is it the son or the thief? Buying a hat to fit the head; eating fish and removing the bones.
Thus, does Tiantong still exercise discrimination? The Sixth Patriarch said: "Ordinary people are Buddhas; afflictions are Bodhi."
"Oṃ. The preceding thought being deluded is an ordinary person; the succeeding thought being awakened is a Buddha. The preceding thought clinging to objects is affliction (*kleśa*);
the succeeding thought departing from objects is bodhi. This is like the saying of turning the palm over. Yongjia said:
'The true nature of ignorance is itself Buddha-nature; the illusory, empty body is itself the Dharma-body. Thus, one penetrates thoroughly the non-duality."
...the gateway.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the beloved younger brother of our Buddha, it was because my heart loved the Buddha that he caused me to leave the household life.
Why should my mind be limited to making offerings only to the Tathāgata? I shall travel through lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, serving all Buddhas, and..."
"Good spiritual friend, it is by means of this mind that one gives rise to great courage and vigor to perform all those difficult dharmic practices;
even if one should slander the Dharma and forever lose their roots of goodness, it is still because of this mind.

If what I have now revealed were not the mind, I would be without a mind and identical to earth or wood. Apart from this awareness and cognition, there is nothing else at all. Why, then, does the Tathāgata say..."

"This is not the mind. I am truly terrified, and there is not one among this great assembly who does not harbor doubt. I pray that you will deign to show great compassion and reveal what we have not yet understood.
Ānanda replied: "My emotions are exhausted and my vision is withered; I have come to believe that being without a mind is the same as being like wood or stone. At this point..."

It would be well to accept this and proceed; you would thereby save a great deal of mental effort. Alas, how can one remain fixated on a single instance of cognitive awareness and refuse to let it go?
Long ago, when Dalaru first visited Mazu, Mazu asked him, "What do you seek by coming here?
He replied, "I seek the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Mazu said, "The Buddha has no knowledge or vision; knowledge and vision are merely demons. From where have you come? He replied:
Nanyue arrived. The Patriarch said, "You have come from Nanyue, yet you do not yet know the essential heart of Caoxi.
You should return there quickly; it is not appropriate for you to go elsewhere. Lang returned to Shitou and asked, "What is the Buddha? Shitou said, "You have no Buddha-nature.
Lang said, "As for the wriggling and moving sentient beings, what then? Shitou said, "The wriggling and moving sentient beings, on the contrary..."
When it was said, "All possess Buddha-nature," Huairang asked, "Why then do I have none? Mazu replied, "It is because you are unwilling to accept it.
At these words, Huairang attained realization. After he became an abbot, whenever students arrived, he would simply say, "Go away!
You have no Buddha-nature! His manner of responding to seekers was roughly like this. How could this mean that there is nothing at all apart from awakening and cognition?

At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to cause Ānanda and the great assembly to enter the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), sat upon the lion throne, rubbed the crown of Ānanda’s head, and addressed him, saying: "The Tathāgata has always taught that all dharmas arise."
All is manifested by the mind alone. All causes and effects, and even the minute dust motes of the world, derive their substance from the mind.
Ānanda, if one examines the fundamental source of everything that exists within all worlds—even down to blades of grass, leaves, and strands of thread—they all possess an inherent nature.
Even empty space has its name and appearance; how much more so the pure, wondrously pure, and luminous mind, whose nature is one?

The mind is entirely without intrinsic nature. If you persist in clinging to the nature apprehended by conceptualization and discursive thought as being necessarily the mind, then this mind ought to exist as a distinct, complete entity apart from all objects of the senses—forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles—and their activities.
Yet, as you now listen to my teaching, you possess conceptualization because of the sound; even if that sound were extinguished, [the mind would still not exist].
All that is seen, heard, sensed, and known—though you maintain an inner state of profound stillness—is still but a reflection of the conceptualization of dharma-dusts.

I am not scolding you for clinging to this as being "non-mind"; rather, you must examine the mind with subtle discernment. If this nature of conceptualization exists independently of the external objects, then it is your true mind.
If this nature of conceptualization has no substance apart from the objects, then it is merely the conceptualization of those external objects.
As for the phenomenon of reflections, external objects are not permanent. If they were to change and perish, this mind would be like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit;
thus, your Dharma-body would be subject to annihilation. Who then could cultivate and realize the patience of the non-arising of dharmas?
Tong said: "The arising of all phenomena is manifested solely by the mind, just as successive images are manifested solely by a mirror.

The six sense-objects are like forms, and discrimination is like the shadow. The shadow exists because of the form; the mind exists because of the objects. This, then, is the matter of shadows of discrimination regarding external objects.
When active, it belongs to the external objects; when still, it belongs to the dharma-object. Therefore, even if one internally maintains a state of profound seclusion..."
There are no shadows of external objects, yet there are shadows of profound stillness; these are still merely shadow-phenomena resulting from the discrimination of *dharmas*.
That which is grasped by them is consciousness (*vijñāna*), not the eternally abiding true mind of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-bodhi*). This is the eternally abiding true mind.
It is far removed from all conceptual discrimination, like a great round mirror, and free from the two defilements of motion and stillness.
This mind is inherently undefiled; therefore, it is called "pure. It is defiled yet remains undefiled; therefore, it is called "wondrously pure.
All causes and effects, as well as the minute dust of the worlds, are established based upon this; it is the fundamental nature of the deluded minds of the nine realms. Therefore, it is said:
The nature of all minds, if this mind is seen, is free from conceptual discrimination and possesses its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
This intrinsic nature does not exist or cease in accordance with conceptual discrimination. It is like a mirror that exists as a substance apart from reflections;
