this mirror-substance does not arise or perish in accordance with dust or reflections. If one clings to conceptual discrimination and cognitive awareness as...
As for "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*): it is merely grasping at reflections as being mirrors. They exist when facing objects, but they do not exist when separated from objects.
Like a reflection within a mirror, they originally possess no self-substance and ultimately end in annihilation. If this were the case, could one thereby realize non-arising?
Therefore, know that the mind has its own substance and is fundamentally not subject to annihilation. As previously stated: "This is not your mind. Why? Because...
That which is recognized is a mind of false delusion and annihilation; it is not the fundamentally real mind. How could it truly be a state of no-mind?
Xuan Sha, ascending the hall, said: "Furthermore, there is another kind who speak of 'bright and clear,' of the 'luminous spirit' and the 'nature of wisdom.'"

Able to see and able to hear, you act as the sovereign within the field of the five aggregates. To act in such a way as a "good spiritual friend" (kalyāṇamitra)—do you realize how greatly this deceives people?
I now ask you: if you identify this brilliant and numinous awareness as your true reality, [you are mistaken].
Why is it that when you are drowsy, this clarity and lucidity does not manifest?
If it were not present during drowsiness, why is there this clarity at other times? Do you understand? This is called "mistaking a thief for one's own son";
it is the root of birth and death, the delusive energy of conditioned phenomena. Do you wish to know its origin? I shall tell you: it is *zhāo* (clarity).
This "bright and lucid" [awareness] arises precisely because of the dharmas of the external objects—form, sound, fragrance, and so forth—and one then says, "This is the bright and lucid.
If those external objects were absent, this bright and lucid awareness of yours would be like the fur on a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit.
Benevolent one, where does your true reality actually reside? If you now wish to escape from these five aggregates, [you must realize this].
Lord of the Field: Simply recognize your secret vajra-body. The ancients said to you:
"Perfectly complete and all-pervasive, it extends throughout the entire dharma-realm. I shall now briefly explain this for you; the wise can attain understanding through analogy.
Do you see the sun over Jambudvīpa? It is that which enables the people of the world to carry out their activities and sustain their bodies.
All forms of livelihood and various mental activities are established by relying upon the light of the sun.
Now, does the very substance of the sun itself possess such manifold mental activities? Is there any place where it does not pervade? If you wish to recognize the adamantine essence:
You must also view it in this way: right now, the mountains, rivers, and great earth; the lands of the ten directions; form and emptiness, light and darkness;
and even your own body and mind—all these are nothing other than manifestations produced by the majestic radiance of your perfect realization.

Indeed, from the various classes of gods and humans down to all sentient beings, the sequence of their karmic actions and the resulting fruits of their rebirths—whether animate or inanimate—are entirely without exception [the product of this].

We rely upon your majestic radiance. Even until all Buddhas attain the Way and achieve the fruit, and engage with and benefit sentient beings—all this is none other than relying entirely upon your majestic radiance.
As for the adamantine essence itself, does it contain ordinary beings and Buddhas? Does it possess the mental activities of the mind?
One must not say "it does not exist" and thereby think one has attained the truth. Do you understand? Once, Xuansha was reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
He revealed the ground of the mind. Consequently, his responses to the capacities of beings were swift and nimble, entering into profound resonance with the *sūtras*.
This single section of his spontaneous discourse accords in every detail with the intent of the scriptures.

When it comes to the statement that all things are received through the power of majestic radiance, and that the arising of all phenomena is a mere manifestation of the mind, it becomes even more brilliant and vital. Furthermore, he was a true successor to the Buddha-eye.
The Venerable Zhuan’an Gui and his paternal uncle, the layman Chi Yi, both delighted in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
Zhuan’an said, “If there is a nature of discrimination that exists apart from the sensory objects before one, this is precisely the root of birth and death.

The layman was startled and asked, “Does the Buddha speak falsely? Zhuan’an replied, “The Buddha certainly does not speak falsely. Furthermore, let us examine and question you right now, face-to-face, layman.”
"Where is the fruit of the mind? The Master sighed and said, "The Buddha taught that the realization of the foremost emptiness is called the Lion’s Roar.
You must go; do not linger here. Later, he ascended the hall and said: "When seeing sees, that seeing is not seeing; even seeing is still..."
Transcending views; views cannot reach it. A fallen flower has intent as it follows the flowing water;
the flowing water is without sentiment as it carries away the fallen flower. All things that can return are naturally not you.
That which does not return to you—what else could it be? [The Master] lets out a shout and says: "Thirty years!"
Later, do not say that Śākyamuni’s teaching corrupts the sons and daughters of others.
According to Zhuan-an’s insight, one immediately departs from sensory objects (*viṣaya*), and there is no separate self-nature to be attained.

Those who naturally and skillfully turn the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* are precisely those for whom "seeing has already departed from seeing, and seeing cannot reach it"—a single segment of true wind that can be considered a fellow student with Xuansha.
At that moment, Ānanda and the great assembly were silent and overcome with despondency. The Buddha addressed Ānanda:

"Among all those in the world who practice and train, even if they have presently attained the nine successive meditative absorptions (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), they cannot yet exhaust their outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) and become Arhats."

All this arises from clinging to these deluded thoughts of birth and death and mistakenly taking them to be real. Therefore, although you have now acquired much learning, you have not attained the fruit of sainthood.

[The Buddha] says in general: "The nine successive meditative absorptions" (navānupūrvavihārasamāpattayaḥ), such as the four dhyānas and the heavens of the four formless attainments mentioned later, merely describe their fruits.
This refers to the nine successive attainments (navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti) practiced by a person in training (śaikṣa).
Entering from one dhyāna to the next, they practice them in succession as described in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*:

"Free from sensual desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and evaluation, born of seclusion, joyful and blissful, he enters and dwells in the first dhyāna; with the stilling of directed thought and evaluation, he dwells in internal..."

With equanimity and purity of mind, one-pointedness, and without applied or sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is born of concentration and characterized by joy and bliss. Free from joy, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending; he experiences with his body that noble bliss of which the Noble Ones say, "He who has equanimity and mindfulness dwells happily. Thus he enters and dwells in the third dhyāna. He abandons pleasure and pain, and with the prior disappearance of elation and dejection, he enters and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity. This is called the perfection of the four dhyānas. Furthermore, having transcended all perceptions of form, with the cessation of perceptions of sensory resistance, and not attending to perceptions of diversity, thinking, "Space is infinite," he enters and dwells in the sphere of infinite space. Having transcended the sphere of infinite space, thinking, "Consciousness is infinite," he enters and dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness. Having transcended the sphere of infinite consciousness, thinking, "There is nothing whatsoever," he enters and dwells in the sphere of nothingness. Having transcended the sphere of nothingness, he enters and dwells in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. This is called the perfection of the four formless attainments. Furthermore, he attains and dwells in the liberation of the mind through loving-kindness, free from ill will; the liberation of the mind through compassion, free from cruelty; the liberation of the mind through sympathetic joy, free from aversion; and the liberation of the mind through equanimity, free from attachment. This is called the perfection of the four immeasurables. Furthermore, perceiving forms internally, he sees external forms, small and beautiful, and having mastered them, he becomes aware of them; perceiving forms internally, he sees external forms, great and beautiful, and having mastered them, he becomes aware of them; perceiving no forms internally, he sees external forms, small and beautiful, and having mastered them, he becomes aware of them; perceiving no forms internally, he sees external forms, great and beautiful, and having mastered them, he becomes aware of them. This is called the perfection of the eight bases of mastery. Furthermore, perceiving no forms internally, he sees external forms, blue, blue in color, blue in luster, blue in appearance—just as the flax flower is blue, blue in color, blue in luster, blue in appearance, or just as the Bārāṇasī cloth, well-dyed and of excellent quality, is blue, blue in color, blue in luster, blue in appearance—so too, perceiving no forms internally, he sees external forms, blue, blue in color, blue in luster, blue in appearance, and having mastered them, he becomes aware of them. This is called the perfection of the first liberation through total purity. Furthermore, perceiving no forms internally, he sees external forms, yellow, yellow in color, yellow in luster, yellow in appearance—just as the karṇikāra flower is yellow, yellow in color, yellow in luster, yellow in appearance, or just as the Bārāṇasī cloth, well-dyed and of excellent quality, is yellow, yellow in color, yellow in luster, yellow in appearance—so too, perceiving no forms internally, he sees external forms, yellow, yellow in color, yellow in luster, yellow in appearance, and having mastered them, he becomes aware of them. This is called the perfection of the second liberation through total purity. Furthermore, perceiving no forms internally, he sees external forms, red, red in color, red in luster, red in appearance—just as the bandhujīvaka flower is red, red in color, red in luster, red in appearance, or just as the Bārāṇasī cloth, well-dyed and of excellent quality, is red, red in color, red in luster, red in appearance—so too, perceiving no forms internally, he sees external forms, red, red in color, red in luster, red in appearance, and having mastered them, he becomes aware of them. This is called the perfection of the third liberation through total purity. Furthermore, perceiving no forms internally, he sees external forms, white, white in color, white in luster, white in appearance—just as the morning star is white, white in color, white in luster, white in appearance, or just as the Bārāṇasī cloth, well-dyed and of excellent quality, is white, white in color, white in luster, white in appearance—so too, perceiving no forms internally, he sees external forms, white, white in color, white in luster, white in appearance, and having mastered them, he becomes aware of them. This is called the perfection of the fourth liberation through total purity. Furthermore, he perceives the earth-kasiṇa, extending upward, downward, and across, undivided, immeasurable, and boundless. This is called the perfection of the earth-kasiṇa. Furthermore, he perceives the water-kasiṇa, the fire-kasiṇa, the air-kasiṇa, the blue-kasiṇa, the yellow-kasiṇa, the red-kasiṇa, the white-kasiṇa, the space-kasiṇa, and the consciousness-kasiṇa, each extending upward, downward, and across, undivided, immeasurable, and boundless. This is called the perfection of the ten kasiṇas. Furthermore, he recollects his manifold past abodes, that is, one birth, two births, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand, many eons of world-dissolution, many eons of world-evolution, many eons of both dissolution and evolution, thinking: "There I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, and such a lifespan; passing away from there, I was reborn elsewhere, and there too I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, and such a lifespan. Thus he recollects his manifold past abodes with their modes and particulars. This is called the perfection of the supernormal knowledge of the recollection of past abodes. Furthermore, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, faring according to their karma—and he understands how beings pass on according to their deeds. This is called the perfection of the supernormal knowledge of the divine eye. Furthermore, by the destruction of the taints, he realizes for himself in this very life, through direct knowledge, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having attained it, he dwells therein, knowing: "Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being. This is called the perfection of the taintless liberation. This is called the perfection of the six supernormal knowledges. Furthermore, he knows the minds of other beings and other persons as they truly are: a mind with lust, he knows it as a mind with lust; a mind without lust, he knows it as a mind without lust; a mind with hatred, he knows it as a mind with hatred; a mind without hatred, he knows it as a mind without hatred; a mind with delusion, he knows it as a mind with delusion; a mind without delusion, he knows it as a mind without delusion; a contracted mind, he knows it as contracted; a distracted mind, he knows it as distracted; a great mind, he knows it as great; a narrow mind, he knows it as narrow; an expansive mind, he knows it as expansive; an unliberated mind, he knows it as unliberated; a liberated mind, he knows it as liberated; a concentrated mind, he knows it as concentrated; a non-concentrated mind, he knows it as non-concentrated; an exalted mind, he knows it as exalted; an unexalted mind, he knows it as unexalted; a surpassable mind, he knows it as surpassable; an unsurpassable mind, he knows it as unsurpassable; a defiled mind, he knows it as defiled; an undefiled mind, he knows it as undefiled; a mind that has transcended the world, he knows it as a mind that has transcended the world. This is called the perfection of the knowledge of the minds of others. Furthermore, he recollects his manifold past abodes, that is, one birth, two births, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand, many eons of world-dissolution, many eons of world-evolution, many eons of both dissolution and evolution, thinking: "There I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, and such a lifespan; passing away from there, I was reborn elsewhere, and there too I had

Possessing mindfulness and dwelling in happiness, he enters and dwells fully in the third dhyāna. With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and sorrow, he enters and dwells fully in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and possesses purity of equanimity and mindfulness.

Transcending all perceptions of form, extinguishing perceptions of sensory resistance, and not attending to perceptions of diversity, he enters the sphere of infinite space; [the sphere of] infinite space...
Abiding fully in the sphere of infinite space, one transcends all space and enters the sphere of infinite consciousness, abiding fully therein.
Transcending all infinite consciousness, one enters the sphere of nothingness, abiding fully therein.

Transcending nothingness, one enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, abiding fully therein. Transcending all spheres of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one enters cessation.

One dwells in the perception of being fully ordained. These constitute the nine successive concentrations (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*). All of these involve conditioned effort and involve the joyful grasping of conditioned, wholesome fruits;
therefore, they are called "being deluded regarding the heavens of outflows (*sāsrava*). To take them as an understanding of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is to be held captive by them.

One practices while entering into the subtle arising and ceasing of delusive thoughts within consciousness, yet one has not yet been able to see the true nature of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmatā*) right here and now.
Quiescence is truly an unconditioned dharma; therefore, as long as one has not yet attained the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), it is not [fully realized].

If a great Arhat has already realized the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodhasamāpatti*), this is called "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*). Now, the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*) also realize the cessation of perception and feeling.

What constitutes outflows (*āsrava*)? It is to realize *nirvāṇa* through discursive thought (*vikalpa*). Even if one attains the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), it is not yet the ultimate reality.

Huangbo said: "All sentient beings who cycle incessantly through birth and death do so because their mental objects run wild and their minds do not rest within the six realms, thereby causing them to undergo all manner of suffering. The Vimalakīrti Sūtra says: "Those who are difficult to transform..."
The human mind is like a monkey; therefore, one uses various methods to restrain it, and only then can it be tamed.
Thus, when the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise; when the mind ceases, all manner of phenomena cease. Hence, one knows that all dharmas are created by the mind.
Even the six realms of existence—humans, devas, hell-beings, asuras, and so forth—are all created by the mind.
Now, simply practice being without mind; suddenly cease all conditions. Do not give rise to deluded thoughts or discriminations. Be without person, without self;
without greed or anger; without hatred or love; without victory or defeat. Simply eliminate these many kinds of deluded thoughts.
The nature is inherently pure from the beginning; this is precisely the practice of the Bodhi-dharma.

O Buddhas and others, if you do not realize this meaning, then even if you study extensively and undergo arduous cultivation—eating wood and wearing grass garments—if you do not recognize your own mind, all such acts are called "perverse practices.
You would all become celestial Māras, externalists, or spirits of water and land. Practicing in such a manner, what would it avail?
Furthermore, Master Zhigong said: "The fundamental substance is produced by one's own mind; how can it be sought within words and letters?
Now, simply recognize your own mind and cease discursive thought and delusion; then worldly afflictions will naturally not arise. As the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* says:
"He prepared only a single bed and lay there ill, his mind remaining unaroused. It is like a person lying ill: all攀緣 (pān-yuán, mental attachments and objective conditions) completely cease.
When deluded thoughts cease and are extinguished, that itself is Bodhi.

If, at present, your mind is still turbid and unsettled, then no matter how much you study to reach the stages of the Three Vehicles, the Four Fruits, or the Ten Grounds, you will ultimately remain seated among ordinary beings and sages;
all conditioned phenomena return to impermanence, and all power has its limit, like an arrow shot into the sky whose force is eventually exhausted.
They fall back again and return to the cycle of birth and death. To practice in such a manner is to fail to understand the Buddha’s intent;

to undergo hardship in vain—is this not a great error? Master Zhi said: "If one has not yet met a world-transcending enlightened teacher, it is in vain that one takes the medicine of the Mahāyāna Dharma. Alas!
If even the medicine of the Mahāyāna Dharma cannot save one from calamity, how much less so the nine successive stages of meditative concentration (*anupūrva-samāpatti*)! Thus we know it is an error.
"To practice in a distracted manner makes it difficult to achieve the fruit of sainthood.
Having heard this, Ānanda again shed tears of grief; prostrating himself with his five limbs touching the ground, he knelt with palms joined and addressed the Buddha, saying:
Ever since I followed the Buddha to leave the household life, I have relied upon the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power and have constantly thought to myself that there was no need for me to practice.
I presumed that the Tathāgata would bestow samādhi upon me; I did not realize that body and mind fundamentally cannot substitute for one another, and thus I lost my original mind.
Although he has left the household life in body, his mind does not enter the Way. He is like a destitute son who abandons his father and flees;

it is only today that he realizes that even if one possesses much learning, if one does not practice it, it is equal to having heard nothing at all. It is like a person speaking of food; in the end, they cannot be satiated.
World-Honored One, we are now entangled by the two obstacles precisely because we do not know the nature of the mind, which is quiescent and eternal.
We only pray that the Tathāgata, out of compassion for us who are destitute and exposed, will give rise to his wondrously luminous mind and open our eyes to the Way.

The interlocutor said: "The Lotus Sūtra also contains this parable of abandoning one's father and fleeing afar. Wandering exposed in foreign lands, one hopes for the pointing out of the jewel within one’s robes;
thus, there gradually arises the hope of returning home. The two obstructions refer to the afflictive obstruction (kleśāvaraṇa) and the cognitive obstruction (jñeyāvaraṇa)."
The afflictive hindrances obstruct the mind; thus the mind is not liberated, and one undergoes retribution for the karma of fetters. The cognitive hindrances obstruct wisdom;

thus wisdom is not liberated, because one does not realize the emptiness of phenomena. Ānanda clearly knew that he was entangled by these two hindrances, yet he also knew what is called the nature of the mind—quiescent and eternal.
Why, then, did his Dharma-eye fail to open? How profound is the difficulty of attaining complete transcendence! —Seng [Dao]
A student asked Youshan, "What should I do when I am about to return to my hometown? Youshan said, "Your parents' entire bodies are covered in red sores, and they are lying in a thicket of thorns.
Where would you go upon returning? The student said, "If that is so, then I shall not return."
Mount [Shan] said, "You must go back. If you go back, I will give you a prescription for ceasing the consumption of grain.
The monk said, "I request it at once. The Master said, "When you ascend to the hall twice daily, you must not chew so much as a single grain of rice.
Later, a monk asked Luopu, "What is it like when a student intends to return to his hometown? Luopu said, "The house is ruined and the people are gone; where can the son go back to?"
The Master said, "In that case, you will not return. Pufu said, "The remaining snow before the courtyard melts under the sun;
who shall sweep the red dust within the chamber? He further spoke in verse: "Resolute in my intent, I return to my home, Boarding a boat to cross the Five Lakes.
As I raise the oar, stars and moon vanish; I halt the rudder, and the sun stands solitary. Unmooring, I leave the shore of error; Setting sail, I emerge [into the truth]."
The Right Path: Upon arriving, the house is utterly emptied; thus one avoids being a fool within the chamber. Danxia’s verse says:
"The road to the peaceful homeland is vast and empty; My longing to return flows on, its thoughts boundless. Casting off the hand, what is there upon arriving home?
In the crystal jewel-palace, the moonlight locks the flowers. These various elders have for a time pointed out the expedient means for returning home; it may truly be said:

When the eye of the Way opened and he truly knew the nature of mind as quiescent and eternal, the Tathāgata immediately emitted a precious light from the svastika on his chest; that light shone brilliantly, possessing hundreds of thousands of colors.

Simultaneously pervading Buddha-worlds as numerous as the motes of dust throughout the ten directions, [the light] universally moistened the crowns of all Tathāgatas in every precious land of the ten directions;
it then returned to Ānanda and the great assembly. Addressing Ānanda, [the Buddha] said:
"I now establish for you the Great Dharma Banner, so that all sentient beings throughout the ten directions may likewise attain the wondrous, subtle, and secret mind of pure and luminous nature."
He attained the pure eye.
Tong said: "Previously, light was emitted from the mouth, and at once the lands of the ten directions were revealed;
these worlds were merged into a single realm to signify that the true and the deluded are non-dual. He revealed two kinds of roots, which must necessarily be..."
The severing of delusion must come first; if discursive thought is not stilled, one will not achieve the fruit of sainthood even if one attains the nine successive meditative absorptions.
This can be verified by examining one's own countenance as in a mirror. Now, light is emitted from the *svastika* on his chest, bathing the crowns of all Tathāgatas.
Turning immediately toward Ānanda and the great assembly signifies that the sacred and the profane are non-dual.

He revealed that while the external objects before one are inherently dark, the seeing-faculty itself suffers no impairment. Even when the head moves and shakes, the seeing remains unmoved; when the hands open and close, the seeing neither expands nor contracts.

While Yangshan was seated, a monk came and paid his respects, but Yangshan did not look at him.
The monk then asked, "Do you know how to write characters? Yangshan replied, "I manage it as best I can. The monk then circled to the right once and asked, "What character is this?
Yangshan wrote the character "ten" (十) on the ground in response. The monk then circled to the left once and asked, "What character is this? Yangshan changed [the character].
He drew a *svastika* with a cross. The monk drew this *maṇḍala* symbol (○) and, with both hands, formed the gesture of an asura grasping the sun and moon.
[The Master] asked, "What character is this? The monk then drew this [symbol] (○@卍) facing it. The monk then made the gesture of *Luzhide* (Lokajyoti).
[The Master] said, "So it is, so it is. This is that which all Buddhas protect and mindfully remember; you too..."
"So it is. I am also like this. Guard yourself well. The monk bowed in thanks and departed, soaring through the air.
At that time, a certain practitioner saw him. Five days later, he asked Baoshan, "Did you see him? Baoshan said, "Did you see him too? The practitioner replied, "I saw him.
He left the gate and soared through the air. Baoshan said, "This was an Arhat from the Western Heaven."
He came to inquire about my Way. The seeker said, "Although I have witnessed various samādhis, I cannot discern their underlying principle.

Guishan said, "I shall explain this for you according to its meaning. These are the eight kinds of samādhi; they are the ocean of awakening transformed into the ocean of meaning. Their essence is identical.
This meaning necessarily involves cause and effect, simultaneity and succession, as well as the general and the particular."

This is not separate from the Samādhi of Concealing the Body. If one understands that the Ocean of Awakening at Mount Yang was transformed into the Ocean of Meaning—the Samādhi—then the *svastika* on the Buddha’s chest surging forth with precious light is likewise a wondrous function within the inconceivable.
This must necessarily take the wondrous, subtle, and secret nature of the pure, luminous mind as its foundation. Once, Guishan asked Yangshan about the "wondrous, pure, and luminous [mind]."
"Mind," [Miaoyan] said. "How do you understand this? Yangshan said, "Mountains, rivers, the great earth, the sun, moon, and stars.
Guishan said, "You have grasped only its phenomena. Yangshan asked, "What did the Master just ask? Guishan replied, "The wondrous, pure, and luminous mind."
Yangshan said, "Can it be called a 'thing'? Miaoyan said, "So it is, so it is.
It is precisely because Yangshan has realized the wondrous, pure, and luminous mind and attained the eye of purity that his samādhi of recognizing characters transcends the ordinary."
Ānanda, you previously answered me that you saw the light of my fist. From what cause does this light of the fist arise?
How is it formed into a fist? And by whom do you see it?
Tong said: "This is the World-Honored One’s third gradual inducement; it can be called a most earnest and compassionate heart.
Previously, when he asked, 'By what do you see? Ānanda replied, 'I likewise see with my eyes. The Master had already rebuked him for mistaking a thief for his own son.
Now, by asking again, 'By what do you see? he intends to lead Ānanda to turn the light back upon itself and reflect inwardly. Suddenly, he beholds..."
"The clarity of seeing is the fundamental source; it does not depend upon the eye. How can you fail to realize this at last? A monk was standing in attendance beside Xuansha.
Xuansha pointed with his staff at a white spot on the ground before him and asked, "Do you see it?
The monk replied, "I see it. He asked this three times, and the monk answered in the same way three times. Xuansha said, "You see it, and I see it too."

"Why do you say you do not see? On another day, he again propped his staff against the ground and asked Changsheng, "What is your view regarding the view of a monk, the view of a layperson, the view of a man, and the view of a woman?
He replied, "Does the Master still see that which is clearly manifest?
The Master said, "Familiarity fills the world; it is thanks to this response of yours, 'clearly manifest,' that I have found my match. Thereupon, he bestowed [the Dharma] upon Xuan.

Sandian saw him face-to-face. Had Ānanda been able to know for himself that the locus of seeing is beyond the reach of the faculty of sight, why would it have been necessary for the World-Honored One to employ so much verbal eloquence?
Ānanda said: "Because the Buddha’s entire body was like Jāmbūnada gold (the juice of a tree named after which enters into water, sand, and stone to form gold), blazing like a mountain of jewels."
Born of purity, there is radiance; I have truly observed this with my own eyes. By curling the tips of the five fingers and showing them to others, there is the mark of the fist.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "The Tathāgata speaks these true words to you today. All those who possess wisdom..."
One must rely on parables to attain awakening. Ānanda, it is like my fist: if there were no hand of mine, my fist would not be formed;
if there were no eye of yours, your seeing would not be formed. If you take your faculty of sight as an analogy for the principle of my fist, is the meaning not the same?
Ānanda replied, "Indeed so, World-Honored One. Since there is no eye of mine, my seeing is not formed. [He continued] by means of my eye...
The sense-faculties (*indriya*) are like, for example, a closed fist. The meaning of the phenomenon is similar [to this]. The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Your statement that they are similar is not correct. Why? Just as a person without hands has no fist at all, one who lacks eyes does not mean there is a total absence of seeing."
Why is this? You should try asking a blind person on the road, "What do you see?
Those blind people will surely answer you, "Right now before my eyes, I see only darkness; there is nothing else for me to behold. Observe it from this perspective.
"The external objects are naturally dark; what deficiency is there in the seeing?

Ānanda asked, "World-Honored One, for what reason do you use the blind person as an analogy? The Buddha replied, "It is because you, Ānanda, cling to the fixed notion that seeing is a faculty belonging to the eyes.
You do not realize that consciousness arises between the sense organ and its object. Since a blind person has no eyes, how could they also see blackness?"
"Darkness. This seeing that depends upon the eye-faculty to perceive is merely the seeing that discriminates external objects;
it is not the seeing that is fundamentally pure. The discrimination of external objects belongs to the sixth consciousness; it exists only as long as the eye exists.

When the eye perishes, it perishes; it necessarily depends upon the sense organ (*indriya*) to manifest. The light of the pure mind does not depend upon the organ to exist, nor does it vanish when the organ ceases.
Therefore, it is without arising or ceasing. This is the vision that is inherently pure and without arising or ceasing;
it is fully possessed by every person and is not absent simply because one is blind. Ānanda, however, clings to the notion that it belongs exclusively to the eye.
"Seeing" is the root of arising and ceasing; yet what deficiency is there in that which the World-Honored One points to as "seeing"?
It is the root of non-arising and non-ceasing. Such a reminder may be said to be an ultimate revelation. Formerly, Prime Minister Cui Qun—
He visited Chan Master Ruhui and asked, "By what means did you attain realization? Rui said, "I attained it by seeing into one's nature.

At that time, Rui was suffering from eye disease. Cui remarked sarcastically, "If you say you have seen into your nature, what can you do about your eyes? Rui replied, "Seeing into one's nature is not the function of the eyes."
"What harm does an eye disease do? Choe bowed his head in thanks. Later, Fayuan remarked separately, "This is the eye of a high official;
how could it be that the answer given at the assembly still involved the meaning of the teachings?"
Ānanda said, “The various blind people before my eyes see only darkness; how can this be called ‘seeing’? The Buddha told Ānanda, “The various blind people have no eyes and see only darkness.
Is there a difference between this darkness and the darkness seen by a person with eyes who is situated in a dark room, or is there no difference?
“Thus it is, World-Honored One. When the darkness of the person in the dark room is compared with the darkness of those various blind people, there is indeed a distinction.”
"It is not so, Ānanda. Suppose a person with no eyes sees only total darkness before them;

if they suddenly regain the power of sight and see various forms within that same field of objects, it is called 'seeing with the eyes. Now, suppose that person in the dark sees only total darkness before them;

if they suddenly obtain the light of a lamp and likewise see various forms within that same field of objects, it should be called 'seeing with the lamp. If it were seeing with the lamp, then the lamp would possess the capacity for vision."
Seeing itself is not called a lamp. Furthermore, if it is the lamp that observes, what concern is that of yours?
Therefore, you should know that while a lamp can reveal color, such seeing is the eye and not the lamp; while the eye can reveal color, such seeing-nature is the mind and not the eye.
Tong said: "This was the World-Honored One’s clear analysis—what he called 'speaking to you with words of truth.

Both the lamp and the eye are conditions for seeing; their substance is not the seer. That which is able to see is the mind. What was previously asked—'Can the gate see?'—already contains this meaning.
Yet here, the lamp is again used as a metaphor for the eye, and the eye is used as an analogy for the mind. Regarding the lamp:
One cannot call this "seeing. Can the eye itself be called "seeing"? That which the eye sees is not the nature of seeing.
If the six sense organs function interchangeably, the ear can also observe; how then could the eye ever be definitively established as "seeing"?
What Ānanda says—"I truly see with my eyes"—is to clearly grasp a delusion as truth. If one knows that a lamp merely manifests color, [one understands the distinction].

The ability to see belongs to the eye; once one is free from the delusion regarding the object, one further realizes that the eye merely manifests color, while the nature of seeing belongs to the mind.

Thus, one is also free from the delusion regarding the subject. When both subject and object are abandoned, there remains only this single mind. Since the mind transcends the eye, it is devoid of arising and ceasing.
With a vision that is neither arising nor ceasing, one beholds the hand of the Tathāgata; it is not that one has never seen it, yet it cannot be said to be "seen by the eye.
Long ago, when the Chan Master Zuoyuan of Kumu was attending upon Dahui at Yunmen Hermitage, he attained full realization while sitting in meditation at night upon seeing a monk trim a lamp.
He composed a verse which said: "To trim the lamp is fire; throughout kalpas..."
Ignorance was shattered by the light. Returning to the hall, he encountered the Holy Monk; he nearly let him slip past right before his eyes. What is it that did not slip away?
It was marvelous fifteen years ago, yet as before, it remains simply this very thing. Hui presented him with a verse, saying:
"Casting off the body at the edge of a ten-thousand-fathom cliff, rising up, one is once again clearly awake. When hungry, one eats; when thirsty..."

Drinking [the wine], one is entirely without affairs; what need is there to discuss whether one is a person of the past or not? Now, what does trimming the lamp have to do with the fundamental matter?
Thereupon, he attained awakening. As the World-Honored One said: "To see in this way is the eye, not the lamp. To see the nature in this way is the mind, not the eye.
Thus, the Patriarch Yuan said: "To trim the lamp is fire; it is like seeing through a wall."
Seeing the horns, one knows it must be an ox. One must attain such thorough realization before it can be called "seeing one's nature.
Although Ānanda and the great assembly had heard these words and their mouths were silent, their minds had not yet attained awakening.
Still hoping that the Tathāgata would proclaim his compassionate voice, they joined their palms with pure hearts and waited expectantly for the Buddha’s merciful instruction.

At that time, the World-Honored One extended his hand, which was marked by the webbed fingers like soft tūla-cotton, and opening his five wheel-like fingers, he exhorted Ānanda and the great assembly.

"When I first attained the Way, in the Deer Park, I spoke for the sake of Ājñāta-kauṇḍinya (which means 'One Who Understands the Meaning') and the other five bhikṣus, as well as you fourfold assembly, saying:
'All sentient beings fail to achieve the state of Bodhi and Arhat solely because they are deluded by adventitious afflictions.
By what means did you all then attain awakening and achieve the fruit of sainthood?"
Tong said: "The World-Honored One’s direct instruction was indeed too plain and clear. This is because Ānanda and the great assembly have not yet attained enlightenment;
the karmic conditions have not yet converged. Out of His compassion, the World-Honored One feared that if His words were too subtle and profound, they would be difficult to understand.
Nevertheless, among the bhikṣus there were some who did attain understanding, and through their understanding, others were led."
This is the explanation. Because this explanation is easy to enter, it causes the various bhikṣus to each recount the origins of their awakening, so that Ānanda may more easily find a point of entry.
Subsequently, the twenty-five [practitioners] of Perfect Penetration each recounted what they had realized; they likewise employed this same pedagogical device.
However, while this [section] clarifies only delusion, the subsequent section realizes the Truth; thus, there is no lack of difference in terms of depth and shallowness. As for this...
The expedient means of guiding and introducing others is but one and the same. What is called "not attaining bodhi" is entirely due to being misled by adventitious afflictions;
this is precisely the news regarding the two fundamental [roots]. Even awakening is not easy.
A monk asked National Teacher Nanyang Zhong, "Which one is the Buddha? The Master said, "This very mind is the Buddha. [The monk] said, "But the mind has afflictions..."

[The questioner] asked, "Is there affliction? The Master said, "The nature of affliction is itself detached. [The questioner] asked, "Is it not then severed? The Master said, "One who severs afflictions is called a follower of the Two Vehicles.
That afflictions do not arise is called Great Nirvana. [The questioner] asked, "Regarding sitting meditation and observing stillness, how should one proceed with this?
The Master said, "It is neither defiled nor pure; why should you give rise to a mind to observe the mark of stillness? Furthermore, [he said]: "Above..."

The *Sheng jing* (Sūtra on Birth) states: "Without cultivating meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and without severing afflictions (*kleśa*), the Buddha prophesied that this person will undoubtedly attain Buddhahood.
The scholar Chen Xiuyu once asked Wansong: "For what reason does Maitreya Bodhisattva not cultivate meditative concentration and not sever afflictions?
Wansong replied: "Because the true mind is fundamentally quiescent, he does not cultivate meditative concentration; because delusive thoughts..."
"Fundamentally empty; therefore, one does not sever afflictions. The gentleman again questioned Master Xiangshan Duren.

Xiangshan said, "The mind of Chan is already settled; there is no need for further cultivation. Afflictions have been completely exhausted; there is no need for further severing. He asked Master Haichuanchen of Zhulin again.
Haichuan said, "Fundamentally, there is neither Chan-concentration nor afflictions. The gentleman said, "Only this is truly refreshing! At that—
Only upon attaining this faith can one truly know that the teachings revealed at the Deer Park were intended solely for those of initial capacity.

At that time, Kauṇḍinya (which means "Fire-Implement" in Chinese), who had stood up and addressed the Buddha, said: "I am now the elder among this great assembly, and it is I alone who has earned the name 'The Liberated.
It was by realizing the two characters 'guest' and 'dust' that I achieved the fruit of enlightenment. World-Honored One, it is like a traveler who takes lodging in an inn."

Whether staying overnight or eating a meal, once the tasks of lodging and dining are finished, one packs for the road ahead and finds no leisure to remain. If one were truly a host, there would be no reason to depart.
Reflecting thus, "not abiding" is called a guest, while "abiding" is called a host; it is because of this non-abiding that [the Bodhisattva] does not abide.

This is what is meant by the meaning of "guest. Furthermore, it is like after a fresh clearing when the bright sun rises in the sky; as its light enters through a crack in a wall, it reveals the various signs of dust within the void.
The substance of the dust wavers and moves, yet empty space remains utterly still. Reflecting in this way, that which is limpid and tranquil is called "space" (ākāśa).
"Shaking" is termed "dust" (*rajas*). That which shakes is given the meaning of "dust.
The Buddha said, "It is so. [The interlocutor] replied: "The metaphor of the 'guest' illustrates the coarseness of the known; the metaphor of 'dust' illustrates the subtlety of afflictions (*kleśa*).

Moment by moment they shift and flow, arising and ceasing without rest. Therefore, it is likened to a traveler who stays at an inn: giving rise to delusions and creating karma, abandoning the old and rushing toward the new."

Therefore, it is likened to having finished a meal and preparing for the journey ahead; yet true nature is eternally abiding and has never been subject to such conditions, which is why it is compared to the host who remains where he is.
Gross obstructions are easily dispelled, but subtle delusions are difficult to clarify.

Only when the sky of the nature-mind is clear and cloudless and the sun of wisdom radiates its light can one seize the opening within the five aggregates to illuminate the emptiness of the fundamental nature, thereby awakening to the delusions therein.
It is because of self-disturbance that it is likened to sunlight entering through a crack in a wall after a fresh clearing of rain, thereby revealing the appearance of dust within the air.
While afflictions cause disturbance, the true nature is quiescent. If one awakens to its fundamental emptiness and remains eternally unmoving, one will know the quiescent and constant mind-nature.
Zhaozhou said: "From the moment you first saw me, you have never been anything other than this."
A person is simply this very host. Why seek this elsewhere? At this very moment, do not turn your head or change your mind;
if you turn your head or change your mind, you will lose it.
Furthermore, one day while sweeping the ground, a monk asked, "The Master is a great *kalyāṇamitra*; why are you sweeping? Zhuzhou said, "Dust comes from..."
A monk asked, "Since this is a pure monastery (*śuddha-ārāma*), why is there dust? Zhaozhou said, "There is not even a single speck.
Zhaozhou’s eye-light pierces through the four worlds; his discernment of the meaning of adventitious dust (*āgantuka-rajas*) analyzes it down to the finest hair of autumn.
If one can discern this, they are truly a śrāmaṇera with a master; dwelling in the dust without being stained, how could they not alone attain the name of "liberation"?
At that moment, the Tathāgata, in the midst of the great assembly, bent his five fingers, having bent them he opened them again, and having opened them he bent them once more.
He said to Ānanda, "What do you see now? Ānanda replied, "I see the Tathāgata’s palms, adorned with the hundred jewels, opening and closing amidst the assembly.
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "Regarding what you see as my hands opening and closing amidst the assembly:
is it that my hands themselves open and close, or is it that your vision itself opens and closes? Ānanda replied, "World-Honored One, it is the precious hands amidst the assembly..."
[The Buddha] opened and closed [his hand]. Ānanda saw the Tathāgata’s hand opening and closing, yet he did not see that the nature of his own vision had any opening or closing.
The Buddha asked, "What moves, and what is still? Ānanda replied, "The Buddha’s hand does not remain still, but as for my nature of vision, it is not even still;
what, then, could be said to be 'not remaining'? The Buddha said, "It is so."
Tong said: "Kauṇḍinya attained awakening through the two characters 'guest' and 'dust,' yet he only understood matters pertaining to the side of affliction (*kleśa*).
The World-Honored One, however, pointed directly to Bodhi to instruct him. First, by means of external objects, he distinguished true nature;
objects have opening and closing, while seeing is without movement or stillness—this is what people easily understand. The World-Honored One, because it was easy for him to understand..."
As he led him [to look], Ānanda indeed saw his own hand opening and closing, yet saw no such movement in the mirror.
Thus, my faculty of seeing is not even subject to stillness; who then could be said to dwell? Seeking the characteristics of motion and stillness, they are utterly unobtainable.
This brings us close to beholding the eternally abiding Lord. Were it not for the wondrous reminder of the World-Honored One, how could this have been possible? In the past—
Xitang asked Baizhang, "How will you instruct others in the future? Baizhang rolled and unrolled his hand twice. Xitang said, "And how else?
Baizhang pointed with his finger and nodded his head three times. Now, tell me:
was Baizhang’s such activity in accord with the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*’s sharp wit, or is there some other principle at work? Furthermore—
When Master Jueyi first resided at his hermitage, there was a nun named Shiji who came to the hut and entered directly without removing her sunshade.
Carrying her staff, she walked three times around the meditation seat and said, "If you can speak the Way, I shall remove my sunshade.
She asked this three times, but Jueyi had no reply. The nun then departed. Jueyi said, "The weather is about to grow dark; please stay for one night."
The nun said, "If you can speak [the Way], you may stay the night. Zhi had no reply, so the nun departed.

Zhi sighed and said, "Though I possess the form of a man, I lack the spirit of a man. He then resolved with indignation to clarify this matter, intending to leave his hermitage to travel to various regions to seek instruction.
That night, a mountain deity told him, "There is no need to leave this place. Tomorrow there will be..."
A flesh-and-blood Bodhisattva arrived and preached the Dharma for the Upādhyāya. The following day, Tiānlóng came to the hermitage;
Zhī then welcomed him with prostrations and related the previous events in detail. Tiānlóng simply raised one finger to show him. Zhī suddenly attained great enlightenment.
Thereafter, whenever anyone questioned him, he would only raise one finger. When the time came for his passing, he said to the assembly: "I have attained..."
"The Zen of a single finger-tip of Tianlong has been used without exhaustion throughout his life.
Do you wish to understand? He raised his finger and then passed away. Tiantong’s verse says: "The Zen of Old Man Juzhi on his finger-tip Has not been exhausted for twenty years.
Truly there exists a transcendent art of the Way-man; Before one's eyes, there is nothing of the mundane to be seen. What he attained was exceedingly simple."
The provision [of the teaching] is exceedingly vast; the ocean of the great trichiliocosm is drunk from the tip of a single hair. Infinite numbers of *qilin* and dragons fall into whose hands?
Reverently, Master Ren grasps the fishing rod. Xuedou’s verse says: Facing the profound love of old Jushi, Since the universe became empty, who else could there be?
Once he cast a floating log into the vast blue sea, Where the night waves together received the blind turtle.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* says: "It is like a one-eyed turtle that happens upon the hole of a floating log; it has no fear of drowning.

From the time the World-Honored One first snapped his fingers, everything he did was none other than revealing the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, enabling people to attain a place of peace and security.
What, then, is not for the sake of the blind turtle?
Thereupon, the Tathāgata emitted a single jewel-light from the wheel-mark on his palm, which hovered to Ānanda’s right;
immediately, Ānanda turned his head to look to the right. He then emitted another light to Ānanda’s left, and Ānanda likewise turned his head to look to the left.
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "For what reason does your head shake today?
Ānanda replied, "I saw the Tathāgata emit wondrous precious light that came to my left and right; therefore, as I looked to the left and right, my head moved of its own accord.

"Ānanda, when you gaze at the Buddha’s light and move your head to the left and right, is it your head that moves, or is it the vision that moves? "World-Honored One, it is my head that moves," [he replied].
"I see that the nature of seeing itself does not even have a place to rest; who could cause it to shake? The Buddha said, "It is so.
Tong said, "This uses the internal body to discern the true nature: while the head shakes of its own accord, the seeing remains unmoved.
Compared to the previous instance where the hands opened and closed, the seeing remained unmoved; this is even more subtle and profound. Within the single body of one person, the seeing—"
When it moves, the head moves. How can you say that the head moves by itself while seeing does not? That which follows the head in moving left and right is emotional perception (*qing-jian*);
that which does not follow the head in its movement or stillness is true seeing (*zhen-jian*). Emotional perception belongs to consciousness (*shi*).
Therefore, there is arising and ceasing. True seeing is the nature of the faculty; fundamentally, it is without activity or cessation. How may this be verified?

The head has movement and stillness that can be perceived, yet seeing itself has no movement or stillness that can be pointed out. Thus one knows that that which has no movement or stillness to be pointed out is called true seeing.
Ānanda, previously you took consciousness to be the mind and regarded only the cognitive perception as seeing. Now, having received [the teaching from] the Tathāgata...
I have come to provide this expedient instruction. When the light of wisdom momentarily appears, you will find that your head shakes of its own accord;

yet, upon looking, you see nothing moving. This seeing-nature is unmoving whether it is thus in motion or thus at rest. When seeing, it does not become existent; when not seeing, it does not become non-existent.
Since there is not even anything to cease, who is there to shake? This is the true essence of detachment from dust, empty and quiescent. A.
It is here that one comes to know the nature [of seeing]. Since it has already been said that one knows the nature, why are there still these various and manifold doubts?
It is because Ānanda, following the Buddha’s initial turning of his fingers and subsequent emission of light, observed the opening and closing of the hand and the shaking of the head;

yet he saw that neither the hand nor the head moved, and he concluded that the same was true for this seeing. This is what is called knowledge derived from inference, rather than direct [realization].

How wondrous is this awakening! Those who enter by way of the gate do not possess the family treasure; at this point, one gains even greater conviction. When Chan Master Wuye first met Mazu, he asked:
"I have roughly exhausted the essential meanings of the literature of the Three Vehicles.

I have often heard that in the Chan gate, 'the very mind is Buddha,' yet I truly have not yet understood this. Mazu said: "It is precisely this very mind that you have not yet understood; there is nothing else besides it."
Another person asked, "What is the mind-seal that the Patriarch secretly transmitted when he came from the West? The Patriarch said, "Virtuous one, you are in the midst of a great commotion;
go now and come back at another time. As soon as the man had stepped out, the Patriarch called out, "Virtuous one! The man turned his head. The Patriarch said, "This is it."
The Patriarch asked, "What is it? At these words, Yè attained realization and prostrated himself. The Patriarch said, "You dull-witted fellow, why do you prostrate?
Furthermore, there was the Zen Master Wuxie Lingmo, who traveled far to visit Shítóu. He immediately asked, "If a single word accords with me, I shall stay;
if it does not accord, I shall leave. Shítóu remained seated as usual. Wuxie was about to depart when Shítóu called out after him, "Dashi! (Venerable One).
Wuye said, "Liyi, turn your head back! From birth until death, it is simply this very thing. Why do you turn your head and look back?
At these words, Liyi attained great enlightenment; he then broke his staff and settled there to dwell. Now tell me:
when Wuye and Liyi turned their heads and looked back, they were thus enlightened—how does this compare to Ānanda?
Thereupon, the Tathāgata addressed the great assembly:

"If there are sentient beings who consider that which is moving to be 'dust' and that which does not abide to be a 'guest,' then you, Ānanda, observe this: while your head moves, your vision remains unmoving."
Furthermore, observe my hand as it opens and closes; you see no actual stretching or rolling up. Why, then, do you now take motion to be the body and motion to be the object?
From beginning to end, moment by moment, things arise and perish; thus you have lost the true nature and act in a state of delusion.
The fundamental mind has lost its true nature; by identifying external objects as oneself, one wanders in saṃsāra, taking this cycle upon oneself.

It is said in general: "The Buddha’s hand does not remain still, yet the seeing-nature is eternally abiding. This is the true master. "The head moves of its own accord, yet the seeing-nature is unmoving.
This is the essence of true emptiness. Now, instead of recognizing the master, you recognize the guest; instead of recognizing emptiness, you recognize...

Dust! Is this not acting in a state of inversion? It is truly because of the arising and ceasing of every thought-moment and the continuous succession of afflictions that one loses the true nature and fails to achieve Bodhi.
To be so utterly misled by adventitious dust reaches such a point. The *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* says:

"One falsely identifies the four elements as the characteristic of one's own body, and the shadows of the conditions of the six sense-objects as the characteristic of one's own mind. This is precisely what [is meant].
This refers to those who take movement as their body and movement as their environment, identifying external objects as themselves.

Having identified with and pursued these objects through deluded movement, they mistake this for their own mind; thus, they fail to recognize the unmoving true mind and remain lost within the flux of change.

Therefore, it is said that [the nature] is "lost. This does not mean that it has been lost and no longer exists; rather, it is like water that has already turned into ice—the nature of water is then lost.
As previously stated, the capacity to give rise to various conditions means that what is lost through those conditions is this fundamental luminosity (*mūla-prakāśa*).

Although one acts all day long, one is unaware of it and mistakenly enters the various realms of existence (*gati*). If this is so, by what means can one escape from birth and death (*saṃsāra*)? Therefore—
It is said: "Within this cycle of saṃsāra, one takes up rebirth for oneself.

What was previously stated—that all sentient beings have, since beginningless time, experienced the continuous succession of birth and death because they do not know the eternally abiding true mind, the essence of pure and luminous nature, yet employ various false thoughts;
and because these thoughts are not real, there is cyclic wandering—refers precisely to this. Formerly, Dongshan asked a monk his name.
"What is it? he asked. The monk replied, "It is I. The Master said, "Which one is your host, O Venerable One?
The monk replied, "The one who is currently responding to you. The Master said, "Alas, alas! People of the present age are all like this;
they recognize only that which precedes the donkey or follows the horse as being themselves. That the Buddha-dharma has sunk into oblivion is due to this very thing. Guest.
"The central host has not yet been distinguished; how can one discern the 'host of the host'? The monks then asked, "What is the host of the host?
The Mountain Master said, "Disciples, you should speak for yourselves. They replied, "If I were to speak of it, that would merely be the 'host among guests.
What then is the 'host of the host'? The Mountain Master said, "To speak thus is easy; to maintain continuity is another matter entirely."
He then presented this verse: "Alas! Behold the practitioners of the Way in these times; By the thousands and tens of thousands, they recognize only the gateway.
It is just like entering the capital to pay court to the Holy Sovereign, Yet stopping as soon as one reaches the Tongguan Pass.

Viewed from this perspective, the discriminating consciousnesses of the intellect, compared to the unmoving essence of seeing, are still separated by many stages; yet even the unmoving essence of seeing, when compared to the quiescent and eternal [nature], is still far removed.
The true nature inherently possesses its own discernment. As the subsequent text states: "Even seeing is transcended by seeing; seeing cannot reach it.
This is as if one has already crossed the Tongguan Pass to behold the Sage Ruler.
The Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause and Realization of the Tathāgata’s Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa, and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas, Volume Two.
At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly, having heard the Buddha’s instructions, felt their bodies and minds become tranquil. They reflected upon their beginningless past.

Having lost my original mind, I falsely identified with the shadows of discrimination arising from conditioned objects. Today, I have attained awakening, like a child who has lost its mother suddenly encountering her again.
With palms joined, I prostrate before the Buddha, wishing to hear the Tathāgata reveal the truth and falsehood, the reality and unreality of body and mind.
The two aspects of manifesting and arising-ceasing versus non-arising and non-ceasing both reveal the nature.

[Ananda] said in general: "Previously, you spoke of 'the seeing being unmoving' and 'the seeing having no expanding or contracting'; this has already clearly pointed out the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing.
Yet, this nature of non-arising and non-ceasing is present within the body of arising and ceasing; it truly reveals the nature."

The very source of non-arising and non-ceasing is the root of deluded manifestation of the nature; it is the root of arising and ceasing. Within this, the void and the real are difficult to distinguish;
therefore, I pray that the Tathāgata will reveal this for us. Formerly, Xie Jian asked the Sixth Patriarch:

"The virtuous practitioners of meditation in the capital all say that if one wishes to realize the Way, one must practice seated meditation and cultivate samādhi. If one does not rely on meditation..."
"There has never been anyone who attained liberation through meditative concentration alone. I do not yet understand the nature of the Dharma you, Master, have taught.
The Patriarch said, "The Way is realized through the awakening of the mind; how could it depend on sitting? As the Sūtra says: 'If one says that the Tathāgata sits or lies down...'"

This is practicing a deviant path. Why? Because there is nowhere from which it comes and nowhere to which it goes; it is without arising and without cessation. This is the Tathāgata’s pure meditation.
All phenomena are empty and quiescent; this is the Tathāgata’s pure sitting. Ultimately, there is nothing to be realized.
"How much more so for sitting? Jian said, "Light is a metaphor for wisdom; darkness is a metaphor for afflictions (*kleśa*).
If one does not use wisdom to illuminate and shatter afflictions, by what means can one escape from beginningless birth and death? The Patriarch said, "Afflictions are themselves bodhi;
they are non-dual and without distinction. To use wisdom to illuminate and shatter afflictions is the view of the Two Vehicles."
Those of the capacities of the sheep and the deer, as well as those of superior wisdom and great roots, are not like this at all.

Jian asked, "What is the insight and understanding of the Mahāyāna? The Patriarch said, "Luminosity and ignorance—ordinary people see these as two. The wise, however, thoroughly realize that their nature is non-dual.
This non-dual nature is the true nature. As for the true nature, it does not cease while dwelling among the foolish and ordinary. It remains...

It is sagely and holy yet does not increase; it exists within afflictions yet is not disturbed; it dwells in meditative concentration yet is not quiescent. It is neither annihilated nor eternal; it neither comes nor goes;
it is not in between, nor is it inside or outside. It is neither born nor extinguished; its nature and characteristics are suchness (*tathatā*).
Constantly abiding and never shifting—this is called the Way (*mārga*). Jian said: "The Master speaks of neither birth nor extinction."

"How does this differ from the non-Buddhists? The Patriarch said, "What the non-Buddhists call 'neither arising nor ceasing' means they use cessation to stop arising, and use arising to manifest cessation;
yet their cessation is not truly ceased, and their arising is called non-arising. As for what I call 'neither arising nor ceasing': [it is not so]."
Originally unborn, it is likewise unextinguished now; thus it differs from the non-Buddhist paths.

Ānanda immediately rose from his seat, prostrated before the Buddha with palms joined, and knelt on one knee to address the Buddha:

"World-Honored One, if this seeing and hearing are necessarily neither produced nor extinguished, why does the World-Honored One say that we have lost our true nature and act in a state of perversion?"

"I pray that you will arouse compassion and wash away my defilements. At that moment, the Tathāgata extended his golden arm and pointed downward with his wheel-marked hand, showing Ānanda and saying, "Do you now see my *mudrā-hasta* (this is translated as 'the hand of seals')?
Is it upright or inverted? Ānanda replied, "In the world, sentient beings consider this to be inverted; yet I do not know which is upright and which is inverted. The Buddha said to Ānanda:
[Ananda] replied, "It is difficult. If worldly people consider this to be inverted, then what do worldly people take to be upright?
Ananda said, "If the Tathāgata were to raise his arm—his hand being like *tūla* cotton (which is called the 'webbed-mark')—and point it upward toward the sky, that would be called upright.
The Buddha then raised his arm and told Ananda, "If this inversion were to exchange its head and tail, worldly people would [regard it as] twice as upright."
Upon observation, you will know that your body and the pure *dharmakāya* of all Tathāgatas are revealed through comparison.
The body of a Tathāgata is called "Right Universal Knowledge" (*samyaksaṃbuddha*), whereas your bodies are termed "inverted by nature.
As you examine them closely, where in your body or the Buddha’s body can the name "inversion" be found? What is it that is designated as inverted?
The Master said: "The pure Dharma-body is precisely the wondrous, luminous, true essence—the wondrous mind.
Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are the objects manifested within that wondrous mind. To return to the root is correct; to pursue the branches is inverted.
It is like bubbles arising from the sea: to recognize the sea as correct and to recognize the bubbles as inverted. The Buddha asked Ānanda: 'Do you now see me?'"
Whether hanging down the hand is considered upright or inverted depends entirely on one's own point of view; one should vigorously examine for oneself who is upright and who is inverted.

One ought not to distinguish between upright and inverted upon the hand of the Tathāgata. When Subhūti sat in meditative seclusion within his cave and beheld the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata, he did so without relying on the faculties or consciousnesses;
this is called "Right Universal Knowledge. As for Ānanda, with his eyes facing [the Buddha]...
The Tathāgata’s hand was further divided on the palm, both upright and inverted. This is the functioning of the six consciousnesses;
turning one's back on the source to pursue the branches, one has already departed from the state of correctness, and is therefore called "inverted by nature.
At first, Ānanda took the hanging hand to be inverted, his words still vague; when asked what should be considered correct, he then took the upraised arm to be correct. Thereafter—
To understand what Ānanda calls "correct" and "inverted," one must discern it upon the hand, not upon the act of seeing.
His gazing has already become inverted. When the hand hangs down, the head and tail follow their natural order; this is inherently correct, yet worldly people consider it inverted.
When the arm is raised, the head and tail are exchanged; this is inherently inverted, yet worldly people consider it [correct].
This is indeed a doubling of the inversion within the inversion of viewing.
Therefore, by way of analogy, it is revealed that to lose sight of the pure *dharmakāya* and instead identify with seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing is already an inversion.

Furthermore, to insist that the seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing within the physical body (*rūpakāya*) must be subject to neither birth nor cessation, claiming this to be correct and not inverted, is likewise an error.
Is this not even more doubled over than inversion? A monk asked Dongshan, "You usually teach students to practice the 'Bird Path.
I do not know what this Bird Path is. Dongshan said, "Not meeting a single person. The monk asked, "How does one walk it?
Dongshan said, "You must simply proceed with no self-interest beneath your feet. The monk asked, "As for walking the Bird Path, is that not just one's original nature?"
"Is it your face? Shanshan asked. The monk said, "Why is it that you, O Ācārya, are so inverted? Shanshan asked, "In what way are you inverted?
The monk said, "If I am not inverted, why do you instead take a servant for the master? Shanshan asked, "What is your original face?
Shanshan said, "Do not walk the path of birds. Dana wrote a verse: "The ancient road stands desolate and leaning..."
The Great Void: practicing the profound is still traversing rugged terrain. Though ascending the Bird Path may be considered subtle, upon close examination, one has already encountered the Way.
Now, the Bird Path is profound and subtle; it is hoped that through the transformation of function, one will attain the station. This is the teaching under Dongshan’s gate.
If one still regards this as inverted, how much more so when one’s perceptions and hearing are vivid and clear, yet coarse traces still remain—
how could such a state be considered non-arising and non-ceasing, or sufficient to correspond to unsurpassed bodhi?

At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly gazed fixedly at the Buddha with unblinking eyes; they were so transfixed that they did not know where their own bodies and minds were, nor the location of their inverted perceptions.
The Buddha, giving rise to compassion and pitying Ānanda and the great assembly, uttered a voice like the tide of the ocean.
(At that time, speaking to suit this capacity and bestowing this Dharma,) he addressed the entire assembly:
"Good sons, I have always said that all conditions of form and mind, as well as the mental factors and all objects of perception, are manifested solely by the mind.

Your bodies and your minds are all things manifested within the wondrously luminous, true essence of the wondrous mind. Why, then, do you lose sight of your original wondrousness, your perfect wondrousness, and your luminosity?"

The luminous and wondrous nature of the mind-treasure recognizes awakening yet falls into delusion; it becomes obscured and darkened, forming emptiness. Within this darkness of emptiness, the accumulation of obscurity forms matter.

Matter mingles with false conceptualization, and these conceptual appearances form the body. As the gathering of conditions causes internal agitation, one rushes outward in pursuit of external objects.

This state of confused turmoil is taken to be the nature of the mind. Once deluded, one takes this as the mind and becomes firmly convinced that it resides within the physical body, failing to realize the true nature of matter.
"From the body outward, including the mountains, rivers, space, and the great earth—all are objects within the wondrously luminous true mind.
[The Master] said in general: "Your body is the *nimitta-bhāga* (the objective aspect), and your mind is the *darśana-bhāga* (the subjective aspect).

The *nimitta-bhāga* encompasses the sense organs, their objects, and all phenomena that serve as conditions, such as the mountains, rivers, the great earth, light, darkness, form, and space. The *darśana-bhāga* encompasses the eight consciousnesses and..."
The fifty-one mental factors (*caitta*), wholesome and unwholesome karmic actions, and the causes and effects of the heterodox and the orthodox—all these flow forth from within the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Therefore, it is said that they are "manifested solely by the mind. This mind is fundamentally wondrous; it does not depend upon cultivation.
How is its fundamental wondrousness to be seen? If one speaks of its essence, it is the perfectly wondrous and luminous mind. From—

It wondrously gives rise to clarity; therefore, it is called "perfect" (*yuan*). Speaking of its function, it is the wondrous nature of precious clarity. Because it is clarity that is wondrous, it is called "precious" (*bao*).
Being wondrous yet clear, and clear yet wondrous, it is entirely free from defilement; this is what is known as the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*).

All aspects of the subjective seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) and the objective perceived-division (*nimitta-bhāga*) are merely reflections manifested within the mirror. This is the extant manuscript.
To recognize seeing and hearing within the wondrous is like discarding the original mirror to recognize a phantom image; though it may seem there is awakening, in reality one is still deluded.
Thus it is said, "delusion within awakening. To take this recognition of delusion within awakening as the nature of the mind—this should be read as a single phrase continuing downward.
Because the wondrous luminosity of the nature of delusion becomes ignorance (*avidyā*), and through this ignorance it transforms into stubborn emptiness (*jaḍa-śūnyatā*). Therefore...

It is said that the state of obscurity and darkness constitutes emptiness (*ākāśa*). This transformed, stubborn emptiness and the transforming ignorance (*avidyā*)—these two dharmas combine to transform and give rise to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), which constitute the external matter of the "retributive environment" (*niśraya-vipāka*).

With these material forms of the four great elements mixed with the mind of deluded thought, they transform and give rise to the internal matter of the "primary retribution" (*mukhya-vipāka*) of sentient beings.
"Roots" refer to deluded thought; "characteristics" refer to deluded matter. Thought and characteristics constitute the body; seeing and characteristics [constitute the faculties].

The two aspects being fully present refers to the eight consciousnesses. "Gathering conditions and churning within" refers to the seventh consciousness. "Rushing outward and fleeing away" refers to the six consciousnesses.
By means of this ignorance, one gives rise to various false conditions that engage with sense objects;
amidst this state of turbid agitation, one mistakenly identifies these as one's own mind—how deluded this is! That wondrously luminous true mind is none other than the pure *dharmakāya*.
Vertically it exhausts the three periods of time; horizontally it spans the ten directions. How could it be confined within the physical body?
Although such seeing and hearing are neither born nor extinguished, they do not exist apart from the eyes for seeing, nor apart from the ears for hearing.

To take this as the mind is certainly to be deluded into thinking it resides within the physical body. One does not realize that outside this physical body—extending even to the mountains, rivers, and the great earth—it is all...
These are objects within the wondrously luminous true mind, like images appearing in layers, all of which are objects within a mirror.

Therefore, to identify with the mirror is "awakening within awakening," termed "Perfect Universal Knowledge" (Samyak-saṃbuddha). To identify with the images is "delusion within awakening," termed "perversion of nature."

Before the light has emerged, there is not even a trace of Buddha or sentient beings;
from where could these mountains, rivers, and lands have come? At that time, a monk asked, "What is the eye of the śramaṇa? The Master said, "It protrudes long and long."
"No. He spoke again: "Whether one becomes a Buddha or a patriarch, one cannot escape it; whether one transmigrates through the six realms of existence, one cannot escape it.
The monk asked, "I do not understand what it is that cannot be escaped. The Shanzhao said, "By day one sees the sun; by night one sees the stars. The monk said, "I, this student, do not understand.
The Shanzhao said, "The colors of Mount Sumeru are green and ever more green. Now tell me, to what does Changsha’s statement point?
The "essence of consciousness" (vijñāna-śukra) is fundamentally luminous; this refers to the wondrous nature of precious clarity. Try to discern and examine it clearly:
it is like casting aside a hundred thousand vast oceans of clear water and instead identifying the substance of a single floating bubble as the entirety of the tide.
To exhaust the vastness of the ocean—such people as you are doubly lost within delusion. It is no different from my hanging down my hand;
the Tathāgata calls such people objects of compassion.
Tong said: "To know that the perception of the river is necessarily subject to arising and ceasing seems to belong to awakening.
However, to cling to the perception of the river as being within the physical body is delusion within awakening. It is like abandoning the ocean to identify with a bubble; one is already deluded.
To then cling to the bubble while denying the ocean—is this not the delusion of delusions? To neglect the true nature and instead identify with seeing and hearing."
You are already deluded; yet you further cling to seeing and hearing as being of a nature that neither arises nor perishes—is this not a delusion upon delusion?

To be deluded through a lack of awakening is merely a single instance of delusion. To be deluded despite having awakened is for the attachments of one's emotions to deepen; is this not twice as grave as delusion?
When I hang down my hand and you perceive it with discrimination, you have already fallen into inversion; to then proceed to confuse head and tail...
To exchange [the correct for the inverted] is already a profound error; is this not doubly as grave as mere inversion?
To be already within the midst of inversion and yet ask, "What is meant by 'acting with inverted conduct'?"—this is inversion upon inversion, delusion within delusion.
