Therefore it is said, "The person who is doubly deluded. The two instances of the character "double" (bei) correspond to one another. —Written by Qinguo of Jingshan.
The Master was sitting in the inner court together with National Teacher Zhong when he saw the Emperor’s carriage approaching.
The Master rose to his feet. The Emperor asked, "Why have you risen? The Master replied, "How can you, O Donor, perceive this poor monk within the four modes of deportment?
The Emperor was pleased. Furthermore, Suzong asked National Teacher Zhong, "What Dharma did you obtain at Caoxi? The Master replied, "Your Majesty, have you..."
"Do you see that single cloud in the sky? The Emperor said, "I see it. The Master said, "Nail it down! Hang it up!
The Emperor asked again, "What is the 'Tamer of the Ten Bodies'? The Master stood up and said, "Do you understand? The Emperor said, "I do not understand.
The Master said, "Hand me the pure water pitcher. The Emperor asked again, "What is 'Non-contention'?"
Samādhi. The Master said, "Donor, you are walking atop the crown of Lulu. The Emperor asked, "What is the meaning of this?
The Master replied, "Do not mistake it for your own pure Dharma-body. The Emperor asked again; the Master did not look at him. The Emperor said:
"I am the Son of Heaven of the Great Tang," [the Emperor said]. "Why do you not deign to look at me? The Master replied, "Do you see empty space? The Emperor said, "I see it.
The Master asked, "Does it blink its eyes and look at Your Majesty? Observing the instructions given by these two masters, [one sees their profound intent].
First, it is because you cannot perceive this poor monk within the four modes of deportment; second, does empty space ever blink its eyes to look upon Your Majesty?
When has it ever been deluded as being within the physical body? This seeing is like the vision of the river at the edge of a cliff.
Heaven and earth are vastly different; yet when one perceives the Buddha’s Dharma-body with Subhūti, they are both given the same name: Samyaksaṃbuddha (the Truly and Fully Enlightened One).
Generally speaking, cognition is based on thought (*manas*), yet the mind (*citta*) is not all-pervasive. As Aśvaghoṣa said: "If the mind is stirred, it is not true cognition.
That which is characterized by movement is the obstruction of thought. When one is free from all obstructions of thought, such that cognition is all-pervasive.
Ānanda, having received the Buddha’s compassionate salvation and profound instruction, wept and joined his palms, addressing the Buddha:

“Although I have received such wondrous sounds from the Buddha and awakened to the wondrously luminous mind—the originally perfect and eternally abiding ground of the heart—I nevertheless perceive the Buddha’s current preaching of the Dharma with my conditioned mind, looking up at him with devotion.
I have merely attained this mind, yet I do not yet dare to recognize it as such.”
"This is the fundamental ground of the mind. I pray that the Buddha, out of compassion, will proclaim the perfect sound to uproot my doubts and lead me back to the Unsurpassed Way.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "You and the others still listen to the Dharma with a conditioned mind; this Dharma is also a condition, and you have not yet attained the nature of reality (dharmatā)."
It is like a person pointing at the moon with their finger to show it to another. That person, because of the finger, ought to look at the moon.
If they instead gaze at the finger and take it to be the substance of the moon, would this person not only lose sight of the lunar orb, but also lose the finger itself?

Why is this? Because they have taken the pointing finger to be the bright moon. Not only do they lose the finger, but they also fail to distinguish between light and darkness. How much more so [if they reject the teaching]?

For this reason, the substance of the finger itself is taken as the nature of the moon’s brightness. Since the two natures of light and darkness cannot be discerned [as distinct], you are likewise so.
Ānanda then said in general: "I have realized that the wondrously luminous mind is fundamentally perfect and complete; it is not originally dependent on conditions. It is the eternally abiding mind."
The ground is originally the master. Yet now, as you gaze upon the Buddha and listen to the Dharma, you still belong to the mind of conditions.
You do not yet know the fundamental source of the mind-ground; by what means can it be recognized? Is it this very thing? Certainly not. Is it apart from this? Where then would it be?
The Buddha, intending to shatter the error of the conditioned mind, first reveals that which he has taught.
The Dharma is also a condition (*pratyaya*). Therefore, it is said that this Dharma is likewise a condition; it is not the attainment of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
The Dharma is established for the purpose of seeing the nature; once the nature is seen, the Dharma has no further use. The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says:

"As with the parable of the raft, even the Dharma should be relinquished, let alone what is non-Dharma. This is further illustrated by the parable of the finger pointing at the moon: once the moon is seen, one forgets the finger.
Ancient worthies have frequently used metaphors that accord with this. One says: "Within the shadows of multicolored clouds, an immortal appears;
holding a red silk fan, he covers his face. You must quickly turn your eyes to look at the immortal; do not look at the fan in the immortal’s hand.
Another says: "A single hare lies across the ancient road; as soon as the blue hawk sees it, he seizes it alive. Later...
Hunting dogs lack spiritual intelligence; they only search for old spots where withered stumps once stood.
This is the origin of the passage in Dongpo’s writings concerning a blind man asking what the sun looks like. When people showed him a copper basin, the blind man struck it and heard a sound;

later, upon hearing the tolling of a bell, he took it to be the sun. A monk asked Fayan, pointing— (Note: The provided text ends abruptly with "pointing," so the translation reflects the fragmentary nature of the source.)
He immediately did not ask. [Zhao]zhen asked, "What is the moon? Yuanzhen said, "Which one is that which you do not ask about?
Point it out. Another monk asked, "I do not ask about the moon; what is the finger? Yuanzhen said, "The moon. The monk said, "I am asking about the finger."
"Why does the Master point at the moon with his eye? he asked. [The Master] replied, "Because you asked about the finger.
If you can understand the house style of the Dharma-eye, then the moon pointed out will be clearly manifest in this very moment; otherwise, you will pass it by right before your own face."

If you consider this discriminating mind that perceives the sounds of my teaching as being your own mind, then this mind should inherently possess the nature of discrimination even apart from the sounds of discrimination.
It would be like a traveler staying overnight at an inn: having rested for a short while, he departs and never remains there permanently.
Yet the attendant at the pavilion has nowhere to go; he is called the "pavilion master. This is also like that:
if it were truly your mind, it would have nowhere to go.
[The Master] said in general: "That which manifests as the sound of the Dharma is the object of perception (*ālambana*). Since that which is the object of perception cannot be grasped as...
It is real. Discernment of the sounds of dharmas is that which is capable of cognition. Yet how can that which is capable of cognition be relied upon as true?
When the mind encounters sound, discernment is vivid and distinct; yet this discernment is merely temporary, like a guest.
When the mind and sound part, discernment completely vanishes, yet the nature of discernment does not vanish. This...
The nature does not exist because of listening to the Dharma, nor does it cease to exist because of not listening to the Dharma; therefore, it is called the "host.

Only when one perceives this can it be called "seeing the nature. If one clings to the mind that conditions the act of listening to the Dharma as one's own nature, this is like mistaking a guest for the host.
When Dadian first visited Shitou, Shitou asked him, "Which of these is your mind? Dadian—

Baizhang said, "The one who perceives speech—this is it. He then shouted at him and drove him out. Ten days later, Huangbo asked, "Since that previous one was not it, apart from this, what is the mind?
Baizhang said, "Setting aside raising eyebrows and blinking eyes, bring forth your mind.
Huangbo said, "There is no mind to be brought forth. Baizhang said, "Originally there is a mind; why do you say there is no mind? There is none."
Xinjin joined in the slander. Under these words, Baizhang Duan attained great enlightenment.

On another day, while standing in attendance, Xutang said, "Are you a monk who practices Chan, or are you a monk who merely tramples through the prefectures and counties? Duan replied, "I am a monk who practices Chan. Xutang asked, "What is Chan?
Duan said, "Raising an eyebrow and blinking an eye. Xutang said, "Setting aside raising an eyebrow and blinking an eye, what about you..."
He presented his original face. Mazu said, "Please, Master, set aside the mirror that reflects the raising of eyebrows and the twinkling of eyes.
Baizhang said, "I have already set it aside. Mazu said, "Then you have already presented it. Baizhang said, "Since you have already presented it, what is my mind like?
Mazu said, "It is no different from yours, Master. Baizhang said, "That is none of your business. Mazu said, "Originally there is nothing at all."
Shitou said, "You, too, have no thing. Dadian said, "Since there is no thing, that is the true thing. Shitou said, "The true thing cannot be obtained;
such is the intent of the scope of your mind's vision. You must protect and uphold this most carefully.
Through their repeated examination and testing, Shitou and his son sought only to verify that the true mind is fundamentally unobtainable; this is what is called the "True Lord."
What is the nature of non-discrimination apart from sound? This is not merely the discriminating mind regarding sound;

it is the non-discriminating nature that discriminates my own appearance while remaining detached from all forms and characteristics. In this way, up to the point where discrimination is entirely absent—neither form nor emptiness.
The Kauśalīyas (namely, those of the school of Maskarī Gośālīputra) take ignorance to be the ultimate truth (*tattva*).
Since it is devoid of the conditions of all phenomena and lacks a nature of discrimination, your own mental natures each have their respective places of return; how then can it be the master?

Tong said: "The two characters 'how' (yú hé) run directly through to the end, forming a single sentence with the phrase 'detached from the conditions of all dharmas, it is the nature of non-discrimination.
To discriminate sounds, and to discriminate the objects of form, fragrance, taste, and touch—these are all merely reflected images of the discriminations of external objects.
How can one be detached from these external objects so that there is no longer the nature of discrimination? Even if one were to extinguish everything..."
Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing—even up to conceptual discrimination—are entirely absent. Internally, one maintains a state of profound stillness that is neither form nor emptiness.

This, however, is the "dark principle" (tamas-tattva) clung to by non-Buddhists; it merely allows for the separation from objects, yet fails to separate from dharmas. It remains a shadowy phenomenon of conceptual discrimination regarding the dust of dharmas.
How could there be an absence of the nature of discrimination simply by separating from the conditions of all dharmas? [It arises] because of the sensory objects (*viṣaya*).

It exists when separated from the external objects (*viṣaya*), yet it ceases to exist once those objects are removed; it exists because of the mental objects (*dharmadhātu*), yet it ceases to exist once those mental objects are removed.
This nature of discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) thus possesses its own point of return. How can it be considered the master? One movement and one stillness both belong to the reflection;
the reflection has a point of return while the mirror has no point of return. One departure and one arrival both belong to the guest; the guest has a point of return, but the host [has none].

There is no returning. To fail to recognize the mirror and instead recognize the reflection, to fail to recognize the host and instead recognize the guest—then your mind-nature would be identical to annihilation.
What, then, could be called the eternally abiding true mind? When Master Dadian ascended the hall, he said: "O practitioners of the Way..."

You must recognize your own original mind. I see that many of the present generation merely take the raising of eyebrows, the twinkling of eyes, a single word, or a moment of silence as a sudden seal of approval, regarding these as the essence of the mind.
This is truly a failure to realize it. I shall now explain it clearly for you;
each of you must listen and receive it. Simply cast away all deluded thoughts and mental constructions, and the immediate manifestation of reality (*pratyakṣa*) is itself it.

The True Mind. This mind has no interaction whatsoever with sensory objects or even when one maintains silent stillness; it is the Buddha-mind itself, requiring no cultivation or refinement. Why is this?
It responds to conditions and reflects accordingly, functioning with a clear, limpid autonomy. Yet, when one exhaustively investigates the locus of this function, it is utterly ungraspable.
What is called "wondrous function" is precisely the original mind. One must guard and sustain it with great care; it must not be... [lost].
Easy. Dadian clearly pointed out the True Lord; he was far too candid. From this alone, one can know that it is vastly distinct from the *tattva* (principles) of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

Among the twenty-five *tattvas* of the non-Buddhists, with the exception of the *mūla-prakṛti* (the Root Nature), which is neither form, nor emptiness, nor mind, all others do not transcend form, mind, and emptiness.
The *buddhi-tattva* (Intellect Principle) is my own mind. The five organs of cognition... the five... [text fragment]
The organs of action, the organs of perception, and the *puruṣa* (the self) are all mind (*citta*). The five sense objects and the five great elements (*mahābhūta*) are all form (*rūpa*).
Among the five great elements, the element of space (*ākāśa*) is itself emptiness (*śūnyatā*). The first principle is called *prakṛti* (primordial nature);
it is reckoned as eternal. The twenty-fifth principle is called the *puruṣa*; it too is reckoned as eternal. Thus I contemplate the holy [truth].
The objective realm is the *avyakta* (the unmanifest primal nature), which transforms into the twenty-three principles (*tattvas*). These serve as objects for my use and enjoyment;
bound by these objects, one cannot attain liberation. If I do not contemplate, the *avyakta* does not transform, and thus there is no bondage;
I am then liberated. This is their fundamental tenet. It is like Gaozi’s principle: "If you do not succeed in speech, do not seek it in the mind. It is not...

One should seek it within the mind; do not seek it in the vital breath (*prāṇa*). It is a single, undifferentiated, profound state of truth (*tattva*), which some commentators point to as the Chan school (*Dhyāna*);
this is greatly incorrect.
Ānanda said: "If my mind-nature each has a place to which it returns, then why does the Tathāgata speak of the wondrously luminous, original mind?"
"Why is there no place to which it returns? I pray that you will deign to show compassion and explain this for me. The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Furthermore, consider my seeing—the fundamental source of the clarity of seeing. Although this seeing is not the wondrous, ultimate, and luminous mind, it is like a second moon;

it is not the reflection of the moon. You should listen attentively. I shall now show you the ground where there is nothing to return to. Ānanda, in this great lecture hall, the eastern [door] is wide open..."
When the sun rises in the sky, there is bright radiance; at midnight during the dark fortnight, when clouds and mist shroud the heavens, it is again dark and murky.
Through the gaps of doors and windows, one perceives openness; within the spaces between walls and buildings, one observes obstruction.

In places where distinctions are made, one perceives conditions; throughout the solid void, there is everywhere the nature of emptiness. When the appearance of dense dust and debris arises, it becomes turbid and obscured.
The dust settles and the mists clear. Observe this purity, Ānanda. You have all observed these various changing phenomena;
I shall now cause each to return to its original source. What is their original source? Ānanda, these various changes:
clarity returns to the sun. Why is this? Without the sun there would be no light; since clarity depends upon the sun, it therefore returns to the sun. Darkness returns to the dark moon.

What flows through returns to the doors and windows; what is obstructed returns to the walls and eaves; what is conditioned returns to discrimination; what is stubborn and void returns to emptiness; what is turbid and thick returns to dust;
what is clear and bright returns to a cloudless sky. Thus, all that exists within the world does not transcend these categories.

As for the eight kinds of seeing you perceive—the luminous nature of your seeing—whom would you have it return to? Why is this? If it were to return to light, then when there is no light, it would not exist.

Furthermore, you see darkness. Although there are various distinctions such as light and darkness, in your seeing there is no distinction. Those things which can be returned to their source are naturally not you;
that which cannot be returned to its source—if it is not you, then who is it? Thus you know that your mind is fundamentally wondrous, luminous, and pure.

It is you yourself who are deluded and distressed, losing your fundamental nature and undergoing the cycle of rebirth, constantly drifting and drowning within birth and death. For this reason, the Tathāgata names you...
"Be compassionate. He replied:
"The perception that discriminates based on sensory objects and the luminous essence of seeing are distinguished by the duality of subject and object.
The luminous essence of seeing and the wondrously luminous mind are distinguished by the division of substance and function. Therefore, the wondrously luminous mind is like..."
True Moon: The clarity of seeing is the fundamental source, yet it is like a second moon; the discrimination based on objects is like the reflection of the moon in water.
Regarding the eight aspects of brightness, darkness, penetration, and obstruction: within the midst of the great void, these comings and goings exist;

therefore, it is said they do not transcend this category. This also roughly corresponds to the Eight Trigrams (*bagua*): when turbid dust is purified, the images of Heaven (*qian*) and Earth (*kun*) appear.
Furthermore, the sun’s brightness and the moon’s darkness represent the images of *kan* (Water) and *li* (Fire). Penetration and obstruction represent the images of *gen* (Mountain) and *zai* (Lake).

Discrimination belongs to movement; it represents the image of *shin* (Thunder). The nature of emptiness resembles wind; it represents the image of *zan* (Wind). As for their presence within the human mind, penetration and obstruction sufficiently encompass delusion and enlightenment.

Conditions arising from the void sufficiently encompass existence and non-existence. Gloom and clearing sufficiently encompass the dust of the senses and awakening. Brightness and darkness likewise suffice.

This fully encompasses both the holy and the ordinary, exhausting all that constitutes the objective realm (*viṣaya*). While there are distinctions among these realms, there is no distinction in the vision [of them].
As for those with distinctions, each returns to its own source; as for those without distinction, they are fundamentally unmoving from the beginning. Of all those things that can be returned—
It is the objective realm; it is a thing; it is not you. That which returns from what is not you back to the realm of things is the faculty of seeing;

it is not a thing. It is truly your own true essence. That which can be returned may be called a guest; that which cannot be returned is called the host—the luminous clarity of the fundamental source of seeing.
If this is so, how much more so is the true mind, which is fundamentally wondrous, luminous, and pure? It does not fall into the realm of seeing;
it is the sovereign among sovereigns. This "sovereign among sovereigns" is the fundamental source, neither arising nor ceasing. It is fully possessed by every person and does not come from without.
Yet, failing to take oneself as the master, one drifts about as a guest—just like failing to recognize the true moon and instead taking the reflection in the water for it.
To take the reflection of the moon in water as one’s own mind—how could such a person possibly escape drowning in the cycle of birth and death?
A monk asked Caoshan, "The ancient masters said, 'Throughout the entire earth, there is only this one person. I wonder, who is this person?
Caoshan replied, "There must not be a second moon. The monk asked, "What is the second moon? Caoshan said, "It is also necessary..."
"Old brother, you have certainly grasped it. [The monk] asked, "What is the first moon? Caoshan said, "Dangerous.
This single word "dangerous" sufficiently shows that Caoshan did not dare lose his fundamental nature or undergo the cycle of rebirth; it is the most intimate point. Baoci Wensui [commented on this].
He once investigated the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* and visited Fayan to recount his own studies; these were found to be in profound accord with the intent of the scripture.
Fayan said, "Does not the *Śūraṅgama* contain the principle of the 'eight returns'? He replied, "It does. Fayan asked, "To what does clarity return?

He replied, "Clarity returns to the sun. Fayan asked, "And to what does the sun return? At this, he was suddenly at a loss for a response. From that time on, he took the Master's words to heart and requested further instruction.
This is the Lord among Lords who can be known; therefore, it is not within the reach of commentaries or sub-commentaries.

Master Duan’s verse says: "The teaching of the eight returns has been handed down for a long time; since antiquity, the patriarchal masters have each analyzed it. Even if one were to attain the state where there is no returning,"
This is also like a shrimp that cannot leap out of its basket; it is the same as the previous discussion on the seven subtle elements, and the underlying principle is likewise the same.
Ānanda said, "Although I recognize that this nature of seeing has no place to which it can return, how can I know that it is my true nature?
The Buddha told Ānanda, "I shall now question you: at present, you have not yet attained the untainted purity of an Arhat, yet by relying on the Buddha’s spiritual power, you are able to see..."

Having attained unimpeded mastery in the first dhyāna, Aniruddha (translated here as "As One Wills") beholds Jambudvīpa (named after the jambu tree found on this continent) as clearly as one gazes at an āmalaka fruit (translated here as "difficult to distinguish") in the palm of one's hand; the various bodhisattvas, however, behold hundreds of thousands of world-systems.

The Tathāgatas of the ten directions exhaustively survey all pure lands as numerous as motes of dust, leaving nothing unseen; yet when sentient beings look through with their physical eyes, they do not see beyond a mere fraction of an inch.
Ānanda, let us for now observe the palaces where the Four Heavenly Kings dwell, and survey everything therein—beings moving in water, on land, and through the air.
Although there are various forms, whether obscured or luminous, they are none other than the distinctions of external objects.
"Obstructed and hindered! You should now distinguish between self and other in this regard. Now I shall lead you to discern within your vision:
who is my own substance, and what are external objects? Ānanda, exhaust the source of your vision all the way back to the palaces of the sun and moon; these are external things and not you."
He proceeded to the Seven Golden Mountains and observed them thoroughly and attentively. Although they possessed various kinds of light, these were still material objects and not you.

Gradually, he further observed the rising clouds, the flying birds, the moving winds, the stirring dust, the trees, the mountains and rivers, the grasses and weeds, and the humans and livestock—all of these were material objects and not you.
Ānanda, although these various natures of things, whether near or far, differ from one another, they are all equally beheld by your own pure visual essence.

Thus, while the various categories of objects possess their own distinctions, the nature of seeing is without difference. This subtle, wondrous, and luminous clarity is truly your own nature of seeing.

Tong said: "At first, when Ānanda asked about the wondrously luminous primordial mind and why it has nothing from which to return, the Buddha [responded that] because the true mind leaves no trace, it is difficult to point out or describe.
Therefore, he relied upon the 'essence of seeing' as a skillful means to provide instruction; for this essence of seeing is most closely proximate to the truth."
It is like the second moon; yet this vision is also illusory and must likewise be returned. Only the true nature, symbolized by the real moon, truly does not return.
As the subsequent text says: "When seeing sees seeing, that seeing is not seeing. Is it not the case, then, that this seeing must also be returned?
Although Ānanda recognized that the essence of seeing has no place to return, he had already realized that [the vision] was like the second moon.
[Ananda] asked: "How can I know that this is my true nature? I wish to thoroughly investigate the meaning of the 'primary moon.

Since this nature of non-retrogression is such, by what skillful means may I come to know it for myself and have confidence in it? The Buddha again distinguished and clarified it for him using the essence of seeing:
"That which is seen is an object; that which is able to see is you. Objects have differences, but seeing has no difference."
That which is without differentiation is the essence of seeing (*darśana-sāra*). It is that which is beheld by the pure clarity;

although it is beheld by the pure four great elements (*mahābhūta*) of the sense-organ of sight, it nonetheless arises from the fundamentally pure nature of the substance itself without depending on artificial construction.
Thus, it is luminous through its own wondrousness, and is called the "nature of seeing" (*darśana-dharmatā*). Since this essence of seeing is your true seeing, it is the nature of seeing.
Is this not your true nature? Therefore it is said: "This subtle, wondrous, and luminous essence is truly your seeing-nature.
Now, while the nature itself is one, the reach of the seeing-essence may vary; this constitutes the distinction between exhausting one's nature and failing to exhaust it.
Those who possess the Buddha-eye can, like the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, exhaustively perceive the pure lands within every atom.
That the earth has no place it does not behold is an example of this. Those who possess the Dharma-eye, such as the various bodhisattvas, see hundreds of thousands of worlds;

this is an example of this. Those who possess the wisdom-eye, such as Subhūti, perceive the Buddha’s Dharma-body; this is an example of this. Those who possess the divine-eye... [is an example of this].
This refers to Aniruddha seeing Jambudvīpa as clearly as observing a fruit in the palm of his hand.

This refers to those with physical eyes (*māṃsa-cakṣus*) who, though able to see through to living beings, do not exceed a mere inch or two. Ānanda had not yet attained the pure state free from outflows (*anāsrava*);

it was by relying on the Buddha’s spiritual power that he saw the First Dhyāna. His was a physical eye that functioned like a divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*). What is seen by the five eyes differs; their respective capacities are such that...
The seer is non-dual; hence it is said there is no differentiation. One must reach the Buddha-eye and exhaust the finest atoms before the capacity of the nature of seeing is fulfilled.
A monk asked Yunmen, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?"
Mendun said, "Look at the mountain in broad daylight. Touzi’s verse says: Tanyan once asked after the Master’s well-being;

How can this compare to the single phrase transmitted by Shaoyang? "Look at the mountain in broad daylight"—dew on the Immortal’s Palm; Deep in the night, the monkey cries as the moon hangs before the eaves.
Furthermore, tell me: when one gazes at the mountains on this day, does one point to the clarity of seeing, or does one point to the nature of seeing?
How do you understand this, the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Yunju Zhi said: "The nature of purity is fundamentally serene and still; it is without movement or agitation.
It does not belong to existence or non-existence, nor can it be grasped or discarded. Its essence is naturally carefree. To see clearly in this manner is what is called [the nature of seeing]."
"To see one's nature. Nature is itself Buddha; Buddha is itself nature. Therefore it is said: 'Seeing one's nature is attaining Buddhahood. [Question:

Since nature is already pure and does not belong to existence or non-existence, by what cause is there seeing? [Answer: Seeing is seeing nothing. [Question: If there is nothing seen, how can there still be seeing?
[Answer: Even the locus of seeing is non-existent. [Question: When seeing occurs in this way, whose seeing is it? [Answer: None."
There is one who is able to see. [The question is asked: "How is its principle ultimately realized? [The answer is:
"To falsely reckon it as existing is to have subject and object; this is what is called delusion. To give rise to understanding following such seeing is to fall into birth and death.

For the person of clear vision, it is not so: though they see all day long, they have never seen. One seeks for its name, location, essence, or characteristics, but none can be found. Both subject and object are utterly transcended."
[The Master] said, "This is called 'seeing one's nature. [The student] asked, 'Does this nature pervade all places? [The Master] replied, 'There is nowhere it does not pervade.
[The student] asked, 'Do ordinary beings possess it? [The Master] replied, 'Since I have just stated that there is nowhere it does not pervade, how could ordinary beings not possess it?
[The student] asked, 'For what reason are the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas not constrained by birth and death, while ordinary beings alone are bound by this suffering?'"
Cengde Bian said: "Ordinary beings, within the nature of purity, conceive of subject and object; they thus fall into birth and death.
The Buddhas and Great Beings, skillfully knowing that within the nature of purity there belongs neither existence nor non-existence, do not establish subject and object."

[The questioner] said: "If it is explained in this way, then there must be people who can realize [it] and those who cannot. [Dongshan] said: "Since even 'realization' itself cannot be found, how could there be a person who realizes?
What do you say about the ultimate principle? [The questioner] said: "Please speak in essence. [Dongshan] said: "I shall tell you the essential point:
within the nature of purity, there are neither ordinary beings nor sages, nor are there people who realize or do not realize. There is neither the ordinary nor the sage."

Both are merely names. If one gives rise to understanding by following these names, one falls into birth and death. If one knows that provisional names are not real, then there is nothing that corresponds to those names.
It is further said: "This is the state of ultimate consummation. If one says, "I am able to realize this," [one has not yet reached it].
That inability to comprehend is itself a great illness. To perceive the existence of purity and defilement, or ordinary beings and sages, is also a great illness.

To form the understanding that there are neither ordinary beings nor sages likewise belongs to the denial of cause and effect. To perceive a pure nature as a place where one may dwell is also a great illness;
to form the understanding that there is no place to dwell is also a great illness. Nevertheless, within the nature of purity, for the time being, one must not disrupt its state.
One should immediately apply this, giving rise to compassion and pity. Where such application arises, it is precisely the nature of total purity;
this may be called "seeing one's nature and becoming a Buddha. Yunju’s words here are, however, most urgent regarding the point that "even seeing must be left behind.
Therefore, I have recorded them in full.
If you see this object, then you can also see my seeing. If you see it as I do, that is called "seeing me.
When I am not seeing, why do you not see the place where I do not see? If you see that which is not seeing, then it is naturally not the characteristic of non-seeing.
If you do not see the ground of my non-seeing, then it is naturally not a material thing; how could it not be you?
Tong said: "Foguo raised the point that while the world, lanterns, and pillars all have names and forms, what would you call the 'essence of the clarity of seeing'?
I wish for you to let me see it. Foguo’s intention was: "When I see the incense altar..."
"How do you see it? Ānanda replied, "I also see the incense altar; this is precisely where I see the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "If I see the incense altar, then it may be known. But when I do not see the incense altar, how do you see it?"
Ānanda said, “I also do not see the Fragrant Terrace; this is precisely seeing the place where the Buddha is not seen.
The Buddha said, “You say you do not see it; that is simply what you know for yourself. As for a place where others do not see, how can you know it?
When an ancient arrived at this point, he could only know it for himself; it cannot be explained to others. It is just as the World-Honored One said: ‘I do not...’”
At the moment of seeing, it is like a deer hanging from its horns; sound, trace, and breath are all utterly extinguished. Where will you search for it? Xuedou’s verse says:
"The whole elephant and the whole ox are no different from cataracts; From of old, the masters have shared in the name 'searching.
If you now wish to see the old man Huangtou, Every land and every dust mote is already halfway there. Xuedou emerges.
The Eye of Teaching. This single verse on seeing the Buddha was composed by the Celestial Youth (Tiantong), who profoundly grasped the intent of the sutras;
this verse brings forth true vision. The verse says: "The vast ocean is drained dry; the great void is filled to overflowing. The nostrils of the patch-robed monk are long;

the tongue of the ancient Buddha is short. A strand of pearls passes through nine bends; the jade mechanism turns but once. Meeting him directly beneath, who can recognize him? Only then does one believe in this man."
It does not accord with the companion. This is a matter of karmic conditions; it is a double case that, though expounded to the utmost of one's ability, can only be described as half-realized.
Furthermore, at the moment you now see an object, since you see the object, the object also sees you; their essential natures become confused and intermingled.
"In that case, you, I, and all the world would fail to be established. Ānanda, when you see, it is you who see and not I;
this nature of seeing is all-pervasive—if it is not yours, whose is it? Why do you doubt your own true nature?
If you consider your own nature to be unreal and seek the truth by taking refuge in me, you are mistaken."
The *Compendium* states: The meaning of this section of the sutra arises from the single phrase, "How can one know that this is my true nature?
Therefore, when the World-Honored One reveals the characteristic of non-seeing, he causes one to understand that the true nature should not be further sought through conceptual discrimination.
As Aśvaghoṣa says: "All Tathāgatas are the Dharma-body; there is no distinction between self and other."
Because they see one another, it is said that "if you see, you do not see. This naturally refers to the characteristic of not seeing;
when we say "not that," we mean it is not the World-Honored One’s characteristic of not seeing, but rather the characteristic of Ānanda’s own failure to see.
Thus, that which is not seen by the World-Honored One is also not unseen by Ānanda; it is simply that the World-Honored One is able to see it.
Therefore it is said: "If one does not see the ground that I do not see, it naturally is not a thing. To say it is not a thing means:
This is not that the World-Honored One does not see; it is merely that Ānanda does not perceive the aspect of seeing.
If the World-Honored One were to see Ānanda’s seeing, and Ānanda were likewise to see the World-Honored One’s seeing, then the nature of purity would clearly become a material object.
Therefore, it is said that the essential nature would be confused and intermingled, failing to establish itself as a stable foundation. This is what is meant by "not seeing."
The "ground" (di) refers to the ground of the original root; it is absolutely impossible to see. It is like a tree-planter who takes up the roots daily to examine them—could that tree ever grow?
Master Fu’s verse says: "There is a thing prior to heaven and earth; formless, it is fundamentally quiescent.
It can act as the lord of the myriad phenomena, yet does not wither along with the four seasons. These few words alone suffice to distinguish [it].
The explanation points out that the true nature is not within the reach of vision; this is the meaning of the "first moon.
It does not merely mean that the essence of the clarity of seeing cannot be seen. [Zhao] Tong said: "This passage of the scripture is most wondrous in its transitions;
it is nothing other than an illumination of this subtle, wondrous, luminous, and sincere nature of your seeing. Why then do you say, 'This seeing is you, not an object'?"
This is because seeing one's nature is not a material object. If seeing were a material object, then my seeing could be seen by you;

however, my seeing can never be seen by you. If you claim that when my seeing and your seeing coincide, it constitutes seeing my seeing, then at the very moment I am seeing, that seeing would already be something visible.
When I am not seen, I am nonetheless visible; why should this not be so?
If one were to say that when I am seen, I am seen by means of seeing, and when I am not seen, I am seen by means of non-seeing—this is called seeing me in the place where I am not seen.
Since you do not see it yourself, how can you see that mark of non-seeing? To cause that mark of non-seeing to be seen by you is simply the mark of seeing;
furthermore, it is no longer the mark of non-seeing. This is the ground of non-seeing.
It is absolutely impossible to perceive it. When it is not being perceived, since it is not visible, it follows that when it is being perceived, it is likewise not visible.
Both seeing and not seeing are equally beyond indication. It is clear, therefore, that my seeing is not a thing.
Since my seeing is not a thing, it is clear that your seeing is also not a thing. Your seeing, once...
That which is not a thing does not belong to things. How could it not be you? This is because it cannot be seen in order to distinguish it as a non-thing.
Even if it were visible, that seeing would itself be a thing; how then could it serve as the lord of the myriad phenomena and establish the world?
Therefore, it is only by having no form that it is able to give form to forms. It has no... [existence].
Only after one has transcended being an object can one then cause all things to become objects. My seeing and your seeing are neither objects; they are beyond all definition.
They pervade the entire dharma-realm, lacking nothing and exceeding nothing. Sentient and insentient beings are all established by means of this;
this is what is called true nature (*dharmatā*). This nature does not belong to you as a personal possession; it must be seen as not belonging to you at all. And yet, when it is seen—
"It belongs to you; it is not mine. Why do you doubt its authenticity yourself, yet seek the truth from me?
That which I could give to you would certainly not be the truth. A monk asked Chan Master Shanglan Chao, "What is the fundamental matter of Shanglan?
Shanglan said, "It is not borrowed from the thousand sages; how could it be sought among the myriad functions? The monk said, "No..."
A student asked, "What is it like when one does not seek to borrow? Lan said, "Can you not pick it up and place it in the hands of the *jiaoli* (the student)?

Danxia’s verse says: "A single piece of numinous clarity is fundamentally wondrous and perfect; Within this, there is neither right nor partiality. The auspicious grass on the Jewel Peak has no roots or stem;
It does not wait for the labor of spring—its color is naturally fresh. If one awakens to this, one knows that the true nature is fundamentally [such].

There is no thing. Where there is no thing, there is no confusion. Because there is no confusion, things and the self share the same source; they are perfectly complete in their undifferentiated wholeness.
If one seeks to obtain this from another, it is entirely mistaken.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if this nature of seeing is necessarily mine and not that of others, then when I and the Tathāgata were observing the Palace of the Supreme Treasury of the Four Heavenly Kings and dwelling in the palaces of the sun and moon, this seeing was all-encompassing, pervading the Sahā world (translated as 'Endurance').
Yet, upon returning to the vihāra, I saw only the monastery grounds (translated as 'Garden of the Assembly'), and when entering the hall with its pure mind, I beheld only the eaves and corridors."
"Venerable One, this vision is thus: its substance is originally pervasive throughout the entire realm, yet now, being within this room, it fills only the room.
Is it that this vision has contracted from large to small? Or is it that the walls and roof have constricted it and severed it? I do not know where the truth of this matter lies;
I pray you will grant me your great compassion and explain it for me in detail. The Buddha told Ānanda: "All worlds..."

The various activities of the intermediate spaces, large and small, internal and external, each belong to their respective objective fields (*viṣaya*). One should not say that the seeing itself expands or contracts.
For example, when a square vessel is used, a square void is seen within it. I ask you again:

Is this square void seen within the square vessel fixed as square, or is it not fixed as square? If it were fixed as square, then when a round vessel is placed there instead, the void should no longer [be square].
If it were circular, then when placed within a square vessel, there would have to be no square space. You say you do not know where this principle resides;

yet the nature of principles is such—how could it "reside" anywhere? Ānanda, if you wish to make it enter a state that is neither square nor circular, you need only remove the squareness of the vessel;
the substance of space itself has no directionality. One should not say that one must further remove the location of the directional characteristics of empty space. If...
As you asked regarding the time of entering a room, you contract your vision to make it small; yet when looking up at the sun, would you ever stretch your vision to equal the face of the sun?
If you build walls and houses, they can obstruct and sever your vision; but if you pierce them with a small hole, how could there be no trace of continuity? This principle is not so.
All sentient beings, from time immemorial, have mistaken themselves for external objects and lost their original mind. For...
It is that which all things revolve around. Therefore, within this state, one contemplates the great as small. If one can revolve things, then one is identical to the Tathāgata;
body and mind are perfectly luminous, unmoving from the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), and yet within the tip of a single hair, one can universally contain the lands of the ten directions.
Tong said: "Ānanda says that because the nature of seeing is all-pervasive, it must be 'I' and not anything else; therefore, what I see should be the same as the Buddha’s vision.
Why is it that when I dwell in the palace of the sun and moon, it pervades the entire Sahā world, yet now being inside this room, it fills only this room?
This seeing expands and contracts, being large and small; how can you say there is no difference? You do not understand the distinction between large and small."
This arises from external objects and does not concern the nature of seeing itself. It is like squareness and roundness, which depend on vessels and do not exist in empty space.

When facing a vessel, emptiness appears to have the characteristics of squareness and roundness; yet, once the vessel is removed, there is no squareness or roundness in emptiness that can be pointed out.

When one discriminates vision based on objects, it appears as if there is a form of expansion and contraction; yet when separated from those objects, no such expansion or contraction can be found in vision itself.
Vision shifts according to the objects, just as one who discriminates space does not perceive it within the vast void, but only becomes habituated to the space within a single vessel.
Thus, to perceive something as large or small therein is to mistake oneself for an object. If...
When one is able to transform objects, then all forms are the Buddha’s form and all visions are the Buddha’s vision.

It is like a single, vast expanse of clear sky where no object presents an obstruction; therefore, it is said that body and mind are perfectly luminous. Because they are perfect, the one is identical to the many.
Therefore, one can universally contain the lands of the ten directions within a single hair-tip. Furthermore, how could the Buddha-eye be otherwise?

A monk asked Huangbo: "If it is said that nature is itself seeing, and seeing is itself nature, then since nature is inherently unobstructed and without limits, why is it that one does not see when an object intervenes?
Moreover, in empty space, when [an object is] near..."
[The Master asked: "If you see when [the object] is near, yet do not see when it is far—how is this so? Huangbo said: "This is you generating false and divergent views.

If you say that one does not see because an object intervenes, yet sees when there is no intervening object, and thereby claim that the nature itself possesses obstruction, then you have absolutely no connection to the truth."
The nature itself is neither seen nor unseen; phenomena likewise are neither seen nor unseen. For one who perceives this nature, where is there that is not my own fundamental nature?
Therefore, the six realms and four modes of birth, as well as the mountains, rivers, and the great earth, are all the essence of my own pure and luminous nature.
Thus it is said: "When seeing form, one sees the mind," for form and mind are not different. It is simply...

If one forms perceptions based on grasping at signs, and attempts to see by setting aside the objects before them, one immediately falls among those of the Two Vehicles who rely on supernatural powers for their views and understanding; thus, they may see when close to empty space, but not when far from it.
This would be categorized among the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas). It is clearly stated that it is neither internal nor external, neither near nor far.
To say that what is near yet invisible is the nature of all things—when even what is near cannot be seen, what is the intent in further saying that what is far cannot be seen?
Jingqing asked a monk, "What is that sound outside the gate?"
The monk said, "It is the sound of raindrops. Qing said, "Sentient beings are inverted; they are deluded about themselves and pursue external objects. The monk asked, "What about you, Master?
Qing said, "I have not even reached the point of being deluded about myself. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'not even reaching the point of being deluded about oneself'?"
Qingyun said: "To leave one's station may still be easy; to shed the body and realize the Way must be difficult. Xuedou’s verse says:
"The sound of raindrops in an empty hall— Even a master finds it hard to respond. If you claim you have entered the stream, You still do not understand as before.
Do you understand? Do you not? The South Mountain and North Mountain pour down in torrents. This can be called "never being hidden anywhere throughout the world. A monk asked:
Chan Master Guyin Cong said, "If one can turn things over, one is identical to the Tathāgata. The myriad phenomena are 'things'—how can they be turned over?
Cong replied, "Once the meal is finished, there is not a trace of intentional intellect. If there were intentional intellect, one would be turned by things.
Furthermore, a monk asked National Teacher Shao, "What is it to turn things over and thus be identical to the Tathāgata? Shao replied:
"What do you call this thing? he asked. [The monk] said, "In that case, it is identical to the Tathāgata. Shaor said, "Do not let out the howl of a jackal;
if you attempt to equate it with the Tathāgata, you are already thousands of miles away.
A monk asked Zhaozhou, "How should one apply the mind throughout the twelve periods of the day? Zhaozhou said, "You are being driven by the twelve periods of the day; I am the one who drives them."
The twelve hours [of the day] are those who can truly transform objects. Baiyun Yuan’s verse says: "If one can transform objects, one is a Tathāgata;
when spring comes, mountain flowers bloom everywhere. One naturally possesses a pair of hands that have reached the ultimate;
they have never easily performed the Three Stages dance. Zhenru Zhe’s verse says: "If one can transform objects, one is a Tathāgata; at every door..."
Upon opening his eyes, he beheld Sudhana; amidst the flowered willow lanes, they performed dances and plays. On the nine thoroughfares, people lay upon towers and terraces, intoxicated with wine.
To contain all the lands of the ten directions within a single hair-tip is possible for the Buddha-eye;
can sentient beings do so? Li Bo, the Regional Inspector of Jiangzhou, asked Guizong: "The scriptures speak of Mount Sumeru being contained [within a mustard seed]..."
"Mustard seed. Pu [Zhicheng] immediately said, "I do not doubt it. Is the saying 'a mustard seed containing Mount Sumeru' not mere idle talk?
Zong said, "It is said that you, Excellency, have read ten thousand scrolls of books; is this true? He replied, "Yes. Zong said, "From the crown of your head to the soles of your feet..."
"If it is as large as a coconut, where would ten thousand scrolls of books be placed? Li bowed his head and remained silent.
Inferring from this, how does the mental capacity of sentient beings differ from that of the Tathāgata?

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if this essence of seeing is necessarily my wondrous nature, and if this wondrous nature is now present before me, then seeing must be my true self.
What, then, are my current body and mind? My current body and mind possess the capacity for discrimination and are real;
yet that seeing has no such distinction and cannot discern my own body. If it were truly my mind, it would cause me to see; [yet] seeing..."
If the nature is truly the self, yet the body is not the self, how does this differ from what the Tathāgata previously refuted, namely that an object can see the self?
We only pray that you will bestow great compassion and reveal the truth to those who have not yet awakened.
Tong said: "The previous statement, 'taking things as oneself,' and this current one, 'being deluded and taking oneself as things,' differ in their approach.

The former distinguishes the false from the true, whereby even one's own body is regarded as a thing. The present [statement] uses the true to dissolve the false, such that all myriad things are none other than oneself."
When one discriminates the false to select the true, claiming that the self and external objects are different, it is still possible to distinguish them.

However, when using the true to dissolve the false, claiming that objects and the self are identical, this is in fact difficult to understand. Thus Ānanda said: "If one can master objects, then one is the same as the Tathāgata."
This very essence of vision pervades the entire Dharma-realm; the mountains, rivers, and all that is seen are all my wondrous nature.
This wondrous nature is now manifest before me. If this vision manifest before me is indeed my true nature, then what are this body and mind that cling to my person?
If you say that the body and mind are not the nature, yet at present the body and mind are truly capable [of sensation].
This is a discrimination. If you claim that all that appears before you is the nature [of the self], then why is that vision unable to distinguish my own body?

If you claim that this vision is formless, being of one essence with all things, and is in fact my fundamental mind which moves in response to conditions, thereby enabling me to see now, then the nature of seeing is truly the self, pervading all that is manifest.
Previously, you were but a solitary body, no longer belonging to "me. How is this different from what the Tathāgata previously found difficult to express:
"Since you see objects, the objects also see you; this seeing is likewise external—how can it be called my true nature?
Based on Ānanda’s perspective, it seems he has caught a glimpse of the principle that quiescence is manifest before one; yet, I...

Seeing has not yet been eliminated; light has not yet penetrated through. Because there is still something vaguely present before one’s face, one is unable to dissolve the distinction between self and object or obliterate right and wrong.
When Shitou was reading Zhaolun, upon reaching the passage, "Only the sage can take the myriad things as himself," he struck the table and sighed, saying:
"The sage has no self; there is nothing that is not his self. The Dharma-body has no..."
"Elephant! Who says there are self and other? Within this perfect mirror of spiritual illumination, the myriad phenomena manifest spontaneously as their essence is profound.

Since mirror-like wisdom is not singular, who can speak of coming and going? How sublime these words! Later, a monk asked Changsha, "How can one turn the mountains, rivers, and the land back into oneself?
Changsha said, "How can you turn yourself [into the mountains, rivers, and the land]?"
[The monk] said, "I have gone to form mountains, rivers, and lands. Xuedou said, "I do not understand. Xuefeng said, "Under the city walls of Hunan, it is good for raising the people;
rice is cheap and firewood is plentiful, sufficient for all four neighbors. The monk was speechless. Xuefeng showed him a verse, saying: "Who asks about the turning of mountains and rivers?
Mountains and rivers turn toward whom? Perfect penetration has no two sides; The Dharma-nature fundamentally has no place of return. [The commentary] reads the words of these two venerable masters.
Thus, those who harbor doubts regarding Ānanda’s doubt may have them completely dissolved like ice melting away.
The Buddha said to Ānanda: "What you have just described as being present before you—this principle is not real.
If it were real and you truly saw it before you, then this essence of vision would have a specific location and could not be without a point of reference. Moreover, as for what is now before you..."
Sitting in the Jeta Grove, he surveyed the groves, the streams, and the halls, reaching upward as far as the sun and moon and facing forward toward the Ganges River.
Now, before my lion throne, you have pointed out and described these various signs: that which is the "grove" refers to the aggregates (*skandha*).
That which is luminous is the sun; that which obstructs is the wall; that which is permeable is space. Thus it extends even to grasses, trees, and the finest hairs;
though they differ in size, as long as they possess form, there is nothing to which [the visual faculty] does not point. If you insist that this seeing must be present before you now—
"You should point it out clearly with your hand: what is seeing? Ānanda, you should know this:
if space were seeing, then since it has already become seeing, what would be space? If matter were seeing, then since it has already become seeing, what would be matter?"
"You may minutely peel away and analyze the myriad phenomena to extract the essence of the bright, pure, and wondrous faculty of seeing.
Point it out and show it to me, so that it may be as clearly understood as those other objects, without any doubt.

Ānanda said, "Right now, within this multi-storied lecture hall, extending far to the Ganges River, looking up at the sun and moon, pointing with my hand, and surveying with my eyes—everything I point to is an object; there is nothing else."

"O World-Honored One, this 'seer'—as the Buddha has taught—is such that even I, a beginner śrāvaka with outflows, and even a bodhisattva, cannot extract a pure seeing from before the myriad objects and phenomena, nor can we find a separate self-nature apart from all things.
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is. The Buddha further addressed Ānanda: "As you have said, there is no such thing as a 'pure essence of seeing.'"
If there were a self-nature existing separately from all things, then that which you point to within these objects would not be the seer.
Now I tell you again: as you and the Tathāgata sit in the Jeta Grove, look further at the groves and gardens, even down to the sun and moon and their various distinct forms;
surely the essence of seeing does not accept being pointed out by you within these things. You must now discern this among all these objects.
"What is it that is not seen? Ānanda replied, "I truly see this entire Jeta Grove, yet I do not know what within it is not seen.
Why is this? If the trees are not the seeing, how can one see the trees? If the trees are themselves the seeing, then how can they be called 'trees'?
This applies even unto the sky: if the sky is not the seeing, how can one see the sky? If the sky is itself the seeing, then how..."
"What is empty? I further contemplated that within these myriad phenomena, even the subtlest manifestations of light are none other than the Seer.
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is."

Tong said: "If Ānanda already knows that all that can be pointed to are objects and that there is no 'seeing' to be pointed out, then within my own body and mind, as well as throughout the mountains and rivers, there is no nature of seeing to be indicated.
Why, then, do you say that this wondrous nature is now present before me?

Furthermore, if he also knows that among the myriad phenomena there is nothing that is not seeing, then within my own body and mind, as well as throughout the mountains and rivers, there is nothing that is not [seeing]."
Seeing one’s nature. What is meant by "seeing one's nature"? It means that while the true self is the nature, the body is not the self.
The World-Honored One provisionally expounded this for his own sake, and the former doubts were instantly resolved. Formerly, the Head Seat Zhao asked Fayan:
"Whom did you, the Abbot, succeed upon opening the hall? Fayan said, "Dizang. Zhao said, "That would greatly betray your late teacher Changqing. Fayan said, "I..."
Jiashan could not respond with Changqing’s "one-turn" phrase. Zhao asked, "Why do you not ask?
Jiayan said, "'Amidst the myriad phenomena, the body alone is revealed. What is the meaning of this? Zhao then held up his whisk. Jiayan said, "This is something you learned from Changqing.
As for your own position as head monk, what is it? Zhao was speechless. Jiayan said, "As for 'amidst the myriad phenomena'..."
"Amidst the myriad phenomena, the body alone is revealed. Does this negate the myriad phenomena, or does it not negate them?

Zhao said, "It does not negate them. Yan said, "Two things. Those attending him on the left and right all said, "It negates the myriad phenomena. Yan said, "Within the myriad phenomena, the body alone is revealed—how so?
Later, the senior monk Zifang also came from Changqing; Yan again raised the previous dialogue with him. Fang...
Baizhang also raised his whisk. Xuedou said, "Even so, how can it be? Xuefeng asked, "What is the Master’s intention here? Xuedou said, "What do you call 'the myriad phenomena'?
Xuefeng said, "The ancients did not negate the myriad phenomena. Xuedou said, "'Amidst the myriad phenomena, the body alone is revealed.
Why speak of negating or not negating? At these words, Xuefeng suddenly attained enlightenment regarding Baizhang’s previous dialogue.
These karmic conditions originally derived from the place of Dizang. Why, then, did they not succeed Dizang?

When Yanchu, Shaoshou, Fajin, and three others went to Dizang’s dwelling, they entered the incense burner room. During their turn, Yanchu raised the passage from Zhaolun that reads, "Heaven and earth share the same root as I.
Dizang said, "Are the mountains, rivers, and the great earth the same as you, Venerable Sir, or are they different?"
“Different,” said Xueyan. Baizhang held up two fingers. Xueyan said, “The same. Baizhang again held up two fingers and then rose to depart.

After the snow had cleared, the three men took their leave. As Baizhang saw them off at the gate, he asked, “Upādhyāya, you usually say that the three realms are mind-only and all phenomena are consciousness-only.
Now, look at this stone in the courtyard—tell me, what is it?”
The Master asked, "Is it within the mind or outside the mind? Yan said, "It is within the mind. Zang said, "What is a traveling monk doing with such pretexts?
Why place a flat stone upon your heart? Yan was at a loss for a reply and immediately set down his pack beneath his seat.
He sought a definitive resolution for over a month, presenting his insights and expounding on principles daily. Baizhang said, "The Buddha-dharma is not like this.
Xiyuan said, "I am at a loss for words; my reasoning has reached its limit. Baizhang said, "If one speaks of the Buddha-dharma, everything is already fully accomplished.
At these words, Xiyuan attained great enlightenment. Only then did he believe that what he had studied under Changqing was still insufficient. —Tiantong.
The Verse says: Leaving behind thought, one sees the Buddha; Shattering the dust, the Sūtra emerges. The family dharma is manifested and established; Who could have founded this gate?
The moon follows the boat as the river’s silk-like waters clear; Spring follows the grass, green upon the scorched earth. Whether you grasp it or not, listen to these earnest instructions.
"The three paths have fallen into ruin, yet upon returning, they are found; the pine and chrysanthemums of old still exude their fragrant scent.
Taking this *gong'an* and this passage of scripture, if one reflects upon and savor them repeatedly, one cannot tell whether Guo Xiang annotated the *Zhuangzi*, or the *Zhuangzi* annotated Guo Xiang.

At that time, the great assembly—none of whom were yet those beyond training—upon hearing these words of the Buddha, were utterly bewildered and did not understand the beginning or end of their meaning;
for a moment they were struck with terror and lost their composure. The Tathāgata, perceiving that their spirits were shaken and cowed, gave rise to a heart of compassion.
He comforted Ānanda and the great assembly, saying: "O sons of good family, the Unsurpassed Dharma King speaks words of truth;
he speaks according to reality, without deception or falsehood. This is not the fourfold evasive discourse on immortality of Makkhali Gosāla."
"Consider this carefully; do not fail me in your sorrowful longing.
Tong said, "I am utterly bewildered and do not understand the beginning or end of this principle. At the beginning, I saw that it was not a thing;

at the end, I saw that there is nothing that is not a thing. At the beginning, the wondrous nature manifested before me; at the end, there was nothing to point out or describe. Therefore, I am bewildered and lost."
That which he maintains is "true speech," and so forth—these are the five phrases of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
"The Buddha’s true speech" (*bhūtavāda*) is shared with the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). "Real speech" (*satyavāda*) is shared with the bodhisattvas.

"As-it-is speech" (*tathāvāda*) is unshared; it is neither unreal nor false. Because it is not false, it is not deceptive speech; because it is not unreal, it is not divergent speech. This is seen from afar.
The term "unprecedented" (*avyākṛta*) means "not different. This is simply a generalization based on its non-falsity.
The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that non-Buddhists reckon the eternal heavens as "immortality," and they maintain that by answering without confusion, one will be reborn in those heavens.

If one were to answer recklessly while actually lacking knowledge, there would be the fear of falling into equivocation (*vāg-vibhramśa*). Therefore, when questioned, one should respond with "secret terminology" (*rahasya-vacana*), which should not [be disclosed].
[The Buddha] would sometimes answer them all, and sometimes give an indefinite response. The Buddha rebuked him, saying, "This is truly evasive and confused. This is detailed in the tenth fascicle.

Once, when a non-Buddhist asked the World-Honored One, "What Dharma did you teach yesterday? he replied, "I taught the Dharma of certainty. The non-Buddhist asked, "What Dharma do you teach today? He replied, "The Dharma of uncertainty.
The non-Buddhist then asked, "Yesterday you taught the Dharma of certainty; why do you teach [the Dharma of] uncertainty today?"
Regarding the indeterminate dharma, the World-Honored One said: "Yesterday it was determinate; today it is indeterminate. Now tell me:
when the World-Honored One spoke these words, was he speaking according to reality, or was it evasive speech? Examine this!

At that time, the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, out of compassion for the fourfold assembly, rose from his seat amidst the great multitude, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One, this great assembly does not yet understand the meaning of the Tathāgata’s illumination regarding the two kinds of refined vision—the seeing of form and the seeing of emptiness, and what is or is not [true]. World-Honored One, if this former...”
If these objects such as form and emptiness are what is seen, they should have something specifically pointed out; if they are not what is seen, there should be nothing gazed upon.
Yet now, I do not know where this principle leads, and thus I am filled with alarm and fear. It is not that my past roots of goodness were meager or slight;
I only pray that the Tathāgata’s great compassion will illuminate this for me: what are these various objects and this essence of seeing fundamentally?
Regarding these things, within that interval, there is neither "is" nor "is not. The Buddha told Mañjuśrī and the great assembly:

"The Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the great Bodhisattvas, while abiding in their own *samādhi* (here translated as 'Right Concentration'), perceive both the seer and the conditions of seeing, as well as all conceived appearances, to be like flowers in the sky—fundamentally non-existent. This seeing and its conditions are originally the wondrous *bodhi*."
[The Buddha said: "This is the essence of pure luminosity.
How can there be 'is' or 'is not' within it? [Ananda] replied: "Mañjuśrī is the teacher of the seven Buddhas and is well-versed in preaching the Tathāgata-dhyāna.
He wishes for the World-Honored One to clarify what these various objects and this seeing-essence originally are. The World-Honored One had previously said: "I do not know the physical body."
"Externally, reaching from the mountains and rivers to empty space and the great earth—all are objects within this wondrously luminous true mind.
This has already been clearly explained; what need is there for further words? However, within this, if one rejects the myriad phenomena, there is the mark of 'non-existence';
if one does not reject the myriad phenomena, there is the mark of 'existence. These two marks of being and non-being are the most subtle. Only those with true insight can transcend them."
Only within the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of bodhi is there a path for emergence. This wondrous, pure, and luminous essence is precisely the samādhi in which the Bodhisattva abides.
Abiding within this concentration, one is utterly detached from the sense organs and their objects; therefore, both seeing and the conditions of seeing—
Neither can be apprehended. Form (rūpa) being empty serves as the condition for seeing, and so on, up to the characteristics of perception (saṃjñā) serving as the condition for the mind (manas).

These belong to the six sense objects (ṣaḍviṣaya). Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing belong to the six consciousnesses (ṣadvijñāna). One who realizes Bodhi finds that not only the object is empty, but the subject is also empty;
therefore it is said that "originally there is nothing at all. When both subject and object are empty, this seeing and its conditions are, in their very essence, quiescent extinction. This is...
The wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of Bodhi admits of no deliberation and admits of no discrimination.
The wisdom of all wisdoms is pure, being non-dual and without duality, uninterrupted and without distinction. How, then, could one discriminate within it by saying: [“...”]?
Is this seeing, or is this not seeing? To forcibly give rise to notions of right and wrong is like a person with cataracts falsely perceiving flowers in the sky;
what connection does it have to the true nature of Bodhi? When Shishuang first visited Daowu, he asked, "What is Bodhi as it meets the eye?
Daowu called out, "Attendant! The attendant responded, "Yes? Daowu said, "Fill the water pitcher."
He entered [the room]. After a long while, he asked Shuang, "What were you just asking? As Shuang was about to raise his voice, Wuye returned to the abbot’s quarters.
Shuang then attained realization. Danxia’s verse says: "Extending a hand is the mechanism of a true master; In ordinary speech, the banners and spears are deployed.
When he asked again and was about to advance, he returned to the quarters; One clear phrase leaves no further doubt. If you wish to know...

This principle that is beyond doubt must be questioned of Shishuang before it can be understood. Later, a monk asked Shishuang, "Within the span of a few feet, why is it that I do not behold the Master’s countenance?
Shishuang, responding from behind a window, said, "I say that throughout the entire world, nothing has ever been hidden.
The monk then raised this question with Xuefeng, asking, "What is the meaning of 'throughout the entire world, nothing has ever been hidden'? Xuefeng—
Yangshan said, "Where is it that Shishuang is not? When Shishuang heard this, he said, "What kind of desperate urgency has this old fellow fallen into?
When Xuefeng heard this, he said, "I, this old monk, am at fault; I have merely added this one character 'is,' leading people into the den of intellectual understanding."
He was immediately subjected to Shishuang’s piercing critique. In a matter of hairs' breadth, none but those with the true eye can discern the difference.
Mañjuśrī, I now ask you: if there were another Mañjuśrī like you who was also Mañjuśrī, would that be Mañjuśrī or not?
"It is so, World-Honored One. I am the true Mañjuśrī; there is no such thing as 'Mañjuśrī. Why is this? If there were such a one..."
[The Buddha said: "Those two are both Mañjuśrīs. However, it is not that I do not have a Mañjuśrī today; yet within this [state], there truly are no such dualistic marks of 'is' or 'is not.

[Mañjuśrī] replied: 'I am the true Mañjuśrī,' thereby answering from the perspective of the primary truth (*paramārtha*). This is analogous to establishing the wondrously pure and luminous essence of bodhi."

"Mañjuśrī does not exist" answers the second proposition; it serves as an analogy to refute the view that form and emptiness are the vision. "It is not that Mañjuśrī does not exist" answers the third proposition;
it serves as an analogy to refute the view that form and emptiness are not the vision. If one were to claim that form and emptiness are the true vision, [it would be refuted by these examples].
This is to distinguish the true from the false; yet, when confronted with the true that is itself free from falsehood, it results in a duality of meanings.

Thus it is said: "If there were such a thing [as a separate true Manjusri], then there would be two Manjusris. If one claims that the emptiness of form is not the true vision, how could it be that the entirety of the false realm is itself the true?
Therefore it is said: "However, today I am not without Manjusri. When Luopo manifested illness, he addressed [his disciples]:
The assembly said, "Now we have a matter to ask you all: if you say this is so, it is like adding a head to what already has one;
if you say it is not, it is like seeking life by cutting off one's own head. The first seat said, "The green mountains constantly lift their feet;
beneath the sun, one does not pick up a lamp. Baofu said, "What kind of time is this to speak such words? At that moment, there was Yan.
The Senior Monk replied, "Apart from these two paths, I ask that you, Preceptor, do not question me.
Baofu said, "Not yet; speak further. The monk said, "Yancong’s Way is inexhaustible. Baofu said, "I do not care whether it is exhaustive or not.
The monk said, "Since Yancong has no source, I simply respond to you, Preceptor. Baofu then desisted. Master Xiu’s verse says: "In this pillar, one does not see the pillar."
If one does not see the pillar because of the cinnamon tree, it is because "is" and "non-is" have already been discarded.
Seek the realization within this "is" and "non-is," and once you have transcended these two principles, then "is" and "non-is" can be extinguished.

Formerly, when Fenggan wished to travel to Mount Wutai, he asked Hanshan and Shide, "If you go with me to travel to Mount Wutai, you will be of my same kind; if you do not go with me to travel there—"
Wuzhu said, "You are not of my school. Guishan asked, "Where are you going? He replied, "To Wutai to pay homage to Mañjuśrī.
Guishan said, "You are not of my school. Guishan entered Wutai alone. There he met an old man and asked, "Are you perhaps Mañjuśrī?
The man replied, "How could there be two Mañjuśrīs? Before Guishan had even finished his prostration and risen, suddenly—

However, [Mañjuśrī] was not seen. Zhaozhou spoke on his behalf, saying, "Mañjuśrī, Mañjuśrī. Furthermore, when Mañjuśrī spent the summer retreats in three places, Kāśyapa intended to strike the gavel to expel him;
as soon as he raised the gavel, he saw hundreds of thousands of millions of Mañjuśrīs.
Kāśyapa exhausted all his supernatural powers, yet he could not lift the gavel. The World-Honored One then asked Kāśyapa, "Which one do you intend to expel?"
"Mañjuśrī," [the Buddha said]. Kāśyapa had no reply. The Celestial Youth (Tiantong) held up the case and said: "The golden-colored dhūta has heart but lacks gallantry.

At that time, he should have carried out the command to its full extent; do not say 'even hundreds of thousands of millions of Mañjuśrīs'—it was simply this Yellow-Faced Gautama who should have been expelled as well.
If one can act thus, not only will the true wind stand like a wall, but it will also cause future generations..."
Know that within my gate of the patch-robed monks (samana), there is no place for you idle Buddhas and patriarchs to settle.

How wonderful, how wonderful! You must know that once this is seen, even the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of bodhi has no place for attachment; how, then, could the two marks of right and wrong arise?
The Buddha said, "This wondrous clarity of vision and these various empty objects are likewise so. Fundamentally, they are the wondrously luminous, unsurpassed Bodhi—the pure, perfect, true mind.
Through delusion, they become form and emptiness, as well as hearing and seeing. It is like a second moon: which one is the real moon, and which one is not?
Mañjuśrī, there is only the one true moon; within it, there is naturally neither 'this is the moon' nor 'this is not the moon.'"
Tong said: "This is fundamentally the wondrously luminous, unsurpassed Bodhi, the pure and perfect true mind. It has falsely become form and emptiness, as well as hearing and seeing.
As previously described, when it was obscured and became emptiness, within that darkness of empty obscuration, it coagulated darkness into form.

Form mixed with deluded thoughts; these thoughts and their appearances became the body. Gathering conditions, it stirs within; rushing outward, it flees in wild abandon. Thus there arises the state of confused and turbulent appearance."
As for the nature of the mind, its arising is roughly the same; in all cases, it is deluded thought that acts as its affliction.
Deluded thought is the very root of illness, just as it is like pressing on the eyes [to see double]. Fundamentally, there is only one wondrously luminous true mind.

Because of deluded thought and discrimination, one perceives form and emptiness, hearing and seeing. Yet how could this perception and its objects of perception exist as a self-substance apart from the true mind? Since...
To name this "the emptiness of form" and to hear and see it is to be far removed from the true mind. It is like a single true moon;
because one presses on the eyes and discriminates, one sees what is called a second moon. Can this second moon exist as a substance apart from the true moon?
Since it is named the "second moon," it is far removed from the true moon. Thus, regarding form—
Hearing and seeing in emptiness, one falsely engages in conjecture. To think that this is the true mind is incorrect;

to think that it is not the true mind is also incorrect. By using the false to discern the true, the true follows the false. It is like a second moon: to conjecture falsely that this is the moon is incorrect;
to think that it is not the moon is also incorrect. This is because of the fabrication.
