Distinguishing the moon: the moon follows the pressure and turns; this is the original reality of the mind. It changes according to deluded thoughts, just as the moon’s original reality changes when the eyes are pressed.
Simply eliminate the deluded thoughts, and there is only the single wondrous, pure, and luminous essence.

One no longer perceives form or emptiness, nor does one perceive hearing or seeing. From where could right and wrong be established? Simply remove the pressure on the eyes, and there is only the one moon.
"True. One does not see a second moon; from where could such 'is' and 'is not' arise?

This is precisely what was meant by the previous passage: 'I am truly Mañjuśrī. Within this, there are in reality no two characteristics of 'is' and 'is not'; therefore it is said, 'it is likewise so.
Long ago, while Yunyan was sweeping the floor, Daowu said, 'You are far too busy. Yunyan replied, 'You must know that there is one who is not busy.'"
I said, "If that is so, then there is a second moon. Yanguan held up a broom and asked, "Which moon is this?
I then desisted. Xuansha spoke differently, saying, "This is precisely the second moon. Changqing said:
He has turned his broom upside down and struck him right across the face. What then? "Sanda, go away. Yunmen said, "The slave shows diligence toward the maid.
Tiantong’s verse says: "Borrowed for the moment to settle the gate; When its use is appropriate, one simply rests.
The hand that plays with snakes before Elephant Bone Rock— What was done as a child brings shame to the old man. Xuefeng... [text ends]
Feng once addressed the assembly, saying, "On South Mountain there is a turtle-nosed snake;
you all must watch it very carefully. Yunmen then thrust his staff toward the front of the hall and made a gesture of fear.
Is this not like a servant being overly attentive to a maidservant? How does it differ from Yunyan holding up a broom? Therefore it is said: "The old fellow knows shame."
One day, while Chan Master Xiyuan Zang was bathing by himself, a monk asked why he did not have a śrāmaṇera do it for him.
Xiyuan clapped his hands three times. The monk reported this to Caoshan, who said, "In one sense, it is the same as clapping one’s hands."
Among these, Xiyuan’s “strange” case and Juzhi’s “one-finger Zen” are both instances where the point of realization was not perfectly grasped.
When a monk asked Xiyuan about clapping his hands, [the monk] said, "Is this not the business of slaves and servants?
Xiyuan replied, "Yes. The monk asked, "Is there anything further beyond this? Xiyuan said, "There is. The monk asked, "What is this matter that is further beyond?"

Shan shouted, "This slave and this servant! Seeing how these venerable elders present their teachings in such a manner, I fear people will mistake the servant for the master and fall into the secondary, conceptual understanding."
Therefore, when you now observe the seeing and the objects, and variously manifest them, this is called deluded thought (*vikalpa*). You cannot, within this, determine what is and what is not.
It is because of the true, essential, wondrous, enlightened, and luminous nature that you are able to distinguish between "this" and "not-this."
Tong said: "If you have not yet seen your nature, then the nature resides within seeing; it is called the 'essence of seeing.

Amidst various deluded thoughts and discriminations, how could one transcend what is right and what is wrong? If you can see your nature, the nature is liberated from seeing and is no longer termed seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing.
All discrimination ceases entirely, and thus one can transcend the pointing and the non-pointing. One cannot transcend them while remaining within [the state of seeing]."
This is not "this. It is like the second moon: who can say it is the true moon, and who can say it is not the moon?
Therefore, I was able to lead you to transcend both "pointing" and "not pointing. There is only the one true moon; in between, there is naturally neither "this is the moon" nor "this is not the moon.
When an object is pointed at, it is what was previously called "all objects are the finger. When that which is not an object is seen, it is what was previously called "there is no 'is'."

It is this very seer. Although Ānanda was able to clarify the two meanings—that these objects are not the seeing and that these objects are themselves the seeing—he remained bound by the duality of "is" and "is not," unable to achieve liberation. This was truly because he did not know where these meanings ultimately converge:
they converge in the nature of seeing. If one perceives the true essence, the wondrously enlightened, luminous nature, then both this seeing and its objects—
Fundamentally, there is nothing at all. Where, then, could a finger be contained? This seeing and its conditions are originally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of Bodhi.
Where, then, could "not being a finger" be contained? Within this, there is neither "is" nor "is not"; only then is there a path for emergence.
The character "emergence" (chū) is most flavorful; that one is able to emerge must necessarily be due to this.
Therefore it is said: "By means of this, one must surely see one's nature before the ultimate goal can be reached.
A monk asked Shao Shan, "In a place where right and wrong do not reach, is there still a phrase? Shan said, "There is. The monk asked, "What kind of phrase is that?
Shan said, "A single sheet of white clouds does not reveal any ugliness. Tiantong commented: "His entire being is turned back and forth; he does not offend the dignity [of the question]."
To step back and draw near requires one to turn about; do you see how Shao Shan acted for him?
With all his might, he pushed his father toward the interior. Dongshan’s verse says: "The green mountains are the white clouds’ father; the white clouds are the green mountains’ child.
The white clouds lean against them all day long, yet the green mountains know nothing of it. Shao Shan said: "A single sheet of white cloud does not expose its ugliness."
Based on this, a monk asked Attendant Jiufeng Qian, "What is external succession? Jiufeng said, "Not borrowing another's household affairs.
"What is internal succession? Jiufeng said, "Pushing the father toward the interior.
Tiantong said, "Exerting all one's strength to push the father toward the interior. Based on this, Touzi also composed a verse: "White clouds do not reach..."
Atop the peak of Mount Zhongfeng, the landscape is filled with mist and clouds; its scenery is extraordinary. A single phrase is a cold melody that has resonated for a thousand ages;
amidst ten thousand layers of azure green, the moon first appears. If you wish to know the wondrously enlightened nature of clarity, it transcends both "is" and "is not," like the primary moon.
One must thoroughly master the fundamental tenets of the Cao-Dong school before one can attain its subtlety.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, it is truly as the Dharma King has said:

that the conditions of awakening pervade the ten directions, remaining profoundly still and eternal, their nature neither arising nor ceasing. This is identical to the 'dark' (míng) spoken of by the former Brahmin Śvāśaraka (herein called a non-Buddhist)."

The Truths. Furthermore, what difference is there between these and the various types of non-Buddhists who smear themselves with ashes (having practiced the concentration of solidifying ash), who assert that a true self exists pervading the ten directions?
The World-Honored One also once expounded this meaning on Mount Laṅkā for Mahāmati and others:
"Those non-Buddhists always speak of spontaneity (*svabhāva*), whereas I speak of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*); it is not their realm. Now, as I contemplate this awakening...

The nature is spontaneous; it is neither born nor extinguished. It is far removed from all false delusions and inversions. It appears as if it were not produced by causes and conditions, being identical to that spontaneity.
How can this be revealed so that one does not fall into the various heterodoxies, but attains the true mind—the wondrously enlightened and luminous nature?
Tong said: "The *tattva* (ultimate principle) discussed by the non-Buddhists is not subject to arising or ceasing;
they claim there is a divine self (*puruṣa*) pervading the ten directions, yet they take the eight consciousnesses as their primary doctrine.

They merely attain a sense of profound, obscure mystery, but this lacks the subtlety of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*). Since they posit a divine self, it is the very root of birth and death; how could it be considered correct?"
"It depends on this. The Buddha said, "The correct cause is the primary truth (paramārtha-satya). It takes non-arising and non-ceasing as its fundamental cultivated cause;
it does not refer to what is called worldly causes and conditions. Ānanda, just as he was coming to believe, suddenly became doubtful and asked:

"This seems to be neither caused by conditions nor something spontaneous (svabhāva), yet you still speak of the nature of awakening as being spontaneous. This is because the nature of awakening is far removed from..."

These two characteristics—affirmation and negation—are profoundly still and eternally abiding; this is called spontaneity (*svabhāva*). Previously, you took the perception of the river as it flows to be non-arising and non-ceasing;
since you had not yet reached the fundamental source, I now point to the nature that is free from such perception as spontaneity.

They have not yet transcended [delusion]. Therefore, I pray that the World-Honored One will reveal the teaching that does not enter into the false views of all causes and conditions, spontaneity, emptiness, or perversion.
A monk asked Master Hui of Changsha Cenling: "How was it before you had seen Nanquan?
Hui remained silent for a long time. The monk said: "And how was it after you had seen him? Hui said: "It cannot be otherwise."
The monk returned and related this to Sandow. Sandow said, "The person sitting atop a hundred-foot pole—though they have gained entry, it is not yet the truth.
One must advance further from the top of that hundred-foot pole; only then will the entire body manifest throughout the worlds of the ten directions. The monk said:
"How does one advance further from the top of a hundred-foot pole? Sandokai said, "The mountains of Langzhou; the waters of Liuzhou. The monk said, "I do not understand.
Sandokai said, "The four seas and five lakes are within the realm of the King’s transformation. Tiantong’s verse says: "The jade man awakens from his dream at the cry of a single cock;
A glance reveals that all aspects of life are complete. With the wind and thunder of faith, the hibernating creatures are roused; Without a word, the peach blossoms bloom."
Li [Zicheng] follows the tracks of others. When the season arrives, he plows with all his might; who fears the mud in the spring fields that reaches up to the knees?
Only if one sits upon a ground of purity, unable to enter the mud or the water, and wanders about with hands cast loose—this is to be opposed to birth and death.
Therefore, although such a person may gain entry, it is not the truth. This is largely what the non-Buddhists call the "Principle of Obscurity" (Tattva).
It is like this. Changsha said, "The ten directions of the world are the entire body.
But non-Buddhists also claim that there is a *ātman* (self) pervading the ten directions. Where is the difference? Try to investigate this.
The Buddha told Ānanda, "I have now thus revealed these skillful means and truly told you this, yet you still do not understand and remain deluded by the notion of spontaneity (*svabhāva*).
Ānanda, if it were indeed spontaneous, one would have to clearly discern a substantial essence of spontaneity.
You should now examine within this wondrously luminous seeing: what constitutes its self? Does this seeing take light as its self, or does it take darkness..."
If you take emptiness as your self, or take obstruction as your self, Ānanda, if light were your self, you should not perceive darkness;

if again emptiness were your essential nature, you should not perceive obstruction. In this way, even if you take various characteristics such as darkness as your self, then at the time of light, the nature of seeing would be severed and extinguished; how then could you see the light?
Tong said: "As for what is called 'spontaneous' (*zìrán*), it means that the self-substance is inherently so, eternally abiding and unchanging.
Now, regarding this wondrously luminous nature of seeing: is it spontaneous to see light? Is it spontaneous to see darkness?
Is it spontaneous to see emptiness or see obstruction? If seeing light were spontaneous, one should not see darkness; if [seeing] light were spontaneous..."
If it were empty, it should not encounter obstruction. If it changes according to conditions, then it is not a spontaneous essence. Some may claim that the "seer" is its spontaneous essence;
yet if light, darkness, emptiness, and obstruction are seen only in response to stimuli, how can this be called spontaneous?
Furthermore, if light, darkness, emptiness, and obstruction were absent, where would the seeing be applied? What you call "spontaneous" would, in fact, be utterly annihilated.
This merely refutes that the nature of seeing can be designated as "spontaneous" (svabhāva);
it does not mean that the nature of seeing exists by itself through light, darkness, emptiness, or obstruction.

If we discuss its mode of arising, although the nature of seeing does not exist because of light, darkness, emptiness, or obstruction, it nonetheless emerges from the wondrous clarity of fundamental enlightenment (mūla-bodhi). Now, by what means, then, does this wondrous clarity of fundamental enlightenment [arise]?
For oneself—truly, one cannot open one's mouth. When Shishuang was first at Guishan serving as the rice-head, one day while he was sifting rice, Guishan said, "This is the property of a donor;
do not scatter it. Shishuang replied, "I shall not scatter it.
Guishan picked up a single grain from the ground and asked, "You say you will not scatter it, but what is this? Shishuang had no reply.

Miaoyan said again, "Do not underestimate this single grain; hundreds of thousands of grains all arise from this one grain. Xiangmo said, "Hundreds of thousands of grains arise from this one grain, but I wonder from where this one grain arises? Miaoyan laughed heartily and returned to his quarters. That evening, Miaoyan ascended the hall and said to the assembly, "Everyone, there is a worm in the rice! All [the monks] looked at one another. Miaoyan said, "I have already told you that there is a worm in the rice; why do you all look at each other? If you can say something, I will grant you a meal of rice; if you cannot, you shall starve to death right here. At that time, a monk stepped forward and bowed. Tong said: "Ananda once heard the World-Honored One refute 'spontaneity' (svabhāva) by means of 'causality' (pratītyasamutpāda).

Now, since this seeing-nature is not spontaneous, it must belong to causality. Yet I am suspicious of the meaning of causality: it involves impermanence and birth-and-death; here there is, while there it is not;

"What constitutes the nature of the causal conditions? This doubt is extremely subtle. The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states:

The Buddha said, "You speak of causes and conditions; I shall question you further. As you now see, the nature of seeing is manifest before you.
Does this seeing exist because of light? Does it exist because of darkness? Does it exist because of emptiness? Or does it exist because of obstruction? Ānanda, [the Buddha continued].
If it exists because of light, one should not perceive darkness; if it exists because of darkness, one should not perceive light.
This applies likewise to all things from space to obstruction, which are identical to light and darkness. Furthermore, Ānanda, this seeing also arises in dependence upon light.

There is seeing conditioned by darkness; there is seeing conditioned by space; there is seeing conditioned by obstruction. Ānanda, if seeing existed conditioned by space, it should not see obstruction;
if seeing existed conditioned by obstruction, it should not see space. This applies likewise to seeing conditioned by light and darkness, which are the same as space and obstruction.
You should know that this wondrously bright, essential awareness is neither caused nor conditioned, nor is it spontaneous, nor is it non-existent.
It is spontaneous. There is neither "not" nor "not-not," and there is neither "is" nor "is-not. It is free from all marks and is identical with all phenomena.
Why do you now attempt to apply your mind within it, seeking to make distinctions through the conceptual names and marks of worldly sophistry?
It is like trying to grasp and rub empty space with the palms of your hands; it only increases your own fatigue. How can empty space ever be seized according to your grasping?
The Master said: "Taking objects as the cause and following objects as the condition—since the cause is intimate while the condition is remote—they are divided into two gates.

It is impossible for emptiness to arise through obstruction; therefore, it is incorrect to call it "caused by conditions" (*pratyaya*). Why? Because the wondrous clarity of refined awareness is fundamentally without characteristics.
If one were to claim it is caused by conditions or is spontaneous (*svabhāva*), it would then belong to the categories of the characteristics of being caused by conditions or being spontaneous.
Thus, it was said at the outset that it is "neither cause nor condition, nor is it spontaneous," which serves to eliminate these characteristics.
There still remains the characteristic of "not-being. Therefore, it is followed by the statement: "It is not that there is no causal condition; it is not that there is no spontaneity.
This dispels the characteristic of "not-being. Yet, there still remains the characteristic of "not-not-being. Therefore, it is concluded with:

"Neither non-being nor not-non-being; neither being nor not-being. This is the ground where both being and non-being fail to reach; it admits of no conjecture and allows of no measurement. That is to say:

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if the nature of wondrous enlightenment is indeed neither caused by conditions nor produced by causes, why does the World-Honored One constantly proclaim to the bhikṣus that the nature of seeing is endowed with four kinds of conditions—namely, the condition of space, the condition of light, the condition of the mind, and the condition of the eyes?"
"The eye—what is the meaning of this? The Buddha said, "I teach that the various marks of worldly causes and conditions are not the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Ānanda, I shall ask you further: when people of the world say 'I can see,' what do they mean by 'seeing' and what do they mean by 'not seeing'?
Ānanda replied, "People of the world rely upon the light of the sun, the moon, or lamps to perceive various forms; this is what they call 'seeing'."
Furthermore, Ānanda, if these three kinds of light were absent, one would be unable to see.

If it were the case that not seeing occurs when there is no light, then one should not see darkness. Since one certainly does see darkness, this is simply the absence of light; how could it be called "not seeing"? Ānanda.
If, when in darkness, one does not see light, it is called "not seeing. Now, when in light, one does not see the characteristic of darkness;
this too is called "not seeing. Thus, both of these characteristics are termed "not seeing. Furthermore, if these two characteristics were to mutually suppress or displace one another...
"It is not that your faculty of vision temporarily ceases to exist within it. Thus, you should know that both [states] are called 'seeing. Why then do you say you do not see? He replied:
"This was the World-Honored One first refuting the characteristics of worldly causes and conditions, and subsequently revealing the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
In the world, seeing exists by depending on the causes and conditions of the sun, moon, and lamp-light. If there were no sun, moon, or lamp-light..."

It is not that there is no seeing; rather, seeing in darkness and seeing in light are equal. Brightness and darkness belong to the external objects before one, while the essence of seeing is fundamentally without arising or ceasing.
From this it may be said that even the worldly faculty of seeing is neither produced by causes nor conditions; how much more so for that which transcends it?

When Master Yunhui of Shimen was serving as a *yuantou* (head gardener) under Qinglin, one day while standing in attendance, Qinglin said, "My son, today..."
"What have you been doing? he asked. "I have been planting vegetables," he replied. Lin said, "The entire world is the Buddha-body; where do you intend to plant them?

Linquan looked at him. Yun said, "If it is a tree without a shadow, how could it receive planting? Linquan said, "It does not receive planting;

let us stop here for now. Have you ever seen its branches and leaves? Yun replied, "I have never seen them. Linquan said, "Since you have never seen them, how do you know it does not receive planting?
Yun said, "Precisely because I have never seen them, it therefore does not receive planting. Linquan said, "So it is, so it is."

It is so. If one awakens to the realization that even seeing is already detached from seeing, then how could all causes and conditions—which naturally harmonize and are established based on seeing—possibly arise?
