Knowing that the shared portion (*sabhāga*) is illusory, one can infer by analogy that the essence of seeing (*darśana-śuddhi*) is also illusory.

Knowing that the essence of seeing is illusory, one can infer by analogy that the seer of seeing (*darśana-draṣṭṛ*) is not illusory. Understanding this thoroughly, one realizes that "seeing" is not [truly] seeing.
You may now understand this clearly and be free of doubt. Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are all equally empty and delusive;
yet why is it that you specifically examine and distinguish "seeing"? It was said previously that what causes you to wander in saṃsāra is the fault of the mind and the eyes.
Thus, when they rush outward toward forms, it is "seeing" alone that is difficult to restrain. Ānanda was deluded by Māraṇḍa, but it was not Māraṇḍa who could delude Ānanda.

Difficult indeed. It is because Ānanda perceives the delusion as a disease. How much more so this deluded vision that flows through thought; fundamentally, it belongs to the realm of arising and ceasing.
Yet, true vision has no place to return; it is profoundly still and eternally abiding. Therefore, when one with sightless eyes sees forms, those forms possess nothing desirable.
When one who perceives darkness sees light, that vision is fundamentally not a conditioned object. One thus directly penetrates the vision of seeing itself.
This is the source [of all things]. To realize that it is beyond the reach of vision, how could there be any fault of transmigration? Long ago, Guishan asked Yangshan:
"The sentient beings of the great earth have a vast, indistinct karmic consciousness with no foundation upon which to rely.
How do you know whether they exist or not? Yangshan said, "Huiji has a way to verify it. At that time, a monk was passing by in front of them.
Yang [Qishan] called out, "Acarya! The monk turned his head. Yang said, "Preceptor! This is precisely what is meant by 'vague and boundless karmic consciousness, with no foundation to rely upon.
Miaoyan said, "This is but a single drop of a lion’s milk that scatters six bushels of donkey’s milk.
Tiantong’s verse says: "Once called, he turns his head—does he recognize me? The hazy moon is once again formed."
Hook. A son of a man worth a thousand pieces of gold, having just fallen into misfortune—how vast is the sorrow on such a desolate road!
This single instance may well be called a "delusive vision of a separate realm. Furthermore, when Minister Chen Cao was ascending the tower with his subordinates:
Seeing several monks passing by, an official remarked, "Those coming are all traveling monks. Baizhang said, "They are not.
The official asked, "How do you know they are not? Baizhang replied, "Wait until they arrive, and I shall examine them. Shortly thereafter, the monks reached the front of the tower.
Cao suddenly called out, "Venerable! and the monks all raised their heads. The official said to the other officials, "I do not believe this.
The officials were at a loss. Tiantong commented: "When Minister Chen personally called him to the front, he could not deceive Changlu by even a hair’s breadth.
This very case may be called a 'shared deluded vision. If there were a man among them..."
When called, he does not turn back; this shall cause Yangshan to stick out his tongue and Chen Cao to apologize.
What is meant by "delusive vision arising from separate karma"? Ānanda, it is like a person in the world who has a red film over the eye.
At night, seeing the light of a lamp, they perceive a separate circular shadow with five overlapping colors. What do you think? Is this what is manifested by the brightness of the lamp at night?
"Is this circular light the color of the lamp, or is it the color of the vision? Ānanda, if this were the color of the lamp, then it would not belong to the person with the cataract;

why then do they not both see it equally? Yet this circular shadow is seen only by the one with the cataract. If it were the color of the vision, then once it has become the object of vision, it would itself be a color."
Then, as for that person with the cataract who sees the circular shadow, what would you call him?

Furthermore, Ānanda, if this circular shadow existed separately from the lamp, it should appear as a circular shadow when one looks at the side-walls, curtains, tables, or mats; yet it exists separately from the act of seeing.
It should not be visible to the eye. How then can a person with cataracts see a circular shadow? Therefore, one should know that the color actually resides in the lamp;

the visual ailment perceives it as a shadow. Both the shadow and the perception are the ailment; the perception of the ailment itself is not the ailment. Ultimately, one should never say that this is the lamp or that this is the vision.
Within this, there is that which is neither lamp nor vision, such as a second moon; it is neither a substance nor a reflection. Why is this?

Because the perception of a second moon is produced by pressing [the eye]. A wise person should not say of this pressed root-cause whether it is a form or not a form, or whether it is apart from vision or not apart from vision.
This case is also like this: it is produced by a cataract in the eye. Now, whom do you wish to name as its reality?
"The lamp is seeing; how much more so the distinction between what is not a lamp and what is not seeing? He replied:
"I used the example of an eye ailment to show that clear seeing is not [inherently] 'seeing.
An eye ailment is a visual disorder, and thus one falsely perceives circular shadows. One who has no ailment does not see those circular shadows at all. This ailment is the disease."
One who perceives the optical illusion has never been ill. By this analogy, one perceives that the essence of seeing is illusory; thus, the mind and its objects are seen as illusory.
To one who is not deluded, there is no perception of a mind and its objects, for it is the act of seeing [objects] that is considered illusory, whereas the seer of seeing has never been illusory.
If, regarding the illusory mind and objects, one again gives rise to views of causality, spontaneity, or right and wrong, it is like—
It is like seeing a circular shadow in a visual impairment and seeking its originating source.
To claim that it is the lamp or the vision, asserting that the circular shadow exists because of the lamp and the vision, is the meaning of "causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*).

To claim that it is neither the lamp nor the vision, asserting that the circular shadow exists apart from the lamp and the vision, is the meaning of "spontaneity" (*svabhāva*). Since it is neither caused by conditions nor...
It is natural. It is merely produced by a cataract of the eyes. This cataract perceives a circular shadow;

it is the same visual affliction as seeing two moons when one presses on the eye. If one thoroughly investigates where this moon arises—whether it is a form or a vision—and yet claims it is "separate from form" and "separate from vision," such a person lacks the capacity for wisdom.
Consequently, regarding that circular shadow, they name it "the lamp" and "the vision. Furthermore...
Since it is distinguished as being neither the lamp nor the vision, how could it be considered wisdom? Thus, these two are clearly known to be illusory.

Even when one investigates the meaning of causes, conditions, or spontaneity, they cannot be found; how much less so for the originally enlightened, luminous mind, which is neither a cataract nor a pressure on the eye?
Since it fundamentally lacks the appearance of a circular shadow or a double moon, where could causes and conditions be established?
Is this not a natural proliferation of conceptual play (*prapañca*)?

Therefore, to argue that the essence of vision arises from the spontaneous conjunction of causes and conditions is like [describing] a cataract. A wise person should not do so; thus, it is called "the deluded vision of individual karma.
Once Master Miaoshan saw a wildfire and asked Daowu, "Do you see the fire? Daowu replied, "I see it. Miaoshan asked, "From where [does it come]?"
[Daowu] arose from his place. I said, "Set aside walking, standing, sitting, and reclining; please ask the Master another question.
Daowu then ceased speaking. Fojian took up the case, saying: "The blazing wildfire—everyone sees it. Only Daowu saw it in a completely different way.
Furthermore, while Xianglin Yuan was weeding, a monk said, "Look, a house is on fire! Yuan [responded].
[The monk] asked, "Where is that fire? The monk said, "I do not see it. Yuan said, "I do not see it. The monk said, "This blind fellow!

At that time, the entire assembly remarked that Elder Yuan had lost the point. Later, when Mingjiao Kuan heard this anecdote cited, he sighed and said, "It must have been my elder brother Yuan who achieved this;
his vision was truly exceptional. He did not depart from the true state (zhengwei), yet he was distinct from the worldly faculty of sight."
They cannot be discussed in the same breath as those who suffer from the visual impairment of illness. Furthermore, Guishan asked Daowu, "Where have you come from?
Daowu said, "I have come to visit the sick. Guishan asked, "How many people are ill? Daowu replied, "There are those who are ill and those who are not.
Guishan said, "Is the one who is not ill perhaps Master Zhi? Daowu said, "Illness and non-illness..."
"Your illness does not concern others at all. Speak quickly, speak quickly! Shan said, "Even if you could speak, it would have nothing to do with it.
Regarding this point of "having nothing to do with it," Tiantong composed a verse: "What wondrous medicine has ever passed through the mouth?
What divine physician can ever grasp the hand? If it exists, it was originally not non-existent; In its ultimate emptiness, it was originally not existent. It arises without perishing."

Without perishing, one attains longevity; completely transcending the era before Vimalakīrti, one walks alone through the void of kalpas. In its perfection, it is like heaven covering all and earth supporting all;
in its operation, it is like the flight of the crow and the running of the hare. This is to uproot the very source of illness within true vision;
when both "illness" and "non-illness" have ceased to interact, how much more so the discrimination between what is a cataract and what is not?
What is meant by "common delusory vision"? Ānanda, in this Jambudvīpa, excluding the great oceans, there are three thousand islands upon the level lands in between.
The central great island, measured from east to west, contains two thousand three hundred large nations;
as for the other small islands scattered throughout the seas, they contain either two or three hundred nations, or even just one.

Or two, or even three, four, five, or ten. Ānanda, if among these there is a small continent containing only two countries, and the people of that single country collectively experience adverse conditions, then the sentient beings of that land on that small continent [will likewise suffer].
They beheld all manner of inauspicious omens: they saw either two suns or two moons;
therein were even halos, solar spots, and crescents, as well as comets, meteors, falling stars, "burdened ears," rainbows, and halos—various evil signs seen only in this land.
The sentient beings of that land had never before seen such things, nor had they even heard of them. The *He lun* states:
"A halo is a vapor encircling the sun. This corresponds to what is called a solar or lunar calamity (*zai*) when it is suddenly observed.

A jade pendant or ring (*peijue*) is a form of atmospheric vapor resembling this; a comet (*hui*) is a so-called "sweeping star," which points in one direction like a broom, its radiant vapor extending in all directions.
That which emerges is called a *bò* (meteor). A flying star that ascends from below; a shooting star that descends from above;
one that carries its vapor away from the sun like a person carrying a load on their back; and one whose vapor flanks the sun like an ear—these are the *hóng* and *ní*.
The bright one is the *hóng*; the dark one is the *ní*. The *Spring and Autumn Annals* states: "In the sixth year of Duke Ai of Lu, there was a cloud in Chu resembling a red bird."
It flew, flanking the sun for three days. The Lord of Chu sent someone to inquire about this from the Grand Historian of Zhou. The Historian said, "It will fall upon the person of the King.
Du Yu’s commentary states: "The sun represents the sovereign; a baleful vapor is guarding it, and therefore it is taken as portending the King's person."
When clouds appear over the state of Chu, only Chu sees them; therefore, calamity does not reach other states.
Furthermore, in the eleventh month of winter in the twenty-sixth year of Duke Zhao of Lu, there was a comet in Qi. The Marquis of Qi sent someone to perform a ritual to avert it, but Yanzi said:
"It is of no benefit; it will only result in further slander. The Way of Heaven does not linger, nor does it double its decrees. How could one perform rites of expiation?
Moreover, the appearance of a comet in the Way of Heaven is for the purpose of clearing away filth. Your Majesty possesses no tainted virtue; what, then, is there to expiate?"
"If it is a defilement of virtue, what harm is there in warding it off? Du Yu’s commentary states: "This belongs to the jurisdiction of Qi.
It is not recorded because Lu did not witness it. Based on this, we can verify that there was a small island where only two states existed;
yet, because the people of that single state collectively experienced these baleful conditions, the sentient beings of that small island witnessed all manner of inauspicious omens.
The realms are thus clarified.
Tong said: "Regarding the influence of evil conditions, there are karmic retributions that are fixed and those that are not fixed. Fixed karma is absolutely impossible to escape;
however, that which is not fixed can, from the outset, be shifted. For example, consider the twenty-third patriarch, Venerable Hualena."
Foreknowing that the twenty-fourth patriarch, Master Shizi, would encounter peril, one day he suddenly pointed toward the northeast and asked, "What kind of phenomenon is this?
Shizi replied, "I see a vapor like a white rainbow piercing through heaven and earth;
furthermore, there are five paths of black vapor stretching crosswise across it. The Patriarch asked, "What does this omen portend? Shizi said, "It cannot be known."
The Patriarch said, "Fifty years after my passing, a calamity shall arise in the kingdom of Northern India;
it shall cling to your person. Later, the Venerable Siṃha was indeed killed by the King of Kaśmīra.
The king’s right arm then fell to the ground, and he died seven days later. Crown Prince Prabhāvatī sighed and said, "For what reason did my father..."
Thus they incurred the calamity. At that time, there was an ascetic named Śvetaśaila (White Mountain), who deeply understood the law of cause and effect.
He then extensively explained the past causes for Kāśyapa’s condition and untied the net of his doubts; this is what is meant by "karmic destiny is fixed and absolutely cannot be escaped.
During the time of Duke Jing of Song, the planet Mars (Venus) appeared in the heart constellation. Terrified, the Duke summoned Ziwei and questioned him. Ziwei said: "Mars..."
"This is a punishment from Heaven. My heart corresponds to the *fenye* (astrological division) of Song; the calamity shall fall upon your person. Nevertheless, it may be shifted onto the Chancellor.
The Duke said, "The Chancellor is the one appointed to govern the state. To shift death onto him would be inauspicious. I, this humble ruler, beg to accept it myself.
Ziwei said, "It may be shifted onto the people. The Duke said, "If the people die, who will there be to serve as my lord? It is better to let me alone [bear it]."
"I shall simply die. Ziwei said, "It may be transferred to the Year Star. The Duke said, "If the year is famished, the people will starve and surely die.
As a ruler, if I were to wish to kill my people to preserve myself, who would consider me their lord?
My fate as a ruler is already exhausted; do not speak further. Ziwei turned back and ran away, facing north and bowing twice, saying, "Your servant—"
"I venture to congratulate you, sir. Heaven dwells on high yet listens to what is below. You possess three words of benevolent man; Heaven will surely reward you thrice.
This very night the stars shall certainly shift their lodgings, and your life shall be extended by twenty-one years.

The Duke asked, "How do you know this? He replied, "Your Lordship possesses three virtues; therefore, there shall be three rewards. The stars must shift their lodgings thrice. As they move from one lodging to another—"
"The Seven Stars; each star corresponds to one year. Seven times three is twenty-one; therefore, it is said that his life will be extended by twenty-one years.
Your servant requests to prostrate himself before Your Majesty to await this event. If the stars do not shift, your servant begs to die for it. The Duke said, "It may be so."
That evening, the stars shifted their positions three times, just as Ziwei had predicted. This is what is meant by saying that even "undetermined karma" can still be altered.
In short, whether karma is determined or undetermined, what addition or subtraction does it make to its own nature?
It is like a magical illusion; those who grasp at an illusion and take it to be real possess nothing but false views.
Ānanda, I shall now clarify these two matters for you through their mutual relationship.

Ānanda, it is like those sentient beings who, due to the deluded vision of their individual karma, perceive a circular shadow appearing within a lamp’s light; although it seems to be an external object, it is ultimately produced by the visual ailment of the observer.
This ailment is simply the fatigue of seeing and is not created by the color itself. Yet, for one who perceives this ailment, there is ultimately no fault in the act of seeing.
For example, as you observe today with your eyes the mountains, rivers, lands, and all sentient beings, these are all produced by the disease of vision that has existed since beginningless time.
Vision and its conditions appear to be present objects before you, yet they are fundamentally the visual faculty of my enlightened awareness perceiving the optical aberration of a cataract.

To perceive and see is itself a cataract. The fundamentally awakened, luminous mind perceives conditions, yet this is not a cataract. It is the perception of that which is perceived that constitutes the cataract;

the perceiving awareness itself is not within the cataract. This is truly the seeing of seeing. How, then, can it again be called "awakening, hearing, knowing, and seeing"? Therefore, what you now see in me and in yourself—
Together with all the ten classes of sentient beings in the world, they all see this as a visual defect; yet it is not that the one who sees the defect sees [it].
Because the true essence of seeing is by nature not a defect, it is not called "seeing."

Tong said: "Using the circular shadow as an analogy for the external object, the eye-cataract as an analogy for the disease of seeing, the fatigue of seeing as an analogy for the clarity of awareness, and the cataract within seeing as an analogy for fundamental awareness—there is nothing that is not made clear. However, the phrasing and meaning are subtle and indirect;

they serve solely to reveal that it is the act of seeing that constitutes the cataract, whereas the seer of seeing is not the cataract. This concerns seeing and the conditions of seeing—the union of the sense organ and its object."
It is so. The currently existing mountains, rivers, lands, and all sentient beings appear as present objects, like reflections in a mirror;

yet, just as a reflection is not produced by material form, these too are not produced by external objects. They are fundamentally the objects perceived by the deluded vision of my own enlightened awareness, formed merely by a cataract of the eye.
This deluded vision of enlightened awareness establishes an objective realm based upon luminosity, thereby engaging in grasping and clinging.

The external object is precisely the eye ailment. If the originally enlightened, luminous mind does not fall into spatial location, is able to perceive the characteristics of all conditioned arisings, and does not follow the shifting flow of those conditions, it is fundamentally not an ailment.

Thus one knows that my original enlightened luminosity, when directed toward an external object, is that which is perceived. That which is perceived is the ailment, whereas the original enlightenment is truly that which perceives it. Fundamentally...
The awakened, luminous mind, being able to perceive the optical illusion and knowing that the illusion is a disease, naturally does not fall into the midst of that illusion.

To say it "perceives the illusion which is the perceived" is to reiterate that my original, awakened, luminous mind perceives the illusion within its field of objects; this is because the conditions of what is perceived by the awakening exist.
To say it "is not within the illusion" is to reiterate that the originally awakened, luminous mind perceives those conditions as not being the illusion; this is because [the mind is] floating...
Dust has not yet arisen; it does not fall into the optical defect of the clear and conscious mental ground (*manobhūmi*).
This is not an object of seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing; therefore, it is called "the true seeing of seeing. Why, then, would one further name it "sensing, hearing, knowing, or seeing"?
If one were to take sensing, hearing, knowing, and seeing as being identical to the nature itself, it would be like using a diseased eye to represent a pure, healthy eye. How could that be possible?
Tonghuo Sanping’s verse says: "This very seeing and hearing is not seeing and hearing; There is no further sound or form to present to you.
If one understands this, there is nothing at all; How could essence and function be hindered by being divided or undivided? Yunmen took it up and said:
This very seeing and hearing is not seeing and hearing. What do you call "seeing and hearing"? There is no further sound or form to present to you;
what head-mouth sounds or forms could there be? If one understands this point, there is nothing at all. What business could there be?
What prevents essence and function from being either distinct or non-distinct? Speech is the essence; the essence is speech. Again, he held up his staff and said:
"The staff is the essence; the lantern is the function. Are they distinct or non-distinct?

Have you not heard it said that "the wisdom of all wisdoms is pure"? Later, Baiyun Cuan commented: "Yunmen only knows how to copy a beauty’s eyebrows by following the original model. Yuan Tong, however—"
Not so. This very seeing and hearing is not seeing and hearing; there is no further sound or form that can be presented before you.
The eye is the eye; the ear is the ear. If one understands this point, there is nothing at all. Whether its essence and function are divided or not—what does it matter?
There are four or five hundred lanes of flowering willows, and two or three thousand towers of pipes and strings. Tiantong’s verse says: "Right face-to-face."
There is no engagement. The six gates are not closed; tracks are severed at the four crossroads. The entire realm is radiance; throughout the whole body there is neither front nor back.
When the shuttle-head is unattached to the warp and weft, the patterns run wild and the meaning is naturally distinct.

Sanping has another verse: Seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving are fundamentally not causes. In their very essence they are void and profound, transcending delusion and being true. As for seeing and form...
The karma of delusion and craving does not arise; it is entirely the body of Śākyamuni, radiantly clear through and through. Furthermore, Huìchāo ascended the hall and said:
"Venerable elders, seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing can only occur once.

As for this very realization—whether it is seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing, or whether it is not seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing—if you wish to understand, I have explained it thoroughly for you, Venerable elders. Wait until you awaken."
This can now be established. Taken together, these suffice as a commentary on this section.
Ānanda, just as those sentient beings share a commonality of deluded vision, so too may one person with a distinct karmic activity be compared to that deluded vision.
A single person with diseased eyes is like that entire country; the circular shadow they perceive is produced by the delusion of their cataract, yet it appears to the commonality of all those people.
Inauspiciousness arises from the miasma of shared karmic vision; it is produced entirely by beginningless false seeing.

This applies to the three thousand continents of Jambudvīpa, including the four great oceans, the Sahā world-system, and all realms of existence throughout the ten directions, as well as all sentient beings—all are, in truth, the untainted, wondrous mind of enlightened clarity.
It is only through the false nature of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing that these delusions arise.
Illness arises falsely through the conjunction of conditions; it dies falsely through the conjunction of conditions.

If one can distance oneself from all conditions of conjunction as well as non-conjunction, then one will further eliminate the causes of birth and death, perfecting the nature of Bodhi which is neither born nor extinguished—the pure fundamental mind, whose original enlightenment is eternally abiding.

Tong said: "It is easy to reveal delusion by means of an eye ailment, whereas it is difficult to reveal delusion by means of miasmic evils; therefore, he uses the individual karma (*bhedakarma*) as an analogy for the collective karma (*sabhāgakarma*).

Furthermore, within the collective karma, the delusion of miasmic evils is easy to recognize, but the illusory causes of disease within the various realms of outflows (*āsrava*) are in fact difficult to believe;
thus, he uses what is easy to illustrate what is difficult. As for the mountains, rivers, and lands that are perceived..."
Together with the ten classes of sentient beings in the world, although they belong to the realm of delusion, they are all equally the enlightened, luminous, and untainted wondrous mind.
This is called "wondrous" because it is identical to things yet not a thing; identical to objects yet not an object.

However, when one turns away from enlightenment and unites with the sensory dust, one becomes tainted. To be tainted is to be turned by external objects, which is the same as being like those suffering from eye-disease or optical illusions. If...

Turning one's back on the dust of delusion and uniting with awakening, one is fundamentally without outflows (*anāsrava*). Being without outflows, one is able to transform objects and become identical to those free from cataracts;
this is the same single luminosity of awakening. Being without outflows is the pure fundamental mind, which is the eternally abiding original awakening.

Having outflows is to be deluded regarding the truth and pursue the false, transmigrating through birth and death. Through the conjunction of conditions, there is false birth; through the conjunction of conditions, there is false death. This is as previously stated.
In this state, the turning of karma corresponding to one's actions occurs.

Fundamentally, because true suchness and delusion are in union, yet we speak specifically of "delusion," it is because true suchness is in a state of confusion. Those who are in union with these [elements] transmigrate within the triple world;
those who are not in union belong to the naturalistic non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) who hold views of non-arising and non-ceasing. This [distinction between] union and non-union...
The conjunction of these two conditions constitutes the root cause of birth and death; collectively, they form deluded views and false attachments.

If these deluded views are extinguished, there remains only the single original enlightenment (*prakṛti-bodhi*). It is like when the eye disease of *taimira* is cured: there remains only the single clear and bright eye.
Is this not the perfect nature of Bodhi, free from arising and ceasing? Even upon reaching the perfection of Bodhi, one must still maintain that faith and vision are already transcended.
"Seeing seeing cannot reach it. Xuan Sha ascended the hall and said: "I now ask you all: what matter do you take charge of?
In what world do you establish yourself and sustain your life? Can you discern this?
If you cannot discern it, it is just like pressing on the eyes and seeing flowers; as soon as you see things, you err. Do you know? What you see right before you now—"

The existence of mountains, rivers, and the great earth; form, emptiness, light, and darkness; and all such various things—all are but the illusory manifestations of a weary delusion, termed inverted perceptions.
Now, one who leaves the household life, recognizes the mind, and penetrates the fundamental source is therefore called a śramaṇa.
Since you have now shaved your head, donned the robes, and assumed the appearance of a śramaṇa, you must immediately possess that which benefits both yourself and others.
This is another portion. Look at it now: it is entirely pitch-black, like a vast expanse of ink. One cannot even save oneself; how then could one possibly save others?
O worthy ones, the matters of the Buddha-dharma involve profound causes and conditions. Do not treat them with indifference or as mere trifles.
Do not gather together to engage in idle chatter or miscellaneous talk, wasting time in pursuit of profit. Time is difficult to obtain; it is truly a pity. Great!
"O man! Why do you not examine yourself? Look at what this matter is! As for the ancestral vehicle of the Buddhas from of old—it is the crown lineage of all Buddhas.
Since you are unable to take responsibility for it, I have used expedient means to advise you:
simply follow the gate of Kāśyapa and proceed directly beyond. This one gate transcends the causes and effects of ordinary beings and sages; it transcends the..."
The ocean-world-realm of Lu Miaozhuangyan transcends the expedient gates of Śākyamuni.
From the very beginning, throughout eternal kalpas, not a single thing has been taught to you as something for your eyes to see. Why do you not urgently investigate and grasp it yourself?
Do not say, "I shall wait for three or two lifetimes to accumulate pure karma. O worthy one, what is this matter of the *zongcheng* (the essential vehicle)?
You cannot depart by means of diligent effort or adornment; you cannot depart through the knowledge of others' minds or past lives.

Do you understand? Consider this: when Śākyamuni appeared in the world, he performed all manner of transformations and expounded the twelve teachings like pouring water from one vessel into another, creating a grand display of Buddhist ritual activity. Yet, within this very gate, not a single point of that can be used.
One cannot employ even the slightest artifice. Do you understand? It is like a dream; it is also like the prattle of one asleep. A śramaṇa should not show his head.
It is not the same as a dream, for he has recognized it. Do you understand? To recognize it is to be a person of great liberation and great penetration.
Therefore, he transcends the ordinary and surpasses the sages; he is born beyond birth and leaves death behind. He is free.
Because you are detached from cause and effect, you transcend Vairocana and surpass Śākyamuni; you cannot be deceived by the causes and effects of ordinary beings or sages.

Nowhere can anyone recognize you—do you understand? Do not merely remain attached to the love-net of birth and death, for you will be bound and carried away by good and evil karma, leaving you no freedom.
Even if you were to refine your body and mind until they are as empty as space, even if...

When you reach a state of lucidity, clarity, and profound stillness that does not waver, you have not yet emerged from the *vijñāna-skandha* (the aggregate of consciousness). The ancients called this "like a rushing torrent of water";
because the flow is so rapid, one is unaware of it and falsely perceives it as tranquility. If you practice in this manner, you will never transcend the boundaries of saṃsāra;
as before, you will continue to be driven by the cycle of rebirth. Therefore it is said: "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent. This applies directly to the Three Vehicles.
Such karmic results are truly fearsome. Without the Eye of the Way, one will never reach ultimate realization.
How can this compare to the ordinary people of this vast world today, who, without expending even a hair’s breadth of effort, suddenly transcend [delusion] and understand the saving of mental energy?
Do you still wish to find joy in this? I urge you to stand firm right now and wait for it to dawn upon you; I shall not require you to apply any further effort.
Refining one's practice: it is not like this now; when else would you wait? Will you consent? He then descended from his seat.
Because Xuansha had read the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and realized the nature of mind, his speech and breath were in every respect in accord with the *Śūraṅgama*.
Having entered into faith through this, he was immediately perfected in the original enlightenment of Bodhi, which is eternally abiding. What, then, is the use of deluded views?
"Is it not so, Ānanda?

Although you have previously realized that the wondrous clarity of fundamental awakening is neither of the nature of causes and conditions nor of spontaneous nature, you have still not clarified that this source of awakening is neither produced through combination nor through non-combination. Ānanda, I shall now further [explain] by means of..."

The external objects have questioned you. You still harbor doubts based on the nature of all worldly delusions and the combination of various causes and conditions, wondering whether the mind that realizes Bodhi arises from such a combination. Yet, as for this wondrous, pure essence of seeing within you now—
Is it in harmony with light? Is it in harmony with darkness? Is it in harmony with openness? Is it in harmony with obstruction? If it were in harmony with light, then observe this light:
when the light appears before you, where would the seeing be intermingled? The characteristics of seeing can be distinguished; what form or image could there be of such an intermingling?
If it is not the seeing, how can it see light? If it is the seeing itself, how can it see the seeing? If the seeing were complete, where would it blend with light?

If the light were complete, it could not blend with the seeing. The seeing must be distinct from the light; if they were mixed, the specific names of their natures as "seeing" and "light" would be lost.
If their natures were lost through mixing, the concept of "blending light" would be meaningless. This applies equally to darkness, openness, and all various obstructions.
It is also like this. Furthermore, Ānanda, as for your wondrous, pure essence of seeing right now:
does it unite with light? Does it unite with darkness? Does it unite with openness? Does it unite with obstruction? If it united with light, then when darkness arrives—
Once the characteristic of light has already ceased, this vision does not conjoin with darkness; how then could it see darkness?
If, when seeing darkness, it does not conjoin with darkness but conjoins with light, then it should not be seeing the light. Since it does not see the light, how can it be said to conjoin with light?
"Clarity is not darkness. That darkness, as well as the state of openness and all manner of obstructions, is likewise so.
Tong said, "Fundamental enlightenment is wondrously luminous; it is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it spontaneous.

Ānanda had previously attained a slight realization that seemed to accord with the teachings on neither causes and conditions nor spontaneity, yet he still clung to the worldly notion that the three lights arise only through external conditions.
The formation of views, as well as doubt and the realization of the bodhicitta, must all arise from the coming together of conditions.
Those worldly views not only perceive light but can also perceive darkness; they do not depend on the condition of light alone.

How much more so for the original enlightenment of bodhi, which is eternally abiding and far removed from seeing—how could it be named through the coming together of conditions? "Coming together" (saṃyoga) is like water.

Earth and clay blend together so that they cannot be distinguished. Now, as for this wondrously pure essence of seeing, how could it be blended with the external objects of light, darkness, penetration, or obstruction?
Seeing is sentient; objects are insentient. They are clearly distinguishable. If these two were blended, what form would they take?
When seeing necessarily sees light, it appears as if they are mixed; yet light does not see itself.
If one perceives only the capacity to see, then there is no admixture. Whatever is subject to admixture must necessarily possess points of incompleteness.
Now, the seeing-part and the perceived-part are each individually complete and fill the entire Dharma-realm; where else could there be room for their blending?
Even if they were capable of being mixed, if one perceives that they are mixed, it cannot be called "seeing," for the perceived-part would then be what is being seen.
If they were mixed, they could not be called "name" and "form"; this seeing would necessarily differ from form and could not be harmonized with it.

To be "joined" is like a box and its lid meeting, adhering so closely that they do not separate. Now, as for this wondrous, pure essence of seeing, it [interacts] with the preceding objects—light and darkness, penetration and obstruction.
What is meant by "conjunction"? If it were conjoined with light, one should not see darkness; yet it is not said that if it were conjoined with darkness, one should not see light.
Since the faculty of vision depends upon four conditions, it is only because it takes light as its object that it sees.

Since it can see darkness even though it is not conjoined with darkness, it should likewise be able to see light even though it is not conjoined with light. If it were conjoined with light, then it would not see [darkness].
This is clear. Since one cannot see light itself, it cannot be said that seeing is conjoined with light. How, then, could it be conjoined with light?

To fully understand that light is not darkness—to see both darkness and light—neither constitutes a conjunction. Thus, this seeing must differ from its objects; it is not something that can be conjoined.
Even this essence of seeing, whether encountering light or darkness, penetration or obstruction, is in every case not the seeing itself. Therefore, it is said:
It is pure. Yet, whether light or darkness, penetration or obstruction, none of these fail to be the seeing; therefore, it is called "wondrous.

As for what is called "wondrous purity," that merely refers to the purity of the physical sense-organ (*rūpa-indriya*), which does not involve delusory objects and is not produced through the combination [of root and object].
How much more so is the fundamental source of seeing and awareness—this is most supremely pure and most supremely wondrous; how could it arise from the combination of the sense-root and its object?
Huhu! Zhangjing ascended the hall and said: "The ultimate truth transcends words, yet people of this age do not understand it.

They strenuously practice other matters, taking them to be spiritual efficacy, unaware that their own nature is fundamentally not an object of the sensory realm; it is this subtle and wondrous gate of great liberation."
All discerning awareness is unstained and unimpeded; such radiance has never ceased or been abandoned.

From past kalpas until the present, it remains eternally without change. It is like the solar disk, which illuminates both the distant and the near; though it reaches all forms, it does not merge with them.
This numinous and wondrous solitary clarity is not produced by artificial refinement; yet because people do not understand this, they grasp at external objects.
It is like an elephant; it is merely like pressing on the eyes and falsely perceiving empty flowers, leading only to self-exhaustion and the wasting of kalpas.
If one can turn the light back upon oneself, there is no second person; every movement and action will not fall short of the true mark (*dharmatā*).

Furthermore, the practitioner Zhītōng of Kōngshì attained sudden realization through contemplating the *Dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā*, and composed two successive verses to express his insight. The first says: "Vast..."
Within the vast expanse of dust, the essence is one suchness; transverse and vertical, intermingling, they seal Vairocana. When the entire wave is water, the wave is not "water";
when the entire water becomes waves, the water itself appears distinct. This is precisely the meaning of non-conjunction (*asaṃyoga*).

It continues: "Objects and self are fundamentally no different; the myriad phenomena are like reflections in a mirror. Clearly and brightly, they transcend the principal and its attendants; perfectly realized, they penetrate the true void. One.
The substance contains manifold dharmas, interlacing within a net of Indra; in this place of infinite layers upon layers, movement and stillness are both perfectly pervasive.
This, moreover, is not a matter of non-harmony.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, as I reflect upon it, this wondrous source of awakening is not in union with the various sense-objects and the mind's thoughts and deliberations?
The Buddha said, "You now say that awakening is not in union. I shall ask you again:
regarding this wondrous essence of seeing which is not in union, is it not in union with light? Is it not in union with darkness? Is it not in union with space?"
Harmony. This is not a harmony that obstructs; it is a harmony that clarifies. If this harmony were not one of clarity, then between vision and light there would necessarily be a boundary.
You should observe closely: where is the light, and where is the vision? Within vision and within light, from what point do they form a boundary?

Ānanda, if within the limit of light there were no vision, then the two would not reach one another, and you yourself would not know the location of the characteristics of light. What boundary could there be?

How could it be established? That darkness and light, as well as all openings and obstructions, are likewise [inapplicable]. Furthermore, this wondrous seeing-essence is not something that comes into conjunction;
does it not conjoin with light, or does it not conjoin with darkness, or does it not conjoin with openness, or does it not conjoin with obstruction?
If it did not conjoin with light, then the nature and characteristics of seeing and light would be mutually contradictory, just as the ear and light do not touch one another at all. Seeing...
Furthermore, since one does not know where the characteristic of light resides, how can one clearly distinguish between what is consistent with reason and what is inconsistent?
This is likewise true for darkness, openness, and all various obstructions.
Tong said: "What Ānanda suspects regarding 'non-conjunction' refers to the two dharmas of the real and the false, which appear not to interpenetrate;
he has not yet been able to harmonize and unify the real and the false. If one were to say they do not conjoin, then there must be a boundary between seeing and light.
If one were to say they do not unite, then the nature and characteristics of seeing and light would be mutually contradictory. Now, in neither case is this so."

Thus, we know it is not a case of non-conjunction. Previously, Ānanda said that one cannot extract the pure vision from before the myriad phenomena, nor can one find a separate self-nature apart from all things. This is roughly analogous [to the present point].
Since he spoke of it as "not a conjunction," he was referring to the wondrous purity of the essence of one's own vision. Because it is pure, it admits no admixture. Furthermore, he said it is not...

This does not refer to a lack of harmony, but speaks solely of the subtlety of the essential spirit (*prajñā*). Because it is subtle, there is nowhere it is not present. The *Yi-hai* (Ocean of Meanings) states:
"One who realizes non-arising understands that the sense objects are the conditions for the mind, and the mind is the cause of the sense objects.

When cause and condition harmonize and combine, illusory appearances then arise. Since they arise from conditions, they necessarily possess no self-nature (*svabhāva*). Why is this? For now, the sense objects..."
Conditions themselves arise depending upon the mind; the mind does not exist as a mind of its own accord, but must depend upon conditions.

Because they depend upon one another, there is no fixed attachment. That which arises from conditions is called "non-arising"; this is not a case of negating the arising from conditions and then asserting non-arising.
Master Shaoshan Shao ascended the hall and said: "It is a ball that cannot be gathered; it is stirred but cannot be dispersed. Sunlight cannot dry it; water cannot rot it. Etcetera.
Leisurely suspended in the great void, it is left entirely to others to gaze upon it with cold indifference.
When Master Bibu was warming himself by the fire, Dao Wu asked him, "What is this? Bibu replied, "Harmony. Dao Wu said, "If that is so, you have escaped right at the head.
Bibu asked, "How long has it been since we last met? Dao Wu then shook his sleeves and departed. One day, Dao Wu...
Returning from outside, Baizhang asked, "Where have you been? I replied, "I went to visit someone.
Baizhang said, "What use is there for these two pieces of skin? I replied, "I borrowed them. Baizhang said, "If he has nothing to lend you, what would you do?
I replied, "It is precisely because he has them that I borrow them. Observe how the various venerable masters raised and proclaimed this point in such a manner.
Is the wondrous enlightenment fundamentally in union with the various sense objects, as well as the thoughts and deliberations of the mind, or is it not in union?
You must possess the eye of wisdom to discern this.
Ānanda, you have still not clarified that all these floating, ephemeral, and illusory phenomena arise from their own place and follow wherever they go.
They are extinguished; they are illusory and false, designated as "characteristics. Their nature is truly the essence of wondrous, enlightened clarity.

Thus, even the five aggregates and six sense bases—from the twelve entrances to the eighteen elements—arise falsely through the conjunction of causes and conditions, and are falsely called "extinguished" when causes and conditions disperse.
They are utterly incapable of knowing that arising and ceasing, coming and going, are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha, which is eternally abiding.
The wondrously luminous, immovable, and all-pervading nature of wondrous True Suchness— within this eternally true and constant nature, one seeks for coming and going,
delusion and enlightenment, and birth and death, yet finds absolutely nothing to be obtained.
Tong said: "This directly reveals the Sudden Gate and points out the path to wondrous Bodhi.

It is within the midst of floating dust and illusory transformations that one realizes True Suchness (Tathatā). Within the nature of True Suchness, one can never find coming or going, delusion or awakening, birth or death.
Among the aggregates, sense bases, and elements, there are only the marks of illusory falsehood; illusion has no self-nature, for it depends upon the True."
It stands like a flower arising in space; its entire substance is space. It is like bubbles arising from water; their entire substance is water.

Therefore it is said that its nature is truly the essence of wondrous enlightened clarity. This essence is the fruit of the Dharmakāya. Because it inherently contains all virtues, it is called the Tathāgatagarbha.

Because it fundamentally has no coming or going, it is called "eternally abiding" (nitya). Because it fundamentally has never tasted [conditioned flavors], it is called "wondrously luminous. Fundamentally...
That which is without arising or ceasing is called "immovable. That which is inherently complete is called "all-pervasive.

Because it is eternally abiding, coming and going cannot be found; because it is wondrously luminous, delusion and awakening cannot be found; because it is immovable, birth and death cannot be found; because it is all-pervasive, it is truly constant.
This is what is meant by the "wondrous nature of True Suchness" (*tathatā*). In reality, it is originally so.
"I have not a single thing. A monk asked Huangbo, "The student does not understand; how will you instruct me, Master?
Huangbo said, "I have no single thing, and from the beginning I have never given a single thing to anyone. Since time immemorial..."
It is simply because you have been pointed toward by others that you seek an accord and seek an understanding; is this not a case where both disciple and teacher fall into royal peril?
You need only know that when for a single thought-moment there is no receiving, this is precisely the absence of a body to receive; when for a single thought-moment there is no thinking.

This is the body of non-conception (*asaṃjñika*), which is definitively without transition or volitional activity. This is the body of non-conditioning (*apratisaṃskāra*), in which one must not engage in deliberation, calculation, or discrimination.
This is the body of non-consciousness (*avijñāna*). Now, as soon as you give rise to a single thought, it is like the twelve links of dependent origination:
ignorance conditions volitional formations, which are both cause and effect; and so on, up to old age and death, which are likewise both cause and effect.

Therefore, although the youth Sudhana sought spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) in one hundred and ten places, he sought them solely within the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).
Finally, he met Maitreya, who in turn directed him to see Mañjuśrī. As for Mañjuśrī:

This is precisely your own fundamental ignorance. If each moment of mind were distinct and separate, and you sought a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) through external means, then every thought would arise and perish in a single instant;
as soon as it perishes, another arises. For this reason, you bhikṣus undergo birth, aging, illness, and death.
From the time you have begun to repay causes and respond to effects, this is simply the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). As for these five aggregates:
These are the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). When not a single thought arises, the eighteen realms (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*) are empty.
This very body is the flower and fruit of Bodhi; this very mind is numinous wisdom, also called the "Numinous Terrace.

If there is any dwelling or attachment, then the body is a corpse, and one is called a "ghost guarding a corpse. If Huangbo’s words were not clarifying that what is called "phenomena" is illusory and false, [how could he have said this]?
"Is its nature truly the wondrously enlightened body of clarity? The Official Haoyue asked Changsha:
"If one has realized it, karmic obstacles are originally empty; if one has not yet realized it, one must surely repay past debts. But what about Venerable Siṃha?"
The Second Patriarch asked, "Why was it that you were able to settle your karmic debts? Shasha said, "Virtuous One, you do not recognize original emptiness.
Yue asked, "What is original emptiness? He replied, "Karmic obstructions are it. Yue asked, "What are karmic obstructions?"

He replied, "It is simply that which is originally empty. Changsha then showed him with a verse: "Provisionally existent, yet fundamentally not existent; Provisionally extinguished, yet also not non-existent.
The meaning of Nirvana as the settling of debts: In its single nature, there is no further distinction.

If Changsha’s words were not clarifying that arising and ceasing, coming and going, are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha—eternally abiding, wondrously luminous, immovable, all-pervading, and the wondrous True Suchness—then they would be nothing more than mere words.

Regarding their natures: Furthermore, while Jia Shan and Ding Shan were traveling together and conversing, Ding Shan said, "If there is no Buddha within birth and death, then there is no birth and death.
Jia Shan said, "If there is a Buddha within birth and death, then one does not become deluded by birth and death."
Neither was willing to concede. Together they went to see Damei. Jia Shan then raised the matter and asked them, "Between the two of you, whose realization is more intimate?
Damei replied, "One is intimate; the other is distant. Jia Shan asked again, "Which one is intimate? Damei said, "Go now."
"He will come tomorrow. The next day, Jiashan went up once more to question him about the plum tree. The Plum Tree said, "Those who are close do not ask;
those who ask are not close. After Jiashan established his own monastery, he remarked of himself, "At that time, I lost an eye.
Does this very case not clarify that within the true permanence of nature, one seeks in coming and going, delusion and enlightenment, and birth and death, yet finds nothing at all?

According to the ancient exegesis, from the section on "Verifying the Mind and Discerning Vision" onwards, there is an extensive refutation of the attachment to persons (*pudgala-grāha*), which corresponds to the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) within *śamatha*.

From this point downward, there is an extensive refutation of the attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*), which corresponds to the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*) within *samādhi*.

Even so, one still remains one stage removed from the direct pointing to the human mind and the realization of Buddhahood through seeing its nature. It has not yet been understood that what Ānanda asked about was the wondrous *śamatha*.
That which has been answered here is the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*). The word "wondrous" is difficult to describe; it is known only by those who have realized it.
Ānanda, why is it that the five aggregates are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness?
Tong said: "The five aggregates (pañca-skandha) are also called the five clusters (pañca-upādāna-skandha). 'Cluster' (skandha) means accumulation; 'aggregate' (skandha) means covering.
They accumulate conditioned phenomena and cover the true nature; therefore, they are collectively termed the 'domain of the five aggregates,' which is extremely difficult to shatter.

This [text] speaks of the 'fundamental Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous true Tathāgata-nature. Is this not to say that one traces back the origin of dependent origination from within the Tathāgatagarbha?"
Does it flow forth? Or rather, does one say that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are all empty, thereby manifesting the Tathāgata’s wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*)?
This belongs to the Sudden Teaching; it is precisely what is referred to above as the Great Dhāraṇī and the various paths of sublime cultivation through Samādhi.
It means that these very five aggregates are the Tathāgatagarbha, and are the wondrous nature of True Suchness—non-dual and without distinction.
They are distinct; therefore, the elimination of the five aggregates does not lack its proper sequence. However, if one speaks in terms of principle, it is sudden awakening.
One must directly perceive that the five aggregates are all inherently unborn and inherently quiescent.

When seeking the characteristics of the five aggregates, they are utterly unobtainable. Furthermore, how could the five aggregates not be True Suchness, and how could True Suchness not be the five aggregates?
A monk asked Guishan An, "Setting aside the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), what is the original body?
An said, "Earth, water, fire, wind, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. The monk said, "These are the five aggregates. An said, "These are distinct from the five aggregates.
He asked again, "When these aggregates have already ceased and those have not yet arisen, what is it like? An said, "These aggregates..."

He did not yet take his leave. [Hui]an asked, "Which one is the Venerable One? [The monk] said, "I do not understand. Hui'an said, "If you understand this aggregate (skandha), you will clearly understand that aggregate.
If you are Hui'an, you may be said to have profoundly understood that the five aggregates are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness."
Ānanda, it is like a person with clear vision who gazes at a bright, cloudless sky. There is only the vast, empty clarity, utterly devoid of anything.
Without cause, that person does not move their eyes, but stares until they become fatigued; then, within the void, they perceive illusory flowers and all manner of other distorted, chaotic forms.
You should know that the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is exactly like this, Ānanda.
These various floating flowers do not come from space, nor do they issue from the eyes. In this way, Ānanda, if they came from space, having come from space, they would return to space.
If there were coming and going, it would not be empty space. If space were not empty, [it would be a contradiction].
It cannot tolerate the arising and ceasing of its own floral characteristics. Ānanda, you should realize this: it does not tolerate Ānanda.

If these flowers emerged from the eyes, then having emerged from the eyes, they would also have to re-enter through the eyes; since the nature of these flowers emerged from the eyes, they ought to possess the faculty of vision.
If there were a faculty of seeing, then as it departed, it would leave the flowers empty in space; upon returning, it should instead obscure the eye itself.

If there were no faculty of seeing, then as it emerged, it would veil the sky; upon returning, it should likewise veil the eye. Furthermore, when you see these flowers, your eyes should be free of any obstruction; why then do you call a cloudless sky "clear and bright eyes"?
Therefore, one should know that the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is empty and false; it is fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.
It is said in general: A verse by Nāgārjuna states: "All phenomena do not arise from themselves, nor do they arise from another;

they do not arise from both together, nor without a cause. Therefore, they are said to be unarisen. Now, as for the statement that all phenomena do not arise from themselves, this is because they depend upon various conditions. They do not [arise] from...
It does not arise from another, because all conditions lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). It does not arise from both together;

for wisdom and cultivation are empty in essence and lack intrinsic nature, being neither conjoined nor dispersed. It does not arise without cause, as it must depend upon awakening and cultivation to manifest, and thus is not spontaneously formed.
Therefore, one should know that this wondrously enlightened, luminous essence is free from all faults and is fundamentally unborn. From the fifth [chapter].
The six sense bases (*āyatana*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), and even the seven great elements—none fail to extensively clarify this meaning.
To realize non-arising is the pure eye; originally there were no flowers. It is through staring that fatigue arises; by turning one's back to the truth and uniting with delusion, one sees flowers.
The flowers have no inherent substance and come from nowhere; one need only remove the cataract from the eye, and the wild flowers vanish.
It subsides of its own accord. If one were to say that these delusory flowers have a source from which they arise, that would be the nature of causes and conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

If one were to say they have no source from which they arise, that would be the nature of spontaneity (*svabhāva*). Now, if we examine their origin: they do not emerge from space, nor do they emerge from the eyes;

thus, it is clear they are not produced by causes and conditions. If they existed spontaneously, then at the very moment one sees the flowers, they should naturally be without obscuration. If they were not...
When one sees flowers due to a cataract, the one who sees those flowers is called "clear-sighted. Seeing the clear and bright sky would, by that logic, be the work of a cataracted eye.
Why then is the clear sky called "clear vision"? These flowers must arise from the cataract; they are certainly not naturally luminous.
Such is the nature of these delusory flowers; the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is likewise so. Fundamentally, all are empty and false; fundamentally, they do not exist.
The self-nature is both form and emptiness; therefore, it is called the fundamental Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness (Tathatā).
Mazu addressed the assembly, saying: "The three realms are mind only. The myriad phenomena and the vast array of forms are all sealed by this single Dharma.
Whatever forms you perceive are all perceptions of the mind. The mind does not exist as a mind of its own accord; it exists because of form. You need only act in accordance with the moment."
Speech is itself phenomena and itself principle; it is entirely without obstruction. The fruit of the path to Bodhi is likewise so:
that which arises in the mind is immediately termed "form. Because one knows form is empty, arising is non-arising. If one understands this meaning, [one attains liberation].
Only then may you dress and eat according to the occasion, nurturing the holy embryo and passing the time with effortless spontaneity. What further matters remain for you?
Having received my instruction, listen to this verse of mine: "The ground of the mind is explained according to the occasion; Bodhi, too, is simply peace."
Phenomena and principle are both unimpeded; that which arises is precisely non-arising. Yunmen addressed the assembly, saying:
"True emptiness does not destroy existence; true emptiness is not different from form. A monk then asked, "What is true emptiness? Yunmen replied, "Do you hear the sound of the bell?
The monk said, "I do. Yunmen said, "When will you ever dream of this? Furthermore, Gaoyuan Ren... [text fragment].
The Zen Master addressed the assembly, saying: "I do not ordinarily wish to dally with the sons and daughters of men regarding the realm before sound or after the phrase.
Why is this? It is because sound is not sound, and form is not form. At that time, a monk asked, "What is meant by 'sound is not sound'?

The Master replied, "Can you call it form? The monk asked, "What is meant by 'form is not form'? The Master replied: [He called out to the monk. "Zhao! The monk responded, "Yes? The Master said, "Where have you been all these years?"
"Can it be called 'sound'? The monk bowed. Ren said, "Tell me, did I speak for you, or did you answer my words?
If one can discern this, there will be a point of entry. Danxia’s verse says: Form is form, and sound is sound;
Where the new oriole sings, the willow smoke is light. Every gate has a path leading to the capital; The three islands slant across the sea moon.

[The Buddha] said, "Clearly! Therefore, know that the nature of the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) is fundamentally the wondrous True Suchness (tathatā). This is precisely to realize the principle of non-arising.
Ānanda, it is like a person whose hands and feet are at ease and whose hundred limbs are in harmony, such that they suddenly forget their very existence;

their nature is neither in conflict nor in accord. For no apparent reason, this person rubs his two palms together against the empty air, and within his hands, he falsely gives rise to [a sensation of fire]."
The various characteristics of roughness, smoothness, cold, and heat—regarding the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), you should know it is likewise so.

Ānanda, these illusory contacts do not come from space, nor do they emerge from the palm. In this way, Ānanda, if they came from space, being able to touch the palm, [they would also touch everything else].
Why does it not touch the body? It cannot be that space selects [a point] to come and touch it. If it were to emerge from the palm, it would not depend on the joining of hands.

Furthermore, because it emerges from the palm, when the hands join, the palm should perceive it; when they separate, the touch should enter the arm, the wrist, and the marrow, such that one should also perceive the traces of its entry.
There must be a conscious mind that knows its emergence and its entry, implying there is a distinct entity within the body that comes and goes.

What need is there to wait for the convergence of cognition and name to be called "contact"? Therefore, one should know that the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is empty and false; it is fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.

It is said in general: within the fundamental nature of the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*), there are originally no sensations; it is only when the mind makes contact with objects and receives those objects into the heart that this is termed [sensation].

It is called "feeling" (*vedanā*). Therefore, the mutual rubbing of two hands is used as a metaphor for the illusory production of various characteristics such as roughness, smoothness, cold, and heat.
Cold and heat are originally non-existent; they exist only because of contact. Thus, it is called "illusory contact," which causes this nature of feeling to arise through causes and conditions.

If it were produced spontaneously, one could say it is not false. Now, since it is neither empty space nor the palm of the hand, it is not produced through causes and conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Since it is only known when the two come together, it is not spontaneous. Being neither produced by causes and conditions nor produced spontaneously, its very substance is quiescent;
it is fundamentally unborn. What else could this be but the wondrous *tathatā* (suchness) nature of the *tathāgatagarbha*? Thus it is said:

He said, "It is subtle; it is receiving yet not receiving. The World-Honored One, because the Brahmacārin Dīrghanakha sought to debate with him, made a preliminary agreement, saying, "If my doctrine falls into error, I shall cut off my own head.
The World-Honored One asked, "What is the fundamental tenet of your doctrine?"
Dazhi said, "I take 'non-acceptance of all things' as my fundamental tenet. The World-Honored One asked, "Do you accept this view or not?

Dazhi shook his sleeves and departed. While walking along the road, he suddenly realized the truth and said to his disciples, "I must return and cut off my own head to apologize to the World-Honored One.
His disciples said, "Since you have achieved victory before the assembly of devas and humans, why would you cut off your head?"
Zhi said: "I would rather have my head cut off before a person of wisdom than achieve victory before an ignorant person.
He then sighed and said: "My doctrine fails in two ways. If this view is accepted, the point of failure is coarse;
if this view is not accepted, the point of failure is subtle. Neither gods, humans, nor those of the Two Vehicles can know where my doctrine falls short."
Only the World-Honored One and the great bodhisattvas know that my argument has fallen into error.

It is fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor is it of spontaneous nature.
It is said in general that perception has no real characteristic; it forms characteristics through the mind, and for this reason it is called "perception" (*saṃjñā*).

When one perceives plums, water flows forth; when one perceives a cliff, acidity arises. The plums have not reached the mouth, yet there is only talk of them. Why does this water come? It is formed [by perception].
It is due to perception (*saṃjñā*). Furthermore, it is like those who speak in a dream—they are not real people—and those who listen—they do not have actual ears.
Yet, upon hearing the mention of sour plums, saliva flows from the mouth. Why does this occur? It is because it is bound by perception.

If this perception were of the nature of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), it would necessarily not exist apart from the plum and the mouth. Now, the speaking does not originate from the plum, and the hearing does not...
From the mouth, water arises within the mouth even though the ears do not emerge from the water; thus, it is clear that this is not [produced by] causes and conditions.
If this perception were of a spontaneous nature (*svabhāva*), then speaking of plums should cause the mouth to become sour, and speaking of a precipice should cause water to flow forth.
Now, each arises according to the seeds of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*); they do not exist without a cause. Thus, it is clear that it is not spontaneous. It is not without cause.
It is conditioned; it is not spontaneous. At the very moment one perceives it, it is non-perception—a single, profound, wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*).

"Quiet! Such a substance of hearing is fundamentally without self-nature. If it were to emerge from emptiness and possess the nature of hearing, it would not be empty space.

Furthermore, if emptiness itself hears, what concern is that for your faculty of hearing? Therefore, you should know that the ear-faculty is illusory; it is fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions, nor is it of a spontaneous nature."
Tong said: "From the eye-faculty to the mind-faculty, all are like flowers in the sky; therefore it is said they are equally the appearance of fatigue produced by staring at the state of Bodhi.
When the ear-faculty is fatigued, sounds arise within the head; when the awakening nature of Bodhi is fatigued, hearing is established within the ear.
That these are produced by delusion is just like flowers in the sky. This hearing is separate from those states of movement and stillness."
The two objects of perception (dust) ultimately have no substance; they exist when the object arrives and cease to exist when the object departs.

This hearing is fundamentally rootless from the start, and is therefore called "false and illusory. Hearing is capable of discerning objects, and thus it does not arise from the objects themselves. Hearing is spiritual while space is inert; thus, it does not emerge from space.
As for the faculty of the ear and the essence of hearing, each has its own specific function. How can it be said that they lack self-nature? For this reason...
When separated from external objects, there is no discrimination. If there were discrimination, it should be possible to point it out;

yet now it cannot be pointed out. Thus we know it has no self-nature (*svabhāva*). When examined in relation to the object, the sense organ, and space, none of them possess a fixed essence that can be apprehended.
This illusory hearing, therefore, is neither produced by causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) nor is it spontaneous (*svayambhū*). This hearing is neither caused by conditions...

It is spontaneous; it is both illusion and reality. If there were something that could be obtained spontaneously through causes and conditions, this hearing would be a phenomenon of arising and ceasing.

Why then would it be called the wondrous nature of True Suchness? A monk asked Xuansha, "I have heard the Master say that the nature of hearing pervades the entire dharma-realm. When Xuefeng beats the drum, why is it not heard here? Xuansha [replied].
He said, "Who knows that which is not heard? Again, a monk asked Caoshan, "What kind of companion must one have in order to constantly hear what has never been heard?
Caoshan said, "One who shares the same single coverlet. The monk said, "This is still the Master’s way of hearing;
how is it that one constantly hears what has never been heard? Caoshan said, "It is because one is not the same as wood or stone. The monk asked, "Which comes first? Which comes after?"

[Ananda] stood behind him. The Mountain [Mahākāśyapa] said: "Have you not heard it said that one constantly hears what has never been heard? Therefore, know that this constant hearing of what was never heard is such that once heard, it is all-pervasive.
Ānanda, it is like a person who pinches their nose tightly; after pinching for a long time, they become fatigued, and then within the nose, they hear a sound."
The sensation of cold. By means of contact, one discriminates between the open and the obstructed, the empty and the solid. Thus it continues even unto various fragrant and foul odors;
together with the nose and its fatigue, these are all but the appearance of exhaustion produced by the staring of Bodhi.

Because of the two kinds of false objects—the open and the obstructed—there arises the faculty of hearing which dwells within, inhaling these objective phenomena; this is called the nature of smelling and hearing. This hearing is ultimately separate from those two objects, the open and the obstructed.
It has no substance. You should know that this hearing does not come from openness or obstruction; it does not emerge from the sense organ, nor is it produced in space. Why is this?

If it came from openness, then when there is obstruction, hearing would cease; how then could one know of the obstruction? If it were dependent on obstruction for its existence, then when there is openness, there would be no hearing;

how then could it perceive fragrance, stench, and other tactile sensations? If it were produced from the sense organ, there would necessarily be neither openness nor obstruction; such is the nature of hearing.

The faculty of the nose has no inherent nature of its own. If it were to emerge from space, then that hearing would naturally turn back to smell your own nose. Space itself possesses the capacity for hearing;

what concern is that for your sense-faculty? Therefore, you should know that the nose-faculty is illusory; it is fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.

The Master said: "Accumulation means stopping. Stopping means contracting the breath so that it neither enters nor exits. Cold arises because of accumulation; without accumulation, it is fundamentally non-existent.

Through accumulation, one comes to know the distinctions between penetration and obstruction, and emptiness and solidity. Based on these penetrations and obstructions, one discriminates between various fragrant and foul odors."
This nature of smelling is, in its entirety, produced through delusion. If there were no obstruction or penetration, where would the nature of smelling reside?
The ear is called the substance of hearing; the nose is called the mechanism of hearing. The magnitude of their respective functions can be seen therein:
the substance is all-pervading, while the mechanism is activated by contact. Nevertheless, the faculty of the nose is illusory and fundamentally cannot be pointed out.
The ultimate source is even more difficult to grasp. A monk asked Chan Master Haiyan of Zhengmi Temple, "What is the single incense burner in the ancient temple?
The Master said, "No one has smelled it throughout the generations. The monk asked, "What of those who smell it?
The Master said, "It reaches none of the six sense faculties. Furthermore, when Baling Jue first arrived at Yunmen, Yunmen said, "Xuefeng and..."
Shangdao opened the door and said, "Dharma has arrived! I ask you, what will you do?
Jian replied, "I have struck the Master’s nostrils. Shangdao said, "The Earth Deity was provoked to anger;
he gave a blow to Mount Sumeru, leaping up to the Brahma Heaven and crushing the nostrils of Śakra. Why then do you hide yourself within the land of Japan?"
Jian said, "Master, do not try to deceive people. Yunmen said, "If you hit my old monk’s nostrils, what then?
Jian was speechless. Yunmen said, "I knew all along that you are merely one who parrots the words of others.
If you can penetrate the lineage of Yunmen’s discourse, it will be like feeling your own nostrils at midnight; you will realize they have been right on your face all along."
Ānanda, it is like a person who uses their tongue to rub against their lips and licks them repeatedly until they become fatigued.

If that person is ill, they perceive a bitter taste; if the person is healthy, there is a slight sensation of sweetness. Through this sweetness and bitterness, the nature of this tongue-root is revealed:

when it is not moving, its quality of neutrality is ever-present. Furthermore, both the tongue and the fatigue are equally the appearance of weariness produced by the staring of Bodhi. Because of the sweetness...
The two kinds of false objects—bitter and bland—arouse cognition which abides in between, absorbing these objective images; this is called the nature of the cognition of taste.
This nature of the cognition of taste, when separated from those two objects of sweetness, bitterness, and blandness, ultimately has no substance.

Thus, Ānanda, you should know that this cognition which tastes bitterness and blandness does not come from sweetness or bitterness, nor does it exist because of blandness, nor does it emerge from the sense organ. It does not [exist]...
“Śūnyatā-jāta, why is this? If sweetness or bitterness arises, then when they are absent, one knows that [the taste] has ceased. How does one know the absence?

If it were to emerge from the absence itself, then as soon as sweetness appears, one would know that [the absence] has perished; how then could one know the two characteristics of sweetness and bitterness?

If it were produced from the tongue, there would necessarily be no objects of sweetness, absence, or bitterness. Thus, one knows that the faculty of taste has no inherent nature (*svabhāva*) from the beginning. If it were to emerge from space, then space itself...”
Taste is not known by your mouth; furthermore, it is space that knows itself—what concern is this for your sense-base? Therefore, you should know that the tongue-base is empty and false;
fundamentally, it is neither caused by conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.

The Master said: "This is the faculty of gustatory consciousness, which perceives sweetness, bitterness, and blandness. Since the sensations of sweet, bitter, and bland are not constant, the consciousness that perceives them likewise changes accordingly.
This consciousness does not come from the sweet, bitter, or bland; nor does it emerge from emptiness. Thus, it is inherently easy to discern.
