Why, then, do you say it does not arise from the tongue? The tongue itself has no taste; therefore, no intrinsic nature can be found. It is simply..."
When contact arises, one knows it is born; when the flavor departs, one knows it ceases. Fundamentally, all is empty and false.
To regard it as existent is like regarding mud as something real, failing to discern its origin. To regard it as nonexistent is likewise clear and immediate. Therefore, it is called "wondrous."
This is not for those who do not know the true taste; it is not worth speaking with them about this.
Once, while Sanzan was performing manual labor picking bracken, Nanquan picked up a single stalk and said, "This is a most excellent offering. Sanzan replied, "It is not only this;
he would pay no heed even to a hundred flavors of rare delicacies. Nanquan said, "Even so, everyone must first taste it before they can say so."
[He] attained [realization]. Xuánjué said, "These are words of mutual seeing; they are not words of mutual seeing.
Tiāntóng’s alternative verse says: "Ask the old teacher Nánquán; everyone eats but a single stalk of vegetable. This may truly be called knowing the flavor.
Ānanda, it is like a person who touches one hand with another; if the coldness of the one is more powerful, the warm hand becomes cold;
if the warmth of the other is superior, the cold hand becomes warm. In this way, through the contact of these joined perceptions, the knowledge of their separation is revealed.
When the momentum of their interaction is established, it arises from the contact of exertion; thus, both the body and the exertion are equally the *bodhi* (awakening) manifested by staring.

The characteristic of effort (*āyāsa-lakṣaṇa*). Based on the two kinds of false objects—separation and union—the faculty of awareness arises from within and absorbs these objective images; this is called the nature of cognitive awareness.
This essence of cognitive awareness, when separated from those two objects of separation and union, as well as opposition and compliance, ultimately has no substance.
Thus, Ānanda, you should know that this awareness does not come from separation or union, nor does it exist through opposition or compliance; it does not emerge from the sense faculties, nor is it...
"Śūnyatā-jāti. Why is this? If [the sense-faculties] come together when they conjoin and are already extinguished when they separate, how can one perceive their separation?

The two characteristics of opposition and compliance are likewise so. If [cognition] were to emerge from the faculties, there would necessarily be no four characteristics of separation, conjunction, opposition, or compliance;

thus, the cognitive awareness of your body would fundamentally lack self-nature. If it were to emerge from space, then space itself would possess cognitive awareness—what connection would that have with your sense-faculties? Therefore, you should..."
One knows that the body enters into emptiness and falsehood; it is fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.
It is generally said: "The touch of contact should exist when there is union and be absent when there is separation; yet, even when separated, it manifests."

Just as with the two types of contact—contrary and compliant—it is only after they have ceased that one knows them. This tactile cognition of the body differs slightly from the cognitions of taste and touch.
When their forces interact, there is a contest of dominance: by applying heat to cold, the cold is made hot; by applying cold to heat, the heat is made cold.
It is like thrusting one's hands and feet into water that is either cold or hot; therefore, it is called "interacting" (shè) with cold and heat.

As these characteristics interact, the two [opposites] are established. It is not through laborious effort that contact reaches this state. When contact is favorable to the body, it is called "conformity" (ānulomika);

when contact is adverse to the body, it is called "opposition" (pratiloma). If there were no four characteristics of separation, union, conformity, and opposition, there would be nothing but this body alone.
And one knows that the nature of touch resides in tranquility. Therefore, it is said that from the beginning there is no self-nature (*svabhāva*).

Thus, this bodily cognition does not arise from objects, nor does it emerge from the sense organs; therefore, it is not produced by causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*). It does not emerge from space; therefore, it is not spontaneous (*svarasataḥ*).

Being neither produced by causes and conditions nor spontaneous is precisely what is called the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā-svabhāva*). The aforementioned seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing—this is indeed...
This refers to the first five consciousnesses. It is the cognition of objects, not the cognition of conceptual discrimination.
It is entirely a manifestation of the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. A monk asked Dongshan: "When cold and heat arrive, how can one avoid them?"
Mount [Shan] said, "Why do you not go to a place where there is neither cold nor heat? The monk asked, "What is the place where there is neither cold nor heat?
Mount Shan replied, "When it is cold, it freezes you to death; when it is hot, it burns you to death. Furthermore, Caoshan asked a monk, "In such heat as this, where do you seek refuge?
The monk said, "I seek refuge within the boiling cauldrons and the glowing furnaces. Caoshan said:
"How can one avoid the boiling cauldrons and glowing coals? The monk replied, "The manifold sufferings cannot reach him.

These are words from within his own house; they emerge as if from a single mouth. Xuedou’s verse says: "Reaching down with the hand is like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high; In 'Correct' and 'Deviant,' why need there be any contrivance?
The ancient palace of lapis lazuli illuminates the bright moon; Yet the clever hound, failing to muster his wit, merely ascends the steps in vain."

Once you have realized this meaning, entering the marketplace with hands hanging down is no different from standing alone on a solitary peak; returning to the source and realizing one's nature is no different from the wisdom of differentiation.
Unless one has profoundly harmonized with the Cao-Dong school, it is not easy to speak of this.
Ānanda, it is like a person who sleeps when weary and awakens from deep slumber; upon encountering sensory objects, there is recollection, and the loss of such recollection is forgetfulness.
These are its inversions. Birth, abiding, change, and extinction—these are drawn in and return within [the mind], never exceeding one another.

What is called the faculty of mental cognition, together with the mind and weariness, is likewise a state of fatigue produced by the fixed gazing of Bodhi. It arises because of these two kinds: birth and extinction.

Regarding false objects: the aggregate of cognition abides in the center, drawing in internal objects; seeing and hearing flow against the current, reaching places where the flow does not reach—this is called the nature of awakened cognition.
This nature of awakened cognition is devoid of the two objects of waking and sleeping, arising and ceasing; it ultimately has no substance.
Thus, Ānanda, you should know that this root of awakened cognition does not come from waking or sleeping, nor does it exist through arising or ceasing. It does not [arise] from...
It does not emerge from the sense organs, nor is it born from emptiness. Why is this? If it came from waking, then it would cease immediately upon sleep; with what, then, would one sleep?

If it must exist at the time of birth, then it would be non-existent upon death; who then would undergo death? If it came from death, then birth would be non-existent; who would know of the one being born?
If it emerged from the sense organs, then the two states of waking and sleeping would merely be the opening and closing of the body. Apart from these two...

This cognizing subject is like a flower in the sky; it ultimately lacks intrinsic nature. If it were born from emptiness, it would itself be the cognition of emptiness—what concern would it have for your sense-faculties?
Therefore, you should know that the mind-faculty is illusory; fundamentally, it is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.
The Master said: "The scenes that appear in a dream exist because of sleep; they are entirely illusory.

Once one has awakened, if one does not realize they were illusory, but instead looks back upon them with recollective thought and regards them as real, this is called 'inversion. The characteristics of dharmas are likewise so:

when the moving mind manifests a scene, it is already false and delusive. Yet the *vijnana* of discerning phenomena does not realize it is a mere object, but remembers it as truly existent—this is the same."
This is called "inversion. It arises when one remembers and ceases when one forgets. Yet the four characteristics—arising, abiding, change, and cessation—are vividly present, flowing incessantly.
Moment by moment, they do not overlap or transcend one another; this is the faculty of mind (*manas*).
When the mind does not engage with objects, it is the same whether awake or asleep. If one seeks the characteristic of waking or sleeping, it cannot be found even there, let alone where birth exists.

Is it not the characteristic of abiding, changing, and ceasing? It is simply that the mind takes phenomena as its object; by inhaling and habituating these within, one returns to this state of weariness.
Thus, although awakening (*bodhi*) does not perceive, the movement [of consciousness] functions as the mind, and both alike return to weariness. The *Zongjing* says:
"When the eyes and other senses grasp external objects, they flow instantaneously into the stage of the mind. Moving from the external into the internal is called 'flowing against the current'."
This means that when the mind has an object of perception, it is like being awake and surveying sensory objects; thus, memory arises.

As for "the flow not reaching the ground," this refers to times of mental obscurity when the sense faculties do not perceive objects; consequently, external objects do not flow into the ground of the mind.
Furthermore, the mind has no object of perception; thus, when one sleeps, memory is lost and forgotten, which is what is meant by "cessation.

To allocate [the states of waking and sleeping] in this manner seems rather forced. Moreover, within sleep there are dreams, and within waking there is forgetfulness; each possesses the characteristics of arising and ceasing.
How can one then claim that waking belongs exclusively to arising and sleep exclusively to cessation? I, the fool, say that regarding the ears and eyes—
Seeing and hearing accord with and reach outward; yet the seeing and hearing of the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) flow back inward.

At the very moment it draws in internal objects, as if the eyes were seeing and the ears were hearing—whether ascending to the heavens or submerging in the abyss—it flows into realms beyond the reach of ordinary seeing and hearing.
This is possible only through the mental faculty, not through the ear.

This is within the range of visual perception. However, each of the five sense organs has its own specific locus, whereas the mental faculty (manas) is formless, merely relying upon the phenomena of waking and sleeping, or arising and ceasing.
Apart from these phenomena of waking and sleeping, arising and ceasing, there is no way to perceive the mind; therefore, it is not so called.
If it were produced from the sense organs, there would necessarily be no awakening or sleep, nor arising or ceasing.

However, if it were to emerge from the organs, then the two states of waking and sleeping would merely follow the opening and closing of the body, rather than opening and closing according to the will. Since the mind is already distinct from these two physical entities, [it cannot be derived from them].
This cognizer, though subject to arising and ceasing, is like a flower in the sky. To what could it possibly cling to manifest my meaning?
Since the mind is already detached from form, and form is likewise detached from the mind, there will necessarily be no signs of waking, sleeping, arising, or ceasing.

How, then, could there be any inherent nature? Therefore, it is incorrect to say that [cognition] arises from the sense organs. The two characters "opening" and "closing" merely describe waking and sleeping.
These two aspects are most subtle. In awakening, the form opens; in sleep, the form merges.

This cycle of awakening and sleep, of birth and extinction, is precisely where the mind resides; therefore, it is called "sleep" and "the cessation of reception. It does not necessarily depend on cognition.
This very awareness neither arises from causes and conditions nor arises spontaneously; it is the very essence of non-abiding.
How could this not be called the wondrous nature of True Suchness? Initially, Yangshan asked Muzhou: "What is the true dwelling place of the Buddha? Muzhou said:
"By means of the wondrous state where thought is non-thought, one returns to the infinite subtlety of the enlightened mind. When thought is exhausted, one returns to the source;
nature and characteristics abide eternally, and phenomena and principle are non-dual—the True Buddha is thusness. Under these words, Yangshan attained realization.
Regarding sudden enlightenment: later, the monk Siyi asked Yangshan, "In the Zen school’s sudden enlightenment, what is the ultimate meaning of entering the gate?
Yangshan said, "This meaning is extremely difficult. If one possesses the highest faculties and supreme wisdom within the ancestral lineage,"

Upon hearing it once, they awaken to a thousand truths and attain the Great Dharani. However, those whose faculties are dull and whose wisdom is inferior will find themselves utterly bewildered if they do not practice dhyāna and samādhi.
He asked: "Aside from this single path, is there no other way of entry?"
Mount said, "Yes. [The monk] asked, "How is it that this is so? Mount said, "Where are you from? [The monk] replied, "I am a man from Youzhou.
Mount said, "Do you still think of that place? [The monk] replied, "I always think of it. Mount said, "That which is able to think is the mind; that which is thought of is the object.
There, there are pavilions and gardens, and crowds of people and horses. Now, turn back and contemplate the very mind that is thinking."
“Are there still many other such things? He replied, “When I arrived here, I did not see anything at all.
The Mountain said, “The stage of faith is indeed this; the stage of the person is not yet this. He asked, “Apart from this, is there another meaning or not?
The Mountain said, “To say there is another or there is not another is already inadequate. He asked, “Having arrived here, what is it that is ‘this’? The Mountain—
He said: "Based on your understanding, you have only attained one mystery. You may sit and don your robes, but look back for yourself later. Tiantong’s verse says:
"Encompassing all without exterior, Vast and unobstructed, it is profound. Gateways and walls rise tier upon tier; Locks and bolts multiply in layers.
Wine is ever full, yet the guests lie down; Food is plentiful, yet the farmers slumber. Suddenly emerging from emptiness— The wind stirs the wondrous."
"Wings! Treading upon the vast blue sea, thunder escorts the roaming dragon. This verse concerns the hundred-foot pole; one must advance further.
One must not cling to the state of awakening and consider it sufficient. Yet, in truth, not a single word is seen here.
One can only empty the faculty of thought; even so, the True Buddha’s suchness remains exceedingly far away.
Furthermore, Ānanda, as for how the twelve bases (*āyatana*) are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrous true nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*):
[The Master] replied: "In the initial section on the five aggregates (*skandha*), the method of analogy was employed to shatter their clinging attachments.

Since the five aggregates are fundamentally empty, no analogy would have sufficed to manifest this truth. Next, in the section on the six sense bases (*āyatana*), provisional matters were pointed out to reveal their delusive characteristics."
This enters into fundamental delusion; therefore, it uses delusion to lead from delusion, which can be understood by analogy.

Now, from the twelve bases (*āyatana*) up to the seven elements (*dhātu*), [the teaching] merely indicates the *tathāgatagarbha* within the objects currently perceived through seeing and hearing—namely, in every land and every atom.

This is to be intensely burning and uninterrupted. The Third Patriarch said: "The six sense objects are not evil; they are identical to perfect enlightenment. One truly perceives this when one understands it thus.
Zen Master Shan-ning of Jinshan ascended the hall and, looking over the assembly, said: "The ancients said that when [the mind] is in the eye, it is called seeing;
in the ear, it is called hearing; in the nose, it is smelling fragrance; in the tongue, it is discourse; in the body, it is sensation."
Contact. It is an object of the mental faculty (*manas*). Although it is thus, one sees only the sharp point of the awl, but does not see the square head of the chisel.

If it were Mount Golden Mountain, it would not be so: there would be eyes that could not see, ears that could not hear, a nose that did not know fragrance, a tongue that did not discourse, a body that did not perceive touch, and a mind that did not take objects as its support. One.
"Mindfulness-correspondence. The liberation of the six sense-faculties. I venture to ask the assembly of Chan masters: tell me, is this the same as what came before, or is it different?
Is there any monk with eyes to come forth and deliver a message? If not, I shall once again break it down for you all, layer by layer:
when opened wide, it allows the passage of private carriages and horses; when clenched shut, not even a hair’s breadth can pass."
It remains so. If one is a true master of the battle, one may freely endure being pierced and stripped by right and wrong.
These words, however, repeatedly provide a commentary that shatters this very passage of the scripture.
Ānanda, you should now observe this Jeta Grove and these various springs and ponds. What do you think?
Do these forms arise and are seen by the eye, or does the eye arise with the characteristics of form? Ānanda, if it were the case that the eye-faculty gives rise to the characteristics of form...
If one perceives emptiness as not being form, the nature of form should be dissolved. Once dissolved, all things are revealed to be utterly non-existent.

Since the characteristics of form no longer exist, who can perceive the substance of emptiness? Emptiness is likewise so. Furthermore, if the sensory object of form were to give rise to visual perception, then observing emptiness as not being form would follow suit.

Upon seeing, it immediately vanishes; when vanished, it is utterly non-existent. Who then can clarify the nature of emptiness and form? Therefore, one should know that vision and both form and emptiness have no location.
Thus, form and vision—these two locations—are illusory; fundamentally, they are neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of a spontaneous nature.
The Master said: "In the previous section on the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), although the objects were used for contrast, the primary intent lay in the faculties (*indriya*).

Now, in the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), although both faculties and objects are mutually refuted, the primary refutation lies in the objects. In the subsequent eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*), the focus is specifically on refuting consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Previously, it was stated that 'all are equally the state of exhaustion produced by staring into the Bodhi-mind,' which began the discourse from the perspective of the faculties. This [present passage] says:"
Observe this Jeta Grove and its various springs and ponds. If visual perception arises from form, then it must not arise from emptiness.
Why is it that one clearly perceives form and yet also clearly perceives emptiness?
Furthermore, if visual perception produces the characteristic of form, it must be unable to produce the characteristic of emptiness. Why is it that it manifests both form and emptiness?
Speaking from this perspective, the eye cannot produce form; the eye is itself quiescent—how could it have anything to do with form? Form cannot produce the eye;
form is itself quiescent—how could it have anything to do with the eye? It is simply by means of empty form that the sensory object of form is spontaneously dissolved.
Vision and form are both empty, and neither has a location. Form being empty, vision is also empty.
Form and perception are both empty. Who is the cause and condition? Who is the spontaneous nature? Is this not what is called the nature of *tathatā* (suchness)?
Long ago, Yangshan pointed to a snow lion and asked, "Is there anyone who can pass through this form? Yunmen said:
At that moment, one should have simply pushed him over. Xuedou said, "He only knows how to push him over; he does not know how to help him up. Fojue’s verse says:
"A single color, nothing surpasses pointing it out to people; Within a world of white silver, he groans repeatedly.
Transcendently he pushes him over and then helps him up; How can this compare to the new warmth of the spring breeze? Tiantong’s verse says: "One down, one up..."

Arise! Snow-Court Lion. Be cautious in avoiding transgression while harboring benevolence; be courageous in action while discerning righteousness. When clear light shines upon the eyes, one is as if lost in one’s home;
when clarity turns the body, one falls back into a position. For the monk, there is nothing to rely upon.
Dying together and living together—what "this" and what "that"? The warm news breaks through the plum blossoms as spring arrives at the cold branches; the piercing wind strips away the leaves.
"The leaves are clear amidst the autumnal floodwaters. Wansong says: "Since it is called 'color,' it must confront the eye.
As for the color that transcends whiteness—only that which is colorless does not confront the eye. This is why Yunmen said, 'At that very moment, I would have pushed him over.
If you recognize it in the place where ultimate whiteness is not white, you are precisely falling into the realm of formlessness."
This is why Xuedou specifically pointed out a separate, living path: at the very point where [the staff] was knocked over, he instead commanded it to be raised up.
Foyan said, "If one attempts to support and raise it from this place, how could there be any sense of order?

Even regarding matters of 'one color' (monochromatic unity), the various venerable masters still insisted on breaking them down completely; how much more so for the myriad phenomena currently before one's eyes?"
"Ānanda, listen further to this: within this Jeta Grove, when the meal is prepared, the drum is struck; when the assembly gathers, the bell is tolled.

Regarding the sounds of these bells and drums, which follow one after another in succession—what do you think? Do these sounds come to the side of the ear, or does the ear go to the place where the sounds are?
"Ānanda, if these sounds were to come to the side of the ear, it would be as if I were to go to the city of Śrāvastī to beg for alms."
In the Jeta Grove, there is no such thing as a "self. This sound must reach Ānanda’s ears;
Maudgalyāyana and Kāśyapa would not hear it simultaneously, let alone the one thousand two hundred and fifty śramaṇas therein who all hear the bell at once.

We have come together to this place of eating. If your ear were to go to the location of that sound, then just as when I return to dwell in the Jeta Grove, I would no longer be present in the city of Śrāvastī;
yet when you hear the sound of a drum, your ear has already gone to the place where the drum is being struck.
The bells sound together, yet they cannot be heard all at once; how much more so for the various sounds of elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep within them?
If there were no coming or going, there would likewise be no hearing. Therefore, one should know that both the faculty of hearing and the sounds have no location.
"Then it would follow that both the hearing and the sound are false in two places; they would fundamentally not be produced by causes and conditions, nor would they possess an inherent nature.
He continued, "It is like this: when I beg for food in the city of Śrāvastī, I do not exist within the Jeta Grove.
By analogy, when a sound comes to the ear, there is no sound elsewhere. Why, then, do one thousand two hundred śramaṇas hear it all together?"
Just as when I reside within the Jeta Grove, I am not present in the city of Śrāvastī; this is like the ear going to the place where sound is, such that the ear is no longer in other places.
How then can it be that [the ear] knows all the various sounds of elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep?
If there were no coming or going, one would fall into a state of inert emptiness. When hearing is not established as the object of meaning, this sound and this hearing, when pressed, leave no trace;
what location could they have? Yet, when left to themselves, they are all-pervasive and penetrate every point. If considered as causes and conditions, there is nothing upon which they depend;
if considered as spontaneous, there is nothing from which they arise. Thus, even this delusion is none other than the true essence. Therefore:

This is called the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Once, while Xuansha was in the midst of his formal meditation session, he heard the sound of a swallow and said, "He speaks profoundly of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) and skillfully expounds the essential teachings. He then descended from his seat.

At that time, a monk requested further instruction, saying, "I do not understand. Xuansha said, "Go away! Who would believe you? Later, when Baoci ascended the seat and heard the cry of a cuckoo, he asked:
"What sound is 'Seng'? he asked. "The sound of a sparrow," [the monk] replied. Ciji said, "If you wish not to incur the karma of the Avīci Hell, do not slander the Tathāgata’s True Wheel of Dharma.
He then descended from his seat. That all sounds are the Buddha's voice is indeed easy to understand.
Xuansha said: "In the bell there is no sound of the drum; in the drum there is no sound of the bell. The bell does not intersect with the drum;
every phrase is without before or after. How do you understand this? This is the essential meaning of dependent origination as non-arising.
To awaken to this, then what is called the essential dharma of the true mark (dharmatā) can be seen."
Ānanda, you should again smell this sandalwood in the incense burner.
If even one *zhu* of this incense were burned, its fragrance would be smelled simultaneously throughout the forty *li* within the city of Śrāvastī. What do you think?
Does this fragrance arise from the sandalwood tree, does it arise from your nose, or does it arise from space? Ānanda, if this fragrance were to arise from your nose...
If it is said that [the fragrance] is produced by the nose, it should emerge from the nose; yet the nose is not sandalwood—how could there be the scent of sandalwood within the nose?

If you say that you "smell the fragrance," then the fragrance must enter the nose and emerge from within the nose; to say one "smells" it is therefore illogical. Furthermore, if it were produced in empty space, [it would have no relation to the nose].
If emptiness were eternal, then fragrance should also be eternally present. Why, then, rely upon burning this withered wood in an incense burner?

If the fragrance arises from the wood, then this fragrant substance, having been burned to become smoke, would cause the nose to perceive it only by encountering the smoke. Now, as that smoke rises into the air, [the fragrance is lost].
It has not yet reached a great distance; within forty li, how is it that [the scent] is already smelled?

Therefore, one should know that the nose and smelling, as well as the scent and the act of smelling, are both without a fixed location. These two locations are false and illusory; fundamentally, they are neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of a spontaneous nature.
Tong said, "This fragrance and the one who smells it are neither the nose, nor space, nor the wood; thus, the locus of the fragrance has no reality.
Yet, within a distance of forty li, it is smelled simultaneously by all. This extraordinary power of the fragrance is likewise inconceivable."
The *Fahua* [Sutra] refers to "six-zhu" incense; its value is equal to that of the Sahā world. The *Zaopo lun* states:
"Regarding the *ulūka-candana* tree, *ulūka* is the name of a snake and *candana* is a fragrant tree.
This clarifies that this snake is most venomous and constantly suffers from heat-poison; by coiling its body around this fragrant tree, its toxic vapors are immediately stilled."

This indicates that if there are sentient beings who, upon hearing it said that both mind and objects are empty—that wood has no essence or characteristics, no location, and that not a single dharma can be apprehended—believe and enter this realization, then all the poisonous vapors of their afflictions will naturally become purified.
Master Xiangyan Xianshen’s verse says: There is a single phrase, entirely beyond the reach of rules; if you attempt to deliberate upon it, [you miss it].
Carrying a companion along, one cannot tread upon it; if one fails to examine its place of origin, the affairs of a lifetime of study will remain unaccomplished.
How earnestly one embraces the sandalwood tree—its source indeed lies herein. Master Zhigong’s way was such that he spent his days picking incense and selecting firewood.

They do not know that the body itself is the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). Tiantong [Jingqing] took up this point and said: "What limit is there for these fellows who dally with their spirits? Xuansha said:
"All day long they handle incense and choose firewood, yet they do not know what the true site of enlightenment is. Tiantong took up this point and said: "How extraordinary!
An eighty-year-old elder entering the examination hall—this is no child's play. But tell me, where does the point of benefit and harm lie?
In what place is there wisdom? Whether one has wisdom or lacks it, they differ by thirty *li*.
Yet, being equally the functioning of the unarisen, there is nevertheless a distinction as slight as a hair’s breadth; those with wisdom discern this.
Ānanda, you regularly carry the alms bowl among the assembly during the two times of the day. In that interval, you may encounter ghee, curd, or clarified butter, which are called superior flavors.
What do you think? Does this flavor arise from space, does it arise within the tongue, or does it arise within the food?
Ānanda, if this flavor were to arise in your tongue, then while it is in your mouth, there would be only one tongue.
At that time, the tongue has already formed the perception of the flavor of ghee. Upon encountering black rock honey, it ought not to shift.
If it does not shift, it cannot be said to know flavors. If it does shift, the tongue is not a single entity; how then could there be many flavors known by a single tongue?
If the cognition of taste arises from food, yet food itself possesses no consciousness, how can it know of itself? Furthermore, if food knows for itself, it would be identical to another's food;
what concern would that have for you? As for the cognition of names and flavors, if they arise from space, then as you consume empty space, what flavor could it possibly have?
If this emptiness were to manifest as a salty taste, then since it would salt your tongue, it would also salt your face; consequently, the people of this world would be like fish in the sea.
Constantly experiencing saltiness, they would not perceive the existence of sweetness; and if they did not recognize sweetness, they would likewise have no awareness of saltiness.
There would necessarily be no object of cognition. What, then, would be called "taste"? Therefore, you should know that taste, the tongue, and the act of tasting are all without location;
thus, both tasting and taste are equally illusory. Fundamentally, they are neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of a spontaneous nature.
Tong said: "This discrimination of flavor-nature does not arise from emptiness, nor does it arise from the tongue; this is easily understood. But why say it does not arise from the food?
Food has no consciousness and cannot say of itself, 'I am savory' or 'I am bitter. Yet the discrimination between the savory and the bitter belongs to the faculty of the tongue.
Furthermore, the tongue has no fixed substance; it shifts immediately upon encountering flavors. From this, one can know the nature of taste."

Taste itself; the tongue itself is the tongue. Both are utterly still. To know that both the tongue and taste are equally still is to realize that which is neither caused by conditions nor produced spontaneously, but is the wondrous *tathatā* nature of the *tathāgatagarbha*. — Chan Master Yin of Shendeng.
Once, while traveling with a group of monks through the region of Xiangmian, one monk was expounding upon the *zongcheng* (the vehicle of the fundamental doctrine) with considerable agility.
At that time, they were having a field meal at a mountain inn where the provisions had been prepared; however, the monk continued his discourse without ceasing.

Hu鼎 said, "The three realms are mind-only; the myriad dharmas are consciousness-only. 'Consciousness-only' and 'mind-only'—are these the words of what kind of person? Is it the Dharma? The monk replied, "The Dharma..."
The Master said, "Eye and speech. Ding asked, "What is the meaning of this? The monk replied, "Because it is mind-only, the sense organs and their objects do not reach one another;
because it is consciousness-only, sounds and forms surge forth. Ding asked, "Are the tongue and flavors not also organ and object? The monk replied, "They are.
Ding took some vegetables with his chopsticks and placed them in his mouth; masticating them, he spoke, "What do you mean by 'mutual penetration'? Those present were struck with amazement.
However, the monk was unable to answer. Yantong said, "The joy of the journey does not mean one has reached home;
insight that penetrates the subtle is not yet called seeing the Way. One must practice authentically and awaken authentically.
King Yama does not fear much talk. The monk bowed and withdrew. Once, while eating lychees, Xuansha asked the assembly, "As for this lychee..."
"It is so red. It is so crimson. How do you all understand this? If you say it is a single color, that is again a state of dull stagnation.
If you say it consists of many colors, you merely fall into the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism. How do you all understand this?
Yantao said, "It is simply that the Master himself makes such distinctions. Sha said, "This is a dull and ignorant person! Thereupon, he struck him.
"What is this engagement? Chongji said, "It all comes down to being but a single color.
Yunshu Sha said, "If everything is thus muddled and indistinct, when will there ever be an end? He then turned to ask Jiaoran, "How would you say it?
Jiaoran said, "One must not fail to recognize the lychee. Sha said, "It is simply the lychee. He added, "All of you..."
Many times here in my presence, people speak in this manner; they fail to distinguish between the black and the white, and they do not recognize good from ill fortune.
I have already told you that when the function is applied, the pivot does not shift. Why do you merely engage in dialogue? What connection is there?
When the ancients took even a single drink or a single meal, they were intent on illuminating the matter that transcends the ordinary. Often...
It is thus. How could it be that this is merely a matter of verbal dexterity? One must have actual realization before one can meet with those of clear vision.
Ānanda, you regularly rub your head with your hand every morning. What do you think? Regarding this act of rubbing, who is it that knows it?
That which is capable of touching—does it reside in the hand, or does it reside in the head? If it resides in the hand, then the head would be without cognition;
how, then, could there be contact? If it resides in the head, then the hand would be useless; how, then, could it be called contact?

If it were present in each separately, then you, Ānanda, should have two bodies. If the head and the hand both produce contact from a single source, then the hand and the head should be considered as one.
If they were of one substance, then contact would not be established. If they were of two substances, for whom would contact exist?
If it exists in the subject, it is not in the object; if it exists in the object, it is not in the subject. It is not logical that empty space should enter into contact with you.

Therefore, you should know that both the perception of touch and the body have no location. Thus, both the body and touch are equally false; fundamentally, they are neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they self-existent.

However, regarding this nature, it is said in general: this clarifies that the nature of contact is empty and false; it exists in the subject but not in the object, it exists in the object but not in the subject, and it exists in neither subject nor object.
That which is contact is itself the nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*). The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "Such a self-nature is like an illusion..."
Dreams are like shadows and like reflections; none of them are truly established. By the nature of *tathatā* (suchness), phenomena naturally follow conditions;
yet while they follow conditions, they naturally return to that nature. When following conditions, there appears to be manifestation, just as when one contemplates illusory phenomena.
It exists though it does not exist, like observing the objects of a dream. It is seen though it is not seen, like observing a reflection in water.
It neither emerges nor enters, like observing an image in a mirror. It is neither internal nor external, because it lacks intrinsic nature and follows conditions.
The principle is not established because all things lack intrinsic nature in accordance with conditions. The phenomena are not established.
Since both principle and phenomena are not established, then all dharmas are likewise unestablished. It is just as, for example, when a person makes a fist toward another person in a dream:
there is no lack of contact, yet ultimately, what is the agent and what is the object? Therefore, all dharmas are exactly like this.
Baofu saw a monk approaching; he struck a pillar with his staff and then struck the monk on the head.
The monk made a sound of pain. Baofu said, "Why does that one not feel pain? The monk had no reply. Xuangjue provided this substitute response:
"He is greedy for the walking staff. Furthermore, Chan Master Baojue once asked Xia Yi, the Commissioner of the Transport Office: "Tell me your sentiment."
"To be of one essence with the insentient. At that time, there was a dog lying beneath the incense table.

[Zhaozhou] then struck the incense table with a ruler and hit the dog, saying, "The dog has sentience and thus departs; the incense table is insentient and thus remains. How can they become one essence?
[The monk] leaned against him, unable to respond. Baoyue said, "As soon as you enter into discursive thought, it immediately becomes a superfluous dharma. Previously—
This is the essential meaning transmitted from one to another by those known as sages.

Ānanda, regarding the three natures—wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate—that you constantly take as objects within your mind, which serve as the principles for the arising and ceasing of phenomena:
do these phenomena arise from the mind itself, or do they exist separately from the mind in some other location? Ānanda, if they were identical to the mind...

Dharmas are not objects of the senses; they are not the objects of the mind’s perception. How, then, could they constitute a sense-field (*āyatana*)? If they existed as distinct locations apart from the mind, then would the intrinsic nature of dharmas be cognizable or non-cognizable?
If it were cognizable, it would be called "mind. If it were different from your [consciousness] yet not an object of the senses, it would be identical to the mental constructs of another.
That which is you is precisely the mind. How could your mind be dualistic toward you?

If it were not consciousness, then since these objects are neither form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, nor the characteristics of union, separation, cold, warmth, or empty space, where would they exist? Now, within form and emptiness—
There is no indication whatsoever. It is not possible for there to be a space outside of the human realm; since the mind is not an object of perception, from what could its location be established?
Therefore, one should know that both phenomena and the mind are devoid of any locus. Thus, both the mental faculty (*manas*) and phenomena (*dharma*) are equally illusory.
These are neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of spontaneous nature.
Generally speaking, when matters of good, evil, or the indeterminate directly confront the sense faculties, those matters are all real;

therefore, they are called "real objects" (*vastu*). When not confronting an object, the mental consciousness alone takes them as its condition; these are merely shadows of real objects, and are therefore called...
The internal objects do not transcend the phenomena that serve as objects of the three natures, such as form and emptiness; therefore, they are called "dharmas.

Because the internal and external mutually perfume one another from time immemorial, they are called "generated and formed. If one claims that these are identical to the mind, it is easy to discern that this is not so:
the mind is the subject that perceives, while dharmas are the objects perceived. If one claims that they exist apart from the mind...
As for this, where does the fruit of this dharma reside? If it is held that there is cognition, then it is identical to the mind.
Since it is identical to the mind, it is not an external object (*viṣaya*). If it is not an external object yet differs from you, it cannot but be called "mind";
it would then be identical to the mental capacity (*citta-pramāṇa*) of another person. If it is not an external object and does not differ from you, how can it be your mind?
Furthermore, you refer to these two as "dharma-objects" (dharmāyatana). Therefore, it is incorrect to define them by having a location or spatial dimension.
If one considers them to be without cognition, then how can these dharma-objects be represented?

Since they possess neither the characteristics of form nor emptiness, and yet are not some distinct place standing apart from form and emptiness—whereas there is emptiness outside of form, that emptiness is not [the dharma-object].
There is that which is external. If emptiness had an exterior, then the dharma-object would have a location, and the mind could still take it as an object.

However, since there is nothing outside of emptiness, where will the mind find an object? Now, the reason the mind takes dharmas as objects is that form and emptiness are themselves without cognition;
they are manifested through cognition. It is because cognition possesses discrimination that they are called "dharmas. Now, since there is neither cognition nor any location, how can the mind...
Even if there were knowing, with what would it form a condition? Therefore, to posit "non-knowing" as having a location or direction is likewise untenable.
Neither possessing knowing nor lacking knowing—where could such a state be established? There is no dharma apart from the mind, and no dharma apart from the mind;
dharmas are inherently devoid of self-nature. How could they be anything other than illusory? Dharmas have no location; the faculty of the mind is itself empty. Thus it is said:

This is the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Zen Master Faben of Qingzhou ascended the hall and, raising his voice to silence the echoes, did not realize that sound is the root of resonance.
He played with shadows to evade his form, yet failed to realize that form is the basis of shadow. Thus, he used the Dharma to question the Dharma.
Not knowing that the Dharma is fundamentally non-Dharma, one transmits mind by means of mind.

Not knowing that the mind is fundamentally no-mind—since the mind is fundamentally no-mind—one realizes that the mind is like an illusion and understands that phenomena are non-phenomena. Knowing that phenomena are like dreams, one sees that mind and phenomena are not real;
do not vainly pursue them. They are but dreams, illusions, and empty flowers; why labor to grasp them? Arriving at this point, the Buddhas of the three periods of time and the One Great...
The teachings of the Treasuries, the words and phrases of the patriarchs, and the manifest entanglements of the old monks throughout the land—none of these will avail. Why?
Because "peace itself was brought about by the generals, yet we do not permit the generals to see that peace. As a verse in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"The eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, mind, and all the sense faculties—by means of these one constantly transmigrates, yet there is no [agent] who can..."
As for "transformation": the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is fundamentally without arising; it manifests as having arising, yet herein there is neither a manifestor nor any manifested object.
The eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, mind, and all the sense faculties are entirely empty and devoid of intrinsic nature; they exist only through the conceptualization of the deluded mind.
Observing in this manner, one sees that all things are without intrinsic nature. This is the general purport of this section. Indeed...
This is in accord with this sutra.
Furthermore, Ānanda, what are the eighteen realms (*dhātu*) that are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness?

The general response is as follows: that which faces the objects is called the sense organ (*indriya*); the organ is internal. That which is encountered by the organ is called the object (*viṣaya*); the object is external. Within these...

That which possesses individual discernment within these intervals is consciousness (*vijñāna*). These three depend upon one another for their existence, like bundles of reeds leaning against each other;

hence they are designated as the eighteen realms (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*). As for these three, when they exist, they all exist together; when they do not exist, they all cease to exist. Originally they have no self-nature (*svabhāva*).
Since they lack self-nature, one knows them to be fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*). (From the *Ruìlùběn*)
Former Chan Master [Xuefeng] ascended the hall and said: "The arising of all dharmas is manifested solely by the mind. Such words are a fine gateway for entry.

Now, let me ask you all: when the eyes see all forms, the ears hear all sounds, the nose smells all fragrances, the tongue discerns all flavors, the body touches all that is soft and smooth, and the mind distinguishes—"
All dharmas are distinct from one another. Just as with the objects encountered by the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind:
are they merely your own minds, or are they not your own minds? If you say they are merely your own minds, [how can this be so?]
Why not simply merge with all of you into a single mass and let it rest?
Why is it that the objects encountered by you remain outside the range of your eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and body?
If you say that the objects encountered by the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue are not your mind, how can you deny that all phenomena arise solely from the mind?
Manifest! These words remain in the world; who would not raise them up? Do you see this speech? Can you understand it?
If you cannot, let us all apply our minds together to discuss and master it. May you find your fortune therein.
"Do not let him grow weary of learning; there is nothing more to do, so withdraw for now. A monk asked Yunju, "When the six gates are not clear, what then?
Yunju said, "It does not involve conditions. The monk said, "What about the matter that transcends this? Yunju said, "One who is cautious does not guard [against it]. Touzi’s verse says:
"When spring arrives, the stone man gazes at the distant mountains; the oriole sings among flowering trees by the tranquil blue waves. One must know..."
Auspicious pines on crags beyond the clouds, for a thousand ages they welcome the wind and endure the cold of the seasons. The first two lines praise that which does not involve conditions;

the latter two lines praise the matter of the upward direction. One must clarify the matter of the upward direction before one can believe that the eighteen realms are fundamentally the nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Ānanda, as you understand it, visual consciousness arises with the eye and visible forms as conditions.

Does this consciousness arise because of the eye and take the eye as its constituent element (dhātu), or does it arise because of visible forms and take visible forms as its constituent element? Ānanda, if it were to arise because of the eye...
Since form is absent, there is emptiness; there is nothing that can be differentiated. Even if your consciousness were present, what would you have it serve?

Furthermore, your vision is not blue, yellow, red, or white; since there is nothing to indicate it, from what could a realm be established? If it arises because of form, then when form is absent in emptiness, [what would arise]?

Your consciousness should cease [with the object]. How then can your consciousness know this nature of empty space? If when form changes you also perceive the shifting and transformation of its characteristics, yet your consciousness does not shift, from what basis could the realm [of consciousness] be established?
If it follows the change [of the object], then it changes; if so, the characteristic of the realm itself would be non-existent.
If it were unchanging, it would be permanent. Since it arises from form, it should not be able to cognize the location of space.

If it were a combination of both, then the eye and form would arise together; yet if they combine, there is a separation in the middle, and if they separate, each would have to combine with its own kind. Their essential natures would thus be confused and disordered; how, then, could they constitute a "realm" (dhātu)?
Therefore, one should know that the eye and forms serve as conditions for the arising of the eye-consciousness element.

Since these three factors are entirely non-existent [in essence], then the eye, forms, and the three [factors] of the form-element are fundamentally neither causes and conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.
Tong said: "These eighteen realms merely refute the six consciousnesses; therefore, it is said that this consciousness does not arise from the eye as a realm.
Consciousness primarily functions through discrimination, causing form to be empty. Since discrimination is what establishes [the objects], it likewise does not arise from form."

Regarding the element (dhātu): form undergoes change and cessation, whereas consciousness is without transition. If both were derived from form alone, what would be the purpose of distinguishing emptiness?
Nor is it produced from the conjunction of the eye and form as an element; do you mean that it is produced by the conjunction of the eye and form?

Since that which possesses cognition conjoins with that which lacks cognition, they must necessarily clash and fail to interpenetrate; therefore, it is said to be "separated in the middle. Do you mean that it is produced by the separation of the eye and form?
If the faculty is separated from the object, they merge; if the object is separated from the faculty, they merge. To which would consciousness then belong? Therefore it is said:
"In confusion, all three locations are equally non-existent. Where could the realm exist? The Dharma Eye pointed to a bamboo and asked a monk, "Do you see it? The monk replied:
[The Master] looked. The Eye said, "The bamboo comes into the eye; the eye goes to the side of the bamboo. A monk said, "It is not like that at all.

Later, Fadelang (Fadeng) offered a different version, saying: "At that time, you should have simply torn open your eyes toward the Master. Guizong Rou offered another version, saying: "The Master simply did not believe me.
These two turns of phrase, however, possess the very breath of this monk. Furthermore, a monk asked Tiantong:
Chan Master Qian asked, "What is the eye that functions without deficiency? Dongshan replied, "It is just like being blind. Danxia’s verse says:
"Blind, deaf, mute—utterly true to the original nature; The eye is like the eyebrows, and only then does the Way draw near.
Last night the Lord of Spring secretly issued his decree; Where the yellow oriole sings, the green willows are in spring. If you can gain conviction in this, [you are one].
It functions freely without deficiency.

Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you understand—that the ear and sound serve as conditions to produce the auditory consciousness—does this consciousness arise because of the ear, taking the ear as its constituent element (*dhātu*), or does it arise because of sound, taking sound as its constituent element? Ānanda, if it arises because of the ear...

When the two characteristics of motion and stillness do not manifest before one, the sense organ does not constitute cognition; there is necessarily nothing known. Since even cognition itself is not established, what form or appearance could consciousness have?
If one takes "hearing" as the basis, since there is neither motion nor stillness, hearing is not established.

How then can the ear, which is a form, together with the objects of color and touch, be called the element of consciousness? From what, then, would the element of ear-consciousness be established? If it were produced from sound, [it would follow that consciousness arises from an object].
If consciousness exists because of sound, it would have no relation to hearing. Without hearing, the locus of the characteristic of sound would vanish.

If consciousness arises from sound, you must admit that the characteristic of sound exists because of hearing; yet hearing should then hear the consciousness. If it does not hear, it is not a sense-element (*dhātu*); if it does hear, it is identical to sound.
Auditory consciousness has already been heard of. Who knows this hearing-consciousness? If there were no knower, one would ultimately be like grass or wood;

thus, sound and hearing should not combine to form a middle realm (*madhyadhātu*). Since there is no middle position within a realm, from what then could the characteristics of internal and external be established?

Therefore, one should know that the ear and sound serve as conditions to produce the auditory-consciousness realm (*śrotravijñānadhātu*). If these three locations are entirely non-existent, then the triad of the ear, sound, and the auditory-consciousness realm [is likewise non-existent].
It is fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.
[The Master] replied: "The Dharma of dependent origination as understood by those of the Hīnayāna is taken to be substantially existent; they do not realize its emptiness.
Therefore, I have analyzed it according to what they habitually hear. If [the consciousness] were produced from the ear, then the ear would possess a *paramārtha-indriya* (ultimate sense-faculty)."
There is the physical sense organ (*tuccha-indriya*), which belongs to the category of conceptualization (*vikalpa*) along with the ultimate sense organ (*paramārtha-indriya*).

If there is no contact with the object of sound, even the cognition of its absence is impossible, let alone its form and appearance. The physical sense organ merely perceives a mixture of color and shape;

if the two characteristics of motion and stillness are absent, even the hearing itself is non-existent, let alone the presence of the element of consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*). Therefore, it is a delusion to claim that consciousness arises from the ear. If [consciousness] were caused by sound...
Sound arises with consciousness of its own accord, without depending on questioning. Since there is nothing capable of hearing, who could discern the characteristics of sound?

If you claim that [characteristics] arise through mutual dependence, and you concede that sound exists because it depends on hearing for its sound-characteristics, then you must likewise concede that hearing exists because it depends on sound for its hearing-consciousness.
Once consciousness has been heard, it is equal to the object of sound; what then serves as the knower? Who knows this hearing-consciousness?
If there were a knower, then there would be two consciousnesses; if there were no knower, it would be identical to grass and trees.

Therefore, the claim that consciousness arises from sound is false. If one claims that sound and the two [consciousnesses] arise through combination, such that one half has knowledge and one half lacks knowledge, then how could these two—the knowing and the unknowing—intermingle to form a middle realm or a middle state?
Since consciousness does not exist, it has nothing upon which to rely; thus, how could the internal faculties and external objects be established?

Therefore, it is said that the notion of the Śrāvakas regarding the "conjoined production" [of consciousness] is false. When these three locations are entirely absent, auditory consciousness does not arise.
Thus, one knows that the non-arising of auditory consciousness is precisely the nature of True Suchness (Tathatā). Once, while the World-Honored One was seated beneath a Nyagrodha tree...
Two merchants asked the World-Honored One, "Did you see any carts pass by? He replied, "I did not see any. They asked again, "Did you hear them? He replied, "I did not hear them.
The merchants said, "Were you in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*)? He replied, "I was not in meditative concentration.
They asked, "Were you asleep? He replied, "I was not asleep. The merchants then exclaimed, "Excellent, excellent! The World-Honored One is awake and yet..."
[The Master] saw [him] and subsequently offered two pieces of white cotton cloth. A monk once asked Chan Master Heze Hui:
"When seeing and hearing illuminate sound and form, do they merely proceed in opposition, or is there a sequence of before and after?

Hui said, "Setting aside for a moment the matter of proceeding in opposition or having a sequence of before and after, what exactly do you take to be sound and form? The monk said, "According to what the Master has discussed, then there are none."
"Sound and form can be apprehended. Thereupon, he bowed twice and departed that very day. Later, he lived in seclusion on Mount Meng.
When a Tripiṭaka Master of Śabda-vidyā arrived in Min from India, the Military Governor of Min requested Xuan Sha to test his realization.
Xuan Sha struck a bronze incense burner with an iron fire-tongs and asked, "What sound is this? The Tripiṭaka Master replied, "The sound of bronze and iron. Xuan Sha said, "Great King, do not..."

The Tripitaka Master was mocked by a foreigner; the Tripiṭaka had no response. Tiantong [Yunwen] took up the case, saying: "When principle accords with reality, the spirit is attained—the poor man finds the treasure within his garment.
When emotion seals the mind, one is bound by things—the strongman loses the pearl upon his forehead.
The Tripiṭaka only understands what lies before him; Xuansha cannot look behind. Do you understand? To accuse another of a crime and then impose that very crime upon oneself."

This is a public case (gong'an). There have been many veteran masters who have offered comments on it. Xuedou said, "Zang said, 'The sound of copper and iron'—this clearly follows after the dust of sound.
Fayan commented differently, saying, "I request the Great Master to act as the King for the Great King.
Fadeng commented differently, saying, "Let the Abbot listen to the question. Xuedou commented differently, saying, "Do not deceive the foreigner," at which Zang was unable to respond.
Chuchu. Fayuan said in his stead, "The Great Master has long received the offerings of the Great King.

Fadeng said in his stead, "On the contrary, it is you, Preceptor, who are deceiving the Great King. These words are most flavorful; they are what Tiantong refers to as "attributing a crime to another and then charging them with it.
According to Xuansha’s intent, what could be called the sound of copper and iron? [He] answered for the Tripitaka Master.
"Mind! What do you call this that is not the sound of copper or iron? These two phrases are extremely easy to deceive people;
you must scrutinize each one through to its core before you will no longer be deceived by them.
Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you understand: with the nose and fragrance as conditions, the nose-consciousness arises.

Does this consciousness arise because of the nose, taking the nose as its constituent element (*dhātu*), or does it arise because of the fragrance, taking the fragrance as its constituent element? Ānanda, if it were to arise because of the nose...
Then, within your mind, what constitutes the nose? Is it the physical form of the two nostrils? Or is it the nature of olfactory cognition and its movement?
If you take it to be the physical form, then that flesh is merely the body; the cognition of the body is contact, which is called the body and not the nose.
What is called "contact" is simply the sensory object. Since even the nose lacks a name, how can you establish it as a constituent element (*dhātu*)?

If you take the act of smelling as the cognition, then within your mind, what constitutes that cognition? If you say the flesh constitutes the cognition, then the cognition belongs to the flesh; fundamentally, it is contact and not the nose. If you say space constitutes the cognition...
If space were itself consciousness, then physical flesh would not be conscious. If this were so, then empty space would be you and your body would have no cognition;
today, Ānanda, you would have no place of existence. If you take fragrance to be consciousness, then that cognition belongs to the fragrance itself; what concern is it to you?
If fragrant and foul odors must arise within your nose, then those two types of flowing air—fragrance and stench—would not arise from the *eranda* and sandalwood trees respectively.
If these two substances do not come to you, yet you smell your own nose, would it be fragrant or foul? If it is foul, it cannot be fragrant.
Fragrance should not be foul. If both fragrance and foulness could be smelled by the same faculty, then you, as a single person, would have two noses.
When I questioned you, there were two Ānandas before me; which one was your true self? If the nose were one, then fragrance and foulness would not be two distinct things.

What is foul becomes fragrant, and what is fragrant again becomes foul; since these two natures do not exist, from what could the realm be established? If it arises because of fragrance, then consciousness exists because of fragrance;
just as the eye has the faculty of seeing yet cannot see itself, so too, because consciousness exists because of fragrance, it should not be able to know that fragrance.
Knowing is itself non-arising; not knowing is not consciousness. Fragrance does not exist through knowing; thus the fragrance-element is not established. Consciousness does not know fragrance;
therefore, the element is not established from fragrance. Since there is no intermediate state, neither internal nor external can be established. Such is the nature of that hearing.

Ultimately, they are all false and illusory. Therefore, one should know that the nose-consciousness element arises with the nose and fragrance as conditions; yet these three locations are entirely non-existent.
Thus, the nose, the fragrance, and the fragrance-element—these three—are fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of a spontaneous nature.

The Master said: "The nose is the faculty; fragrance is the object; that which lies between the two is consciousness. Generally speaking, when one speaks of 'dhātus' (realms), one specifically refers to consciousness.
This consciousness does not arise from the faculty, nor does it arise from the object; the general meaning is roughly the same, though the phrasing and logic here are slightly more complex.
By borrowing the object to refute the faculty, it is shown that consciousness does not emerge from emptiness, yet its autonomy resides therein."

Thus, by refuting consciousness through its objects, it is clearly seen that consciousness does not arise from their conjunction. First, the ephemeral sense organ (*bāhyendriya*) is refuted; since it is not known by the flesh, it is already refuted.
Furthermore, the ultimate sense organ (*paramārthendriya*) is also refuted; since it is not known by space, the cognition must reside in the fragrance itself and has no concern with the nose.
If the odor arises within the nose, it requires no external object. If this were so, one would be able to smell both fragrant and foul odors simultaneously.
"There ought to be two nostrils; thus, the sense organ (indriya) is insufficient as a basis. Since the nose is but one, how can there be two breaths?
Thus, the object (viṣaya) is insufficient as a support. Therefore, it is incorrect to say that consciousness arises from the sense organ.

If you claim that consciousness arises from the fragrance, then it should not perceive the fragrance—just as vision, which issues from the eye, does not see the eye itself. If you say it can indeed know [the fragrance], then..."
Fragrance itself possesses consciousness; why must one say it is "produced"? If it were said that [fragrance] does not know [itself], then it could not be called "consciousness.
How, then, could the realms (dhātus) be established? Therefore, the claim that [consciousness] is produced from fragrance is incorrect.

Since fragrance does not know its own fragrance, the object and the faculty are separate and cannot be joined. If consciousness were produced from fragrance, it would not know the fragrance; therefore, it certainly is not produced from fragrance.

Only then can one know fragrance. This faculty and its object are separate; fundamentally, they are not the cause [of consciousness]. Therefore, it is incorrect to say that consciousness arises from the union of the faculty and the object.
Since the realm of fragrance is not established, there is no intermediate state. If there is no intermediate state, how can there be "internal" or "external"?
Nose-consciousness is illusory and has no original location. To thoroughly understand that the nature of hearing is itself emptiness is to realize it is without cause.

Conditions are naturally obtainable. In the "Dharmadhātu" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, there is the merchant of incense Utpalabhāra, who was skilled at discerning all varieties of incense, as well as the methods for blending all types of incense and the origins of the king of incenses.
Furthermore, he was skilled at discerning incense that cures various illnesses, incense that eliminates all evils, and incense that gives rise to joy and increases [virtue].
The fragrance of afflictions; the fragrance that extinguishes afflictions; the fragrance that causes attachment to the conditioned; the fragrance that causes revulsion toward the conditioned;
the fragrance of relinquishing all arrogance and negligence; the fragrance of generating the mind to recollect the Buddha; the fragrance of realizing the dharma-gates of liberation;
the fragrance enjoyed by the noble ones; the diverse fragrances of all bodhisattvas; and the fragrances of all the bodhisattva stages.
"O Fragrance, I know only this method for blending incense. As for the Bodhisattvas, they remain far removed from all evil habitual tendencies and are untainted by worldly desires.
Seeking to sever the snares of the afflictions and the Māras, they transcend all realms of existence and adorn themselves with the fragrance of wisdom.
They are entirely free from attachment to any world and have fully accomplished [these qualities]."
The precept of non-attachment; the pure wisdom of non-attachment; practicing within the realm of non-attachment; being entirely without attachment in all places;
with a mind that is equanimous, unattached, and without dependence. Once, an elder passed by a lotus pond, and the deity of the pond rebuked him, saying:
"Do not steal my fragrance! The elder then asked: "Ordinary people who come and go do not fail to smell the fragrance. Why [do you rebuke me]?"
"I alone am stealing," [the thief] said. The deity replied, "An ordinary person acts with a distracted mind; therefore, it is not called stealing.
For a Venerable One with a pure mind, attachment itself is forbidden. Thus, the nose-consciousness is not easily subdued.
Therefore, one who wanders through the world with a mind free from attachment is well able to discern all various fragrances; this is not improper."
Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you understand: with the tongue and flavors as conditions, the tongue-consciousness arises.

Does this consciousness arise because of the tongue, taking the tongue as its constituent element (dhātu), or does it arise because of flavors, taking flavors as its constituent element? Ānanda, if it were to arise because of the tongue...
Then all worldly things—sugarcane, *ume* plums, *heliicterus*, rock salt, *achyranthes*, ginger, and cinnamon—would have no taste at all.
You yourself should taste your own tongue: is it sweet or bitter? If the nature of the tongue were bitter, who would come to taste the tongue? The tongue does not taste itself.
What constitutes cognition? The nature of the tongue is not bitter; since flavor does not arise [independently], how can a realm (dhātu) be established?

If consciousness arises because of flavor, then consciousness itself would be the flavor, just like the tongue-organ; it should therefore not taste itself. How then could consciousness discern whether something is a flavor or not a flavor?

Furthermore, no single taste arises from a single substance. Since tastes arise from many [substances], consciousness should likewise have multiple entities. If the entity of consciousness were one, its essence would necessarily be produced by taste alone;
yet salty, bland, sweet, and pungent flavors arise together in combination, and their various changing characteristics are unified into a single taste.
It should be without discrimination. Since discrimination is absent, it cannot be called consciousness. How, then, could it be called the "consciousness-element of tongue and taste"?
It is not from empty space that your mind-consciousness arises; when the tongue and taste combine, therein they are fundamentally without self-nature.
How does the element arise? Therefore, one should know that with the tongue and flavors as conditions, the tongue-consciousness-element arises.
Since these three locations are all non-existent, then the tongue, the flavors, and the tongue-element—these three—are fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.

The Master said: "First, because of the tongue, self-arising is refuted. Second, because of flavor, arising from another is refuted. Third, that it cannot arise from empty space refutes causeless arising.
Fourth, the conjunction of tongue and flavor refutes co-arising. Thus, within this very context, there is fundamentally no intrinsic nature.
The tongue does not taste itself, and flavor does not taste itself; from where, then, could consciousness arise? This is the correct [view].
This reveals the principle of non-arising: know that the tongue-consciousness is fundamentally without arising, and that the tongue-root is inherently pure;
this is precisely the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Formerly, Master [Name] ate without discrimination, and many of his disciples emulated him.
One day, he ordered his disciples to prepare food at the abode of a *nirmāṇakāya* (an emanation being). They took the remains of the *nirmāṇakāya* and ate them together.
His followers all vomited their hearts out and dispersed. The Master then said, "I have been pure for many lifetimes; therefore, I have no aversion.
Only those among you who can share this with me may take the food. Thereupon, the entire assembly submitted to this and followed his lead.
Regarding the precepts: Caoshan was also fond of wine. A monk asked, "What is it like when the spirit-clothes are no longer worn?
He replied, "Caoshan’s filial piety is complete. The monk asked, "After filial piety is complete, what then?
He replied, "Caoshan is fond of wild wine. His disciple Shuiqing asked, "I am solitary and poor; I beg the Master for relief. Caoshan called out, "Disciple Shui! Shui responded, "Yes? Caoshan said:
Qingyuan drank three cups of Baijia wine, yet he still said, "I have not even touched my lips. Xuangjue asked, "Where did you give him the wine?
These three cases demonstrate that the nature of flavor is fundamentally empty, and the tongue-consciousness is likewise fundamentally empty.
One who realizes this is said to know the flavor.

Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you have clarified—that body-contact serves as a condition for the arising of body-consciousness—does this consciousness arise because of the body and take the body as its constituent element (*dhātu*), or does it arise because of contact and take contact as its constituent element? Ānanda, if it arises because of the body...

If there were necessarily no conditions for the two perceptions of union and separation, what would the body perceive? If it arises because of contact, then there would necessarily be no such thing as "your body.
Who, then, is not the body that perceives union and separation? Ānanda, objects do not perceive through contact; the body perceives that there is contact.

To know the body is itself contact; to know contact is itself the body. Thus, that which is contact is not the body, and that which is the body is not contact. The two characteristics of body and contact are fundamentally non-existent.
As for location: if it coincides with the body, it is the very nature of the body itself; if it is separate from the body, it is merely a characteristic such as empty space.

Since neither internal nor external can be established, how could a middle be posited? If a middle cannot be posited, and both internal and external natures are empty, then from whom would your consciousness arise to establish the realms?
Therefore, you should know that with body and touch as conditions, the triad of body, consciousness, and realm is entirely non-existent. Thus, the body—
Regarding the three—contact (*sparśa*), the body (*kāya*), and the element (*dhātu*)—they are fundamentally neither causes and conditions nor inherent natures.
It is said in general that "things do not touch cognition; it is not that non-things do not know contact. Things truly know the void, yet the real does not touch the void.
Therefore, all things can only touch objects; they cannot touch cognition. It is precisely this single word "cognition" [that distinguishes them].
This clearly reveals the pure *dharmakāya*, which is beyond the reach of tactile contact. That the body perceives the existence of touch is merely the discerning cognition of the *rūpakāya*.
Because it takes the two perceptions of conjunction and separation as conditions, one knows that touch exists.
Touch cannot be separated from the body, nor can the body be separated from touch. To speak of touch is not to speak of the body; to speak of the body is not to speak of [touch].
Contact. Second, is the fruit stable? Therefore, when combined, they are but a single body with no state of contact; when separated, they are equal to empty space with no function of contact.
In both cases, there is no location; internal and external are not established. Since both body and contact are non-existent, from what could consciousness arise?
Since there is no intermediate consciousness, the faculties and objects are entirely empty. Thus, one knows that the elements of body and consciousness are void.
This is delusion. When the Great Meditation Master Si of Mount Nanyue had already attained the supernormal power of recollecting past lives, obstacles soon arose again;
his four limbs became weak and flaccid, and he was unable to walk. He thought to himself: "Illness arises from karma, and karma arises from the mind.
At the source of the mind there is no arising; what form can external objects take? Illness, karma, and the body are all like clouds and shadows. Having contemplated in this way, [he was healed].
Perverted perceptions are extinguished, yet lightness and ease remain as before. If one reflects upon this, it can be said that one has profoundly clarified that bodily consciousness is illusory.
Chan Master Poxi of Xingyang was lying ill when Dayang asked him: "This body is like a bubble or an illusion; within bubbles and illusions, one accomplishes the task.
If there were no bubbles and illusions, there would be no way to accomplish the Great Matter. If you wish to accomplish the Great Matter, you must recognize..."
Yangshan asked, "Taking hold of this bubble-like illusion—how so? Fengbo said, "This is still a matter of 'this side. Yangshan asked, "What about the matter of 'that side'?
Fengbo said, "The crimson wheel shines across the earth; no flowers grow beneath the sea. Yangshan laughed and said, "Is that how alert you are?
Fengbo shouted, "I thought I had forgotten! and immediately passed away. Such was Fengbo.
This may be called a profound clarification of the matters that transcend the Dharma-body. A monk asked Da Long, "The physical body is subject to decay;
what is the indestructible Dharma-body? Da Long replied, "Mountain flowers bloom like brocade;
stream water is as deep blue as indigo. Xuedou’s verse says: The question was never understood; The answer was not grasped. The moon is cold, the wind is high; Ancient cliffs and frosty cypresses.

It is truly laughable that when meeting a person who has attained the Way, one does not respond with either speech or silence. Grasping a white jade whip in hand, one smashes the "black dragon pearl" (the *li-zhu*) to pieces.
Had it not been smashed, flaws and impurities would have increased. The state has its laws and regulations; there are three thousand articles of crime.
According to this verse, even the solid *dharmakāya* must be smashed to pieces—how much more so the physical body (*rūpakāya*)?
