Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you have clarified: with the mind and mental objects as conditions, the mental consciousness arises.

Does this consciousness arise because of the mind, taking the mind as its constituent element (dhātu), or does it arise because of mental objects, taking mental objects as its constituent element? Ānanda, if it arises because of the mind...
Within your mind, there must be something you are contemplating. To clarify your intention: if those preceding dharmas did not exist, consciousness would have no basis for arising.
Devoid of conditions, it would have no form; what, then, would consciousness be used for? Furthermore, your conscious mind, along with its various modes of deliberation and its nature of discernment—

Are they identical or distinct? If they are identical, then the mind is itself the mental faculty (*manas*). How then could there be that which is produced? If they are distinct, then the mind is not the same as the mental faculty;

in that case, there would be no cognition. If there is no cognition, how can the mental faculty arise? If there is cognition, how can one cognize the mental faculty? It is only a matter of identity and difference.
If the two natures are not established, how can the realms be posited? If phenomena arise from causes, then all worldly phenomena do not depart from the five sense objects.
Observe the phenomena of form, the phenomena of sound, the phenomena of fragrance, the phenomena of taste, and the phenomena of touch; their characteristics are clearly manifest.
Since these correspond to the five sense faculties and are not subsumed under the mental faculty, your consciousness must certainly arise in dependence upon dharmas. Now, observe closely:

what is the nature of each dharma? If it is apart from form and emptiness, motion and stillness, openness and obstruction, conjunction and separation, or arising and ceasing—transcending all such characteristics.
Ultimately, nothing is obtained. When there is birth, form, emptiness, and all dharmas arise together; when there is cessation, form, emptiness, and all dharmas cease together.

Since the cause itself does not exist, what kind of form or characteristic could consciousness—which arises dependent on that cause—possibly have? Since no such characteristics exist, how could the realms (dhātus) be produced?
Therefore, one should know that with the mind and mental objects as conditions, the sphere of mental consciousness arises.

When these three locations are entirely absent, then the mind, mental objects, and the sphere of mental consciousness—these three—are fundamentally neither causes and conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.
Tong said: "This realm of consciousness is the nature of the sixth consciousness that cognizes and distinguishes.

Since its nature is defined by this cognition and distinction, it has no object apart from dharmas; thus, the mental faculty (manas) would not arise. Without objects, it has no form; what use would consciousness have?

This shows that consciousness takes dharmas as its object and is clearly not produced from the mental faculty. If one were to claim that the mental faculty can perform discrimination and serves as the root for the arising of consciousness,"

The seventh consciousness (*manas*) is the思量 (思量 *sīlāng*, deliberation) that serves as the basis for defilement and purity. The eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is the 識心 (識心 *shixin*, cognizing mind) that serves as the fundamental basis.
Are its nature of discerning (*vijñapti*) the same as or different from that of the preceding six consciousnesses? The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "The mind (*citta*) is able to accumulate karma;

the intellect (*manas*) is able to extensively accumulate it; the nature of discerning is called consciousness (*vijñāna*). In relation to manifest objects, five [consciousnesses] are spoken of. The treatise (*śāstra*) states: "That which arises through accumulation is called mind (*citta*); deliberation..."
"Measuring" is called *manas* (mind); "cognizing objects" is called *vijñāna* (consciousness). These are merely different names for a single dharma.

Since it is but a single dharma, it may equally be called *citta* (mind), *manas*, or *vijñāna*. However, there is a subtle distinction: they receive their names based on whichever aspect is predominant.
When the eight consciousnesses and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) are all stilled, it can only be called *citta*. When [the eighth consciousness] is present in the seventh...

Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is neither mind (*citta*) nor consciousness; it can only be called the intellect (*manas*). When the six consciousnesses and the mind both confront their objects, it is therefore called the "consciousness that discriminates phenomena" (*vṛtti-vijñāna*).
In reality, they are one and the same entity. It is like waves arising from the ocean: they are neither different nor not different.

When the winds of objective realms arise as the six consciousnesses pursue sensory dust, they immediately stir up the waves of the seventh consciousness’s deliberation (*manovijñāna*), which ultimately...
It does not depart from the profound, tranquil ocean-store of the eight consciousnesses. These six, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses are neither identical nor different;

for now, let us set aside such debate. To speak instead of the realm of mind-born consciousness: if one were to say that consciousness is identical to the mind, then consciousness would simply be the mind.
How, then, could it be said that the mind is the producer and consciousness is the produced? To claim they are identical is untenable.

Furthermore, if the various consciousnesses were different from the mind (*manas*), being utterly distinct from it, then one would belong to the realm of sentient beings and the other to the realm of insentient things;
thus, there would be no object of cognition. To claim they are different is untenable. If there is no object of cognition, it necessarily does not arise from the mind.

The mind is capable of discernment; that which is produced must necessarily involve consciousness (*vijñāna*). If there is something cognized, at the moment the mind arises, there would be no dharma to serve as an object-condition (*ālambana*), yet there is only the mind itself.
How, then, could it cognize its own self? If it were able to cognize the mind, then the mind would instead become an object and could not function as a faculty (*indriya*).
If it does not cognize the mind, it is the same as being without consciousness; it would not be the domain of the mind.
It arises. To seek consciousness apart from dharmas is most difficult to describe. Thus, if one calls it "identical," it cannot be named "arising";

if one calls it "different," it cannot be named "consciousness. Since these two natures—identity and difference—are both unestablished, and since consciousness has no fixed location, how can the realms (dhātus) be established?
Therefore, to say that consciousness arises from the sense organs is false. If, however, one says it arises in dependence on dharmas...
Manifestation arises from causal dharmas; there must necessarily be a dharma that can be characterized before it becomes the cause for the production of consciousness.

Now, the various dharmas of the world do not depart from characteristics such as form and emptiness. When these are confronted by the five sense organs, they are apprehended solely by the five organs, and thus constitute the causes of the five consciousnesses.
The mental faculty (*manas*), however, is able to depart from these five objects of sensory dust and [perceive] separately...
Is there a phenomenon that serves as the causal basis for the characteristics of phenomena? The internal objects upon which the mind itself relies do not outwardly depend on the five sense faculties;
yet, they ultimately do not transcend phenomena such as the shadows of form, emptiness, arising, and ceasing.

Even when the mind conditions supramundane phenomena—those so-called states that are neither form nor emptiness, neither arising nor ceasing—they still do not transcend being neither form nor emptiness.
Form is manifested through emptiness; it is neither born nor extinguished. Birth and extinction are manifested through form;

ultimately, one cannot depart from form, emptiness, birth, and extinction to find something else called "dharma-objects" (dharmas) that serve as the cause for the arising of consciousness. Is it the five sense-objects themselves that constitute the dharma?
These are the causes for the five sense-faculties, not the cause for the mind. If one seeks the dharma apart from the five sense-objects, then it does not exist.
Dharmas can be apprehended; since there is nothing that can be apprehended, this is the absence of a cause. Since the cause is absent, how could anything arise?
If one claims that a causeless consciousness can arise, that consciousness would necessarily not be able to differentiate dharmas such as form and emptiness.
What dharma would it differentiate, and what kind of characteristics would it assume? Since no characteristics exist, consciousness does not truly arise. Therefore, it is said:
That which arises from dharmas is delusion. Since it is neither born of the mind nor born of dharmas, where could consciousness have a location?
To have no location is itself the true location. Long ago, the Venerable Guoqing Qingshang asked Xuansha:
[The Master] said: "It is as taught in the scriptures: one must not use the mind of discursive knowledge to fathom the unsurpassed wisdom and vision of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, how is this so? Zhaozhou said: "If you say that you have thoroughly investigated the mind of discursive knowledge to its very bottom, would you then be able to fathom it?
From this point on, enter through faith. Later, someone asked: "When my disciple sits in meditation at night, my thoughts..."
"Chaos and distraction! I do not yet understand the method for subduing them; I pray you will deign to grant me instruction. Jing said:
"If, while sitting in quietude at night, your mind wanders in flight, take that wandering mind and investigate the place where it flies.

When you investigate and find no place, then where can the wandering thought exist? Turn back and investigate the investigating mind itself; then the mind that performs the investigation will become still."
Furthermore, the wisdom that is able to illumine is fundamentally empty, and the objects upon which it focuses are likewise quiescent.

That they are "quiescent yet not quiescent" is because there is no person who can bring about such quiescence; that they are "illumining yet not illumining" is because there is no object to be illumined.
When both object and wisdom are quiescent, the mind is at ease. One does not seek out branches externally, nor does one dwell in meditative concentration internally.
When these two paths are both extinguished, the single nature is serene. This is the essential path for returning to the source.
While Yaoshan was sitting, a monk asked, "What are you pondering so intently? Yaoshan said, "I am pondering that which is not to be pondered. [The monk] said, "No..."
"How does one contemplate that which is beyond contemplation? The Master said, "It is not contemplation. A monk asked Master Xichan of Shuzhou, "What is the state beyond contemplation?
The Master said, "Who sees the void nod its head at night? Danxia offered this verse:
"A single point of numinous clarity is not contained within the six gates; How could one need to fix one's gaze upon it so intently? Within this, lies the vital message."

It is difficult for people to entrust themselves to this. Only empty space nods its head in the dark. Thus it is clear that where the mind and consciousness cannot reach, consciousness itself is fundamentally luminous.
Ānanda said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, the Tathāgata has often spoken of the causes and conditions of conjunction; all things in the world are like seeds..."
All such transformations are manifested through the combination of the four great elements. Why, then, does the Tathāgata reject both the doctrines of causality and spontaneity?

I do not yet understand the meaning of this; I only pray that you will take pity on me and reveal to all sentient beings the definitive meaning of the Middle Way—the Dharma free from conceptual proliferation.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying: "Previously, you were weary of and detached from sound..."
Having heard the various teachings of the Pratyekabuddhas and the Hīnayāna, you have resolved to diligently seek unexcelled Bodhi;
therefore, I now reveal the ultimate truth for your sake. Why do you further entangle yourself with worldly frivolous discourse and delusive conceptualizations?
Although you are well-versed in many teachings, you are like a man who knows the names of medicines but cannot distinguish them when the actual medicine appears before him. Just so...
"It is truly pitiable. Listen attentively now; I shall analyze and explain it for you, so that those who cultivate the Mahāyāna in the future may also penetrate the true reality (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*).
Ānanda remained silent, receiving the Buddha’s holy instruction."
Tong said: "Ānanda wished for the World-Honored One to reveal the Middle Way.
He knew that if one adheres to the causes and conditions of worldly conjunction, one is stuck in existence; yet if one rejects both causes and conditions and spontaneity, one sinks into emptiness.
To be neither existent nor empty—this is the Middle Way. However, he did not realize that in supreme Bodhi, even the Middle Way has no place of attachment."
This is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). This ultimate truth is precisely the aforementioned aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*);
it is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature. To perceive all marks as being without marks is the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) of the Mahāyāna.

Ānanda wished to abandon the Hīnayāna in order to seek unsurpassed bodhi; now, [the Buddha] has shown him the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*), yet he remains utterly bewildered and ignorant.
This is a matter of no small consequence. It is like the story of the man who speaks only of medicine with his mouth;
when the true medicine appears before him, he is unable to recognize it. This is truly pitiable! Alas, how difficult it is to recognize medicine!
One day, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva commanded Sudhana to gather medicine, saying, "Bring back whatever is medicine. Sudhana looked everywhere throughout the great...
"Nothing on the ground is not medicine. Wumen then asked, "As for 'nothing is not medicine,' what does this mean? Wenshu said, "Bring me that which is medicine.
Shancai then picked up a blade of grass from the ground and handed it to Wenshu.
Wenshu took it, held it up, and showed it to the assembly, saying, "This medicine can kill a person, and it can also bring a person to life. Yunmen...
Addressing the assembly, he said: "Medicine and disease treat one another; the entire earth is medicine. Which of these is oneself? Xuedou composed a verse on this: "The entire earth is medicine;
How great a mistake has occurred from ancient times! Shut the door and do not build a carriage; The thoroughfare is naturally vast and open. Mistake upon mistake!
Even the nostrils that pierce through the heavens have been pierced. According to the meaning of this verse, the true medicine is manifest before us.
You must also spit it out. How much more so for one who cannot discern?
Ānanda, as you have said, the four great elements combine to manifest the various transformations of the world. Ānanda, [this is not so].
If those great elements were by nature not composite, they could not intermingle with one another, just as space does not mix with material forms.
If they were composite, they would be like transformations, wherein beginning and end mutually establish one another, and arising and ceasing continue in succession.
Birth and death, death and birth; birth, death, birth, and death are like a whirling firebrand, never ceasing for a moment.
Ānanda, it is like water turning into ice, and ice returning to water.
Tong said: "If one says that the four great elements are not in combination, then this contradicts the principle of True Suchness responding to conditions;
it would be no different from inert emptiness. If one says that the four great elements are fixedly combined, then this contradicts the principle of the unchanging nature of True Suchness."
It is merely a matter of transformation, like water becoming ice and ice returning to water. The four great elements are fundamentally the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha;
there is no ice apart from water. How could water combine to become ice? How could ice combine to become water? Originally there is but one thing;
there is no other entity that intervenes to harmonize them. Seek the harmony, and you shall find it.
Its characteristics are utterly unattainable; therefore, it is neither a composite nor a non-composite.
When deluded, True Suchness is the four great elements, like water forming ice. When awakened, the four great elements are True Suchness, like ice returning to water.
Water is but one. A monk asked Linji: "What are the four kinds of signless realms?"
Ji said: "If for a single moment of thought you harbor doubt, you will be obstructed by earth. If for a single moment of thought you harbor attachment, you will be drowned by water.
If for a single moment of thought you harbor anger, you will be burned by fire. If for a single moment of thought you harbor joy, you will be blown away by wind.

If you can discern in this way, you will not be bound by conditions; you will employ conditions everywhere—surging east and subsiding west, surging south and subsiding north, surging center and subsiding in the periphery."
Surging from the edges, they sink in the center; surging from the center, they sink at the edges. Treading upon water as if on land, entering the earth as if into water—why is this so?
It is because one has realized that the four great elements are like dreams and illusions. Disciple of the Way, you who are listening to the Dharma right now are not these four great elements;
it is that which uses your four great elements. If you can see it in this way, then going and staying will be entirely up to yourself.
Indeed, as Linji said: "If there is no abiding, it is not water; how then could there be ice?
When Yaoshan was presented with a loincloth by a donor, he held it up and showed it to the assembly, asking, "Does the Dharma-body possess the four great elements or not?"
"If you can explain it, I will give you a pair of trousers. Daowu said, "The nature of the ground is not emptiness; emptiness is not the nature of the ground.
This is the element of earth; the other three elements are likewise so. Guishan said, "I give you a pair of trousers.
Why is Daowu’s realization so utterly different from this sutra? Try to investigate this.
Observe the nature of earth: that which is coarse is the great earth; that which is subtle is fine dust, down to the *paramāṇu* (the infinitesimal particle).
If one analyzes the boundary of the characteristics of that ultimate minute form into seven parts, and further analyzes the *paramāṇu*, it is simply the nature of true emptiness.

Ānanda, if this *paramāṇu* is analyzed until it becomes empty space, you should know that empty space gives rise to the appearance of form. As for what you have now asked regarding "by means of harmony..."
Because they combine, they give rise to all the various manifested forms of the world. You should observe this single *paramāṇu* (subtle atom):
by how much empty space must it combine to exist? It cannot be a *paramāṇu*. Furthermore, if one were to analyze a *paramāṇu* into its constituent parts...
Regarding emptiness: by how many material forms (*rūpa*) is empty space synthesized? If it were synthesized by material forms, then that which is synthesized by material forms would not be empty.
If it were synthesized by emptiness, then that which is synthesized by emptiness would not be material form. Material form may still be analyzed, but how can emptiness be synthesized?

You fundamentally do not know that within the *tathāgatagarbha*, essential material form is true emptiness, and essential emptiness is true material form; that it is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire *dharmadhātu*, and follows along with sentient beings.

The arising of the mind corresponds to the scope of what is known; it manifests in accordance with karma. The ignorant of the world deludedly regard this as being due to causes and conditions, or as having a nature of spontaneity.
All of these are merely the conceptual calculations of the discerning consciousness; they consist only of verbal expressions and possess no real meaning whatsoever.
Tong said: "The *Dharmadhātu-gāthā* states: 'If one wishes to know the principle of true emptiness, the true suchness within the body pervades the external as well.
Sentient and insentient beings share a single substance; everywhere they are identical with the true Dharmadhātu.

This is the essential purport of the seven great elements (*mahābhūta*). 'True emptiness' is the substance of the One Suchness (*tathatā*). The 'seven great elements' are the function that accords with karma. Substance..."

They function through non-duality; they support one another and mutually manifest without departing from the wondrous nature. Therefore, each and every thing is called "nature. There is only this single nature.
Emptiness is the emptiness of nature; form is the form of nature. Thus, that which is empty is form, and this is called "wondrous existence" (*miao-you*).
That which is form is emptiness, and this is called "true non-existence" (*zhen-wu*). This true non-existence and wondrous existence is what is called the "wondrous *tathatā*-nature."
It is simply that it does not fall into the categories of existence or non-existence; therefore, it is called "pure. Yet, it has never been without existence or non-existence;

therefore, it is called "primordial. To say it is "pure" means it is not defiled by causes and conditions. To say it is "primordial" means it is not something produced through the combination of elements.
Generally, that which arises from the combination of causes and conditions possesses form and characteristics and occupies a specific location; it cannot pervade the entire Dharma-realm.
Only that which does not arise from the combination of causes and conditions is without form or characteristics and has no fixed location; therefore, it can pervade the entire Dharma-realm.
Pervading the Dharma-realm is the very nature [of reality], and thus there is nothing that is not comprised within the seven great elements. Pervading the Dharma-realm constitutes these seven.
Great! That which is not non-nature is precisely the mind of the Tathāgata. It is only this that is pure; only this that is primordial;
only this that is all-pervasive. Therefore, it cannot be known and cannot be measured. As for the minds of sentient beings, regarding that which is pure, they sometimes become defiled;
regarding that which is primordial, they sometimes do not remain so; regarding that which is all-pervasive...
At times, it is not all-pervasive; it follows the mind capable of knowing and accords with the measure of that which is known.
Knowledge accumulates to form karma, and karma accumulates to form results—whether good or evil—which transform and create the phenomena of the ten realms, both the environment and its inhabitants.
The minds of sentient beings are boundless; the karma of sentient beings is likewise boundless.
Were it not for the nature that pervades the entire Dharma-realm serving as their substance, how could they manifest according to their karma, emerging ever more inexhaustibly?
The karmic forces of sentient beings are each different; yet, within the pure and fundamental nature, there is not the slightest addition or subtraction.
Therefore it is said that all moving creatures and living beings possess Buddha-nature. The world is ignorant and fails to realize that the three realms are nothing but mind.

"All phenomena are but consciousness. Thus, regarding the manifestation of things according to one's karma, those who perceive them as arising from causes delude themselves into thinking they possess the nature of causes and conditions;
those who perceive them as arising without cause delude themselves into thinking they possess the nature of spontaneity (*svabhāva*).

They do not know that [the mind] is fundamentally pure, transcending both existence and non-existence, and that neither causes and conditions nor spontaneity provide a basis for attachment. This is what is called "causality" (or "the cause").
How can conditions give rise [to things]? By what condition does the atom (*paramāṇu*) arise from space? By what condition does space arise from form?
Space is conditioned only by space; form is conditioned only by form.
Even if one could analyze the atom until it becomes space, one would not know how many spaces combine to form an atom. Thus, since the atom does not exist because of space, space is not...

It is certain that [things] exist through the analysis of atoms (*paramāṇu*). It is likewise certain that emptiness and existence cannot give rise to one another, and thus the arising of the great earth has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Therefore, those who explain this by means of the conjunction of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya-samnipāta*) are in error.
This means that [emptiness] arises spontaneously. Why would emptiness exist without a cause? Why would form exist without a cause?
One cannot perceive emptiness without the analysis of atoms (*paramāṇu*), nor can one establish the great earth without the accumulation of atoms.
Thus, how could the arising of the great earth be something that suddenly exists without a cause? Therefore, by means of...
The proponents of "spontaneity" (zìrán) are likewise in error. Their formulation of this doctrine arises from the conceptual calculations of the discerning mind.
They insist on calling it "causes and conditions" when it is not so; they insist on calling it "spontaneous" when it is not so.

There is merely verbal expression, all of which constitutes groundless frivolous proliferation (prapañca). How could they know that the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha does not arise from views? It does not...
Because one does not give rise to views while attached to signs, it is beyond the reach of conceptual speculation. Because one does not attach to signs, it is beyond the arrival of verbal expression.
Where the movements of the mind cease and the path of language is cut off—this may be called the true mark (dharmatā), and this may be called the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
The Qin-era Dhyāna Master Bodhidharma asked Master Sheng which sūtras and śāstras he was lecturing upon.
Sheng said, "The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*. Da said, "How do you explain the meaning of the emptiness of form (*rūpa-śūnyatā*)? Sheng said, "The aggregation of atoms is called form;
the lack of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) in those atoms is called emptiness. Da said, "Before the atoms have aggregated, what would you call them?
Sheng was at a loss. Da then asked, "What other sūtras or śāstras do you lecture on? Sheng said, "The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. Da said:
"How do you explain the meaning of nirvāṇa? Daosheng said, "Nir (nie) means non-arising; vāṇa (pan) means non-extinction. Therefore, it is called nirvāṇa.
Daotuo asked, "This is the nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata; what then is the nirvāṇa of the Dharma Master? Daosheng replied:
"Does the meaning of *nirvāṇa* have two aspects? I, So-and-so, understand it only thus; I do not yet know how the Meditation Master explains *nirvāṇa*.
Dahui picked up his *añjali* (fly-whisk) and asked, "Do you see it? He replied, "I see it. Dahui asked, "What do you see?
Sheng said, "I see the *añjali* in the Meditation Master’s hand. Dahui threw the *añjali* to the ground and said, "See! Sheng said, "I see it."
Wuzhuo said, "I see. Huairang asked, "What do you see? Wuzhuo replied, "I see the *ruyi* (ceremonial fly-whisk) in the Zen Master’s hand falling to the ground.
Huairang rebuked him, saying, "Judging by your understanding, you have not yet emerged from the common stream. How can you claim your fame will resound through the universe?
He then brushed off his robes and departed. His disciples remained filled with doubt and pursued Huairang to question him further, asking, "Our master says that form is emptiness..."
[The monk] said, "This does not accord with Nirvana. I do not yet understand how the Chan Master explains the principle of the emptiness of form (*rūpa-śūnyatā*.
Dharma-ta replied, "I do not say that your master’s explanation is incorrect; however, your master only understands the emptiness of form in the state of fruition (*phala*).

He has not realized how to explain the emptiness of form within the causal stage (*hetu*. The disciple asked, "What is the emptiness of form in the causal stage? Dharma-ta replied, "Because a single atom (*paramāṇu*) is empty."

The collection of atoms is empty; because the collection of atoms is empty, a single atom is empty. Within the emptiness of a single atom there is no collection of atoms, and within the emptiness of the collection of atoms there is no single atom.
This was not something newly invented by Deva; it is because each individual sense-faculty is pure.
The various faculties are pure. Because the various faculties are pure, a single faculty is pure. Within the purity of a single faculty, there are no various faculties;
within the purity of the various faculties, there is no single faculty. By means of this illumination, it is not difficult to understand.
This, in turn, points out the path of entry into the true emptiness of the nature of form and the true form of the nature of emptiness.
Ānanda, the nature of fire is without self; it depends upon various conditions. Observe the households in the city that have not yet eaten:
when they wish to cook, they hold a magnifying lens in their hands and seek fire from the sun.

Ānanda, what is called "conjunction" is like myself and you, along with these one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, who now form a single assembly. Although the assembly is one, if one examines its fundamental basis...
Each has a body, and all have their respective clans and names: such as Śāriputra of the Brahmin clan;
Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa (which translates as "Wood-Claw-Lame") of the Kāśyapa clan; and even Ānanda of the Gautama clan (the name of a lunar mansion, also known as the Solar Clan).
Ānanda, if this nature of fire exists because of a combination of conditions, yet that person holds a mirror in his hand and seeks fire from the sun—
Does this fire emerge from within the mirror? Does it emerge from the tinder? Or does it come from the sun?
Ānanda, if it comes from the sun, it should naturally burn the tinder in your hand; furthermore, all the forests from which it originates should likewise be consumed by fire.
If it emerges from within the mirror, it should naturally emerge from the mirror and ignite the tinder; why then does the mirror not melt? Even as you hold it in your hand, it remains unscathed.

Regarding the characteristic of heat: how does it melt and dissolve? If it were produced within the moxa itself, why would it depend on the meeting of the sun’s rays and the light of the mirror before the fire could arise?
You should observe this closely: the mirror is held by the hand, the sun comes from the heavens, and the moxa grows from the earth.
From what direction does the fire travel to reach here? The sun and the mirror are far apart; they are neither blended nor joined. It cannot be that the fire-light has no source.
"It exists inherently. You still do not know that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of fire is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true fire;
it is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm. It accords with the minds of sentient beings and manifests according to the scope of their cognition.

Ānanda, you should know that if one person holds a mirror in one place, fire arises in that one place; if one holds mirrors throughout the Dharma-realm, fire will arise filling the entire world. Thus, its arising pervades the whole world."
How could there be any fixed location? They manifest according to one's karma. The world is ignorant and deludedly regards them as being caused by external conditions, or as arising from spontaneity;
these are all merely the conceptualizations and calculations of the discriminating mind. There are only words and explanations, but no actual reality whatsoever.
Tong said: Nāgārjuna stated that all phenomena do not truly exist as suchness; they should not be known to have characteristics by means of mind and consciousness.

If they were known to exist by means of mind and consciousness, then they would not be existent. For example, the characteristic of solidity in earth is known to exist by means of the body-faculty and body-consciousness;
if the body-faculty and body-consciousness were absent, then the characteristic of solidity would not exist. [The opponent] asked: What of the body-faculty and body-consciousness?
Whether one knows it or not, the earth always possesses the characteristic of solidity. The answer is:

if one first knows for oneself that there is the characteristic of solidity, or if one hears it from another, then one knows that the characteristic of solidity exists. If one has neither previously known nor heard of it, then the characteristic of solidity does not exist.
Furthermore, if the earth were eternally the characteristic of solidity, it should not abandon that characteristic, just as congealed butter, wax, or honey do not abandon their own characteristics.
Resin, when melted, abandons its solid characteristic and falls into the state of moisture. It is the same with gold, silver, copper, iron, and so forth.
Just as water possesses the characteristic of moisture but turns into a solid characteristic when cold, all such various things likewise abandon their characteristics.
Furthermore, it is said: if fire truly possessed the nature of heat, why is it that some people enter fire and are not burned? And as for people...
Although fire is within the body, it does not burn the body; although water is within the clouds, fire cannot extinguish it.

This is because fire lacks a fixed nature of heat, and by the power of supernormal faculties (*ṛddhibala*), fire cannot burn the body. By the causal conditions of karma (*karmapratyaya*), the five viscera do not become hot.
By the power of the divine dragon (*nāga*), water cannot extinguish [the fire]. If the nature of heat were distinct from fire, then fire would not be hot.
If heat and fire were one and the same, how could one speak of "heat"? The nature of fire is such, and the others are likewise.
Thus, because there is no distinct nature apart from the general nature, it is called "emptiness of nature. By means of this principle, one investigates the natures of earth, water, and fire;
like tracing a stream to find its source, all are empty. This is what the World-Honored One has taught. From [the *Śālistamba Sūtra*].
The manifestation of its nature is called "arising in accordance with karma. It corresponds to the measure of what is known. This is what Nāgārjuna discussed:
he traced the nature back from its manifestations, specifically clarifying that matter (rūpa) and mind (citta) are non-dual.
A magnifying lens is also called a *huo fangzhu*. The *Lun heng* states: on the day of Bingwu at noon during the fifth month, one melts stones from the five directions.
It is round like a mirror; its center is concave. When it reflects objects, the image appears inverted; when directed toward the sun, fire emerges.

In the world, people know only of these three—moxa, the mirror, and the sun—and assume that fire arises through the conjunction of these causes and conditions. They do not realize that the mirror, the moxa, and the sun are far apart and cannot truly conjoin;
therefore, this is not [true] dependent origination. If one were to claim that fire arises spontaneously and ex nihilo, it would follow that it does not depend [on anything].
The sun-stirring mirror (yangsui) seeks fire by facing the sun; therefore, it is not natural.

If one were to claim that each of these three possesses the nature of fire, then the moxa should burn itself, the mirror should melt itself, and wherever the sunlight reaches, it should incinerate the forest trees.

Since none of these three possess the nature of fire, it is sufficient to know that the nature of fire is empty. Nevertheless, due to the karmic power of these three, fire manifests in accordance with karma.
One can know for certain that its nature is empty. Thus, when fire arises pervading the world, how could it have a fixed location?
Therefore, one obtains fire by drilling wood and obtains fire by striking stone; it manifests according to karma, not limited to the single instance of the sun-stone (*sūryakānta*).

It all originates from within the inherently pure nature; the nature itself is the fire. What need is there for causes and conditions? Fire is the fire of the nature itself—how could it be said otherwise?
It is spontaneous. Therefore, know that the fire-element is neither caused by conditions nor is it spontaneous; yet that which "natures" it is one who is profound in the true mark (*dharmatā*).

When Xuefeng was opening the fire, he pointed to the fire and showed it to the assembly, saying, "The Buddhas of the three periods turn the great Dharma wheel within this flame. Yunmen said, "The flame is for the Buddhas of the three periods..."
[He] was preaching the Dharma. The Buddhas of the three periods of time stood on the ground and listened. Xuansha said, "Lately, the royal decree has become quite strict. Feng asked, "How so?
Xuansha said, "They do not permit anyone to jostle others while walking through the marketplace.
Feng then stuck out his tongue. One day, Caoshan entered the monks' hall to warm himself by the fire. Zeng said, "It is very cold today. Caoshan said, "You must know that there is something which..."
When it was cold, the monk asked, "Who is it that is not cold? Dongsan held up a torch to show him. The monk said, "Do not say there is no one here.
Dongsan threw down the torch. The monk said, "I do not understand this point. Dongsan said, "The sun shines upon the cold pond; it is even brighter.
When the ancients encountered a situation, they immediately revealed the path that goes beyond—this is for the sake of the nature.
Fire is true emptiness; the nature of emptiness is true fire. There is a point of genuine penetration and liberation.
Ānanda, the nature of water is not fixed; its flowing and ceasing are without constancy.
For instance, there are the great sages such as Kapiḷa (translated here as "yellow-red") of Śrāvastī, Kāla (translated here as "wheel"), and Padma-hrasva (translated here as "red lotus").

"O Ānanda, suppose a magician seeks the essence of the moon to mix with his magical elixir. These magicians, during the daytime of the bright fortnight, hold a *fangzhu* (a concave crystal) in their hands to catch the water from the moon.
Does this water emerge from within the crystal, does it exist spontaneously in the air, or does it come from the moon?

If, Ānanda, it comes from the moon, then since it can cause the crystal to produce water even from such a great distance, why do the trees and forests through which it passes not likewise produce water?"
All [the waters] should flow forth. If they flow, why wait for what is produced by the *fangzhu* (concave mirror)? If they do not flow, it is clear that the water does not descend from the moon.
If it were to emerge from the pearl, then this pearl should constantly produce flowing water; why then wait until the middle of the night to receive it under the white moon?
If it were produced from space, then since the nature of space is boundless, water would likewise be limitless; from humans to devas, all would be submerged and drowned.

How, then, could there still be those that move on water, land, or through the air? You should observe this more closely: the moon ascends from the heavens, and the pearl exists because it is held in the hand.
Regarding the pearl and the water basin: you yourself have set them out. From what direction does the water flow into this? The moon and the pearl are far apart; they are neither blended nor joined.
It cannot be that the water-crystal arose spontaneously from nowhere. You still do not understand [the nature of] the Tathāgatagarbha.

The nature of water is true emptiness; the nature of emptiness is true water. Pure and fundamentally so, it pervades the entire Dharma-realm. According to the minds of sentient beings, it responds to the measure of their cognition.
If one person grasps a pearl in one place, water appears in that place; if all throughout the Dharma-realm grasp them, water arises filling the entire Dharma-realm.

Beings fill the world; how could there be any fixed location? They manifest according to their karma. The world is ignorant and deludedly regards these as causes and conditions, or as arising from a nature of spontaneity.
All of these are merely the conceptual calculations of the discerning mind; they are nothing but words and have no real substance.
The Master said: "Fangzhu is also called yinsui (the 'yin-concave'). Its shape is like that of a clam shell.
If one polishes it until it is hot and directs it toward the moon, moisture will emerge from it in the form of water. Fang means 'stone' and zhu means 'pearl'; it is produced by refining stone.

It should be fashioned on the *renzi* day of the eleventh month at the hour of *zi*. Before the full moon it is called 'white,' after the full moon it is called 'black,' and at midday it is called 'day.'"
It also means that the moon is as bright as day. In meditative concentration, non-Buddhists may behold the disks of the sun and moon, or see red lotuses, as well as yellow and red colors;
thus, they each receive their names based on these techniques. The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says:
"For example, the forms of the sun and moon, the *padma* [lotus], the deep abyss, the void, and the embers of fire—such various signs as these [are seen by] the non-Buddhists..."
This is what is meant by the saying, "Every path leads to Chan. As for these illusory arts (*māyā*), they are all produced using medicinal substances.
The illusory arts of the immortals (*ṛṣi*) transmitted in the present age frequently employ *vājigandhā* (yangqishi) and lodestone, which belong to this same category.

The production of the "square pearl" from water is neither a result of synthetic combination nor is it spontaneous; it is certainly no different from the *sūryakānta* (sun-crystal). It is said that...
Emptiness is boundless; water should likewise be without limit. How could there then be movement on land, in water, or through the air?
Would this not contradict the true nature of water as emptiness? Generally speaking, when considered in terms of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), it has form;

thus, even if water fills space, one sinks together with it. When considered in terms of essence (*svabhāva*), it is formless; thus, space manifests as water without exhaustion. This is the true water of essence.
"Emptiness. "The nature of emptiness is true water. This refers to the nature of the pure four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

Because their nature is fundamentally empty, emptiness and emptiness mutually contain one another; emptiness and emptiness are non-dual. Who, then, could perceive any sign of one usurping or displacing the other?
Later, when Pūrṇa raised his doubt, he doubted only that the nature might be usurped, not the characteristics themselves. Characteristics are not [the issue].
[The Master] said, "The World-Honored One has already spoken of this previously. Why then do you still harbor doubts?
Yaoshan asked a monk, "Where have you come from? The monk replied, "From Hunan. Yaoshan said, "Is the water in Lake Dongting full yet? The monk said, "Not yet.
Yaoshan said, "After so much rain, why is it not full? The monk was speechless. Daowu spoke on his behalf, saying, "It is full."
Yunyan said, "Profoundly still. Dongshan asked, "In what kalpa has it ever increased or decreased?
Yunmen said, "It is right here. Furthermore, Xuefeng said, "Sitting by a grain basket, countless people die of hunger;
sitting by the sea, countless people die of thirst. Xuansha said, "Sitting inside a grain basket, no one dies of hunger."
[The story goes that] countless people were drowned by the seawater; they died of thirst in numbers beyond count. Yunmen said, "His whole body is rice; his whole body is water.
Tiandong took up this case and said, "I am not like that. Sitting inside a rice basket, he causes countless people to die of bloating."
The seawater submerges one's head, indiscriminately killing countless people. Beforehand, they are harmed because you do not swallow it; afterwards, they are harmed because you do not spit it out.
It is just as Yunmen said: "The whole body is rice; the whole body is water. When you reach this point, there is no place for you to swallow or spit out.
The ancients raised the theme of the waves of the ocean of nature, layer upon layer and inexhaustible; yet when it comes to Yunmen, [it is resolved].

The entire body is water; the words are now complete. This is precisely identical to the true emptiness of the nature-water and the true water of the nature-emptiness—pure and fundamental from the beginning, pervading the entire Dharma-realm, like two halves of a tally fitting together.
Thus, one should know that those who attempt to fathom the nature-emptiness and nature-water through conceptual thought and measurement fall short by far more than a mere fraction.
Ānanda, the nature of wind has no substance; its movement and stillness are not constant.

When you regularly adjust your robes to enter the great assembly, the corner of your saṃghāṭī (herein called the "great robe") may move and touch those beside you, causing a slight breeze to brush against their faces.
Does this wind emerge from the corner of the kāṣāya (herein called the "dyed robe"), arise from empty space, or is it produced on the faces of those people? Ānanda, if this wind were again...
"Pull out the corner of your *kāṣāya*. You are now exposed to the wind; as your robe flutters and billows, it ought to detach from your body.
Now that I am preaching the Dharma, look at my robes hanging within this assembly. Observe my robe: where is the wind? There should be no place within the robe where the wind could be hidden."
If wind were produced from space, your robe would not move; for what reason is there no stirring? Since the nature of space is eternally abiding, wind should be constantly produced.

If there were no wind, space itself would perish. If the extinction of wind could be perceived, what would the extinction of space look like? If there were such arising and ceasing, [space would be impermanent].
It is not called a false name; it is named "empty space. How does the wind emerge?

If the wind were produced from the face itself that is being brushed by it, then it should brush you as you yourself adjust your robe. Why, then, does it brush you in the opposite direction? Examine this carefully.
The adjustment of your robes belongs to you; your face belongs to that person. Space is tranquil and does not participate in movement. From which direction does the wind come to stir here?
The natures of wind and space are distinct; they are neither blended nor joined. It cannot be that the nature of wind exists of itself without a source.
"You are entirely unaware that within the Tathāgata-garbha, the nature of wind is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true wind.
It is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm; it accords with the minds of sentient beings and responds to the measure of their cognition.

Ānanda, suppose you, as a single person, slightly move your robe—there is a subtle breeze produced that sweeps throughout the Dharma-realm, fills the lands, and pervades the world. How could this not be so?"

As for spatial locations, they manifest according to one's karma. Those in the world lack understanding and are deludedly attached to them as being caused by external conditions, or as arising from a self-nature;
these are all merely conceptualizations and calculations of the conscious mind. They are nothing but verbal descriptions and possess no actual reality whatsoever.
Tong said: "The robe is on you, yet it does not flutter away; your face belongs to that person, yet the wind does not strike it.
Space is tranquil, yet it does not arise or perish along with the wind. These three do not participate in the nature and characteristics of the wind's movement.
What causes their conjunction? It cannot be that the nature of the wind emerges without a root. Who says it is self-originated?"

However, because wind is identical to nature (*dharmatā*) and nature is identical to wind, it manifests specifically in accordance with karma; it is simply like the arising of wind when a garment moves.
Since nature pervades the *dharmadhātu*, wind likewise pervades the *dharmadhātu*; therefore, they are both equally termed "Great.
Confucianists state that Kun represents earth, Kan represents water, Li represents fire, and Xun represents wind; in total, these do not go beyond yin and yang.
From what do yin and yang arise? They emerge from the movement and stillness within the Great Ultimate (Taiji).

Each individual thing possesses its own Great Ultimate, while all things collectively constitute the single Great Ultimate. There has never been a case where principle and phenomena are not identical, nor where phenomena and principle are not identical.
Yet, those who realize that the mind is the Great Ultimate are rare. Once one has realized that the mind is the Great Ultimate, throughout the world...
"How could there be any object outside of the mind? Once, while Magu was fanning himself, a monk asked, "The nature of wind is eternally abiding;
it is all-pervasive, reaching everywhere. Why, then, does the Master still shake his fan?
Magu said, "You only know that the nature of wind is eternally abiding, but you do not yet know that it reaches everywhere. The monk asked, "In what way does it reach everywhere? Magu—
He then shook his fan. The monk bowed, and Gu said, "What use is there for you, monk? Even if you were to wear a thousand of them, what benefit would it be?
Furthermore, Nanquan asked a monk, "The night breeze was fine last night. The monk replied, "The night breeze was fine last night."
Zhuanzi said, "The wind blew down a pine tree in front of the gate. A monk said, "The wind blew down a pine tree in front of the gate.
He then asked another monk, "There was a fine breeze last night. The monk said, "What kind of wind was it? Zhuanzi said, "It blew down a pine tree in front of the gate.
The monk said, "What kind of pine tree was it? Zhuanzi said, "One gained, one lost. According to these two monks—
The answer is: Both possess the breath of a true monk. Why did Nanquan say one gained and one lost?
If you can definitively determine who gains and who loses, you may be said to have personally seen Nanquan.
Ānanda, emptiness has no form; it is manifested through form.

For example, in the city of Śrāvastī, at a place far from the river, there dwell various Kṣatriyas (here translated as "royal lineage"), Brāhmaṇas (here translated as "pure-vowed ones"), Vaiśyas (merchants), Śūdras (farmers), as well as Purohitas.

(These are called "wise people") such as the caṇḍālas and others. (The executioners and fools) have newly established their dwellings; they dig a well seeking water, and having excavated one foot of earth—
Within it, there is one chi of empty space. In this manner, even until the earth has been excavated by one zhang, one likewise obtains one zhang of empty space in the interim.
The depth of this empty space corresponds to the amount of earth excavated. Is this space produced because of the earth being removed?

"It arises from causes; it does not arise spontaneously without a cause. Ānanda, if this space were to arise spontaneously without a cause, why was there no unobstructed openness before the earth was excavated?
One would have seen only the great earth, with nothing penetrating through it.

If it arose because of the earth, then at the moment the earth is removed, one should see the space entering. If the earth had already emerged first and there were no space to enter, how could space be said to arise because of the earth?"

And yet it emerges. If there were no entering or exiting, then empty space and the soil would fundamentally have no distinct causes. If they were not distinct, they would be identical; if they were identical, why does space not emerge when the soil emerges?
If it emerges because of digging, then the digging produces space and should not produce soil.

If it does not emerge because of digging, then the digging itself produces the soil—how then can one perceive space? You must examine this more carefully, examining it with the utmost precision. From where does the digging arise...
In the hands of people, it turns according to their movements; the earth shifts because of the ground. If such is the case with empty space, by what cause does it arise?

If one digs into emptiness, one encounters solidity; the void and the solid do not function as one another. It is neither a blending nor a conjunction. Thus, it should not be that empty space arises from nowhere on its own.
If this nature of empty space is perfect, pervasive, and fundamentally unmoving, you should know that the earth, water, fire, and wind presently before you are all likewise named [empty space].
The five elements are by nature truly interfused; they are all the Tathāgatagarbha, fundamentally without arising or ceasing. Ānanda, your mind is deluded and confused;
you do not realize that the four great elements are originally the Tathāgatagarbha. You should contemplate empty space: does it emerge, does it enter, or is it neither emerging nor entering?
"You do not know at all that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of awareness is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true awareness.

It is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm; it accords with the minds of sentient beings and responds to the measure of what they know. Ānanda, it is like a single well’s emptiness: the emptiness arises within that one well.
The empty space of the ten directions is also like this—it is perfectly full throughout the ten directions; how could it have a specific location? It follows karma."
I have discovered that the world is ignorant, deluded by causes and conditions as well as inherent nature; all of these are merely the conceptualizations and calculations of the conscious mind.
They consist only of verbal expressions and possess no real meaning whatsoever.
Tong said: "The nature of emptiness is formless; how could it have coming or going? It is only because it is manifested through form that we know there is emptiness.
Where there is form, there is no emptiness; where there is no form, that is emptiness itself. Form has coming and going, but emptiness has neither arising nor ceasing.
Not only can earth obstruct emptiness, but water, fire, and wind are all likewise form. It is not only by digging into the earth that one can perceive it."
Space. When water is drained, fire extinguished, and wind stilled, space can likewise be perceived. Thus, when the four great elements arise, space has never been absent;
when the four great elements cease, space does not begin to exist. While the four great elements come and go, space fundamentally has no entering or exiting.
The nature of space is all-pervasive and easy to understand: the four great elements are empty of intrinsic reality.
It is just like this. Before one follows after karma, [the mind] is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm;
it has never been non-existent. Once it has manifested, responding to conditions as they arise, it fills the world; yet it is not something that begins to exist now.

Its *lakṣaṇa* (phenomenal marks) undergo birth and extinction, but its *svabhāva* (intrinsic nature) is without birth or extinction. That which possesses birth and extinction necessarily lacks universal pervasiveness; only [that which is without birth and extinction] is universally pervasive.
As for "pervasive," it is itself without arising or ceasing; that which is called the Tathāgatagarbha comes from nowhere and goes nowhere—how could there be room for arising and ceasing within it?
If one were to discuss "insentient emptiness" (wankong), although it lacks coming and going, it still possesses arising and ceasing, as will be illustrated later:
"Within the Great Enlightenment, emptiness arises like a single bubble emerging from the ocean. Thus, throughout the ten directions, it is empty...
All [conditioned] emptinesses are utterly extinguished; only true emptiness is true awakening. Originally, it is devoid of arising and ceasing.

The preceding four great elements—true form, true fire, true water, and true wind—are all spoken of in terms of the "True" (Zhen). These are precisely what are later called the "Pure Four Great Elements.
They are all spoken of in terms of their intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*), without grasping at appearances; therefore, they are said to be "inherently true, perfectly interfused," and are the Tathāgata.
The Treasury (the *dharmadhātu*) is fundamentally without arising or ceasing. To speak clearly of the true nature of self-existence:
if all phenomena possessed form, how could they be perfectly interfused and unimpeded? What is meant by "interfusion" (*yōng*) is that form is emptiness and emptiness is form;
one perceives no trace of the five great elements, but only this single emptiness. What is meant by "perfection" (*yuán*) is that emptiness does not obstruct form, and form does not...
Obstructing space, the five great elements emerge in infinite alternation, yet they do not depart from the one true reality. Previously, the four great elements were integrated with true emptiness;
here, true emptiness is dissolved back into true awakening. This clarifies that what is called "true emptiness" is precisely "true awakening."
This is not comparable to a dull, blank emptiness. When Zen Master Huanglong Zuoxin ascended the hall, he said: "The mind is identical to the realm of empty space;
it manifests dharmas equal to empty space. When one realizes empty space, there is neither 'is' nor 'is-not. Simply rest thus."
Ceasing the oars and grasping the ropes, they moor the boat within the bay for a while. Yet, according to the gate of the patch-robed monks (śramaṇas), this is worlds apart.

But tell me, what excellence is there in the gate of the patch-robed monks? "Carrying a knotted staff slung across the shoulder, one goes straight into a thousand peaks and ten thousand peaks, regardless of others.
Furthermore, Hu Dingjiao went to visit Baoshou. Baoshou asked, "Are you not Hu Dingjiao?"
Huangbo asked, "Are you a tacker? Huangbo said, "No, I am not. Baoshou asked, "Can you still tack the void? Huangbo said, "Please, Master, break it open so that I may see it.
Baoshou then struck him. Huangbo was dissatisfied. Baoshou said, "In the future, there will be a talkative master who will point this out for you.
Later, he went to visit Zhaozhou. Zhaozhou asked, "Are you not that Huangbo tacker? Huangbo—
Wuye said, "I dare not. Zhaozhou asked, "Can you still nail the void? Huguo said, "I ask the Master to break it open and bring it here.
Zhaozhou said, "For now, let us nail this single crack. Huguo then cited the karmic incident of Baoshou striking with his staff.
Huguo asked, "I do not know where the fault lies. Zhaozhou said, "Even this single crack cannot yet be dealt with; how much less could he [Baoshou] have been told otherwise?"
He came breaking through empty space. On his behalf, [Zhaozhou] said, "For now, let us nail this seam shut.
Zhaozhou said, "My speaking thus is thousands of miles and ten thousand leagues apart from Baoshou. At this, Hu attained awakening. Considering these two cases together:
neither the one who realizes empty space is right, nor is the one who breaks through empty space right. What, then, is the path for emerging?
"Ānanda, the seeing-nature has no cognition; it exists because of form and emptiness. As you are now in the Jeta Grove, there is brightness in the morning and darkness in the evening;
even if it were midnight, there would be light during the bright fortnight and darkness during the dark fortnight. Thus, brightness and darkness alike exist because of seeing."
Analyze this: does this seeing share the same substance as light and darkness, as well as the great void of space;
or is it not of one substance? Is it both the same and not the same, or different and not different?

Ānanda, if this seeing were fundamentally of one substance with light, darkness, and space, then light and darkness—being two distinct substances—would cancel each other out; thus, when it is dark, there would be no light.

When there is light, there is no darkness. If light were identical to darkness, then when light appears, seeing would vanish. Conversely, if they were necessarily one with light, then darkness should cease to exist;
if it ceased, how could one see both light and darkness? If light and darkness are distinct, then seeing itself is without arising or ceasing. How, then, can they be said to be one?

If this essence of vision were not of one substance with darkness and light, then, setting aside light, darkness, and empty space, what form or shape would you discern as the fundamental source of vision?
Apart from light, apart from darkness, and apart from empty space, this fundamental source of vision would be like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit.
Since light, darkness, and empty space—these three things—are all distinct, from what could vision be established? Light and darkness are mutually opposed.

How can they be said to be the same? Apart from these three, there is nothing else. How can they be said to be different? They are distinguished as space and as vision. Since they originally have no boundaries, how can they not be the same?
When one sees darkness and when one sees light, their nature does not change; how can they not be different?

You should examine this more minutely—examine it with great care, examine it with precision, and observe it with discernment. Light comes from the sun; darkness comes from the dark moon; their pervasion belongs to empty space.

It returns to the great earth. In this same way, from what source does this essence of seeing arise? The faculty of seeing is conscious, while space is insentient; they are neither blended nor joined.

Thus, it cannot be that the essence of seeing arises spontaneously from nowhere. If the natures of seeing, hearing, and knowing are perfect, pervasive, and fundamentally unmoving, [how could they arise from elsewhere?]
You should know that the boundless, immovable space, together with its shifting earth, water, fire, and wind, are all equally called the six great elements (*ṣaḍdhātu*).
Their nature is truly perfect and harmonious; they are all the Tathāgatagarbha, fundamentally without birth or extinction.

Ānanda, your nature is submerged in saṃsāra because you do not realize that your seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha. You should contemplate these faculties of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing: are they born...?
Is it cessation? Is it identity or difference? Is it neither arising nor ceasing? Is it neither identical nor different?

You have never known that within the *tathāgatagarbha*, the nature of seeing is luminous awareness, and luminous awareness is the essence of seeing; it is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire *dharmadhātu*.

In accordance with the minds of sentient beings, it responds to the measure of what is known. Just as a single faculty of sight perceives throughout the *dharmadhātu*, so too do hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and the awareness of touch [function].
Awakened awareness is wondrously pure and radiant, pervading the entire Dharma-realm and filling the ten voids; how could it have a fixed location? It manifests according to karma.
Those in the world lack understanding and, deluded, regard it as having causes and conditions or as being of a spontaneous nature;
all such views are merely the conceptual calculations of the conscious mind. There are only words, but no real meaning at all.

Tong said: "The five great elements—earth, water, fire, wind, and space—already possess the six objects of the senses: form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and dharmas; these are what are called the 'objective divisions' (nimitta-bhāga).
Now, the six sense organs—seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing—are likewise composed of the pure four great elements.
When color and space appear before one, consciousness arises in response to the object; this is the stage prior to entering into discrimination."
The five consciousnesses are what is called the "seeing portion" (*darśana-bhāga*). Therefore, by means of the "great seeing," they are subsumed as one.

Just as the faculty of sight sees throughout the Dharma-realm, so too do hearing, smelling, tasting, and touching perceive their respective objects. This wondrous virtue is luminously pure and pervades the entire Dharma-realm.
Why is it uniformly called "wondrous"? Because when there is form, there is seeing; when there is sound, there is hearing. It is swift without haste and reaches without moving.
It arises spontaneously; it does not result from deliberation, nor does it depend on artificial arrangement. Therefore, it is called "wondrous. This seeing has no inherent substance;
it exists only because of objects. If the preceding object is absent, seeing does not arise.

How could there be a single substance or multiple substances that either separate from or unite with objects, such that they could be discussed through the four propositions of identity and difference? Those who establish their arguments based on these four propositions are all...
This is idle proliferation (*prapañca*). Thus, light and darkness, penetration and obstruction, alternate before one's eyes, just as earth, water, fire, and wind manifest alternately within space.
While objects undergo arising and ceasing, the seeing-nature is without arising or ceasing; while objects are subject to movement and agitation, the seeing-nature is without movement or agitation.
Its pervasiveness throughout the Dharma-realm is non-dual with empty space. Nevertheless, the seeing-faculty is aware and cognizant, whereas empty space is inert; they cannot be blended.

They are unified. Awakening is itself emptiness; this is called "true emptiness. Now, inert emptiness (*wankong*) possesses arising and ceasing, whereas true emptiness is devoid of arising and ceasing.
Inert emptiness arises and ceases within true awakening, just as the four great elements arise and cease within space.
Space and the four great elements cannot be discussed in terms of identity or difference regarding arising and ceasing; yet, through seeing awakening, one realizes this.
Regarding the emptiness of form, how could one observe it through arising and ceasing, or sameness and difference?

All that is spoken of as arising and ceasing, or sameness and difference, belongs to delusory objects. All that is spoken of as neither arising nor ceasing, and neither the same nor different, belongs to delusory conceptualization.
This is distinguished only with respect to the object, not with respect to the nature; therefore, it constitutes conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
If it were distinguished with respect to the nature, this vision would take the nature as its object, like a second moon that does not depart from the true moon.
Thus, when the nature manifests as vision, it is precisely the true awakening manifesting as clarity. Awakening is the essence of that vision; clarity is that vision’s...
This is its function. It is like a lamp that has light: the lamp is the essence of illumination, while the light is the function of illumination.
To see is to awaken; to awaken is to be empty. Fundamentally, there is no defilement, hence it is called "pure.

Fundamentally, there is no contrived activity, hence it is called "original. Fundamentally, there is no location, hence it is called "pervasive. This is discussed in terms of the three bodies (*trikāya*).
Purity is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); original suchness is the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*); pervasiveness is the Transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*). Discussed in terms of the three virtues:
purity is principle (*li*); original suchness is wisdom (*jñāna*); pervasiveness is practice (*caryā*). These three are integrated and subsumed;
raising one implies all three, and raising all three implies the one. When there is no stimulus, it is pure, originally such, and pervasive.
The Dharma-realm: this vision does not sink into non-existence. Since it is in accord [with reality], its wondrous virtue is brilliantly radiant, pervading and encompassing the entire Dharma-realm.
This vision does not cling to existence. The six sense organs are pure, and they fill the ten voids.

Therefore, there are those who see a hundred Buddha-realms, and those who see a thousand Buddha-realms; yet they must see that which encompasses the entire Dharma-realm before the purity is truly fulfilled.

[Objection: It is not so. Furthermore, it should be understood that all objects of cognition merely manifest according to one's karma. Later [the text] says: "If you take emptiness as clarity, then emptiness appears;
if you individually clarify earth, water, fire, and wind, then each of these appears. This refers to the phenomena within the scope of what is known.

Because one turns one's back on awakening and unites with the dust [of sensory objects], one gives rise to worldly toil (*rajas*); because one turns one's back on the dust and unites with awakening, one gives rise to... [liberation].
Suchness (*tathatā*). This is a matter that manifests according to karma. The nature of awakened clarity is without action, without creation, and without a recipient;
yet the karma of good and evil does not perish. This is why it is called the *Tathāgatagarbha*.
The official Haoyue asked Changsha Chengyan: "When an earthworm is cut in two, both ends move. I do not know—"
"Buddha-nature resides in Anantamukha. The Śramaṇa asked, "As for 'moving' and 'non-moving,' what kind of realm is this?

Yuezhou said, "These words do not accord with the scriptures; they are not the talk of the wise. As for your question, Master—what kind of realm are 'moving' and 'non-moving,' and from which sutra do they originate?
The Śramaṇa said, "It is evident that these words do not accord with the scriptures; they are not the talk of the wise..."
Regarding what was discussed: Great Virtue, do you not see that the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:

"One should know that the boundless, immovable space of the ten directions, together with the shifting earth, water, fire, and wind, are all equally named the six great elements. Their nature is truly perfect and harmonious;
they are all the Tathāgatagarbha, fundamentally without arising or ceasing. It then presents this verse: "Most profound, most profound, the Dharma-realm..."
The human body is itself the mind. When deluded, one mistakes the mind for the myriad forms; when awakened, the realm of lands is the true mind.
Both the body and the objective field lack any real characteristic. One who clearly realizes this is called a "true knower.

Changsha was excellent at expounding the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, even to the point of saying that the body and the objective field have no real characteristics, and that internally there is no faculty capable of seeing, nor externally...

Regarding the realm of seeing, both the subject and object are empty; when sought, the act of seeing cannot be found at all. How, then, can one further speak of the arising and ceasing, or the identity and difference [of this seeing]?
Ānanda, the nature of consciousness has no source; it arises falsely due to the six kinds of faculties and objects. You should now survey this entire assembly.
The noble assembly uses their eyes to survey them; as those eyes look all around, it is merely like [seeing] within a mirror, with no further analysis.

As you, O consciousness, identify them one by one—pointing out, "This is Mañjuśrī," "This is Pūrṇa," "This is Maudgalyāyana," "This is Subhūti," "This is Śāriputra"—does this conscious cognition arise from seeing, or does it arise from marks, or does it arise...?

"Empty space arises suddenly without any cause. Ānanda, if the nature of your consciousness were born within seeing, then the four—namely darkness, light, form, and emptiness—would necessarily not exist;
since they are fundamentally absent, your seeing would have no basis. If the nature of seeing itself does not exist, how could consciousness arise?"

From what does consciousness arise? If the nature of your consciousness arises within the objective form and not from the faculty of seeing, then since you do not see light nor do you see darkness, and light and darkness are not perceived, there would be neither form nor emptiness. If even that objective form does not exist, from what could consciousness arise?
If one arises within emptiness, it is neither a mark nor a vision. Without vision, there is no discernment; one cannot, of itself, know light, darkness, form, or emptiness.

Since marks are extinguished and conditions cease, seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing have no place to be established. Abiding in this state where both are non-existent, emptiness is then the same as nothingness.
There is no object that is not identical to its own substance; even if you were to give rise to consciousness, what would there be to discern?
If it emerged suddenly without any cause, why do you not discern the bright moon at midday? You should examine this more closely, scrutinizing it with great care: the seeing relies upon your pupils.
Mutually pushing against the external objects before them, they can be manifested as existing; they do not mutually establish non-existence. Thus, from what source does this consciousness arise?
When consciousness moves, the seeing remains clear; it is neither a blending nor a union with hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, or cognizing, which are likewise so.

It should not be that the conditions of consciousness arise spontaneously from nowhere. If this conscious mind fundamentally has no source, then one should know that the discernment of seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing [is likewise without source].
Perfectly full and profoundly still, their nature does not arise from external conditions; including space, earth, water, fire, and wind, these are all equally called the "Seven Great Elements.
Their nature is truly perfect and harmoniously fused; they are all the Tathāgata-garbha, fundamentally devoid of arising and ceasing. Ānanda, your mind is coarse and flighty;

you do not realize that seeing, hearing, awareness, and cognition are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha. You should contemplate these six empty consciousnesses of the mind: are they the same [as the elements]?

Is it different? Is it empty or existent? Is it neither identical nor different? Is it neither empty nor existent? You fundamentally do not know that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature-consciousness is luminously aware;
the awakened luminosity is the true consciousness. This wondrous awakening is profoundly still, pervading and encompassing the entire Dharma-realm.

It contains and exhales the ten voids; how could it have a fixed location? It manifests according to karma. The world lacks knowledge and is deludedly grasping at it as being caused by conditions or arising from itself.
However, these natures are all merely conceptualizations and calculations of the discerning mind; they exist only as verbal expressions and possess no real meaning.

It is said in general that earth, water, fire, and wind depend upon space to constitute the five great natures of the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*), which are what are called the "objective aspects" (*nimitta-bhāga*).
That which is called seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing depends upon consciousness to constitute the five great natures of the root-body (*mūla-kāya*), which are the... [subjective aspects].
This refers to the aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*). Both the aspects of seeing and appearance (*nimitta-bhāga*) arise equally from the eighth consciousness;

therefore, the eight consciousnesses are profoundly still, which is termed "wondrous enlightenment" (*miao-jue*) and is termed the "Tathāgata-garbha. Now, the first five consciousnesses are taken as the "greatness of seeing," which refers to the objective realm (*xing-jing*) and belongs to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
The sixth consciousness is taken as the "greatness of cognition," which refers to the discriminative consciousness of phenomena (*fen-bie shi-shi*).

This belongs to the category of inference (*anumāna*) and is not a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*). Followers of the Two Vehicles do not know that there are the seventh and eighth consciousnesses.
They take this [sixth consciousness] as the master and lord, which performs good and evil karma and possesses a preeminent power. Therefore, the first five consciousnesses are non-conceptual;

it is only upon reaching the sixth consciousness that one is able to conceptualize. Thus it is said: "When consciousness moves, seeing is still. This refers only to this consciousness, which does not arise from...
Seeing does not arise from form, nor does it arise from emptiness; it is not produced by causes and conditions, nor does it suddenly emerge without cause.

It is not produced spontaneously. Furthermore, these six consciousnesses possess all three natures—wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate—and each has its own seeds and active manifestations (pravṛtti) corresponding to the six sense organs and their objects.
They are neither blended nor combined; all three are equally non-existent [as independent entities].

Being utterly without a place of reliance, from where could this consciousness possibly have come? If it were produced from views, produced from marks, or produced from emptiness, then it would have a point of origin.
Having a point of origin implies having a location, which would mean it is not all-pervasive.

Only when there is no place from which it comes—neither coming from existence nor coming from non-existence—is its nature such that it does not originate from any locus; this is its fundamental state.
