It is boundless; it is fundamentally all-pervasive and perfect. Therefore, this clear and luminous discerning consciousness (*vijnana*) gives rise to the aforementioned two divisions of subject and object, both of which are termed the "Seven Great Elements.
When consciousness returns to its profound stillness, these six consciousnesses merge with the eighth consciousness; hence, it is called the *Tathagatagarbha*.
If the six consciousnesses merge with sensory objects, they are said to be "identical" or "existent"; when they depart from sensory objects, they are said to be...
Difference is emptiness; it is neither conjoined nor separated, and no trace can be found. Only then can it be called "serenely still.

Why is this serenely still consciousness called the "consciousness of nature" (*xing-shi*) and the "true consciousness" (*zhen-shi*)? It gives rise to cognition from clarity, rather than arising from emotion;
it produces illumination from awareness, rather than arising from objects. This consciousness flows forth from within true nature and true awareness.

Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is itself the nature. Consciousness is itself awakening. This refers to what is called the transformation of the eighth consciousness into the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*).
This luminous clarity of the nature-consciousness is precisely the true consciousness of the luminous clarity of awakening; it is simply what is meant by "the wondrous clarity is clearly wondrous.
Therefore, it is said that "wondrous awakening is profoundly still, pervading and encompassing the Dharma-realm. The preceding six [consciousnesses] are all likewise described as such.
It is pure and fundamentally so. Here, it is specifically described as "wondrous enlightenment, profound and still," which distinguishes it by being regulated by both "equality" and "wondrousness.
Thus, there is a subtle difference. The previous six [consciousnesses] are said to "perfectly fill the ten directions," which seems to accord with the meaning of the nature itself;

here, it is specifically said to "contain and expel the ten voids," which seems to accord with the meaning of its manifestation. The nature of consciousness has no source, yet it is able to be the source of the myriad dharmas. Regarding all that was previously...
That which is called the Tathāgatagarbha all returns to this. Regarding emptiness, it is said:

"Your mind is deluded," meaning you are confused about the difference between the four great elements and emptiness; for the nature of emptiness is awakening. Regarding views, it is said: "Your nature is submerged."
This means to flow and revolve after sensory objects without returning. Because one perceives the awakening yet does not move, regarding consciousness it is said:

"Your mind is coarse and floating. This means that while the essence of consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*) is latent within, "floating" refers to merely identifying with the floating sense-faculties (*indriya*), and "coarse" refers to failing to penetrate the essence of consciousness.

Although the five aggregates (*skandha*) are distributed among the eighteen realms (*dhātu*), this section alone provides a detailed analysis of consciousness, because— [as in the original text]... as such.
Within the *ālayavijñāna*, that which is neither arising nor ceasing yet is in conjunction with what arises and ceases constitutes the *ālaya-vijñāna*.
That which is ultimately able to return to the state of non-arising and non-ceasing is called the ninth consciousness; it is both consciousness and nature (*dharmatā*).
That which cannot ultimately do so and still retains arising and ceasing, though it may be profoundly still and undisturbed, is consciousness but not nature. This is seeing the nature.
One who does not become deluded regarding consciousness finds the subtle within the awakening of the mind. Baoshou ascended the hall and said: "The three realms are but mind;
the myriad dharmas are but consciousness. Clouds arise beyond the railing; raindrops fall before the eaves. The mountain stream is as clear as indigo; wild flowers bloom like woven patterns.
If you do not investigate the source at this very moment, you will vainly ask Maitreya in the future. Do you understand?
Do you understand? Do not trouble yourself by standing for long. Danxia’s verse says: Spiritually resonant, it does not involve past, present, or future.
The entire triple world is but a single point of mind. Outside the railing, peach blossoms and spring butterflies dance; Before the gate, willow trees and morning orioles sing.
Furthermore, the *Weixin jue* (Secret Instructions on Mind-Only) states: "The cragside trees and the branches in the courtyard each manifest boundless wondrous forms;

the howling of monkeys and the chirping of birds all discourse upon the perfect sound of non-duality. Only by awakening to this can one believe that throughout the entire earth, there is nothing that is not medicine—not merely the seven elements.
Otherwise, a profound discourse on the principle would instead become a poisonous drug; how could this be?
To insist that things must arise through causes and conditions is mere conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). A monk asked Yaoshan, "My own matter is not yet clear; I beg the Master for instruction.

Yaoshan remained silent for a long while and said, "It would not be difficult for me to speak a single phrase for you right now, provided you could see it immediately upon hearing it—this would still leave some room for progress. If you further enter into deliberation, however, you will instead become my... [disciple].

This is a transgression. It would be better for each of you to simply keep your mouths shut to avoid implicating one another. Therefore, know that when the mind of wisdom engages in speculative calculation, it moves further and further away from the Way.
As long as there is verbal expression, it is not the true meaning.

At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly, having received the subtle and wondrous instruction of the Buddha-Tathāgata, felt their bodies and minds become utterly expansive and free from all obstructions.
Each member of this great assembly came to know for themselves that the mind pervades the ten directions and perceived the emptiness of the ten directions.
Just as one observes the object held in one's hand, so too all things existing within the entire world are none other than the wondrous, luminous, and primordial mind of Bodhi.
This essence of mind is pervasive and perfect, encompassing the ten directions. Turn back and observe the body born of your parents.

It is like a single mote of dust blown into the empty space of the ten directions, existing yet vanishing; or like a single bubble floating upon a vast, still ocean, arising and ceasing without trace.
Thus, one clearly knows for oneself that the fundamental, wondrous mind has been attained—eternally abiding and never extinguished.
He prostrated to the Buddha with palms joined, experiencing what he had never known before. Before the Tathāgata, he spoke verses in praise of the Buddha, saying:
"The essence of mind is all-pervasive and perfectly round, encompassing the ten directions. The magnitude of the mind is vast and great; it is inherently so.
Even the emptiness of the ten directions appears as an object in the palm of one's hand, and one’s own physical body is equal to a mote of dust. This was the beginning.
To bring delusions back to the truth while still maintaining dualistic views is to remain several houses' distance from the state where body and mind are one and nothing exists outside the body.
When Grand Master Lu asked Nanquan, "Master Zhao is truly extraordinary;
he understands that heaven and earth share the same root as I, and that all things are one body with me," Nanquan pointed to the peony flowers in the courtyard.
The Master said: "At that time, people saw this single stalk of flowers as if it were a dream.
Lu was at a loss for words. Xuedou’s verse says: "Hearing, seeing, sensing, and knowing are not each distinct; Mountains and rivers do not exist within a mirror.
In the frosty sky, the moon has fallen and night is half spent; Who, with the clear pool, reflects the cold image? Tiantong’s verse says: "Illuminating through to the subtle and the manifest..."
The root of creation: amidst the bustling appearance and disappearance, one beholds its gate. Wandering the spirit beyond kalpas, one asks what exists;
fixing the gaze before the body, one knows the wondrous presence. The tiger’s roar sighs as the mountain breeze blows; the dragon’s cry lingers as the cave clouds darken.
Nanquan pierced through the dreams of people of his time. If you wish to recognize the majestic Honored One who is the successor to the position [of Buddhahood], an ancient worthy said:
"In every place is Maitreya; there is no gate and no Sudhana. This means that all things existing within this entire world are none other than the wondrously luminous, original mind of Bodhi.
If one recognizes this, one will know for oneself that it is eternally abiding and indestructible, and thus have faith.
When bubbles are gathered, they become the ocean; one does not perceive any signs of arising or ceasing. Therefore, it is said that their arising and ceasing have no source.
Emperor Shunzong of the Tang dynasty asked Foguangman: "From what direction does the Buddha come? Toward what direction does he go when he passes away?
Since you say he dwells eternally in the world, where is the Buddha now? Foguangman replied: "The Buddha comes from the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); he passes away toward the unconditioned."
As for departing: the Dharmakāya is equal to empty space; it eternally abides in the state of no-mind. Where there is thought, one returns to no-thought;
where there is dwelling, one returns to non-dwelling. One comes for the sake of sentient beings; one departs for the sake of sentient beings.
The ocean of pure True Suchness is profound and its essence eternally abiding. Let the wise contemplate this well and harbor no further doubts. The Emperor asked again: "The Buddha, toward..."

Born in the royal palace, he passed away beneath the twin śāla trees; he remained in the world for forty-nine years. Furthermore, it is said that there is no dharma to be taught: mountains, rivers, and the great ocean;
heaven and earth, as well as the sun and moon—when their time comes, they all return to extinction. Who can say they are not subject to birth and death?
Doubtful thoughts remain like this; the wise should discern them well. Man-da replied: "The essence of the Buddha is fundamentally unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);

it is through deluded sentiments that false discriminations arise. The Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is equal to empty space; it has never undergone birth or cessation. When conditions are met, a Buddha appears in the world."
The Buddha enters nirvana without conditions, yet transforms sentient beings everywhere;
like the moon reflected in water, he is neither permanent nor annihilated, neither arising nor ceasing. Arising has never truly arisen, and ceasing has never truly ceased.
To clearly perceive the state of no-mind is naturally beyond verbal expression. Emperor Xunzong was greatly delighted. One day, Prime Minister Pei entered Kaiyuan Temple.
At a temple, he saw a mural and asked the temple master, "What is this painting? The temple master replied, "It is a portrait of a high monk.
Pei said, "The form and shadow are here; where is the high monk? The temple master was speechless. Pei said: [This is the meaning of the encounter.]
"Is there any Chan master here? The abbot replied, "There is one. He then invited Huangbo to meet him and recounted the previous conversation to ask Huangbo about it.
Huangbo called out, "Pei Xiu! Pei responded, "Yes. Huangbo asked, "Where are you? At these words, Pei had an awakening.
This may serve as evidence that the permanent abiding is neither born nor extinguished; therefore, I have appended this record.
"The Wondrous, Profound, Total-Holding, Immovable Honored One, the King of Śūraṅgama, is rare in the world.
Dinglin said: "The essence of consciousness is water; when the water does not ripple, it is called 'profound' (zhan)—this is what is meant by 'perfect profundity' (yuan-zhan)."
This [nature] is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire dharma-realm. When it is not divided into six, it is profoundly perfect.
What is called "wondrous profundity" means that through wondrous power it maintains total retention without movement; thus it is profoundly wondrous.

What is called "the nature of awakened, profound clarity" means that awakening merges with the essence of consciousness, like the sun merging with water to possess the nature of clarity. This is what is called "profound essence."

"Perfectly constant" refers to the essence of consciousness (*vijñāna-śuddha-sāra*), which is perfectly still and translucent. Because it has already extinguished arising and ceasing, it is called "constant.
This so-called stillness is not a state of non-flowing; it is like a rapid current that appears tranquil from a distance. As the Sūtra says: "When consciousness moves, vision is clear;
thus, consciousness possesses a nature of movement, which is termed the source of ideation (*saṃjñā-mūla*). Unless one attains the wondrous stillness of total retention (*dhāraṇī*), then thoughts...
The perfuming of mindfulness and the torrent of habitual tendencies give rise to the various formations (*saṃskāra*). The sūtra uses the metaphor of a flowing stream for these formations;
yet, compared to the formations, consciousness is still called "still" (*zhan*). This is what is meant by "the stillness entering and merging with stillness":

it is like when waves and ripples subside and transform into clear water, which is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*). Internally and internally, there is still, luminous clarity; one enters where there is nothing to enter.
This is called the domain of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). That which is termed "penetrating clarity" (*zhan ru*) is precisely the aggregate of consciousness.

Since penetrating clarity constitutes the aggregate of consciousness, this clarity is the luminous awareness of the nature of consciousness; this luminous awareness is itself wisdom (*jñāna*). Wisdom and consciousness—this is the boundary of consciousness.

Therefore, it is said that the five aggregates consist of "the profound entry merging with the profound," returning to the limits of consciousness (*vijñāna*). Why is the nature of consciousness not called "the profound entry"?

Because it pervades the entire Dharma-realm and thus has no coming or going. What is called "innermost profound clarity entering where there is nothing to enter" means that the emergence of the profound constitutes activity (*saṃskāra*), which is like the flow of water;
the entry of the profound constitutes consciousness. When consciousness ceases, the aggregate of activity (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is extinguished. Then...
Internally and internally, it is profoundly clear and bright; one enters until reaching the source of perception, where there is nothing further to enter.

That which is called the "essence of consciousness" (*vijñāna-dhātu*) is precisely the *ādāna-vijñāna*. That which is called "adhering to the profound clarity" adheres to this essence of consciousness. This essence of consciousness—
It is like water that is pure and clean; originally it has no viscosity. Because of the false arising of discrimination, it combines with form, and thus water and earth become mixed.

Only then can viscosity be produced. If one recognizes this consciousness—that it is like pure and clean water, originally devoid of viscosity—and is able not to combine with form, then it will detach from viscosity and settle within.
Therein lies the profound clarity of the perfectly clear, the wondrously clear, and the awakened clarity.

Exquisite. There is profound clarity (*zhan-ru*), and there is sticky clarity (*nian-zhan*). These meanings are as explained previously; they are distinguished by the finest nuances, serving as metaphors for the totality of the Dharma.
As Aśvaghoṣa said: "Relying on non-awakening, the mind takes movement as its activity; when awakened, it does not move.

Now, this state of awakening where there is no movement is what is called "wondrously profound and total retention" (*miao-zhan zongchi*). When there is movement, it becomes activity, flowing and shifting to become the various [phenomena].
"Go! That which is called the King of Śūraṅgama is the Śūraṅgama Samādhi. Because Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages are able to attain it, the Buddha is its king.
One day, while Master Fu was lecturing on a sutra, the Emperor arrived.
The entire assembly rose, but the Master alone sat upright and did not move. An attendant reported, "The Imperial carriage is here; why do you not [rise]?"
He rose. The layman said, "If the earth of the Dharma were to move, all would be unsettled. If you are a Great Being such as this, you have truly attained the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
A monk asked Chan Master Fang of Jiangshan, "What is the Immovable Honored One?
Fang said, "Wearing only his cotton robe, he passes through the marketplace. The monk said, "I do not yet understand. Fang said, "Riding a donkey, he tramples through the mountain caves."
Tinghu. The monk said, "Having passed through the three-tiered waves, one listens intently for a single roll of thunder. Huangbo said, "Stretching out a hand, one does not see one's own palm.
The monk asked, "Is it still permitted for a student to advance further? Huangbo said, "Treading upon the ground, one addresses the void."
The monk said, "Under the Leimen Gate, whose cloth drum is being beaten? Fang said, "On an eight-petaled flower ball, there is no need for embroidered red banners.
The monk said, "Thirty years from now, these words will spread far and wide; it is a skillful means to strike. Jiangshan is naturally a man of that other side;
he is not hindered by following the current to attain the wondrous. Yet, this monk mistakenly identified the compass needle.
"It is difficult to converse with you.
You have dissolved my inverted conceptions of billions of kalpas, attaining the Dharma-body without passing through the *asaṃkhyeya* eons.
He replied: "Even 'billions of kalpas' has a number that can be pointed out; 'asaṃkhyeya' refers to the three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*). There is no beginning."
From that time onward, those who were deluded regarding the truth and identified with the false all held inverted views.

Now, having brought the false back to the true, they have attained their original wondrous mind, which is eternally abiding and imperishable—just as previously described, this is what is called the *tathāgatagarbha*, or the *dharmakāya*. A monk asked Huangbo:
The teachings state: "Dissolve my inverted conceptions of billions of kalpas; without passing through the *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, I shall obtain the Dharma-body.
How is this so? Baizhang said: "If one were to attain something through cultivation over three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, one would not attain it even in kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
If, however, one obtains the Dharma-body within a single *kṣaṇa*, directly perceiving one's nature, that is still..."
This is the ultimate discourse of the teachings of the Three Vehicles. Why is this? Because it views the Dharmakāya as something that can be attained;
thus, it is all subsumed within the category of teachings of incomplete meaning (*neyārtha*). Huangbo’s utterances and exhalations of breath truly reveal him to be a vessel for the Mahāyāna.
Since Ānanda had already attained the Dharmakāya, why did he further say, "I hope you will further examine and eliminate even the most subtle delusions"? This was because he [still] perceived...

Because there is a *dharmakāya* that can be attained. When the Venerable Fu of Taiyuan was first lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* at Guangxiao Monastery in Yangzhou, a practitioner of Chan who had been stranded by the snow went to listen to the lecture.

When the discourse reached the section on the three causes of Buddha-nature, the three virtues, and the *dharmakāya*, and the Venerable Fu expounded extensively upon the subtle principles of the *dharmakāya*, the Chan practitioner could not help but laugh. After Fu finished his lecture, he invited the Chan practitioner to eat.
Cha said, "I, [Name], have always been of narrow and inferior resolve, interpreting the meaning according to the literal text. I have just now incurred your laughter; I hope you will instruct me.
The Chan practitioner said, "I truly laugh because you, Master of Commentaries, do not recognize the Dharma-body. Fu said, "If this is how you explain it..."
"Where is it not so? [Feng] said, "Please, Master, explain it once more. Fu said, "The principle of the Dharma-body is like the vast void:
vertically it exhausts the three periods of time, horizontally it spans the ten directions; it encompasses the eight poles and includes the two polarities."
"Responding to conditions and meeting with stimuli, there is nowhere he does not pervade. A Chan practitioner said, "I do not say that you, Master of the Tripitaka, are wrong;
however, what you have described is merely the extent of the *dharmakāya*. You have not yet truly realized the *dharmakāya* within yourself.
Fufu said, "If it is so, then may you, Virtuous One of Chan, explain it for me. The practitioner asked, "Do you believe it? Fufu replied, "How could I dare not believe?"
The Chan practitioner said, "If it is so, the Preceptor shall suspend his lectures for ten days and sit upright in quiet meditation within his chamber.

He must withdraw his mind and collect his thoughts, casting aside all conditions of good and evil at once. Trusting solely in what has been taught, he shall practice from the first watch of the night until the fifth.
Upon hearing the sound of the drum and horn, he will suddenly achieve realization. Thereupon, he went to knock on the door. The Chan practitioner said:
"Who are you? Hu replied, "I am so-and-so. The Chan master rebuked him, saying, "I have instructed you to transmit and uphold the Great Teaching and preach the Dharma on behalf of the Buddha.
Why did you come here last night drunk and lying in the street? Hu said, "Virtuous Chan Master, since I began lecturing on the sutras, I have been twisting the nostrils of my biological parents.
From this day forward, I shall never dare to act like this again. The Chan master—
He said, "Go now; let us meet tomorrow. If you have true conviction, you shall truly attain the Dharmakāya without passing through the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.
A monk asked Master Lishan, "Please point directly to the attainment of the Dharmakāya without passing through the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*. Lishan said:
The son inherited his father’s legacy. [A monk] asked, “How should one comprehend this? Shanshan said, “To diminish and strip away is not compassionate.
The monk said, “If that is so, then the great assembly will have someone to rely upon. Shanshan said, “Setting aside the great assembly for a moment, what is the Dharma-body?
The monk had no reply. Shanshan said, “Ask me; I will tell you. The monk then asked, “What is the Dharma-body? Shanshan said:
Like flowers in the sky or a mirage—tell me, how does the Dharma-body preached by Mount Li compare to that of Ānanda?
May you now attain the fruit and become a Treasure King, once again delivering as many beings as there are sands in the Ganges.
Tong said: "To attain the Dharma-body without passing through the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*—this is precisely the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*). The stage of ordinary humanity is not yet it.
Therefore, when practice is perfected and the fruit is fulfilled, one truly realizes true wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*), like pure lapis lazuli containing a precious moon within;
only then does one become a Treasure King (*ratnarāja*). Reaching this point, one universally observes that all sentient beings possess the Tathāgata’s wisdom, virtues, and marks. My...
I shall deliver each and every one of them. Sentient beings are inexhaustible; my vow is inexhaustible. To give rise to loving-kindness and exercise compassion is something I cannot help but do.
This is truly because the Triple Gem of Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha serves as the bridge and ferry for the masses.
At the beginning of Dongshan’s life, he first visited Yunmen. Yunmen asked, "Where have you recently come from? He replied, "From Chadu. Yunmen asked, "Where did you spend the summer retreat?"
The Master said, "I am from Baoci in Hunan. Zhimen asked, "When did you leave there? He replied, "On the twenty-fifth of the eighth month.
Zhimen said, "I grant you three blows of the staff. The next day, he went up to inquire after the Master’s health, saying, "Yesterday I received the Master’s three blows of the staff;
I do not know where my fault lay. Zhimen said, "You rice-bag! You have been [running] back and forth between Jiangxi and Hunan..."
"Go thus. At these words, he attained great enlightenment. He then said, "In the future, I shall go to places where there is no human habitation;
I will not store a single grain of rice nor plant a single stalk of vegetable.

I will receive those coming and going from the ten directions, thoroughly helping them to pull out their nails and extract their wedges, cast off their greasy hats, and strip away their foul-smelling cloth robes, so that they may be free and easy."
To become a "non-active" monk on this very earth—how joyful that would be! Nanquan said, "Your body is as small as a coconut, yet you open such a large mouth.
At these words, Baizhang immediately prostrated himself.
"To offer this profound mind to every dust-mote world is what is called repaying the Buddha's kindness.

Tong said, "The two characters 'profound mind' (shenxin) have a rich flavor; they cannot be fathomed by anything shallow or superficial. Dust-mote worlds are boundless, and wisdom and compassion are immeasurable.
To share the same compassion as the Buddha is sufficient to be called repaying his kindness. When Linji took his leave of Huangbo, Huangbo asked him what [he had learned].
"Where have you been? Mazu said, "Neither south of the River, nor north of the River. Huangbo struck him. Mazu grabbed him and gave him a slap.
Huangbo laughed heartily and called to his attendant, "Bring the meditation board and desk of our late master Baizhang.
Mazu said, "Attendant, bring fire! Huangbo said, "Even so, you may take them away. [He then departed.]
Later, while sitting, he silenced the tongues of all people under heaven.
Afterwards, Guishan asked Yangshan, "Did Linji fail Huangbo? Yangshan replied, "Not so. Guishan said, "How about you, my son?"
Yangshan said, "Only by knowing gratitude can one understand how to repay it. Guishan asked, "Among the ancients of old, was there anyone like this?
Yangshan replied, "There was, but because the times were so distant, I did not wish to cite him. Guishan said, "Even so, I do not yet know;
you simply go ahead and cite him. Yangshan said, "It is just like on the occasion of the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* assembly, when Ānanda..."
Nanzenbutsu said: "To offer this profound mind to every dust mote and land is what is called repaying the Buddha's kindness.
Is this not an act of repaying kindness? Miaoyan said: "So it is, so it is. When one's insight is equal to that of the teacher, one has diminished the teacher’s virtue by half;
only when one's insight surpasses that of the teacher is one fit to receive the transmission. Furthermore, Miaoyan asked Yangshan: "After Linji..."
"How is this? Yang said, "There is a person between Wu and Yue, but he stops whenever he encounters a great wind. Mui asked, "What can be done about that?
Yang replied, "To offer this profound mind to the dust-motes and lands—this is what is called repaying the Buddha's kindness.
Later, Xuefeng Zhao succeeded Shoushan Nian as his heir; people considered him to be a reincarnation of Mount Yang. If it were Mount Yang...
How can those who truly possess the profound resolve be fathomed? How can they be fathomed?
I prostrate and entreat the World-Honored One to bear witness: I vow to enter the evil world of the five turbidities first.

Tong said: "If the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are not yet empty, then the five turbidities (*pañca-kāṣāya*) will be difficult to shatter; how then could one deliver others from all suffering and calamity?

It is precisely because one has attained the fruit and realized the supramundane Dharma that it does not hinder one from entering the marketplace to extend a helping hand and awaken others through awakening.
This is what is meant by 'dedicating this profound mind to the dust-motes of the lands,' which must first be applied to this world of the five turbidities."
Ānanda had such a vow in his past karma, and the Great Virtuous One (Dashi) Fu of this land was well-suited to fulfill it. The Great Virtuous One’s name was Xi.
At the age of sixteen, he took Liu Shi’s daughter Miaoguang as his wife, and they had two sons named Pu Jian and Pu Cheng.
At twenty-four, he sold his wife and sons to provide for a water and land assembly (*shuilu hui*). During this time, he visited with a fellow villager at Jiting Port.

He filtered fish. Having caught them, he submerged the basket in the water and made this prayer: "Those who wish to go, may they depart; those who wish to stay, may they remain. People called him a fool.
Later, the Indian monk Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa said to him, "I and you both made a vow before the Buddha Vipaśyin.
Now, the robes and bowl in the Tuṣita Heaven are still present there. On what day shall we return? He then ordered [the monk] to look at his reflection in the water.
He saw a halo of light and a precious canopy. The Great Being smiled and said to him, "The forge produces many pieces of dull iron;
the gate of a skilled physician is filled with the sick. To deliver sentient beings is the urgent task; why dwell on that pleasure?
Huìsōng pointed to the summit of Mount Sōng and said, "This is a place where one may dwell. The Great Being personally tilled the soil and resided there. Someone stole some beans, wheat, and melons.
Guo Dashi immediately took it away, placing it in a basket. In the second year of the Tianjia era, he was moved by the appearance of the seven Buddhas following him:
Śākyamuni led from the front and Vimalakīrti followed behind. Only the World-Honored One Śākyamuni frequently looked back and spoke with him, saying, "I am your successor."

Directly pointing to the human mind, seeing one's nature and attaining Buddhahood—this treasury of the true Dharma eye was transmitted from Kāśyapa and Ānanda down to Bodhidharma, spanning twenty-eight generations.
Although there were scriptural teachings in this land, the most supreme style of our school had not yet been heard.
Before Bodhidharma had arrived, the Great Being had already been born; is this not clear evidence that he had entered [the Way] beforehand?
"As long as even a single sentient being has not attained Buddhahood, I shall never enter nirvana here."

Why did they so hastily enter nirvana and depart? The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:

At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, being among the great assembly, rose from his seat and bared one shoulder.
With his right shoulder bared and his right knee touching the ground, he joined his palms in reverence and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"O World-Honored One of Great Majestic Virtue, you have skillfully expounded for the sake of sentient beings the Tathāgata’s ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Among those who preach the Dharma, the World-Honored One has always designated me as the foremost;
yet now, hearing the subtle and wondrous sound of the Tathāgata’s Dharma, I am like a deaf person listening from beyond a hundred paces."

As for mosquitoes and gnats, they have never been seen by us, much less heard of. Although the Buddha has clearly proclaimed this to remove our delusions, we still do not yet fully understand the ultimate meaning of this principle;

World-Honored One, if all the world’s faculties, objects, aggregates, bases, and elements are indeed the Tathāgatagarbha, pure and inherently so, how is it that the mountains, rivers, the great earth, and all conditioned phenomena suddenly arise?

Their natures are perfectly interfused, pervading the entire Dharma-realm, serene and eternally abiding. World-Honored One, if the nature of earth is pervasive, how can it contain water?

World-Honored One, because they do not understand this, You told them: "If you maintain the view that there must be something illuminated for it to be called 'luminous enlightenment'..."

This absence of sameness and difference is the truly unconditioned dharma. As Aśvaghoṣa said: "If the mind is moved, it is not true cognition;

The "object" (所) is established; once the object is established, true awakening is obscured. Since the object has been falsely established, one discriminates it, saying, "This is the object.
That which performs this act of establishing is the "subject" (能). The act of discrimination is the object, while that which performs the discrimination is again the subject.
Once subject and object are established, identity and difference immediately manifest: the subject must differ from the object, and the object must differ from the subject.

The fundamental, singular, true awakening is originally devoid of identity or difference. That it nevertheless blazes forth with such diversity is due to the establishment of objects based on the perception of light.
Not only does this result in diversity, but in order to differentiate these diverse characteristics, one further establishes names that are identical.

that which is the same is the same as this state where there is no perception of sameness or difference. Within this, one may discern that it is both different and the same.

Thus, there are characteristics of identity and characteristics of difference, as well as characteristics that are neither identical nor different.
Such turmoil involves the mutual dependence of subject and object, and the mutual definition of identity and difference, whereby purity cannot be attained; hence, there are characteristics of toil.
The characteristic of toil is ignorance (*avidyā*). Through long-term toil, dust arises; its own characteristic becomes turbid.

To intermingle with the true nature is called "turbid" (*hun*); to sully the pure essence is called "muddy" (*zhuó*). From this, the afflictions of worldly toil—the two delusions of views and thoughts—are incited.
Due to these afflictions, the two retributions of the environment and the inhabitants arise through transformation: movement forms the world, and stillness forms empty space. Empty space...

The former establishes sameness based on difference; although there is neither subject nor object, it is nonetheless a state of inert emptiness. The latter is the world where things are intensely formed as difference;
movement constitutes the substance of the world, and difference constitutes the substance of the realm. Herein, there is both subject and object, consisting entirely of a realm of movement.

This "sameness and difference" refers to the dependent retribution (*pariṇāmanirmita*). It is indeed a coarse trace of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). As for the primary retribution (*pratyakṣavipāka*) of those sentient beings:
because they possess a mental nature, they are not the same as the world; because they possess material form (*rūpalakṣaṇa*), they are not the same as empty space.
Nevertheless, while all that exists is subject to arising and ceasing, they are able to be without arising and ceasing; ultimately, they are able to manifest arising and ceasing.
That which is free from subject and object is without arising or ceasing. Reaching the state of no-arising-and-no-ceasing, there is neither sameness nor difference;

yet these too are all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). Because consciousness (*vijñāna*) possesses discrimination, it is conditioned; because wisdom (*jñāna*) is without discrimination, it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Being conditioned, it possesses karma, its fruits, and the various characteristics of the conditioned. That which is unconditioned is devoid of karma, its fruits, and the various characteristics of the conditioned. [Like] a mountain.
The rivers, the earth, and the great world have been fundamentally unborn from the beginning; they exist only because of the establishment of objects through clarity, arising from deluded vision.
A monk asked Chan Master Xueju Ying, "From what do the mountains, rivers, the earth, and the great world arise? Ying replied, "They arise from deluded thoughts."
The monk said, "Could you give me one ingot of gold on credit? Daoying then simply left. The monk was not satisfied.
Later, Yunmen said, "That was already a tangle; it could not be settled. Had he waited until the monk asked, 'Could you give me one ingot of gold on credit?
he would have taken up his staff and struck him. What kind of function is this? Therefore, Yunmen [said...]"
Holding up his staff, he addressed the assembly, saying: "The staff has transformed into a dragon and swallowed up heaven and earth.
Where, then, do the mountains, rivers, and the great earth come from? Xuedou’s verse says: "The staff swallows heaven and earth; In vain they speak of peach blossoms and surging waves.
Those who 'burn their tails' do not need to seize the clouds or snatch the mist; Those who 'expose their gills' need not lose heart."
Startled souls! It has been grasped. Whether you hear it or not, you must be free and easy; do not remain in such confusion and turmoil.
Seventy-two blows shall be lightly pardoned, but one hundred and fifty are difficult to let go of for you. The Master suddenly took up his staff and descended from the seat;
the assembly scattered all at once. If one can penetrate this point, not only will the mountains and rivers remain as they were.

Furthermore, when the clarity of awareness has no point of emergence, the clarity of awareness and the vacuity of darkness interact to produce agitation; thus, there arises a wind-circle that sustains the world. From this vacuity, agitation is born.
Solidity and clarity establish obstruction. That which is the precious metal is clear awareness establishing solidity; thus there is the golden wheel that sustains the land.

Solid awareness achieves the treasure, and the shaking of clarity gives rise to wind. Wind and metal rub against each other, and thus there is the fire-light which serves as the nature of transformation.

The brilliance of the jewels produces moisture, and the flames of fire rise as steam; thus there is a water-circle that contains the worlds of the ten directions. As the fire ascends and the water descends, they interact and produce solidity:
the moist becomes the great oceans, and the dry becomes the continents and sandbanks. For this reason, within those great seas...
The fire-light constantly rises. Within the shallows of that continent, rivers and streams flow perpetually. Because the force of the water is weaker than the fire, it solidifies into high mountains;

therefore, when the mountain rocks are struck, they burst into flame, and when melted, they turn into water. Because the force of the earth is weaker than the water, it draws forth as grasses and trees.
Therefore, forests and thickets, when encountered by fire, become earth; through condensation, they become water. Delusions arise from one another, serving as seeds for each other in turn.
By these causes and conditions, the world continues in succession.
He asked: "If it is fundamentally pure and serene, how did the mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise?

Previously, you said that the five great elements—earth, water, fire, wind, and space—are all the Tathāgatagarbha, fundamentally pure and serene, pervading the entire Dharma-realm; yet they manifest according to karma."
How could it have a fixed location? Its manifestation arises due to the karmic power of sentient beings. The karmic power of sentient beings originates from ignorance (*avidyā*).
Because there was no wondrous, profound, and all-holding [wisdom], a single thought suddenly stirred;

as awareness departed from emptiness, clarity arose, and as emptiness departed from awareness, obscurity arose. From the clarity of awareness, consciousness (*vijñāna*) was produced. When this consciousness is refined and remains unmoving, that is—
It is water. When emptiness and obscurity congeal into form, it is earth. When they interact and become agitated, they become wind and water;
this is like earth overcoming water to produce wood. Because the agitation arises from the earth of empty obscurity, it becomes wood;
yet when the clarity of awareness does not waver, it becomes solid obstruction—this is like wood overcoming earth to produce metal. When metal and wood combine, fire is produced.
Therefore it is said: when wind and metal rub against each other, there is the light of fire; when fire and metal combine, water is produced. Thus it is said:

when the light of fire rises and steams upward, there is a wheel of water; when water and fire combine, earth is produced. Fire ascends and water descends, and thereby islands and sandbanks are formed.
When earth and water combine, wood is again produced; because earth is weak and water is strong, grasses and trees flourish.
Xun represents wind and wood. Wind is the nature of that wood. When they first meet and interact, there is movement;
thus, there is the "wind-wheel" (*vāyu-maṇḍala*), which possesses only the nature of wood. Upon emerging as grasses and trees, it becomes manifest wood with a distinct form.
In the Five Elements (*pañca-bhūta*), the relationship of production and overcoming constitutes husband and wife, while mutual production constitutes father and son. The son is born from the wife.
Birth must occur through the union of Yin and Yang following a state of deficiency before a child is conceived.

Once the child is born, the vital breath (*qi*) of the parents remains within it. Thus, mountains and stones can become fire and can become water, because they are produced through the overcoming of fire by water.
Grasses and trees can become earth and can become water, because they are produced through the overcoming of water by earth.
Extending this principle to all things, there is none that is not thus. I have often compared it with the *Yījīng* (Book of Changes), and they accord like two halves of a tally.
Truly, it is as the sages of past and future have held: their fundamental measure is one and the same. From the awakening of luminosity, consciousness arises as the primordial, profound stillness.
Does this not accord with the principle that "Heaven first produces Water"? Water produces Wood in the East—the trigrams Zhen and Xun;
Wood produces Fire in the South—Li; Fire produces Earth in the Southwest—Kun; Earth produces Metal in the West—Dui; and Metal in the Northwest—Qian—furthermore produces Water in the North—Kan.
Like a ring without end, they successively serve as seeds for one another. Therefore it is said: "The Sovereign emerges."
Zhen (Thunder) corresponds to Xun (Wind). Zhen signifies movement; Xun represents wind. Is this not the principle that motion arises through mutual dependence?
Zhen is wood; Dou (Joy) is metal. As they face each other east and west, they form a couple, and from this, fire is produced.
Is this not the very principle of wind and metal rubbing against one another? Li is fire; Kan is water.
South and North face each other as husband and wife, and from this, Earth is born. Is this not the very principle of their interaction giving rise to firmness?
Kun represents the earth; Gen represents the mountain. Both belong to the element of Earth, wherein all things begin their formation and reach their completion.

Thus, in spring and summer, when all things sprout and flourish, they constantly abide upon the earth and are visible. In autumn and winter, when all things contract and gather, they constantly abide beneath the earth and are invisible.
This is why the *Hetu* (River Diagram) accomplishes transformation and carries out the operations of the spirits.

The Spirit not only wondrously accords with the functioning of phenomenal flow, but also perfectly merges with the source of origination. Thus, at the very bottom of this world, it rests upon the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*);
at the very bottom of the great earth, it rests upon the gold-circle (*kāñcana-maṇḍala*). Earth and gold share the same nature of solidity and both belong to the element of earth (*pṛthivī-dhātu*).

As for fire, it is not called a "circle" but is termed "transformative nature," because it... [exists] in... (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment. The translation reflects the available portion while maintaining the technical terminology and philosophical context.)
Regarding the external realm, the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) undergo transformation and alteration. Regarding the internal realm, the primary elements arise and perish in accordance with it.
Fire is able to melt, disperse, and ripen all things; therefore, it is said to have the nature of transformation.

The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states that through the predominant power of the karma of sentient beings, first, based upon space at the very bottom, a wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*) arises. This wind-circle...
Above that is the water wheel. Above the water wheel, there is the vajra; this is slightly different from the present case.

That [text] describes the established order, ascending from below to above to form the sequence. This [text] describes the process of origination; thus, it does not preclude speaking of them in a crosswise or intermingled manner.
Master Yong of Yangshan addressed the assembly, saying: "A single word exhausts the mountains and rivers. A monk then asked:
"What is this one word? Shan inserted a fire-tongs into the side of the brazier, then withdrew it to its original place.
Touzi composed a verse: "A single phrase brings forth the myriad phenomena; In Magadha, they needlessly shut the heavy gates.

If at that time the patch-robed monks had opened their eyes even slightly, They would have seen the tongs inserted by the brazier as if they were being burned by fire. If one is a person of great and thorough realization, they will view these three...
The arising and ceasing of the realms occur within Great Awakening; they are truly like the birth and extinction of bubbles. How much more so, since they are fundamentally unborn from the start?
One seeks the characteristics of the three realms, yet they are utterly unfindable.

Furthermore, Pūrṇa, this delusion of clarity does not come from another; the fault lies in the awakening-clarity itself. Once that which is delusory has been established, the principle of clarity cannot transcend it.
For this reason, hearing does not go beyond sound, and seeing does not surpass form. Thus, the six delusions of form, fragrance, taste, touch, and so forth are accomplished.

From these, the functions of seeing, awakening, hearing, and knowing are divided. Through the mutual entanglement of similar karma, combinations and separations form the transformations of the world. One sees the clarity of form.

When consciousness arises, it clearly perceives the notion [of a form], which becomes established. Diverse perceptions give rise to aversion; identical notions give rise to craving. Craving flows forth as the seed;

the grasping of the notion serves as the womb. Through their union, birth occurs, attracting those of similar karma. Thus, by means of causes and conditions, there arise the *kalala* (translated as "coagulated mucus"), the *arbuda* (translated as "bubble"), and so forth.
Whether born from a womb, an egg, moisture, or transformation, each follows its appropriate course. Birth from an egg arises solely through the power of thought; birth from a womb is due to emotion.
There is. Moisture arises through conjunction; transformation occurs through separation. Sentient thoughts conjoin and separate, undergoing mutual change and transformation.
Thus, they receive karma and follow its flight or descent. By these causes and conditions, sentient beings continue in succession.
Tong said: "The world takes emptiness and obscurity as its substance; this is what is meant by 'the clarification of thought forming the land.
Sentient beings take awakening and clarity as their nature; this is what is meant by 'awareness being the sentient being. Emptiness and obscurity manifest because of awakening and clarity;
therefore, the world is formed through the karmic power of sentient beings. These two continue one another, and both have awakening and clarity as their fault. This is it.

The delusion of establishing an object through cognition does not arise from the four great elements and so forth; it arises solely because one takes awareness to be "illumination," whereby there is that which is illuminated.

This results in the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) and the subjective aspect (*darśanabhāga*). When the four great elements exist within the vessel-world (*bhājanaloka*), they constitute the remote objective aspect;

when the four great elements exist within the sense-organ body (*indriyakāya*), they constitute the immediate objective aspect. Once this delusive object is established, it consequently causes the six sense-faculties to become obstructed.
Though obstructed, the luminous principle within the seeing-part does not exceed its bounds.

This fundamentally one, perfectly interfused, precious awakening divides into seeing, hearing, smelling, and knowing—the three of sense organs, objects, and consciousness—which give rise to deluded karma. Thereupon, those of similar karma entwine with one another;
because the karma of the parents and the self is identical, they form sentient beings in the womb or egg. Through union and separation, they are transformed into various forms.
It does not arise from parents; rather, it is formed through one's own karma as a combination of moisture and heat, or as a separated and transformed entity.
That which attracts those of similar karma is seen clearly as being due to its veneration. One perceives false objects with a deluded mind, and form arises from this perception;
without perception, there is no form. One pursues false forms with a deluded perception, and thought [arises] from...
Seeing is established; without seeing, there is no perception (*saṃjñā*). Seeing forms a fetter that becomes perception; consciousness has already become emotion.

Therefore, at the moment when similar karma draws one together, differing views give rise to hatred—the father becomes the object of hatred. Shared perceptions give rise to love—the mother becomes the object of love.
For a woman who enters the womb, it is the reverse: the flow of perception becomes love, and through love, [the process continues]. Love is... [not]... [complete].
Detachment. From this, the seeds arise. Thus, craving is the root of saṃsāra. Once the mother has conceived the thought [of conception], that thought coalesces into vital energy (*vāyu*).
From this, the embryo is formed. Thus, thought is the medium for transmitting life. Through their union, the seminal essence and blood combine.
In the first week, they coagulate into a *kalala*; in the second week, a *budbuda*; in the third week, soft flesh; in the fourth week, firmness.

Flesh. Regarding the five stages of the seven positions, this applies to both womb-born and egg-born beings. For moisture-born and transformation-born beings, there is not necessarily the presence of the *kalala* (congealed slime) and *arbuda* (bubble).
Why does the egg-born come first? Because the movement of thought occurs first, followed by the arising of emotional attachment;
furthermore, the egg-born encompasses the other three modes of birth—womb-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born. Humans also possess all four types of birth, such as Viśākhā Mīramātṛ. Three.
The twelve sons were all born from eggs. The cakravartin king Rāvaṇa was born from the crown of his mother’s head; he is called "moisture-born.
While the Buddha was traveling with the fourfold assembly, among the bhikṣuṇīs there was a bhikṣuṇī named Āḷavī.

They are born by transformation within the earth; thus one knows that the transformation of feeling becomes perception, and the transformation of union becomes separation. Originally there is no fixed karma:

the egg-born may change into the womb-born, and the moisture-born may change into the transformation-born. There is likewise no fixed substance; they follow their flight or sinking, responding according to what is appropriate.
Furthermore, there is no fixed destination; it is merely through the cause of conceptual craving and the condition of parents that sentient beings continue in succession, thus becoming infinite.
Daotong Ji went to visit Layman Pang. The Layman said, "I remember when I was in my mother’s womb, there was a saying I would like to share with you, Master.
You must not interpret it through intellectual reasoning. Daotong Ji said, "Still..."
"This is a matter of separate lifetimes. The scholar said, "I was told that one must not apply intellectual reasoning.
Nanquan said, "This is a startling statement; how could one not be afraid? The scholar said, "According to your understanding, Master, it may indeed be called startling.
Nanquan said, "Not applying reasoning, yet applying reasoning. The scholar said, "It is not merely a matter of one or two lifetimes. Nanquan said, "The one who eats his morning gruel."
"Monk! You may examine and reprimand me as you please. Master Shi snapped his fingers three times. Furthermore, regarding Chan Master Guizong Kequan:
because the Prefect was resentful that the Master would not pay him formal respects, he was driven to great distress. He then wrote a letter to Guo Gongfu, saying:
"My worldly karmic ties still have six years remaining. Yet, I am oppressed by the Prefect; I must entrust my remaining breath to be reborn into your household. I pray that you will not..."

Seeing this obstruction, Gongfu was startled and delighted as he read the letter, and he took its meaning to heart. In the middle of the night, his wife saw the Master enter her bedchamber in a dream;
she cried out in alarm, "This is not the place where a monk comes from! Gongfu shook her awake and questioned her.
His wife related the matter in detail. She called for a lamp, took out the letter, and showed it to him; they laughed together without ceasing. Consequently, she became pregnant.

When he was born, they named him Xuānlǎo (Xuánlǎo). At one year of age, his memory and questioning were as they had been before. When he reached three years old, Bái Yún Duān arrived at his home. Upon first seeing him, Duān said, "My nephew has come!
Duān asked, "How many years have passed since you met with the Master? Xuānlǎo counted backward on his fingers.
[Daowei] said, "Four years. Xuedou asked, "Where did you part? He replied, "At Bailian Zhuang. Xuedou asked, "What is the proof?
He replied, "Tomorrow, Father and Mother will invite the Monk for a meal. Suddenly, the sound of a cart being pushed was heard.
Xuedou asked, "What is that sound outside the gate? Xuande made a gesture with his hand as if pushing a cart. Xuedou said, "Afterward, it was like..."
"What? he asked. [The master] replied, "Two ditches on level ground. Six days later, he passed away without illness.
This was likely because Old Xuan did not habitually engage in intellectual reasoning during his tenure; thus, even across a lifetime, he remained so clearly conscious.
Had there been even a hair’s breadth of discerning clarity or conceptual thought lingering in his breast, he would have been exposed by Baiyun Wenzhun.

Pūrṇa, when conceptualization and craving form a common bond, and one cannot separate oneself from that craving, then the succession of parents and children throughout the world continues without interruption.

These are rooted in desire and greed; as craving and love increase together and greed cannot be halted, then among all beings in the world—whether born from eggs, wombs, moisture, or by transformation—they devour one another according to their respective strengths and weaknesses. These are rooted in killing.
Greed is the root. Because humans eat sheep, when the sheep dies it becomes a human; when the human dies, they become a sheep.
Thus it continues through ten species of birth, dying and being born again and again, mutually devouring one another. These evil karmas arise together and persist until the end of the future.
Such beings take the greed for theft as their root. "You owe me my life; I shall repay you with my debt. For this reason, throughout the sutras...
For hundreds of thousands of kalpas, they have constantly remained within birth and death. You love my mind; I cherish your form.
Because of these causes and conditions, for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, we have constantly been bound in entanglement. Only killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct constitute the three roots.
Because of these causes and conditions, karmic fruits continue in succession. Pūrṇa, these three kinds of inverted continuities are all the clear manifestation of awakening itself.
Cognitive awareness arises from the manifestation of conditions; it is born from deluded vision. The mountains, rivers, and the great earth—all conditioned phenomena—successively flow and change.
Because of this delusion, they end and then begin again.
Tong said: "The world belongs to the dependent retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*); as the dependent retribution is insentient, it does not form karma.

Sentient beings belong to the primary retribution (*mukhya-vipāka*); as the primary retribution is sentient, there is indeed karma. Among karmas, none is greater than the three—killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct—and yet their root begins with sexuality.

Through the perception of sameness, one forms attachment; through the perception of difference, one forms aversion. It is precisely this attachment and aversion that constitute [the source of suffering]."
The root of karmic activity is conceptualization and craving; if these are not bound together, one may still achieve liberation.

Once both parties are bound together, then from life to life and age to age, one cannot separate from them. Parents and children, sons and grandsons, are born in succession without end—all this has lust as its foundation.
When greed and craving flourish together, one perceives a "flavor" therein, and from this, killing arises. Greed for this flavor—
Cease! One must inevitably seek to obtain it, and thus theft arises. Its root begins with a single attachment (*tṛṣṇā*).
When this attachment is not fulfilled, one forcibly swallows [the object] as killing and secretly takes it as theft; both are means to satisfy that attachment.

Therefore, within lust itself are inherently present the two karmas of killing and theft. When resentment and bondage arise, one repays debts and repays lives, remaining perpetually within birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
The fetter of craving is a heart of pitying attachment toward forms; it is constantly bound in entanglement.

This attachment and aversion are the cause of karma, while the entanglement of birth and death is the fruit of karma. This encompasses the three kinds of perversion among sentient beings throughout the worlds above:

they turn their backs on the Truth and unite with the delusive, all of which is produced by the luminosity of awareness. Since the luminosity of awareness is itself false and illusory, it falsely establishes the subject and object; thus, there are mountains.

The great earth, the rivers, the continuity of worlds, the karmic fruits of sentient beings, and all conditioned phenomena—arising and ceasing, ceasing and arising, continuing without end—if one awakens to the fact that these delusions lack intrinsic nature, then their very substance is non-arising.
Who then undergoes this sequential flux? Who begins anew after an end? Thus, the faculties, objects, sense bases, and elements are, in their essence, utterly pure.
This is the fundamental nature; it is the *tathāgatagarbha*. Yongjia said: "If one understands, karmic obstacles are fundamentally empty;
if one does not understand, one must repay past debts. How flavorful his words are!
When Yunju Ying was performing manual labor at Dongshan, he accidentally killed an earthworm. Dongshan asked, "What about this? Ying replied, "It will not die. Dongshan said, "Two..."
"When the Patriarch went to the capital of Ye, what then? Yingshou did not answer.
Later, a monk asked, "Regarding the story of the Master cutting and killing earthworms at Dongshan, was it not the case that you had nothing to say? Yingshou said, "I did have words at that time;
it was simply that no one could testify to them. Observe how Yunju is one who stands outside the three realms; thus, he is beyond the reach of conceptual thought.
Furthermore, he spoke at length on the characteristics of the karmic fruits of sentient beings.
Pūrṇa said: "If this wondrous enlightenment is fundamentally wondrously enlightened clarity, and is neither increased nor diminished in relation to the mind of the Tathāgata..."
Without apparent cause, the mountains, rivers, the great earth, and all conditioned phenomena suddenly arose.

Now that the Tathāgata has attained the wondrous, luminous enlightenment of emptiness, when will the conditioned habits and outflows of the mountains, rivers, and the great earth ever arise again? The Buddha told Pūrṇa:
"It is like a person who, in a certain village, mistakes south for north. Does this delusion exist because of further delusion, or does it exist because of awakening?"
[The Buddha] emerged. Pūrṇa said: "Such a deluded person does not arise because of delusion, nor do they arise because of awakening.
Why is this? Delusion fundamentally has no root; how, then, could it arise because of delusion? Awakening does not produce delusion; how, then, could it arise because of awakening? The Buddha said:
"When that deluded person is in the midst of delusion, suddenly there is an awakened person who points it out and causes them to awaken. Pūrṇa, what do you think?"
"How so? Even if this person were deluded, would they become further deluded within this village? "No, World-Honored One. "Pūrṇa, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions are also like this.
This delusion has no root; its nature is ultimately empty. From the beginning, there was never any delusion."

It is as if there were delusion and awakening; when awakening perceives delusion, delusion is extinguished, and awakening no longer gives rise to delusion. It is also like a person with cataracts who sees flowers in the sky;

once the disease of the cataracts is removed, the flowers vanish from the sky. Suppose, however, there were a foolish person who, at that spot in the empty space where the flowers had vanished, [continued to search for them].
"Wait for the flowers to grow again. Observe this person: is he foolish or wise? Pūrṇa replied, "In emptiness there were originally no flowers;

it was a false vision that gave rise to their appearance and disappearance. To perceive the flowers as they vanished into emptiness was already an inversion; to command them to appear once more is truly madness."
"How can such a madman be called either foolish or wise? The Buddha said, "It is as you understand it.
Why do you ask how the wondrous, enlightened, luminous emptiness of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas could ever again produce mountains, rivers, and the great earth?
It is like gold ore mixed with refined gold; once that gold is pure, it cannot become mixed again. It is like wood turned to ash, which does not return."
It is like wood. So too are the Bodhi and Nirvana of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
It is said in the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*, where the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha asked the World-Honored One:

"If all sentient beings have been fundamentally enlightened from the beginning, for what reason do they still possess all ignorance? If this ignorance has existed in sentient beings from the very beginning..."
"For what reason does the Tathāgata further say that all beings of the ten directions have been enlightened from the beginning, yet subsequently give rise to ignorance?
At what time could any Tathāgata ever again produce afflictions? The World-Honored One replied:
"Good son, throughout all worlds, there is beginning and end, arising and ceasing, presence and absence, gathering and dispersing."
Beginning and ending, the continuous succession of thought-moments, the revolving cycle of coming and going, and all manner of grasping and rejecting—all these are saṃsāra.

To attempt to discern perfect enlightenment while not yet having emerged from saṃsāra is for that nature of perfect enlightenment to become identical with the flow of transmigration. If one would avoid saṃsāra, [one must first emerge from it].
This is impossible. What Pūrṇa now doubts is no different from that of Vajragarbha;

the World-Honored One merely refutes it by means of their views regarding arising and ceasing, citing four successive metaphors: the first metaphor illustrates awakening such that one no longer falls into delusion;

the second illustrates cessation such that there is no further arising; the third, using gold that is not re-mined from ore, reiterates the meaning of awakening such that one no longer falls into delusion; the fourth...

The ashes do not weigh down the wood; this reiterates the meaning that once extinguished, there is no further arising. Therefore, the phrasing here is brief. Awakening that does not fall back into delusion is precisely *bodhi*;
extinction that does not arise again is precisely *nirvāṇa*. This uses the fact of having emerged from saṃsāra to distinguish perfect awakening (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).
That nature of perfect awakening is itself without saṃsāra; therefore it is said: "The *bodhi* of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas..."
The attainment of Nirvana is likewise so. Sentient beings are lost in delusion; what they value is simply awakening. Originally, there was no delusion;
this beginningless delusion is merely a semblance of delusion. At the very moment of delusion, how could it have ever been lost?

Therefore, it is called a "semblance of delusion. Now, there is likewise no awakening; that which awakens from delusion is a semblance of awakening. At the very moment of awakening, there is furthermore...
How can this be attained? Therefore, it is called "semblance-awakening" (*sajiao*). When awakening dispels delusion and delusion is extinguished, that is "initial awakening" (*shijiao*).

When awakening reaches the point where the initial and the fundamental are not distinct—being solely the wondrous awakening (*miaojiao*)—delusion will no longer arise. Since one is simply not deluded oneself, awakening is also of no further use.
National Teacher Zhong asked Zilin Gongfeng, "What is the meaning of 'Buddha'? Zilin replied, "It is the meaning of awakening. The Master said, "Buddha..."
"Have you ever been deluded? Ling said, "I have never been deluded. The Master said, "If so, what use is there for awakening? Ling was speechless.
Furthermore, Master Mihu instructed a monk to ask Yangshan, "Do people of the present age still require awakening?
Yangshan said, "Awakening is not non-existent; however, how can one avoid falling into the 'second place'? Mihu deeply approved of this. Touzi commented: "Yangshan..."
Shan may indeed speak thus, but has he yet managed to avoid falling into his own trap?
If he has avoided it, there is still one person who utterly refuses to consent. If he has not avoided it, he likewise falls into the "second head.
Although Mishu may grant him approval, does he himself still possess a way to emerge? Everyone, try to examine this for yourselves. If you examine...
If you can investigate and find [the truth], both [subject and object] will dissolve like ice melting away. If you cannot investigate and find it, do not act rashly.
The verse says: "Seeking someone at the peak of the green mountain crags, He points to the end of the mountains, yet one has not yet found rest.
Though one may thus avoid the Chongyang decree, How does this compare to the numinous sprout that never offends spring? Later, Tiantong’s verse says: "The second head is divided."

Awakening breaks through delusion; one must quickly let go and cast aside the trap. Merit, if not yet perfected, becomes a redundant appendage; wisdom, difficult to fathom, leads to the realization that one has bitten one's own heel.
The rabbit grows old on the ice-disk as autumn dew weeps; the bird shivers in the jade-tree as the morning wind blows chill.
"Bring it here; with great reverence, distinguish the true from the false. Being entirely free of blemishes, a white jade tablet is precious.
In short, without the spring breeze the flower will not bloom; yet once the flower has bloomed, the wind blows it away. Even if you possess wondrous awakening, you must still spit it out."

Pūrṇa, as for what you asked regarding earth, water, fire, and wind—how their fundamental natures are perfectly interfused and pervade the entire Dharma-realm—and your doubt that the natures of water and fire would not mutually overcome or extinguish one another;
furthermore, your inquiry as to how empty space and the great earth, both being pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm, could possibly coexist without conflict:
Pūrṇa, it is like empty space, whose essence is not any of these manifold phenomena, yet which does not obstruct those various phenomena.
"Manifest it! Why is this so? Pūrṇa, that great empty space is bright when the sun shines upon it; it is dark when clouds gather; it moves when the wind stirs;
it is clear when the sky is serene; it is turbid when vapors condense; it becomes a haze when earth accumulates;

and it becomes a reflection when water is still. What do you think? Are these various conditioned characteristics of different directions produced because of those things, or are they produced by the space itself?"

"There is. If it were produced by that [the sun], Pūrṇa, then at the moment of illumination, since it is the brightness of the sun, the worlds of the ten directions would all be of the same solar color;
how then could one still see the round sun in the sky? If it were the brightness of space, space itself should illuminate."

Why is it that during the time of clouds and mist at midnight, no radiance is produced? One should know that this light is neither the sun nor the sky, yet it is not different from the sky and the sun.

When one contemplates their essential characteristics, they are fundamentally illusory and cannot be pointed out or described; it is like seeking flowers in the sky and binding them into a fruit of the sky.
How can you question the meaning of their mutual subjugation and extinction? Contemplate the original truth of their nature: it is solely the wondrously enlightened clarity.

This mind of wondrously enlightened clarity was originally neither water nor fire; why, then, do you ask again how they could be mutually incompatible? True, wondrously enlightened clarity is also like this.
If you manifest through clarity in emptiness, then emptiness appears. If earth, water, fire, and wind each manifest individually, then they appear individually.
If they manifest together, then they appear together. How do they appear together? Pūrṇa, it is like the reflection of the sun appearing in a single body of water.
When two people look at the sun in the water together and walk off in opposite directions—east and west—the sun follows each of them.
The two depart—one to the east, one to the west—without any prior fixed point of reference. It should not be difficult to ask:
if this day is one, how can they travel separately? Since each day is dual, how can they manifest as one? This is a circular, empty fabrication with nothing to rely upon.
Tong said: "In the previous answer, it was stated that the fundamental nature is pure and quiescent; why, then, do mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise?

If we speak in terms of phenomena (*lakṣaṇa*), there is arising, for they arise from deluded vision. If we speak in terms of the nature (*dharmatā*), there is no arising, for awakening does not return to delusion."
Phenomenal characteristics are fundamentally illusory; what could possibly be suppressed or extinguished? Nature is fundamentally unborn; who could fail to be accommodated within it?

Therefore, the seven elements are all the wondrous true suchness-nature of the Tathāgata-garbha. The Tathāgata-garbha is originally not the seven elements, yet it does not obstruct their manifestation.
It is like empty space: its essence is not the various phenomena, yet it does not obstruct the emergence of those various forms.

"Swung away, it is but a single void. When earth accumulates, the characteristic of earth appears; when water settles, the characteristic of water appears; when the sun shines, the characteristic of fire appears;
when the wind stirs, the characteristic of wind appears; when the sky clears and becomes serene, the characteristic of space appears.

Because of light and darkness, they belong to seeing; because of turbid vapor, they belong to consciousness. These seven metaphors illustrate the seven elements. The seven elements do not arise of themselves."
Therefore, it is not born from itself; it is not born from another. Thus, it does not exist as emptiness alone, nor is it the sun or the sky. Therefore, it is not born from both together.
It is not distinct from the sky and the sun, yet it is not born without cause. From this it may be said that, fundamentally, there is no birth.
Since there is fundamentally no birth, although things manifest according to karma, they are like flowers in the sky. Flowers in the sky cannot ripen into fruits in the sky; how could this be?
Is there anything that, through its attributes, suppresses and excludes others such that they cannot coexist? Although these attributes are illusory, their nature is fundamentally true.
This purity is all-pervasive; originally, it did not take the form of water or fire. Since it is formless, it does not obstruct one another.
How could there be suppression and exclusion such that they cannot coexist? Such is the case with the attributes of the seven great elements. As for the seven great elements themselves...
The nature is likewise thus. Therefore, the Tathāgatagarbha—the wondrously enlightened and luminous mind—is also like this.

To explain it through the analogy of space: when one seeks clarity through space, then space appears. In terms of physical phenomena, it is like digging a well; in terms of karma, it is like stillness resulting in empty space;
and in terms of the mind, it is like the false arising of the perception of space, whereby one sees only emptiness, [obscuring] earth, water, fire, and wind.

It is also like this. If each person clarifies and brings forth [the light], then each person’s manifestation appears. If they clarify and bring it forth together, then there is a simultaneous manifestation.

It does not matter whether clouds rise on the southern mountain or rain falls on the northern mountain; in all cases, there is no obstruction within empty space. This is just like the sun in the water:
as the sun moves east and west, the reflection follows it accordingly. One need not seek confirmation from the sky above.
[The opponent] says: "I only harbor doubts regarding the water. It is like the moon appearing to move when the clouds pass, or the shore appearing to shift as a boat moves;
these arise from deluded perception. How can one distinguish whether what is seen in such a false manner is one or many?
Is this not a great delusion? Another asks: "Earth, water, fire, and wind exist as actual realities before us. Why do you call them false? The answer is: "Because they lack wisdom."
People say that things exist as substantial realities; however, when observed with the eye of wisdom, this is not so.
It is like a small child who sees a reflection in a mirror and, filled with joy, desires to seize it; an adult, knowing the truth of the matter, is not deluded by it.

Ordinary worldlings see the aggregation of atoms and call it real earth; yet one who possesses the divine eye can disperse this earth, finding that from the very beginning it cannot be apprehended as a reality.
Thus, one knows that appearances are fundamentally empty and illusory. Fayen asked the Elder Baozi, "An ancient said, 'Mountains and rivers have no obstructions;
light penetrates everywhere. Now, what is this light that penetrates everywhere?"
Zi said, "The sound of the pestle beating on the eastern side. Niu of Guizong spoke differently, saying, "The Master intends to create an obstruction.
As for the dialogue between these two venerable elders, it does not constitute a leakage; yet even this was subject to Guizong’s critical examination.

When the Tripitaka Master Mahākarṇa from the Western Heaven arrived at the capital, he claimed to have attained the power of knowing others' minds. Emperor Suzong ordered National Teacher Huizhong to test him. The Master said, "You..."
"Tell me, where is the old monk right now? Zang said, "The Master is the teacher of the entire nation;
why have you gone to Xichuan to watch the boat races? After a long silence, he asked again, "Tell me, where is the old monk right now?
Zang said, "The Master is the teacher of the entire nation; why are you here at Tianjin Bridge?"
Looking up, he was playing with a monkey. After a long while, he asked again, "Where do you say the old monk is right now?
Zang could not fathom this, and the Master rebuked him, saying, "You wild fox spirit! Where is your 'penetration of others' minds'? Zang had no reply.
A monk asked Yangshan, "For what reason did the Great-Ear Tripitaka Master fail to see the National Teacher for the third time?"
Mount [Zhaozhou] said, "The first two times were when he was still within the realm of the mind; the last time he entered the samādhi of self-enjoyment, which is why he did not see him.
A monk cited this and asked Xuansha, who said, "Tell me, did you see him during those first two times?
Another monk asked Zhaozhou, "The Tripitaka Master did not see the National Teacher on his third visit. I wonder where the National Teacher was at that time?"
The Master of the Tripitaka said, "It is right above the nostrils. Later, a monk asked Xuansha, "Since it is right above the nostrils, why can one not see it?
Xuansha replied, "Precisely because it is too close. Tiantong commented: "The Tripitaka Master did not see the National Teacher."
"Setting that aside for a moment, do you say that the National Teacher knew his own place of descent?
If you say he knew it himself, then the hundred birds carry flowers and the various devas make offerings without a day’s rest. Tell me, at such a time as this, where does he fall?
You should know that the National Teacher’s mind engaged with the objective realm twice; each instance served to manifest the truth."
