Thus, each manifests individually. If even the wondrously enlightened and luminous mind does not know where its own self-enjoyment samādhi falls, how can one interrogate it regarding the meaning of their mutual exclusion and sublation?
Pūrṇa, you have used the characteristics of form and emptiness to overturn and supplant one another within the Tathāgata-garbha;

yet the Tathāgata-garbha, in accordance with them, pervades the entire Dharma-realm as form and emptiness. Therefore, within it, there is the movement of wind, the clarity of space, the brightness of the sun, and the obscurity of clouds.

Sentient beings become confused and bewildered, turning their backs on awakening and uniting with the dust of the senses; thus they give rise to worldly toil and the appearances of the mundane world. By means of my wondrous luminosity...
The cessation of birth merges with the *tathāgatagarbha*. This *tathāgatagarbha* is solely wondrous, enlightened clarity, perfectly illuminating the *dharmadhātu*.
Therefore, within it, one becomes the infinite, and the infinite becomes one. The small manifests the large; the large manifests the small.

Without moving from the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), it pervades the worlds of the ten directions. Its body contains the inexhaustible space of the ten directions, yet within a single hair-tip, it manifests...

In the Jewel-King lands, sitting within a mote of dust, he turns the Great Dharma Wheel; extinguishing the dust and merging with awakening, he thus brings forth the wondrously enlightened nature of True Thusness.
It is said in general: "If one discriminates Perfect Awakening while still not having escaped saṃsāra, that nature of Perfect Awakening is identical to the cycle of transmigration. If...
To seek liberation from saṃsāra [while remaining thus] is impossible. This passage uses the phenomenon of the mutual sublation of form and emptiness to discern the *tathāgatagarbha*.

Yet, the nature of the *tathāgatagarbha* follows along with form and emptiness as it flows through the *dharmadhātu*. To wish to escape the worldly dust and toil [of existence while failing to realize this] is impossible.
Sentient beings are deluded and distressed because they do not understand that form and emptiness are fundamentally one and the same with themselves. For...
Constrained by form, it encounters obstruction wherever it touches. Because it turns its back on awakening, although it is luminous, it is not subtle; therefore, it is called delusion.

Sensory objects belong to the realm of arising and ceasing and are fundamentally not inherently existent. Awakening is neither subject to arising and ceasing nor does it depend on anything external; yet it is not something that exists as a primal essence.
Therefore, it can be extinguished; yet because it does not come from without, it can be integrated. Thus, the wondrous awakening of true suchness perfectly illumines the dharma-realm:
the one is all, and all is the one. Transverse and vertical, they are sovereign and free; every phenomenon is unimpeded—this is the inconceivable function.
This is not something accomplished through cultivation; it is merely called "arousing" [the mind]. The Great Master Dharmatrata’s *Dharma-gate for Settling the Mind* states:
"In delusion, the person pursues phenomena; in awakening, phenomena pursue the person. In awakening, consciousness subsumes form; in delusion, form subsumes consciousness.
Whatever involves mental discrimination and calculation regarding the manifestations of one's own mind is entirely a dream. If...
When the consciousness-mind is quiescent and extinguished, such that there is not a single place where a thought stirs, this is called Right Enlightenment.
Shenxiu’s verse says: "The body is the Bodhi tree; the mind is a stand for a bright mirror. At all times diligently wipe it clean; do not let it gather dust.
This very act of diligent wiping is precisely using a mind of arising and ceasing to unite with the Tathāgatagarbha; therefore, he remained outside the gate. (6)
The Patriarch’s verse says: "Bodhi originally has no tree; A bright mirror likewise has no stand. From the beginning, there is not a single thing— Where, then, can dust settle?
This very "not a single thing" is the union with the Tathāgatagarbha through non-arising and non-ceasing;

it is the succession to the Patriarchal seat. Zhaozhou, ascending the hall, said: "It is like a bright pearl in the palm of one's hand: when a barbarian comes, a barbarian appears; when a Han Chinese comes, a Han Chinese appears."

When the Han monk arrived, the old monk took a blade of grass and used it as a sixteen-foot golden body; he took the sixteen-foot golden body and used it as a blade of grass. "The Buddha is affliction; affliction is the Buddha. A monk asked, "Whose affliction is the Buddha?

Zhaozhou said, "It is the affliction for all people. The monk asked, "How can one escape it? Zhaozhou said: [He] came to the Han region. The old monk took a blade of grass and used it as a sixteen-foot golden body; he took the sixteen-foot golden body and used it as a blade of grass. "The Buddha is affliction; affliction is the Buddha. A monk asked, "Whose affliction is the Buddha?
Zhaozhou said, "It is the affliction for all people. [The monk] asked, "How can one be exempt from it? Zhaozhou said:
"What is the use of trying to avoid it? This Zhaozhou does not employ the extinction of dust, nor does he employ the unification of awakening;
yet he is able to manifest the great within the small and the small within the great. He is truly fit to walk hand-in-hand with the Sixth Patriarch.
Yuanzhao ascended the hall and said: "Upon a single hair-tip, he manifests a jeweled royal land; sitting within a mote of dust, he turns the Great Dharma Wheel. [He] raised his staff.
He said, "This is dust. How do you explain the principle of turning the Wheel of Dharma? Today, this mountain monk will not spare his eyebrows to explain it through for all of you.
When he lifts it up, the waters of the sea surge into waves and Mount Sumeru rears its peaks.
When he sets it down, the four seas are calm and clear, and heaven and earth are serene and still. I dare ask you all: when he lifts it up..."
Arising is it; letting go is it. To sever what should be severed yet remains unsevered—this is a double case. [The Master] struck the meditation seat and descended from it.

Furthermore, when the nun Miaozong ascended the hall, he said: "When the school of the Patriarchs is proclaimed once, the Three Baskets are cut off from all expression. When the Patriarchal command is put into practice..."
Severing the ten directions at their seat, the followers of the Two Vehicles flee in terror upon hearing it; even those on the Tenth Ground still harbor doubts when reaching this point.

If one belongs to the elite stream, they understand before a word is spoken. Even if one were to employ the skillful means of shifting stars and changing constellations, or the mechanisms of seizing the banner and snatching the drum, these would still be mere empty fists—how could they possess any real meaning? As for the single path leading upward, not a thousand sages have traveled it.
The tradition says that scholars exhaust their bodies like monkeys grasping at reflections. At Vulture Peak, the entrustment was made in accordance with the needs of the times;

the Three Vehicles were proclaimed, each according to the capacity of the faculties. Beginning at the Deer Park, the Wheel of the Four Truths was turned, delivering hundreds of thousands of millions of beings.
Today, this mountain monk, together with this very realm and its lands, with the Buddhas and the Patriarchs, and with the mountains, rivers, and the great earth—[all are present].
The grasses, trees, and forests, as well as the fourfold assembly present before us, each turn the Great Dharma Wheel; their intermingling lights entwine like a net of precious threads.
If even a single blade of grass or a single tree did not turn the Dharma Wheel, it could not be called turning the Great Dharma Wheel.
Thus it is said: "Upon the tip of a single hair, one manifests a jewel-king realm; sitting within a mote of dust, one turns the Great Dharma."
The Wheel: At times, within this [wheel], one performs immeasurable and boundless, vast Buddha-works that pervade the entire Dharma-realm.
One becomes many; many become one. Within the small, the large appears; within the large, the small appears. Without moving a step, one travels to Maitreya’s pavilion;
without turning back to listen, one enters Avalokiteśvara’s Universal Gate. Sentient and insentient beings—[their] nature...
The marks are equal; this is neither a wondrous application of supernatural powers nor a matter of natural law.
If one is clear and decisive regarding this, the imperial grace and the Buddha’s grace will be fully repaid at once. But tell me, what is the phrase for repaying this grace?
The heavens are high and the myriad phenomena are upright; the ocean is vast and the hundred rivers flow with the tide.
The various venerable masters have profoundly realized the realm of wondrous luminosity, proclaiming it with their utmost voices and taking great delight in its flavor.
Yet the Tathāgatagarbha is the fundamentally wondrous and perfect mind; it is neither mind nor emptiness. It is not earth, water, fire, or wind.
It is not the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind. It is not form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental objects. It is not the sphere of visual consciousness.
In this way, it extends even to: not the sphere of mental consciousness; not clarity or ignorance, nor the exhaustion of clarity or ignorance. In this way, it extends even to:
not old age and death, nor the exhaustion of old age and death; not suffering, not its origin, not its cessation, not the path; not knowledge, not attainment.

It is not dāna (herein called "giving"), not śīla (herein "precepts"), not vīrya (herein "diligence"), not kṣānti (herein "patience"), not dhyāna (herein "meditative concentration"), not prajñā (herein "wisdom"), and not pāramitā (herein "perfection"). Thus it continues:
it is not tathāgata (herein called "Thus-Come One"), not arhat (herein "Worthy of Offerings"), and not samyaksaṃbuddha (herein "Perfectly Complete Enlightened One"). It is not the Great...
Nirvana is neither permanent, nor blissful, nor self, nor pure, for it is neither mundane nor supramundane.
It is the Tathāgatagarbha, the fundamentally luminous and wondrous mind. It is the mind itself and it is emptiness. It is earth, water, wind, and fire;
it is the eye, and the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; it is form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental objects; it is the sphere of visual consciousness—and so forth.
...even up to the very sphere of mental consciousness (*manovijñānadhātu*). It is precisely illumination and non-illumination; it is the exhaustion of illumination and non-illumination.

In this same way, it extends even to old age and death, and the exhaustion of old age and death. It is precisely [the truths of] suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. It is precisely knowledge and attainment.
It is precisely *dāna* (generosity), *śīla* (ethical discipline), *vīrya* (vigorous effort), *kṣānti* (patience), *dhyāna* (meditative concentration), *prajñā* (wisdom), and *upāya* (skillful means).
Pāramitā. In this way, it extends even to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, and Great Nirvāṇa;
it is permanence, bliss, self, and purity. This is because all these are identical to both the mundane and the supramundane.
This is the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrously luminous source of the mind, which is neither identical to nor distinct from phenomena, and is both identical to and distinct from them.

How can the sentient beings of the three realms of existence, as well as the supramundane Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, attempt to fathom the unsurpassed Bodhi of the Tathāgata with their minds of limited knowledge,
using worldly language to enter the Buddha’s wisdom and vision?
Tong said: "Regarding this passage of the sutra, only Changshui has provided a brief sequential explanation. He states:
'The fundamentally wondrous, perfect mind is neither mind nor emptiness,' etc., which clarifies the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) by way of negating characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

'The originally luminous, wondrous mind is precisely mind and precisely emptiness,' etc., which clarifies the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) by way of affirming characteristics. The wondrously luminous source of the mind is detached from both affirmation and negation."

"This is precisely 'neither-is-nor-is-not'" refers to clarifying the Middle Way Truth (madhyamā-satya) by means of simultaneous negation and illumination. Because it doubly negates both the ultimate (paramārtha) and the conventional (saṃvṛti), it is said to be "detached from is and detached from is-not.
Because it doubly illuminates both the ultimate and the conventional, it is said to be "this is precisely neither-is-nor-is-not. Thus, the three truths are of one essence.
Therefore, all say that it is precisely the *tathāgatagarbha*. First, one negates characteristics by means of "not"; next, one negates "not" by means of "precisely.
Yet, as long as one remains bound by names and words, one has not reached the ultimate principle of the single truth (*ekasatya*).

Only when one is free from both "precisely" and "not," where there is neither "not" nor "not-not," and where the path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity ceases, does the one true *dharmadhātu*, the mind of the *tathāgatagarbha*, finally manifest. Thus, the *Vimalakīrti*...
In the thirty-first fascicle of the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, the bodhisattvas each expound the dharma-gate of non-duality, all using words to eliminate conceptual signs.
Mañjuśrī uses words to eliminate words, while Vimalakīrti eliminates words through wordlessness; this alone constitutes the ultimate.

Generally speaking, worldly dharmas do not transcend the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the seven elements (*sapta-dhātu*), and the bases of sense-faculties, objects, and spheres (*āyatana*). World-transcending dharmas do not transcend those of the śrāvakas.

Regarding the two vehicles of the Pratyekabuddhas: while Bodhisattvas and Buddhas pertain to both the mundane and the supramundane—and are not exclusively supramundane—their minds belong to consciousness (*vijñāna*), which subsumes the five aggregates (*skandha*).
The visual consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) and so forth subsume the twelve bases (*āyatana*); these are the six realms of ordinary beings.

The Pratyekabuddha contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), observing that they possess the characteristic of arising and the characteristic of being abandoned through cultivation. This is the Pratyekabuddha.
The realm of the *dhātu*. To know suffering, abandon its origin, realize cessation, and cultivate the path—this is the realm of the *śrāvaka*.

To possess wisdom and attainment, as well as the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) reaching the other shore—this is the realm of the *bodhisattva*. The three titles of the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha.

The four virtues of *nirvāṇa* collectively constitute the Buddha-realm; both the mundane and the supramundane do not exist outside of this. If one has attachment to each [aspect] individually, then it is not perfect.
Therefore, regarding "non-identity" (*bipolar negation*), if one perceives its perfection while remaining exclusively attached to "non-identity," that is not subtle.

Thus, regarding "identity" (*affirmative assertion*), one perceives its subtlety. Subtle yet luminous, luminous yet subtle—neither identical nor non-identical, yet both identical and non-identical. It is able to...
It is free from all that is associated with it; neither influence nor trace can be found. This is true, unsurpassed Bodhi. Aśvaghoṣa said:
"True emptiness" means that from the very beginning, it is dissociated from all defiled dharmas; it is free from the differentiated characteristics of all phenomena;
and because there is no mind of false conceptualization, one should know that True Suchness (Tathatā) does not possess any marks of existence.

It is not signless; it is not characterized by both existence and non-existence; it is not characterized by neither existence nor non-existence; it is not a single characteristic; it is not diverse characteristics;

it is not characterized by both unity and diversity; it is not characterized by neither unity nor diversity. In brief, this is because it cannot be touched by the false conceptualizations of all sentient beings.
Therefore, the sentient beings of the three realms of existence perceive its provisional nature, while the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas perceive...
Regarding that emptiness, even among Bodhisattvas it cannot be fathomed within the Truth of the Middle Way, let alone the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Only Buddhas and Buddhas can exhaustively realize it; though Bodhisattvas who have ascended the stages (*bhūmi*) may not perceive it, how could worldly language ever approximate it?
Unsurpassed Enlightenment (*anuttara-bodhi*) cannot be known by the cognitive mind.
"It cannot be entered through words; one must instead contemplate and perceive its subtlety. A monk asked Mazu, "Why does the Master say 'this very mind is Buddha'?
He replied, "To stop a small child from crying. [The monk] asked, "After the crying has stopped, what then? He replied, "Neither mind nor Buddha.
[The monk] asked, "When people other than these two types come, how do you instruct them? He replied, "I..."
[The monk] said, "This Way is not a thing. [Baizhang] asked, "What if someone who has already realized it comes along? [Baizhang] replied, "Just let him realize the Great Way for himself.
Mazu had already attained the wondrous mind of *nirvāṇa*; his every word and breath were in secret accord with this.
Furthermore, when Mazu heard that Damei was dwelling in the mountains, he sent a monk to ask him, "Did you see Master Mazu?"
"What have you attained that you have settled on this mountain? Baizhang asked. Muzhe replied, "The Master told me, 'This very mind is Buddha,' and so I have settled here.
The monk said, "Lately, the Master’s teaching of the Dharma has changed.
Muzhe asked, "How so? The monk said, "He also says, 'Neither mind nor Buddha. Muzhe said, "This old fellow is merely confusing people; he hasn't yet [attained anything]."
One day, the monk returned and reported this to Mazu. Mazu said, "The plum has ripened.
Chan Master Huizang of Dongsi was often troubled by his disciples who would incessantly recite and memorize the phrase "this very mind is Buddha.
He asked, "Where does the Buddha dwell? How can you say 'this very'?"
"Mind. The mind is like a painter; yet it is said to be 'this very mind is Buddha. He then addressed the assembly, saying:
'The mind is not Buddha; wisdom is not the Way. The sword has long since been lost, and you are merely marking the boat.
Nanquan once said: 'In Jiangxi, Mazu says "this very mind is Buddha. Old Wang does not speak thus: it is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not..."
"This is a thing. When he said this, was there any fault? Zhaozhou bowed and left.
At that time, a monk asked Zhaozhou, "Master, you bowed and then left; what was your intention? Zhaozhou said, "You should ask the Abbot instead.
The monk then asked Master Quan, "Just now, what was the intention of Abbot Shen? Quan said, "He, however—"

If you have grasped the meaning of this old monk’s intent, you will certainly have no doubts regarding the applications of the various venerable masters; only then can you enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
It is like the lute, the harp, the *konghou*, and the *pipa*: though they possess exquisite sounds, if there are no skillful fingers, they can never produce them.
It is the same for you and all sentient beings: the precious, awakened true mind is each and every one of you fully complete.

Just as when I press my finger, the Ocean-Seal manifests its radiance, so too when you momentarily raise your mind, the afflictions of worldly toil arise first. This is because you do not diligently seek the unsurpassed path of awakening.
Those who cherish the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) and consider a little attainment sufficient are addressed collectively as follows:
"The wondrous is luminous; luminous is the wondrous. This is precisely the "wondrous" of the Wondrous Sound and the Wondrous Finger. In sum, it transcends the reach of thought and deliberation.
It is like my pressing a finger, where the Wondrous Sound issues forth accordingly; it is like the Sea-Seal (Sāgaramudrā) manifesting radiance, wherein every form is perfectly complete.
How could there be any intentional fabrication? The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states: "All forms and images existing in Jambudvīpa are reflected as seal-impressions within the great ocean;
therefore, it is called the 'Ocean Seal' (*sāgaramudrā*). When you briefly raise your mind, it is like a vessel and a hand that have not been practiced together;

you do not attain its subtle mastery. Consequently, the afflictions arise first, for you are attempting to unite the mind of birth and extinction with the Tathāgatagarbha, and thus cannot follow [its nature].
One contemplates through the sequential cultivation of concentration and wisdom; yet, by following along with afflictions and ignorance, there arise the defilements.
When these defilements obscure and veil [the mind], although the precious awakened true mind is fully present within each and every being, how can it manifest?
One day, while Chan Master Dongming Qian was reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the practitioner Zhong asked: "As it says, 'When I press my finger, the Ocean Seal emits light.'"
"What is the Buddha’s intention? Xuan said, "Śākyamuni the Old Man deserves twenty blows. [The Master] asked, "Why is it so?
Xuan said, "What need is there to use pointing fingers? [The Master] asked, "If you momentarily raise your mind, worldly toil arises first;
what then? Xuan said, "That too is the radiance of the Sea-Seal. How wondrous, how wondrous! One must see it thus."

This can indeed be called "turning the *Śūraṅgama*. Chan Master Wuben of Jianfu ascended the hall and said: "When the Gandharva King once performed music, the mountains, rivers, and great earth all danced. How can this compare to the lame old Yunmen, who could say, 'The twenty-fifth day of the twelfth month'?

Today at Boshan, if there is a branch, I grasp the branch; if there is no branch, I follow the precedent. **Attainment:** This may truly be called "turning the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. When Chan Master Wuben of Jianfu ascended the hall, he said:

"When the Gandharva King once performed music, the mountains, rivers, and the great earth all danced. How can this compare to the lame old Yunmen, who understood how to say, 'The twenty-fifth day of the twelfth month'? Today at Boshan, if there is a branch, I grasp the branch; if there is no branch, I grasp the precedent."

"It must be the right moment. He suddenly picked up his staff, laid it across his knees, and made the gesture of playing the lute, saying, "Is there anyone here who can hear the strings and appreciate the music?
After a long silence, he said, "Even if one were to produce the cry of a phoenix, in the end, who would truly know the technique of the fingers?
He struck the ground once with the staff and descended from the seat. Alas! Is it not true that the technique of the fingers has never been transmitted?
"By diligently seeking the path to unsurpassed enlightenment, one shall naturally attain it.
Pūrṇa said, "I and the Tathāgata’s precious, awakened, perfect, bright, true, wondrous, and pure mind are non-dual and complete."
Yet I, having encountered beginningless delusive thoughts in the past, have long remained in saṃsāra; though I have now attained the Noble Vehicle, I am not yet ultimate.

World-Honored One, when all delusions are completely extinguished, there remains only the wondrous, true, and eternal. I venture to ask the Tathāgata: regarding all sentient beings, [how can they attain this?]
"For what reason is there delusion? Why do you obscure your own wondrous clarity and undergo this drowning? The Buddha told Pūrṇa:
"Although you have removed your doubts, other delusions remain unexhausted. I shall now question you again using various matters present before us in the world.
Have you not heard of the one named Yaśoda (translated here as Cishou) in the city of Śrāvastī? One morning, he suddenly looked at his face in a mirror and became attached to it."

In a mirror, one’s head is reflected; the eyebrows and eyes are visible. Yet, when one scolds and rebukes one’s own head, one does not see its face or features, and taking it for a *chimei* (a mountain sprite), one runs about wildly and without cause.
What do you think? For what reason does this person run about wildly without cause? Pūrṇa replied, "This person’s mind is deranged; there is no other reason.
The Buddha said, "The wondrous enlightenment is perfectly bright and complete; its fundamental nature is perfectly bright and wondrous. Since it is called..."
Delusion. What is its cause? If it has a cause, how can it be called delusion? These various delusive thoughts themselves arise from one another in succession;

from confusion they accumulate further confusion, passing through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust. Even if a Buddha were to illuminate them, they still could not turn back. Such a cause for delusion exists inherently within delusion itself.
Once one recognizes that delusion has no [ultimate] cause, then delusion has nothing upon which to rely. Since it does not even have birth, what could it possibly do?

Extinction. One who attains Bodhi is like a person awake recounting the events of a dream; though the mind may be sharp and clear, for what cause or condition could one seek to grasp things within a dream?

How much more so when there is no cause, as they were originally non-existent? It is like that city-dweller, Yantradatta, who ran away in terror of his own head—could there have been any cause or condition for this?
When his madness suddenly subsides, the head is not obtained from outside; even if it has not yet subsided...
Madness—what could possibly be lost there? Pūrṇa, such is the nature of delusion; by what cause would it exist?
You need only not follow after the threefold continuity of worldly karma, its fruits, and sentient beings. Because these three conditions are severed, the three causes will not arise.

Then, the madness of your own *yaktadatta* within the mind will naturally subside. This subsiding is itself *bodhi*. This supremely pure and luminous mind has always been coextensive with the *dharmadhātu*;
it is not obtained from others. Why rely on arduous toil or the laborious cultivation and realization of the "sinews and sinewy knots"?
Tong said: "Pūrṇa has already realized the exhaustion of outflows and has attained the fruit of sainthood; why, then, do residual delusions still remain?

It is simply because from the past he has applied his efforts toward the cessation of delusion. This very mind that seeks to cease delusion is precisely the discriminating, enlightened clarity that, terrified of its own head, runs about in madness.
To seek the Truth by ceasing delusion implies there is a Truth to be attained, like [seeking] something within a mirror."

The head is present; the eyebrows and eyes are visible. The true substance has not been lost, yet it is difficult to fathom. It is like having the head itself without losing it, yet finding the face and eyes difficult to see.
Throughout one’s life of discrimination, one perceives this world, these sentient beings, and these karmic fruits as being dissimilar to my True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Even if one were to attain True Suchness, it would be attained by severing delusions through realization; it is not the self-nature of the primordial heaven.
This is the true Buddha. Pūrṇa has not yet reached this realization; therefore, since delusion can be extinguished, birth must have a cause.

One must recognize that cause in order to sever delusion. Since the previous section established the "object" through the principle of luminosity, it is indeed the arising of delusion. Such conceptual discriminations are precisely what constitutes delusion.
The World-Honored One directly reveals the sudden gate (*tongo*), which does not concern itself with the extinction of delusion, but merely brings it to rest.
It is distinct. Bodhi is self-sufficient; it merely requires the cessation of frantic wandering. The head is fundamentally sovereign.

Thus, that which is falsely discriminated and falsely wandered in frenzy arises due to the accumulation of delusion. Delusion is originally without cause; it does not arise from delusion, nor does it emerge from awakening.
Since delusion has no root, where can the false be attached? Since the false has no support, the false is fundamentally unarisen. The false is originally...
There is no arising; there is nothing that can be extinguished. Extinction itself is unextinguishable, and thus quiescent extinction manifests before one.

Therefore, the wondrous enlightenment is perfectly complete; it is fundamentally perfect, bright, and wondrous. Originally, there is neither arising nor extinction, for there is no such thing as delusion.
One who attains Bodhi finds that even "reality" cannot be grasped—how then could they find delusion? Thus, one does not follow or conform to the three kinds of differentiated characteristics.
As for why continuity arises and why it does not arise when conditions are severed: if the one mind does not arise, then the myriad dharmas are without fault.
How could the supreme, pure bodhi be obtained through the cultivation and realization of human effort?
Because the three conditions are severed, the three causes do not arise; therein, one realizes the samādhi of cessation. Pūrṇa and others constantly [practice]...
To differentiate in this way is why bodhi is attained through cultivation and realization.
However, if one does not differentiate in this manner, there is no delusion to be extinguished and no truth to be attained; it is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire dharma-realm.
If you claim that the Tathāgata’s uniquely wondrous, true, and eternal nature must necessarily be realized through the complete extinction of all things, you have not yet seen its wondrousness.
The flesh between the bones is called *ken*. Where the muscles and tendons are knotted and obstructed upon the bone where it can be peeled away is called *kei*.
When an experienced butcher dissects an ox, these are the places where he exerts effort; using these characters as a metaphor for that which requires no exertion of effort.
A monk asked Huangbo, "Since there are currently all manner of delusive thoughts, why do you say they do not exist?
Huangbo replied, "Delusion has no inherent substance; it is merely what arises from your own mind.

If you recognize that the mind is Buddha, the mind is fundamentally without delusion—how could you give rise to a mind that further identifies with delusion? If you do not produce thoughts or stir the mind, naturally there will be none."
[The Master] said, "False! Therefore it is said: 'When the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise; when the mind ceases, all manner of phenomena cease.
Baizhang asked, 'Right now, at the very moment a false thought arises, where is the Buddha? Huangbo said, 'Right now you are aware that a false thought has arisen.'"
Awakening itself is precisely the Buddha. If, within this state, there were no deluded thoughts, even the Buddha would not exist. Why is this so?

It is because you give rise to the thought of becoming a Buddha, and thus claim there is a Buddha to be attained; you give rise to the view of sentient beings, and thus claim there are sentient beings to be saved.
Every stirring of the mind and every movement of thought is entirely your own point of view. If all such views are absent, where could a Buddha be found?
"In what place? [Baizhang asked. "Just as Mañjuśrī gave rise to the thought of seeing the Buddha, he was immediately banished to the Two Iron Ring Mountains," the monk said.
Baizhang said, "At this very moment of awakening, where is the Buddha? From where does your question come? From where does your realization arise?
Speech and silence, movement and stillness—all sounds and forms—are entirely the work of the Buddha. Where would you seek the Buddha? You must not look for him elsewhere."
Place the head upon the head; place the mouth upon the mouth. Do not give rise to divergent views. Mountains are mountains; waters are waters; monks are monks;
laypeople are laypeople. The mountains, rivers, and great earth; the sun, moon, and stars—none of these transcend your own mind.
The three thousandfold world-system is, in its entirety, your very self. Where is there any multiplicity? Outside the mind, there is no dharma.
Green mountains fill the eyes; the world of empty space is brilliantly clear. There is not so much as a single hair’s breadth for you to form a conceptual understanding of.
Therefore, all sounds and forms are the Buddha’s eye of wisdom. Dharmas do not arise in isolation; they depend upon conditions to manifest.
Because there are sentient beings, there is manifold wisdom. Though one speaks all day long, when has one ever spoken? Though one hears all day long, when has one ever heard?
"I have heard it said that although Śākyamuni taught for forty-nine years, he never spoke a single word.
The monk asked, "If this is so, where is Bodhi? Huangbo said, "Bodhi has no such location.
Even the Buddha did not attain Bodhi, and sentient beings do not lose Bodhi. It cannot be attained through the body, nor can it be sought through the mind."
"All sentient beings are themselves the mark of bodhi. The monk asked, "How does one arouse the bodhicitta? Baizhang said, "Bodhi is unobtainable.
You should now simply arouse a mind that is without attainment. To be certain not to grasp at even a single dharma is the bodhicitta.
Bodhi has no place of arising; therefore, there is nothing to be attained. Thus it is said: 'I [attained it] from Dīpaṃkara.'"

In the Buddha’s realm, there is not the slightest dharma that can be attained. The Buddha has already bestowed upon me a prediction of enlightenment, clearly knowing that all sentient beings are fundamentally Bodhi and need not attain anything further.
You now ask about generating the Bodhicitta, as if you were taking a single mind to study and become a Buddha;
you merely intend to take the path of Buddhahood as your task, and even if you were to practice for three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, it would still be nothing more than this.
What connection does obtaining a reward-body or transformation-body Buddha have with your original source, the true-nature Buddha?
Therefore it is said: "Seeking outwardly for a Buddha with form is not like you. Furthermore, Linji said:

"Followers of the Way, the various quarters claim there is a Way to be cultivated and a Dharma to be realized. But tell me, what Dharma do you realize? What Way do you cultivate? What do you employ now?"

"Where is there a deficiency? What needs to be repaired? Later generations of young monks, failing to understand this, immediately place their trust in such wild fox spirits and allow them to claim authority over matters, thereby binding others.
To speak of the 'characteristics of principle' and say that one only attains Buddhahood by guarding the three karmas—such talk is like spring drizzle. (The ancient...)
It is said: "When you encounter a person who has attained the Way, first of all, do not speak of the Way. Therefore it is said:
"If a person cultivates the Way but the Way does not function, ten thousand kinds of deviant states will vie for their attention. When the sword of wisdom is drawn forth, there is not a single thing;
before the bright side is revealed, the dark side is already clear. Thus the ancients said: "The ordinary mind is the Way. What is it that you, Virtuous One, are seeking?
What thing is this? It is the person who follows no dependence, listening to the Dharma right before your eyes now, distinct and clear, never lacking anything.
If you wish not to be distinguished from the Buddhas and Patriarchs, simply see in this way; do not allow yourself to be misled by doubt.
If your mind is not different [from its true nature], it is called the "Living Patriarch. If the mind were different, then essence and appearance would be separate; yet the mind is not different.
Therefore, mind and its manifestations are not distinct. Furthermore, a monk asked Chan Master Siji of Jianfu Temple, "What is it like when there is no Buddha in the ancient hall?
Siji replied, "From where does the Brahma-sound come? The monk asked again, "Without relying on cultivation or realization, how can one achieve success?
Siji said, "Cultivation and realization are themselves non-attainment. When the insights of these various venerable masters were each perfectly realized, what need was there for anything else?
The essence of diligent cultivation and realization is none other than the wondrous mind of *nirvāṇa* and the treasury of the true Dharma-eye;
how could it wait for the plucking of a flower at Vulture Peak and Kāśyapa’s smile before being termed the "separate transmission of the mind-seal"?
It is like a person who has tied a wish-fulfilling jewel within his own garment, yet remains unaware of it.
Wandering through distant lands on the road, he runs about begging for food; though he is truly impoverished, the jewel has never been lost.

Suddenly, a wise person points out the jewel to him, and his every wish is fulfilled according to his heart, leading him to great abundance. Only then does he realize that the divine jewel was not obtained from without.

Tong said: "The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* both point directly to the human mind and teach that seeing one's nature leads to Buddhahood; they both employ the metaphor of the jewel in the garment.
The Tathāgatagarbha-nature is shrouded by the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), like a jewel tied within one's clothing, and for this reason it is not easily seen."
One runs outward in pursuit, daily seeing only insufficiency; one wanders in exhaustion to foreign lands, frantically rushing through the nine realms.

Seeking the pleasures of humans and devas, one takes up the limited benefits of the partial and small vehicles—this is like a beggar running about for alms. Once the original mind is attained, one is full and has more than enough.
The jewel is named "Wish-Fulfilling. Whatever one desires is granted according to the mind. How unexpected that its self-nature is inherently complete!
How unexpected that its self-nature can give rise to the myriad dharmas! Thus, its wondrous functions are never deficient, leading to great abundance. This is the first divine jewel.

Delusion has never been lost; awakening has never been attained. It is simply that when one receives the pointing-out instruction from a wise person, one immediately enjoys it inexhaustibly of oneself—how could there be any need for cultivation or realization?
One day, the World-Honored One showed a multicolored mani jewel and asked the kings of the five directions, "What color is this jewel?
At that time, the kings of the five directions each described it as a different color. The World-Honored One then...
The Buddha tucked the pearl into his sleeve, then raised his hand and asked, "What color is this pearl? The Heavenly King replied, "There is no pearl in the Buddha's hand;
where could there be a color? The World-Honored One sighed and said, "How can you be so deluded?
When I show you a worldly pearl, you each insistently describe it as blue, yellow, red, or white. But when I show you the true pearl..."

They were entirely unaware of this, yet at that time the Heavenly Kings of the Five Directions all attained realization of the Way. When Dazhu first visited Mazu, Mazu asked him, "Where have you come from?
He replied, "From Dayun Temple in Yuezhou. Mazu asked, "What do you intend to do by coming here?
He said, "I have come to seek the Buddha-dharma. Mazu said, "Disregarding the treasure-trove within your own house, you have abandoned it and wandered away."
"What are you doing? Here I have not a single thing. What Buddha-dharma do you seek?
Huizhu then prostrated and asked, "Which one is my own treasure-trove? The Patriarch said, "It is that which is now asking me."
"Your treasure-store is already fully manifest; there is nothing lacking, and its use is at your command. Why do you need to seek it elsewhere?
At these words, the pearl suddenly recognized his own original mind without relying on intellectual cognition. He leaped for joy and paid his respects, serving the Master for six years.
Later, he returned home and composed the *Tunwu rudao yaomen lun* (A Treatise on the Essential Gate of Entering the Way through Sudden Enlightenment) in one fascicle. The Patriarch saw it.

He addressed the assembly, saying: "In Yuezhou there is a great pearl; it is perfectly round and luminous, its brilliance penetrating through, existing in a state of spontaneous freedom without obstruction.
Yangshan went to visit Chan Master Hui of Dongsi Temple. Hui asked him, "Where are you from? Yangshan replied, "I am a man from Guangnan.
Hui said, "I have heard that there is a 'Taming the Seas' Bright Pearl in Guangnan; is this true? Yangshan replied, "It is. Hui—
Yangshan said, "What is this pearl like? Yunyan replied, "It is hidden during the dark moon and appears during the bright moon.
Yangshan asked, "Can you bring it here or not? Yunyan said, "I can bring it here. Yangshan said, "Why do you not present it to me, old monk?
Yunyan joined his palms, stepped forward, and said, "Yesterday I went to Mt. Gui, and there too I was asked for this pearl; I was left with nothing to say in response."
There is room for further elaboration. It was said: "A true lion cub is well able to roar.

For thousands and hundreds of years thereafter, it has been fortunate that various venerable masters have each obtained the divine pearl; it was not acquired from without. This serves to further confirm that the Buddha’s words are not erroneous.
At that moment, Ānanda prostrated at the Buddha’s feet amidst the great assembly, rose, and addressed the Buddha:

“World-Honored One, you have just explained that because the three conditions for the karma of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct are severed, the three causes do not arise; thus, Cūḍapanthaka’s madness has naturally subsided within his mind.”
"Cessation is itself Bodhi; it is not obtained from others. Thus, the nature of causes and conditions is clear and manifest.
How could the Tathāgata suddenly discard causes and conditions? "World-Honored One, I attained awakening through causes and conditions.
Is this principle [applicable] only to us junior śrāvakas in training? Within this assembly, there are also Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Śāriputra, Subhūti..."

Purāṇa and others, having heard the causes and conditions of the Buddha from the aged brahmin, gave rise to the aspiration for enlightenment and attained realization, thereby achieving the state of outflowlessness (*anāsrava*).
Now, if you say that Bodhi does not arise from causes and conditions, then the "spontaneity" (*svayambhū*) taught by Kauśārī and others in Rājagṛha would constitute the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
We pray only that you will bestow great compassion upon us and dispel our confusion.
Tong said: "The World-Honored One taught that because the three conditions are severed, the three causes do not arise.

He correctly instructed Pūrṇa and others that if they do not follow after the conceptualization of the laws regarding the severance and extinction of the three kinds of continuous causal conditions, then the nature of madness will naturally subside."
When Bodhi manifests before one, one should not desire to unite the mind of arising and ceasing with the Tathāgatagarbha.

Even the opening of a separate gate of sudden enlightenment—which seeks to attain the non-arising and non-ceasing by severing causes and conditions—is not permitted; how much less so when there are actual causes and conditions?
Ānanda has long been habituated to extensive learning, well-acquainted with the principles of causes and conditions and spontaneity, as well as their mutual interaction.
Refutation: You have misunderstood the principle that because the three conditions are severed, the three causes do not arise.

In the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), when the three karmas of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct lack their conditions, then the three causes of greed, hatred, and delusion do not arise. There are causes and conditions; there is mutual correspondence.
This is perfectly clear and evident—how can you claim there are no causes and conditions? It is just as when Mahāmaudgalyāyana and Śāriputra met.
The bhikṣu Aśvajit taught that all phenomena arise from conditions and all phenomena cease from conditions; upon hearing these words, he immediately realized the first fruit [of the path].
He attained enlightenment through causes and conditions, and it was the same for all the elders.

Now, to suddenly abandon causes and conditions—is this not like the doctrine of Makkhali Gosāla, who claimed that although sentient beings experience suffering and pleasure, there are no causes or conditions?
Nevertheless, how do they differ? It is simply that by hearing the causes and conditions of the Buddha, one attains the state of outflowlessness (*anāsrava*).

What is called "arising from conditions and ceasing from conditions" allows for a profound realization and vision of the principle of non-arising (*anutpāda*); as for those [phenomena] of arising and ceasing—
All are conditioned by the ear; thus, one attains the outflow-free (anāsrava). How could this be obstructed by causes and conditions?
One day, Huìtōng, the attendant of Niǎokē, wished to take his leave. Niǎokē asked, "Where are you going now? He replied, "Huìtōng has left the household life for the sake of the Dharma."
"The Master has not bestowed his compassionate instruction; I shall now go to various quarters to study the Buddha-dharma," said Tōng.
The Master said, "As for the Buddha-dharma, we have a little here as well. Tōng asked, "What is the Master’s Buddha-dharma?
The Master plucked a tuft of cloth from his body and blew upon it. Tōng thereupon attained realization. Fen-yang offered this verse: The Attendant’s Initial Resolve.

Longing for superior conditions, he took leave of his teacher, intending to go and study Chan meditation. When Niaoke perceived that his karmic affinity had ripened, he blew on his razor-sharp blade, and [Zhaozhou] attained peace of mind in that very instant.
Is such a karmic affinity not indeed what is meant by "causes and conditions"?
The Buddha told Ānanda: "It is just as with the case of the city-dweller Yan-ruo-da-duo (Śaṇḍaka).

If the causes and conditions for his madness were to be extinguished, then his non-mad state would naturally emerge. Causes and conditions are themselves natural; this is the ultimate limit of principle. Ānanda, the head of Yan-ruo-da-duo was originally natural.
It was fundamentally so of itself; there is no 'so-ness' that is not self-so. For what cause and condition, then, did he fear his head?"

He runs about wildly. If the head were natural, why would it run wild due to causes and conditions? Why would it not be natural? It is lost due to causes and conditions; yet the original head is not lost.

This wild panic is a false projection that has never undergone any change; how could it depend on causes and conditions? If the original state were wild, then the wild panic already existed naturally.
Before one was wild with panic, where did that panic lie hidden? If the non-wild state were natural, then the head originally had no delusion; why then [is there this fear]?

He ran about frantically. Had he realized that his original head was there all along, he would have known that this frantic running arose from causes and conditions and was, by its very nature, mere idle speculation.
It is said in general: to claim that the true nature of Bodhi emerges spontaneously only after causes and conditions have been severed is not the correct teaching.
To investigate this through the single instance of Yajñadatta’s fear of his own head, one finds it is neither caused by external conditions nor produced spontaneously.
Nevertheless, the severing can be understood. It begins with the head; the head is fundamentally spontaneous (*svabhāva*) and must not be usurped by causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
For what reason, then, does one go mad because of the cause and condition of looking into a mirror? If one takes causes and conditions to be real, then spontaneity cannot act as the master.
Why, then, would the true head be lost for no reason of causes and conditions? Yet, the head is fundamentally [spontaneous].
Lost! He runs about in his own madness. Seeing that madness is fundamentally a false manifestation makes it clear that it has nothing to do with causes and conditions.

Since it does not arise from causes and conditions, nor does it cease because of causes and conditions, it is incorrect to claim that the nature of madness can be extinguished through causes and conditions.
Since you speak of madness, and madness is fundamentally spontaneous (*svabhāva*), where could it have been hidden? As for the state of non-madness, it is likewise spontaneous.
Furthermore, whether one runs about in madness or is not mad, all such states lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). It is clear that this has nothing to do with spontaneity (*svayambhū*).
Since it neither emerges from spontaneity nor is hidden by spontaneity, it is incorrect to say that the non-mad nature emerges spontaneously.
Thus we know that whether one speaks of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) or speaks of spontaneity, what does this have to do with the head? Whether one speaks of being originally mad or...
The original state is not madness; how could it be rescued by madness? Both belong to conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and are not yet the ultimate reality.
One need only awaken to the original head; the head was never lost from the beginning. To recognize the frantic running is to see that madness originally emerged as a delusion.

This single word "awakening" and this single word "recognizing" constitute one's own true and authentic utilization; they are beyond the reach of verbal discourse. To awaken to the head is to awaken to the original source.
The face and eyes are fundamentally without change; it is only the delusion of consciousness that causes one to run wild through the nine realms, giving rise to false discriminations.

This awakening and this consciousness last but a moment, like a flash of lightning or a spark from a flint. How could they be a place where one can take a stand through causes and conditions or spontaneity?
Therefore, it is said that when [delusion] ceases, that is Bodhi; it is not obtained from others, for it is far removed from causes and conditions.

That he attained such spontaneity was precisely due to this. Chan Master Zhinan of Mount Niutou served as a lieutenant general during the Daye era of the Sui dynasty and frequently achieved military victories.
During the Wude era of the Tang dynasty, at the age of forty, he requested ordination and became a disciple of Chan Master Baoyue.
Two former comrades who had served with him in the army heard that the Master had retired to the Way and...
They entered the mountains together to search for him. Upon finding him, they said to him, "General, are you mad? Why do you dwell here?

Huiyan replied, "My madness is about to subside, while yours is now fully unleashed. Those who indulge in lustful sights and lewd sounds, and who covet glory and seek favor, wander through birth and death;
by what means can they emerge from this on their own? The two men were moved to realization, sighed, and departed. Later, they went to pay their respects to Master Daorong.
When the Master elucidated the Great Matter, Huigong said to him, "I have received the true instructions of the Great Master; that which I had attained has entirely vanished.
Even if there were a dharma superior to nirvana, I would say it is like a dream or an illusion.
Now, a single speck of dust flying can obscure the sky, and a single mustard seed falling can cover the earth. You have now transcended such views; what more need I say? Thus it was.
As for those such as Xi Kuang and Zhi Yan, they may be said to have attained true awakening.
Therefore, I say that because the three conditions are severed, it is the bodhicitta; when the bodhicitta arises, the mind of arising and ceasing is extinguished.
This is merely arising and ceasing; when both cessation and arising are exhausted, there is the path of non-effort (*anabhoga*).

If there were such a thing as spontaneity (*svabhāva*), then it would follow that the spontaneous mind arises and the mind of arising and ceasing ceases—yet this too is arising and ceasing. That which is without arising and ceasing is called spontaneity.
It is like the world, where various phenomena intermingle and blend to form a single entity; this is called the nature of combination (*saṃyoga-svabhāva*).

That which is not combined is termed the primordial nature (*prakṛti-svabhāva*). The primordial is not "primordial," and combination is not "combined. Both combination and the primordial are transcended; both transcendence and combination are negated.

Only this phrase may be called the Dharma free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*). Bodhi and Nirvana remain far distant; they are not to be realized through your arduous cultivation over kalpas.
Although you may recall and uphold the pure and wondrous principles of the twelve divisions of the scriptures of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, [you have not yet attained them].
[To say it is] "like the sands of the Ganges" merely increases frivolous proliferation.
[The Master] replied: "This section clarifies that there is no need for the toil of refining and realizing the 'tendons and sinews' (of practice).

When madness suddenly ceases, it is not due to the toil of severing conditions; therefore, it is not caused by causes and conditions. If one were to claim that the three conditions are severed, then the three causes..."
It is non-arising. By means of these causes and conditions, one attains the bodhicitta. This bodhicitta arises because the arising-extinguishing mind is extinguished;
by extinguishing the false, one realizes the true. Yet even this "true" becomes false; this is merely the nature of the dharma of arising and extinguishing, not bodhi.
That it belongs to the category of arising and extinguishing is certainly easy to understand. As for the point where both extinction and arising are exhausted—
Not only does the mind of arising and ceasing come to an end, but that which extinguishes arising and ceasing also comes to an end.
Since there is no longer any arising to be extinguished, there is no further function to be employed.

If, within this state, there were something neither arising nor ceasing called "spontaneity" (*svabhāva*), such a spontaneous mind would manifest because both arising and ceasing have been exhausted. This spontaneous mind arises precisely because of arising.
The cessation of the mind is also called the dharma of arising and ceasing; it is not the bodhicitta. Furthermore, the characters [of this term] possess a profound significance.
That which is without arising and ceasing is called "spontaneous" (*svayambhū*). Why, then, is it also called arising and ceasing? It is because it is manifested in contrast to arising and ceasing;
since there is a state of relative opposition, it is like the manifestation of non-composition in contrast to composition. Thus it is.
There are cases where this is not so. There is conjunction and there is non-conjunction; their mutual opposition remains distinct.

For example, when one speaks of the existence of an ox-horn in contrast to the non-existence of a rabbit-horn, it belongs to the realm of arising and ceasing. Such [emptiness] can only empty away arising and ceasing, but cannot empty away its natural state.
It is like saying that a certain house is empty of people, yet not empty of the house itself;

this is not true insight, and is therefore called conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). One should simply transcend all dualistic opposites—whether "fit" or "unfit," "so" or "not so"—remaining entirely free from them, yet without even a mind of detachment.
Thus, both union and separation vanish; having abandoned the object of abandonment, one further abandons [the subject].

That which is capable [of action] and that which is acted upon are both transcended; there is only the single reality. Only this phrase may be called the Dharma free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*).
If one relies on this phrase to grasp at non-existence, even the supreme Bodhi and Nirvana will remain far distant.

Why is this? Because one remains seated within the merit of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*). Supreme Enlightenment and the wondrous mind of Nirvana can only be realized and entered in a single instant.
This is because it is not something you can cultivate and realize through diligent toil over kalpas.
That which is attained without being cultivated and realized through diligent toil over kalpas is attained spontaneously without depending on causes and conditions.

That which must be attained by relying on cultivation and realization through diligent toil over kalpas is necessarily attained spontaneously through causes and conditions. Although you may further recollect and maintain [the teachings] throughout the ten directions...
The Tathāgata’s pure and wondrous principle is entirely the dharma free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*).
It is merely the natural proliferation of causal conditions; how could there be any actual attainment? Therefore, I say that because the three conditions are severed, the three causes do not arise.
To claim that one attains the bodhicitta by following such conceptual discrimination is not true attainment. This is because...
The arising and ceasing mind merges with the Tathāgatagarbha; yet, by not following this discrimination, the nature of madness naturally subsides.
This subsiding is itself Bodhi. That one does not merely "attain" it is what constitutes true attainment, for it is through the non-arising and non-ceasing that it merges with the Tathāgatagarbha.
This is the most supreme karmic condition; how could it be constrained by the naturalistic theories of Śāriputra? It may be so.

"Are these the same as what the heterodox teachers speak of? The Sixth Patriarch said, "What the heterodox teachers call 'neither arising nor ceasing' means they attempt to stop arising by means of cessation, and manifest cessation by means of arising;
thus, though it is cessation, it is not yet ceased, and though it is arising, they say it does not arise.

What I call 'neither arising nor ceasing' is that fundamentally there has been no arising from the beginning, and now there is likewise no cessation. This is why it differs from the heterodox teachings. He then proceeded to question the Mountain Master.

Xiu, the Master of the Mountain, said: "If you clearly know the nature of arising and non-arising, why are you detained by arising? Xiu replied: "A bamboo shoot must ultimately become a bamboo. Now, could it still be used as a strip of bamboo? The questioner said: "In the future, you will realize this for yourself. Xiu said: "I am just like this. What is your intention, Reverend? The questioner [remained silent]. Xiu said: "I have already answered. The questioner said: "What did you say? Xiu said: "I said nothing at all. The questioner said: "Why do you speak of 'nothing'? Xiu said: "Because there was nothing to say. The questioner said: "If there is nothing to say, why do you say 'nothing'? Xiu said: "It is because there is nothing that I say 'nothing'. [The Master] said: "This is the Director’s quarters; that is the Head Cook’s quarters. Xiu then prostrated. Tiantong’s verse says:
Vast and open, free from dependence; lofty and closed, unrestrained. The realm is peaceful and quiet, reaching a place where few people dwell.
With a modicum of power, one distinguishes the ranks; With a vast and empty mind, one transcends right and wrong. Right and wrong are transcended—standing alone in the Great Square.
There are no tracks or paths. Observing it thus, those who realize unsurpassed *bodhi* fundamentally do not descend through stages;
how then could any traces be seen?
Although you discuss causes and conditions and spontaneity with such certainty and clarity that people call you the foremost among the learned, [you have not yet realized this].
If, despite the熏習 (xūnxí—perfuming/habituation) from extensive learning accumulated over many kalpas, one cannot avoid the peril of Mātaṅga’s daughter, why wait for my Buddha-peak divine mantra?
The lustful fire in Mātaṅga’s heart was instantly extinguished, and she attained the stage of Anāgāmin within my Dharma.
Thus the Forest of Diligence is perfected and the River of Craving is dried up, bringing you liberation.

Therefore, Ānanda, though you have for kalpas maintained the Tathāgata’s secret and wondrous adornments, it is not equal to practicing untainted karma for a single day, thereby distancing yourself from the two sufferings of worldly hatred and love.
Just as Mātangī was formerly a courtesan, yet by the power of the divine mantra, her lustful desires were dissolved.

Among the Dharma, she is now known as the Bhikṣuṇī Śīlabhadra. Together with Yaśodharā (translated here as "Flower-Colored"), the mother of Rāhula (translated here as "Obstructing the Sun"), they simultaneously awakened to their past causes.
Knowing the causes from successive lifetimes—that craving and attachment are suffering—they cultivated untainted goodness for a single thought-moment.
If one can emerge from the bonds of affliction and receive the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*), how can you deceive yourself by still lingering to watch and listen?
It is said in general that although Ānanda had accumulated much learning over many kalpas, he could not avoid the calamity of the Mātanga woman;

this clearly shows that merely memorizing the Tathāgata’s pure and wondrous principles does not lead to the realization of the fruit. The Buddha-śikhara Divine Mantra is capable of [protecting] Mātanga...
That Dengga’s lewd mind suddenly ceased was the manifestation of liberation from bondage through inconceivable cultivation.
To recollect and maintain the secret "Sublime Adornment" (Guhyasamāja) is itself a state of outflows; to abandon the false and pursue the true is termed the dual suffering of aversion and attachment.

Suffering cannot be avoided; how much less can the attainment of the fruit be achieved? When the熏習 (perfuming) of the sudden and perfect Dharma-gate becomes untainted (*anāsrava*), one awakens to the causes of former lives, craving no longer arises, and one receives a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). How could this be limited merely to the attainment of the fruit?
Mātanga attained the third fruit of the path and was called "One Who Has Transcended the Envelopments.

Yaśodharā, who was also a karmic connection for the World-Honored One throughout successive lifetimes, was prophesied to attain Buddhahood at the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. She was but a woman; yet, by turning her mind for a single thought-moment, she still achieved such vigor.
How much more so for you, Śrāvakas—how can you deceive yourselves by failing to achieve sudden awakening? You must certainly rely on the severing of delusions.

Due to these causes and conditions, why do you allow the conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) of non-Buddhists to linger between your observation and hearing? Master Chunan ascended the hall and said:

"Sons of the Buddha, even if you could understand the teachings of the Buddhas of the three periods of time as fluently as pouring water from one vessel into another, and even if you were to attain hundreds of thousands of *samādhis*, it would not equal a single moment of cultivating the path free from outflows (*anāsrava-mārga*).
This allows you to avoid being fettered by the causes and effects of the realms of humans and devas. At that time...
A monk asked, "How does one cultivate the untainted path? Nan said, "Apprehend it before you were a śrāmaṇera.
The monk asked, "Before I existed, who was taught to apprehend it? Nan said, "The one who apprehends is also non-existent.
If one grasps these one or two turns of phrase, the intent of the Tathāgata that had not yet been fully exhausted will be entirely revealed.

Ānanda and the great assembly, having heard the Buddha’s instructions, had their doubts and delusions eliminated. Their minds awakened to the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*), and they attained an unprecedented lightness and tranquility of body and mind.
Weeping again with deep sorrow, they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“O Unsurpassed King of Pure Jewels of Great Compassion! You have skillfully opened my mind, enabling me through these various [teachings]...”
Through causes and conditions and skillful means, you uplift and encourage others, leading those submerged in darkness out of the ocean of suffering. World-Honored One,
although I have now received such sounds of the Dharma and know that the Tathāgata-garbha— the wondrously enlightened and luminous mind— pervades the worlds of the ten directions,

containing and nurturing the pure, jewel-adorned, and wondrously enlightened royal lands of the Tathāgatas throughout the ten directions, the Tathāgata has further rebuked me for my lack of merit despite my extensive learning.
I have not yet attained through cultivation. I am now like a traveler who has suddenly been granted a magnificent mansion by the Heavenly King.
Although I have obtained this great residence, I must enter it through its gates.

I only pray that the Tathāgata will not abandon his great compassion, and will show me and all the ignorant ones gathered here how to cast aside the Lesser Vehicle and fully attain the path of the Tathāgata’s original resolve—the Nirvāṇa without remainder.
He caused those in training to ask: "From what [source] do they subdue their past objects of attachment, attain dhāraṇī, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision?
Having spoken these words, they prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground and, with single-minded attention within the assembly, awaited the compassionate decree of the Buddha.

The Master said: "From the initial discernment of the true and the false to reveal the nature of enlightenment, up to the proclamation of the ultimate reality within the supreme meaning, I have resolved and cleared away all doubts and obstructions so that you may believe and understand the true nature as the mind of the causal stage.

Since the causal mind is now true, one can then perfectly accomplish the cultivation and realization of the fruition stage. Therefore, the preceding section constitutes the 'Path of Vision' (darśana-mārga), and from here below—"
A separate arising constitutes the factors for the cultivation of the Path. Although Ānanda had already attained the Dharma-body, he still possessed subtle delusions;
now that those delusions have been eliminated and he has realized the true mark (dharmatā), he nevertheless laments his lack of proficiency in cultivation.
In short, he remains outside the gate; though he knows of the celestial king’s flowered mansion, he is as yet unable to enter it. Therefore...
Those who fail to enter through the gate do so for two reasons: first, because they cherish the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) and do not clarify the path of their original resolve;
second, because they grasp at conditions as suffering and are unable to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
While this is indeed due to the habit of excessive learning, it is also at the request of those among the assembly who are still in training. Muzhou said to the multitude: "You all..."
"Have you people yet found a point of entry? If you have not yet found a point of entry, you must seek one;
later on, do not let me down. Master Xian of Yao Peak ascended the hall and said:
"Winter departs and autumn arrives; the gates of the pavilions stand open. If you can enter, there is no need to linger. You venerable monks, have you [yet entered]?"
"Have you been able to enter here yet? If you have been able to enter, as the ancients said:
'Every place is Maitreya; there is no gate and no Sudhana. If you have not yet been able to enter, it is simply because you, venerable elders, have been running about in vain;
I shall say no more. I have stood for a long time, so take care. A celestial messenger asked Muzhou, "The three gates are all open."
The Master entered through that gate. The Governor called out, "Come forward! The messenger responded, "Yes. The Governor said, "Enter through the Gate of Faith.

The messenger then saw the murals on the wall and asked, "What were the two Venerable Ones discussing as they conversed? The Governor struck the pillar and said, "Which of the three bodies does not preach the Dharma?
Muzhou’s teaching style was lofty and steep; here, he has explained everything clearly and transparently.
If one attains such faith, one shall no longer pass through the successive stages.
At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for those among the assembly—pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas—who had not yet attained mastery over the bodhicitta, [spoke thus].

Furthermore, for the sake of sentient beings in the age of the Dharma’s decline after the future Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, he has brought forth the Bodhicitta and opened the path of sublime practice of the Unsurpassed Vehicle.
He proclaimed to Ānanda and the great assembly: "You all must resolutely bring forth the Bodhicitta."
Regarding the wondrous samādhi of the Buddha-Tathāgata, one should not give rise to weariness; rather, one ought first to clarify the two definitive meanings of the initial resolve for enlightenment.
[The Master] replied: "Ānanda’s question contains two meanings: the first concerns the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa without remainder as the original resolve for enlightenment."
First, the path. Second, subduing discursive attachments to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Therefore, the Buddha spoke to him using two definitive meanings.

If one wishes to know the path of the original aspiration for enlightenment, one must discern the root of birth and death and attain the nature that is without arising or ceasing to serve as the mind of the causal stage;
only then can one perfectly realize the wondrous virtue of Nirvana, which is neither born nor extinguished. This is the first step for the beginner.
This is the first meaning. To subdue and control discursive attachments, one must carefully examine the root of afflictions (*kleśa*).

Knowing that the six sense-faculties act as intermediaries for thieves, one realizes that one creates the conditions and must suffer the consequences oneself. Therefore, simply select a faculty of perfect capacity (*mūla-indriya*) and enter deeply through a single door;

then those six faculties of cognition will all become pure at once. This is the second meaning for a beginner. To attain the state of non-arising (*anutpāda*), one must subdue the afflictions and be able to sever them.
Afflictions are themselves the realization of non-arising; these two have never failed to be mutually constitutive. This is called "wondrous samādhi" and also the "wondrous path of cultivation.

At all times, one must be reminded of the single character "wondrous" (miao), ensuring that the wondrous and the luminous are in resonance with one another, so as not to fall into grasping at signs while seeking bodhi. Those pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas cannot yet avoid such attachment.

Because of these characteristics, one has not yet attained mastery over Bodhi. To awaken solely to this wondrous [truth] without relying on arduous toil or the laborious cultivation and realization of the "sinews and sinewy knots" (kenkō)—this is what is called the Vehicle of Non-arising (*anutpāda-yāna*).

When the Great Master Bodhidharma arrived in Jinling, Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty asked him: "Since I ascended the throne, I have built monasteries, transcribed scriptures, and ordained monks beyond measure. What merit do these bring?"
[The Emperor asked about] "merit. The Patriarch said, "There is no merit at all. The Emperor asked, "Why is there no merit?

The Patriarch said, "This is merely a minor fruit of the human or celestial realms, a cause subject to outflows (*āsrava*). It follows one like a shadow follows a form; though it exists, it is not real.
The Emperor asked, "What, then, is true merit? The Patriarch said, "Pure wisdom is wondrously perfect; its essence is inherently empty and quiescent. Such is merit..."
The Emperor asked again, "What is the primary meaning of the Noble Truths? The Patriarch replied, "Vast emptiness; there is no sage.
The Emperor said, "Who is it that faces me? The Patriarch replied, "I do not know. The Emperor did not understand.
Knowing his opportunity was not met, the Patriarch subsequently crossed secretly to the north of the river. Xuedou’s verse says: "The Noble Truth is vast and empty; how can one discern its mark?"
"Who is it facing me? he asked. The reply was, "I do not know. Because of this, he crossed the river in secret; how could he avoid the thorns that grew there?
The entire nation pursued him, but he did not return; for ten thousand ages, people have only remembered him in vain. Do not remember him! The pure breeze pervades the earth—how can it have limits?
Looking around at those present, he said, "Is there a Patriarch here? He himself replied, "There is."
"Summon him here to wash the old monk’s feet. Tiantong’s verse says: Vast and open, there is no sage;
the responsive capacity comes directly and abruptly. Is this not like striking the nose while wielding the axe? Or missing the opportunity, failing to look back as one falls into the cauldron?

Silently sitting in the cold stillness of Shaolin, silently upholding the true command. The autumn is clear as the moon turns its wheel of frost; the river is pale as the Dipper hangs its handle in the night.
The lineage of robes and bowls is entrusted to one's children and grandchildren; from this point on, humans and devas become medicine for the sick.

If we speak of the path of wondrous cultivation in the Unsurpassed Vehicle—that is, the primary meaning of the Noble Truths—even that is not permitted, let alone falling into the second or third [vehicles].
How are the two meanings of the initial mind determined? Ānanda, as for the primary meaning:

if you wish to cast aside the vehicle of the śrāvakas, cultivate the bodhisattva vehicle, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, you should carefully examine whether the mind generated at the stage of the causal ground is identical to or different from the awakening at the stage of the resultant fruit.
Ānanda, if, at the causal ground, you take a mind subject to arising and ceasing as the basis for cultivating the cause—
"To seek the Buddha-vehicle while [clinging to] birthlessness and deathlessness—this is impossible.
He replied: "This is the primary meaning for revealing the nature of seeing. If one speaks of seeing the nature, it does not depend upon effort or achievement."
One simply observes whether the mind generated at the stage of the causal ground is identical to or different from the awakening at the stage of the fruition.
Therefore, the sages attained it without thinking and hit the mark without striving; even infants know without deliberation and can do so without learning.
Not learning and not deliberating is the cause; not thinking and not striving is the fruition. Hence it is said: "The great man does not lose [his original nature]."
This is the heart of an infant. When cause and effect are in accord, there is neither increase nor decrease. One who has not realized their nature is insufficient to speak of this.
Mazu was residing at the Chuanfa Temple on Mount Nanyue; he lived alone in a single room, practicing only seated meditation.
Whenever anyone came to visit him, he would not look at them. When Master Shengrang went to see him, Mazu likewise did not look at him. The Master observed him...
His divine countenance appeared different. He then recalled the prophecy of the Sixth Patriarch and employed various means to guide him. One day, he began grinding a brick in front of the hermitage;
the Patriarch paid him no heed. After some time had passed, the Patriarch asked, "What are you doing? The Master replied:

[He] ground it to make a mirror. The Patriarch said, "How can grinding a brick produce a mirror? The Master said, "Since grinding a brick cannot produce a mirror, how can sitting in meditation enable one to become a Buddha?
The Patriarch then rose from his seat and asked, "What then is the way? The Master replied, "It is like driving a cart:
if the cart does not move, do you strike the cart or do you strike the ox? The Patriarch was speechless. The Master spoke again.
The Master said: "Do you study sitting meditation, or do you study sitting as the Buddha? If you study sitting meditation, meditation is neither sitting nor lying down.

If you study sitting as the Buddha, the Buddha is not characterized by the posture of sitting. Within the dharma of non-abiding, one should neither grasp nor reject. If you sit as the Buddha, that is precisely killing the Buddha;
if you cling to the form of sitting, you have not realized its principle. The Patriarch prostrated himself and asked: "How should I apply my mind?"
He immediately entered the Samādhi of Signlessness (*animitta-samādhi*). The Master said, "Your study of the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground is like sowing seeds below;
my preaching of the essential Dharma is like the moisture from heaven. Because your conditions have converged, you shall perceive the Way.
The Patriarch asked, "The Way has no form or appearance; how can it be seen? The Master replied, "The Dharma-eye of the Mind-Ground can see the Way. The Samādhi of Signlessness..."
Mèi replied, “It is likewise. The Patriarch asked, “Is there arising and ceasing?
