[The Master] said, "An outsider cannot do it. [Fengxue] said, "Suddenly he is caught and defeated; to whom does the merit belong? Fuyou said, "As for the reward, I have never heard of it.
[The Master] said, "If that is so, then there is labor but no merit. Fuyou said, "Merit is not non-existent; it is accomplished, yet it is not dwelt upon."
He asked: "Since he has already achieved success, why does he not remain in it? Fokuang replied: "Have you not heard it said:
'Peace itself was brought about by the generals, yet we do not permit the generals to witness that peace'? From this, one can see that the function is used to clarify the position;
this has never been abandoned in the Chan school. How could it ever have been the case that they spoke exclusively of "unconcerned Chan"?
Ānanda, what is meant by the "world of sentient beings"? "World" (*loka*) refers to the passage of time; "realm" (*dhātu*) refers to spatial direction.
You should now know that east, west, south, north, southeast, southwest, northeast, northwest, above, and below constitute the realms;
the past, future, and present constitute the worlds. There are ten directions and three periods of time. All sentient beings weave together their delusive falsehoods.

They are mutually constituted. Within the body there is exchange; worlds intersect one another. Yet the nature of these realms, even if they extend throughout the ten directions, has a fixed location that can be clearly discerned.
In the mundane world, one merely speaks of east, west, south, and north; above and below have no fixed positions, and the center has no definite direction.
The four numbers must be clear as they intersect with the mundane world: three times four and four times three, revolving to twelve, flowing and transforming through three cycles, totaling ten.
In total, throughout the beginning and the end, within the six sense organs, each possesses one thousand two hundred merits.

Ānanda, you should further determine their relative superiority and inferiority among them; for instance, as the eye perceives, it is dark behind and bright in front, and fully bright in the direction before it.
The area behind is entirely dark; looking to the left and right, it covers only two-thirds. Considering the functions performed as a whole, its merit is incomplete:
of the three parts attributed to its function, one part lacks virtue. One should know that the eye possesses only eight hundred merits. As for the ear, it hears all around.
Nothing is left out throughout the ten directions; when active, it reaches both near and far, yet when still, it has no boundaries.

You should know that the faculty of hearing is endowed with one thousand two hundred merits. It is like the sense of smell: it passes through inhalation and exhalation, yet while there is out-breathing and in-breathing, it lacks the interval between them.
Examining the faculty of the nose, three parts are missing one; one should know that the nose possesses only eight hundred merits.
As for the tongue, it proclaims all mundane and supramundane wisdom; its expression has spatial divisions, yet its principle is inexhaustible.

One should know that the faculty of the tongue is complete with one thousand two hundred merits. As for the body, it perceives touch; it recognizes the adverse and the favorable, being able to perceive them when they come into contact.

When separated, there is no cognition; when one is absent, the pair cannot unite. Examining the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), it lacks one of its three parts; thus, one should know that the body possesses only eight hundred merits.
Yet, as with the mind, it silently accommodates all mundane and supramundane phenomena of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
Only the holy and the ordinary are embraced without exception, reaching to the very limits of existence. You should know that the faculty of mind (*manas*) is complete with twelve hundred merits.

It is said: all sentient beings, weaving together delusions, bring about their mutual formation; within their bodies they trade and shift, and their worlds interpenetrate one another. This is called...
The karmic power of sentient beings binds together the world; the physical body is the primary retribution (*vipāka*), while the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*) is the secondary retribution.
Relying solely upon the fruition of karma, they load their burdens and travel through the inn of saṃsāra, transmigrating without end.
Their entanglement with worldly dust is entirely mediated by the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*). Within these six faculties, each possesses twelve hundred merits.

This is based on the fact that the nature of discernment is the same; however, below, in relation to the six sense organs, their specific functions differ, and thus they are entirely incomplete and unequal.
As it was said previously: "That which causes you to transmigrate has its fault in the mind and eyes"; therefore, there follow the seven investigations and the eight returns.

Having already clearly seen that [the faculties] are delusive, I now further explain in detail how the six [faculties] act as intermediaries for thieves, and provide a thorough analysis of the relative merits and defects of the six sense organs.
This is so that one may select the perfect penetration of the ear organ as the foundation for cultivation and realization.
While the eyes, nose, and body lack one-third of their full capacity, the tongue and mind, though complete in their functional qualities, are no different from the ear.

However, once one falls into verbal expression or conceptual thought, it is not as close to the essential nature (xingti) as the faculty of hearing—which is without sound or odor—and therefore this [method] should be followed.
Regarding the "three layers" (sanyie) for engaging with the world:
first, each of the four directions is discussed in terms of the three periods of time, totaling twelve; second, within the three periods of time of the eastern direction, one is transformed.
This constitutes ten. The same applies to the south, west, and north. Thus, by multiplying one by ten, one reaches one hundred and twenty.
In the third stage, thirty in the east transforms ten into one hundred; the same applies to the south, west, and north.
Thus, by multiplying ten by one hundred, one reaches one thousand two hundred. Since there are three sequences of flow, three layers are used; since there are ten directions, [one...]
It transforms into ten; this is the natural number. In the *Yī Jīng*, the Great Proliferation number (*dàyǎn zhī shù*) is fifty.
Multiplying five by ten, or multiplying ten by five, follows the same principle as the Sage’s application of these methods; the sequence and the ultimate aim are one and the same.

Thus, there are two hundred for each of the four cardinal directions and one hundred for each of the four intermediate corners; totaling this, there are three hundred for each direction. Now, regarding the eye...
That which is seen in the front and the three directions to the left and right has already formed six hundred [parts]. Together with the two corners in front, they collectively form eight hundred.
Only the single direction behind and the two corners behind are not seen; because three parts are clear, there is "function" (gōng), and because the rear direction is dark, there is no "virtue" (dé).
"Function" and "virtue" are merely interchangeable terms; in reality, the six sense organs are pure and function interchangeably.

There is no fixed direction. If one practices according to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, having already given rise to a semblance of understanding, then even though one may possess eight hundred eyes, one will likewise be endowed with the merits of the other five sense organs.
However, if the six [sense organs] act as intermediaries for thieves to plunder the family treasures, then one will trade away the wares of fabrication;
what end could there be to such a process? Therefore, if one cultivates them, the merits are fundamentally inexhaustible; if one does not cultivate them, there is only the fruit of karma.
It is also inexhaustible. Fayen ascended the hall and said: "The ancients said: 'What is Chan? The three realms are continuous.
What is the Way? The ten directions are vast. Why do they say the three realms are continuous?
Where is the principle that the ten directions are vast? Do you wish to understand? Block the eyes; block the ears; block the tongue."
Body and mind: there is no place of vacancy, no place of movement. Elder, how do you understand this? It cannot be grasped horizontally; it cannot be grasped vertically;
it cannot be grasped lengthwise; it cannot be seized away. There is no place for the application of the mind, nor is there any place for its establishment.
If you can understand it in this way, only then will you understand that the Dharma-gate is utterly free from selection and that all words are [empty].
"Severing all leakage. Once, a monk asked, "What are words that sever all leakage?
I told him, "They are like nostrils; they are very good. If you, Venerable One, understand it in this way, naturally there will be no passage for the wind.
If you recognize it, the entire world of the ten directions is the adamantine eye. There is nothing more to do; take care. — Huanglong Zhen.
The Zen Master ascended the hall and said: "I cite an ancient precedent to ask you, *śrāmaṇeras*: you must not understand it as something of the past;
if you understand it as something of the past, you lose the eye right before your face. I cite a present-day precedent to ask you, *śrāmaṇeras*:
you must not understand it as something of the present; if you understand it as something of the present, you obstruct the *śrāmaṇera*s' original eye."

Even if one were to claim that there is no loss and no obstruction, and that it is neither ancient nor modern, this would still be a case of medicine treating an illness—a mere device to stop a child’s crying.
As for that single phrase of "transcendent liberation," can you, O Ācārya, speak it?
If you cannot, wait until I am at the deep heights of Luohan Peak to discuss the true mark (*dharmatā*), and then I shall tell you. Although such talk clarifies the matter alone...

Moving upward, this indeed complements the present sutra. Only when one reaches the state where the mouth resembles the nostrils and the eyes resemble the eyebrows, such that the six sense faculties have no place of attachment, will one realize the wondrousness of non-arising.
This culminates in the realization that the entire earth is the single eye of a śramaṇa.
There is no further place for inhalation or exhalation. This merit is not to be sought through worldly means.

Ānanda, if you now wish to go against the current of the flow of birth and death and trace it back to its root until you reach that which is neither born nor extinguished, you must examine these six faculties of sensory reception:
which are conjoined and which are separated; which are deep and which are shallow; and which constitute perfect penetration and which do not.
Perfected. If you can awaken to this faculty of perfect penetration, you will reverse the beginningless flow of delusory karma and attain the circulation of perfect penetration;

compared to those with imperfect faculties, your progress will be many times greater than theirs—days and eons multiplied against one another. I have now fully revealed these six profoundly still and perfectly luminous faculties;
their fundamental merits and quantities are as such. Choose from among them according to your own discernment that which you may enter, and I shall clarify it for you, so that you may...
To advance further: the Tathāgatas of the ten directions each practiced within the eighteen realms and all attained the perfect, unsurpassed Bodhi.

Throughout this process, there was no distinction of superiority or inferiority; it was only because you are of inferior capacity that you have not yet been able to achieve perfect mastery of wisdom therein.
Therefore, I proclaim this so that you may enter deeply through a single gate; once you have entered one without delusion, those six [realms]—
The faculty of cognition (*jñendriya*) is at one time pure;

it is generally termed the flowing faculty (*sravendriya*), which is that which is wondrously profound and immovable. When it is determined [by distraction] and emerges, it flows away and rushes toward objects.
This is called the current of birth and death. To enter it by going against the flow and returning the current to its source until it becomes entirely one is called non-arising and non-ceasing.

Arising and ceasing are delusion; non-arising and non-ceasing are the absence of delusion. Although the six faculties of sensory reception are attached to the illusory merit of clarity, they are originally portions of a single, pure, bright essence.
They share the same nature of profound, pervasive, and perfect luminosity. It is only by entering deeply through a single gateway that one can proceed directly...
One reaches the ground of the fundamental source and attains the path of universal penetration (*pariṣvaṅga*), so that no further entanglements arise.
Having subdued former objects of clinging, one enters the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, whereby the six faculties of sensory experience all become sublime functions. The Sixth Patriarch said:
"If one gives rise to the true contemplation of *prajñā*, in a single instant all deluded thoughts are extinguished. If one recognizes one's own nature..."
Awakening is itself the stage of Buddhahood. Good friend, when wisdom contemplates and illuminates, it is clear and penetrating both within and without;
one recognizes one’s own original mind. If one recognizes the original mind, that is liberation. If one attains liberation, that is the samādhi of prajñā.
The *prajñā-samādhi* is precisely non-thought (*amanasikāra*). What is meant by "non-thought"?
If one perceives all phenomena (*dharma*) without the mind becoming stained or attached, this is called non-thought. Its function pervades all places, yet it does not cling to any place.
It merely purifies the fundamental mind so that the six consciousnesses emerge through the six gates; amidst the six sense objects, they are neither stained nor confused as they come and go.
Freedom. Universal and unimpeded, it is precisely the *prajñā-samādhi*. This sovereign liberation is called the practice of non-thought.
These words of the Sixth Patriarch entered through the faculty of mind; he directly inherited the tradition of Kāśyapa’s lineage.
Once, while Yangshan was herding an ox on the upper slope of Mount Weishan, he saw a monk ascend the mountain and soon descend again. Yangshan asked him about his ascent.
Yangshan asked, "Why do you not remain in the mountains for a while? The monk said, "It is simply because our karmic conditions do not harmonize.
Yangshan said, "What are those conditions? Try citing them for me. The monk said, "When the Master asked me what my name was, I replied, 'Returning to Truth.
The Master then asked, 'Where is this Returning to Truth? I had no answer. Yangshan said, "Go back to the Master and say this to him:"
"Someone has spoken it. The Master asked, "How did he speak it? The monk replied, "In the eyes, in the ears, in the nose.
The monk returned exactly as instructed. Yangshan said, "You empty-headed, talkative fellow! These are the words of a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) for five hundred people.
Chan Master Cheng of Tan’an ascended the hall and said: "Sound in the nose, fragrance in the ear, [and] the eye..."
The tongue discerns bitter, salty, sweet, and bland; the mind can perceive touch while the body makes distinctions. In an ice chamber it is like spring, and in the ninth month of summer it is cool.
When one perceives it thus, one will know that within a man’s body one enters meditative concentration (*samādhi*), while within a woman’s body one emerges from concentration.
The sunflower turns with the sun; the rhinoceros horn pattern reflects the moon. Fragrant maples transform into an old man; the larvae of the *mínglíng* insect [transform into cicadas].
The fruits are meager. If you do not realize this, how bitter it is for the Buddha! I grant you a single eye;
only when you see exactly as the various venerable elders have seen will you obtain the news of the purification of the six sense faculties.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One, how is it that by flowing against the current and entering deeply through a single gate, one can cause all six faculties to become pure simultaneously?

The Buddha told Ānanda, “You have now attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*. You have already extinguished the afflictions of the three realms belonging to the world of sentient beings that are abandoned through insight (*darśana-heya*).
Yet, you still do not know the beginningless, empty habitual tendencies accumulated within the faculties throughout successive births.”

The acquisition of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) must be attained through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*); how much more so for the distinctions of their arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing, as well as their specific categories and numbers?

It is said in response: those abandoned by seeing the truths (*darśana-heya*) are the eighty-eight proclivities (*paryavasthāna*). Those abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) are the eighty-one volitions (*cetanā*).
Although the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) abandons the coarse delusions of discrimination (*vikalpa*), the subtle innate delusions (*sahaja-kleśa*) still remain unabandoned.
Therefore, one cannot realize the limit of suffering. To be able to realize the limit of suffering, one must reach the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣabhūmi*).

Not only does one know the number and limits of the birth, abiding, change, and cessation of a single sentient being, but one also knows, in every moment, the subtle modes of activity and the constant transformation of both sentient and insentient beings within the trichiliocosm. This is the state of total lucidity.

This ultimate state must necessarily be attained through that which is severed by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). A monk asked Mount Mui (Shigong): "For one who has attained sudden enlightenment, is there still further cultivation?
Mui said: "If one truly awakens to the source, he knows it for himself; then 'cultivation' and 'non-cultivation' are both dualistic extremes.

Now, although the beginner's mind may have been attained through conditions, having suddenly awakened to the principle in a single thought-moment, there still remains [the residual habituation of]..."

The habitual tendencies accumulated over beginningless kalpas cannot be suddenly purified; one must teach them to cleanse and eliminate the flowing consciousness of present karma, which is itself cultivation.

There can be no separate dharma taught to lead them toward practice. By entering the principle through hearing, the hearing of the principle flows with subtlety, and the mind becomes spontaneously perfect and luminous, no longer dwelling in the realm of delusion.
Even if there were hundreds of thousands of subtle meanings to be emphasized or refuted, [the mind remains thus].
At that time, one may sit and don the robe; only then can one begin to understand how to make a living for oneself. To state the essential point:
on the ground of ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), not a single speck of dust is admitted; within the gateway of the myriad practices (*sāhasra-caryā*), not a single dharma is abandoned.
If one enters directly with a single blade, then all sentiments of ordinary and sage are exhausted, the true permanence is revealed, and principle and phenomena are non-dual—this is suchness.
As it is with the Buddha: principle and phenomena are not two; they are not realized apart from cultivation.
Although Guishan spoke extensively of the single path of the supreme vehicle, he never once swept away the practice of gradual cultivation, nor did he ever so much as mention it again.
Now, you should observe these six faculties present before you: are they one, or are they six? Ānanda, if you say they are one, why does the ear not see?
Why does the eye not hear? Why does the head not tread? Why do the feet not speak?
If these six faculties are definitively established as six, then as I now proclaim this subtle and wondrous Dharma-door to you in this assembly, which of your six faculties comes to hear it?
“I receive it,” Ānanda replied. “I hear it with my ears. The Buddha said, “It is your ears that hear; what concern is this for the body or the mouth?
The mouth comes to inquire about the meaning, and the body rises to show reverence and acceptance. Therefore, you should know that they are neither one nor six, yet ultimately neither six nor one.
Ultimately, your faculties are neither one nor six. Ānanda, you should know that these faculties are neither one nor six, arising from the beginningless past.”

Due to the arrival of perversion and decline, the meanings of "one" and "six" arise within the perfect and湛 (zhàn) [profoundly still] nature. You, Srotāpanna, although you have attained the dissolution of the six, have not yet eliminated the one.
It is like the great void of space which enters into and unites with various vessels; because the shapes of the vessels differ, the space is named differently.
When the vessels are removed and one contemplates the space, one speaks of the space as being "one. How could that great void of space ever become the same as what belongs to you?
The same applies here; how much more so when one claims that they are both one and not one? Thus, your understanding of the six faculties of reception is likewise so. [The Master] said in general:
"This precisely explains the doubt regarding 'entering deeply through one gate' and the purification of the six faculties, so as to make the six faculties fundamentally..."

First: It is inherently pure from the beginning; there is no need to further speak of the "six thieves. If the six faculties were originally six distinct entities that did not function as one, how could they ever be pure at once?
Now, consider it like the great void of space, which is fundamentally one. When it encounters and merges with various vessels, it becomes sixfold.

Because the shapes of the vessels differ, the space within them is given different names, leading one to say there are six spaces rather than one. Yet, if the vessels are removed, [the space remains one].
Contemplating emptiness, one speaks of emptiness as "one," meaning that the six have dissolved and only one remains. This metaphor illustrates the arising of the meanings of "one" and "six.

That great empty space cannot combine with forms; fundamentally, it is neither identical nor different. Since there is neither identity nor difference, where could the names "one" and "six" possibly be established?
This metaphor shows that [emptiness] is fundamentally neither one nor six. To perceive that it is fundamentally neither one nor six is the perfection of the round.
Profoundly and eternally quiescent—what could possibly be impure? The Srotāpanna is called "one who has entered the stream," yet there is nowhere he enters.
He does not enter form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas; thus these six are dissolved. Yet, he still clings to the existence of nirvana.
Therefore, not even one has been lost. From where does this "one" come? From where does emptiness arise? Thus, we know that there is still something further above.
Yaoshan asked Yunyan, "Apart from staying at Baizhang, where else have you been? He replied, "I have been to Guangnan.
Yaoshan said, "I heard it said that outside the eastern gate of the city of Guangzhou, there is a slab of stone. It was..."
The Governor moved away. "Is that so? Yan said, "Not only the Governor; even if the entire nation were to move, it would not budge.
The Mountain (Shishuang Qingzhu) asked again, "I have heard you are skilled at playing with lions; is that true? He replied, "It is true. [The Mountain] asked, "How many times have you played them?
He replied, "I have played them six times. The Mountain said, "I too can play them. He asked, "How many times has the Master played them? The Mountain said:
I performed a display. Yaohan said, "One is six; six is one. Later, he went to Miaoshan.

Miaoshan asked, "I have heard that you, Elder, were performing the lion’s dance at Yaoshan; is this true? He replied, "It is. Miaoshan said, "When you perform it for a long time, there must be times when you set it aside.
Yaohan said, "If I wish to perform it, I perform it; if I wish to set it aside, I set it aside. Miaoshan asked, "At the moment you set it aside, where is the lion?"
Chu Yan said, "Set it down! Set it down! You must know that when Yunyan plays with the lion, he is not playing with a mere spirit;
for him, there is a single stone that the entire nation could not move."

Due to the mutual conditioning of the two aspects of light and darkness, within the wondrous perfection, the clarity becomes adhered to and gives rise to vision. The essence of vision reflects forms, and by binding these forms, the sense organ is formed.
The fundamental source of this organ is termed the "pure four great elements," and for this reason it is called the substance of the eye; it is shaped like a cluster of grapes.

The four sensory objects float upon the faculties; they flow and disperse, rushing toward forms. Through the mutual impact of the two aspects of movement and stillness, within the wondrous perfection, the clarity becomes adherent and gives rise to hearing.
The essence of hearing reflects sound, and by coiling back the sound, it forms the faculty. The source of this faculty is termed the "pure four great elements."
Therefore it is named the "body of the ear," resembling a fresh, rolled leaf. The four sensory objects float upon its root-faculty; as they flow and escape, they rush toward sounds.

Through the two conditions of openness and obstruction, the faculty is activated. Within the wondrous perfection [of the mind], turbidity adheres to stillness to produce the sense of smelling. The essence of smelling reflects odors, and by receiving these odors, the faculty is formed.
The root source is designated as the pure four great elements; hence it is named the substance of the nose. It resembles two hanging claws.

The superficial faculties of the four objects flow outward and rush toward fragrances. Through the intermingling of the two aspects of tranquility and transformation, within the wondrous perfection, turbidity adheres to stillness and gives rise to the sense of taste.

It constantly refines and reflects flavors, condensing the essence of flavor to form its root. This root-source is termed the "pure four great elements" (mahābhūta), and for this reason it is called the substance of the tongue.

Its shape is like a newly waxing crescent moon; as a floating root, it perceives the four sensory objects. It rushes toward flavors with flowing dissipation, through the friction of two kinds of contact: separation and union.

Within this wondrous perfection, the stillness of clarity becomes adherent and gives rise to awareness. The essence of awareness reflects upon contact, and by seizing upon contact, it forms the sense organ.

The fundamental source of this organ is termed the "pure four great elements," and because of them, it is called the physical body. Like the head of a waist drum, the floating organ [of the ear] encounters the four sensory objects; its flow disperses as it rushes toward contact.

Through the two kinds of continuity—arising and ceasing—within the wondrous perfection, the clarity becomes adherent and gives rise to cognition. The essence of cognition reflects the dharmas, and by grasping these dharmas, the sense-faculties are formed.

The source of these faculties is termed the "pure four great elements," and because it is the cause of mental activity, it is called "mental intention" (*manas*). It is like seeing within a dark chamber.
The floating faculties and the four sensory objects flow and rush toward phenomena.
It is said in general that they originally depend on a single brilliant spirit, which divides into six harmonious combinations; this is seen in detail herein.
From the origins of the knots of the six faculties up to the manner in which they rush toward external objects, everything is fully and minutely provided. This is just like...
The great void merges with all vessels. Its essence is lucid and penetrating; when it encounters form, vision arises;
when it encounters sound, hearing arises. How wondrous and perfect! Yet, when still water is turbid, the entry of dust causes it to become sticky.
These pure and clear four elements constitute the supreme sense organs (*indriya*); they can illuminate objects and give rise to consciousness, and are thus the pure material organs (*rūpīndriya*).
"Floating roots and four objects" refers to the floating root of clarity (*prabhāsvara-mūla*), which can flow toward and rush after external objects, creating these various karmas.

The natures of earth, water, fire, and wind are fundamentally all empty; therefore, they are called the "pure four great elements. The characteristics of earth, water, fire, and wind are fundamentally all shifting and unstable;
therefore, they are called the "four objects. As seen in the dark chamber, how could there be a floating root of clarity?
Dust. Obscurity becomes space; within the obscurity of space, the coagulation of darkness becomes form.
Because this dark form mingles with false conceptualization, it stirs inwardly as it gathers conditions. Because there is darkness that can be seen, it is called the "floating root";
because it is agitated and wavering, it is also called "dust. Just as among the five kinds of form, the form induced by feeling (vedanā) is formless, yet it is experienced through recollection.

This refers to that which maintains [the senses]. The faculties (*indriya*) sink within, while the objects (*viṣaya*) float without. Since the objects serve as the basis, how can one say they "flow away"?
This is to reveal the dependent by citing its support. As Master Puan said in a verse: "It cannot be pinched into a ball, nor can it be pushed open; Why seek Nan-yueh or T'ien-t'ai?
At the gateways of the six sense-faculties, no one employs them, Yet they provoke the barbarian monk."
A monk from Baofu came specifically to visit Lohan. Chan Master Lohan Chen asked him, "How do they teach the Buddha-dharma there?
The monk replied, "Baofu has sometimes addressed the assembly, saying: 'Block up your eyes so that you cannot see;
block up your ears so that you cannot hear; sit upon your faculty of thought so that you cannot think.'"
[The Master] could not distinguish them. Baolin Chen said, "I am asking you; I have not blocked your eyes—what do you see?
I have not blocked your ears—what do you hear? I have not sat upon your faculty of thought—how do you make such distinctions?"
Upon these words, a monk attained realization; he found a path of entry at the gateway of the six sense faculties and was able to catch a glimpse of a segment of wondrous, perfect, and true wind.
Furthermore, there was another monk who, upon hearing a tune from the western wing, said: "How can one resist it as you depart?"
A single turn of the autumnal gaze, and one attains great awakening. Why must a foreign monk come specifically for this?
Ānanda, these six sense organs arise from that awakened clarity; there is clarity within clarity, yet they lose that essential lucidity, and through clinging to delusion, they emit light.
Therefore, at this moment, when you are neither in darkness nor in light, the essence of seeing does not exist; when you are neither in motion nor in stillness, it fundamentally does not exist.

Listen to this inquiry: hearing has no penetration and no obstruction; the nature of smelling does not arise; it is neither changing nor tranquil; tasting has nothing from which it issues; it is neither separated nor joined;
the perception of touch is fundamentally non-existent; it has neither cessation nor arising. To understand where these rest:

you need only cease following the twelve conditioned characteristics—movement and stillness, union and separation, tranquility and change, penetration and obstruction, arising and ceasing, light and darkness—and pull them out one by one as they appear.
One faculty: when it is freed from its attachment and turns inward to rest, it returns to the original truth; the fundamental luminosity is then manifested.

As this luminous nature becomes manifest, the remaining five attachments should be uprooted for complete liberation. Thus, the cognitive awareness that arises from external objects no longer follows the sense-faculties; instead, the luminosity is manifested by relying upon the faculties.
Consequently, the six faculties function interchangeably as one another's instruments.
Tong said: "Previously it was stated that 'the clarity of delusion is not from another; the fault lies in the clarity of awareness.

Once the object of delusion is established, the principle of clarity does not transcend its limits—it is confined to the sense faculties. Here it is said that 'due to that clarity of awareness, there arises a clarity within awareness; thus one loses that essential discernment.'"

Adhesive delusion gives rise to light, which pursues the sensory objects. This generally clarifies the accomplishment of the six delusions; it divides that profound and perfect [nature], causing its refined radiance to reflect and manifest.

Internally it does not depart from the faculties, and externally it does not depart from the objects; yet the original true luminosity is consequently shrouded by the faculties and objects, leaving no means for it to manifest as vision.
One should know that the six objects are empty and false, having no inherent nature from the beginning. As for the six faculties...
They are false and illusory. Apart from their objects, they have no substance; as objects alone lack intrinsic nature, [the faculties] can both adhere and detach.
Since the faculties alone have no substance, they exist when facing an object and cease to exist when separated from it. As stated in the *Eight Consciousnesses’ Rules*:

"The three—eye, ear, and body—dwell in two stages," meaning the first dhyāna of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), which is the second stage. This is because there is no solid food (*kavadīkārāhāra*) there. [The tongue...]
Consciousness does not arise because there is no defilement; thus, olfactory consciousness does not manifest, and only the three consciousnesses of the eye, ear, and body abide therein.
Upon reaching the third stage, as they are born of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), even these three consciousnesses do not arise.

This is the contemplation of emptiness that eliminates the vessel [of the senses]. When all is empty, what further could exist? Thus one knows that "either one or six" is a delusion; it is neither one nor six.
This is the True. When delusion is subdued, the True manifests. When the True manifests, delusion no longer adheres.

Once one is liberated from this adherence, the radiance that is emitted does not arise from external objects. Since it does not arise from objects, it is the original, fundamental luminosity of the True Nature.
It does not emerge by following the sense organs. This profoundly still, perfectly luminous nature, though it does not follow the organs, merely manifests by relying upon them as its medium.

Since the organs are said to be "relied upon," they originally have no fixed location; therefore, hearing does not necessarily depend on the ears, and seeing does not necessarily depend on the eyes, such that the six organs can be used interchangeably.
This is not like what occurred previously, where hearing could not transcend sound and seeing could not go beyond form, leading to the arising of self-centered attachments.
Bound by fetters, one cannot transcend them. The verse of Viśvabhū Buddha says: "The body is provisionally borrowed from the four great elements;
the mind is originally without birth, arising only because of objects. If the external object is absent, the mind is likewise non-existent;
sin and merit are like illusions—arising and then ceasing. This passage from the scripture serves as its commentary. A monk asked National Teacher Shao: "I have received the teachings..."
[The student] asked: "It is said that the eye does not see forms and the mind does not know dharmas.

How is it that the eye does not see forms? The Master said: "Rather, it is the ear that sees. [The student] asked: "How is it that the mind does not know dharmas? The Master said: "It is the eye that knows."
[The student] said, "If that is so, then the path of seeing and hearing is cut off, while sounds and forms are clamorous. The Master said, "Who told you that?
He then continued, "Indeed, all questions and answers are like the meeting of needle points; there is not the slightest discrepancy.
There is no matter that is not penetrated and no principle that is not complete. This is truly because all speech and all *samādhis*—whether horizontal or vertical, deep or shallow—are one."
Manifestation and concealment, coming and going—these are the gateways to the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all Buddhas. To verify this based on the present moment alone:
furthermore, when Master Xinding Hui asked a monk, "How do the venerable elders of the South discuss National Teacher Huizhong’s teaching that 'insentient things preach the Dharma'?
The monk replied, "Everywhere it is said that the six sense faculties function interchangeably. Xinding said, "The scriptures state that there is no..."
The eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind—what do they use to interact with one another? When a monk hesitated, Xìn struck him across the back with his staff.
If one has such faith, this mutual functioning is manifest right before one; it is even superior to National Teacher Shao’s seven steps.
Ānanda, do you not know that within this assembly there is Aniruddha (translated as "Non-extinction"), who sees despite having no eyes;
Upananda (translated as "Good Joy") the Nāga, who hears despite having no ears; and the goddess of the Gaṅgā (translated as "Heavenly River"), who perceives fragrances despite having no nose?
Kauṇḍinya (translated as "Ox-Aspect") perceives flavors through his extraordinary tongue; Śūnyatā-deva (translated as "Wind-Nature") perceives touch despite having no body.
The light of the Tathāgata reflects it so that it appears for a moment; yet, being of the nature of wind, its substance is fundamentally non-existent.

As for those who have attained the extinction samādhi and the peace of śrāvakas—such as Mahākāśyapa in this assembly, whose mental faculty has long been extinguished—he possesses a perfect and clear understanding.

"It is not because of mental thought. [The Master] replied: "It is clear that they do not follow their respective sense organs, even to the point of the six organs functioning interchangeably. How can this be verified?
Sudarśana obtained a 'half-head' heavenly eye; thus he did not rely on his eyes. Dragons hear with their horns; thus they do not rely on their ears. The River God heard..."
Fragrance is not originally distinguished from other flavors by the nose-flesh of a cow; the Śūnyatā-deva can perceive touch.

As for those śrāvakas who have cultivated the meditative absorption of cessation and attained the realization of stillness—such as Mahākāśyapa, whose mental faculty has long since ceased—it is known that the six faculties may be non-existent yet are fundamentally the six. The six faculties can be used interchangeably; this is not... [text ends].
The Origin is One. It is neither one nor six; yet the essence of profound stillness and perfect roundness is fully possessed by every person.

Is this not a further source of conviction? When Puyong Zhi-zang reached the Fifth Patriarch’s hall for his formal entry into the lineage, the Patriarch brought up the story of the "Two Women and the Separated Souls" to question him.
Having attained resonance with it, he presented a verse, saying: "The two women merge into one daughter-in-law; the wheel of mechanism cuts..."
Severance is difficult to reverse; from the beginning, coming and going have been utterly free of indulgence. "The traveler need not ask the path by which they came.
Furthermore, when Zhang Zishao went to Jingshan, he discussed "investigating things" (*gewu*) with Official Feng and several other gentlemen.
Huì said, "You gentlemen only know 'investigating things,' but you do not know 'things being investigated' (*wugé*. The gentlemen were at a loss. Huì laughed loudly. The official said, "Master..."
"Can you explain this? Hui said, "Have you not seen it recorded in a minor collection of tales? There was a man from the Tang dynasty who conspired with An Lushan to rebel.
This man had previously served as the Governor of Langzhou, and a portrait of him exists there. When the Emperor Minghuang visited Shu, he saw it."
Enraged, he ordered his attendants to strike the head of the statue with a sword. At that time, the Governor of Minglang was stationed in Shaanxi; suddenly, the head fell to the ground.
Upon hearing this, the Duke immediately grasped its profound meaning. The *Six Verses on the Ministers of Fenyang* states:
"Seeing is Aniruddha—clearly, there is not a single thing. The great earth and the mountains and rivers proclaim the *pāramitās*. Hearing is Upananda."
The faculty of sound is all-pervasive and unsurpassed; near and far are perceived simultaneously. One need not further recite "Mahā. Fragrance is the daughter of the Gaṅgā;
her heart of compassion is universal, and she can discern the pure and the impure entirely. She is none other than the mother of this very self. Taste is Kāvaṇava;
though sweetness and bitterness are commonly spoken of, it distinguishes between the pungent and the sour as soon as it enters the mouth, just like the moon in the sky. Touch is...
Śūnyatā: good and evil are harmonized as one; in slaughter and dismemberment, there is neither anger nor joy. This very thing is Amitābha; its essence is Mahākāśyapa.
Vairocana and [Amitābha] share this single Dharma; though the dark chamber is clearly divided, it branches out into a thousand petals.
Fenyang’s realization was exceptionally profound; he used these six sense faculties to point out, one by one, the single aperture of the Ultimate.
In sum, it is nothing other than subduing the mind to return to the original source and manifesting the fundamental radiance.
Ānanda, if your faculties were now completely uprooted, their inner luminosity would shine forth.
Then these superficial phenomena, as well as all the changing appearances of the vessel-world, would—like ice melting in hot water—be transformed in an instant into supreme awareness.

Tong said: "To extract one root at a time, detach from its clinging, and turn inward to subdue it, tracing back the flowing roots until reaching the state of non-arising and non-extinction—this belongs to the realm of gradual cultivation;

the faculty still resides within me. To extract all the faculties simultaneously, so that they shine with inner clarity and radiance, such that birth and death are extinguished and quiescent extinction manifests before one—this belongs to the realm of sudden enlightenment;
the faculty no longer resides within me. Therefore, if one does not awaken, one remains adrift."
The sensory faculties, the physical body, the mundane world-receptacle, and all manifested phenomena all return to the law of arising and ceasing, just as water freezes to become ice.
Once awakened, one immediately transforms arising and ceasing into the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing, just as hot water melts ice back into water.
Water is its original state; supreme awareness is inherently possessed by oneself from the beginning. Having already been realized...
Since there is unsurpassed awakening, what need is there to worry about the six thieves?
Longtan Xian asked Tianhuang Wu, "Since I first arrived here, I have not received the Master’s instruction on the essential point of the mind.
Huang said, "Ever since you arrived, I have never failed to instruct you on the essential point of the mind. Xian asked, "Where did you instruct me? Huang replied, "When you were holding up..."
"Tea is served; I shall receive it for you. Food is brought; I shall accept it for you. When you perform a prostration, I simply lower my head.
Where have I not pointed out the essential heart of the Dharma to you? While Tan stood there lost in thought, Huang said, "If you see, you see directly right now.
Any conceptual deliberation is a deviation. Tan was enlightened on the spot. He then asked again, "How does one preserve this?"
Ren said, "Follow your nature in carefree wandering; go with the flow in expansive ease. Simply exhaust the ordinary mind; there is no separate 'sage's understanding'.
Furthermore, one of Jiashan’s junior disciples had attended him for a long time. Ren sent him away to travel on pilgrimage and visit various Chan centers.
Later, hearing that Jiashan was gathering a great assembly and his reputation for the Way resounded far and wide, the disciple returned to pay his respects. He asked, "Does the Master have..."
"This is a most extraordinary matter. Why did you not tell so-and-so about it sooner? The mountain master said, "You were steaming rice while I was lighting the fire;
you were walking away while I was spreading out my bowl. What part of this constitutes a betrayal of you? From this, the junior monk attained awakening.
All these may be said to have, through mindfulness, been transformed into supreme awakening.

Ānanda, it is like those people of the world who gather their visual consciousness in the eyes; if they were suddenly to close them, the appearance of darkness would manifest before them, and the six sense organs would become dark and indistinct, with head and feet appearing as one.
If such a person were to run their hand over the exterior of their body, although they do not see it, [they still perceive] the head and feet.
First, to distinguish them: awareness and perception are identical. When conditioned by seeing, they arise from light; when darkness occurs, they constitute non-seeing.

If non-illumination were self-originated, then all appearances of darkness could never obscure it. Since the faculties and their objects have already been dissolved, how could the luminous awareness not achieve perfect wonder?
Tong said: "Previously it was shown that profound stillness and perfection do not follow the sense organs; now it is shown that profound stillness and perfection do not depend on external conditions.
That person with eyes closed, using their hand to trace another's body, is immediately able to distinguish their head from their feet.

This awareness in the dark is no different from seeing clearly in the light. If ordinary people can still make such distinctions without relying on the condition of light, how much more so [is this true for the enlightened mind]?"
How could the true awakening of the Sage depend upon conditions? Seeing depends on light; in darkness, it becomes non-seeing.

These are conventions following worldly truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). If the essence of awakened clarity were to become clear because of light and dark because of darkness, then consider now a person with eyes closed:
they would not perceive the features of their head and feet within the state of darkness without depending on the condition of light.
It is not a view of non-existence; it is a view in which clarity cannot manifest and darkness cannot obscure.

Not only is it beyond the constraints of the sense organs (*indriya*), but it is also beyond the obstructions of sensory objects (*viṣaya*). When the organs and objects have both dissolved, how could it be that the hand alone becomes the eye?
The eye may likewise become the ear. When a single organ returns to its source, all six organs become pure. How so?
If the clarity of awakening arises from the six sense faculties, its luminous principle does not transcend them; thus, it is not perfectly wondrous.

Only when it arises spontaneously without depending on the sense faculties or their objects is it the marvelous function of spiritual power, responding to stimuli without fixed direction—this is the mutual functioning of the six faculties, which serves as the foundation for Avalokiteśvara’s perfect penetration and his thirty-two manifestations.
Yunyan asked Wudao, "For what purpose does the Bodhisattva of Great Compassion employ so many hands and eyes?
Wudao replied, "It is like a person at midnight reaching back with their hand to feel for their pillow. Yunyan said, "I understand. Wudao asked, "How do you understand it?
Yunyan said, "My whole body is hands and eyes. Wudao said, "You have spoken quite well; however, you have only spoken..."
Bashou said, "What do you say, elder brother? I replied, "The whole body is hands and eyes. Tiantong’s verse says: A single aperture, void and penetrating;
On all eight sides, the lattice windows. Formless and impartial, spring enters the regulations; Neither lingering nor obstructing, the moon travels through space.
Pure and precious eyes, merit-filled arms— How can they compare to having them throughout the entire body? Manifested.
The hands and eyes of the former [master] reveal the total mechanism; in the deployment of great function, what need is there for hesitation or avoidance?

Xuedou’s verse says: "Everywhere it is; throughout the body it is. Even picking it up, it is still ten thousand miles away. With wings spread, the Peng bird soars through the clouds of the six realms;
Gathering the wind, it stirs and surges the waters of the four oceans. What speck of dust has suddenly arisen? Which hair’s breadth has not yet appeared?"
Stop! Do you not see that the net of pearls hangs down, its reflections layer upon layer? From where do the hand and eye at the tip of the staff arise?

*Duḥ!* Now, as for "pervading the body" and "penetrating the body," why go so far as to compare them to a distance of a hundred thousand li? To pervade the body is still not to have left behind the view of the body.
To pervade the entire body is to forget the body itself. This difference is as slight as a hair’s breadth; none but those with the true eye can discern it.
Xuedou forgets both hand and eye, while Tiantong does not hinder the functioning of his spiritual mechanism—thus it is the mystery within mysteries.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, as the Buddha has taught, if one wishes to seek the permanently abiding mind through the ground of practice, it must correspond with the designations of the fruit-stage. World-Honored One, within the fruit-stage there are these seven names:
Bodhi, Nirvāṇa, True Suchness (Tathatā), Buddha-nature, the Amala-vijñāna (here translated as ‘the stainless consciousness’), the empty Tathāgatagarbha, and the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom.”
That is to say, although they are distinct, they are pure and perfect; their essential nature is firm and solid, like a diamond king, eternally abiding and indestructible.

If this seeing and hearing were to exist apart from light and darkness, motion and stillness, penetration and obstruction, they would ultimately have no substance at all—just as the thinking mind has nothing whatsoever by nature when separated from its objects.
How can one take that which is ultimately subject to annihilation as the cause for cultivation? One who desires...

One attains the seven fruits of the Tathāgata’s eternal abiding. World-Honored One, if one is free from light and darkness and perceives ultimate emptiness, then, as there are no external objects before one, the nature of thought ceases.
Whether advancing or retreating in this cyclical investigation, one minutely seeks and finds that fundamentally there is neither the self-mind nor the mental factors associated with the self.

With what, then, could one establish a cause for seeking unsurpassed enlightenment? The Tathāgata previously spoke of the profound, quintessential, perfect, and eternal; [yet this current state] contradicts that truth.

[The interlocutor] said: "In the end, this becomes mere conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). How is it that the Tathāgata’s speech is true? Please, out of great compassion, dispel my ignorance and delusion.
[The Master] replied: "Ānanda, because the cause is the real cause and the fruit is the real fruit, [the cause] is devoid of substance once separated from its objects."
Being free from thought and without mind, one may suspect this to be annihilation. Yet you have not yet realized that the mind which confronts objects is fundamentally subject to arising and ceasing;

that which arises and ceases can indeed be severed. However, the mind that is detached from objects does not belong to the realm of arising and ceasing, and that which neither arises nor ceases is never severed.

When one reaches the state of profound clarity, essence, perfection, and constancy, there is ultimately nothing to be attained. Through subtle investigation, one finds that, fundamentally, there is no "self-mind. And...
This is what my mind intends. To establish the cause by means of this is called the "correct cause"; to realize the fruit by means of this is called the "true fruit.
It is profoundly pure, essential, perfect, and eternal; it has been thus from the very beginning. Why, then, do you further doubt that it could be violated?
This fundamental, singular, profound purity, perfection, and eternity has seven designations. The *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* states: "The empty Tathāgatagarbha is free from non-understanding."
Liberated from all afflictions through wisdom, it is the non-empty Tathāgatagarbha, endowed with inconceivable qualities of the liberative wisdom of Buddhas exceeding the sands of the Ganges;
as the empty-and-non-empty Tathāgatagarbha, it conforms to the emptiness of form, universally responding to all.
The empty Tathāgatagarbha is the eternally abiding fruit. The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom clearly perceives all things without discrimination;
the Amala-vijñāna discerns all things without defiled attachment. Because this clear and lucid spiritual cognition is present, it is called Buddha-nature.
This clear and lucid spiritual cognition is ultimate awakening; therefore, it is called Bodhi. Ultimate...
The essence of awakening is fundamentally quiescent and extinguished; therefore, it is called *nirvāṇa*. Being quiescent and extinguished, it cannot be touched by any deluded mind;

therefore, it is called *tathatā* (Suchness). These seven fruits are originally one and the same entity. The First Patriarch, Bodhidharma, used only eight characters to encompass them all without omission:
"Pure wisdom is wondrously perfect; its essence is inherently empty and quiescent. Here, "pure" refers to the *amala-vijñāna* (white-pure consciousness).
"Intelligence" (zhi) refers to the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*). "Emptiness" (kong) refers to the empty Tathāgata-garbha. "Quiescence" (ji) refers to *nirvāṇa*.
Furthermore, True Suchness (*tathatā*), Bodhi, and Buddha-nature are all not outside of the "wondrous perfection" (*miaoyuan*). As for these two characters, "wondrous perfection":
It is precisely discrimination; it is not discrimination. It is precisely arising and ceasing; it is not arising and ceasing. One feels even more that they are perfectly fused.
A monk asked Huangbo, "What is the Way? How does one practice? Huangbo said, "What thing is the Way? You wish to practice."
He asked, "Regarding the succession of the masters of various schools, how do they instruct those who study the Way through Zen?

Baizhang said, "Those are words for guiding those of dull faculties; they should not be relied upon as the ultimate truth. He asked, "Since these are words for guiding those of dull faculties, I wonder what Dharma is taught to those of superior faculties?
Baizhang said, "If one is of superior faculties, where would they go to seek it from another?"
When seeking others, even one's own self cannot be found; how much less could there be any other dharma to be grasped by the mind?
As it is said in the teachings: "What is the nature of dharmas? If this is so, then there is absolutely nothing to seek or find. Baizhang said:
"If it is thus, then one would save mental effort. Baizhang said, "If it were so, then everything would become utterly severed;
it cannot be that he does not exist. Huangbo asked, "Who taught him that he does not exist? Who is he? You intend to seek him out.
Huangbo said, "Since you are not permitted to seek him, why do you say again, 'Do not sever him'? Huangbo said, "If you do not seek him, then simply rest. Who [is there to sever]?"
[The Master] said, "I will teach you how to cut off this void before your eyes. How do you cut it off?
[Huangbo] asked, "Can this Dharma be attained such that it becomes identical to empty space? Huangbo said, "Empty space, I have never told you whether it is identical to or different from [anything].

I was merely speaking thus for a moment, yet you immediately gave rise to conceptual interpretations here. [Huangbo] said, "It should be that one does not give rise to conceptual interpretations for others."
Baizhang said, "I have never obstructed you; however, you must understand that this belongs to the realm of emotion (*qing*). When emotion arises, wisdom is blocked.
The monk asked, "In this state, is it not the case that emotion does not arise? Baizhang said, "If emotion did not arise, who would say 'it is'?"
Even after a thousand or ten thousand years, there may still be those who harbor doubts like Ānanda;
having obtained these few words from Huangbo, they shall once again be able to proclaim the profoundly deep purport.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "Though you have studied much and possess great learning, you have not yet exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*).
In your mind, you merely know the causes of inversion, but when true inversion actually manifests before you, you truly cannot recognize it.

Fearing that your sincere heart may still not be convinced and submissive, I shall now test you with matters of the mundane world to dispel your doubts. Thereupon, the Tathāgata commanded Rāhula to strike the bell once.
The Buddha asked Ānanda, "Do you hear it now? Ānanda and the great assembly both replied, "We hear it.
When the bell had ceased and there was no sound, the Buddha asked again, "Do you hear it now? Ānanda and the great assembly both replied, "We do not hear it.
Then Rāhula struck it once more, and the Buddha asked again, "Do you hear it now? Ānanda and the great assembly again replied, "We all hear it."
The Buddha asked Ānanda, "How do you hear? How do you not hear? Ānanda and the great assembly together replied to the Buddha, saying, "If the bell is struck, we hear it.
Once the striking has ceased and the sound has faded, when both the resonance and the echo have utterly vanished, that is called 'not hearing.'"
The Tathāgata further commanded Rāhula to strike the bell and asked Ānanda, "Do you hear the sound now? Ānanda and the great assembly both replied, "There is a sound.
After a short while, the sound faded away. The Buddha asked again, "Do you hear the sound now? Ānanda and the great assembly—
He replied, "There is no sound. After a short while, Rāhula came again and struck the bell. The Buddha asked once more, "Is there a sound now?
Ānanda and the great assembly both replied, "There is a sound. The Buddha asked Ānanda, "In what way is there a sound? In what way is there no sound?"
Ānanda and the great assembly together addressed the Buddha, saying: "When the bell is struck, it is called 'having sound.

When the striking has ceased and the sound has faded, such that both resonance and echo are cut off, it is called 'having no sound. The Buddha said to Ānanda and the great assembly: "How is it that you now speak with such self-contradictory confusion?
The great assembly and Ānanda simultaneously asked the Buddha: "In what way do we speak with self-contradictory confusion?"
The Buddha said: "I asked you about what was heard, and you said you heard it; I asked you about the sound, and you said it was a sound.
Since your answers regarding 'hearing' and 'sound' were not fixed, how can this not be called evasive? Ānanda, when the sound has ceased, there is no resonance."
"You say there is no hearing. If there truly were no hearing, the nature of hearing would have already ceased, becoming like a withered tree. When the bell is struck again, how could you know it?

Whether one knows 'there is' or 'there is not' is simply a matter of the sound-object being present or absent; how could that nature of hearing itself be subject to existence or non-existence for you?
If hearing were truly non-existent, who would know its absence? Therefore, Ānanda, regarding sound within the field of hearing—"

Birth and cessation belong to the sounds themselves; it is not that your hearing arises when sound arises or ceases when sound ceases, such that your faculty of hearing would thereby become existent or non-existent.
You are already inverted, mistaking sound for hearing; how much more so to be deluded by confusion, taking the permanent to be the intermittent?
One must never say that apart from all movement and stillness, or closure and opening, there is no nature of hearing. It is like a person in deep sleep, fast asleep upon their pillow and bedding.

While there were people in his household pounding silk and husking rice during his sleep, the man heard the sounds of pounding and husking in his dream and perceived them as something else—either the beating of drums or the striking of bells.
While in that dream, he wondered at the source of the bells himself.
It was the sound of wood, stone, and a pestle. At that moment, he suddenly woke up and immediately recognized the sound of the pestle.

He told his family members, "While I was dreaming, I was confused by this sound of pounding rice and took it to be the sound of drums. Ānanda, how could that person in his dream have recalled whether things were still or moving, open or closed, or whether sounds were penetrating or obstructed?
His body was merely asleep, yet the nature of his hearing was not clouded. Even if your physical form were to dissolve and the radiance of your life-force were to pass away, this nature—

How can this be extinguished for you? Because all sentient beings, from time immemorial, have followed after forms and sounds, flowing with the movement of thoughts, never awakening to the pure, wondrous, and eternal nature of their own essence.
Failing to follow that which is eternal, they pursue birth and death; thus, life after life, they wander through defilement.
If one abandons birth and death and maintains the true and eternal, the light of eternity will manifest before them, and the faculties and their objects—
The consciousness-mind will, at that moment, dissolve and fall away. Conceptual appearances are the dust; the conscious mind is the grime.
When you are free from both, your Dharma-eye will become clear and bright at that very moment. How could you then fail to achieve unsurpassed perfect enlightenment?
The Master said: "The Tathāgata has taught that 'liberation from attachment and inward stillness' is precisely the profound, pure, perfect, and eternal nature.

Ānanda doubted that the faculty of hearing could exist apart from its objects, fearing it might be subject to annihilation like them. Therefore, the Buddha used the sound of a bell to reveal the nature of hearing.

When the sound ceased and there was no resonance, this was merely the absence of sound, not the absence of hearing. Sound undergoes arising and ceasing; hearing does not arise or cease. If one were to say..."
Hearing arises because of sound; hearing ceases because of sound. When there is no hearing, who knows that it is absent?

Therefore, while that which is non-existent or existent may cease, the one who knows existence and knows non-existence never ceases. It is not only when awake that this knowledge does not cease in relation to objects;
even in dreams, when separated from objects, it does not cease. It is not only in dreams that the faculty remains...
When it ceases, its form dissolves and its faculties perish, yet it does not cease. This is roughly similar to the previous observation of the river’s sight;

however, while the purpose of the sight revealed previously was to demonstrate non-arising and non-ceasing, the purpose of the hearing revealed here is to demonstrate the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty.
To turn the hearing back to hear one's own nature is precisely to awaken to the purity of one's inherent nature.
Wondrous constancy. When the light of constancy manifests before one, it is the manifestation of quiescent extinction (*śānti*).
When the skin and flesh have all fallen away, there remains only the single reality. Only in this way can one be said to possess the clarity of the Dharma-eye and achieve unsurpassed enlightenment.
Master Wuzhu of Baotang Monastery was asked by Du Gong Hongjian: "I, your disciple, have heard Master Jin speak of 'no recollection' (*amṛta*)."
"Are the three phrases 'no-recollection,' 'no-thought,' and 'do not delude' a single teaching or three? The Master replied, 'Yes. The official asked, 'Are these three phrases one or three?
The Master said, 'No-recollection is called precept; no-thought is called concentration; do not delude is called wisdom.
When the one mind does not arise, it possesses precept, concentration, and wisdom; thus it is neither one nor three. The official asked again, 'Does the Master still employ these three phrases...'"

"Will you receive visitors? the Master replied, "For a beginner practitioner, one must first cause the thoughts to cease and settle the waves of consciousness. When the water is clear, the reflection appears; when one awakens to the essence of non-thought, quiescence manifests before one. Even 'non-thought' is not established. At that moment, a crow cawed in a tree by the courtyard. The official asked the Master, "Did you hear it? The Master said, "I heard it. After the crow had long since departed, the official asked again, "Master, did you hear it? The Master replied, "I heard it. The official said, "If you heard it, why do you say you heard it only after it was gone? The Master said, "When I heard it, I heard it; now that it is gone, it is gone. The official was greatly enlightened. He bowed and withdrew. Later, he composed a verse: "Before the sound arose, there was no hearing; After the sound ceased, there was no hearing. Now, hearing and sound are both forgotten; Only the true nature remains. He then sent a messenger to invite the Master to his residence. The Master went with him. Upon entering the gate, the official descended from his sedan chair and bowed. The Master raised his hand in greeting. The official said, "I have long been a man of the world, yet I have never encountered such a person as this. Huineng said, "I transmit mind by means of mind. The monk asked, "If it is mind that is transmitted, why do you say that mind also does not exist?
Baizhang replied, "Not grasping a single dharma is called 'transmitting the mind. If one realizes this mind, it is precisely no-mind and no-dharma.
The monk asked, "If there is neither mind nor dharma, how can it be called 'transmission'? Baizhang said, "When you heard the Way of transmitting the mind, you took it to mean—"
There is something to be attained. Thus the Patriarch said: "When one recognizes the mind-nature, it may be called inconceivable;

when it is thoroughly understood, there is nothing to be attained. When there is attainment, one does not speak of knowing. If this matter were taught through conventional instruction, how could it ever suffice?
Even the single word 'knowing' is already inadmissible; only then can it be called the Truth."
In the interim, there is no substantial nature. Therefore, as with the interlaced reeds, both bondage and liberation share the same cause;

for the sage and the ordinary person, there are not two paths. You should observe the nature within the interlacing: it is neither emptiness nor existence. When obscured by delusion, it is ignorance; when illuminated and clarified, it is liberation.

Tong said: "The 'intermediate' refers to that which sees and that which is seen; it is the intermediate state. Knowledge arises from the objects (*viṣaya*); this knowledge is consciousness (*vijñāna*) and belongs to the subject that sees.

Because of the sense organs (*indriya*), there are appearances (*nimitta*); these appearances are the objects and belong to that which is seen. Thus, there are these three: the object, the consciousness, and the organ."
They exist by depending upon one another; fundamentally, they have no real nature. They are like intertwined reeds: standing in mutual dependence, they originally lack self-nature.

If one examines the nature within the interweaving and considers it empty, then their mutual dependence appears to exist. If one considers it existent, then that which does not depend on anything is originally non-existent.
It is neither the nature of existence nor the nature of emptiness; this is called "naturelessness. That which is fundamentally natureless is the ultimate reality. Thus it is concluded.
These six sense faculties are not subject to diminution; these six sense faculties are not subject to augmentation.
Why is it that when one understands them they are called "sages," yet when one is bound by them they are called "ordinary people"? It is because they have not attained the principle of non-arising;
they are deluded in a single thought, with a perceiving subject within and an perceived object without, thereby being bound by the sense organs and their objects.
There is no portion of freedom. This obscurity and darkness is the very root of ignorance (*avidyā*); it is that from which all fetters arise.
If one truly perceives the wondrous naturelessness [of phenomena], then, detaching from sensory clinging and withdrawing inwardly, one awakens the radiance of the fundamental luminosity.

When this luminosity does not follow the sense organs and seeing does not rely on external conditions, the six faculties function interchangeably, transcending the mundane world. Thus, the awakening of this luminosity is the cause of liberation.
This explains the origin of its name. When bound, it is co-arising ignorance, the root of the fetters of birth and death; thus one is an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
Because of these six sense faculties—and no other entity—one is so designated. When liberated, one swiftly realizes peace and bliss, the wondrous permanence of quiescence.
Therefore, they are called "sages. These [realities] are based on these six sense faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*) and are not other things. Within these same six sense faculties, there is no second path.
Those who are bound by the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) take the interlaced reeds (*naḍakalāpikā*) as their nature of existence;
yet that nature is never actually existent. Those who are bound by the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) take the interlaced reeds as their nature of emptiness; yet that nature...
In reality, it has never been empty. Only when one realizes that there are no views of emptiness or existence, of ordinary or holy beings, and so forth, can one speak of true nature.

A monk asked Huangbo, "If the fundamental substance is already Buddha, how is it that there are further the four modes of birth and the six realms of existence, with their various and differing forms?
Huangbo replied, "The essence of all Buddhas is perfect and complete, with neither increase nor decrease; yet it flows into the six realms. Where it dwells...
In every place they are perfectly round; within the myriad species, each and every one is a Buddha. It is like a single mass of mercury:
when divided and scattered in various places, every grain is perfectly round; yet if not divided, it remains but a single block. This one is all.

All is one. The various forms and appearances are like houses; they are merely places where you take up or discard [a dwelling], such as leaving the house of an ass to enter the house of a human, or leaving a human body to reach a celestial body, and so on, up to the houses of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas.

It is only because of these acts of taking and discarding that distinctions arise. How could there be any distinction in the fundamental nature of the source? How profound these words are! Regarding this—
This elucidation can enable ordinary people of the mundane world to immediately ascend to the rank of the sages.

As for the sequence of the causes for untying the knots: once the six are untied, even the "one" vanishes. By selecting the most appropriate faculty for perfect penetration, one enters the stream and achieves true awakening.
Tong said: "To realize and manifest [the truth] is itself liberation; this is the Sudden Teaching. Why, then, is there a teaching regarding the sequence of untying the knots?
The Sudden does not discard the Gradual; it is for this reason that it is called the Perfectly Sudden Dharma-gate. This is so for those of great capacity and great vessels."
Upon a single awakening, one immediately reaches the stage of Buddhahood, requiring no further cultivation or realization. Next best is the selection of the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty:
by returning the single faculty to its source, all six faculties are liberated; first the six faculties are dissolved, and subsequently even that one is extinguished.
This is the sequence of Avalokiteśvara’s entry into the stream, the forgetting of objects, up to the manifestation of quiescence and the attainment of perfect enlightenment.
It is just like the Sudden Gate (Dunmen), where great and small awakenings occur beyond counting; how could there not be a sequence?
Formerly, when Chan Master Guankui Xian first visited Linji, Linji seized him and held him for a long time. Guankui said:
Linji said, "I will let you have one more meal. After Xixian took up residence there, he addressed the assembly, saying, "I see that Linji had no words;
even until now, I remain full and never hungry. Later, when he arrived at Mount Mo, he first made a vow to himself:
"If the place is worthy, I shall stay; otherwise, I shall overturn the meditation seat. Once he had entered the hall, Mount Mo heard of it.
When Xingxiu arrived, Master Shishuang instructed his attendant to ask him, "Have you come from traveling the mountains, or have you come for the sake of the Buddha-dharma?
Xingxiu replied, "I have come for the sake of the Buddha-dharma. Shishuang then ascended the seat. Xingxiu did not prostrate before him. Shishuang asked, "Where did you depart from today?"
Xixi said, "The road intersection. Moshan asked, "Why not cover it over? Xixi was speechless. Moshan spoke on his behalf, saying, "How could you have reached this point?
Only then did Xixi prostrate and rise to ask, "What is Moshan? Moshan replied, "It does not expose its crown. Xixi asked, "What is the master of Moshan?
Moshan replied, "He is neither male nor female, nor any such form. Xixi asked, "Why do you not transform?"
He departed. Mount [Moshan] said, "It is neither a god nor a ghost; what could it possibly transform? At this, Xixi submitted to his teaching.
He served as the head gardener for three years, finally receiving a blow from Linji only upon reaching this point. Later, he gave a turning word, saying: "I received one ladle at Linji's place;
I received one ladle at Moshan's place. He further said: "The ten directions..."
"There are no walls or enclosures; on all four sides there are no gates. It is starkly exposed, bare and open, with nothing to grasp.
Tiantong (Tian-tong) took up the case, saying: "When Guanying spoke in this manner, tell me, did he obtain it from Linji or from Moshan?
Although he may have shot two eagles with one arrow, he still sometimes kills by running and sometimes kills by sitting. For now—"
"How can one attain the state of being exactly right? Clenching and releasing both depend on me; picking up and casting away—who else could do it?
Only when one penetrates this completely does one begin to lose that 'one,' and only then can it be called true liberation."

The *ādānavijñāna* (appropriating consciousness) is a subtle consciousness; its habitual tendencies form a violent torrent. Fearing that one might confuse the real with the unreal, I have never openly expounded it. [The Master] said:
"The six sense organs are neither the cause of being ordinary nor the cause of being holy; that which presides over them is consciousness (*vijñāna*).

When the six consciousnesses have dissolved yet the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) still persists, this is the realm of the seventh consciousness. When the six are liberated and the one is extinguished, one returns to Suchness."
The "Ocean of the Ālayavijñāna" is the realm of the eighth consciousness. As Vasubandhu stated:

"Based upon the Tathāgatagarbha, there arises the mind of birth-and-death, which transforms and merges with that which is non-arising and non-ceasing; being neither identical nor different, it is called the Ālaya-vijñāna.

This consciousness is most subtle; it contains and stores seeds as habitual tendencies (vāsanā), such that its hidden store cannot be known, yet it accumulates the consciousnesses throughout successive lifetimes.
The waves form a violent torrent, and one knows not whence they arise; therefore, it is called "subtle.
Because it relies upon that which is neither arising nor ceasing, it is termed the "Tathāgatagarbha outside the entanglements," appearing as if it were truly real.

Because it relies upon the mind of arising and ceasing, it is termed the "Tathāgatagarbha within the entanglements," appearing as if it were not truly real. Yet, whether real or not real, it is always this very same thing.
Consciousness is difficult to discern. If one takes it to be real, there is the fear of mistaking a thief for one's own son;
if one takes it to be unreal, there is the fear of mistaking one's own son for a thief. This is why the World-Honored One did not speak of it lightly.
If one can transform the eighth consciousness into the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom, which is neither real nor unreal, only then can one speak of unsurpassed Bodhi and True Suchness (Tathatā).
This is the Buddha-nature. Later on, the school of Nature (Xingzong) became unclear, precisely because the school of Characteristics (Xiangzong) did not penetrate deeply enough;

they took the view of self within the seventh consciousness to be the Buddha-nature, and took the marks of arising and ceasing within each moment of the eighth consciousness to be True Suchness (Tathatā).

Therefore, it is called "blunt buddha-nature" and "uncouth true suchness. By fixating on the state of profound stillness and non-fluctuation as the ultimate, one knows that a portion of the [dualistic] self has not yet been extinguished.
A monk asked Changsha Chengyan: "The sixth, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses ultimately have no substance.
How can the eighth consciousness be said to be transformed into the Great Perfect Mirror?"
