The Master Zhi Sha showed the verse, saying: "Seven births depend on one cessation; one cessation sustains seven births.
When one cessation ceases, they all cease; the six and the seventh never again migrate. From this perspective, it is not merely that the six are liberated and the one perishes;
there is even what is called the liberation of the seven and the perishing of the one. How subtle, how subtle!

The self-mind grasps the self-mind; that which is not illusion becomes illusory phenomena. If one does not grasp, there is nothing that is not illusion. Since even non-illusion does not arise, how can illusory phenomena be established?

Tong said: "The true nature is empty of conditioned phenomena because they arise through conditions and are thus like illusions. Since the true nature is fundamentally empty, how could illusions arise from it?
It is simply because the eighth consciousness internally takes True Suchness as its object and externally gives rise to conditioned phenomena; therefore, they are like illusions."
The *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* states: "The ālayavijñāna is extremely subtle; all its seeds are like a violent torrent.
I do not reveal it to the foolish and the ignorant, fearing that they would conceptually grasp it as a self. This is the mind itself grasping the mind itself."
It is precisely through one's own discrimination that one clings to it as a self. First, by clinging to it as a self, illusory phenomena arise within what is not illusory;
from this, stillness (*zhan*) is divided, and from this, bondage begins. This is why these six faculties pursue sensory objects and revolve in saṃsāra.
If one does not cling to it as a self, then even the non-illusory does not exist—how could the illusory be established? Stillness enters and merges with stillness, becoming one.
The source is non-dual; this is why the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) are pure, yet both are simultaneously extinguished.

The six faculties belong to the illusory, while the one belongs to the non-illusory. When both the one and the six are extinguished, it is said: "If even the non-illusory does not arise, how can illusory phenomena be established?
This transformation of consciousness into wisdom (*vijñāna-parāvṛtti-jñāna*) occurs precisely in the interval between grasping and non-grasping. As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "Discrimination..."
This is consciousness (*vijñāna*). Non-discrimination is wisdom (*jñāna*). Arising and ceasing is consciousness; non-arising and non-ceasing is wisdom.

That which is simply without discrimination is the true nature of non-arising and non-ceasing; therefore, one is not covered by the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*). A monk asked Huangbo:
Regarding Mañjuśrī holding a sword before Gautama: how is this?

Huangbo said, "Five hundred bodhisattvas attained the knowledge of past lives and saw the karmic obstacles of their previous existences. These five hundred are precisely your own five aggregates (skandhas).
Because they saw these obstacles from past lives, they sought the Buddha, the bodhisattvas, and nirvana; therefore, Mañjuśrī brought forth wisdom and understanding."
"Sword. "Because it harms this mind that perceives the Buddha, I say you have harmed it well. The monk asked, "What is this sword?
Baizhang said, "The mind of understanding is the sword. The monk said, "If the mind of understanding is the sword, then it cuts off this mind that perceives the Buddha."

"If it is simply the mind that perceives [existence] which must be severed, how can it be eliminated? Baizhang said, "Use your own non-discriminating wisdom (*avikalpa-jñāna*) to sever this mind of discriminative perception.

The monk asked, "If one is acting with the perception of existence and the desire to seek Buddhahood, and uses the sword of non-discriminating wisdom to sever it, what then becomes of the sword of wisdom itself? Baizhang said, "As for non-discriminating wisdom..."
Harm arises from both the view of existence and the view of non-existence; even non-discriminative wisdom cannot be apprehended.
The Master Seng said, "One cannot use wisdom to further sever wisdom, nor can one use a sword to further sever a sword. Huangbo said, "The sword harms itself;

as sword meets sword, they harm one another, and thus even the sword cannot be apprehended. Wisdom harms itself; as wisdom meets wisdom, they harm one another, and thus even wisdom cannot be apprehended."
It may be so. That both mother and child perish together is likewise.
These subtle discourses not only do not permit the head to emerge from the place of grasping, but even at the place where there is no grasping, there is no trace. It is most subtle indeed.
One must penetrate this thoroughly before one can speak of transforming the eighth consciousness into the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom.
This is called the Wondrous Lotus, the Jewel-Awakening of the Vajra King, the Illusion-like Samādhi, by which one transcends the stage of No-More-Learning in the snap of a finger.
This is the incomparable Dharma (Abhidharma), through which one swiftly realizes quiescent permanence—the single path to Nirvāṇa for the Bhagavans of the ten directions.
The Master said: "At first, Ānanda claimed that from the beginningless past, he had been born and perished together with all forms of ignorance, and was unable to subdue the Mātaṅga woman.

He therefore earnestly entreated the Tathāgatas of the ten directions for the primary expedient means of the wondrous śamatha, samādhi, and dhyāna through which one attains Bodhi. Now, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, with one voice..."
It is the same sound. If you wish to recognize the co-nascent ignorance that causes you to revolve in birth and death as the root of bondage, it is none other than your six faculties;

there is no other thing. Furthermore, if you wish to know the unsurpassed Bodhi that enables you to swiftly realize peaceful liberation—quiescent, pure, wondrous, and eternal—it is likewise your six faculties and nothing else. It is just as with the ice mentioned before.
The analogy of water: when water freezes, it becomes ice; how could any other substance be allowed to intervene and become ice? When ice melts, it becomes water;

how could any other substance be allowed to intervene and become water? "The six [senses] act as intermediaries for thieves, robbing one of the family treasure"—this refers to the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*).
"When the six are liberated, the one perishes, and one swiftly ascends to perfect enlightenment"—this also refers to the six sense organs. This is the delusion.
It is precisely the real; it is precisely the real and the delusory. There exists a wondrous awakening within this interval. The single word "wondrous" is difficult to describe in words.
It must involve the transformation of consciousness into wisdom, [realizing] the wondrous clarity of intrinsic awareness and the luminous wondrousness of original awareness.
Only when one possesses the corresponding capacity can one speak of unsurpassed bodhi.
It is like a lotus flower that emerges from the mud yet remains unstained; this is true of ordinary lotuses as well.
However, the udumbara flower is unlike anything in the mundane world—it is the so-called auspicious and wondrous lotus. This alone elucidates the supreme path for entering [enlightenment].
The Buddha’s knowledge and vision are fully adequate to correspond to this. The "Vajra King Jewel-Awakening" refers to the initial stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*) within the Vajra-mind.
Because the Vajra can destroy all things, each of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) is called the "Vajra-mind," as it likewise destroys and extinguishes the preceding stages;
this is what is known as the "sword of wisdom. Once this awakening manifests, not only [does it eliminate] that which has no beginning...
Ignorance is suddenly extinguished; this is the vision of the Buddha and the vision of the Bodhisattva, yet there is no place from which they emerge. Samādhi is right reception (*samyaksamāpatti*).
That it is said to be "like an illusion" means that the actions of an illusory person are fundamentally based on non-action; it is quiescence that is luminous.
It is illumination that is itself stillness; with emotions forgotten and interpretations severed, it is inconceivable.
This is what is called the Vajra Samādhi of hearing and cultivating through illusory-like listening. This wondrous śamatha, samādhi, and dhyāna depend solely upon a single awakening;
once awakened, one immediately reaches the stage of Buddhahood. Therefore, in the mere twinkling of an eye, one transcends the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) of the two vehicles.
Even those beyond training (aśaikṣa) still fall short of ultimate merit; they still cling to the view of non-existence.

When this true nature manifests, one is free from both existence and non-existence, entering directly and transcending all at once without relying on gradual stages of cultivation; this is the Sudden Gate.

It is like a prince in the womb whose nobility already surpasses the ministers, or a kalaviṅka chick whose cry exceeds that of all other birds; how could this be compared to ordinary meditative concentration and contemplation?
How could one possibly fathom its practice? Therefore it is said: "This peerless Dharma is that by which one swiftly realizes quiescent permanence.
The Bhagavat possesses six meanings: sovereignty, brilliance, majesty, renown, auspiciousness, and nobility;
because he has perfected all virtues, his name is not translated. A monk asked Qianfeng: "The ten directions..."
"Bhagavān, regarding the single path to the gate of Nirvāṇa, I do not know where the beginning of that path lies.
Yunfeng drew a line with his staff and said, "It is right here. The monk then requested further instruction from Yunmen.
Yunmen picked up his fan and said, "The fan leaps up to the Thirty-three Heavens, striking the nostrils of Śakra. A carp from the Eastern Sea strikes—"
A single blow—rain pouring down like an overturned basin. Do you understand? Do you understand? Huanglong Nan said:
"Qianfeng’s one-time pointing of the way was a concession to beginners; Yunmen then brought forth its transformations, so that later generations would not grow weary.
Zhuan’an’s verse says: "Qianfeng need not point it out; Yunmen should cease his collection of old bones. Naturally, the carp of the Eastern Sea..."
"The fish struck the nostrils of Śakra. The Celestial Child’s verse says: "Once it has entered the hand, one uses a dead horse to treat the illness;
with the *reviving-soul incense*, one seeks to raise you from peril. Only when a full-body sweat is forced out in a single day does one finally believe that our house spares no eyebrows.
What kind of matter is this? How could it be explained through intellectual understanding to enable others to enter? It must be realized by oneself.
Only through complete and thorough awakening can one grasp its subtle mystery.

Thereupon, Ānanda and the great assembly, having heard the unsurpassed compassionate instruction of the Buddha-Tathāgata—composed of *geya* (here translated as "repeated verses") and *gāthā* (here translated as "recited verses"), interwoven with such brilliance and purity, so wondrous, refined, and lucid—their minds and eyes were opened and enlightened; they marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.

Ānanda joined his palms, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said to him: “I have now heard from the Buddha these words of the Dharma—unrestricted, great compassion, pure by nature, wondrously eternal, and true.
Yet my mind has not yet fully grasped the sequence for loosening the knots so that the six may be resolved and the one vanish. I pray only that you will bestow upon me your great compassion.”
Again, out of compassion for this assembly and for those of the future, he bestowed the sound of the Dharma to wash away their deep-seated defilements.

Thereupon, the Tathāgata, upon the lion throne, adjusted his *nirvāṇasaṃghāṭī* (herein called the inner robe), gathered his *saṃghāṭī* (herein called the great robe), and took hold of a seven-jeweled desk.
He extended his hand toward the table and took the flowered silk scarf offered by the deva Kāpala (which in this context refers to the Yāma Heaven).
In front of the great assembly, he tied it into a single knot and asked Ānanda, "What is this called? Ānanda and the entire assembly replied together to the Buddha, "This is called a knot.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata folded and stacked the flowered silk scarf and tied another knot, asking Ānanda once more.
"Difficult. "What is this called? Ānanda and the great assembly again addressed the Buddha, saying: "This is also called a 'knot.
In this manner, by successively folding and overlapping the flowered handkerchief, six knots were formed in total.
As each knot was completed, [the Buddha] took the knot formed in his hand and held it up, asking Ānanda: 'What is this called? Ānanda and the great assembly likewise responded in succession."
The Buddha said, "This is called a knot. The Buddha told Ānanda, "When I first tied the cloth, you called it a knot.
This folded flower-cloth was originally a single strip; as for the second and third folds, why do you and the others again call them knots?
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, this precious folded flower-cloth was woven into a handkerchief; although it was originally a single entity, according to my contemplation—"
When the Tathāgata ties it once, it receives the name of "one knot. If one were to tie it a hundred times, it would ultimately be called "a hundred knots.
How much more so with this cloth, which has only six knots; it will never reach seven, nor will it remain at five. Why, then, O Tathāgata, do you allow that there is only the first [knot]?
"The second and third [knots] are not called 'bonds. The Buddha told Ānanda: 'Regarding this precious flowered cloth, you know that this cloth originally consists of only a single strand.
When I tied six knots, there were six named bonds. You should examine this carefully: the substance of the cloth is the same.'"
"Because the knots formed are distinct. What do you think? The first knot tied is called the first. In this way, up until the sixth knot is formed.
Now, I wish to take the name of the sixth knot and establish it as the first. Would that be so? "No, World-Honored One."

"As long as these six knots remain, this sixth name can never become the first. Even if I were to exhaust my eloquence throughout successive lifetimes, how could I cause these six knots to change their names?
The Buddha said, "It is so. The six knots are distinct. If one traces them back to their original cause,"

If one attempts to create [different items] from a single piece of cloth, they will become entangled and disorderly, and in the end, nothing will be accomplished. Your six sense organs are exactly like this:
within that which is ultimately identical, you seek that which is ultimately different. The Buddha told Ānanda: "If you truly find these six knots unsatisfactory,"
"You wish for the six to become one; how, then, can this be achieved? Ānanda replied, "If these knots remain, disputes will arise:

within them, one will naturally think, 'This knot is not that,' or 'That knot is not this. If the Tathāgata were to untie them all today, and the knots did not arise again, then there would be neither 'this' nor 'that';
they would no longer even be called 'one,' so how could the six be established? The Buddha said, "When the six are untied, the one is realized."
It is likewise with that which has perished. Because your mind-nature has been deranged since beginningless time, false cognition arises;

as this delusion does not cease, the wearying faculty of sight gives rise to dust. It is like having blurred vision: from the clear and brilliant essence, there arise without cause all the mountains, rivers, and great earth of the world, as well as birth-and-death and nirvana—all of which are but the flowers of a deranged and wearying inversion.
Xiang said in reply: "It was previously explained in detail that the single, pure luminosity is divided into the six harmonious combinations.

Why, then, is this analogy presented again? Previously, it was shown that the six sense organs were triggered by the attachment of the turbidities—such as light and dark, motion and stillness—to the profound clarity."

From the external toward the internal. Therefore, by simply not following after characteristics such as movement and stillness, or light and darkness, one detaches from sensory "glue" and turns inward to rest;

the fundamental radiance of clarity is then manifested, whereby the six sense-faculties immediately attain mutual function. This is the reversal of the flow to restore the single unity; thus, one restrains the external.
Now, because the mind-nature is deranged and the wearying faculty of sight gives rise to dust, the process proceeds from the internal toward the external. Thus, if the knots of the faculties...
Eliminate them; as the characteristics of dust naturally cease, one first attains the emptiness of persons, and eventually attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

This is the dissolution of the fettered mind, whereby its interior is harmonized. Within this profound, brilliant, and pure clarity, there is no cause for the arising of confusion; delusion regarding the fundamental source is itself without cause.
"Establishing objects through the causal consciousnesses: this is the false manifestation of cognition and vision; it is the very cause from which the knots arise.
By turning back that profound stillness to reverse its false arising and ceasing, once arising and ceasing have been extinguished, quiescent extinction manifests before one.

This is the meaning of the knots being untied: at that time, the six functions do not operate—listening does not go beyond sound, and seeing does not transcend form. These knots are not those other [senses]."
Bondage is not this [true nature], like the fatigue of the eyes which causes distinct floating flowers to appear.

When one is released from it, once the six [senses] have dissolved, that "one" [remaining essence] also perishes. Since even "one" has no name, how could there be "six"? It is like clear, bright eyes which originally have no floating flowers;
therefore, the name "bondage" refers to birth and death, yet it never actually diminishes [the essence]. The name "release" refers to Nirvana, yet it... [does not increase it].
This is merely an augmentation. It is like wild flowers: arising and ceasing without cause, what increase or decrease could they possibly bring to the great void?
Thus, one knows that birth and death are but inversions; once these six are understood, they are liberated. One knows that *nirvāṇa* is but a flower in the sky;

once this one is realized as vanished, it perishes. When the flow is reversed and the One is perfected, even that "One" has not yet vanished. Only when that One itself vanishes is the binding mind finally liberated.
A monk asked Chan Master Fengxue Zhao, "One is six, and six is one. When both 'one' and 'six' have vanished, what then?
Fengxue said, "A single arrow shoots two vultures. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of this? Fengxue said, "The body perishes and the tracks vanish.
Furthermore, when the scholar Zhang Zhuo first met Shishuang, Shishuang asked, "What is your name? Zhuo replied, "My surname is Zhang and my given name is..."
Zhuo said, "If even 'cleverness' cannot be found when sought, from where does 'clumsiness' come? Under these words, Zhuo attained awakening and presented this verse:
"Radiant and silent illumination pervades the sands of the Ganges; Ordinary beings and sages, all sentient creatures, share one family.
When a single thought does not arise, the entire body is revealed; As soon as the six sense-faculties move, they are shrouded by clouds. To sever deluded thoughts is to increase them once more."

To be ill is so; to incline toward True Suchness is likewise erroneous. Flowing in accordance with worldly conditions without obstruction, one regards nirvana and birth-and-death as equal to flowers in the sky.
If one is skillful, one deeply attains the principle of "the six dissolving and the one vanishing"—how could this be achieved through gradual stages?
Ānanda said, “This knot is identical to a binding; how can it be untied?
The Tathāgata took the knotted cloth with his hand and pulled its left side askew, then asked Ānanda, “Is it untied like this? “No, World-Honored One.
He then turned the cloth over and pulled its right side askew, asking Ānanda again, “Is it untied like this? “No, World-Honored One. The Buddha told Ānanda, “I...”
Now, pull with both hands from the left and right; yet you cannot untie it. By what skillful means can you untie it so that it is released?
Ānanda said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, one should untie it at the very center of the knot, and then it will immediately fall apart. The Buddha told Ānanda, "So it is, so it is.
If you wish to remove a knot, you must do so at the center of the knot."
Yong said: "The old explanation of 'pulling from the left or the right' is a metaphor for relying on the two extremes of emptiness and existence;

such methods cannot untie the knot. One must rely on perfect contemplation (*yuan guan*): if one does not give rise to discrimination regarding the faculties and does not give rise to grasping or attachment regarding objects, then the knot will be untied.

Now, to wait for contemplation before the knot is untied is still like pulling from the left or the right. What does this have to do with the mind that forms the knot? It is no better than [the former method]."
The speech of the patch-robed monks (nanseng) is even more subtle and profound. Shousheng said, "Before the fifteenth day of the month, use the hook;
after the fifteenth day of the month, use the awl. A monk then asked, "What about when it is exactly the fifteenth day? Shousheng replied, "The clay ox tramples the moon in the clear pool.
Tiantong commented, "Shousheng was a master who could employ both ends; he directly forgot all effort. Who is this?"
"To realize the essence" means to let go. "To interchange host and guest" means to hold fast. "To leave no trace"—is there anyone who can realize this?
A jade maiden at night casts her shuttle, weaving brocade in the western house. Furthermore, Yunmen addressed the assembly, saying:
"If you do not speak before the fifteenth day, then after the fifteenth day, bring me a single phrase. [Tianyi] himself said, "Every day is a good day.
Tiandong [Yuanwu] commented, "For those whose birth year is the Tiger, it is their own destiny;
for those whose birth year is the Monkey, it is a clash. Shimen Cong said, "Before the fifteenth day, all Buddhas are born; after the fifteenth day, all..."
Before the fifteenth day of the month following the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, all Buddhas are born; you must not leave my presence.
If you leave my presence, I shall hook you with my hook. After the fifteenth day, all Buddhas enter parinirvāṇa;
you must not remain in my presence. If you remain here, I shall pierce you with my awl. Now tell me: what is it exactly on the tenth day?
On the fifth day, using a hook is precisely it; using a chisel is precisely it. Thus, there is a verse that says:
"Precisely on the fifteenth day, the hook and the chisel cease at once. If you further intend to ask 'How?', turn your head—the sun has already risen.
Yunmen, however, was not like this: "Before the fifteenth day, the Buddhas were never born; after the fifteenth day, the Buddhas..."
It has never been extinguished. Before the fifteenth day, if you leave me here, I will not use my hook to catch you;
feel free to carry your staff slung across your shoulder and tie your straw sandals tight.
After the fifteenth day, if you stay here with me, I will not use my awl to prick you; feel free to break your staff and go high.
He hung up his alms-bag and said, "Tell me, on this very fifteenth day, what should be done?
Regarding the period before and after the fifteenth, the hook and the awl are used in vain. This morning, on the fifteenth day itself, it is precisely the time to employ the hook and the awl.
But how is one to use them? When you encounter a dead snake on the road, do not strike it down; carry it home in a bottomless basket. If, at this point—
With these numbers, you will attain the definitive point; the knots of the mind will be suddenly and completely released at once.
Ānanda, I say that the Buddha-dharma arises from causes and conditions; it does not grasp the coarse characteristics of worldly conjunctions.

When the Tathāgata elucidates mundane and supramundane dharmas, he knows their fundamental cause and how they emerge according to their respective conditions. This is so even up to the sands of the Ganges.

Even a single drop of rain outside the boundaries of the world, he knows its number; the various things appearing before him—pines straight and thorns crooked, cranes white and crows black—he fully understands their fundamental causes.
Tong said: "The Buddha knows that both mundane and supramundane phenomena arise from the mind. Following defiled conditions, they emerge as the nine realms;
following pure conditions, they emerge as the Buddha-realm. This principle of cause and condition is still understandable. But as for the raindrops falling like the sands of the Ganges—"
Furthermore, regarding the various phenomena that appear before one, by what cause and by what condition does one know their fundamental origins?

The Buddha possesses two kinds of wisdom: ultimate wisdom (*paramārtha-jñāna*) and provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*). Ultimate wisdom darkly accords with principle, while provisional wisdom clearly discerns phenomena. Therefore, that which knows the fundamental origins of these various phenomena is entirely the discernment of provisional wisdom.
The Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is perfect, complete, and all-pervasive; there is not a single thing that can exist outside of this Dharma-body.
"What is external to the body—how could the Tathāgata not know it? Dongshan Chong ascended the hall and said: "If you ask this mountain monk what he should say, [I would say]:
'The past is the present; the present is the past. Therefore, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: 'Pines are straight and thorns are crooked;
cranes are white and crows are black. Do you understand this? Nevertheless, even so, it is not necessarily the pine."
The pine is always straight; the thorn is always curved. The crane is white; the crow is black. Dongshan said:
"Here too there are curved pines, there are straight thorns, there are black cranes, and there are white crows."
I have stood for a long time; take care. Now tell me: did Dongshan revolve the *Śūraṃgama Sūtra*, or was it the *Śūraṃgama Sūtra* that revolved him?
Ultimately, how do you understand this statement?
Therefore, Ānanda, according to your own mind, choose among the six sense-faculties. If the knots of the faculties are untied, the appearances of sensory objects will naturally cease.
When all delusions have been extinguished, what need is there for that which is not real? Ānanda, I now ask you:

regarding this *karpāsa* cloth, when the six knots appear before you, could they be untied simultaneously so that they are all removed at once? "No, World-Honored One. These knots were originally tied in succession;
today they must be untied in succession. Although the six knots share the same substance, the knots themselves do not arise at the same time."
At the time of untying the knots, how are they removed simultaneously? The Buddha said: "The liberation of the six sense faculties is likewise so.

When this faculty is first liberated, one first attains the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). When the nature of emptiness is perfectly luminous, it constitutes the liberation from phenomena (*dharma-vimokṣa*). Once liberated from phenomena, both [person and phenomenon] are empty and do not arise;
this is called a Bodhisattva attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) from within samādhi."
Tong said: "Once a single faculty returns to its source, all six faculties achieve liberation. To explain this in detail through analogy:
when deluded, the six faculties are bound together as one; when awakened, the six faculties function interchangeably. What sequential order could there be?

It is merely that delusion accumulates through delusion, proceeding from the subtle to the coarse, while awakening enters through awakening, proceeding from the coarse to the subtle; thus there is no lack of gradual progression. This does not mean—"
When one strand is pulled out, the remaining five are pulled out in succession. The Buddha’s words are perfectly integrated and fundamentally free from dogmatic attachment.
For example, the first is called a "knot," yet the location of that knot is essentially the same as the second and third; it cannot be called a "knot" again.
How could there be such a thing as binding what is already bound? Therefore, the binding is itself one.
Since the binding is one, the first is the sixth, and the sixth is the first; these are merely different names for the same thing, and there is nothing inherently improper in this.
However, in the birth of a person, from conception in the womb until the formation of the physical body, the six sense organs do not arise simultaneously; they have their own sequence.
Once the eighteen realms are established, some of these faculties are fully functional while others are not. Therefore, one should follow that which is fully functional.
To realize the Way in a single day leaves one with a surplus; to cultivate the Way for a hundred kalpas is still insufficient.

Thus, the relationship between a day and a kalpa differs by a factor of ten million. Because the six sense faculties possess varying degrees of sharpness and dullness, there are those whose faculties are easily uprooted and those whose are not.
Confucius attained the stage of "ear-harmony" at sixty—this was the transformation of his faculty of hearing—and at seventy, he followed [his heart's desires].
"The mind desires, yet it does not overstep the square" (*ju*). This refers to the transformation of the faculty of thought (*manas-indriya*). There is a sequence to this:

these knots were not accumulated in a single day, nor can they be removed in an instant. From first attaining the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) up to attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), one enters the stream and loses the objects of perception;
this is the sequence. Thus, "returning the hearing" (*fanwen*) is implicitly established as the perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*).
First, it depends on Ānanda himself to choose. The emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) is the breaking of the provisional name of the five aggregates;

this is the severing of the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). The emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) is the breaking of the substantial reality of the five aggregates; this is the severing of the delusions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*).

Furthermore, the breaking of even the pure phenomenon of *nirvāṇa* is the eternal severing of fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*). When both are empty and non-arising, this is the emptiness of equality (*samatā-śūnyatā*).

When that which is empty has been exhausted, that which empties also ceases. When both object and wisdom are simultaneously dissolved, and both subject and object are equally stilled, this is the wondrous, profound, and all-encompassing Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
Hence it is said: "One attains the patience of non-arising. A monk asked Baizhang, "What is the essential teaching for the sudden enlightenment of the Mahāyāna?
Baizhang replied, "You must first bring all conditions to rest and cease from all affairs."
Do not recall or mentally engage with any phenomena whatsoever—whether wholesome or unwholesome, mundane or supramundane.
Relinquish body and mind, allowing them to be at ease. Let the mind be like wood or stone, devoid of discrimination; let the mind have no movement.
If the mind-ground is empty, the sun of wisdom manifests of its own accord, like the sun rising when the clouds part.
Simply cease all攀缘 (pán yuán—clinging to objects), greed, anger, craving, and grasping; let the defilements of both impurity and purity be exhausted.

Then, one remains unmoved by the five desires and the eight winds, is not bound by seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing, and is not deluded by various sensory objects. Thus, one naturally becomes fully endowed with wondrous spiritual powers.
This is the liberated person. Facing all objects, the mind is neither pure nor disturbed; it is neither gathered nor dispersed.
Penetrating through all sounds and forms without obstruction, such a one is called a "person of the Way.
Neither employing good, evil, right, nor wrong, and neither clinging to nor abandoning any phenomena, such a one is called a "person of the Mahāyāna. Not...
When one is bound by all that is good or evil, empty or existent, defiled or pure, conditioned or unconditioned, and by worldly merit and wisdom—

this is called the "wisdom of a Buddha. When one is no longer bound by likes or dislikes, beauty or ugliness, what is rational or irrational, and when all attachments to knowledge and views have been exhausted,
such that one is free and sovereign in every situation, this is called a "Bodhisattva who has first resolved to attain enlightenment."
Thus, he immediately ascended to the stage of Buddhahood. Indeed, whatever Baizhang spoke from his lips was in silent accord with the essential purport of the sutras;
were he not a person of great liberation, he could not have uttered such words of liberation.
Ānanda and the great assembly, having received the Buddha’s instruction, attained perfect clarity through wisdom and were freed from all doubt.
At once, they joined their palms, prostrated at his feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "Today our bodies and minds are radiant and clear; we have swiftly attained unimpeded understanding.
Although we have realized the meaning of the 'one' and the 'six' being non-existent, we have not yet reached the fundamental root of perfect penetration. World-Honored One," [they said].
We have drifted and wandered, orphaned and exposed for accumulated kalpas. With what heart or what concern could we have anticipated becoming fellow members of the Buddha’s celestial kin?

We are like infants who have lost their mother’s milk, suddenly encountering a compassionate mother. If, through this fortunate encounter, the Way is realized, then the secret words we receive will be identical to our original awakening.

"Then there would be no difference between this and not having heard it at all. I pray only that you will bestow great compassion and grant me the secret adornment, so as to fulfill the Tathāgata’s final instruction.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, withdrawing into a state of profound stillness, hoping for the Buddha’s silent transmission.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed all the great Bodhisattvas and the great Arhats whose outflows were exhausted within the assembly, saying:
"You Bodhisattvas and Arhats, having been born into my Dharma and attained the state of no-more-learning, I now question you."
Regarding the initial Dharma-mind that awakens to the eighteen *dhātus*: who attains perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa*), and by what skillful means does one enter *samādhi*? He replied:
"To reveal the perfect penetration of wisdom-awakening is to first dissolve the six [consciousnesses] so that the one [mind] perishes;

this continues until one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Because the six are dissolved, the body attains non-obstruction; because the one perishes, the mind attains non-obstruction. Although...
Although they have not yet reached the state of the six sense organs being purified, once the one is uprooted, the six dissolve; once the six dissolve, the one perishes.

Thus, they are already luminously free from delusion. Yet, they simply do not know where the fundamental root of perfect penetration lies, which organ is the most perfectly penetrating, through which organ one should enter to immediately realize perfect penetration, or by following the organ of perfect penetration to realize the fruit of perfect penetration. This depends upon...
Ānanda attained the Way because of this; it was the final instruction bestowed by the Tathāgata.
Therefore, I pray that the World-Honored One will not withhold its profound and majestic essence, but grant it through secret transmission.
As for the perfect faculties, it has already been shown that the Tathāgatas of the ten directions all practiced within each of the eighteen realms and attained the fullness of unsurpassed Bodhi.
"Ti. Within this interval, there is likewise no superiority or inferiority. Now I further announce to the Bodhisattvas, Arhats, and others:
regarding the initial arousal of the mind and the realization of the eighteen realms, who has attained perfect penetration? By what skillful means did they enter samādhi?

While it may still be possible to compare and evaluate their perfected faculties, as for the skillful means by which they awakened and entered [enlightenment], these vary according to each individual."

To know for oneself and realize for oneself—how could this be reached through verbal expression? That which is beyond the reach of verbal expression can it be transmitted through silent communion (*mingshou*)?
Based on Ānanda’s request, he hoped that the Buddha would grant him this silent transmission, not through words spoken, but through what is not spoken;
not through hearing heard, but through what is not heard. Not through words spoken—this is called the secret word (*miyan*). Not through hearing heard—this is...

This refers to the original awakening; thus, one attains the Buddha’s secret words, which are identical to my own original awakening. Although it may seem as though there is hearing, it is the same as not hearing at all.
To hear without hearing—this is called true hearing. For this reason, I withdrew and concealed the secret mechanism, hoping that others might attain it.
Had the Buddha been able to transmit it and Ānanda been able to receive it, it would not have been a secret; it would not have been esoteric.
To take this as proof of *yuan-tong* (perfect penetration) would mean it is not true *yuan-tong*. Awakening comes through one's own awakening; how could it be something that others can bestow?
Chan Master Jizhi of Panshan ascended the hall and said: "The path that leads upward is not transmitted by the thousand sages.
Students exhaust their bodies, like a monkey grasping at reflections. If a reflection could be grasped, then the secret seal could be bestowed. The Regional Commander of Jingnan...
He sent Cheng Rui to enter Yunju Monastery to provide offerings. Cheng asked, "The World-Honored One had secret words; how is it that Kāśyapa did not conceal them?
Cheng Ying summoned the Minister (Cheng Rui), who responded with an assent. Cheng Ying said, "Do you understand? Cheng Rui said, "I do not understand.
Cheng Ying said, "If you do not understand, the World-Honored One had secret words. If you do understand, Kāśyapa did not conceal them. Therefore...
"To understand this matter, it cannot be achieved except through one's own thorough awakening.
Then the five bhikṣus, including Kauṇḍinya—who had previously managed the fire implements—rose from their seats, prostrated themselves at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
In the Deer Park and at the Cock Garden, I beheld the Tathāgata’s initial attainment of the Way.

Through the Buddha’s voice, I realized and clarified the Four Noble Truths. When the Buddha asked the bhikṣus, "Who first declared their understanding? the Tathāgata certified me with the name Ajñāta.
(Chih-yen translates this as "Understanding") My subtle voice is secret and perfect. Regarding sounds, I have attained Arhatship.
When the Buddha asked about the most direct path to penetration, according to my realization, sound is the supreme means.
Tong said: "Kauṇḍinya first attained the name 'understanding' upon realizing the two terms 'adventitious dust. Now, through the Buddha’s voice, he has realized and clarified the Four Noble Truths.
When the Buddha first turned the Wheel of Dharma of the Four Noble Truths at the Deer Park, there were three turnings:

first, the turning that reveals the characteristics; second, the turning that exhorts practice; and third, the turning that constitutes realization. As for 'revealing the characteristics,' it means showing their specific marks, stating: 'This is suffering.'"
"This is the origin of suffering; this is its cessation; this is the path leading to the cessation of suffering. To "exhort to practice" means to urge them to cultivate it, namely:
"Suffering should be known," up to "the path should be known. To "bear witness" means to cite one's own realization as proof for others, namely:
"Suffering has been known by me; there is nothing further to be known," up to "the path has been cultivated by me; there is nothing further to be cultivated. This is clear awakening.

Regarding the Four Noble Truths, they merely understand that all phenomena are subject to arising and ceasing; in this regard, there is no difference between them and those who speak of adventitious defilements (*āgantuka*).

It is by means of this [understanding] that one attains Arhatship. How could it be said that while sounds are all subject to arising and ceasing, I am not of the same category as those subject to arising and ceasing?
Or that while sounds are all adventitious defilements, I am not of the same category as those adventitious defilements? Yet, it is said that the wondrous sound is subtle and perfect; its perfection—
The wondrous lies in sound itself. How could it be that sound is subject to arising and ceasing while that which is not subject to arising and ceasing is not?
How could it be that sound is adventitious dust while that which is not adventitious dust is not? This realization is known only by Kauṇḍinya himself;
it cannot be spoken of to others, and for this reason it is called "esoteric. Since his realization was found within sound, [it is thus].
He took sound as his means of attaining perfect penetration. Chan Master Xián of Xiāngyán was of keen intelligence while at Bǎizhàng;
however, he could not attain realization through Zen practice. After Bǎizhàng passed away, he went to study under Wúshān.
Wúshān asked him, "I have heard that when you were with your late teacher at Bǎizhàng, you would answer ten for one question and a hundred for ten. This is your cleverness."
Those with sharp faculties and keen understanding recognize that the root of birth and death lies in conceptualization and perception. Try to utter a single word before your parents were even born;
when suddenly questioned thus, you will find yourself utterly bewildered. Returning to your quarters, take up the texts you have studied during your ordinary days.
From beginning to end, he sought a single phrase with which to respond, yet in the end he could not find one.

He then sighed to himself, saying, "A painted cake cannot satisfy hunger. He repeatedly requested that Guishan explain it to him, but Guishan said, "If I were to explain it to you, you would later curse me away.
What I say belongs to me; it ultimately has nothing to do with you. Xian then took [the matter]...
He burned all the texts he had previously studied and said, "In this life, I shall not study the Buddha-dharma.
I will instead become a simple monk who provides gruel and rice, so as to spare my mind from its labors. Weeping, he took leave of Master Muzhou and traveled directly to Nanyang.
There, seeing the traces left by National Teacher Huizhong, he settled down to stay. One day, while clearing away grass and trees, he happened to throw aside some tiles and rubble.
When he struck the bamboo and it made a sound, he suddenly attained enlightenment. He immediately returned to bathe, prostrated from afar toward Mount Miu, and praised him, saying:
"The Master’s great compassion exceeds that of my own parents. Had you explained this to me at that time, how could there have been the events of today?
He then composed a verse: "One strike causes all knowledge to be forgotten; No further cultivation is required. A movement of the countenance reveals the ancient [truth]."
The Path does not fall into the trap of silence; it leaves no trace anywhere. Its majestic demeanor lies beyond sound and form.
Those who have attained the Way in all quarters all say this is the highest level of capacity. When Guishan heard of this, he said to Yangshan, "This boy has penetrated through."
Yang said, "This was composed through the workings of the mind, intellect, and consciousness. Wait until I have personally examined it myself.
Later, Yang saw Xian and said, "The Master praised you, his disciple, for having realized the Great Matter. Try to explain it to me."
Xian recited the previous verse and said, "This was accomplished through the retention of past habituation. If there were true awakening, it would be expressed differently.
Xian then composed another verse, saying: "Last year’s poverty was not yet poverty; this year’s poverty is the true poverty.
Last year’s poverty left no ground even for a monk’s staff; this year’s poverty has not even a staff. Yangshan said, "The Tathāgata..."
"You may understand Chan, but you have not even dreamed of the Patriarchal Chan. Xiangyan further offered this verse: "I have a single device;
with a blink of an eye, I look at him. If he still does not understand, I shall call for another novice. Yang then reported this to Guishan, saying:
Furthermore, it is a joy that Master Xián’s disciple has realized the Zen of the Patriarchs.
Xuánjué said, "Tell me, are the Buddha-dharma Zen and the Patriarchal Zen distinct or not? Chángqìng Líng said, "I settle them both at once.
Also, regarding the monk who requested instruction on the story of Zhaozhou’s "cypress tree," Master Shěng of Yèxiàn said, "I do not refuse to explain it to you."
"Do you still believe me? The monk said, "Since you, Master, have spoken with such gravity, how could I dare not believe?
Xing said, "Do you hear the sound of raindrops falling on the eaves? At that, the monk was suddenly enlightened; unconsciously, he let out a cry of "Ya! Xing asked, "What principle have you seen?
The monk immediately responded with a verse: "The raindrops at the edge of the eaves are clear and distinct; they strike—"
He shattered heaven and earth; in that very moment, his mind was stilled. His realization was identical to that of this monk, who also took sound as supreme.
Upāniṣad then rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said to the Buddha: "I, too, have observed..."
When the Buddha first attained the Way, he contemplated the signs of impurity and gave rise to great revulsion. He realized the nature of all forms (*rūpa*), seeing that they proceed from impurity;
that white bones dissolve into subtle dust, which returns to empty space. When both emptiness and form are non-dual, one achieves the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).

The Tathāgata bestowed upon me the name Niṣadha (which means "the nature of dust is empty"). Once the color of dust has been exhausted, the wondrous color becomes subtle and perfect. I [have realized this] through the marks of form.
He attained Arhatship. When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration, he said, "As I have realized it, the sense-object of form (*rūpa*) is the foremost.
He continued: "Upānisaṭha was greedily attached to the dust of form; therefore, the Buddha taught him the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) to serve as an antidote.
Although form may appear beautiful, because it originates from impurity, it is utterly loathsome. How much more so is the corpse after death!"
The various impure signs of skeletal dust are as follows: first, bloated; second, festering; third, bloody; fourth, livid;
fifth, being devoured; sixth, scattered; seventh, skeletal remains; eighth, cremated; ninth, the unreliability of all worlds. These are called the nine perceptions.
When these nine perceptions are perfected, the nature of form ultimately returns to emptiness, and emptiness has no location.
Emptiness. This constitutes the non-duality of form and emptiness; one attains liberation through wisdom and achieves the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
Once the defiled forms have been exhausted, the wondrous form is subtle and perfect. How could there be some so-called "wondrous form" that exists apart from defiled form?

How could it be that by emptying the characteristics of form, that which is capable of being emptied is itself the wondrous form? Is it not the case that while the characteristics of form undergo arising and ceasing...
If the nature of form is without arising or ceasing, is that itself the wondrous form? Or rather, is it because the mind is free from attachment that all forms are wondrous forms?
This point of realization by Niṣadha is difficult to express through the medium of speech;
one can only call it "wondrous," "mysterious," and "perfect. Long ago, when the Seven Virtuous Women were wandering in the Śītavana cemetery, one—
The woman pointed to the corpse and said, "The corpse is here; where has the person gone? Another woman asked, "How? How?
The sisters observed closely and each attained realization. Moved by this, Śakra devānām indra scattered flowers and said, "I pray only that you, O divine sister, may let me know what you require;
I shall provide for you for the rest of my life. The woman replied, "My household possesses the four requisites and the seven treasures."
"All these are fully provided; I require only three things: first, a single trunkless tree;
second, a patch of ground where neither sun nor shade falls; third, a mountain valley where a cry goes unanswered.
Śakra said, "I possess everything you require; as for these three things, I truly have none to give. The woman said, "If you..."
"It is not so. How could one possibly explain and save others? Śakra was at a loss; he then went together with him to inform the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "Kauśika, even my great Arhats do not understand this meaning; only the great Bodhisattvas understand it.
This, too, is one who has attained realization by contemplating the sign of impurity. Furthermore, regarding Lingyun:
Upon seeing peach blossoms, he attained enlightenment. He spoke a verse: "For thirty years I have sought the swordsman; Time and again the leaves fell and branches sprouted anew.
Since the moment I first beheld the peach blossoms, To this very day, I have had no further doubt.
He presented this to Guishan, who said, "Those who enter through conditions shall never again fall back or lose [their realization]. You must protect and maintain it well. Xuansha then said:
"Truly correct, most truly correct! I dare say you, elder brother, have not yet reached the ultimate. [The Master] continued, "Has your elder brother reached it yet?
Juefan’s verse says: "Once Lingyun saw it, he did not see it again; On every branch, red and white, no flowers cling.
How vexing is that guest on the fishing boat, Who comes back to the level ground to scoop for fish and shrimp! Touzi’s verse says: "Before the mountain..."
The peach blossoms bloom with spring in the old garden; as the flowers open upon the red branches, I reflect upon this body. At the moment of realization, I thank you for exerting effort beside me;

though the smile spreads, the mind gives rise to resentment. Smoke locks the green willows as the oriole’s song lingers slow; rain invades the stone pillars as they lean against their neighbors in the void.
The golden crow is released, yet there is no news; the wooden horse’s neighing passes beyond Han and Qin. Relying on Lingyun—
Regarding the locus of views, it likewise takes form as its primary cause.
At that time, the youth Gandhahastin rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I have heard the Tathāgata instruct me to carefully contemplate the characteristics of all conditioned phenomena. I then took my leave of the Buddha and retired to a quiet, secluded retreat for purification. There, I beheld the bhikṣus..."
I burned aloeswood incense. Its fragrance was serene as it entered my nostrils. I observed this scent: it was neither wood nor empty space, neither smoke nor fire;
departing, it had no place of attachment; arriving, it had no point of origin. Through this, my conceptual mind dissolved, and I gave rise to the realization of the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*).
The Tathāgata bestowed upon me the seal of the name "Ultrasonic Fragrance" (Gandharva). In an instant, the dust-like vapors were extinguished, and wondrous fragrance became subtle and pervasive.
Through this Ultrasonic Fragrance, I attained Arhatship. When the Buddha asked about the most perfect penetration, according to what I have realized, Ultrasonic Fragrance is supreme.
Tong said: "All that has marks is entirely illusory. To see all marks as non-marks is to see the Tathāgata. 'Tathāgata' means the suchness of all dharmas.
He comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; therefore, he is called the Tathāgata. This is the essential purport of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
Having heard this teaching, Xiangyan constantly contemplated it with earnest attention. One day, by chance—"
Upon touching the fragrance, an illumination was suddenly revealed to me. This fragrance is tranquil; it enters my nostrils, yet it is neither smoke nor fire, neither wood nor space.
It possesses no self-characteristic, no other-characteristic, no common characteristic, and no characteristic of being causeless.

In departing, it leaves no attachment; in coming, it has no point of origin. It is fundamentally unborn from the beginning. To see that all these characteristics are not characteristics is to see the Tathāgata.
This is the meaning of "coming. Thus, one attains the untainted (*anāsrava*). That ordinary beings cannot attain the untainted is because the faculty of mind (*manas-indriya*) has not yet dissolved.
Because the faculty of mind has not dissolved, they cling to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). To cling even once to the conditioned is to fall into arising and ceasing (*utpāda-vyaya*).

When the mind dissolves, one realizes the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); the unconditioned is precisely the absence of arising and ceasing. Therefore, while the vapors of sensory objects arise and cease in an instant, the wondrous fragrance—
"Neither arising nor ceasing"—this is the point of awakening for Xiangyan, which cannot be fully explained by any conceptual analysis.
To call it "mysterious" or "perfect" is merely to describe what he himself has realized.

Formerly, the Grand Historian Huang Shan-gu, having been inspired by Yuan-tong Xi, went to rely on Hei-tang and requested him to point out a direct and swift path. Hei-tang said: "Just as when Confucius spoke of the disciples..."
"Am I being secretive? I am not secretive toward you. How could Grand Historian Jichang have provided such a theoretical explanation?

When the Master (Dongshan) was about to offer a response, the Hall Master said, "Not so, not so. The Master remained in a state of confusion and distress. One day, while attending the Hall Master on a mountain walk, the Master asked:
At that time, the rock-peonies were in full bloom. The Hall Master asked, "Do you smell the fragrance of the *muguihua* (wood-lily)?
The official replied, "I do. The Hall Master said, "I have hidden nothing from you. The official was suddenly relieved and prostrated himself, saying, "Master, why such a grandmotherly urgency?
The Hall Master laughed and said, "I simply wish for you to reach home. Furthermore, there was a nun who attained enlightenment, whose verse began: "In the end..."
Day after day seeking spring, yet not seeing it; my straw sandals have trodden through the clouds atop the ridges. Returning home, I laugh as I pick up a plum blossom and smell it;
the spring is already fully present upon the branches. This nun and Huang Gong (Shan谷) attained realization in this very way, taking Xiangyan’s verse as supreme.

The two Dharma-Prince sons of the Buddha, Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata, together with five hundred Brahmā gods present in the assembly, immediately rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Since beginningless kalpas, we have served as skilled physicians for the world.
We have tasted every herb, wood, metal, and stone within this Sahā world; there are some eighteen thousand such names and species, all of which we know thoroughly.”
Whether tastes be bitter, sour, salty, bland, sweet, or pungent; whether they arise from combinations or through transformation; whether they are cold or hot;
whether they are poisonous or non-poisonous—he is able to know them all completely. Serving the Tathāgata, he thoroughly understands that the nature of taste is neither empty nor existent.
They are neither identical to body and mind, nor are they separate from body and mind. By discerning the cause of their flavor, they attained awakening.
The Buddha-Tathāgata bestowed upon us brothers, the two bodhisattvas Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata, the seal of his approval; we are now Dharma princes within this assembly.

"By means of the clarity of gustatory sensation, I ascended to the stage of a Bodhisattva. When the Buddha asked about the most perfect penetration, I replied that, according to what I have realized, the cause of taste is supreme.
I said: 'Since beginningless kalpas, I have been a skilled physician in the world; I could merely cure diseases by knowing whether a taste was cold or hot.

However, upon serving the Tathāgata, I first came to know that the nature of taste is empty, that it is neither existent nor non-existent, and that it is neither identical with nor different from [the sense organ or the object].'"
Separation. Now, both emptiness and existence are neither identical nor separate. Within the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrously luminous and perfect mind, its essence is fundamentally thus.
Because he attained awakening through the flavor [of the teaching], he realized the self-nature of enlightened clarity; thus, he ascended to the rank of a Bodhisattva.
That which is called "awakening" therein is the nature-flavor of true emptiness within the Tathāgatagarbha, and the true flavor of the nature-emptiness—pure and inherently so, all-pervading.
Pervading the entire Dharma-realm, it is flavor itself and awakening itself; it is awakening itself and flavor itself. This is that realization which is difficult to explain to others.
Dayu (Da-yu) took his leave to return to the Patriarch (Linji). The Patriarch asked, "Where are you going? He replied, "I am going to the various regions to study the 'five flavors' of Chan.
The Patriarch said, "The various regions have five flavors of Chan, but here I have only one flavor. [Dayu] asked, "What is it like?"
"This is the 'one-flavor' Chan," said Mazu, and he struck him. Yuyue said, "I understand! I understand! Mazu said, "Speak, speak!
As Yuyue was about to open his mouth, Mazu struck him again. Later, a monk went to Huangbo and recounted this previous conversation.
Huangbo ascended the hall and said, "Master Mazu produced eighty-four *kalyāṇamitras* (spiritual friends). When questioned, every one of them was dripping wet. There was only..."
Guizong was slightly superior; only Huangbo deeply understood the single flavor of Chan.
Thus, when he met Guizong, he later used this very device to receive Linji. When Linji did not attain realization, Huangbo directed him to go to Dayu.
Upon seeing Dayu, Linji recounted the circumstances of his three times being beaten by Huangbo. Dayu said, "Huangbo has thoroughly exhausted you for my sake; yet you have come here."

He asked whether there was fault or no fault. Linji said, "Underneath my words, you have attained great enlightenment. Linji said, "It turns out that Huangbo’s Buddha-dharma consists of nothing more than this.
Yunju grabbed him and said, "Speak quickly! Speak quickly! Linji struck him three times under the ribs.
Yunju let go and said, "Your teacher is Huangbo; it has nothing to do with me. Just as Yunju was about to display the ancestral style of his own house, he was already... [interrupted].
Linji snatched it away; thus we know that Linji’s realization was already one step ahead. Chan Master Faju of Longxing saw Huanglong late in his life and received his deep seal of approval.
In a formal address, he said: "This matter is like a physician diagnosing an illness.
When poison is already filling the belly, it is not easy to treat; it requires a medicine that causes dizziness and nausea before it can be cured. Regarding this:

To force them to comply with your wishes by casting them into this situation would only serve to nourish their madness and delusion, and increase the depth of their chronic ailment. To seek to cure a disease that has not yet arisen—is this not a misguided approach?
The weeds before the Dharma Hall grow deep; yet you feel no shame in your heart. It is precisely through these few principles that one attains integration.
"Not only do they know the flavor, but they can also heal others.

Then Bhadrapāla (translated here as Xiànhù, "Worthy Protector"), together with his sixteen companions, Bodhisattvas, rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In the past, we heard the Dharma under the Buddha Vīkṣaṇarāja and left the household life. At the time of our bathing..."
At that time, as the monks followed the custom of entering the chamber, he suddenly awakened to the cause of water: it neither washes away dust nor washes the body;
in the midst of this, there is tranquility, and one attains the state of non-possession. His former habitual tendencies were not forgotten, and they continue until the present day.

Having left the home-life under the Buddha, he attained the stage of No-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). That Buddha named me Bhadrapāla. Through the manifestation of wondrous touch, I became established as a son of the Buddha. Thus the Buddha questioned him.
Yuantong said, "As I have realized it, the sense-base of touch is supreme.
Tong said, "Xuedou cites the sixteen *āryapudgalas* who, during the time of the monks' bathing ceremony, entered the room according to custom."

Suddenly he realized the cause of the water. How do you all, venerable practitioners of dhyāna, understand this? He said, "The wondrous touch proclaims clarity; one becomes a son of the Buddha and dwells therein.
You must also penetrate it through and through before you can attain it. The verse says: "One who understands affairs accommodates the monks and consumes one."
Lying with legs extended upon a long couch, he spoke of realizing perfect penetration within a dream.
Washing with fragrant water, one spits directly in the face—this is a case already established. Later, various elder masters further elucidated it layer upon layer.
When National Teacher Shao first visited Longya, he asked: "Heaven does not cover it; earth does not support it. What is the principle of this? Longya said:
"The Way is thus. The Daoist asked this seventeen times, and Ya replied in this same manner each time.
When the Daoist requested instruction once more, Ya said, "Daoist, you shall understand it for yourself in the future. Later, while bathing at Tongxuan Peak, [the Daoist attained realization].

Suddenly, he realized the meaning of their previous conversation. He then prepared his formal robes and, gazing toward Longya from afar, prostrated himself and said, "If you had told me this back then, I certainly would have cursed you!
Later, he went to attend upon Fayan. A monk asked Fayan, "What is a single drop of water from Caoxi?
Fayan replied, "It is a single drop of water from Caoxi. The monk withdrew, feeling bewildered.
The Master attained sudden enlightenment by the side of his seat; the doubts and obstructions of his life were dissolved like ice melting away.
Only upon reaching this point did he gain complete mastery. He once had a verse that said: "At the summit of Tongxuan Peak, it is not of this world;
outside the mind there is no dharma, only green mountains filling the eye. Fayan heard of this and said, "By this single verse alone, you can revive our school. Furthermore—
Master Shiti was once asked by his attendant to take a bath. Shiti said, "Since you do not wash away dust, nor do you wash the body, how will you do it?
The attendant replied, "Venerable Sir, please go ahead first; I will bring the soap.
Shiti laughed heartily, nearly causing the attendant to spit right in his face. A monk asked Chan Master Tiangai You: "There is one..."
The name of the monastery was Wugou Jingguang Chan Monastery (Stainless Pure Light Chan Monastery). [The Master] constructed a bathhouse.
Someone asked, "Since it is already 'Stainless Pure Light,' why have you built a bathhouse? The monk was speechless. Tiangai spoke on his behalf, saying:
"On a bright moonlit night in the third month of autumn, one does not merely display its full orb. Danxia further provided a verse for him, saying: "Although he has answered exhaustively..."
Profound is the underlying meaning; alas, how can one avoid failing to encounter the pivotal phrase?

If you wish to realize that which is fundamentally stainless, you must further enter the water to see the tall man. The practitioner of the Empty Chamber, Zhitong, was the daughter of Fan Xun of the Longtu Pavilion.
She once visited Sishi for formal certification and resided in Jinling. She established a bathhouse and posted a notice at its door that read: "There is not a single thing."
What is there to wash? If even a speck of dust exists, from where does it arise? Speak a single phrase of the profound mystery, and only then may we all enter the bath together.
Guling merely knew how to rub backs; when did this Bodhisattva ever clarify his mind?

When one wishes to realize the Stage of Freedom from Defilement, one must have filth flow out from one’s entire body. Everyone says that water can wash away grime, but who knows that water [itself]...
This too is a dust. Even if the water-sediment is suddenly removed, one must still wash it away upon reaching this point. Later, she became a nun named Weijiu.
The various venerable elders spoke of dreams within dreams, repeatedly pointing out that wondrous touch proclaims clarity;
she may thus be considered a fellow student of the sixteen bodhisattvas.
Mahākāśyapa, the Bhikṣuṇī Jālinīprabhā, and the others immediately rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In a past kalpa, within this world-system, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Candrasūryapradīpa."

I have been able to draw near to you, hear the Dharma, and practice its study. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, I have made offerings to his relics, lit lamps to maintain the light, and applied purple-gold luster to the Buddha’s images.
From that time until now, in birth after birth and life after life, my body has always been perfectly formed.
"O Assembly of Purple-Gold Light! These bhikṣuṇīs of the Purple-Gold Light and others were my kinsmen; they resolved their minds for enlightenment at the same time as I.
I observed that the six sense-objects in this world are subject to decay and transformation, and thus I cultivated the extinction of all things through emptiness and stillness.

Only then could my body and mind pass through hundreds of thousands of kalpas as easily as a finger-snap. By means of the dharma of emptiness, I attained arhatship. Thus did the World-Honored One speak of me.
Practicing *dhūta* (here translated as "shaking off") is supreme. It illuminates the wondrous Dharma and extinguishes all outflows (*āsrava*).
When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, according to what I have realized, the causal factor of the Dharma is the foremost.

Tong said: "As for what was mentioned previously regarding those who attain the state of tranquility through the various meditative absorptions of cessation—the Śrāvakas, with the sole exception of Mahākāśyapa, whose mental faculty has long since ceased, yet who possess a perfect and clear understanding that does not depend on mental ideation—they have merely awakened to the emptiness and stillness of dharmas and attained the stage of Arhat."

The arising of the six sense objects occurs in dependence upon emptiness; the cessation of the six sense objects returns to emptiness. While the sense objects have arising and ceasing, the nature of emptiness is indestructible.
To shake off the dust of phenomena is itself the dharma of emptiness. When the mind does not take phenomena as its object, one attains the state beyond arising and ceasing;
thus, one can pass through hundreds of thousands of kalpas as swiftly as a finger-snap. To this day, he maintains the Buddha’s golden brocade *kāṣāya*.
Śāriputra entered meditative absorption on Mount Kukkuṭapāda to await Maitreya’s descent and the transmission [of the Dharma]; this too is a testament to that.
The Bhikṣuṇī Jinguang was formerly a poor woman, and Kāśyapa was a smith; the woman offered him a small amount of gold.
Entrusting the casting of this Buddha’s face, I vow that in birth after birth I shall become a devoted husband and wife;

may we be moved by this merit to be reborn in the heavens for ninety-one kalpas, our bodies always perfect and radiant with a mass of purple-gold light. Now, having encountered the Buddha and left the household life, the fruit of my past vows has been fulfilled.
Chan Master Xuangjue of Yongjia had extensively investigated the Tripitaka and mastered the profound and wondrous Dharma-gate of Tiantai *śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
Throughout the four modes of deportment, he constantly remained in silent meditative contemplation. Later, inspired by Chan Master Lang of Zuoxi, he traveled with Chan Master Ce of Dongyang to Caoxi.
Upon his initial arrival, he shook his mendicant’s staff, circumambulated the Patriarch three times, and stood firm and resolute.
As he stood there, the Patriarch said, "A śramaṇa is one who possesses the three thousand modes of dignified conduct and eighty thousand subtle practices.
From where have you, Great Virtue, come, that you give rise to such great arrogance? Huìjué replied, "The matter of birth and death is great; impermanence is swift."
The Patriarch said, "Why do you not realize non-arising? Is there anything more swift than realization? Huairang said, "Realization itself is non-arising;
fundamentally, there is nothing swift. The Patriarch said, "So it is. At that time, the entire assembly was not without astonishment.

Huairang then assumed his full ceremonial demeanor to pay his respects, and after a short while, he announced his departure. The Patriarch said, "Your return is very swift! Huairang said, "Fundamentally, there has been no movement from the start."
"Is there any swiftness? The Patriarch said, "Who knows that it is not movement? Huizhao said, "The benevolent one merely gives rise to conceptual discrimination.
The Patriarch said, "You have thoroughly grasped the meaning of non-arising. Huizhao said, "If there is non-arising, how can there be 'meaning'?

The Patriarch said, "If there is no meaning, who would engage in discrimination? Huizhao said, "Discrimination itself is not the meaning. The Patriarch sighed in praise, saying, "Excellent! Excellent!"

He stayed for one night; thus he was called "One-Night Awakened" (Ekāṃśa-buddha). This was not merely the temporary cessation of the mental faculty (manas), but the attainment of the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
How could it be otherwise that his responses were as swift as echoes? From Kauṇḍinya to this sixth sage, [the sequence of realization was thus established].
They are called wondrous sound, wondrous form, wondrous fragrance, and wondrous touch; all are termed "wondrous" because they are not bound by sensory objects.
These are the means by which one realizes perfect penetration through the six sense objects.
Aniruddha immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "When I first left the household life, I was constantly fond of sleep.
The Tathāgata rebuked me, saying I was of the same class as beasts. Upon hearing the Buddha’s rebuke, I wept and reproached myself."
I did not sleep for seven days and consequently lost both my eyes. The World-Honored One showed me the *Vairocanābhisaṃbodhi-vajrasamādhi*.
Without relying on my eyes, I perceived the ten directions; their essential reality was transparently clear, as if I were looking at fruit in the palm of my hand.

The Tathāgata certified me as an Arhat. When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration, according to what I have realized: by turning back the seeing and returning to the source, this is the foremost method.
The messenger replied: "Aniruddha was the son of King Śuklodana and the Buddha's cousin.
In a past life, he offered a single meal to a pratyekabuddha and, as a result, experienced bliss at will for ninety-one kalpas.
The Buddha once rebuked him, saying: 'Alas! Alas! Why do you sleep? You are like a snail, a clam, or an oyster; you may sleep for a thousand years and yet never hear the Buddha.'"
Because of this [name], his eyes were lost, yet he attained the "half-head" divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"The divine eye of Aniruddha is composed of the four great elements and derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), and is pure over half the head. The Buddha’s divine eye is composed of the four great elements and derived matter, and is pure throughout the entire head.
The "Samādhi of the Vajra that Illuminates Joyful Vision" is precisely the Dharma-gate of "revolving vision to follow the source. This clarity belongs to...
The object belongs to that which is illuminated; where clarity resides, it is the capacity to illuminate. Where illumination resides, it is the capacity to see.
From what does illumination arise? From what does seeing come? Ultimately, there is nothing seen in seeing, and nothing illuminated in illumination.
One immediately attains the Vajra Samādhi and perceives the source directly. Because the Vajra is capable of crushing and destroying, both seeing and illumination vanish together.
Samādhi is right concentration; it is the essential body of quiescent illumination. To delight in this contemplative illumination is to turn back the faculty of sight and follow the source.
Upon attaining the divine eye, one reaches a state beyond the reach of thought or deliberation. When Deshan first arrived at Long...
Dongshan arrived at the Dharma Hall and said, "I have long heard of Dragon Pond; yet now that I have come, the pond is not to be seen and the dragon does not appear.
Dragon Pond straightened his body and said, "You have truly arrived at Dragon Pond. Based on this initial karmic encounter, Dongshan was destined to receive the robe and bowl of Dragon Pond.
One night, while standing in attendance, Dragon Pond said, "It is deep in the night; why do you not go out? Dongshan replied, "The mountain delicacies..."
Dongshan went out again, then returned and said, "It is dark outside. Guishan lit a paper candle and passed it to him.
As Dongshan was about to take it, Guishan blew it out. At this, Dongshan attained great enlightenment and prostrated himself. Guishan asked, "What have you seen?"
Mount Shishuang said, "From this day forward, you shall no longer doubt the tongues of the old monks throughout the world.
The next day, Dayuan Tan ascended the seat and addressed the assembly, saying, "Among you there is a man whose teeth are like a forest of sword-trees and whose mouth is like a blood-basin."
"A single blow of the staff does not turn one back. "In the future, atop a solitary peak, you shall establish my Way.
He then piled his commentaries and sub-commentaries before the Dharma Hall, raised a torch, and said: "To exhaust all profound dialectics is like placing a single hair in the vast void;
to exhaust all worldly mechanisms is like casting a single drop into a great abyss. Having said this, he burned them all. Then, having paid his respects and taken his leave, he departed.
And he departed. As for the Dharma-eye attained by Deshan, how does it compare in measure to that of Aniruddha?
When Linji was about to pass away, he spoke this verse: "Following the current without ceasing—ask how it is? True illumination is boundless—explain it to him as such.
Free from characteristics and free from name, no one receives it; Having used the 'blow-off-the-head' blade, one must quickly polish it. He further said to the assembly:
"After my extinction, you must not extinguish my Treasury of the True Dharma Eye. San-sheng came forward and said, "How would we dare extinguish the Master’s Treasury of the True Dharma Eye?
Linji said, "In the future, if someone asks you, what will you say to them?
San-sheng then gave a shout. Linji said, "Who would have known that my Treasury of the True Dharma Eye would be extinguished by this blind donkey?"
[He] set it aside. Tiantong’s verse says: "The robe of faith was bestowed upon Lu Neng at midnight; The seven hundred monks of Huangmei were thrown into turmoil.

Linji’s single branch of the True Dharma Eye— The blind donkey extinguished it, earning him the people's loathing. Mind-to-mind, the seals are impressed; from patriarch to patriarch, the lamp is transmitted.
Mountains and rivers are leveled; the Kun and Peng birds are transformed. This very name and phrase is difficult to compare with; great!"
When all means of liberation have been overturned and one reaches this state, even the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye must be extinguished, let alone the divine eye.
Cūḍapanthaka (translated as "Snake-Slave") then rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "I..."
I lacked the practice of recitation and retention, and possessed no nature of great learning. Having first encountered a Buddha, I heard the Dharma and left the household life.
I memorized a single verse (*gāthā*) of the Tathāgata; for one hundred days, however, I was able to grasp the preceding line but forgot the following, or grasp the following but forgot the preceding.

The Buddha, pitying my folly, instructed me to dwell in retreat (*anagārika*) and regulate my inhalation and exhalation. At that time, I contemplated the breath with subtle precision, exhausting its arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing. All...
As I practiced this moment-to-moment mindfulness, my mind suddenly opened wide and I attained great non-obstruction.

Eventually, with the exhaustion of outflows, I became an Arhat, sat beneath the Buddha’s seat, and was certified as one beyond training. When the Buddha asked about the most perfect penetration, according to what I have realized, it is the reversal of the breath to follow emptiness;
this is the foremost.
