The Master said: "This is none other than the Bhikṣu Sūcī. In a past life, he was a Dharma teacher who was stingy with the Dharma;

consequently, he received the retribution of being dull-witted. Although he lacked extensive learning, he was ultimately free from distraction; thus, he was able to enter the practice of regulating the breath.

The coarseness or subtlety of the breath arises from the arising and ceasing of the mind. As the mind gradually subsides, the breath becomes increasingly subtle. Mind and breath depend upon one another until they reach their ultimate limit."
Exhausting the extremely subtle characteristics of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*)—birth, abiding, change, and cessation—at every moment, there is no cessation, and the mind is no-mind.
In a single kṣaṇa, one penetrates into the stage of adamantine dry wisdom (*vajropama-śuṣka-prajñā-bhūmi*), thereby attaining a state of sudden, unimpeded clarity.

This is the realm of awakening; it is beyond the reach of words and thought. Formerly, when Minister Mo Jiang was serving in Western Shu, he visited Chan Master Nantang Jing to inquire about the essentials for resolving his mind.
The Master instructed him to maintain mindfulness toward the "good place.

One day, while entering the latrine, he suddenly smelled a foul odor and quickly covered his nose with his hand; at that moment, he attained realization. He immediately presented this verse: "From the beginning..."

His bearing was elegant and refined; he often laughed at those of his time who sought [the truth] outside themselves. Though there are ten thousand distinctions and a thousand differences, there is no place to find it;
once attained, it is originally right at the tip of one's own nose. Nantang replied: "When a single dharma is penetrated, all dharmas are complete.

When its wondrous function is applied freely in all directions, what more is there to seek? When the green serpent emerges from its scabbard, the demonic armies submit; the blue-eyed barbarian monk smiles and dots his eyes."
[Śāriputra] said, "This too is the reversal of the breath following emptiness; one suddenly realizes entry [into the path]. It is almost as if one were face-to-face with the bhikṣu Śūcivṛtti.
Then Kātyāyanāvavādaka rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying, "I have karmic afflictions of the mouth."
In a past kalpa, I mocked and ridiculed śramaṇas; consequently, in life after life and birth after birth, I suffered from the disease of rumination (bovine eructation).
The Tathāgata showed me the Dharma-gate of the Single Flavor of the Pure Mind-ground. Having attained this, I extinguished the mind and entered samādhi, contemplating the cognition of flavors.

Neither a substantial entity nor a material object, he should contemplate so as to transcend all worldly outflows (*āsrava*). Internally detached from body and mind, externally relinquishing the world, and far removed from the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*), he is like a bird escaping its cage.
Free from defilement and with dust extinguished, his Dharma-eye becomes pure, and he attains the state of an Arhat.

The Tathāgata personally certified me, and I attained the path of no-more-learning. When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration, according to what I have realized: returning to the flavors and revolving the faculty of cognition—this is the foremost.
The Master said, "Kauṇḍinya, you possess a distinct tongue that perceives flavors; this is because you have the affliction of rumination. As a beast among cattle, one knows only grass and trees.
Now, your tongue-appearance is like that of an ox, yet you are able to discern all varieties of flavor.

By focusing on the root of the tongue, you observe the flavor and turn it back toward awareness. Flavor has many kinds, but the knowing is of no two types. This knowing has not yet turned back to the mind."

That which has not yet been extinguished is, for that very reason, with-outflow (*sāsrava*). Upon realizing that it returns to non-existence, and knowing that there is nothing to be known, one attains the state without-outflow (*anāsrava*).
This realization does not arise from the sense-faculties; it is not their substance. It does not exist within objects; it is not a material thing.

Because it is not a substance, one is inwardly liberated from body and mind. Because it is not a material thing, one externally relinquishes the world. By this, one departs from the defilements of the mind and dissolves [them].
Regarding external objects, he attained a mind-born body (*manomayakāya*) and constantly dwelt in the heavens, receiving offerings from devas and humans.
To prevent slander against him, the Buddha bestowed upon him a rosary, commanding him to constantly recollect the Buddha. This is called the Dharma-gate of the Single Flavor of Purity.

All karmic actions created by the faculty of the tongue since beginningless time were purified at that moment. By means of this, he attained a mind of quiescent extinction and entered [the state of non-arising].
"Right Concentration. This truly captures the essence of the Way. Yangshan sent some fruit to Muzhou;
when Muzhou received it, he asked, "Where did you get this? Yangshan replied, "From my own garden. Muzhou asked, "Is it even fit to eat? Yangshan said: [It is.]
He did not dare to taste it first, but offered it to the Master. Guishan asked, "Whose is this? Yangshan said, "It is Huaiji’s.
Guishan said, "Since it is yours, why do you have me taste it first? Yangshan said, "The Master has tasted it a thousand times and ten thousand times.
Guishan then ate it and said, "It still retains a sour and astringent taste. Yangshan said, "As for the sour and astringent taste, surely you know it yourself."
Miaoyan did not answer. Furthermore, while Xuansha was eating fruit with General Wei, Wei asked, "What is it that is used daily yet remains unknown?
Xuansha picked up a piece of fruit and said, "Eat. After Wei had finished eating the fruit, he asked the question again.
Xuefeng said, "This is precisely what is used daily yet remains unknown. Yangshan said, "I know it myself. Xuefeng said, "I do not know it.
To know while not knowing, and to not know while knowing—this is the revolving taste of awareness. You should see it thus and know it thus;
only then can it be called the pure Dharma-eye."
Piliṅgavatsa (which means "residual habit") immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"When I first resolved to attain enlightenment, I followed the Buddha to enter the Way. On many occasions, I heard the Tathāgata speak of the various things in the world that are not to be enjoyed.
While begging for alms in the city, my mind was contemplating the Dharma-gates; I did not notice that a poisonous thorn on the road had pierced my foot, causing pain throughout my entire body."
I was mindful and aware, cognizing this profound suffering. Although I perceived the perception of pain, my perceiving mind was pure and free from the perception of pain.
I further reflected: "In such a single body, how could there be two perceptions? Before long, having gathered my mindfulness, my body and mind suddenly became empty.
Within twenty-one days, all outflows were exhausted; I became an Arhat, received the seal of personal realization, and attained the state of No-more-learning. The Buddha—
[Śāriputra] asked about the realization of perfect penetration: "As for my own realization, I have attained pure awareness such that the body is cast aside;

this is the foremost. Puming said: "Pindola Bharadvāja called the river spirit a 'servant boy. Because he still possessed the residual habitual tendencies of nobility from previous lives, he was unable to cast aside his body;
thus, when a poisonous thorn pierced his foot, his entire body felt pain, and only then was he able to achieve introspection."
Entering [this state], although there is the capacity for awareness to perceive what is painful, that awareness is the pure mind.
It is free from subject and object, and is not within the reach of pain. Pain is the object of perception, while awareness is that which perceives it;

awareness is the perceiver, whereas pain cannot perceive itself. There is one pain and one non-pain; having already perceived the pain, one further perceives the non-pain. How could a single body possess both?
Is it awakening? Awakening is the sole reality; to perceive pain is delusion. By means of this, one gathers the mind, forgetting the body externally;

as that which is perceived dissolves, one forgets the mind internally. Even the capacity for awakening transforms, and body and mind suddenly become empty. This is the realization of the stage of No-More-Learning (aśaikṣa).
It is simply one pure awakening; therefore, it is called "pure awakening. Once pure awakening is realized, both subject and object are transcended, and one is thus able to relinquish the body.
Being able to relinquish the body, all worldly things that are not conducive to joy are immediately liberation.
Formerly, when the fourth patriarch Upagupta was asked for ordination by someone with the view of self-existence (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the Patriarch said: "Seeking ordination—"
"Follow the Dharma; you must believe my words and not disobey my instructions. The man replied, "Since I have come to take refuge with you as my teacher, I shall certainly obey your commands.
The Master then manifested a steep precipice with towering trees upon it and ordered him to climb the tree.
He then manifested a great pit beneath the tree, a thousand cubits deep and wide, and ordered him to let go of his feet. Following these instructions, the man immediately let go of both feet.
"Let go of one hand. He let go of one hand. "Let go of both hands. The man replied, "If I let go of both hands, I will fall into the pit and die.
The Patriarch said, "We previously agreed that you would receive my instruction; why do you now disobey me? At that moment, the man's attachment to his body was extinguished.
He let go of both hands and fell, no longer seeing either the tree or the pit, and immediately realized the fruit of the Way. This was Xuan Sha’s initial [encounter].
Desiring to travel extensively through all directions to seek out spiritual friends, he set out over the mountain passes with his bag slung over his shoulder.
He stubbed his toe on a rock, and as blood flowed and pain ensued, he sighed, saying: "This body is not truly existent; from where does this pain arise? He then returned to Xuefeng.
Xuefeng asked, "Which one is the Bhikṣu Bei? Sandou replied, "I would never dare to deceive anyone. On another day, Xuefeng called to him.
Beidoutuo, why do you not travel everywhere to seek instruction? Beidoutuo replied: "Dharma did not come to the Eastern Land;
the Second Patriarch did not go to the Western Heaven. Fengran approved of this. When Yunmen first visited Muzhou, as soon as Muzhou saw him coming, he closed the door.
Yunmen then knocked on the door. Muzhou asked, "Who is it? Yunmen said, "It is I. Muzhou asked, "What are you doing? Yunmen said:
"My own matter is not yet clear; I beg the Master for instruction. Mazu opened the door, and as soon as [Xuedou] saw him, he closed it again.
[Xuedou] knocked on the door like this for three consecutive days. On the third day, Mazu opened the door; [Xuedou] pushed his way in immediately.
Mazu seized him and said, "Speak! Speak! As [Xuedou] hesitated, Mazu pushed him out, saying, "A cart-rut from the time of Qin! Thereupon he shut the door.
When Yunmen stepped on a threshold, he damaged one of his feet. Yunmen then attained thorough enlightenment.

Later, when the Governor pointed him out to Xuefeng, he remarked that those such as Xuansha and Yunmen were like Pindola Bharadvaja reborn; yet they still suffered from injured feet, for their habitual tendencies had not been eliminated.
Subhūti immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "Since the beginning of kalpas beyond measure, my mind has been free from obstruction.
I recall as many births as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River; from the very moment I was in my mother’s womb, I knew emptiness and stillness.
In this way, even until the ten directions became empty, I also enabled sentient beings to realize the nature of emptiness, having received the Tathāgata’s inspiration of their inherent nature."
Awakening to true emptiness, wherein the nature of emptiness is perfectly luminous, one attains Arhatship and suddenly enters the Tathāgata’s precious, luminous ocean of emptiness.

Sharing the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, one is certified as having reached the stage beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*). Liberation through the emptiness of nature—this I consider supreme. When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, according to what I have realized:
all phenomena enter into non-existence; that which is non-existent is itself exhausted. Turning back the dharmas to return to nothingness—this is the foremost method.
Tong said: "Since beginningless kalpas, Subhūti has recognized the nature of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), yet he has known only partial emptiness (*pradeśa-śūnyatā*).

Having received the Buddha’s illumination regarding the true emptiness of the awakened nature (*prakṛti-prakāśa-śūnyatā*), he now understands that emptiness arises within great awakening, like a single bubble emerging from the ocean.
Therefore, it is called the 'Jewel-Bright Ocean of Emptiness. Partial emptiness is not perfect; true emptiness is perfect. Partial emptiness is..."
One is not yet liberated. True emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is itself liberation. Those who do not enter true emptiness suddenly still sit within the views of the two vehicles;
they cannot share the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*). Regarding "all marks entering non-being": first, one uses single emptiness to empty all marks.
Regarding "non-being being exhausted by what is non-being": next, one uses double emptiness to empty the mark of emptiness itself. At the beginning, one turns the marks back toward their source.
There is nothing. Since phenomena have already returned to non-existence and both person and phenomena are empty, one is able to return to the ocean of jewel-like luminous emptiness.
This is like sitting in meditation amidst a mountain crag and beholding the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata. The Buddha also said that Subhūti first saw my Dharma-body;
this is likewise one verification of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. When the monk Zhichang visited the Sixth Patriarch, the Patriarch—
He asked, "Where have you come from, and what do you seek? He replied, "I, a student, recently went to White Peak Mountain in Hongzhou to pay my respects to the Great Penetrating Master.
I received his instruction on the meaning of seeing one's nature to become a Buddha, yet I have not resolved my doubts."
"I have come from afar to pay my respects and humbly hope that the Venerable Master will grant me instruction. The Patriarch asked, "What words did he say?
Try reciting them for me. Zhichang replied, "I arrived there and stayed for three months, yet I did not receive any instruction. Because of my earnest desire for the Dharma..."
One night, he entered the master’s chamber alone and asked, "What is this original mind and original nature of mine?
Dàtōng then said, "Do you see empty space? He replied, "I see it. Daotong asked, "Do you see that empty space has any form or appearance?
He replied, "Empty space is formless; how could it have any appearance? Daotong said, "Your seeing of your original nature is just like this."
In empty space, there is not a single thing that can be seen; this is called right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*). There is not a single thing that can be known;
this is called true knowledge. There is no blue, yellow, long, or short; one sees only the fundamentally pure source and the perfectly luminous essence of awakening.

This is what is called "attaining Buddhahood by seeing one's nature" and is also called the "Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision. Although the student has heard this teaching, they have not yet [realized it].

“I have reached a definitive conclusion,” he said. “I beg the Master to grant me further instruction. The Patriarch replied, “The teachings of that master still involve the persistence of cognitive views;

therefore, you have not yet attained realization. I shall now show you a verse. The verse says: ‘To see not a single dharma while maintaining the view of non-existence Is much like floating clouds obscuring the face of the sun.
Not knowing a single dharma while guarding a knowledge of emptiness Is like flashes of lightning arising within the great void.’”
"Thunder! This knowing-seeing arose in a flash; what a mistake, for how could it ever have understood the skillful means?
You should, in a single thought-moment, recognize your own error; your own numinous light is constantly manifesting. This is precisely the jewel-bright ocean of emptiness.
After hearing this verse repeatedly, his mind was suddenly enlightened, and he composed a verse, saying: "Groundlessly, knowing-seeing arose; I clung to appearances to seek Bodhi."

Ti. When the mind dwells upon a single thought of awakening, how could it transcend its former delusion? The source-body of self-nature’s enlightenment follows illumination and erroneously undergoes flux.
Failing to enter the chamber of the Patriarchs, one wanders in confusion toward two extremes. This may be called knowing error in a single thought; thus, that which is not the "non" is exhausted.
From Aniruddha to these five sages, there are those who speak of "revolving vision" and "reversing the breath."

These are called "returning to flavor" and "revolving the dharmas"; both involve returning the flow to restore the single essence, thereby realizing perfect penetration through the six sense faculties.
The reason Avalokiteśvara’s method of "returning the hearing" is not listed here is that it represents the ultimate fruit of perfect penetration, standing adjacent to the rank of Buddhahood.

"Therefore, after the pressing [of the earth], Śāriputra immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: 'Since the beginningless kalpas, my mind and vision have been pure.
Thus I have undergone births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, manifesting various transformations within both the mundane and supramundane realms.'"

Upon seeing [the Buddha], my vision was unimpeded; I attained freedom from all obstructions. On the way, I encountered the brothers Kāśyapa following one another as they expounded upon causes and conditions.
I awakened to the boundlessness of the mind and left the household life under the Buddha. Seeing that enlightened clarity is perfect and full, I attained great fearlessness and became an Arhat.
As the Buddha’s eldest son, I was born from the Buddha’s mouth and transformedly born from the Dharma. When the Buddha asked about the most direct path to perfect penetration, it was as follows:
"What I have realized is that the mind perceives the radiance of light, and this supreme insight is the foremost.
Śāriputra replied, "When I was first in my mother’s womb, her wisdom and eloquence surpassed those of my maternal uncle.
My uncle said, 'Once this child is born, his wisdom will be matchless. Consequently, I went to South India to study the Dharma, having no leisure even to trim my nails."
He was the bhikṣu Dīrghanakha. When Śāriputra was nine years old, he was already able to debate and defeat his assembly, earning the high esteem of the king.
He had long been close friends with Maudgalyāyana, and they made a pact, saying: "Should either of us attain the taste of the Deathless (amṛta), we shall surely share it with one another.

While on the road, Maudgalyāyana encountered the bhikṣu Aśvajit and asked him: "What doctrine does your teacher preach? Aśvajit replied: [The verse beginning with] "Whatever exists... (yam kiñci samudayadhammam...).
He said, "All phenomena arise from conditions; all phenomena cease from conditions. This is what my teacher, the Great Śramaṇa, constantly proclaims.
Upon hearing this, Lián immediately attained realization and the first fruit of the path. He quickly went to inform Śāriputra, who also realized the first fruit at those very words.
The two men went together to visit the Buddha. Seeing the two youths from afar, the Buddha addressed the assembly, saying, "These are my..."
These were the two great disciples. One was foremost in wisdom; the other was foremost in supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). Śāriputra possessed the sharpest insight of mind.
Having left the household life with the Buddha, he thoroughly mastered the Buddha-dharma in seven days and attained the state of an Arhat after fifteen days;
therefore, he is called foremost in wisdom. As the Buddha’s eldest son, his mental vision does not depend upon the sense faculties or consciousness.
Therefore, one can internally polish the mind until it emits light; when this light reaches its ultimate limit, it becomes gnosis and vision.

This is precisely what is meant by seeing the luminosity of awakening and fully attaining great fearlessness (*mahā-vaiśāradya*). Those whose vision has not yet penetrated are possessed of doubt and thus possessed of fear.

Śāriputra attained fearlessness through debate at the age of nine, but it was only upon reaching a comprehensive mastery of the Buddha-dharma that he was truly named "Great Fearless One. (As recorded in the *Chángqìng Lèng Chán*)
When the Master first visited Xuefeng, he asked, "I request that you, Master, grant me an instruction on the single path transmitted by all the sages of antiquity.
Xuefeng remained silent for a long time. Ling bowed and withdrew. Xuefeng then smiled.

Thus he traveled back and forth between Xuefeng and Xuansha for twenty years, wearing out seven meditation cushions, yet he did not clarify this matter. One day, as he rolled up the curtain, suddenly—
He attained great enlightenment and uttered this verse: "How very strange! How very strange! Rolling up the curtain, one sees the whole world.
If someone asks what school I understand, I raise my whisk and strike them right on the mouth.
Fengju said to Xuansha, "This boy has reached through to the bottom. Xuansha said, "Not so. This is merely the composition of the conscious mind; you must further examine him."

It was only then that he attained it. When evening arrived, the assembly of monks came up to pay their respects. Xuefeng said to Shouling, "The Dharma Master Bei has not yet consented to your presence here.
If you truly possess correct awakening, bring it forth before the assembly. Shouling then offered this verse: "Amidst the myriad phenomena, the body alone is revealed;
Only when one consents for oneself does one become intimate with it. In the past, I mistakenly sought it along the road; now..."
"Looking at it, it is ice within fire. Feng then looked at Sha and said, "It must not be a fabrication of the conscious mind.
To 'look at it as ice within fire'—upon a single glimpse, one penetrates it and attains non-obstruction.
Master Leng may truly be said to possess the eye."
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I have already served as a Dharma Prince for Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Whenever Tathāgatas of the ten directions instruct their disciples who possess the faculties of bodhisattvas,"
I shall cultivate the practices of Samantabhadra and receive my name from you, World-Honored One. With my mind-ear, I shall discern all the knowledge and views of sentient beings.

If, beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in other directions, there is a single sentient being who gives rise to the realization of the practices of Samantabhadra within their heart, at that time I shall mount my six-tusked elephant and manifest hundreds of thousands of bodies, arriving at that very place. Even if...

Their obstructions are deep; they have not yet attained the vision of me. I personally place my hand upon their heads in the darkness, providing protection, consolation, and encouragement so that they may achieve success.
When the Buddha asks about the perfect penetration, I declare its fundamental cause: the illumination of mental hearing brings forth mastery in discernment;
this is the foremost.

The Master said: "Pervading the entire Dharma-realm is called 'Universal' (Samantabhadra). Occupying a station adjacent to the ultimate sages is called 'Worthy' (Bhadra). Universal-Worthy has already realized the stage of fruition; here we speak of his original cause.
Through the manifestation of hearing from the mind, his discernment is sovereign. Throughout the entirety of the void realm, there is nothing that does not reach the range of this mental hearing.
He discriminates those who practice the conduct of Universal-Worthy and protects them. Within this [text], there is one...
In the Samādhi of Sovereignty over All Seeds, there is not even a hair’s breadth of deliberate effort involved.

This is because the Dharmakāya that has been realized is already fully pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm. Wherever a thought first arises, that very place becomes the locus of practice and vows; its virtuous functions are unimpeded.

The substance is itself the function; the function is itself the substance. Therefore, it is called "sovereign mastery. Guanyin attained the manifestation of quiescence by reversing the hearing from the ear-faculty;
Puxian attained sovereign discernment by illuminating through the ear-consciousness. To say "manifestation" does not mean there has never been discernment;
to say "sovereign mastery" does not mean there has never been quiescence. Such are the attainments of these two sages.
In truth, there is no distinction of superiority or inferiority between them. When Tanyi first entered Mount Lu, he relied upon Master Huiyuan.
Later, he returned to Kuaiji and recited the *Lotus Sūtra* for twelve years at Qinwang Mountain.

He was moved by the manifestation of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, who appeared in the form of a woman wearing colorful garments, carrying a bamboo basket and two bulbs of garlic, along with a white pig, and came before Tanyi, saying: "I have entered..."
She had been gathering bracken in the mountains when the sun slanted low; wolves and jackals roamed about, and she had no means of returning home.
She ventured to ask for one night’s lodging, and her husband, Yi, granted her request. The woman wailed incessantly; he then had her stay upon a bed of grass.

At midnight, she cried out in pain from her abdomen and asked Yi to massage her. Yi declined on the grounds that he observed the precepts and ought not to touch her with his hands. The woman’s wailing grew even more intense.
"It is truly so. Daoyi then wrapped his *khakkhara* in cloth and pressed it down from afar. On the following day, the woman transformed into auspicious clouds while wearing her colorful robes;
the pig changed into a white elephant; and the garlic turned into twin lotuses. They ascended into the air, and she said to Daoyi, "I am the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra.
I came specifically to test you. When Meng Yi, the Prefectural Governor, reported this to the court, an imperial edict was issued to establish a Buddhist monastery.
The story of Huasi Temple is quite similar to the account of Guanyin testing Wu Daozi;

the manifestation of his divided body and the touching of heads in consolation are beyond full description. If such things occur in the Eastern Land, they may be known to exist throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
A monk asked Changsha: "Why did Sudhana travel through worlds within the body of Samantabhadra for immeasurable kalpas [without seeing them]?"
The monk said, "Pervasive. Zhaozhou asked, "Since immeasurable kalpas past, have you ever traveled everywhere? The monk asked, "What is the body of Samantabhadra?
Zhaozhou said, "Seeking Chang'an within the Han-yuan Palace. Furthermore, a monk took his leave of Dashi. Dashi asked, "Where are you going?
The monk said, "I am going to Mount Emei to pay homage to Samantabhadra. Dashi held up his whisk and said, "Wen... (He left it unfinished.)
"Samantabhadra is right here. The monk drew a circle, threw it behind him, and followed this by saying, "Attendant, give this monk a cup of tea.
Tiantong commented: "Those who know the Dharma are afraid; those who deceive the enemy perish.
To select milk from water, one must be a king of geese. Since this monk said he was going to pay respects to Samantabhadra, yet again—"
Cast it behind you; it is unavoidable that one must conduct a thorough examination of the great accompaniments. Do you recognize them as being right here?
It would be improper to seek Chang’an elsewhere.
Then Sunda-ra-nanda (which means "Good Love" or "Joyous Delight") rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

When I first left home and followed the Buddha to enter the Path, although I was fully endowed with the precepts, my mind was constantly distracted and agitated regarding *samādhi*, and I had not yet attained the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*).
The World-Honored One instructed me and Kauṣṭhila (translated here as "Great Thigh") to contemplate the white [light] at the tip of the nose.

When I first contemplated this earnestly for twenty-one days, I saw the breath entering and exiting through the nostrils like smoke; my body and mind became internally luminous, and there was a perfect, hollow clarity.
The world became entirely empty and pure, like lapis lazuli. As the traces of smoke gradually vanished, my nasal breath turned white; my mind opened and outflows were exhausted.
All inhalations and exhalations transformed into radiant light, illuminating the worlds of the ten directions. I attained Arhatship. The World-Honored One prophesied that I would attain Bodhi.

The extinction of the outflows (*āsrava*)—this is the foremost.

His teachings flourished greatly and spread throughout the world. It is said that there were over three thousand monasteries following his lineage during the Tang dynasty. Among them, the five houses and seven schools emerged, each developing distinct styles of teaching. This is known as the Hongzhou school of Chan. Later generations refer to it simply as the Baizhang school. It is the most flourishing among the various Chan lineages. Its influence remains vast today. The patriarchs and masters of the past were all of this lineage. Their words and deeds are recorded in the various *Yulu* (Recorded Sayings) collections. One should study them extensively to understand the essence of the Way. If one studies them without understanding the intent, one will merely grasp the literal words and miss the true meaning. Therefore, one must first seek the source and clarify the root before engaging in practice. Only then will one truly realize the ultimate truth. If one practices without knowing the source, one will wander aimlessly and fail to reach the goal. Thus, it is essential to first investigate the origin and then apply oneself to cultivation. This is the fundamental principle for entering the path. If one does not first investigate the source, one will be like a blind person trying to find their way. Even if they exert themselves, they will only increase their confusion. Therefore, the ancients said, "First, clarify the mind-ground; then, cultivate the path. This is the correct sequence. This is the final destination of all Buddhas and patriarchs. It is the very lifeblood of the Dharma. One must not treat it as a mere academic pursuit or a ritualistic exercise. It requires a profound and sincere resolve to cut through delusion and awaken to the truth. Only through such earnest application can one hope to attain liberation. This is the legacy of the ancestral teachers. It is a path that has been transmitted from generation to generation. Furthermore, Chan Master Cheng of Pan’an addressed the assembly, saying: "Virtuous ones, you should know that my present single shout can penetrate the five teachings.
After a long silence, he let out a loud shout and asked: "Did you hear it? The assembly replied: "We heard it."
Zhaozhou Cheng said, "Did you just hear that one shout? If you did, that would mean it exists, which is the teaching of the Lesser Vehicle. He asked again, "Do you hear it now?
Cheng replied, "I do not hear it. Zhaozhou said, "Since you do not hear it now, then this one shout does not exist."
This is the entry into the Initial Teaching (Shijiao) of the Mahāyāna. When I first uttered the shout, you said there was;
when the sound had long since faded, you again said there was not. Yet, to say there was not implies that it previously existed, and to say there was implies that it is now non-existent.
This is neither existent nor non-existent—this is the entry into the Final Teaching (Zhongjiao) of the Mahāyāna. At the time when I first had the shout, existence was not...
This is existence. Because of non-existence, there is existence; at the moment of shouting, non-existence is not itself non-existence.
Because of existence, there is non-existence; this is precisely existence and non-existence simultaneously. This is entering the Sudden Teaching. I do not employ the single shout as a single shout;
existence and non-existence are not established. Awakening and understanding are both forgotten. When the Way exists, not even a hair’s breadth is established; when the Way does not exist—
It extends horizontally throughout space. This single shout is itself hundreds of thousands of millions of shouts; these hundreds of thousands of millions of shouts are themselves this single shout.
This is the entry into the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). There were many such debates, and those who heard them were instantly subdued. It was not long before—
