Upāli (translated here as "the Prince’s Attendant") immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I personally followed the Buddha when he left the city to renounce the world; I personally witnessed the Tathāgata’s six years of diligent austerity; I personally saw the Tathāgata subdue..."
I have subdued all Māras and restrained all non-Buddhists. I am liberated from the outflows of worldly greed and desire.
Having received the Buddha’s instructions, I have purified all three thousand modes of deportment and eighty thousand subtle categories of natural and proscribed offenses.
With body and mind in total stillness, I have become an Arhat. I am the pillar of the Tathāgata’s assembly; he has personally sealed my heart, and I uphold [the Dharma].

I cultivated the body through the precepts; the assembly ranked me as foremost. When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, I replied: "By means of disciplining the body, I attained mastery over the body;
then, in succession, I disciplined the mind and achieved thorough penetration of it. Thereafter, both body and mind became entirely unimpeded and sharp. This is my primary method."
The messenger said: "The Tathāgata practiced austerities for six years, performing everything that ordinary outsiders were unable to do;
thus he was able to subdue all the non-Buddhists. Furthermore, because he attained liberation from worldly greed and all outflows (*āsrava*), Māra could not disturb him.
When Māra attacked him with his armies, they were all transformed into lotus flowers, and the demons were subdued—all this was due to his body."

He maintained the precepts and practices; of the thirty thousand and eighty thousand [rules], there were none that were not perfected. Thus, the Māras and heretics folded their hands and sighed in admiration.

His conduct in walking, standing, sitting, and reclining was governed by the code of discipline known as the two hundred and fifty rules; when categorized according to the three aggregates (*triskandha*), these constitute three thousand.
Furthermore, by assigning three thousand [rules] to the three actions of the body and the four of the mouth—making seven branches—one arrives at twenty-one thousand.

These are further assigned to the four categories of afflictions, resulting in eighty-four thousand. The Buddha established this Vinaya to instruct and admonish śramaṇas, causing them to attain purity of both body and mind.
Regarding the faults and calamities of the turbid margins, such as killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying: their nature is inherently sinful. It is not...

It is prohibited for the sake of restraint; once committed, it constitutes karma. Therefore, it is called "inherent karma" (*prakṛti-sāvadya*). Other [actions] were prohibited only after faults arose; prior to the prohibition, committing them incurred no offense.
Therefore, they are called "prohibited karma" (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*). When both types of karma are eliminated, one attains quiescence (*nirvāṇa*). One begins by disciplining the body.

This refers to the mastery over the body and the purity of its nature and karma. It refers to the sequential grasping of the mind and the attainment of penetration by the mind, which is the purity of obstructive karma.
As for "grasping the body and extending to the mind," the mind constitutes bodily consciousness;
once bodily consciousness has ceased, true wisdom manifests. Possessing pure precepts and wisdom, one then attains the foremost path. This—
Upāli was foremost in upholding the precepts and served as the guiding pillar for the assembly. His attainment reached the point where body and mind were entirely proficient;
he had clearly advanced toward enlightenment. How could this be merely a matter of physical discipline?

As for the Venerable Pārśva—here translated as "Universal Practice"—he always ate but one meal a day, never lay down to sleep, and performed prostrations to the Buddha during the six periods of the day. Pure and free from desire, he was [held in high esteem] by the assembly.
Returning, the twentieth patriarch, Venerable Śayananda, wishing to deliver him, first asked the assembly:
"Can this Parivrajaka ascetic, who is able to cultivate the holy life, attain the Way of the Buddha? The assembly replied: "Our teacher is diligent."

"Why is this not possible? The Patriarch said, "Your master is far removed from the Way. Even if he were to practice asceticism for kalpas as numerous as dust motes, it would all be the root of falsehood.
The assembly asked, "What virtues and conduct do you, Venerable One, possess that you should speak thus of our master?"
The Patriarch said: "I do not seek the Way, nor am I inverted. I do not prostrate to the Buddha, nor am I disrespectful.
I do not sit in perpetual meditation, nor am I indolent. I do not eat only once a day, nor do I eat at irregular intervals. I am not one who knows contentment."

"Furthermore, he is without craving and his mind has no expectations; this is what is called the Way. When Pūrvācārya heard this, he gave rise to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) and joyfully praised him.
The Patriarch then said to the assembly, "Do you understand my words? It was because his desire for the Way was so intense that I did not praise him.
For if a string is too tight, it will snap; therefore, I did not praise him, so as to allow him—"
Abiding in the stage of peace and bliss, he entered the wisdom of all Buddhas. He then addressed Viśvāmitra, saying, "I have just rebuked you before this assembly;

has it not caused distress within your heart? Viśvāmitra replied, "I recall that seven kalpas ago, I was born in the Land of Constant Peace and Bliss as a disciple of the wise Moon-Pure (Candraprabha).
He prophesied that before long I would realize the fruit of a Sakṛdāgāmin."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāprabhāsa appeared in the world. Because I was old, I leaned on a staff to pay my respects to him.

The Master rebuked me, saying, "You value your son and slight your father; how can you be so base? At that time, I considered myself without fault and requested the Master to show me where I had erred.
The Master said: "You prostrated to the Bodhisattva Mahāprabha while leaning your staff against the wall and drawing the face of a Buddha.

Because of this arrogance, you consequently lost the two fruits [of the path]. Since I have taken responsibility for my own person and repented my transgressions, even when hearing various evil words, they have been like the wind or an echo.
How much more so now that I have obtained the drinking of the unsurpassed nectar—would I instead give rise to feverish affliction? I only pray for your great compassion."
He bestowed his instructions with the wondrous Way. The Patriarch said, "You have long cultivated manifold virtues; you shall succeed to my lineage. He then transmitted the Dharma verse, saying:
"In a single word, one accords with the unborn, identical to the nature of the Dharma-realm. If one can understand it thus, one will thoroughly penetrate both phenomena and principle.
This was the twenty-first patriarch. Indeed, one cannot hope to attain the unsurpassed [enlightenment] without cultivating pure conduct (*brahmacarya*).
"Bodhi (Awakening) is something that has never been heard of since antiquity.
Then Mahāmaudgalyāyana rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"When I was first begging for alms along the road, I encountered the three [kings]: Uruvilvā (translated as 'Pumpkin Cave'), Gayā (the Elephant Head Mountain), and Nadī (the name of a river)."
Yepa (of the Great Tortoise clan) proclaimed the profound meaning of the Tathāgata’s causes and conditions. I immediately gave rise to the bodhicitta and attained great penetration.

The Tathāgata bestowed upon me a *kāṣāya* robe, which I wore upon my body; my beard and hair fell away of their own accord. I travel throughout the ten directions, attaining freedom from all hindrances.

My supernormal powers were manifested and ranked as unsurpassed; I attained the state of Arhat. Not only did the World-Honored One praise me, but the Tathāgatas of the ten directions also extolled my spiritual power as perfectly bright, pure, sovereign, and fearless.
When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the Way, I replied that it was through the revolving of the stillness of the mind.
The light of the mind radiates forth; it is like settling a turbid stream until it becomes long-lasting, clear, and limpid—this is the foremost [method].
Tong said: "That people cannot achieve perfect clarity and purity is because their consciousness flows outward and rushes toward sensory dust.

Thus, their minds serve the functions of the physical form rather than the functions of the spirit. If consciousness does not flow outward, it returns to the wondrous stillness, like settling [a stream]."

The turbid flow, having long attained clarity and brilliance, causes the light of the mind to manifest and spiritual powers (*abhijñā*) to become sovereign; this is the attainment of non-obstruction by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

Among the six supernormal powers, only the extinction of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) is an internal realization; the remaining five all belong to external applications. The *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states:
"The samādhi like an illusion is like a sprout gradually growing; therefore, one must accumulate [merit] for a long time before it can become brilliant."
Jie (the monk Baozhi). At first, he practiced only meditative concentration (*samādhi*). After practicing for a long time, he suddenly attained supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).

Chan Master Deng Yinfeng resided at Mount Heng during the winter and stayed at Mount Qingliang during the summer. During the Yuanhe era, Wu Yuanji obstructed the military way and defied the imperial mandate.
When the government troops and the rebels were locked in combat and had not yet determined victory or defeat, Yinfeng said, "I shall go and resolve this calamity."
He then cast his *śikya* staff into the air and passed through it with his body flying. The officers and soldiers of both armies looked up in awe;

the event corresponded exactly to their prior dream, and their hearts to fight were instantly stilled. Since the Peak had manifested such divine wonders, he feared it would delude the masses, and so he entered Mount Wutai.
Standing before the Vajra Cave, as he was about to demonstrate his passing, he first asked the assembly: "When those in other regions pass away, they do so sitting or lying down. As for me..."
"Have you ever seen anyone pass away while standing upright? they asked. "Yes," the assembly replied. "Is there anyone who has passed away while standing on their head?
they asked. "I have never seen such a thing," the assembly replied. Thereupon, Feng stood on his head and passed away; he remained perfectly erect, his robes falling naturally over his body.

At that time, the assembly attempted to move him to perform the cremation, but he remained motionless and immovable. Those from near and far who gazed upon him could not cease their expressions of wonder and admiration.
Feng had a younger sister who had become a nun; she was also there at that time.

She then patted him and rebuked him, saying, "Old brother, you did not follow the laws and precepts in your past life, and now you have died to delude people. Thereupon, she pushed him with her hand, and he fell down flat on his back.
Supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) are indeed the fruit of the stages of realization; yet, those with clear eyes do not prize them. When Yangshan ascended the seat, a foreign monk arrived through the air.
Yangshan asked, "Where have you recently departed from? He replied, "From the Western Heaven. Yangshan asked, "When did you leave there?
He replied, "This morning. Yangshan said, "Why so late? He replied, "I was traveling among the mountains and enjoying the waters. Yangshan remarked, "That is merely playing with supernatural powers."
"It is not that it does not exist, O Ācārya. The Buddha-dharma must still be realized by an old monk like me.

[The monk] said, "I came specifically to this Eastern Land to pay homage to Mañjuśrī, yet instead I encountered a 'lesser Śākyamuni. He then produced a Sanskrit manuscript on *bīḍūka* leaves and gave it to Yangshan, who then ascended into the air and departed.
Yangshan addressed the assembly, saying, "I have now clearly explained to you matters concerning the side of the holy; do not take them..."
Settle the mind and simply practice according to reality within the ocean of your own nature. You do not need the three clarities or the six supernatural powers.
Why? Because these are merely peripheral matters for the sages. For now, you must recognize the mind and reach the root.
If you attain the root, you need not worry about the branches; at some future time, they will naturally be present. If you have not attained the root, even if...
Even if you were to apply your emotions to study this, you would still not attain it. Have you not seen what the Venerable Master Guishan said:
"When all sentiments of ordinary and sagely beings are exhausted, the essence reveals the true permanence; when phenomena and principle are non-dual, one is the Buddha of Suchness.
This is the direct lineage of perfect clarity and purity. From Śāriputra down to here, [the teachings] have been called the seeing of the mind, the hearing of the mind, and the light of the mind.
Not dependent on the faculties, not dependent on objects, having transcended both faculties and sense-fields, and being entirely free from the habits of delusion—
this is the realization of perfect penetration through the six consciousnesses.
Ucchuṣma (Fire-Head Vajra), before the Tathāgata, joined his palms in prostration at the Buddha’s feet and addressed him:
The Buddha said: "I always first recall that in the distant past, many kalpas ago, my nature was full of lustful desire.

There was a Buddha who appeared in the world named King of Emptiness (Kongwang), who taught that those with much lust become a mass of fierce fire. He instructed me to contemplate everywhere throughout my hundred skeletal members, four limbs, and all the cold and warm vital energies.
As the divine light coalesced within, it transformed my lustful mind into the fire of wisdom. From this time on, all Buddhas have called me..."
The Buddha summoned me and named me "Fire-Head" (Jietou). By the power of the Samādhi of Fire-Light, I attained Arhatship. Therein I made a great vow:
"When all Buddhas attain the Way, may I become a powerful Malla and personally subdue their demonic enemies. When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, I replied:
"By clearly observing that the warmth and touch within my body and mind flow unimpededly, all outflows were extinguished and a great jewel-flame arose; thus I ascended to the stage of no..."
This supreme awakening is the foremost.
It is said in general that, among the preceding seven elements, the nature of fire is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true fire;
it is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire dharma-realm. Because the *Agnimukha Samādhi* (Fire-Head Samādhi) inherently possesses inconceivable power, [the deity] Fire-Head...
Vajra, by means of internal concentration of the divine light, one transforms the mind of excessive lust into the fire of wisdom.

At the very point where this true fire first stirs, one returns to the root and source, reverts to purity, and thus achieves wisdom. In those with excessive lust, the warmth of their vital energy erupts;
while alive it becomes the fire of desire, and at death it becomes the fire of karma. As the power of karma intensifies and blazes, it becomes a fierce fire.
"A mass of fire. Maitreya Bodhisattva said: "Men and women alternate and couple two by two, whereby impurity flows out.

Although the various devas of the desire realm engage in sexual desire, they have no such impurity; rather, from their sense organs, a wind-like vapor issues forth, and the feverish affliction is thereby stilled.
Among the gods of the Four Great Kings, they couple two by two, and the feverish affliction is likewise stilled. As it is said:
Among the gods of the Four Great Kings and likewise the gods of the Thirty-three, their feverish affliction ceases merely by holding one another in mutual embrace.
Among the gods of the Heaven of the Hours, it ceases merely by holding hands. Among the gods of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations, it ceases merely by looking at one another and smiling.
Among the gods of the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations, their feverish affliction ceases merely by gazing at one another with their eyes.
Is this not because their desires gradually diminish as their station gradually rises? When the lustful mind of Mātanga was extinguished, he immediately realized the third fruit;
when the various outflows of the Fire-Head Vajra were exhausted, he ascended to supreme enlightenment—how could this be considered strange?
While Guishan was standing in attendance by the side of Baizhang, Baizhang asked, "Who is there? Guishan replied, "It is I. Baizhang said, "You, sweep away..."
"Is there fire in the brazier? Baizhang prodded it and said, "There is no fire. Mazu rose personally and prodded deeply, finding a small amount of fire.
He held it up to show him and said, "You said there was none; what about this? Thereupon, Baizhang attained awakening, prostrated in thanks, and set forth his understanding.
Mazu said, "This is merely a temporary crossroads. As the Sutra says: 'If you wish to know the meaning of Buddha-nature...'"
One should contemplate the conditions of time and season. When the time has arrived, it is like suddenly awakening from a delusion or suddenly remembering what was forgotten;
only then does one realize that one’s own property was never obtained from another. Thus the Patriarch said: "Awakening is the same as non-awakening; there is no mind and no dharma.
This merely means being free from the false and delusive minds of ordinary and sage. The fundamental mind and dharma have been complete from the very beginning.
"Since you are now thus, protect and maintain yourself well. The next day, he entered the mountains with Baizhang to perform manual labor.
Baizhang asked, "Have you brought fire? Muzhou replied, "I have brought it. Baizhang asked, "Where is it?
Muzhou then picked up a piece of wood, blew on it twice, and handed it to Baizhang. Baizhang said, "It is like a worm gnawing through wood. Miaoxi remarked, "Baizhang..."

Had it not been for his later words, how much trouble would have been caused for the kitchen steward? This [attainment] also arose from the greatness of his fire-element, leading him to ascend to unsurpassed enlightenment.
Why must one necessarily contemplate the various cold and hot energies within the body to realize perfect penetration?
The Bodhisattva Dharaṇīdhara rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I recall that in the past, when the Tathāgata Samantaprabhāsa appeared in the world, I was a bhikṣu who constantly stood at all major roads and ferry crossings."
Where fields and roads were rugged and narrow, or where conditions were unfitting and obstructed or damaged carts and horses, I leveled and filled them all;
or I constructed bridges, or carried sand and earth on my back. Through such diligent toil, immeasurable Buddhas appeared in the world.

Furthermore, when there were sentient beings in the marketplace who required someone to carry their goods, I would first carry them for them until they reached their destination; once the goods were set down, I would depart.
I did not take their payment. During the time when Vipaśyin Buddha (translated as "Pervasive Sovereignty over All") was present in the world, there was widespread famine.
I worked as a porter; regardless of whether the distance was far or near, I took only a single coin. Sometimes, oxen pulling carts became mired in the mud.
"I possess supernatural powers; I shall push his wheel for him and uproot his suffering. At that time, the Great King of the country invited the Buddha to partake in a vegetarian feast.
I then leveled the ground to await the Buddha. Viśvabhū Tathāgata rubbed the crown of my head and said to me: "You should level the mind-ground."

Then the ground of the world became entirely level. My mind was immediately opened, and I saw that the subtle atoms of my own body were equal and indistinguishable from all the subtle atoms that compose the world.
These atoms, by their very nature, do not touch or rub against one another, even when weapons of war are present.

Furthermore, there is nothing to be contacted. Regarding the nature of dharmas, I have realized the patience of non-arising and attained arhatship; now, having turned my mind, I enter the stage of a bodhisattva.
Having heard the Tathāgatas proclaim the ground of the Buddhas’ wondrous Lotus wisdom and vision, I was formerly their witness.

I served as their leader. When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the Way, I replied: "By contemplating the two objects—the body and the realm—I saw that they are equal and without distinction, being fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha.
These objects arise from false delusion; when the objects are eliminated, wisdom becomes perfect, and one achieves the Unsurpassed Way. This is the foremost."
Tong said: "All dharmas are equal; there is no high or low. If the ground of the mind is level, one does not give rise to discrimination.
Thus, one does not perceive the marks of self and other, high and low, and so forth; then all things are level.

From this, the Bodhisattva Dhṛtarāṣṭra entered into the wondrous nature of True Suchness, the Tathāgatagarbha. In this nature, form is true emptiness, and emptiness is true form. [Even] a mote of dust..."
Intrinsic nature does not involve mutual contact or friction; it is fundamentally equal and fundamentally unarisen.

These very atoms—internally, the atoms of the body, which are accumulated from atoms; and externally, the atoms of the realms, which are likewise accumulated from atoms—are originally devoid of intrinsic nature.
They arise through false conceptualization. At the very point where they are false, that is precisely where [reality lies].
Abiding in non-arising is precisely the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*).

If this body of mine is the wondrous nature of True Suchness, then the dust of this world-realm is likewise the wondrous nature of True Suchness. Since the nature is fundamentally non-dual, how could there be any differentiation among phenomena?
As there is no differentiation, even weapons of war cannot touch it. Upon awakening to this Dharma-nature, contact is fundamentally unarisen; contact is itself...

Because there is no contact, one enters the Buddha’s knowledge and vision through the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). To enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is what is called wisdom (*jñāna*).
Since the sensory objects (*viṣaya*) are neither objects nor non-objects, the objects vanish of their own accord. One realizes wisdom without departing from the objects; thus, wisdom becomes perfect.
When wisdom is perfected, one is able to realize and testify to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and thereby achieve the Unsurpassed Way.
One day, Master Guishan pointed to a field and asked Yangshan, "In this field, which end is high and which end is low?
Yangshan replied, "In fact, this end is high and that end is low. Guishan said, "If you do not believe me, stand in the middle and look at both ends."
Yangshan said, "There is no need to establish a middle; nor should one dwell at either extreme. Guishan said, "If it is so, look at water. Water can level all things.
Yangshan said, "Water has no fixed nature; it levels itself high where there is high ground and levels itself low where there is low ground.
Guishan then desisted. If Master Guishan and his disciple Yangshan do not establish the two extremes and do not settle upon the Middle Way, they may truly be called [the masters of non-duality].
Because he has well pacified the mind-ground, all things are thereby pacified.

There was a Master named Dazhu (Beat-the-Ground), who, having received the essential instruction from Mazu Daoyi of Jiangxi, constantly concealed his brilliance. Whenever a student posed a question, he would respond only by striking the ground with his staff;
thus, he was known as "Master Beat-the-Ground. One day, a monk hid his staff away before approaching him. [The Master then struck the ground.]
Question: [The Master] merely opened his mouth. A monk asked a disciple, "As for the Master’s daily practice of striking the ground whenever someone asks him a question, what is the meaning of this?
The disciple immediately took a piece of firewood from the hearth and threw it into the cauldron.

Unless one has thoroughly exhausted all dust-like delusions, dissolved them, perfected wisdom, and attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), one cannot understand this principle.
The youth Candraprabha immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I recall that in the past, during kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Jaladeva. He taught all the bodhisattvas to practice the contemplation of water."

Entering into samādhi, he contemplates within his own body that the nature of water is not to be displaced. Beginning with mucus and saliva, he thus exhaustively examines the lymphatic fluids, semen, blood, feces, and urine;
as they circulate and revolve within the body, the nature of water is seen to be uniform throughout. Thus, he perceives the water within his body.
It was no different from the fragrant water seas of the World-Beyond Floating Banner King realm.
At that time, I first accomplished this contemplation; I saw only the water and had not yet attained the bodiless state. I was then a bhikṣu, practicing dhyāna within my chamber.
I had a disciple who peered through the window to observe the room; he saw nothing at all except clear water filling the entire space.
Being a young child without understanding, he took a piece of tile or rubble and threw it into the water, which caused the water to splash and make a sound as he looked around and departed.
After emerging from samādhi, I suddenly felt pain in my heart, like that experienced by Śāriputra when he was struck by a malevolent spirit. I reflected to myself:
"I have now attained the path of Arhatship and have long been free from the conditions for illness; why does this heartache suddenly arise today?"
"Lest you should suffer any loss or decline. At that time, the youth came quickly before me and related the matter as described above.
I then told him, "If you see water again, you may immediately open the door and enter this water to remove the tiles and debris. The youth followed my instructions.

Furthermore, when entering meditative concentration again, he once more saw the water; the tiles and rubble were exactly as before. He opened the door and emerged. After I had emerged from concentration, my physical form was as it was at first.
There he encountered immeasurable Buddhas, continuing in this manner until he reached the Tathāgata King of Sovereign Penetration of Mountains and Seas.
Only then did I attain the dissolution of the self. My nature became one with the true void of the fragrant water-oceans throughout the worlds of the ten directions, without duality or distinction.
Now, from the Tathāgata, I have received the name "Childlike Purity" and am included in the assembly of Bodhisattvas.

When the Buddha asks about the perfect penetration, I say that through the single flavor of the flowing nature of water, I attained the patience of non-arising and perfected Bodhi; this is the foremost method.
Tong said: "The Great Yin is the water-essence (*āpa-maṇi*). The nature of water is round and luminous; therefore, it is called Moonlight.
When first practicing the contemplation of water, one contemplates that the nature of water cannot be displaced.

Whether it be the internal vital essence and blood, or the external oceans of worlds (*kṣetra-samudra*), although their watery forms differ, their nature cannot be displaced by one another. Only because they cannot be displaced does this contemplation first take form; one sees only the water."
This refers to the ten *kṛtsnāyatana* (totality) meditative absorptions. They exist when one has entered meditative absorption, but do not exist when one has emerged from it.
As for the ten totalities—blue, yellow, red, white, earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness—when one forms the perception of blue, for example, everything becomes blue;

this is the fruit of that concentration. It manifests according to the transformations of the mind, and the same applies to the fire-light concentration (*tejodhātu-samādhi*). Although one may attain these concentrations, [the faculties remain...]
Fundamental ignorance still persists; therefore, one does not know the causes of the illness and has not yet attained the dissolution of the body.
The presence of the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) is precisely fundamental ignorance. Seeing only the water, one perceives everything as water, and thus throws tiles and rubble into it.
It was also transformed into water. Śāriputra entered meditative absorption on the bank of the Ganges;
a malevolent yakṣa struck him, and upon emerging from concentration, he suffered a headache. The Buddha said, "You lack the power of meditative stability; your body shall be shattered.
"Malevolent" (Wéihài) is the name of a yakṣa king and was a former enemy of Śāriputra. Regarding the *Pṛthivī-kūṭarāja* world-system, it accords with the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Within the Flower Treasury Ocean, there is a great lotus flower. Within that lotus flower are various seas of fragrant water;

each of these seas of fragrant water serves as the seed for the worlds of the Buddha-fields. Because the Flower Treasury World rests within these seas of fragrance, it is called the Floating Banner King Realm (*Puḍgala-rāja-kṣetra*).
The Flower Treasury consists of twelve layers, rising high like a banner; it is the most lofty and vast of all. Therefore...
He was titled King Moonlight. Only upon first realizing the Dharma-body did he attain a body beyond death and transformation.
Within the Tathāgatagarbha, his nature merged with the true emptiness of the various fragrant water-seas; therein, the nature-water is true emptiness, and the nature-emptiness is true water.
Pure and inherently so, it pervades the entire Dharma-realm, flowing as a single flavor, such that even the characteristics of mutual conflict or competition were forgotten.
Thus it is. This [attainment] relies on the greatness of water to realize perfect penetration; only after meeting immeasurable Buddhas can one achieve success.
How could this be spoken of lightly? When Dongshan took his leave of Yunyan, as he was departing, he asked:

"After a hundred years, if someone suddenly asks whether you can still capture the true likeness of the Master, how would you respond? Yunyan remained silent for a long while and said: "Just this. Dongshan was struck with realization.
Yanguan said, "Reverend Jia, in taking up this matter, you must be extremely careful and discerning; I still harbor doubts.
Later, while crossing a stream, he beheld his reflection and attained great enlightenment. He composed a verse which says: "By all means, do not seek it from another;
To do so would distance it from me. Now I go forth alone, And everywhere I encounter It. It is now truly myself; I am now no longer..."
"This is the channel. You must understand it in this way before you can realize suchness (*tathatā*).
Only when Dongshan reaches this point does he attain the dissolution of self, his nature merging with the true void, being neither two nor distinct.
After the Boatman Monk had parted from his fellow practitioner Daowu, he said to Daowu: "In the future, if there is a sharp-witted lecturer, send one of them here. Daowu—
When I arrived at Jingkou, I encountered Jiaoshan ascending the hall. A monk asked, "What is the Dharma-body?
Jiaoshan replied, "The Dharma-body is without form. The monk asked, "What is the Dharma-eye? Jiaoshan replied, "The Dharma-eye is without flaw. Daowu could not help but laugh.
Jiaoshan then descended from his seat and asked Daowu, "Just now, when I responded to the monk’s words, I must—"
"There is something incorrect about this, which has caused the Venerable One to laugh. I hope the Venerable One will not withhold his compassion.
I said, "The Master was one who entered the world [to teach], yet he had no teacher. He went to visit the Boatman Master at Huating.
[The Master asked: "Did you find him? I replied, "This man has no tile to cover his head above, and no place to stick a锥 (chui-needle) into below."
Shan then changed his robes and went straight to Huating. As soon as Chuang-tzu saw him, he asked, "Virtuous One, in what monastery do you reside?
He replied, "As for a monastery, I do not reside in one; as for residing, it is not like that. Chuang-tzu asked, "If it is not like that, then what is it that is not like?"
He said, "It is not the Dharma of the present moment. The Master asked, "Where did you learn this? He replied, "It is not something reached by the ears or eyes.
The Master said, "A single phrase that fits the head is a tethering stake for ten thousand kalpas. Having thus exposed him, the boatman asked again.
"A thousand feet of dangling line; the intent lies in the deep pool. Three inches away from the hook—why do you not speak?

As Shanshan was about to open his mouth, the boatman struck him with a pole, knocking him into the water. Just as he climbed back onto the boat, the boatman said again, "Speak! Speak! As soon as Shanshan was about to open his mouth, he struck him once more.
At that moment, Jia Shan suddenly attained great enlightenment and nodded his head three times. The boatman said, "The line on the tip of the fishing rod—"
"From you, I play; not violating the clear waves, my intent is naturally distinct. These very points constitute the lineage transmission.

Zhaozhou then asked, "As for casting the line and throwing the hook, what is your intention, Master? The boatman replied, "A thread hangs in the green water; there is the meaning of whether it floats or sinks.
Zhaozhou said, "The words carry the profound yet there is no path; the tongue speaks, yet there is nothing spoken. The boatman said, "Fishing."
"Only when the waves of the Yangtze River have run dry will the golden-scaled fish finally be encountered. Mazu then covered his ears. The boatman said, "So it is, so it is!
You are truly a clever presiding master. He then instructed him, saying, "In the future, where you hide your body, there must be no trace;
where there is no trace, do not hide your body. For twenty years I was at Yaoshan, and I understood nothing other than this matter."
"Now that you have attained this, you must not dwell in cities or villages hereafter. Go instead into the deep mountains;
by the side of your mattock, seek out one or two [disciples] to carry on the lineage, ensuring it does not come to an end. Having said this, Jiashan took his leave and departed.
He looked back again and again. The boatman then called out, "Dharma-heir! Dharma-heir!
Jia Shan turned his head, and the boatman held up his oar and said, "You thought there was something else. Thereupon, he capsized the boat and entered the water, passing away.
Later, at Huating, there was the hermitage master Xingkong, who sent a letter to Chan Master Chishi of Xuedou, saying: "I shall undergo a water burial. Later, Chishi...
When he arrived, he saw that Xingkong was still alive. He mocked him with a verse, saying: "Alas, old Xingkong!

You insist on feeding fish and turtles. If you were going, you should have gone properly; instead, you do nothing but talk to people. Xingkong laughed and said, "I am waiting for my brother to come and bear witness.

He then announced this to the fourfold assembly. When the assembly had gathered, he preached the essentials of the Dharma and further spoke a verse: "To depart while sitting or to pass away while standing."
"It would be better to perform a water burial. First, it saves the firewood for cremation; second, it avoids the excavation of a grave.

To cast off one's hands and simply depart—how unimpeded and exhilarating! Who is the true connoisseur? The Monk-Fisher of old. Whose lofty spirit shall be inherited after a thousand years? Few sing his single strain of the fisherman’s song.
Thereupon, he sat cross-legged within the basin and drifted downstream with the current. The assembly followed him all the way to the seashore.
He hoped to blind himself. The Master took a plug to block the water and turned back; the crowd gathered to watch, but the water did not enter.
He then went downstream with the current, chanting: "The Boatman of old returned to his hometown; where his traces vanished, his subtlety is immeasurable.
The true wind rests solely with those who know the sound; he blows his iron flute crosswise to conclude the performance. The sound of the flute resounded.

He swallowed it. A moment later, amidst the vast expanse, he saw [the monk] cast his flute into the air and vanish. This truly demonstrates that those who have attained the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) allow the single flavor to flow through.
A monk asked Yunmen, "Is it true that the Buddha-dharma is like the moon reflected in water? Yunmen said:
"In the clear waves there is no path through. Yangshan asked, "From where did you enter, Master? Muzhou said, "If you ask again, from where would you come?
Yangshan asked, "At such a time as this, what is it like? Muzhou said, "Layer upon layer are the mountain passes; you must still go see the boatman before you will succeed."
The Dharma Prince Vairocanaraśmiprabha rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I recall that in the past, after kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, a Buddha appeared in the world named Amitaghoṣa.

He revealed to us the wondrous clarity of the Bodhisattvas' fundamental enlightenment, showing that this world and the bodies of sentient beings are all driven by the power of illusory conditions and wind. At that time, I...
At that time, I contemplated the establishment of the realms, the movement of the world, the motion and stillness of the body, and the thoughts and stirrings of the mind.
All such movements were non-dual and without distinction. I then realized the nature of these manifold movements: they come from nowhere and go nowhere.
The myriad sentient beings throughout the ten directions, as numerous as motes of dust, are all equally illusory. This extends even to the three thousand [great thousandfold worlds].

All sentient beings within the single world-system of the great trichiliocosm were like a hundred mosquitoes contained within a single vessel, chirping and clamoring in disorder, creating a frantic noise within a mere fraction of space.
Not long after encountering the Buddha, they attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

At that moment, their minds opened and they beheld the land of the Buddha Akṣobhya in the eastern quarter; there they became Dharma-princes, serving the Buddhas of the ten directions with body and mind.
"Radiant and penetrating, unimpeded. When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the Way, I observed that the power of wind has no basis;
through this, I awakened to the Bodhicitta and entered samādhi. Unifying with the Buddhas of the ten directions, I transmitted this single wondrous mind. This is the foremost."
The Master said: "In the East there is the Tathāgata Vairocana-prabhāsa (Lapis Lazuli Light). His vows and practices are no different from those of Amitābha.
This Dharma Prince should be like Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and others. Why then does he enter samādhi through the 'Wind-Power Without Support'?
The nature of wind is movement; because of movement there is sound. Therefore, he reveals himself to Bodhisattvas as 'Immeasurable Sound. Observe this."
The sentient beings of the world are like a hundred mosquitoes and gnats contained within a single vessel, chirping and clamoring in confusion;
all are driven by the power of the wind of delusive conditions. The movement of this wind is most subtle, yet its power is greatest, pervading the entire dharma-realm.
There is nowhere it does not pervade. It is like the movement and stillness of the body, or the stirring of thoughts in the mind—these are near and visible.
It is like the transformation of the realms or the circulation of the world—these are distant and invisible.
Whether visible or invisible, they are all equally this movement. This very nature of movement comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; it is all-pervasive.

Pervading the entire world, it has no location; because it has no location, it is fundamentally without arising or ceasing. Because it is without arising or ceasing, it is fundamentally immovable from the outset.
By observing in this way, one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), whereby one awakens to Bodhi and enters samādhi.
This is precisely the nature of immovability existing within movement; it is not that one must depart from movement to find something else.
This refers to immovability. The East corresponds to the trigram Zhen, which signifies movement. Yet, in the East lies the Buddha-land of Akṣobhya (the Immovable), which is movement within stillness;
this is precisely the principle of the wondrous luminosity of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-bodhi*). The nature of enlightenment is wondrously luminous and fundamentally non-moving;

fundamental enlightenment is luminously wondrous, such that it is without movement even amidst movement. To speak of these in their various combinations, they are all one wondrous True Suchness (*tathatā*).
In essence, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions share this single wondrous mind. If one seeks stillness apart from movement, it is no longer wondrous.
Innate enlightenment is firm and luminous; when the wind and metal rub against each other, light shines like lapis lazuli, penetrating all things with unimpeded clarity.

He transmits a single wondrous mind; not only does he personally realize perfect penetration, but he causes all sentient beings in the world who possess this nature of movement to likewise realize perfect penetration.
When the novice Gao first visited Yaoshan, the Master asked, "Where have you come from?
He replied, "From Mount Heng. The Master asked, "Where are you going? He replied, "I am going to Jiangling to receive the full precepts. The Master said, "Regarding receiving the precepts..."
"What do you seek? he asked. "To escape birth and death," [Gao] replied. "There is one person who does not receive the precepts, and for whom there is no birth and death to escape.
Do you know this yet? At these words, Gao attained great enlightenment. He said, "If that is so, then what use are the Buddha’s precepts?
Mount Shan said, "This novice still has them hanging from his lips and teeth. Gao bowed and withdrew. Daowu then arrived.
They stood in attendance. Master Shàn said, "Just now there was a limping śrāmaṇera who seemed to have some measure of spiritual breath.

I said, 'Do not yet place full trust in him; you must further examine him before you can be certain. That evening, as he ascended the hall for the formal lecture, the Master called out, 'Where was that śrāmaṇera from this morning?
Gāo stepped forward from among the assembly and stood there. The Master asked, 'I hear that Chang'an is very noisy.'"
"Do you still know? Gao replied, "My country is at peace. Shanshan said with joy, "Did you obtain this from reading the sutras, or did you obtain it from seeking instruction?
Gao said, "I obtained it neither from reading the sutras nor from seeking instruction. Shanshan said:
"There are many who do not read the scriptures and do not seek instruction; why is it that they do not attain [realization]? Gaofeng said, "I do not say they cannot attain it;
it is simply that they themselves are unwilling to take responsibility. Shan turned back and said to Daowu and Yunyan, "Do not disbelieve what I have said."
Touzi’s verse says: "Rising and falling, clouds go and clouds come; He has no land, and is free from all dust.
Upon the summit of Mount Sumeru grows rootless grass; It does not wait for the spring breeze to bloom.
If a śrāmaṇera perceives this, he sees the Land of Akṣobhya Buddha in the East, unswayed by the winds of delusive conditions. Magu held his staff.
He went to Zhangjing, circumambulated the meditation seat three times, struck his mendicant’s staff once, and stood there upright. Zhangjing said, "It is so; it is so.
He then went to Nanquan, circumambulated the meditation seat three times, struck his mendicant’s staff once, and stood there upright.
Nanquan said, "It is not so; it is not so. Gu said, "Zhangjing said it was so; why did you say it was not?"
Quán said: "Zhāngjìng is precisely this; it is you who are not. This is turned by the power of the wind; in the end, it will fall into ruin. Tiantóng’s verse says:
"It is you who are not—look well at the rolled-up sleeves! It seems suppressed, yet it seems raised; a difficult elder brother, a difficult younger brother.
To let go—when he arrives at that moment, to seize it—why do I act so abruptly? One shake of the golden staff is too much!"
Stands alone in majesty. He circles the meditation seat three times, strolling at ease. The monastic groves are in turmoil, and right and wrong arise.
One might imagine seeing ghosts before a skeleton. Xuedou’s verse says: "This is wrong, that is wrong; one must avoid picking them up and discarding them.

The waves of the four seas have smoothed over, and the tides of the hundred rivers have receded. The ancient staff’s wind is high across the twelve gates; in every gate there is a path, yet all is empty and desolate."

It is not desolate. The author is fond of seeking "medicine for those who are not ill. If one knows this medicine for those who are not ill, then the disputes of the monastic community will not arise, and one will not be turned by the power of the winds.
The Bodhisattva Gaganagañja rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"In the presence of the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, I attained the Boundless Body (*anantakāya*). At that time, I held four great precious jewels in my hands, which illuminated as many Buddha-fields as there are motes of dust throughout the ten directions, transforming them into empty space.
Furthermore, within my own mind, I manifested a great round mirror, from within which I emitted ten—"
The light of various subtle and wondrous jewels flows and permeates the ten directions, reaching to the very limits of space.
All the lands of the Sovereign Banners enter within the mirror and penetrate my body; my body becomes identical to empty space, without mutual obstruction.

My body is able to skillfully enter lands as small as motes of dust, extensively performing the Buddha-work and attaining great accordance. This great spiritual power arises from my contemplation that the four elements are...

"Based on this, deluded thoughts arise and perish; yet empty space is non-dual, and the Buddha-lands are fundamentally the same. By illuminating this sameness, I attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, I replied: 'By contemplating the boundlessness of empty space, I entered *samādhi*.
Its wondrous power is perfectly luminous; this is the foremost.'"
The Master said: "The Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha has already, together with the Tathāgata, realized the three bodies and four wisdoms at the abode of Dīpaṃkara Buddha.
Among the three bodies, he emphasizes the Dharmakāya; therefore, it is said that he attained the boundless body. Among the four wisdoms, he emphasizes the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom;
therefore, it is said that he further manifested the Great Perfect Mirror within his own mind as the boundless Dharmakāya."
Space is boundless; how is it able to coexist with the four great elements without mutual obstruction?

This is truly because one observes that the four great elements have no basis and that their material substance is entirely empty. These pure great elements are like precious jewels, through the power of contemplative observation.
It illuminates the ten directions and transforms into empty space; that is, the four great elements become empty space, and empty space becomes the Dharma-body.
What obstruction could there be? Originally it is the one Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom; why then does it emit ten kinds of precious light?

This is truly because the ten *pāramitās* have been cultivated to such a subtle and perfect completion that they all manifest with sovereign clarity within the mirror, flowing and permeating the ten directions to the very limits of empty space, yet remaining entirely subsumed by this single mirror. This mirror is the body;
the body is the mirror. The three bodies (*trikāya*) are the four wisdoms (*caturjñāna*); the four wisdoms are the three bodies. Body and wisdom—
They are mutually integrated; mind and environment are both transformed. Therefore, it is said that the various kingly banners of the lands come within one's realm and enter into one's own body.
Light and shadow interpenetrate, such that they cannot be distinguished. Since the body is solely wisdom, it is identical to empty space and does not create mutual obstruction.
Since wisdom is solely the body, one is able to skillfully enter the lands and extensively perform Buddha-works, thereby expounding the three [vehicles].
The method of the vehicle attains great accordance and follows the capacities of the four *siddhāntas*. One views the arising and ceasing of delusive thoughts as being identical to empty space;
empty space and the arising and ceasing of delusive thoughts are non-dual. One views the land as being identical to Buddha-nature.
Buddha-nature and the buddha-land are not distinct. Principle does not obstruct phenomena, and phenomena do not obstruct principle.

By illuminating this identity, one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and realizes the boundless body of empty space. With wondrous power perfected and luminous, the body and the lands mutually interpenetrate.
It is simply a matter of realizing the Dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena (*li-shi wu-ai fajie*).
If mirrors reflect one another in infinite layers like Indra’s net, such that the one is all and all is one, this is the Dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between phenomena (*shi-shi wu-ai fajie*).
It is not that the Tathāgata has failed to realize this; even the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha remains among the ranks of his disciples because he was still hindered by [clinging to] empty space.
Regarding the "limitless realms" (*anantya-āyatana*): because a body can still be perceived there. Huangbo said: "The Buddha’s true Dharma-body is like empty space.

This metaphor indicates that the Dharma-body is precisely empty space, and empty space is precisely the Dharma-body. Ordinary people say that the Dharma-body pervades the realm of empty space, or that empty space contains the Dharma-body;
they do not realize that the Dharma-body is precisely empty space, and empty space is precisely [the Dharma-body].
It is the Dharmakāya. If one definitively asserts that space exists, space is not the Dharmakāya;
if one definitively asserts that the Dharmakāya exists, the Dharmakāya is not space. However, do not interpret it as being merely space; space is itself the Dharmakāya.
Do not form an interpretation of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). The Dharma-body is itself empty space; empty space and the Dharma-body have no distinct characteristics.
Buddhas and sentient beings have no distinct characteristics; birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and nirvāṇa have no distinct characteristics.
To be free from all characteristics is itself the Buddha. If you understand these words of Baizhang, you will truly see the boundless body of the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja. —Cao Shan.
He asked Elder De, “The Buddha’s true Dharma-body is like empty space; it manifests forms in response to things, like the moon reflected in water.
How do you explain this principle of ‘responding’? De said, “It is like a donkey looking down a well.
Shan said, “Your explanation is quite thorough, yet you have only explained it eighty percent. De asked, “And how about you, Master? Shan replied, “It is like...”
The well gazes at the donkey. Tiantong’s verse says: The donkey gazes at the well; the well gazes at the donkey. Wisdom encompasses all without limit; stillness contains all with abundance.
Who among them holds the seal behind the elbow? Within the house, no books are kept. The shuttle-head is not entangled by the warp and woof.

The patterns of its expression range freely, and its meaning is inherently distinct. By clarifying this, one may know how to skillfully enter the lands. It is like looking at a donkey from within a well:
it is fundamentally unborn, and thus merges with empty space.
Maitreya Bodhisattva then rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I recall that in the past, after the passage of kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Candrasūryapradīpa. From that Buddha I went forth into homelessness;

yet my mind was heavy with worldly fame, and I delighted in frequenting the houses of the noble families. At that time, the World-Honored One instructed me to practice the cultivation of mind-only consciousness."
In meditative concentration, I entered samādhi. Throughout kalpas past, by means of this samādhi, I served Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;

the mind seeking worldly fame ceased and was extinguished, leaving nothing behind. When Dīpaṃkara Buddha appeared in the world, I then attained the unsurpassed, wondrously perfect samādhi of the cognitive mind.
Even throughout all the lands of the Tathāgatas in the entirety of space—whether pure or defiled, existent or non-existent—all are my own.

"O Bhagavān, these are manifested through the transformations of the mind. Because I have realized that all is but mind-consciousness (*citta-vijñāna*), immeasurable Tathāgatas flow forth from the nature of consciousness.

I have now received the prediction that I shall succeed the Buddha in his place. When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration [of the Dharma], I said: 'I have clearly observed that the ten directions are but consciousness;

the mind of consciousness is perfectly luminous, entering the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), and having distanced itself from the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the grasping of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*'), I have attained [this realization]."
The patience regarding non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)—this is the foremost. [Dong] said:
"I have observed with clarity that the ten directions are consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*). These two characters, 'consciousness-only,' possess profound implications.

'Only' (*mātra*) excludes the existence of external objects; 'consciousness' (*vijñapti*) distinguishes the emptiness of the mind. Furthermore, the term 'consciousness' generally manifests [the nature of reality], while 'only' merely excludes [external objects]. Regarding 'generally manifesting':"

This refers to all sentient beings, each of whom possesses eight consciousnesses, six categories of mental factors (*caitta*), as well as the perceived and perceiving aspects (*nimitta-bhāga* and *darśana-bhāga*) that they transform, along with their various modalities and the suchness (*tathatā*) revealed by the principle of emptiness.

Since all such phenomena do not exist apart from consciousness, the name "consciousness" is used here to manifest them collectively. The term "only" (*mātra*) serves merely to negate the deluded attachment of ordinary beings to a mind that exists apart from consciousness.
Externally, there truly exist phenomena such as form and so forth; therefore, the statement "only" (*kevala*) merely negates the views of the ignorant.

When the mind of consciousness is perfectly luminous, one enters the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (the perfected nature). By initially practicing the concentration on consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), one proceeds until the attainment of the unsurpassed, wondrously perfect samādhi of the mind of consciousness.
Having thus transformed consciousness into wisdom, it is said that one "enters the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*. [This has not yet been completed.]
When the evolving consciousnesses arise, the first is bound by objects; this is a coarse affliction called the grasping of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*).

Subsequently, it is bound by phenomena; this is a subtle affliction called the grasping of the dependent nature (*paratantra*). Seeking worldly fame is the prototype of the grasping of pervasive conceptualization;
the cessation and non-existence of the mind that seeks worldly fame is the prototype of the grasping of the dependent nature. This concludes.
Thus, because it is solely mind and consciousness, the nature of consciousness flows forth as immeasurable Tathāgatas; this is the model for the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

The *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* states: "The person with cataracts is like the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); the appearance of blue, yellow, and so forth is like the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*)."
The *Ratnāvalī* states: "It is like a person who sees a moving object and thinks it is a snake; after looking at it for a long time, they realize it is merely a rope.
Although the mind that suspected it was a snake does not cease immediately, it subsides of its own accord. This is like being free from the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature).
Yet the rope still remains. Then, upon closer inspection, one says: 'This is not a rope; it is simply hemp. Thus, the grasping at the rope [is abandoned]."
The mind, moreover, ceases of its own accord without being severed. This is like the relinquishing of attachment to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Hemp and rope are fundamentally one: when there is a knot, it is called "rope"; when there is no knot, it is called "hemp. By this analogy, nature and consciousness are fundamentally one:

when there is bondage, it is called "consciousness"; when there is no bondage, it is called "nature. Upon reaching the realization of *vijñapti-mātratā* (consciousness-only), there is no nature apart from consciousness; consciousness itself is [the nature].
"Nature" refers to the wondrous true *tathatā*-nature of the eighth consciousness, the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Since it is free from both the dependent and the imputed attachments, the seeds of birth and death are melted away, and one relies upon the true nature that is neither born nor extinguished.
Thus, one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). All lands—whether pure or defiled, existent or non-existent—are merely transformations of my own mind.
Manifesting yet non-discriminating, one attains quiescence in that very place; this is the realization of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) regarding the division of marks.

From the nature of consciousness flow forth immeasurable Tathāgatas: principle is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), wisdom is the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*), and practice is the Transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
Wisdom is Mañjuśrī, practice is Samantabhadra, and compassion is Avalokiteśvara—all of which flow from the one mind.

When one emerges from this, there is no discrimination; it is immediately and right where it is quiescent and extinguished. This is the direct realization of the patience regarding non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) within the aspect of seeing.
The *Dharmacakṣus-gāthā* says: “The three realms are mind-only. The eye [perceives] sound, and the ear [perceives] form. Form does not reach the ear; how then can sound touch the eye?

The eye, form, ear, and sound— All phenomena are thus established. If all phenomena were not dependent on conditions, How could they be observed as being like illusions? Mountains, rivers, and so forth...”
The Great Earth: what is firm and what changes? Because the Dharma-eye, consciousness, and mind are perfectly luminous, one is able to utter these perfect words.
Panshan gave this instruction: "In the three realms there is no dharma; where can one seek the mind? The four elements are fundamentally empty;
upon what does the Buddha rely to dwell? The celestial sphere does not move; it is still and silent, leaving no trace. Face-to-face presentation—there is nothing more. Xuedou [commented].
The verse says: "No phenomena exist within the three realms; where can one seek the mind? White clouds form a canopy, flowing water serves as a zither. One or two strains, no one understands;
After the rain has passed, the autumn waters in the night pond are deep. Furthermore, a monk asked Shishuang:
"I do not ask about the time when ten thousand doors are all closed; what is it like when ten thousand doors are all open? Shishuang said: "The matter within the hall."
"How so? The monk had no reply. After half a year, he finally managed to say, "No one can receive him.
Xuefeng said, "You have spoken quite well, but you have only reached eighty percent. The monk asked, "How about you, Master? Xuefeng said: [The text ends here.]
"No one recognizes him. Touzi’s verse says: "The ancient hall opens upon the cliffs as the moon locks the pines; frost gathers and snow falls, its resonance inexhaustible.
Before the stars, a person lies within the chamber of a thousand peaks; Buddhas and patriarchs have no means to recognize him.
Maitreya Bodhisattva cultivated the samādhi of mind-only consciousness and entered *samādhi*. Now, where does Panshan say he is?

"Seeking the mind. Shishuang said, "No one recognizes him. These two turning words await his descent in a future age to succeed the Buddha in his position, where he will expound them in ever-deepening detail.
The Dharma Prince Mahāsthāmaprāpta, together with fifty-two bodhisattvas of his same rank, rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I recall that in the past, during kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there appeared a Buddha in the world named Amitābha.
Twelve Tathāgatas followed one after another for the duration of a single kalpa; the last of these Buddhas was named Sūryaprabhācandraprabhābhibhū."
That Buddha taught me the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha. It is like this: suppose there is one person who is single-mindedly mindful and another who is single-mindedly forgetful;
such two people may meet yet not meet, or see yet not see. Because these two people are mindful of each other, their mutual mindfulness is profound.
In this way, from birth to birth, they are like a form and its shadow, never diverging or differing from one another.

The Tathāgatas of the ten directions cherish and pity sentient beings as a mother remembers her child. If the child has run away, what can the mother’s remembrance accomplish? But if the child remembers the mother...
Just as when a mother remembers her child, the mother and child will not be separated throughout their successive lives;

so too, if sentient beings remember the Buddha and recite his name, they will certainly see the Buddha in the present and in the future. They will be near to the Buddha, and without relying on expedient means, their own minds will naturally open.
Just as a person who has been perfumed with incense carries the fragrance of that scent upon their body, this is called "Adornment of Fragrant Light.

When I was originally on the causal ground, I entered the patience of non-arising through the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha; now, within this world-realm, I gather those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha and lead them back to my Pure Land.

When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the Way, I made no selection among them; rather, I gathered all six sense faculties into one, maintaining a continuous flow of pure mindfulness, thereby attaining samādhi—this is the foremost method.

Tong said: "The *Amitābha Sūtra* states that with the light of wisdom, one universally illumines all things; now, having escaped the three miserable realms and attained supreme power, he is named Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
There are fifty-two bodhisattvas of his same rank, which is sufficient proof that those who attain rebirth in the Pure Land achieve it with ease.
Furthermore, as for those who practice nianfo, they must not fail to do so for even the duration of a finger-snap."

The five worldly desires are what bind one’s mindfulness. When pure mindfulness succeeds itself continuously—like a child remembering its mother—one will certainly see the Buddha in the present and the future.

With the mouth reciting and the mind remembering, the ears and eyes focused on nothing else, one’s deportment solemn and dignified, fully gathering the six sense faculties, the single mind remains undisturbed.
Within such *samādhi*, seeing the Buddha is certain; one will not be far from the Buddha.
The light of wisdom blazes forth; without relying on deliberate cultivation, one spontaneously attains awakening. It is like a person who has been perfumed with incense:
they do not expect to become fragrant, yet they naturally do so. This power of Amitābha’s vows is wondrous and inconceivable.

Having already attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) through the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha, Mahāsthāmaprāpta further gathers those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha and leads them back to the Pure Land. Thus, he awakens himself and awakens others—truly...
In the practice of the Bodhisattva, the six sense faculties all belong to the seeing portion (*darśana-bhāga*). Since this emphasizes seeing the Buddha, it subsumes them under the "Great Seeing.
Why is the Great Seeing placed after the Great Consciousness? It is because one must transform the eighth consciousness to realize the subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*).

Only after this can one transform the preceding five consciousnesses. Once the consciousnesses have been transformed into wisdom and one has been born into a Buddha-land, that constitutes the ultimate fruit.

Yet, why does Avalokiteśvara’s "turning back the hearing" follow even after that? Now, the reason for valuing birth in a pure land and the realization of perfect penetration is not merely for one's own liberation, but for the sake of delivering sentient beings. It must be as [described in] the thirty-two...
It should be that wherever one may be, all places become pure lands and one realizes perfect penetration; only then will one fulfill their allotted measure.
Chan Master Yongming Shou recited the Lotus Sūtra from his youth, reading five lines at once, and finished it in sixty days.
Later, he visited National Teacher Shaor to clarify the essentials of the mind, and subsequently went to Zhiyi’s Rock on Mount Tiantai to practice for ninety days.
He was settled in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). A bird once built its nest in his *kaṣāya* robe. He once prepared two lots:

one said, "Dwell in meditative concentration for life," and the other said, "Recite the sutras and adorn the Pure Land with myriad virtues. He then focused his mind and prayed with diligence; upon reaching the seventh attempt, he drew the lot for "reciting the sutras and myriad virtues" each time.
Thereupon, he devoted himself exclusively to the practice of the Pure Land. After three years of reciting the sutras, he saw [a vision] within his meditative contemplation.
Avalokiteśvara poured nectar into his mouth, whereupon he attained eloquence. King Zhongyi invited him to reside at Lingyin;
after two years, he moved to Yongming. He recited one hundred and eight items daily, never failing for even a moment. Students came to seek his instruction and inquiry.
He took the pointing to the mind as his school and enlightenment as his standard. At sunset, he would go to a separate peak to practice the Way and recite the Buddha’s name.
King Zhongyi sighed, saying, "Since antiquity, there has never been one who sought the Western Paradise with such single-minded intensity.

He then established for him the Xifang Xiangyan Hall (Western Paradise Incense-Veneration Hall) to fulfill his aspiration. His disciples numbered one thousand seven hundred; he once [practiced] together with the assembly.
He received the Bodhisattva precepts, offered food to ghosts and spirits, and released living beings during the day; he dedicated all these acts toward the adornment of the Pure Land.

He transcribed one hundred scrolls titled *Zongjing* (The Mirror of the Source), and further composed the *Wanshan Tonggui* (The Convergence of Myriad Good Deeds) pointing the way back to the Pure Land.
After he had passed into extinction, a stupa was erected on the mountain. A monk came from Linchuan and said:
"While I was ill, I entered the underworld and was granted permission to return. I saw a statue of a monk in a hall, to which King Yama himself came to pay homage.
I asked who this image was, and the presiding official replied, 'This is Chan Master Shou of Hangzhou. Upon hearing this, I attained rebirth in the highest grade in the Western Paradise."
He was reborn. Because the King revered this man, he paid him homage here. Yang Jie, whose courtesy name was Cigong, was the younger brother of Da-nian.
The consort of the Prince of Jing also saw him in a dream sitting upon a lotus flower, appearing carefree and self-possessed.
Once, while Cigong beheld the sun rising like a platter surging forth, he attained awakening and composed a verse, which said: "When a man grows up, he must..."

Marriage. When a woman reaches maturity, she must be married; what leisure time could there be for further discussing talk of non-arising? [This was] intended to overturn the case against Master Pang.
Later, his verse on departing this world said: "There is nothing to be attached to, and nothing to be abandoned. Within the great void,"
"Zhi-hu-ze-er. To take a wrong turn and follow it. "Western Paradise of Ultimate Bliss"—this refers to Yongming Yanshou and Cigong being reborn together in the Pure Land.
This is as clear as day. As for the Samādhi of Buddha-recitation, it is like a child yearning for its mother.
Dongshan said: "I told you not to go; returning now, you have turned your back on your father. A monk asked Caoshan: "The child returns to join the father—why [is this so]?"
The monk paid no attention at all. Shanshan said, "It is only fitting that it should be so. The monk asked, "Where is the bond between father and son?
Shanshan said, "Only then is the bond between father and son established. The monk asked, "What is the bond between father and son? Shanshan said:

"A blade or axe cannot split it open. Tiantong took up this saying and said: "The emerald curtain hangs down; the imperial decree has not yet been issued. The purple silk screen is closed; sight and hearing cannot penetrate.
To stir even a hair’s breadth is to invite disaster. When the moon rises at the night gate, one takes a secret step forward and the crane emerges from its silver cage.
Do you know? Shedding oneself from the single color leaves no trace; not sitting in the same wind avoids falling into a great error."
[Case] Again, a monk asked Hugu: "What is one's original parent? Hugu said, "One whose head does not turn white.
The monk said, "With what do you offer them? Hugu said, "Sincere, rice-less meals; in the hall, one does not inquire after kin. Danxia’s verse says:
"Stepping out the door, the entire world has no known kin; Entering the room, what fills the eyes is not one's parents. In the empty chamber..."

In the cold of night, what else is there? The azure sky and the bright moon serve as its neighbors. These two lines clearly elucidate the Amitābha of one’s own nature and the Pure Land of the sole mind.
One must perceive it in this way; only then can it be called "true seeing. Long ago, there was a nun who paid homage to Yunyan.
Yunyan asked, “Is your father still alive? The nun replied, “He is. Yunyan asked, “How old is he? The nun said—
"Sixty-five. Yankou said, "You have a father who is not sixty-five years old; do you know him yet?
The nun asked, "Is it this one who comes in such a manner? Yankou said, "One who comes in such a manner is still but a descendant.
Dongshan said, "Even one who does not come in such a manner is likewise a descendant. Alas! The original parents—"
Is this not easy to perceive? Therefore, one who can see their original parents sees the Amitābha of self-nature;
thus, Chan and the Pure Land are fused as one, both belonging to the inconceivable realm.
The sixth fascicle of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* (Lengyan jing) states: "From hearing, reflection, and cultivation, one enters samādhi. Initially, within hearing, one enters the flow and loses the object.
Once that which is entered has become still, the two characteristics of movement and stillness clearly cease to arise. In this way, gradually..."

Increase. When that which is heard is exhausted, one does not abide even in that exhaustion of hearing. When that which is perceived is realized as empty, emptiness and perception reach ultimate perfection.

When both emptiness and that which is emptied are extinguished, birth and death are extinguished, and quiescent extinction manifests before one. This is the gateway through which Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva entered the Way.
Its principle is profoundly subtle and refined, beyond the reach of verbal explanation. Once, while conversing with Dharma Master Qian about this, there was—
Regarding the flavor [of this teaching], I shall briefly describe it here.

What is meant by "entering samādhi through hearing, contemplation, and cultivation" refers to contemplating from the point of returning the hearing, cultivating from the point of returning the hearing, and thereby entering from the point of returning the hearing until one reaches the ground of right concentration, which is neither arising nor ceasing.
This samādhi is fundamentally without movement; it is profoundly still and eternally quiescent. It is only because...

The auditory object (śabda-viṣaya) stimulates it; the faculty of hearing (śrotra-indriya) adheres to the profound stillness and emerges from it. Consequently, one hears sounds and pursues them, flowing along until one forgets the source. One is then far removed from *samādhi*.
Only by entering through hearing, reflection, and cultivation does one realize that the nature of hearing is itself the Principle (*li*).
Reflection is Wisdom (*jñāna*); cultivation is Practice (*caryā*). When these three virtues—Principle, Wisdom, and Practice—are perfectly integrated, they are simultaneously and entirely present.
Therefore, with a single instance of hearing, reflection is contained therein; with a single instance of hearing, cultivation is contained therein.

Reflection and cultivation give rise to sagely wisdom from this turning-back of hearing. Step by step one returns to the Truth, progressing through stage after stage, as detailed in the subsequent text.
This is the sequence for entering *samādhi*. First, within the midst of hearing, one turns the flow back...
Entering. One does not enter through the sensory object of sound, but enters the stream of the sages; thus one relies upon the self-nature and externally loses its locus.
Every stimulus from the sensory object of sound must have its locus; now, though the locus is lost, one is still not yet tranquil.
When the sound moves, one perceives a moving aspect and desires to lose it; when the sound is still, one perceives...
I desire to pursue the characteristic of stillness, yet these two characteristics remain distinct;

thus, I have not yet attained quiescence. Only by following the path of non-abiding can one reach the ground of profound stillness. Therein, that which moves moves of its own accord, and I do not know its movement.

From what source does the characteristic of movement arise? That which is still is still of its own accord, and I do not know its stillness. From what source does the characteristic of stillness arise?
It arises because there is ultimately nowhere for it to go. Not only is the characteristic of motion unattainable, but the characteristic of stillness is likewise unattainable.
These two characteristics—motion and stillness—are the objects perceived by the faculty of hearing; they are certainly the realm of what is heard.

When these two characteristics do not arise, they are clearly and vividly understood to be, moreover, the faculty of hearing itself. It is easy to lose the object of hearing, but difficult to lose the subject that hears.
The capacity to hear undergoes difficulty. Thus it gradually increases, progressing without ceasing. Once its object is lost, its faculty is further lost;
then both the capacity to hear and the object heard are exhausted together. That which is heard is the sense-object of sound (*śabda-viṣaya*).
From the loss of its object, one gradually reaches the exhaustion of what is heard; when there is nothing further to be heard, the sense-object of sound vanishes. As for the capacity to hear...
The faculty of hearing is the root. From the initial entry into the stream, one gradually reaches the point where the capacity to hear is exhausted;

when there is no longer any one who hears, the faculty of hearing has vanished. When both the faculty and its object vanish together, one returns to the ground of exhaustion. If there were a "mark of exhaustion" to be grasped, that would be attachment to emptiness.
If one dwells in emptiness, although one may have attained the emptiness of the perceived, one has not yet attained the emptiness of the perceiver. Now, externally...

Exhausting all dust, exhausting the internal faculties—thus exhausting even hearing without dwelling in or clinging to it, then not only is that which is perceived empty, but the perceiver is also empty.
