At the bottom of the mechanism, it is continuous—there naturally exists the golden needle and jade thread. Before the seal, it is vast and expansive—originally there is no bird-script.
The "Insect Script" (Chongwen). This uses the golden-winged bird (garuḍa) to elucidate the matter of the upward direction; that is, there is none who can rival it.
Therefore, the golden-winged bird should be considered the foremost among those who preach the Dharma.
If there are kinnaras who desire to be liberated from their kind, I manifest before them in the form of a kinnara and preach the Dharma for them,
causing them to achieve success.
Tong said: "Kiṃnara" means "the doubtful person" (疑人). Because they have human bodies but with horns, those who see them doubt their nature.
They are the deities of the Dharma-music of the Heavenly Emperor. While the Gandharvas play the music of the mundane world, the Kiṃnaras play the music of the supramundane world.
Leaning against [their instruments], they play upon the Four Noble Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, and the Six Pāramitās.
The Dharma cannot be compared to worldly pleasures. Formerly, at the Shaolin Monastery, the sacred precinct manifested supernatural power:
the Buddha spanned Mount Tai and Mount Shao with his two feet and, wielding a staff, struck down the bandits. The bandits were terrified and fled in disarray, not daring to enter the monastery.

For this reason, the monks of the monastery mostly practiced boxing and staff-fighting. Whenever they were mobilized for military expeditions, they would simply recite the name of the Bodhisattva Kinnara-raja.
He was renowned by this name; relying upon it, he was without fear and frequently defeated his opponents. Some say he was an emanation of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
While Fengxue was serving as the garden head under Nanyuan, one day Nanyuan went to the garden and asked, "How do you deliberate upon 'a single blow from the South'?
Fengxue replied, "I deliberate upon it as something extraordinary. After a long silence, Fengxue then...
Xue asked, "How do you resolve this matter here, Preceptor? Nan-yuan raised his staff and said, "Under the staff there is no patience with birth;
when confronting the situation, the teacher is not seen. At this, Xue attained sudden and great enlightenment.
While few have transmitted the staff-method of Linji, the staff-method of Kinnara has been discussed without end until the present day. Is there something different about it? Or is there not?
It is because they are different.
For example, there are mahoragas who delight in being liberated from their own kind;
before them, I manifest the body of a mahoraga and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve accomplishment.
Tong said: "Mahoraga; this translates as 'Great Python' or 'one who crawls on its belly. It is also called the dragon that guards the grounds of the *kālāma* (monastery).
When the Thirteenth Patriarch, Venerable Kāpimāra, was traveling several li through the mountains, he encountered a great python.
The Patriarch walked straight ahead without looking back. The python coiled itself around the Patriarch’s body, whereupon the Patriarch bestowed upon it the Three Refuges."
Having heard this, they departed. When Nanyue Huairang arrived at the stone cave, an old man dressed in plain white robes came out, joined his palms in greeting, and paid his respects.
The Master asked, "Where do you reside? He replied, "In the past, I was often a bhikṣu who greatly delighted in solitude.
However, many beginners would come to seek my instruction; I grew weary of responding to them and gave rise to thoughts of resentment. Consequently, when my life ended, I fell [into this state]."

“I have been in the form of a python, dwelling in this cave for a thousand years. Having just encountered the Venerable One and been able to hear the Dharma of the precepts, I have come to offer my thanks.
The Patriarch asked, “Are there any other inhabitants living on this mountain?
He replied, “Ten li from here, there is a great tree that provides shade for five hundred great nāgas. The king of those trees is named Nāgārjuna, and he constantly serves the nāgas.”

"The assembly is preaching the Dharma; I have come here merely to listen. The Patriarch then proceeded there. Nāgārjuna came out to meet him and said, "This deep mountain is desolate and lonely, a dwelling place for dragons and pythons.
Great Virtue, Most Honored One, why have you deigned to trouble your divine feet? The Patriarch replied, "I am not a most honored one; I have come to visit a worthy man.
Nāgārjuna thought to himself, "This master has attained the nature of certainty and possesses the clear eye of the Way."
"No," [the Master] replied. "Is this the Great Sage continuing the True Vehicle? The Patriarch said, "Though you speak with your mind, I already know it with my mind.
Simply prepare for ordination; why worry that I am not a sage? Upon hearing this, Nāgārjuna repented and apologized.

The Patriarch immediately granted him and five hundred dragon followers the tonsure and conferred the full precepts upon them all. He transmitted the Dharma verse, saying: "The Dharma is neither hidden nor manifest."
This is called the true limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). To awaken to this law of concealment and manifestation is neither through folly nor through wisdom.
Precisely because it is neither folly nor wisdom, even dragons and pythons can attain liberation.
If there are sentient beings who delight in being humans or who cultivate themselves as humans, I manifest in a human body to preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve their goal.
Generally speaking, among the fourfold assembly—consisting of kings, ministers, elders, and householders—who is not a human?

Furthermore, there are those who delight in cultivating themselves as human beings; this refers to those among the scholar, farmer, artisan, and merchant who have no intention of pursuing the Three Vehicles.
They are fully endowed with Buddha-nature, yet they remain unaware of it throughout their entire lives while preaching the Dharma.
Once, when Chan Master Panshan Ji was walking through a marketplace, he saw a customer buying pork and said to the butcher:
"Bring me one *jin* of the finest meat. The butcher set down his knife, joined his palms, and said, "Magistrate, which of these is not the finest?
At this, the Master attained realization. On another day, as he was leaving the gate, he saw a funeral procession being carried out.
A singer shook his bell and sang: "The crimson wheel is certain to sink to the west; I know not to which realm the soul has departed. Below the curtain...
The filial son wept, crying out, "Alas! Alas! Suddenly, the Master’s body and mind leaped with joy. Upon returning, he related this to Mazu, who gave his seal of approval.
Formerly, when Baoshou was serving as the *kōmyō-shu* (offering master) at Baoshou Temple, he asked, "Before your parents were born, bring me back your original face.
The Master stood there until deep into the night; his response did not accord with the truth. The following day—
The Master was about to take his leave. Baoshou asked, "Where are you going? The Master replied, "Yesterday I received the Master’s questions, but I did not find them to my satisfaction.
I am going south to study under other teachers. Baoshou said, "In the south, summer retreats are observed but winter retreats are not.
Here, we observe winter retreats but not summer retreats. You should stay here for the summer as a wandering monk (*pindadāra*). As for the Buddha-dharma—" [He left the sentence unfinished.]
Amidst the bustling crowds and vast red dust, he constantly preached the True Dharma, and his disciples did not dare to disobey him.
One day, seeing two people quarreling on the street, he struck out a single fist and said, "How can you be so shameless? At that moment, the Master attained great enlightenment.
He rushed to see Baoshou; before he could utter a word, Baoshou said, "You understand! There is no need to speak."
The Master then paid his respects. These two instances show that one need only manifest in human form to be able to preach the Dharma;
why must it necessarily be a Great Being who manifests [in such a way] before something is accomplished?
If there are non-human beings— whether with form or without form, with perception or without perception— who delight in transcending their own kind,
I shall manifest my body before them all and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve accomplishment.

The Master said: "Devas and Nāgas are called 'emerging. Devas can weary of pleasure, and Nāgas can fear suffering; they naturally possess a path for emerging [from saṃsāra] and are the easiest to deliver.
Gandharvas and others are called 'liberating. Bound by karmic retribution, they are the most difficult to liberate.
Non-humans (amanuṣya) and Yakṣas are called 'crossing. Having already sunk into profound suffering, as if submerged in a great ocean, they must necessarily be delivered by means of a raft."
All are equally called "liberated," yet the difficulty or ease of their liberation varies in this way.
Those that are formless but possess consciousness are spirits, ghosts, and numinous essences. Those that have form but lack consciousness are earth, wood, metal, and stone.
The Yogi, the Flaming Mouth, and the Ghost King with the Scorched Face are all emanations of the Great Being Avalokiteśvara. As the Monk Pòzhuò Duò of Mount Song said:

His conduct was unfathomable. In a mountain valley there was a shrine that was extremely efficacious; within its hall stood nothing but a single hearth, upon which offerings were made by those near and far without ceasing.
One day, the Master led his attendant monks into the shrine and struck the hearth three times with his staff, saying:
"Tsk! This hearth is merely composed of clay and tiles. From where does the 'saint' come? From where does the 'efficacy' arise? Yet you continue to slaughter [animals] in this manner!"
He struck it three more times, and the hearth immediately tilted, broke apart, and fell down.
A moment later, a man dressed in green robes and wearing a tall cap appeared before the Master and bowed. The Master asked, "Who are you? He replied, "I am originally the Hearth God of this temple."

Having long endured the retribution of karma, today we have been graced by the Master’s teaching of the Dharma of non-arising (*anutpāda*). Having attained liberation from this place, we are now born among the devas;
we have come specifically to express our gratitude. The Master said, "This is your own inherently existing nature;

it is not something I have forcefully spoken. The spirit bowed again and vanished. A short while later, an attendant monk asked, "We have served the Master for a long time, yet we have not received his instructions."
"What essential principle did the Stove God obtain that he was able to be reborn in heaven? The Master said, "I simply told him that he was made of clay and tiles;
I had no other principle to impart to him. When the monk remained silent, the Master asked, "Do you understand?"
The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master asked, "Why do you not understand the nature that is inherently present?
The attendant monks then prostrated themselves. The Master said, "Falling! Falling! Broken! Broken!
Later, Zen Master Yifeng recounted this to National Teacher An, who sighed and said, "This man has fully realized that things and self are of one suchness; he may truly be called a bright moon."
He dwelt in seclusion; there was no one who did not see him. It was difficult to fathom the flow of his discourse. Feng asked, "I wonder what kind of person is able to grasp the flow of his speech?
An said, "One who does not know. At that time, he was known as "Puo-zao-duo" (The Oven-Breaker).
It is unknown where he was from; might he not have been an emanation of Avalokiteśvara?

This is called the thirty-two kinds of wondrously pure bodies that enter various lands; all are accomplished with mastery through the effortless, wondrous power of cultivation based on hearing and the permeation of hearing via samādhi.

The *Compendium* states: That which is called the "spontaneous, wondrous power of sovereign accomplishment" refers to the physical body manifested by Samantabhadra as described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, and the "Samādhi of All Physical Bodies" as described in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.

This is because, through the power of his compassionate roots that secretly permeate the Dharma-realm, he remains unmoved from the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) while manifesting traces throughout the ten directions. By means of this sanctity...
When practicing compassion in response to those whose faculties are dull, one carries a vessel for excrement as if in fear;

yet when practicing heavenly compassion in response to those with middling faculties, it is like a swift horse seeing the shadow of a whip. One practices the Great Straight Path, remaining without fear or hesitation.
Therefore, by means of the Brahma-conduct and compassion, one should respond to the various capacities [of beings].

Thus, seated upon the lion throne with a jeweled footstool supporting the feet, merchants and traders travel throughout foreign lands, engaging in the exchange of goods and profits in every possible way. These are the three types of capacity.
Emptiness, Provisionality, and the Middle. [The Buddha] himself declares that he causes all sentient beings to see such phenomena; this is the Lotus Sūtra’s *rūpakāya-samādhi*.

Through the Tathāgata’s divine power, he manifests in accordance with the faculties of beings throughout the ten directions. By the power of his great compassion and vows, he does not abandon sentient beings;
thus, he is able to pervade everywhere in a single thought-moment without a creator. This is like the benefit bestowed in the eleventh stage (*ekādaśabhūmi*).

Sentient beings are identical to the Dharma-realm. According to their faculties and according to the time, the physical body manifests before them; it functions without being contrived and responds without being produced.

By means of the wisdom of universal radiance, it does not belong to any specific location; it accords with the minds of sentient beings and manifests forms according to things, for there is no coming or going.
This is the manifestation of the physical body as described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. All these manifestations in accordance with conditions...
It is precisely like an illusion. Therefore, through the Illusion-like Samādhi (*māyopama-samādhi*), one achieves mastery by means of hearing and cultivating what has been heard.
Linji said: "What I, this mountain monk, speak of is simply that person who is currently listening to the Dharma with solitary, vivid clarity right before their eyes.
This person is unimpeded in every place; they penetrate the ten directions and the three realms with mastery, entering into all things."
Distinguishing between objects, one cannot be diverted; in a single kṣaṇa, one penetrates the Dharma-realm. Encountering a Buddha, one speaks of the Buddha;
encountering a Patriarch, one speaks of the Patriarch; encountering an Arhat, one speaks of the Arhat; encountering a hungry ghost, one speaks of the hungry ghost.
Traveling through all lands and realms to transform sentient beings, one never for a moment departs from this single thought-moment. Everywhere is pure and luminous.
Pervading the ten directions, the myriad dharmas are of one suchness. O practitioners of the Way! You great men will only now realize that, fundamentally, there is nothing to do.
It is only because you have not had sufficient faith that you pursue it moment after moment, abandoning your head to seek your head, unable to rest of your own accord.
This is the teaching of Linji, who attained the True Dharma Eye of Avalokiteśvara. If you can believe that, fundamentally, there is nothing to do—
Then the thirty-two responsive, effortless, and wondrous powers will immediately manifest before me.
World-Honored One, because I further employ the effortless, wondrous power of the Vajra Samādhi— cultivated through hearing and practicing what has been heard—

and because I share in the same compassion and longing for all sentient beings throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time across the six realms, I cause those sentient beings to [perceive] me...
Body and mind attain fourteen kinds of fearless merits.

Generally speaking, "loving-kindness" (maitrī) must be spoken of as "power," for when power is sufficient to respond universally, it is called "Great Loving-Kindness. "Compassion" (karuṇā) must be spoken of as "looking up," for it answers that which is looked up to;
thus it is called "Great Compassion. That which sentient beings fear is birth and death; I, by means of non-arising—

Śāriputra said, "I have just entered the city, while you have just left it; how can you say that you have gone just as I have?
The woman asked, "In what should the disciples of the Buddhas dwell? He replied, "The disciples of the Buddhas dwell in accordance with the Great Nirvāṇa."
The woman said, "The disciples of the Buddhas already abide in reliance upon the Great Nirvāṇa;
I, too, shall depart in this same manner as Śāriputra. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī asked the woman Aṅgulimālā, "What is the meaning of birth?
The woman said, "Birth takes the non-arising of birth as its meaning. Mañjuśrī asked, "How is it that birth takes the non-arising of birth as its meaning?"

[The Master] asked, "What is the meaning of birth? The woman replied, "If one clearly understands that the four conditions of earth, water, fire, and wind have never been self-originated and yet can harmonize according to what is appropriate, this is the meaning of birth. [The Master] asked, "What is the meaning of death?
The woman replied, "Death takes the non-death of death as its meaning. [The Master] asked, "How is it that death takes the non-death of death as its meaning?"

"Not dying is the meaning of death. The woman said, "If one can clearly understand that the four conditions of earth, water, fire, and wind have never been obtained as something of one's own, and yet can act according to what is appropriate for them, this is the meaning of death.
The woman Ātreyī asked Mañjuśrī, "If one clearly understands the principle that birth is non-arising, why is it that one is nevertheless..."
Regarding the cycle of birth and death, Shu said: "Their power has not yet reached full maturity. These two women appeared during the era of a Buddha;
they were not only endowed with merit and gentle compliance, but were also able to manifest the matters that transcend the ordinary.
Could it be that they were those who, having received and mastered secret Dharma-gates in past lives, manifested themselves in this way?"
Fourteenth: Within this trichiliocosm, there are ten billion suns and moons.

Among the various Dharma princes currently dwelling in the world, there are those numbering as many as sixty-two Ganges-sands who cultivate the Dharma, establish models, and teach and transform sentient beings.

Their skillful means and wisdom, which accord with the capacities of sentient beings, are each different. This is due to the wondrous [realization] arising from the fundamental root of perfect penetration attained by me.
The Gate of the Ear. Thereafter, body and mind become subtle and wondrous, encompassing and pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
This enables sentient beings to hold my name together with sixty-two Ganges-sands of Dharma-princes; the merit of these two individuals—[my follower and those princes]—is [equal].
"It is perfectly equal and without difference, World-Honored One. My single name is no different from those many names.
Because I have cultivated this and attained true perfect penetration, it is called the fourteenth power of bestowing fearlessness, which provides all beings with complete merit."
Tong said: "At the beginning, by observing their sounds, one immediately attains liberation; this reaches those of the highest faculties.

However, by simply perceiving that the five aggregates are all empty, one crosses over all suffering and calamity. To observe with observation requires nothing less than subtle and wondrous contemplative practice.
At the end, he shows that merely upholding the name provides blessings for all sentient beings; this reaches those of middle and lower faculties, providing them with blessings."
The term "it is said" (*yún zhě*) refers to [the benefits] ranging from escape from water and fire to obtaining sons and daughters; thus, there is no request that is not fulfilled.

Therefore, regarding the thirty-two manifestations, what is called "liberation" (*jiětuō*) refers to realization and awakening, while the remaining accomplishments merely involve the preparation of merit.

Because the faculty of hearing is sharp among the sentient beings of this region, those who receive the Way are numerous; for this reason, Avalokiteśvara’s transformation is superior, whereas the other faculties are dull.

Consequently, those who receive the Way are few, and thus the transformations of the various sages are inferior. Whether complete or incomplete, the difference between a day and a kalpa multiplies by ten million times.
Thus, it has already been secretly determined that the faculty of hearing is the essence of the teaching for this region.

Master Shanjue of Hualin Forest would often carry his mendicant’s staff and go out into the mountain foothills at night; every seven paces he would strike the staff once and recite the name of Avalokiteśvara once.
Jiashan asked, "I have heard that Master Yuanwen recites the name of Avalokiteśvara; is this true? The Master said, "Yes. Jiashan said, "What is it like when one has already mounted the head?
The Master said, "If you put your head out, I will let you mount it; if you do not put your head out, what is there to mount? Jiashan had no reply.
The Inspector Pei Xiu visited him and asked, "Do you have an attendant? The Master said, "I do."
"There are one or two, but they simply cannot see guests. Pei asked, "Where are they? The Master then called out, "Dàkōng! Xiǎokōng!
At that moment, two tigers emerged from the hermitage. Seeing them, Pei was struck with terror. The Master said to the two tigers, "Guests are here;
depart now. The two tigers roared and left. Pei asked, "What practice does the Master perform?"
"Karma has brought about such a result as this. The Master then remained silent for a long while and asked, "Do you understand? Pei replied, "I do not understand.
The Master said, "This mountain monk constantly recites the name of Avalokiteśvara; that is why I am able to know. Hualin remained silent for a long while, yet did not emerge from his state.
[The Master said,] "If one does not skillfully observe the observer, then simply recite the name of Avalokiteśvara."

World-Honored One, I have also attained this perfect penetration for the purpose of cultivating and realizing the unsurpassed Way. Furthermore, I have skillfully attained the four inconceivable, unconditioned, wondrous virtues.
The first is that, because I initially attained the wondrously wondrous faculty of hearing, the essence of the mind left behind the act of hearing.
Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing cannot be separated; they form a single, perfectly integrated, pure, and precious awakening.
Therefore, I can manifest many wondrous forms and can preach boundless secret and divine mantras.
Among these, some may appear with one head, three heads, five heads, seven heads, nine heads, eleven heads, and so on, up to one hundred and eight heads, a thousand heads, or ten thousand heads.
Heads: eighty-four thousand śakara heads (adamantine and firm). Arms:
two, four, six, eight, ten, twelve, fourteen, sixteen, eighteen, twenty, up to twenty-four;
and so on, even unto one hundred and eight arms, a thousand arms, ten thousand arms, and eighty-four thousand mudrā-arms (each bearing a sublime seal). Eyes: two.
With three eyes, four eyes, or nine eyes, and so on up to one hundred and eight eyes, a thousand eyes, ten thousand eyes, or eighty-four thousand pure jewel-eyes—
whether manifesting compassion or majesty, meditative concentration or wisdom— they rescue and protect sentient beings, attaining great sovereign mastery.
The Master said: "Because he shares in the compassionate power of the Buddhas, there are the thirty-two manifestations;
because he shares in the sorrowful longing of sentient beings, he bestows the fourteen fearlessnesses. These are already the wondrous power of non-action, inconceivable.
Furthermore, regarding the four inconceivable wondrous virtues of non-action, they arise from the cultivation and realization of the unsurpassed Way. That Way is unsurpassed; its..."
Its divine mystery becomes increasingly unfathomable. The previous teachings on the Dharma and the invocation of names can still be discerned;
but reaching this point, its form and its mantra enable sentient beings to attain great sovereign mastery—this is truly a state of great inconceivability.
All of it flows forth from the wondrously wondrous hearing-mind. Initially, the sense organs and their objects vanish; the mind itself is already wondrous, yet this [state] surpasses it.
This is the subtlety of the coarse, not the subtlety of absolute transcendence. Subsequently, both wisdom and its object vanish, and both subject and object are stilled;
thus it is called "subtlety upon subtlety. Initially, one turns the hearing back and abandons external objects; now, the essence of the mind abandons hearing itself—since even hearing is abandoned.

The six sense organs are transformed together; thus, seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognition cannot be partitioned, forming a single, perfectly integrated, pure, and precious awakening—this is what is meant by "the manifestation of quiescent extinction.
Because it is solely perfect, integrated, and pure, its responsive transformations are without fixed direction:
the head represents the totality of the six functions; the arms symbolize the compassion that uplifts and receives others; and the eyes symbolize illuminative discernment.
Regarding the statement that the heads, arms, and eyes each number eighty-four thousand:
this reveals the remedial Dharma-gates corresponding to the eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*). The Sixth Patriarch said:
"This Dharma-gate of mine produces eighty-four thousand wisdoms from a single prajñā. Why is this? Because worldly people possess eighty-four thousand afflictions."
If there is no defilement, wisdom is constantly manifest and does not depart from its own nature.

Grand Master Lu Xun asked Nanquan, "For what purpose does the Bodhisattva Mahākāruṇika employ so many hands and eyes? Nanquan replied, "Just as the state employs you, Grand Master, for what purpose do you exist?
Magu asked Linji, "Regarding the thousand hands and eyes of Mahākāruṇika, which one is it?"
Zhengyan seized Jie and held him fast, saying, "The Great Compassionate One has a thousand hands and eyes; what is the True Eye? Speak quickly! Speak quickly!

Gu pulled Jie down from the meditation seat and sat back down himself. Jie offered his greetings, saying, "How do you do? As Gu hesitated, Jie let out a shout, pulled Gu down from the meditation seat, and sat back down himself.
Gu then departed. Furthermore, Magu asked Twelve: [Note: The source text provided ends abruptly with "Magu asked Twelve," suggesting the narrative continues beyond this point.]

Regarding the Twelve-Faced Avalokiteśvara: "Which one is the front face? Nanquan seized Guishan by the neck as he descended from his meditation seat and said, "Where has the Twelve-Faced Avalokiteśvara gone?
Speak quickly! Speak quickly! As Guishan turned around and prepared to sit, Nanquan struck him.
Guishan caught the staff and they grappled each other back to the abbot's quarters. These two venerable masters each manifested their spiritual powers; it was truly inconceivable.
Consider this: if one perceives the mechanisms of others' giving and taking, one may be said to possess the hands and eyes of Avalokiteśvara.

Second, because I have emerged from the six sense-objects through hearing and reflection, just as sound passes through a wall without obstruction, I am thus able to manifest every form and recite every mantra with wondrous skill. These forms and mantras can bestow fearlessness upon all beings.
Sentient beings. For this reason, throughout the lands as numerous as motes of dust in the ten directions, all name me the "Bestower of Fearlessness.
It is said in general that the perfect penetration of hearing and thought is like sound passing through a wall;

because it can transcend the six sense objects without being obstructed by them, one is able to manifest forms and recite mantras, revealing inconceivable functions. Only the nature of hearing is truly inconceivable.

Therefore, the power of the mantra is likewise inconceivable. Previously, by means of the perfectly interfused, pure, and enlightened awareness, one protects and delivers sentient beings and attains great sovereignty;
this is because one employs the full power of that awareness to lead them to the shore of the Way.
Therefore, they are endowed with arms, hands, eyes, compassion, majestic power, concentration, and wisdom, which bring about liberation.

These merely manifest individual forms and involve the recitation of individual mantras; while they can cause sentient beings to be free from fear, this is only freedom from the suffering of birth and death, and has not yet reached great sovereign mastery (*mahāvaśitā*).
Once, there was a person who was captured by those who prey upon living beings and used as fodder for ghosts. He was bound in chains...
In the middle of the night, a giant python arrived at a pillar inside the temple and was about to devour him.
Throughout his life, this man had mastered only a single mantra of great compassion; by reciting it incessantly, the python could not approach him, as if there were a barrier separating them.

The python eventually departed. When dawn broke and the lock was opened, [the monk] was found unharmed. The crowd marveled and asked for the reason; he told them that by reciting the Mahākaruṇā-dhāraṇī, he had escaped.
From this point on, the licentious sacrifices were consequently abolished. Such is generally the power of the dhāraṇī to bestow fearlessness.
When Zhang Sengyou was painting an image of Baozhi, as soon as he applied the brush, he could not settle upon it; Baozhi then...
He sliced open his own face with his fingernails, revealing twelve-faced Avalokiteśvara with exquisite and extraordinary features, some compassionate and others majestic.
Zhi Sengyao was ultimately unable to paint them. A monk asked Chan Master Wenshu, "Why was it that Sengyao could not capture the likeness of Master Zhigong?
Wenshu replied, "It is not only Sengyao; even Zhigong himself could not capture his own likeness. The monk said:

The monk asked, "Why was it that Master Zhigong could not be portrayed? Zhishu said, "Colors and paints cannot bring him forth. The monk asked, "Can you, Master, portray him? Zhishu said, "I too cannot portray him. The monk asked, "Why, Master, can you not portray him? Zhishu said, "He does not conform to my colors; how could I be expected to portray him? Dana’s Verse: The Ancient Sage, the Great Master, Is beyond the reach of brush and ink. If one seeks to capture his likeness, One must first understand the mind that conceives. The myriad forms are but empty shadows; How can they represent the true reality? If you wish to see the Original Man, Look directly at the face before your eyes. Do not seek him in words or images, For he is not within the realm of thought. If you can perceive him in this way, Then you have truly met the Buddha. If you still harbor doubts and hesitations, You will wander forever in birth and death. The ancient mirror is bright and clear; It reflects all things without distortion. If you can see your own nature, You will realize the Way yourself. Do not rely on external forms, For the essence is not found therein. If you can cast off all attachments, You will attain liberation and peace. This is the path of the Buddhas and Patriarchs; Do not seek it through conceptualization. It is said: "The radiance of his body blazes forth, his features are majestic and lofty; how could a skilled hand ever paint him?
Do not ask of Xuanzang or Wu Daozi; Master Zhi, he himself could not know him. That even Master Zhi could not know him allows us to perceive the inconceivable realm.
Third, because I have cultivated the fundamentally wondrous, perfect, and penetrating root of purity,
all the worlds I traverse cause sentient beings to relinquish their bodies and precious treasures to seek my compassion.
The Master said: "The fundamental, wondrous, perfect penetration, and pure root is precisely the faculty of hearing.

Being far removed from dust and defilement, it is fundamentally free of affliction; therefore, it is called 'pure. Yet, the world and its sentient beings suffer from afflictions and cannot achieve liberation;
thus, they earnestly entreat for deliverance. Among the six perfections cultivated by Bodhisattvas, giving is primary; therefore, he instructs them [to practice it]."
Generosity consists in abandoning greed and stinginess as the causal basis for cultivation.
Within this very act of giving, one perceives no giver, no recipient, and no object given; this is called the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*).
Without pure and complete penetration, one cannot reach this sublime state. Therefore, the inexhaustible [merit] received by Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva is attained through this.
The Bodhisattva took the precious jewel necklace and offered it back to the Buddha. At first, the Buddha was unwilling to accept it; through this, one may observe his precepts.
That he offered it to the Buddha without weariness allows one to observe his diligence. That he did not use it for himself allows one to observe his patience.

When giving and receiving are devoid of sentient attachment, one may contemplate meditative concentration (*samādhi*). When seeking solely to provide for the welfare of all sentient beings, one may contemplate wisdom (*prajñā*).
Thus, by citing the single practice of giving, the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) are contained therein. How could it be that giving alone constitutes the teaching?
A monk asked Baizhang, "Nowadays, all śramaṇas claim, 'I rely on the Buddha's teachings; I have studied a sutra, a śāstra, a dhyāna, and a vinaya;
I possess knowledge and understanding. Is it appropriate for them to receive the fourfold offerings of the donors? Are they able to digest [such offerings]?
Baizhang said, "Just consider, as it is now, a single sound and a single form, a single fragrance and a single flavor—at one..."
Regarding all phenomena of existence and non-existence, upon each and every object, there is not even a speck of dust of grasping or defilement;
nor does one dwell in a state of non-grasping or non-defilement, nor is there any conceptual understanding of not dwelling. Such a person may consume ten thousand taels of gold daily.
It can indeed be extinguished. Right now, as you illuminate all phenomena—whether existent or non-existent—at the gateway of the six sense organs, you must scrape away and eliminate all craving.

If there is even a hair’s breadth that cannot be removed, then even for begging a single grain of rice or a single thread from a donor, each and every one of you will have to wear fur and horns, pulling plows and bearing heavy loads, to repay them all.
Only then can one truly attain it. This is because one does not rely upon the Buddha. The Buddha is one who is unattached, one who seeks nothing, and one who has no reliance.
If you now continue to greedily search for the Buddha step by step, you will end up turning your back on him entirely. Believe these words:
only by cultivating the pure fundamental root can one rightfully receive the offerings of others.

Fourth, having attained the Buddha-mind and realized the ultimate, I am able to offer various precious treasures as offerings to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, extending also to all sentient beings within the six realms of the Dharma-realm.
Those who seek a wife shall obtain a wife; those who seek a son shall obtain a son;
those who seek samādhi shall obtain samādhi; those who seek longevity shall obtain longevity; and so on, even unto those who seek Great Nirvāṇa shall obtain Great Nirvāṇa.
Nirvana. It is said in general that when one realizes the ultimate, their wisdom is sufficient; thus, they can bestow upon others the bliss of transcendence from the world.
When one makes offerings to the Tathāgata, their merit is sufficient; thus, they can bestow upon others worldly blessings. Both [arise] from this.
Accomplishment is achieved within the inconceivable. If one perceives a seeker or a recipient, the act of giving is narrow.

To obtain merit is not as good as obtaining the fruit; to obtain the fruit is not as good as obtaining the ultimate fruit. Therefore, attaining Great Nirvana is considered the ultimate. Baizhang said:
"Suppose there is someone here who, with the four requisites of merit and wisdom, makes offerings to the Four [Noble Ones]."
After eighty years have passed, during which he has fulfilled the desires of the sentient beings of the six realms throughout hundreds of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* worlds, he reflects:
"These sentient beings are all now aged and infirm;
I shall instruct and guide them with the Buddha-dharma, enabling them to attain the fruit of *srotāpanna* up to the path of *arhat*. Thus he practices giving.

Lord, if merely bestowing all the requisites for happiness upon sentient beings produces immeasurable merit, how much more so is it when one causes them to attain the fruit of *srotāpanna* up to the path of *arhatship*; such merit is immeasurable and boundless.
Yet, even this does not equal the merit of the fiftieth person who rejoices upon hearing the sutra. As the *Bao'en jing* (Sutra on Requiting Kindness) says: "Queen Māyā gave birth..."
Five hundred crown princes all attained the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood and entered parinirvāṇa; stupas were erected for each of them and offerings were made.
Yet, as each one prostrated and sighed, they said: "It would have been better to give birth to but a single son who attains unsurpassed bodhi.
To consider my own mental strength and effort—if even among hundreds of thousands of millions of sentient beings there is but one person who attains it, that alone repays the value."
Throughout the trichiliocosm, one must exclaim: "Ah! Avalokiteśvara has already attained the Buddha-mind, yet he is able to cause all sentient beings to likewise attain the Buddha-mind.
His compassionate vow is truly inconceivable."

When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the Way, I replied: "I have attained the Samādhi of Universal Illumination through the gateway of the ears. By means of the mind that conditions objects, I attained mastery;
through the sign of entering the stream, I achieved Samādhi and realized Bodhi. This is the foremost method.

World-Honored One, that Buddha-Tathāgata praised me for having well-attained this Dharma-gate of Perfect Penetration, and in the midst of the great assembly, he bestowed upon me the name Avalokiteśvara. It was because of me...
Because he observes and hears the perfect clarity of the ten directions, the name Avalokiteśvara pervades the worlds of the ten directions.
It is said in general that the *Book of Documents* states: "He brightens the four eyes and extends the four ears," meaning that he takes the eyes and ears of the four quarters as his own.
It further states: "The vision of Heaven is through the vision of the people; the hearing of Heaven is through the hearing of the people. This means that Heaven’s—

Sight and hearing cannot be seen; they are seen in the people. Since Guanyin takes the sight and hearing of the ten directions as his own sight and hearing, the sight and hearing of the ten directions is itself Guanyin. How could his name not pervade the ten directions?
Baofu asked a monk, "Where have you come from? The monk replied, "From Guanyin. Baofu said, "Do you see Guanyin?"
Mo said, "I see. Fú asked, "Do you see the left side? Do you see the right side? Mo replied, "When one sees, one does not pass through left and right.

Fǎyǎn commented separately, "It is just as the Master sees. When Upādhyāya Fú attended the Dharma assembly at Mount Jìngshān, a monk once asked him in front of the Great Buddha Hall, "Have you ever been to Wutái? He replied, "I have been there. The monk asked, "Did you see [the Bodhisattva]?"
Wen-shu-ma said, “I see him. [The Master] asked, “Where do you see him? He replied, “In front of the Buddha Hall at Mount Jing.
When Xuefeng heard these words, he marveled at them. Linji said, “There is a class of students who seek Mañjuśrī on Mount Wutai;
they have already made a mistake. There is no Mañjuśrī on Mount Wutai. If you wish to recognize Mañjuśrī, it is simply—”
Your current functioning is always without change; wherever you are, there is no doubt. This is the living Mañjuśrī.
Your single thought-moment is the light of non-differentiation; everywhere it is the true Samantabhadra. Your single thought-moment naturally unties its bonds;
liberation occurs wherever one is. This is the samādhi-dharma of Avalokiteśvara. They mutually serve as both host and attendant.
When they emerge, they emerge all at once. One is three; three is one. If you can understand it in this way, only then will you be able to truly contemplate the teachings.
Alas! These words of Linji show that there is no difference whatsoever between explaining the essence (the *zong*) and explaining the teachings (*jiao*).

At that time, from his five limbs, the World-Honored One emitted jewel-like light simultaneously, which reached far to drench the crowns of the heads of Tathāgatas as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions,
as well as the various Bodhisattvas who were Dharma Princes. Those Tathāgatas likewise emitted jewel-like light from their five limbs,
coming from the directions of motes of dust to drench the crown of the Buddha’s head, and to drench the crowns of the heads of all the great Bodhisattvas in the assembly.
As well as the Arhats, the forest trees, ponds, and marshes all emitted the sounds of the Dharma; their interlacing lights entwined like a net of precious threads.
This great assembly attained what they had never experienced before, and all universally obtained the Vajra Samādhi.

Immediately, the heavens rained down lotus flowers of a hundred jewels—blue, yellow, red, and white—blended and intermingled in profusion. The empty space of the ten directions became the color of the seven treasures.
The great earth, mountains, and rivers of this Sahā world all vanished simultaneously; only the lands as numerous as motes of dust in the ten directions were seen, merging into a single realm.
There, the sounds of *brahman* chants and songs were spontaneously performed and presented.
Tong said: "The perfect penetration realized by all the Bodhisattvas and Arhats has already entered the inconceivable realm.
Therefore, from within this inconceivability, the Buddha manifested auspicious responses and precious lights; both the primary and secondary retributions revealed perfect penetration.
As for the primary retribution, light was emitted from his five limbs—identical in every Buddha—which revealed the twenty-five modes of perfect penetration. [The head...]

The head is the Way. Each person possesses a physical body, yet the Buddha attains its perfection. As for the environment that supports life, the intermingling lights are interlaced like a net of precious threads;
even the empty space of the ten directions takes on the color of the seven treasures.

This reveals that the eighteen realms and the seven elements are all the true suchness and wondrous nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. They interact and mutually fuse, constituting a single ocean of jewel-like luminosity and emptiness.
Furthermore, this Sahā world merges into a single realm; this is the sign of the vanishing of dust and the returning of hearing.

Forests, trees, ponds, and marshes all proclaim the sound of the Dharma; this is the sign of pure sound devoid of dust. The precious awakening is perfectly luminous, pervading the entire dharma-realm;
thus, returning the hearing is implicitly established as the primary faculty. When Dongshan arrived at Guishan, he asked: "Recently..."

[Daowei] heard that National Teacher Zhong had taught the Dharma through insentient things, yet he had not yet fathomed its subtlety. Guishan said, "I also have this here, but it is difficult to find someone capable of receiving it. Daowei said, "Please, Master, speak of it. Guishan said, "The mouth born of my parents shall never speak for the sake of my son. Daowei asked, "Are there others at present who admire the Way alongside you, Master? Guishan replied, "There are. Daowei asked, "Who are they? Guishan said, "They are the ones who do not hear me when I speak. Daowei said, "If that is so, then I am one of them. Guishan said, "You are indeed one of them. Miaoyan said, "Not far from here, connected to this stone chamber, there is a practitioner named Yunyan. If you can part the weeds to catch his wind, he will surely be one whom you hold in high esteem.
Once he arrived at Yunyan’s place, he asked, "Regarding the 'Dharma preached by the insentient,' who is it that can hear it?
Yunyan replied, "The insentient themselves can hear it. He asked, "Does the Master also hear it? Yunyan said, "If I were to hear it, you..."
[The monk] said, "Then you did not hear me preaching the Dharma. [Yunyan] asked, "Why did you not hear it? Yunyan held up his whisk and said, "Do you hear it now? [The monk] said, "I do not hear it.
Yunyan said, "If you cannot even hear me preaching the Dharma, how much less can you hear the insentient preaching the Dharma?
[The monk] asked, "In which scriptures does the insentient preaching the Dharma appear? Yunyan said, "Have you not seen [the passage concerning] Maitreya?"
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The water birds and the forest trees all recollect the Buddha and recollect the Dharma; the insentient grasses and trees play the flute and sing in harmony.
Dongshan attained realization upon these words and composed a verse, saying: "How truly marvelous! How truly marvelous! The insentient preaching the Dharma is inconceivable.
If one listens with the ears, it will ultimately be difficult to understand; Only by hearing sound through the faculty of sight does one finally attain it."
"Know this. Zen Master Yunju You ascended the hall and said, "All sounds are the Buddha’s voice. He struck the meditation seat and said, "This Brahma-sound is clear and far-reaching;
it causes people to delight in hearing it. He further said, "All forms are the Buddha’s form.

Thereupon, he picked up his whisk and said, "Now the Buddha emits light, illuminating and revealing the meaning of the true reality (*dharmatā*). Those who have already arrived wear it upon their heads in reverence."
Those who have not yet reached this state should know it thus and believe it thus. Striking the meditation seat, he descended from his position.
These venerable elders have personally arrived at the assembly of Perfect Penetration; therefore, they are able to expound upon it in such a layered and profound manner.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata addressed the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī:

"Observe now these twenty-five great Bodhisattvas and Arhats beyond training, each of whom has spoken of the expedient means by which they first attained the Way, all claiming to have cultivated true and perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*).
In their respective practices, there is truly no distinction of superior or inferior, nor any difference of priority or sequence. I now wish..."
To cause Ānanda to attain awakening, [the Buddha spoke] in twenty-five sections. "Who among them corresponds to his faculties?

Furthermore, after my parinirvāṇa, for the sentient beings of this world who enter the Bodhisattva Vehicle and seek the unsurpassed path, by what gate of skillful means can they easily achieve success?

Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, receiving the Buddha’s compassionate command, immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, [spoke].
He spoke a verse in response to the Buddha, saying:
"Their cultivation of practice is truly without distinction of superior or inferior, or of before or after;
they have all already awakened to and entered unsurpassed bodhi, and are certified by the Buddhas. Huangbo said: "Since the Tathāgata entrusted the Dharma to Kāśyapa..."
Seal the mind with the mind; mind and mind are not different. If the seal adheres to emptiness, the seal does not form a pattern.
If the seal adheres to things, the seal does not form the Dharma. Therefore, one seals the mind with the mind, yet mind and mind are not different.

Since that which seals and that which is sealed are both difficult to harmonize, those who attain it are few. Yet, the mind is itself no-mind, and attainment is itself non-attainment. It is only because it is thus "non-"...

The mind has nothing to be attained; therefore, there is no distinction between before and after. These twenty-five types of those beyond training (aśaikṣa) are in reality neither superior nor inferior, for they are sealed by the mind, and mind-to-mind is without difference.
The nature of the ocean of awakening is serene and perfect; this perfect serenity of awakening is fundamentally subtle and wondrous. When primordial clarity shines forth, the "object" arises;

once the object is established, the nature of the shining subject perishes. [The Master] Tong said: "Awakening is fundamentally subtle and wondrous" means that it is inherently subtle and eternally luminous. Because one discriminates external objects, it is called "primordial clarity.
Having already fallen into the stage of the conscious mind (*manas*), this is "semblance-cognition" (*sadr̥śa-pramāṇa*). Once semblance-cognition is established, the perfect luminosity [is lost].
Direct perception has ceased. Previously, the World-Honored One said: "The beginningless essence of bodhi and nirvana is fundamentally pure;
it can give rise to all conditions, yet that which is lost amidst these conditions [is not perceived]. This was brought forth as a verse. Master Puming addressed the assembly, saying:
"The mind-dharma of the Patriarchs penetrates the ten directions; it has been thus from antiquity to the present, for such is the nature of reality. Such a dharma does not..."

Cultivated through expedient means, it is spontaneously attained; not acquired through expedients, it is spontaneously perfected. All things are manifest and complete; this is called the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*).
It functions yet is not existent; it does not function yet is not non-existent. Its wondrous essence is serene and eternally unchanging.

Its essence accords with its wondrous function, responding fully to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). It reflects and manifests in successive layers of boundless forms and appearances. The mind has no self-nature; it engages with all phenomena.
The Immovable Bodhimanda is fully revealed throughout the worlds of the ten directions.

In such a realm, if one briefly turns the light back, turning away from dust and merging with awakening, one will no longer be occupied with shadows. This principle is like a great royal highway; simply walk upon it.
Even if one does not practice, one is nonetheless on that path. Such discussions as these are merely teachings from the gate of transformation (*nirmāṇa*).
If you wish to uphold and proclaim the fundamental vehicle (*mūlayāna*), it would be better simply to disperse at once.

If you disperse, you will be free from affairs and may perhaps realize the clear, perfect essence of the ocean of awakening. Otherwise, you will remain sitting within the cave of non-action (*asaṃskṛta*).
From delusion arises space; based on space, worlds are established. When thought becomes clarified, it forms a land; when awareness awakens, it becomes sentient beings.
Space arises within the Great Awakening, like a single bubble surfacing from the ocean. All these tainted lands of subtle dust arise entirely dependent upon space.
When the bubble ceases, emptiness is fundamentally non-existent; how much more so, then, are the various realms of the three existences?
It is answered: "Awakening" is called "Great Awakening" (Mahābodhi) to distinguish it from the awakening of ordinary cognition. Great Awakening is like the ocean.
It is beyond all measure and calculation. Its nature is fundamentally empty, yet it cannot be named by "emptiness. Its nature is fundamentally awakened, yet it cannot be named by "awakening.
When there are signs, they accord with the deluded mind; when there are no signs, they are hidden. Once the true nature is hidden, emptiness and awakening become divided.
A fleeting view of emptiness arises, and the perceived world (the *nimitta-bhāga*) is produced; thus, the lands of the three realms are all established upon this emptiness. One merely recognizes...
When the clarity of awakening gives rise to the aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*), sentient beings with outflows (*sāsrava*) all follow after delusion and emerge from it.
These objective aspects (*nimitta*) do not exist as aspects apart from seeing; they are formed by the solidification of thought. Seeing does not exist as seeing apart from these aspects.

This is precisely that which flows through the three realms and unites with sensory objects; it consists of these marks and these views. Born within the Great Awakening, it is like a single bubble upon the ocean.

If one can turn back and exhaust the flowing roots until reaching the state of non-arising and non-extinction, then the bubble will vanish and return to the sea, remaining as the great, wondrously luminous Great Awakening. Even emptiness cannot be found there, let alone [any other phenomena].
"Are the various triple-world realms, with their atoms of sentient and insentient beings, established within space?
A monk asked Baizhang, "The void arises within the Great Enlightenment, like a single bubble emerging from the sea. How is this so? Baizhang replied, "The void is a metaphor for the bubble."
The ocean is used as a metaphor for the nature [of mind]. One’s own numinous awareness-nature exceeds even empty space; thus it is said:

"Emptiness arises within great awakening, like a single bubble emerging from the sea. Chan Master Muping asked Luopo: "Before the single bubble has emerged, how does one discern the current of the water?
Luopo replied: "By shifting the boat one understands the force of the water; by raising the oars one distinguishes the waves."

They did not reach an accord. Having already attended upon Pánlóng (Pang Long), he returned and asked about their previous conversation. Pang Long said: "If you move your boat, you will not recognize the water;
if you raise your oars, you will lose the source. Thereupon, he attained realization. Dánxiá (Danxia) offered this verse:

"The golden crow and jade hare shine together, Illuminating the time before even Wēiyīn (Vipaśyin) had appeared. If one says there is another path in the azure sky, The wooden man remains as before, with his two hands folded."
Meyi. Generally speaking, where the coiled dragon appears, there is no trace of its body; where Luopu sees it, where there is no trace of it, do not hide the body.
If you understand this, it is simply one path; there is nothing different. Later, a monk asked, "What is Muping?
He replied, "No need for the axe. The monk said, "Why is there no need for the axe? He replied:
Muping: "If one can truly illuminate and penetrate that great matter prior to the unmanifested state of Vītarāga, then the nature of returning to the source is non-dual.
Expedient means have many gates; the sacred nature is all-pervasive. Whether following the current or going against it, all are expedient means."
"Those who first enter samādhi differ in their speed of progress; this is a matter of debate.

Tong said: "What was previously stated—that the Tathāgatas of the ten directions all attained perfect, unsurpassed bodhi by practicing within each of the eighteen realms—refers precisely to this sacred nature which is universally pervasive: whether through direct or inverse methods, all are skillful means. Furthermore:

[Zhi]yun said: "If one can awaken to the faculty of perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa*) therein, thereby reversing the beginningless flow of fabricated karma, then the time required to follow the path of perfect penetration versus that which is not perfectly penetrated will differ by factors as vast as a day compared to an eon.
Thus, for those at the initial stage of mind, the speed of entering samādhi differs according to their respective categories.
Huangbo said: "'The nature of returning to the source is non-dual' means that the true nature of ignorance is itself all phenomena."
Regarding the Buddha-nature and the many gateways of skillful means: Śrāvakas perceive the arising of ignorance and perceive the cessation of ignorance.
Pratyekabuddhas perceive only the cessation of ignorance and do not perceive its arising; they realize quiescence in every thought-moment.
The Buddhas perceive that sentient beings, throughout their entire lives, arise yet are without arising, and cease yet are without cessation—neither arising nor ceasing.
Cessation is the fruit of the Mahāyāna. Thus it is said: "The Way-fruit is full and Bodhi is perfected; the flower blooms and the world arises. Chan Master Kumu ascended the hall and said:
"The nature that returns to the source is non-dual, yet there are many gates of expedient means.

If you only understand the nature that returns to the source, what need is there to worry about the gates of expedient means? Do you all wish to understand the nature that returns to the source? Bring forth the pillar!"
He made a wooden ladle. Those around him were unwilling to comply with him. Do you wish to understand the gate of skillful means? Take this wooden ladle and turn it into a pillar;
it will be equally suitable for propping up heaven and supporting the earth. But tell me, how would you express that single phrase which does not fall into the gate of skillful means?
After thirty years, do not let it be cited incorrectly. These two venerable masters each followed [their own way].
The manifestation of the ground of insight must be non-dual with the principle of returning to the source.

When form and perception coalesce to form dust, the essential clarity cannot penetrate through; how could one fail to achieve clear penetration? It is in this state that one attains perfect penetration.

Tong said: "Those who enter by way of the ten contemplations (daśasaṃjñā) form internal dust; therefore, their true essence, though clear and bright, cannot penetrate through, because they are bound by dharmas.
When Shitou asked a newcomer, 'Where have you come from? he replied, 'From Jiangxi.
Shitou asked, 'Have you seen the Great Master Ma? He replied, 'I have. Shitou then pointed to a piece of firewood and asked, 'How does the Great Master Ma compare to this?'"
The monk had no reply. He returned and related this to Mazu. Mazu said, "Did you see how large that wedge of firewood was?
The monk said, "It was of immense size. Mazu said, "You must have great strength. The monk asked, "Why?
Mazu said, "You carried a wedge of firewood from Nanyue; is that not being strong? [Mazu continued,] "If this monk were a true man, he would have set it down."
"Indeed," [the Master] replied.
"Sounds and various languages merely consist of names, phrases, and meanings; since one does not contain all, how can one attain perfect penetration?

Ananda said, "I have realized that the entry through the auditory faculty (*śrotra-indriya*) and the entry through the object of sound (*śabda-viṣaya*) are different. Sound is the Buddha's speech, whereas the faculty is my own."
The mind: to recognize sensory objects is to become attached to names and phrases; to turn the hearing inward is to realize the source of one’s own nature.
Names and phrases stagnate at a single point, whereas the source of nature is all-pervasive. Therefore, even awakening to the Way through hearing sounds is something that must be set aside.
Master Yunju Ye said in a formal lecture: "You people here, even if you were to master the matters on the Buddha's side, you would already be misapplying your minds."
The ancients did not speak of "heavenly flowers falling" or "stones nodding their heads," nor was it a matter of one's own self; what else could these be but idle talk?
To attempt to employ this finite body and mind within the infinite is like trying to fit a square block into a round hole—how much confusion and error there will be!
If there were no such thing [as this], then even if you were to gather flowers and cluster brocades together, it would be of no avail.
It is likewise of no use; one has not yet transcended emotional consciousness. All matters must reach their ultimate exhaustion right here.
If even a single hair’s breadth remains unexhausted, it constitutes a breach of the dust-accumulations, let alone if there is more.
To err by a hair’s breadth is to commit a transgression as vast as a mountain. As the ancients said: "If the place of study is not profound, it is entirely mundane; it belongs to the inner chambers."
If one fails to let go of things, both will result in leakage. One must simply, right here, exhaust all affairs—whether grasping, departing, or arriving—and only then will one be free from fault.
It is like a person who is clear-headed in every respect and penetrating in every thing.
They merely call him a "man of affairs" and never call him "Noble and Precious. From this, one knows that the path of the Noble and Precious is distinct.
Have you not heard it said: "That which enters through the gate is not the treasure"? Do you understand that a dragon is not produced upon a staff?
This should serve as a stern warning to those who find flavor in mere words and phrases.
Fragrance is known when combined with other substances; separated, it fundamentally does not exist. Since that which is perceived is not constant, how can one attain perfect penetration?
The nature of taste is not intrinsic; it exists only when there is flavor. Since its perception is not consistently uniform, how can one attain perfect penetration?
The Master said: "Fragrance and flavor arise from conjunction and separation; they are not constant, nor is their substance all-pervasive.
Those who take attachment to fragrance and flavor as the entrance will ultimately fail to resemble the perfect essence; therefore, both are to be excluded. A monk asked Yunju Ying:
"Who is it that can eat the food of the Fragrant Accumulation? Ying said: "You must know the person who eats it; even when it enters the mouth, one must pluck it out."
[The Master] came out. Again, a monk asked Shoushan Nian, "What is the path of true cultivation? Shoushan said, "A poor child does not eat mixed food.
The monk said, "I shall cast off my hands and return home. Shoushan said, "I have never smelled incense or stench.
Foyin ascended the hall and said: "I have this one point; everyone chews it in their mouths. Those who can chew it through must spit it out quickly."
However, that which cannot be chewed turns instead into a poisonous drug. He then summoned the various masters of Chan, saying, "What flavor is there?
Please tell me. After a long silence, he said: "The King of Physicians is not without prescriptions; the fragrance of the *sū* from a thousand miles away does not turn back the elephant.
Foyin then provided a further commentary for the two venerable elders: "If one hears this fragrance, if one knows this..."
Taste is simply that which is constantly perceived.
Touch is clarified by what is touched; there is nothing it does not clearly touch. Since its nature of union and separation is not fixed, how can it attain perfect penetration?
Tong said: "If 'contact' necessarily has an object, it is already not the meaning of perfection. Furthermore, when joined there is contact, and when separated there is no contact;
yet one knows contact through separation, so its nature is not fixed. If its own nature is not fixed, how can it be pervasive?
When Master Shuilao first visited Mazu, he asked, "What is the precise meaning of the coming from the West? Mazu said, "Prostrate yourself."
As Baizhang was about to prostrate, the Master gave him a kick. Baizhang attained great enlightenment; rising up, he clapped his hands and laughed heartily, saying, "How marvelous!
How marvelous! Hundreds of thousands of samādhis and immeasurable subtle meanings are all recognized at the very tip of a single hair!
Later, he told the assembly, "Ever since I took that one bite from the horse..."
The Master stepped on it. "Right up until now, people cannot stop laughing. Although this is so, what was touched upon in the past still lingers.
How does this compare to Linji’s liberation? Linji said: "For twenty years I was at the place of my late teacher Huangbo;
three times I asked about the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma, and three times I received his blows with the staff. It was as if being brushed by the tip of a boat pole."
"Now I am thinking of having one more meal. Who among you can serve it for me? At that time, a monk stepped forward from the assembly and said, "I, so-and-so, can serve it.
Nanquan took up his staff and gave it to him; as the monk was about to receive it, Nanquan struck him. "The sword has already gone far away; you are merely marking the boat."

The dharma-object (dharmāyatana) is called the internal dust. Since there must be a locus for the dust, and since the subject and object do not pervade everywhere, how can one attain universal penetration?

He replied: "The dharma-object has no form; it dwells secretly within the faculty of the mind. Once it falls into the duality of subject and object, it possesses a fixed direction and therefore cannot pervade everywhere.
Although this empty dharma can pervade the ten directions, it cannot pervade that which is not empty."

Therefore, they cannot achieve perfect penetration. This does not mean that the subject can exist without involving the object, or that the object can exist without involving the subject, such that the two stand independently.
Linji said: "All dharmas, mundane and supramundane, have no self-nature and no nature of arising;
they possess nothing but empty names, and even these names are empty. If you simply take these idle names to be real, you are profoundly mistaken. Suppose...

There are. All are objects of transformation based upon something. There is a basis for Bodhi, a basis for Nirvana, a basis for liberation, a basis for the three bodies, a basis for object and wisdom, a basis for Bodhisattvas, and a basis for Buddhas. What do you seek within these lands of transformation based upon something?
Even the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings are all just worn-out, filthy scrap paper. The Buddha is...
This is an emanation body. The Patriarch is an old bhikṣu. Are you still your mother’s child? If you seek the Buddha, you will be seized by the demon of the Buddha.
If you seek the Patriarch, you will be bound by the Patriarch. If you have any seeking, it is all suffering.

It is better to remain without such concerns. It is true that by relying on the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍāyatana*), one will inevitably encounter obstacles and be unable to attain perfect penetration (*pariśuddha*).
Thus, the above selection of those who enter through the six objects demonstrates that they are not suitable for those at the initial stage.

"Though the seeing-nature is brilliantly clear, it sees what is before it but not what is behind; the four directions are thus deficient by half. How, then, can one attain perfect penetration? Ananda replied:
"It is indeed true that with the eyes one sees what is before but not what is behind. However, the seeing-nature is not the eyes; it is the mind that sees."
Why is it that even a single half is deficient? It is because as soon as one falls into the realm of dualistic perception (*dṛṣṭi-bhāga*), one loses the perfect and eternal nature.

Therefore, the faculty of the eye (*cakṣur-indriya*) must be carefully examined. Nanquan went to visit National Teacher Zhong. The Master asked, "Where have you come from? Nanquan replied, "From Jiangxi.
The Master asked, "Have you brought back the portrait of Master Ma? Nanquan said, "This very thing is it. The Master said, "What about the one behind it? Nanquan [remained silent].
He then simply stopped. Changqing Ling said, "It is very much like not knowing. Baofu Zhan said, "I almost failed to reach you here, Master.
Yunju Xi said, "Both of these venerable elders were merely supporting him from behind;
as for Nanquan stopping there, was he supporting him in front or supporting him from behind? Xuansha once pointed out that for a deceased monk, everything before one's eyes is manifest."
Bodhi. The mark of divine light extending ten thousand miles from behind the crown of the head. There is a verse that says:

"The mark of divine light extending ten thousand miles from behind the crown— When it has vanished from the crown, where can one look for it? The task is accomplished; the intent has ceased. This trace of its coming is present everywhere.
If a wise person encounters it, they seize it immediately; Do not wait until, in an instant, you lose your head. These are the two cases.
They stimulate one another; in their equilibrium, they do not value being seen.

The inhalation and exhalation of the breath pass through, yet in the present moment there is no mingling of airs. Being fragmented and disjointed, they do not achieve mutual penetration; how then can one attain perfect penetration?
Tong said: "The universe is one great respiration. Spring and summer are exhalation; autumn and winter are inhalation. The white moon is exhalation; the black moon is inhalation.
Before midnight is exhalation; after noon is inhalation. That humans breathe through in this way, thereby penetrating Heaven and Earth, is like fish being in water.
To regulate the incoming and outgoing breath until it reaches the state where no breath is exchanged before one's eyes is what practitioners of longevity cultivation do."
To act in accordance with nature is to be unaware of the profound obscurity and the state of hazy indeterminacy; it is merely the mechanism of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Its essence and its substance are merely the spirit of discernment (*vijñāna*). Fragmentation and pervasive affliction—what connection do they have with one's own nature?
A practitioner of the Way asked Dazhu, "Is there any dharma in the world that surpasses nature? Dazhu replied, "There is. The practitioner asked, "What dharma?"
[The Master] said, “I have understood. Zhuzhu asked, “One who can know the spontaneous—do you say that the primal qi (*yuanqi*) is the Way?
Zhuzhu said, “Primal qi is primal qi; the Way is the Way. [The Master] said, “If it is thus, then there should be two. Zhuzhu said, “In knowing, there are not two people.
He asked again, “What is called heterodox? What is called orthodox? Zhuzhu said, “When the mind pursues external objects, it is heterodox.”

This is erroneous. Objects follow the mind; this is what constitutes correctness. Viewed from this perspective, the doctrine of regulating the breath is a case of the mind chasing after objects—it is excessively fragmented and disjointed.
How much less could it lead to the attainment of perfect penetration?
"The tongue is not an entrance without cause; it gives rise to cognition because of flavors. When flavor ceases, cognition no longer exists.
How, then, can one attain perfect penetration? Tong said: "If the tongue were not a faculty, how could it know flavor? To know flavor without a faculty is what is called 'without cause.'"
It is not that the words are inverted. Since this faculty exists, it gives rise to perception through the sense-sphere of taste;
when taste ceases, perception ceases. Thus, this faculty takes the presence or absence of taste as its own existence or non-existence—how can it be considered perfect?
When Jiashan was serving as the head cook at Weishan, Weishan asked him, "What vegetables are you eating today? Jiashan replied, "For two years we have been together."
One spring, Guishan said, "Cultivate the matter well. Jia said, "The dragon dwells in the phoenix’s nest. Touzhu’s verse says:
"Meeting, we ask about the porridge of sentient beings; Do not compare it to the fragrant meal offered in the hermitage garden.

Purple qi follows the vermilion phoenix through the night; The golden dragon coils at dawn around the branch of the moon. Furthermore, when Xiyan Zhi ascended the hall, after a long silence he said: "Fortunately..."
"What a fine dish of rice! It must not be sprinkled with pepper and ginger. Even so, try and taste it. With these words, he descended from his seat.
These two cases are likewise of the same springtime. If one succeeds in tasting it, one may be granted the distinction of knowing the flavor with a different tongue.

"The body and its objects of touch are likewise; each is not the contemplation of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*). Since their boundaries do not merge, how can one attain perfect penetration? Guanyin replied:
'The wondrous touch proclaims clarity, yet it is merely the body manifesting cognition. Pure enlightenment transcends the body, yet this too is not Perfect Enlightenment.
Only by contemplating according to Perfect Enlightenment—transcending both body and mind so as to be beyond all measure—can one finally merge with all phenomena in profound stillness.'"
Ji Shi said: "Now that one has a body and has contact, there is a limit to what can be known; this is not universal penetration.
When the Grand Historian Huang Shanggu visited Chan Master Xin of Sishi, he entered the room with the assembly.
Xin opened his eyes wide and asked, "The Elder Xin dies, and the Scholar dies; when we are both reduced to two heaps of ashes, where shall we meet? Shanggu was speechless.
[The Master] said: "The *New Translation of the Vinaya* has been published. [Dahui] remarked that what he had attained through his studies under Huitang had not yet truly taken root.

Later, while serving as an official in Qian-nan, his power of the Way grew even more superior. Amidst a state of non-conceptualization, he suddenly clarified the meaning of the question posed by Siji.

He sent a letter in reply, saying: 'In years past, I was burdened by your persistent exhortations; for a long time I remained as if in a drunken dream, with only a vague sense of things within a realm of light and shadow.'"
Because my doubts were not yet exhausted and the life-root remained unsevered, I retreated in dismay at the sight of the precipice.
Recently, while traveling on the road through Qian-nan during my official exile, I woke from a midday nap and suddenly reflected: "How much have I been deceived by the old monks of the world?
Only the monk Sīxin refused to grant me his seal of approval; that alone was the foremost act of true concern for me. I could not bear [to remain in this state].
How fortunate! Thus, a hidden convergence such as that between a mountain and a valley cannot even be found within oneself; what more need be said of meeting one another?
One who has not severed the life-root is not fit to speak of this.

"The faculty of cognition (*manas-indriya*) is characterized by chaotic thinking; in its profound clarity, there is ultimately nothing to be seen. Since conceptualization cannot be escaped, how can one attain perfect penetration?
Ananda replied, "Since the faculty of cognition belongs to the realm of knowing, knowing gives rise to chaotic thoughts that arise in confusion, like waves rising upon the sea.
Within the nature of profound clarity, there is ultimately nothing to be perceived. Even if one were to return knowing to non-knowing and thought to non-thought,"
This also belongs to conceptual thought; it is not easily liberated, and therefore one cannot attain perfect penetration. A monk asked National Teacher Shao, "What is 'not realizing a single dharma'?
The Master said, "Wait for the words. The monk asked, "What is 'realizing all dharmas'? The Master said, "Why are you drunk?
He then said, "Just as when I respond to you in this way, what do you all think?"
How do you understand this? Is it that this is the true manifestation? Is it that at this very moment there is not a single dharma to be realized?
Is it that you recognize his place of origin? Is it that the whole body is fully revealed? Do not misunderstand!
Such a view is called "clinging to the grass and leaning on the wood"; it is worlds apart from the Buddha-dharma.
[This is] a barrier. Even if one’s ability to respond and discern were like a cascading torrent, it would only result in inverted views.
If you merely valued responding and discerning, what difficulty would there be? I only fear that it would be of no benefit to others and would instead lead to deception and error.
As for the discerning questions and answers you have studied in the past, you have mastered and expounded many principles of logic; however—
Why does your doubt not cease? Upon hearing the skillful means of the ancient sages, you fail to understand them at all; this is simply because there is much emptiness and little substance.
Upādhyāya, it would be better for you to see through everything at once from the very root. Look: what kind of principle is this?
How many dharma-gates are there that could provide you with a basis for doubt and seeking a solution? Only then will you realize that all you have studied until now was in vain.
This matter is precisely the root-source of birth and death, the livelihood within the realms of the aggregates. Therefore, the ancients said:

"If seeing and hearing are not yet liberated, one is like the moon in water. Be careful with this non-action. If even seeing and hearing cannot be liberated, how much less so can thoughts and memories?
Those who possess the aforementioned five faculties are not suitable for those at the beginning stage.

"Consciousness and seeing are a mixture of the three harmonies; when one interrogates their source, they are called 'without marks. Since their own essence has no fixed prior existence, how can one attain perfect penetration? Ananda replied:

"The object belongs to the *nimitta-bhāga* (the perceived portion), and consciousness belongs to the *darśana-bhāga* (the perceiving portion). Now, as for this 'seeing' of consciousness and seeing, it is the faculty that conjoins with the object."
Consciousness arises within them; these three elements combine to form it. When one examines its root, this vision originally has no self-nature and no characteristics can be apprehended.
It exists when there is a combination, and does not exist when there is no combination. Therefore, it is said to be "not fixed.
