How could that which lacks a fixed nature of its own ever realize perfect penetration? Shen Hui was thirteen years old when, from [Master] Yu...
Quan came to visit the Sixth Patriarch. The Patriarch said, "My son, you have come from afar with great hardship; have you brought your original nature with you?
If you possess this original nature, you should recognize its master. Try to explain it to me. Huai would replied, "I take non-abiding as the original nature;
seeing is itself the master. The Patriarch said, "How can you, a novice monk, speak so recklessly? Huai then asked, "What is the Master doing while sitting here?"
Chan. [Nanquan] asked, "Do you see or not see? The Patriarch struck him three times with his staff and said, "When I strike you, is it painful or not painful?
He replied, "It is both painful and not painful. The Patriarch said, "I too both see and do not see.
Huai asked, "What is meant by 'both seeing and not seeing'? The Patriarch said, "That which I see is that I constantly observe the faults of my own mind."
One does not perceive the right or wrong, the good or bad of others; therefore, one both sees and does not see.
As for your question, "How can it be that there is both pain and no pain? if you felt no pain, you would be the same as wood or stone; if you did feel pain, you would be the same as ordinary people.
He immediately gave rise to resentment and anger, saying, "Whether you saw those two extremes or not when you went forward, whether it was painful or not painful—these are birth and extinction.
You have not even seen your own nature, yet you dare to mock people. Shenhui prostrated himself in repentance and apology.
The Patriarch said, "If your mind is deluded and you do not see, ask a virtuous friend for the way. If your mind is awakened, you will immediately see your own nature yourself."
"One practices according to the Dharma; it is you who are deluded and do not see it. Yet you come to ask me whether I see or not.
I see for myself; why wait for your delusion? If you could see for yourself, you would not wait for my delusion either.

Why do you not know and see for yourself, but instead ask me whether I see or not? Shenhui prostrated himself more than a hundred times, seeking forgiveness for his transgressions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
He attended at the Master’s side. One day, the Master addressed the assembly, saying:
"I have an object that has no head and no tail, no name and no character, no back and no front. Do you all recognize it? Shenhui stepped forward and said:
"It is the original source of all Buddhas; it is the Buddha-nature of Shenhui. The Master said: "I told you it has no name and no character, yet you immediately—"

To call this the "original source Buddha-nature" means that even if you go forth in the future and cover your head with a thatched roof, you will still only become a follower of the school of intellectual understanding.
If, at that time, the Second Patriarch had merely bowed and stood in his place, what fault would there have been?
"Mind-hearing penetrates the ten directions and arises from the power of the Great Cause. Since the initial mind cannot enter [this state], how can one attain perfect penetration?
Ananda replied: "It does not use the ear to hear, nor does it use consciousness to hear; therefore, it is called 'mind-hearing. This refers to one who has already realized the stage of fruition."
This is no different from Avalokiteśvara’s observing and hearing the ten directions with perfect clarity. This too should be called "I also realize it from within.
It is not only Samantabhadra whose mental hearing penetrates through to the external affairs of the sands of worlds in the ten directions, knowing them all without exception;

this is because at the stage of the causal ground, he gave rise to the aspiration for enlightenment, and his practices and vows were so vast that they pervade the realm of empty space, reaching everywhere without fail.
Upon arrival, because there is this great cause, one realizes this great fruit. This is not something that those who lack great roots or great capacity can undertake.
It is better to instead practice "returning the hearing" (*fanwen*), permeating it with hearing and cultivating it through hearing; thus one may gradually enter.

This means that for a beginner, it is not easy to find a foothold, and it is difficult to attain perfect penetration (*yuantong*). This differs slightly from other explanations. Master Dongshan Bing was daily only in a state of tranquil repose.
While seated one day, he called his attendant and went down to the Dharma Hall, saying, "Those dragging wood must not damage the steps.
The attendant went out to look, but there was no one there; upon returning, he reported that it was silent and devoid of human traces. The Master instructed him to search again.

As the attendant leaned over the eaves and looked down, he saw a swarm of ants dragging the wings of a dragonfly as they crawled up the steps. This was surely because of the extreme stillness [of the environment].
It is the one who possesses numinous awareness. Thus, when they hear the sound of ants, it is like thunder; how much more so for the mind-hearing of Samantabhadra, which is even greater than this?

The practice of olfactory concentration is originally a provisional device intended only to cause the mind to settle. Once settled, the mind becomes attached to that which it dwells upon; how, then, can one attain perfect penetration?
Tong said, "How difficult it is to restrain the mind! At first, when it is scattered and distracted, one fears only that it will not abide;
later, when it becomes still and silent, it again becomes something that abides. Both abiding and non-abiding are neither the fundamental essence of non-abiding;
therefore, one cannot attain perfect penetration. One day, while Shigong was performing chores in the kitchen, Mazu saw him and asked, "What are you doing?"
Mogong said, "I herd oxen. The Patriarch asked, "How do you herd them? Mogong replied, "Whenever one enters the grass, I seize the nose and drag it out.
The Patriarch said, "You truly herd oxen. Nanquan gave this teaching: "Master Wang herds a water buffalo.
If he intends to go east of the stream, he cannot avoid damaging the crops of the public; if he intends to go [west of the stream]..."
"Going westward, one cannot avoid the official's gaze upon the crops; how can this compare to 'accepting a little bit according to one's lot'?

Yet, even this is not seen at all. Tiantong took up the case and said: "Nanquan’s 'herding the ox' may indeed be called extraordinary, reaching a point where it cannot be blocked or guarded against in any place.
Why is this so? It is because he accepts a little bit according to his lot. Yunmen then asked: "Now tell me—"
"Inside the cow, he brings it in; outside the cow, he brings it in. Even if you can explain clearly where he brings it in, I will further ask you:
"Where is the cow? Daowei criticized him, saying, "Yunmen only knows how to rope the cow; he does not know how to pass the halter through its nostrils."
Holding up his staff, he said: "The Buddhas of the three periods and the nostrils of all the old monks under heaven have been pierced through at once by this mountain monk’s staff.
Now tell me, where are the nostrils of this mountain monk? After a long silence, he said:
To falsely accuse another of a crime and sentence them to the full penalty— should one penetrate such a pivotal opportunity,
one will surely seize the nostrils [of the truth] and certainly attain supreme, perfect penetration.

"Explaining the Dharma by manipulating sounds and characters awakens those who have already achieved prior success. Since names and phrases are not themselves untainted (*anāsrava*), how can one attain perfect penetration through them?
The practitioner replied: "The faculty of the tongue can only distinguish flavors; it is the tongue-consciousness that is able to manipulate sounds.
By explaining mundane and supramundane dharmas, one awakens others. However, such awakening is only bestowed upon those who have already achieved prior success, much like timely rain."
This transformation cannot be conveyed through words and speech. This is because the body of names (*nāmakāya*) and the body of phrases (*padakāya*) do not exist apart from written characters;

they are not themselves the untainted (*anāsrava*) Dharma. It is like a finger pointing at the moon: the finger is not the moon. How could one thereby attain perfect penetration? A former master said:

"To realize [the truth] before words are spoken is to do a disservice to our school’s tradition; to take responsibility after the sentence has been uttered is to sink into oblivion. Regarding the Buddha... [text ends].
The Patriarch said: "Therefore, awakening comes first; it is only then that one may use words to verify and establish it. If one waits for words to awaken, one is far removed from it.
Fayen entered the hall, and after the assembly had stood for a long time, he said to them:
"If you were to disperse right now just as you are, would there be any principle of the Buddha-dharma? Try to say something. If there is none, then come back here."
"How so? If it exists, it also exists in the midst of a crowd in a great marketplace; why must one come here?
Everyone has once read the *Guanyuan guan*, the *Baimen yihai*, the *Huayan lun*, the *Nirvana Sutra*, and many other treatises.
In which of these teachings is there such a moment? If it exists, try to cite it. If it is indeed thus..."
How could such words exist within this sutra? Is this not the very moment [of realization]? What connection could there possibly be [between them]? Therefore it is said:
"Subtle words stagnate at the forefront of the mind, constantly becoming a field for discursive thought; ultimate reality dwells right before one's eyes."
It is instead turned into the realm of names and forms. Furthermore, how can it be turned back?
And if it is turned back, how can it be made correct? Do you understand? What use is there in merely reciting these "encouragement slips" (cezi) in such a manner?
Truly, names and phrases are not untainted; they cannot lead to perfect penetration.

Observing precepts and violating them merely restrain the body; where there is no body, there is nothing to restrain. Since these are fundamentally not pervasive across all things, how can one attain perfect penetration through them?
Tong said: "The Dharma-body is immeasurable and does not depend on cultivation;

the Response-body has limits and easily creates karma, thus it must rely on precepts to restrain it. This restraint is applied only to the Response-body, yet it cannot penetrate the principle of the Dharma-body;
therefore, it is not universal. Without universality, one cannot attain perfect penetration. Huang—
Chan Master Po-hui left home to become a monk in his youth and specialized in the study of the sūtras and śāstras. Later, upon being further conferred the Bodhisattva precepts, he sighed and said:
"The Great Being’s (Mahāyāna) restraint of discipline and my original Śrāvaka precepts are identical in terms of what is maintained and what constitutes an offense.

However, they differ in their formulation regarding the increase or decrease of the categories of offenses, the primary and secondary rules, and the specific and general prohibitions; furthermore, the underlying intent of these regulations is distinct. Yet, both are subtle and difficult to guard against. Furthermore...
Among the practices for gathering virtue, he had never performed even a small portion, let alone those for benefiting sentient beings.

Furthermore, how could one feel attachment to this worldly body and life, which are like bubbles and illusions? Thinking thus, he set aside his lectures and intended to cast his body into the water to feed the scales and shells [of aquatic creatures].
Just as he was about to depart, two practitioners of the second dhyāna happened to meet him and engaged him in a detailed discussion.
It was said that there were many spiritual friends in the south. Why linger in one corner? He turned his resolve from there and went to Shushan.
He asked, "When one departs in a single kṣaṇa, what is it like? Shushan said, "It fills the void; how will you go?
He replied, "If it fills the void, it is better not to go. Shushan then ceased speaking and descended from the hall. This is the first case for study.
A monk asked, "Just now, your response was most extraordinary. The Master said, "That was merely an impulsive remark. I venture to hope for your compassion in instructing this ignorant one.
The Master said, "In the span of a single *kṣaṇa*, can there still be any deliberation? At these words, [the monk] attained sudden enlightenment.
Furthermore, Chan Master Yuan’an Ci relied on Chengdu Zhengfa Temple to leave the household life as a youth and received full ordination.

Later, while visiting lecture halls and listening to a discourse on the *Nirvāṇa-parivarta* chapter of the *Awakening of Faith*, he reached the passage: "When the four great elements have each departed, where then does this deluded body abide?
Ultimately it has no substance; it is truly like an illusion. Thereupon, he attained a realization and composed a verse, saying:
"A single bright pearl is here within me; touch it or move it, and it emits light that shakes the earth. These two venerable masters—[the former] and [the latter].
Without departing from the illusory body, one realizes the Dharma-body; how could it not be universal?

Spiritual powers are fundamentally due to past causes; what connection have they with the discrimination of dharmas? Since mindfulness depends on conditions and is not separate from objects, how can one attain perfect penetration through it?
Tong said: "The supernatural powers of the Hīnayāna are all produced through intentional effort; they exist when directed toward objects and cease when separated from them.

They cannot manifest by being detached from objects because they involve conceptualization and objective conditions. These are achieved through the power of past causes and are not realized through the discernment of the wondrous Dharma.
Since one is already attached to such supernatural powers, it is impossible to speak of [the ultimate truth] with them."
Regarding Yuancong: When Huangbo first traveled to Tiantai, he encountered a monk who appeared like an old acquaintance, and they set out together.
Upon reaching a mountain stream where the water was surging, Huangbo leaned on his staff and stopped. The monk urged Huangbo to cross with him, but Huangbo said, "Please, brother, go ahead.
The monk immediately floated his straw hat upon the water and crossed over. Huangbo remarked, "I, however, am with this one..."

The servant boy formed a group; [Baizhang] regretted not having struck him dead with a single blow. That monk then prostrated from afar in the water, praising him and saying, "Truly a vessel for the Mahayana Dharma;
I am not his equal. This was the supernatural power of the Hinayana, which is why he was rebuked by Baizhang.
Mazu, Nanquan, and two or three others went to visit Jingshan. On the road, they encountered an old woman. It was...
He asked, "Which way should one go? [The Master] said, "Go straight ahead. Gu said, "The water ahead is deep; can you cross it?
He replied, "Without getting my feet wet. Gu asked again, "The rice on the upper bank is so lush, while the rice on the lower bank is so frail.
He replied, "It has all been eaten by crabs. Gu said, "The grain is so fragrant. He replied, "It has no scent."
Tang asked, "Where does the old woman dwell? She replied, "Right here. When the three men reached the shop, the old woman brought a pot of tea and three cups.
She said, "If you monks possess supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), then drink the tea.
While the three looked at one another, the old woman said, "Watch as this old crone displays her own supernatural powers," and she picked up a cup.
He tilted the teapot and departed. Such spiritual powers as these are no small matter; thus, even Magu and Nanquan could not fathom their limits.
The aforementioned methods of entering through the six consciousnesses are not appropriate for those at the beginning of their practice.

If one contemplates through the nature of earth, it is solid and firm rather than penetrative; it is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and not the nature of the sages. How, then, can one attain perfect penetration? He replied:
"Since earth is solid and firm, its nature is fundamentally not penetrative; furthermore, the Earth-Holding [Samādhi] is a conditioned phenomenon and not the fruit of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Therefore, it is not suitable for perfect penetration. A former master said: "If a person recognizes the mind... [The text continues: ...Great.
"There is not an inch of ground to be found. If you can see it thus, what further obstruction could there be?
While Baofu was standing with a monk in attendance, Baofu said, "How can you be so careless? The monk asked, "In what way am I careless?"
Fengxue picked up a clod of earth and handed it to the monk, saying, "Throw this outside the gate.
After the monk had thrown it, he returned and asked, "In what way was I careless? Fengxue said, "I saw you bumping and knocking against things; that is why I said you were careless.
Had this monk been suddenly awakened by these words, he would have attained penetration into the sacred nature. Thus it is said: [the text continues].
He attained perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa*). [The Buddha asked:

"If one contemplates through the nature of water, then thoughts and perceptions are not real; if suchness (*tathatā*) is beyond both awakening and observation (*vitarka-vicāra*), how can one attain perfect penetration?
Āniruddha replied: "Contemplation of water is likewise among the ten modes of perception; it is formed by thoughts and perceptions. How could it be the same as reality? For it is true that—"
The principle of reality is suchness, immovable and not produced by artificial construction; therefore, it is beyond the reach of vitarka and vicāra (discursive thought).
A monk asked Xuefeng, "What is it like when there is a cold spring in an ancient ravine? Feng said, "Staring with wide-open eyes, one cannot see the bottom.
The monk asked, "And what of those who drink from it? Feng said, "It does not enter through the mouth. The monk reported this to Zhaozhou, who said, "It must not enter through the nose."

He entered through the gate. A monk then asked, "What is it like when there is a cold spring in an ancient ravine? Zhaozhou said, "Bitter. The monk asked, "And what of those who drink from it? Zhaozhou said, "Dead.
When Xuefeng heard of this, he remarked, "Zhaozhou is an ancient Buddha," and from afar he prostrated himself.
From that time on, he no longer engaged in dialogue. Tiantong commented: "To uphold and establish the lineage of the school, one must rely upon a master craftsman; Xuefeng has prepared himself."
The physical and mental state of fifteen hundred people’s spiritual friends—Zhaozhou employs the skillful means of a veteran master of one hundred and twenty years;
it is truly extraordinary. Nowadays, among the multitude, people settle upon meanings according to mere words and recklessly engage in disparagement and denigration, deeply wronging the ancients.
Nevertheless, as they strike the gong together at the banquet, there seem to be those who understand; let this be engraved upon their bones and inscribed upon their hearts.
It is rare to encounter a clear mirror. This monk’s realization is stalled in a state of profound stillness where nothing stirs.
Zhaozhou’s tongs and hammer are precisely Xuefeng’s needle and thread; how could they be different?

"If one contemplates through the nature of fire, one becomes weary of existence and seeks to leave it, yet this is not true liberation. This is not a skillful means for a beginner; how, then, can one attain perfect penetration? Ananda replied:

"When I heard the teaching on the fire of desire, I felt a sense of weariness and detachment. This was my weariness with existence. Since there is both longing and aversion, it is not true liberation.
Furthermore, for a beginner entering the Way, it is better to exhaustively investigate principle than to merely restrain desire. As principle becomes increasingly clear,"
Then one’s desires will daily diminish. If you wish to exhaustively investigate principle, try to observe what this fire actually is.
Once, while a monk was attending him, Zhaozhou pointed to the fire and asked, "This is fire; you must not call it 'fire. I have already said it. The monk had no reply.
Zhaozhou then poked the fire with a poker and asked, "Do you understand? The monk said, "I do not understand. Zhaozhou said, "This..."
"There is Master Touzi in Shuzhou. Go there to pay your respects and question him;

he will surely explain it for you. If the conditions are in accord, you need not come back; if they are not in accord, then return. The monk went to Touzi, who asked, "Where have you recently departed from?
He replied, "Zhaozhou. The Master said, "What words or phrases did Zhaozhou have? The monk related the previous conversation.
The Master said, "Do you understand? The monk replied, "I do not. He requested instruction from the Master. The Master then descended from his meditation seat, walked three steps, and sat back down.
He asked again, "Do you understand? The monk replied, "I do not. The Master said, "Go back and report this to Zhaozhou.
The monk returned and reported it to Zhaozhou. Zhaozhou asked, "Do you understand now? The monk replied, "I do not. Zhaozhou said, "Touzi..."
It is not that they do not compare well; indeed, such were the skillful means employed by those two venerable elders, yet even they did not attain awakening—how much less others?

If one contemplates the nature of wind, movement and stillness are not without their counterparts, and these counterparts are not themselves the Unsurpassed Enlightenment. How, then, can one attain perfect penetration?
Tong said: "This nature of universal movement comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; fundamentally, it has no counterpart.
When one observes that the power of wind has no basis, one awakens to the Bodhicitta, which is itself supreme enlightenment. How could there be two characteristics—movement and stillness?
It is only for those of initial capacity that, amidst movement, they recognize the unmoving nature and thus distinguish between the two characteristics of movement and non-movement."
This is clearly a state of duality. Being subject to duality, it is a phenomenon of arising and ceasing; it is far removed from unsurpassed Bodhi.
The seventeenth patriarch, Saṃghanandin, ordained the youth Dharmadatta, who was renamed Gayāsata.
One day, hearing the sound of wind blowing the temple bells, the patriarch asked: "Is it the bell that rings, or is it the wind? Śata replied: [The text ends here.]
Heshang Moheyan said, "It is not the wind-bells that ring; it is my own mind that rings. The Patriarch asked, "And who is it that has this mind?
Heshang Moheyan replied, "Because all things are utterly tranquil. The Patriarch said, "Excellent, excellent! He who shall succeed to my Way—if it be not you, then who?
Later, when two monks were debating the meaning of the wind and the banner, one said, "The wind moves," and the other said, "The banner moves. They engaged in such discussion.
[The monk] did not stop. Guishan Zuzheng stepped forward and said, "It is not the wind moving; it is not the banner moving. It is the mind of the worthy one that moves.
This was identical to what Śāradvatīputra had said. Xuefeng cited the Sixth Patriarch’s words, "It is not the wind moving; it is not the banner moving.
It is the mind of the worthy one that moves," and remarked, "How great is the Patriarch! He is like a dragon's head with a snake's tail. I should give him twenty blows!"
"Strike! At that time, the Venerable Daigen Fu was standing in attendance; he unconsciously gnashed his teeth. The Peak said, "I just now spoke in such a manner;
you too deserve twenty blows of the staff. National Teacher Yao ascended the hall and said: "The skillful means of the ancient sages are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
The Patriarch said, 'It is not the wind or the banner that moves; it is the mind of the observer that moves. This is the unsurpassed mind."
The Seal Dharma-gate: We are disciples under the patriarch; how should we understand the patriarch’s intent?
Do not say, "The wind and the banner do not move; it is your mind that moves falsely. Do not say, "Without stirring the wind or the banner, one directly apprehends through the wind and the banner.
Do not say, "What is it at the place where the wind and the banner move? Some say, "One clarifies the mind by relying on objects," but this is unnecessary.
Regarding the recognition of objects: some say "form is emptiness," while others say "it is neither the wind nor the banner that moves. One must understand this with subtle penetration.
But if one understands it in such a way, how does it relate to the intent of the Patriarchs?
Such an interpretation is not permitted; you venerable elders ought to know this. If you attain thorough awakening here, what Dharma-gate would there be that you could not [master]?
"Once enlightened, the skillful means of hundreds of thousands of Buddhas are all at once and thoroughly understood. What further doubt could there be? Therefore, the ancients said:
'One thing understood, a thousand things are clear; one thing deluded, ten thousand things are confused.
Elder, how could it be that you understand one case today and do not understand another tomorrow? Is it not because there is a portion of the 'matter above' that is difficult to comprehend?"

A certain class of inferior ordinary people will not understand this view; even if they were to pass through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, they would only exhaust their own spirits and weary their thoughts—there is no other possibility.
When National Teacher Shao spoke in this manner, how does he compare to Xuefeng?
He too deserves twenty blows of the staff.
"If one observes through emptiness (*śūnyatā*), then dullness and insentience are not originally awakening. Since non-awakening is distinct from Bodhi, how can one attain perfect penetration?
Tong said: "If one is biased toward mere emptiness, then it is dullness and not awakening; if it is true emptiness (*bhūtakoṭi-śūnyatā*), then it is awakening and emptiness simultaneously.
Beginners who aim for emptiness easily go astray; therefore, one must discern with care. Xuan Sha ascended the hall and said: "People of the present age do not realize this..."
According to the Middle Way principle, one falsely involves oneself in worldly affairs and sensory dust, becoming stained and attached at every turn and bound by every circumstance.

Even if one attains some awakening, the realms of dust remain chaotic and names and forms are seen as unreal; thus, one then intends to settle the mind and withdraw thoughts, seeking to subsume all phenomena back into emptiness.
To close one's eyes and hide the essence, such that as soon as a thought arises it is immediately broken and eliminated, and as soon as a subtle perception is born it is instantly suppressed—
such a view is precisely that of an externalist who has fallen into nihilism, a dead man whose soul has not yet dispersed.
Obscure and indistinct; without sensation or cognition. Plugging one's ears to steal a bell is merely self-deception.
Here, where things are clearly manifest, it is not so. It is not a matter of leaning against the door or huddling by the window; every word is present before you, beyond all deliberation.
It does not involve literary ink; it fundamentally transcends the realm of dust. It has no original rank or position, yet is provisionally called "a child who has left the home-life.
Ultimately, it leaves no trace. Whether True Suchness, ordinary beings, sages, hell-dwellers, or humans and devas—these are merely expedient methods for healing the mad child.
Even empty space undergoes no change; how could the Great Way have rising or sinking? To awaken is to move freely in all directions without departing from the fundamental limit (*bendi*).
If one reaches this point, there is no place for either ordinary beings or sages to stand. If one applies intentional thought within the words, one will be drowned and destroyed.
If one rushes outward in pursuit, one falls again into the realm of Māra. As for that which is above suchness (*tathatā*), there is nothing to be established.
Set it aside! It is just like a blazing furnace that harbors no mosquitoes or gnats. This principle is fundamentally level; why use a shovel to clear it away?
Whether moving or still, whether raising an eyebrow—this is the true path of liberation. Do not forcibly employ mental calculations; to establish such constructs is to deviate from the truth.

If you arrive here, you will not admit even a hair’s breadth [of conceptualization]. To point toward it with the intellect is already an error; even if a thousand sages were to appear, they would be no different.
Do not rest for even a single moment. Take care. If you can clearly understand Xuan Sha’s words, you will penetrate the principle of true emptiness.
Even "unsurpassed bodhi" is but a provisional name; is it not then that perfect penetration is manifest before you?
"If one observes by means of the nature of consciousness (*vijñāna*), observing that consciousness is not permanent, and yet maintains the mind as something [real], this is merely delusion;

how, then, can one attain perfect penetration? Ananda replied: "The wondrous true suchness-nature of the Tathagatagarbha is precisely the eighth consciousness. It is fundamentally not delusive. Those who have not yet seen their nature cannot transform consciousness;
rather, they are transformed by consciousness. If one employs contemplative observation, even that observation is consciousness; it is but a thought."

Because one is mindful of arising and ceasing, it is not permanent. Even if one can maintain the mind so that it remains tranquil and unmoving, this is still sustained by the power of contemplation and thus belongs to the realm of the illusory.
How could the wondrously profound and total retention (*dhāraṇī*) be such that it is originally without mind, yet does not fail to remain without even waiting for one to maintain it?
When the sixteenth patriarch, Rāhulata, arrived at the place of Saṃghanandin, he encountered...
He entered meditative absorption. The Patriarch and the assembly waited for him; after twenty-one days had passed, he finally arose from his concentration.

The Patriarch asked, "Is your body in concentration, or is your mind in concentration? Daitō replied, "Both body and mind are in concentration. The Patriarch said, "If both body and mind are in concentration..."
"How can there be coming and going? Daiten replied, "Though there is coming and going, the characteristic of concentration is not lost;

it is like gold in a well—the essence of the gold remains eternally tranquil. The Patriarch said, "Whether the gold is in the well or the gold has come out of the well, the gold itself is neither moving nor still. What is it that comes and goes?
Daiten replied, "If one speaks of the movement or stillness of the gold, what is it that comes and goes? If one speaks of the coming and going of the gold, the gold itself does not move."
Jing said, "If gold is in the well, what is the gold that has been taken out? If the gold has been taken out of the well, what is the thing remaining inside?
Tidi said, "If the gold has been taken out of the well, then what remains is not gold. If the gold is still in the well, then what was taken out is not the object.
The Master said, "This interpretation is not correct. Tidi said, "That interpretation is not established either. The Master said, "This interpretation must fall into error. Tidi said, "..."
"That argument is not established," the Patriarch said. "That argument is not established; my argument is established. Dì said, "Although my argument is established, the Dharma is not mine.
The Patriarch said, "My argument is already established, because I have no self. Dì said, "If you have no self, what argument is thereby established?
The Patriarch said, "Because I have no self, your argument is established. Dì said, "Virtuous sir..."
"Who is your teacher? Who has realized this non-self? The Patriarch said: "My teacher is Gaṇapati;
he has realized this non-self. Gaṇapati praised him with a verse: "I bow my head to Teacher Gaṇapati, who has emerged from you, O Benevolent One.
Because you, O Benevolent One, are without self, I wish to take you as my teacher. The Patriarch answered with a verse: "Since I am already without self, you must see [the truth]."

“I am the self; you are the self. Because you have taken me as your teacher, you know that the self is not the self. At these words, Nandi’s mind was suddenly enlightened, and he immediately sought ordination and liberation.
The Patriarch said, “Your mind is autonomous; it is not bound by me. He then entrusted him with the Eye of the True Dharma, speaking this verse:
In the reality of dharmas, there is truly nothing to be realized; there is neither grasping nor abandoning. Dharmas possess neither the mark of existence nor non-existence;

how, then, could they arise internally or externally? One should know that the transformation of consciousness into wisdom occurs within the space of a hair’s breadth. Failing to perceive the truth, one ultimately reverts to delusion.

"All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent; the nature of mindfulness is fundamentally subject to arising and ceasing. Since cause and effect now yield such disparate results, how can one attain perfect penetration?
Ananda replied: "According to the Dharma-gate of Buddha-recollection (*buddhānusmṛti*), mindfulness itself is the Buddha, practice itself is the Buddha, and the mind alone is the Buddha."
The Buddha is made by mind alone; cause and fruit are in perfect accord, originally not distinct in their resonance.

Now, Mañjuśrī points toward the path that transcends the mundane, whereby practice is categorized as impermanent and mindfulness as subject to arising and ceasing. To seek the eternally abiding fruit of Buddhahood through such means is therefore untenable.
This is absolutely impossible to obtain. Chan Master Qi Ji, at the invitation of friends from the Lotus Society, ascended the hall and said:

"Gradually the skin becomes like chicken skin and the hair like crane feathers; the father grows old while the son grows young. Look at these staggering steps—how they put even Wood Seat Monk to shame!
Even if gold and jade fill the halls, one must still watch out for the 'white-thief' (the thief in plain sight). How can one avoid decay, frailty, aging, and illness?"
Just as it reaches its peak brilliance, let you enjoy a thousand kinds of happiness; he has attained freedom. Yet impermanence will inevitably arrive.
"Return to the hall to drink tea. There is only the direct path for cultivation; as before, strike and circumambulate.
"Simply recite the name of Amitābha Buddha. If you merely recite it, it will not suffice. He spoke again: "Aha!
This direct path has been pointed out straightaway by Master Shandao. You all travel back and forth along this very road morning and evening;
why do you pass Amitābha Buddha right before your eyes? If you can realize it here and now—"

Then you may eliminate the obstacle of delusion, pull out the arrow of hesitation, sever the net of doubt, cut through the river of ignorance and craving, clear away the dense forest of the mind, wash away the turbidity of mental defilements, rectify the mind’s crookedness, and sever the mind’s cycle of birth and death.
Only then do you turn toward that other shore; lift up your feet and head toward the place where even Buddhas and patriarchs have never trodden. Take one more step forward and open your mouth.
Addressing the Buddhas and Patriarchs at the place where verbal explanations fail, I shall utter a single phrase to call back Master Shandao.
Do not seek other shortcuts for your practice; otherwise, you will again abandon your father and flee, wandering through foreign lands, bumping into things here and there.
How bitter! Amitābha Buddha! Furthermore, Huanglong Xin ascended the hall and said: "A pure pearl cast into turbid water..."
Turbid water cannot fail to become clear; when one recites the Buddha’s name while immersed in a distracted mind, that distracted mind cannot fail to become the Buddha.
Since the Buddha is not distracted, the turbid water naturally becomes clear. Once the turbid water has become clear, to whom does the merit belong?

After a long silence, he said: "How many times have black winds overturned the great ocean? Yet I have never heard of a fishing boat capsizing. Thus, one must fully restrain the six sense faculties and practice.
Even the Buddha-remembrance method is subject to uniform critique regarding its gradual path and meritorious efforts; by contrast,
this "hearing the sound and directly penetrating the source of nature" avoids all such faults and is truly the supreme capacity for cultivation and realization of perfect penetration.
I now address the World-Honored One: Since the Buddha has appeared in this Sahā world, the true essence of the teaching in this region consists in purity found within sound and hearing.
If one wishes to attain samādhi, it must truly be entered through the midst of hearing.
The Master said: "The Sage establishes his teachings according to different circumstances. There are those who perform buddha-work through the light of a Buddha;
there are those who perform buddha-work through a Buddha’s bodhi tree;

and so on, up to those who do so through gardens, pavilions, and towers, or through empty space, or through silence without verbal instruction—such as in the land of the Buddha Gandhottamakūṭa, where there are no written words."
It is said that it is solely by means of empty space that all devas and humans are led to enter the practice of discipline (*vinaya*).
In this teaching, the essence of the Dharma resides exclusively in sound and hearing; unmixed with worldly dust, it is most pure.
Because it is pure, one easily attains entry into *samādhi*. In this Sahā world, hearing is what accords with the capacity of the practitioner. A monk asked Xuansha: "The student..."
When a man first enters the monastery, he asks the Master to point out a way of entry. Baizhang said, "Do you hear the sound of the Yan River water?
He replied, "I hear it. Baizhang said, "Enter from here. This may be called a direct pointing-out instruction.
Free from suffering, they attain liberation. How excellent is Avalokiteśvara! Throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he enters buddha-lands as many as motes of dust.
Having attained the power of great mastery, he bestows fearlessness upon sentient beings. O Wondrous Sound, Avalokiteśvara; your Brahma-sound is like the tide of the ocean.
He saves the world so that all are at peace; he transcends the world so that one attains eternal abiding.
It is said in summary: "How excellent is Avalokiteśvara! Having already departed from suffering, he is thus able to save the world so that all are at peace.
Having already attained liberation, he is thus able to cause people to transcend the world and attain eternal abiding throughout the eternally wondrous kalpas, entering into the subtle."
In the realm of dust, the thirty-two manifestations are nowhere not pervasive. Bestowing the fourteen fearlessnesses, one attains the power of great sovereignty;
thus, the four inconceivables are wondrous and unfathomable. This wondrously wondrous hearing-mind is like a sound passing through a wall.
All are transformed into a single wondrous sound. When its wonder lies in purity, it is called the Brahma-sound (*brahmasvara*);
when its wonder lies in resonance, it is called the Tide-sound; when its wonder lies in seeking out sounds, it is called Avalokiteśvara.
This is not like the sounds of the mundane world; it is the wondrous sound of one's own nature. A monk asked Guizong, "What is the profound principle? Zong said—
[The Master] said, "No one is able to comprehend it. [The monk] asked, "What was it like before? Zong said, "If there is 'before,' you have already deviated.
[The monk] asked, "What is it like if there is no 'before'? Zong said, "Who seeks the profound meaning? He further said, "Go! There is no place for you to apply your mind.
[The monk] asked, "Is there not some skillful means (upāya) that allows students to enter? Zong said, "The wondrous power of Avalokiteśvara’s wisdom can save the world."
[The monk] asked, "What is the wondrous power of wisdom of Avalokiteśvara? Zong struck the lid of the cauldron three times and asked, "Do you hear it?
The monk replied, "I hear it. Zong said, "Why do I not hear it? The monk was speechless. Zong drove him away with his staff.
On another day, he ascended the hall and said, "I now wish to speak of Chan; all you disciples, come forward together.
Zong said, "Listen to the practice of Avalokiteśvara, which skillfully responds to all places. He then asked, "What is the practice of Avalokiteśvara? Zong then snapped his fingers and said:
"Did you all hear that? they asked. "We heard it," they replied. Zong said, "You lot! What are you looking for here?
He drove them out with his staff and returned to the abbot’s quarters, laughing heartily. Guizong remarked, "That group of people possessed a wondrous sound that dwells in peace and constancy;
he pointed it out again and again without sparing himself. How truly compassionate he was!"
I now address the Tathāgata as Avalokiteśvara has spoken: "Suppose a person is dwelling in stillness, and drums are struck simultaneously in the ten directions;
they hear them all at once in ten places. This is the perfection of reality."
Tong said: "The Avalokiteśvara Samādhi of Perfect Illumination is unconditioned and non-active.

Thus, it is like a person sitting in stillness who hears the drum being beaten in the ten directions simultaneously; this is not comparable to a situation where four sides are deficient by half. This demonstrates its perfection within the objective realm.
Once, when Chan Master Huangbo Weisheng happened to strike a window lattice with a fan, making a sound, he suddenly recalled the teachings."

The Middle Way. When drums are struck simultaneously in all ten directions, they are heard at once in all ten places. Because of this, he attained great enlightenment. Later, the Governor of Ruizhou commissioned Huanglong to select a master for Huangbo.
Huanglong assembled the community and presented this koan: "Reciting hymns on the bell tower; planting vegetables under the bed.

He said, "If anyone can explain this, they shall go to serve as the abbot. Shengchou replied: [He remained silent. Huanglong said, "This fellow has the capacity to maintain the Dharma. He was subsequently sent to take charge of Huangbo.
A fierce tiger sat blocking the road. The Dragon was greatly pleased and consequently sent him forth. That he emerged victorious may be called personally verifying its perfect reality.
The eyes do not see beyond obstructions; the mouth and nose are likewise so. The body knows only through contact; the mind’s thoughts are chaotic and without order.
"Listening to sounds through a wall, one can hear them both from afar and nearby. That the five sense organs are not uniform in this regard is precisely what constitutes the penetration of reality.

Tong said, "It is not that the five sense organs do not come into contact with their objects; however, if they must first come into contact before cognition occurs, then it is already turbid and confused."
Only the sound of a voice can be heard across a wall without losing its pure essence; thus, those whose capacity is not boundless cannot attain union with it.
This demonstrates the pervasiveness of the sense-faculties (*indriya*). Zhang Wugou stayed at the residence of the Sū family;
one night, while using the toilet, he investigated the "pine-needle" koan. Upon hearing the croaking of frogs, he attained sudden enlightenment. He composed a verse:
It is said: "On a spring night, a single frog croaks; it shatters heaven and earth, making them one family.
At such a moment, who can understand? Xuan Sha suffered aching feet at the mountain pass. If one were free from defilement, this could be called personally realizing that pervasive reality.

The nature of sound consists of movement and stillness; within hearing, it appears as existence or non-existence. When there is no sound, it is called "no-hearing," yet this is not a truly existent nature of non-hearing.
Since sound is absent, there is no cessation; since sound is present, there is no arising. Being perfectly free from both arising and ceasing, this is the eternal reality.

"Even when one is in a dream, it is not the case that hearing does not exist because one is not thinking. It is through the activity of investigation and reflection (*vitarka-vicāra*) that thought arises;

the body and mind cannot reach [the nature of hearing]. He said in general: 'Sound has movement and stillness, therefore hearing has the presence and absence of sound. But the nature of hearing is eternally abiding;
it does not arise because of the presence of sound, nor can it be extinguished because of the absence of sound. How is this verified? Even within a dream, it is capable [of hearing]."
The sound of the pestle used for pounding grain produces a resonance like that of bells and drums; in a dream, this is as if one were awake, occurring without the need for deliberate thought.

This differs from those states where what is perceived is not constant. Thus, through consciousness, one can perceive its permanence. Even when the other five sense organs are present in a dream, they are able to perceive objects with vivid clarity;
yet it is not necessarily the case that these perceptions arise solely in response to external objects before one, for there is a distinct element of volitional thought involved.
Because these are merely conditioned constructs, the other five faculties exist when there is deliberation and do not exist when there is no deliberation;

they exist when confronting objects during the waking state and do not exist when confronting objects during dreams. Remaining stagnant within body and mind, they are bound by the roots and their objects.
Only the nature of the ear-consciousness does not exist because of deliberation during the waking state, nor does it cease to exist because of a lack of deliberation during dreams. Its...
The nature has already transcended the realm of both thought and non-thought;
therefore, returning to listen to the source of awareness and observation is neither thinking nor non-thinking, and differs from ordinary contemplation that employs discursive thought.
Having emerged from the sphere of thought, it departs from the sense organs, beyond the reach of the body; it departs from consciousness, beyond the reach of the mind.
"This is what is meant by 'when arising and ceasing have both ceased, quiescent extinction manifests. Is this not called the true, eternal Buddha-nature?
Zhang Wugou said to Daohui, "Whenever I am in a dream, I invariably recite the *Yuyan* and *Mengzi*. What do you think of this?
Daohui cited the *Complete Enlightenment Sutra*, saying, "Because of quiescence, the minds of all Tathāgatas throughout the worlds of the ten directions manifest therein."
[The manifestation] is like an image in a mirror. Wugou said, "Unless one is a true teacher, one cannot hear this discourse.

Wugou’s dream-like state suggests that his residual habit-energies (*vāsanā*) have not yet been eliminated. Mahamati points out that the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) does not preclude the emergence and subsidence of habit-energies;
this can be called penetrating the path of ultimate permanence and truth.

Now, in this Sahā world, the treatises on sound and language have been proclaimed and clarified. Yet sentient beings are deluded regarding their fundamental hearing; because they follow after sounds, they wander through the cycle of rebirth.

Even though Ānanda possesses a powerful memory, he cannot avoid falling into deviant thoughts. Is this not because he follows that which he has sunk into? By reversing the flow, one attains freedom from delusion.
Ānanda, listen attentively. Relying on the Buddha’s majestic power, I shall proclaim the Vajra King, the inconceivable, illusory-like True Samādhi of the Mother of Buddhas.
You have heard all the secret gateways of countless buddhas; yet if you do not first eliminate the outflows of desire, [you will not realize them].
Accumulating learning leads to error and delusion; yet you intend to uphold the Buddhas through hearing. Why do you not hear that which hears itself? He replied:
"Regarding the capacities of those in this land, the nature of mind is not clearly understood.

Since clarity is attained by relying on discourse based on sound, it is common for one to awaken to the Way through words. Nevertheless, sentient beings fail to reach the fundamental source and instead wander along with the flow of sounds."
This is what is called delusion. However, to pursue external objects is to be heterodox; to return to the root is to be orthodox.

If one can flow against the current to exhaust the source and reach the state of non-arising and non-ceasing, this is "returning to hearing" (*fǎnwén*). One may then realize the true and eternal, avoiding being swept away by the whirlpool.
This is the single path to *nirvāṇa* for all Buddhas, as numerous as motes of dust—the Vajra Samādhi of perfuming through hearing and cultivation—called "Suchness."
The illusory one is so called because of the absence of volitional action; being without action and without conditioning, they penetrate the primordial hearing from which all Buddhas emerge.
If there is volitional action and conditioning, the outflows of desire will not be eliminated; even if one extensively upholds the secrets, it will instead result in error.
It is not merely a defiled mind lingering with attachment that is called an "outflow of desire" (*kāma-āsrava*); even the mere flicker of a thought directed toward seeing a Buddha is termed "deviant.
Therefore, turning the hearing back to hear one's own nature (*śrutvā svabhāvam*) is the foremost method for counteracting excessive learning.
Emperor Xiaozong of the Song dynasty asked a monk from India: "Since this is Flying Peak (*Feilai Feng*), why does it not fly away? The monk replied: "A single movement..."
"It is not as good as being alone in stillness. He asked again, "What do you recite with the rosary in your hand? He replied, "I recite the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
He asked again, "Why do you recite your own name? He replied, "Seeking from others is not as good as seeking within oneself."
A monk asked Zen Master Zhichao, "What is the Buddha? Chao replied, "Who are you? The monk said, "Are you not he yourself?
Chao said, "If it were so, there would be no connection. These two statements both accord with the principle of hearing that which hears itself.
Hearing is not born of itself; it exists because of sound. When hearing turns back and detaches from sound, who could there be to name that which is capable of such detachment?
Once a single faculty returns to its source, all six faculties achieve liberation. Seeing and hearing are like illusory cataracts; the three realms are like flowers in the sky.

Upon hearing this, the obscuring faculties were removed; as the dust of delusion vanished, awareness became perfectly pure. When purity reached its ultimate limit, light permeated everywhere, and silent illumination encompassed the void.
He said: "From here on, I shall clarify the path of entering through one's own hearing.

First, one must carefully examine whether this hearing arises from causes and conditions, or whether it arises spontaneously. Hearing is fundamentally non-arising; therefore, it is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it spontaneous."

Birth is manifested specifically through sound; therefore, the name "hearing" is established. If one turns back the faculty of hearing until it reaches the state of non-arising and non-ceasing, there is no longer a subject that hears, and naturally, there is nothing heard. Being detached from sound, they do not interfere with one another.
This capacity to detach from sound can no longer be called "hearing. Who then could give it a name? Only he can bestow names upon all things.
Nothing can be given a name by another; it can only be metaphorically described as a "source.

Therefore, returning to the source and reverting to the root, one finds that even "hearing" has no name—how could there be any bondage? This very single faculty is, in its essential nature, liberation, and thus the six faculties are simultaneously purified.
The six faculties are inherently pure from the beginning; it is only when they suddenly give rise to seeing and hearing that they become [defiled].
This capacity is like the illusory film produced by staring fixedly; suddenly perceiving the triple world and being governed by it is like seeing flowers in the sky with cataracts in one's eyes.
These illusory films and flowers in the sky are fundamentally non-existent, yet by following the current and forgetting the source, one fails to realize they are delusions.
Now, upon hearing the restoration of original hearing, the cataracts of the sense-organ are first removed; thus, the six objects of perception dissolve, and the original...
Awakening is perfectly pure, like the clear orb of an eye; from where could flowers arise?

What is called "perfect purity" does not reject the myriad phenomena, yet both the sense faculties and their objects are simultaneously purified. This is the ultimate state of clarity, seeing through the ten directions as clearly as pure lapis lazuli containing a precious moon within;
how could its light fail to penetrate everywhere? This is internal luminosity radiating forth—tranquil yet imbued with illumination.

This is what is called the illumination of the primordial clarity (*yuan-ming*). When this illumination does not give rise to objects, stillness contains the void like a single cloud in the great purity of space;
thus the ocean of awakening is limpid and perfect, and one attains its primordial subtlety.
For those who seek great liberation, can they afford to cease their "returning of the hearing"? Huangbo said: "This Dharma is equal; it has no high or low. This...

This is called Bodhi. This very source, the pure mind, is identical with sentient beings, Buddhas, worlds, mountains, and rivers—whether possessing form or lacking form—it pervades the ten directions, all-pervasive and equal, without the marks of "self" or "other.

This source, the pure mind, is eternally self-perfected, luminous, and universally illuminating; yet worldly people do not realize this, instead recognizing only seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.
It is because of the mind. It is obscured by seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing; for this reason, one does not perceive the essential body of brilliant purity.
Simply by being directly without-mind, the essential body manifests of itself, like the great solar orb rising in the void and illuminating the ten directions everywhere.
There is no further obstruction. Therefore, the practitioner on the Path should recognize that seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, as well as all activities and movements, are empty.

By emptying out seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, the path of the mind is cut off and there is no way for it to enter. One should simply recognize the fundamental mind within the very place of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.
Yet, this fundamental mind does not belong to seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, nor is it separate from them.
Do not give rise to views based upon seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing. Do not stir thoughts based upon seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing.
Nor should you seek the mind apart from seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing, nor abandon seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing to grasp at dharmas.
Neither identical nor separate, neither abiding nor clinging, free and sovereign in every direction—there is nothing that is not the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
As Huangbo said, once the cataracts of delusion have been completely ground away, this too serves as an aid in returning to the source.
Returning to observe the world, it is like events within a dream. Mātanga is but a dream; who can detain your form?
It is like a skilled worldly illusionist who conjures various men and women; though one sees their faculties move, it is all pulled by a single mechanism.
When the workings of the mind cease, one returns to stillness; all illusions are revealed as being without inherent nature.

Tong said: "If one can attain such purity that the radiant light penetrates everywhere, and silent illumination encompasses empty space—since even empty space is contained within it, how much more so the things that exist within that space?
Therefore, if the cataract of delusion is removed, not only are the three realms empty."
Flowers are originally non-existent. Within the triple world, whether it be the sense organs (*indriya*) or their objects (*viṣaya*), all are like dreams and illusions.
How could Māraṅgaka in a dream detain the form of one who is awake? Even if the mind were sharp and brilliant, it cannot grasp anything within a dream.
This is one sign that the sense organs and their objects are fundamentally liberated from the very beginning. The *Liezi* records an account of illusion: [text continues].
A master skillfully creates an illusory person, complete with the five internal organs within and the five sense faculties without. He drives it about as a performer, appearing perfectly human.

Once the performance ends, the illusory person beckons the king’s favorite consort. The king becomes enraged. The illusionist then explains that the illusory person is entirely composed of wooden parts.
Only then does the king’s anger subside. The king’s wrath was not directed at the illusory person; the illusory person had no [agency].
It is because of the mind. Since illusion has no inherent nature from the start, how could there be room for joy or sorrow within it?
This, moreover, is a sign that the faculties and their objects are fundamentally liberated from the very beginning. Master Chan Master Wuzu Yan addressed the assembly, saying:
"Yesterday, when I entered the city, I saw a stage of puppet shows. I could not help but draw near to watch them. Sometimes they appeared dignified and extraordinary."
Or, one might see someone so hideous as to be unfit for movement, walking, or sitting;
seeing them in blue, yellow, red, or white, and observing them closely, one finds that there is actually a person behind a blue cloth curtain.
Unable to restrain my amusement, I asked the Chief Secretary his surname. He replied, "Old Monk, stop looking! Why do you ask about a surname? I was thus [interrupted].
He uttered a single phrase, leaving one with nothing to say in response and no ground on which to stand.
Is there anyone who can speak for this mountain monk? Yesterday he fell from his station; today here he uproots the very source.
If you can understand the message of uprooting the source, you may bring the workings of the mind to rest and return to stillness.

The six sense organs are also like this. Originally they depend on a single brilliant spirit, which divides into six harmonious combinations. When one of these is brought to rest and restored, the functions of all six cease to operate.
As soon as the thought arises, defilements dissolve; one achieves perfect, bright, pure, and wondrous clarity. Only when the remaining traces of dust are gone does one reach the stage beyond study.
"Ultimate clarity is itself the Tathāgata. Huangbo said:
"The same single luminous clarity is divided into the six harmonious unions. "Single luminous clarity" refers to the one mind;
"six harmonious unions" refers to the six sense faculties. These six faculties each unite with their respective objects: the eye unites with form.
The ear conjoins with sound; the nose with fragrance; the tongue with flavor; the body with touch; and the mind with mental objects (*dharma*).

From the midst of these, the six consciousnesses arise, forming the eighteen realms (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*). If one realizes that these eighteen realms are non-existent, the six [faculties] are bound together into a single brilliant clarity.
This single brilliant clarity is precisely the mind. Those who practice the Way all know this.
However, he could not help but provide an interpretation based on intellectual cleverness and the six harmonies; consequently, he was bound by the Dharma and failed to accord with his original mind.
When the Tathāgata appeared in the world wishing to preach the True Dharma of the One Vehicle, sentient beings did not believe it and instead raised slander, sinking into the sea of suffering.
If [the Buddha] had not preached at all, he would have fallen into stinginess and greed, failing to universally bestow the wondrous Way upon sentient beings. Thus...

He established expedient means and taught that there are three vehicles (*yāna*). These vehicles have their great and small, and their attainments have their shallow and deep; yet none of these are the fundamental Dharma.
Therefore, it is said: "There is only the path of the One Vehicle; the other two are not the truth. Nevertheless, he was ultimately unable to manifest the Dharma of the One Mind.
Thus, he summoned Kāśyapa to share his seat and separately entrusted to him the teaching of the One Mind that transcends words. This is one branch [of the transmission].

"Let them practice separately. If they can achieve realization, they will immediately reach the stage of Buddhahood. This statement by Huangbo does not concern those who still have residual dust or are merely students;
he is truly a vessel for the Mahāyāna. The *Zhēnlùn* says: "A bodhisattva at the initial stage perceives the medium-grade function.
Because they have deep faith in True Suchness (Tathatā), they obtain a partial vision and know that the body of the Tathāgata neither comes nor goes."
There is no interruption in their departure; they are merely manifestations of the mind, not separate from *tathatā*.
Nevertheless, these bodhisattvas have not yet been able to abandon subtle conceptualization because they have not yet entered the stage of the *dharmakāya*.

Bodhisattvas with purified minds perceive these subtle functions, which become increasingly refined until, within the final stage of the bodhisattva path (*niṣṭhā-bhūmi*), they are seen to be completely exhausted. Subtle...
The subtle function is called the *saṃbhogakāya* (Enjoyment Body). Because there is the *karmavijñāna* (karmic consciousness), one perceives the *saṃbhogakāya*.
If one were separated from the *karmavijñāna*, it would be invisible. All Tathāgatas are the *dharmakāya*.

The *dharmakāya* possesses no differentiated marks of self or other, nor of color or form, because they perceive one another. Now, that which exhausts the subtle function is named the *saṃbhogakāya*; this is because [it exists]...
The subtle characteristics of karmic consciousness are said to pertain to the stages of the Bodhisattva; thus it is said, "When residual dust remains, one is still a learner.

If one is free from karmic consciousness, there is nothing further to be seen; this is called the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya; thus it is said, "When clarity reaches its ultimate limit, that is the Tathāgata."
The great assembly and Ānanda: Turn back the mechanism of inverted hearing; by hearing back toward the self-nature, that nature will achieve the Unsurpassed Way.
Such is the true nature of perfect penetration. This is the single path to Nirvana for the Buddhas as numerous as motes of dust. All Tathāgatas of the past—
This gate has already been accomplished. All bodhisattvas of the present now each enter into perfect clarity.
Those who practice and study in the future should rely upon this Dharma; I, too, have realized it through it—not only Avalokiteśvara.

Tong said: "When hearing follows outward-moving conditions, one becomes deluded regarding the source and pursues only the branches; thus it is called 'reaching' [the ear]. To turn back the hearing is the means to revolve those conditions.
When one turns back the hearing toward the self-nature, one turns away from dust and unites with awakening; thus it is called 'correct. Once one hears the self-nature,"
One immediately beholds one's original face; this very faculty of hearing thus becomes unsurpassed bodhi—perfect, penetrating, true, and eternal, not to be obtained through external means.
This is the sudden gateway through which the Buddhas of the three periods of time realize unsurpassed bodhi.
A monk asked Changsha, "What is Mañjuśrī? Changsha said, "The walls, the tiles, and the rubble are. The monk said, "If so..."
"What is Avalokiteśvara? The monk said, "Sound and speech are. "What is Samantabhadra?

The monk said, "The mind of sentient beings is. "What is the Buddha? The monk said, "The physical body of sentient beings is. "The bodies of all Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are identical;
why then are there various names? The monk said, "It is because one returns to the source from the faculty of the eye."
The one named Mañjuśrī returns to the source through the faculty of hearing and is thus called Avalokiteśvara; returning to the source through the mind, he is called Samantabhadra.
Mañjuśrī is the Buddha’s wisdom of wondrous observation; Avalokiteśvara is the Buddha’s great compassion without conditions;
Samantabhadra is the Buddha’s wondrous practice of non-action. These three sages are the Buddha’s wondrous functioning, and the Buddha is the true essence of these three sages. This is functioning.
Thus, although there are as many provisional names as there are sands in the Ganges, their essence is collectively designated as one Bhagavān.

Therefore, know that those who individually enter perfect illumination are in no way different from all Buddhas; yet, because the faculty of hearing is most perfect, one must take Avalokiteśvara as the method.
It is truly as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has taught: he inquired after various skillful means to save those of the final age who seek to transcend the world and achieve the mind of nirvana;
among these, Avalokiteśvara is supreme. All other skillful means are likewise the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha.
One immediately abandons worldly toil through this very matter; it is not a matter of long-term cultivation. Whether at a shallow or deep level, one speaks the Dharma alike.

I prostrate to the Tathāgatagarbha, which is untainted and inconceivable. I pray that you will bestow your grace upon future generations, so that they may have no delusions regarding this gateway and easily achieve success through skillful means.

It is fit to teach Ānanda and those submerged in the final age of decay; by cultivating this faculty alone, one attains perfect penetration that surpasses all others—such is the nature of the true mind.
The Master said: "Among all the methods for selecting the perfect penetration in response to the Buddha’s inquiry, none compares to the Dharma-door of Avalokiteśvara’s 'reversing the hearing.

It is capable of instructing Ānanda to remedy his fault of fixating on external sounds; it is capable of saving those in the final age to uproot the suffering of saṃsāra. No other expedient means can match it.
By chance, a single faculty was touched, and he realized his own fundamental matter. For those of deep capacity, it leads them into the subtle."

This is not within the reach of those at the initial stage of practice; for those of shallow capacity, it would cause them to stagnate in mere traces and thus conflict with the state of perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa*).
It is not a study that can be practiced from beginning to end by all. Only those who enter through this faculty of the ear-root (*śrotra-indriya*) are suitable regardless of their depth of capacity;

they may practice it long-term, it is most easily accomplished, and is the supreme expedient (*upāya*). Therefore, I pray that the World-Honored One will silently bestow his grace upon it, and that Mañjuśrī [will likewise confirm] its reality.
The heart of one who serves others is also truly comforted. On this occasion, Chan Master Qi of Zhongta ascended the hall and said:
"The circumstances of the rice and gruel here are for the sake of you, my brothers, whom I have brought forth and proclaimed; they are by no means ordinary.

If you wish to attain the essential, it is rather the mountains, rivers, and the great earth that shall reveal it to you. Since the Way is eternal, it can also lead to ultimate realization. If you follow Manjusri..."
As for those who enter through the Gate of All Things: all unconditioned phenomena—earth, wood, tiles, and rubble—assist you in triggering the catalyst.
If you enter through the Gate of Avalokiteśvara: all sounds and noises—even frogs and earthworms—assist you in triggering the catalyst.
If you enter through the Gate of Samantabhadra: you arrive without moving a step. These three gates of skillful means are shown to you, like holding up a single finger.
"Breaking an arrow and stirring the waters of the great ocean, so that the fish and dragons therein know water is their life—do you understand?

If one lacks the eye of wisdom to examine this with discernment, then no matter how many hundreds of skillful means you employ, they will not lead to the ultimate realization. Furthermore, a monk asked Chan Master Daofu:
"Those of us who are beginners and recent students have recently entered the monastic groves. Within the gates of expedient means, we beg the Master for instruction."
Fupu struck the door-bolt. A monk asked, "Is there anything further above this? Fupu said, "There is. The monk asked, "What is this matter that is further above?
Fupu struck the door-bolt again. Now, Puxian said, "The hearing-mind penetrates the ten directions," and Wenshu said, "I also realize it from within.
These three sages struck and sang to one another, leading people to enter through the faculty of hearing.

This is because it accords with the spiritual capacities of those in this region. If the various venerable masters had not clarified the ultimate reality from beginning to end to guide others, how could they have ever followed the tracks of universal penetration?
Furthermore, why is it that those who achieve swift realization are so rare?

While it is certainly no easy matter to enter and realize the manifestation of nirvana before one's eyes, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The faculty of hearing has no [independent] cognition."
Because it is known [by another], it should not be heard. Since auditory consciousness lasts for only a single moment, it cannot perform discrimination;

thus, it should not hear. Mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) likewise cannot hear. Why is this? First, the five consciousnesses cognize the five objects, and only thereafter does mental consciousness cognize them.
Mental consciousness cannot cognize present five-objects; it cognizes only past and future five-objects. If mental consciousness...
If one could perceive the five sense-objects of the present, then even the blind and the deaf should be able to perceive sounds and forms. How marvelous is this discourse!

It perfectly accords with the principle of this quiescent extinction (*śānti*). Since sound alone lacks sentience and lacks faculties, the two characteristics of movement and stillness clearly do not arise.
Since the faculty alone lacks sentience, the act of hearing reaches its limit and does not abide. Since consciousness alone lacks form, it is without opposition and without obstruction.

Because the locus [of perception] is thus, that which perceives and that which is perceived are both empty. When both the perceived and the perceiver are empty, birth and cessation are extinguished; one then swiftly realizes it in a single thought-moment.

This is fundamentally not a different path from those who progress through gradual increase and gradual transformation. Therefore, by turning the hearing inward to enter the stream, one reaches the state of non-birth and non-cessation.
This is what one should follow.
Thereupon, Ānanda and the great assembly attained clear understanding in both body and mind, receiving a profound revelation.
They beheld the Buddha’s Bodhi and Great Nirvāṇa as being like a person who has traveled far away on business and, though not yet returned, clearly knows his home.

On the road where they were returning, there was a vast assembly of the eight classes of beings, including devas and nāgas, those of the two vehicles still in training, and all the newly resolved bodhisattvas, numbering as many as ten Ganges-sands;

all of them attained their original mind, became free from dust and defilement, and achieved the purity of the Dharma-eye. Upon hearing these verses, the bhikṣuṇī Śrīprabhā became an arhat. An immeasurable multitude [of beings likewise attained realization].
All those born [in that realm] gave rise to the peerless mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Ānanda adjusted his robes, joined his palms in homage before the great assembly, and prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet. His mind and its traces were perfectly luminous; he was filled with a mixture of sorrow and joy.
Desiring to benefit all sentient beings of the future, he bowed his head and addressed the Buddha: “O Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One, I have now realized how to attain Buddhahood.”
This is the Dharma-gate. By practicing within it, one attains freedom from doubt. One constantly hears the Tathāgata speak these words:

"He who seeks to deliver others before he has delivered himself is a bodhisattva who has resolved for enlightenment; he who, having perfected his own awakening, is able to awaken others is a Tathāgata appearing in the world.
Although I have not yet been delivered, I vow to deliver all sentient beings of the final kalpa, World-Honored One. As for these sentient beings—
As they move further away from the Buddha, false teachers will preach the Dharma as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River. How may one cause them to gather their minds and enter samādhi?
How may one cause them to establish themselves at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), remain far removed from demonic activities, and attain no retreat or discouragement regarding the bodhicitta?
Tong said: "The Peerless, Unsurpassed, Perfectly Equal and Perfect Enlightenment—this is what is called the Supreme Vehicle.
Because there is nothing with which it can be equaled, yet it is able to be equal to all things, it is called 'Peerless' (asama-sama).
Because it is free from afflictions, it is called Buddha-Bodhi. Because it is free from birth and extinction, it is called Great Nirvana. All immeasurable sentient beings know this."

This arousal of the bodhicitta clearly understands that afflictions are not the home, while awakening-nature is the home; it clearly understands that birth and extinction are not the home, while nirvana is the home.
Through the dharma-gate of "turning the hearing inward," one enters the stream and causes what is lost to vanish, thereby reaching the manifestation of quiescent extinction.
Within this, one practices and attains the path of wondrous, perfect penetration, which is as clear as pointing at something with one's finger.

Master Ānanda, although he has not yet personally crossed over to reach the other shore by exhausting the two deaths, he desires to deliver future sentient beings so that they may all enter right concentration and not be disturbed by Māra.
Since demonic affairs are exceedingly numerous and difficult to guard against, consider the bhikṣuṇī Śīlabhadrikā:
had she not obtained the Tathāgata’s divine mantra, how could her lustful mind have been suddenly extinguished? Thus it was accomplished.
"Arhat. This final answer regarding the fifty kinds of *skandha-māra* serves to repay this question and further clarifies the path by which one returns to one's home.
Chan Master Nian of Shoushan addressed the assembly, saying: 'I, an old monk, intend to return to my hometown.
Who can go along with me? At that time, a monk asked: 'I wonder, Master, when will you do so?'"
Xuanjian departed. He thought to himself, "I will tell you when I have a companion. The monk asked, "What about the matter for one who has no companion?
Xuanjian said, "Throughout the day one meets no person; though it is clear, one knows not where. The monk asked, "And what if one suddenly encounters a person?
Xuanjian said, "The lost child does not return home; he has lost the path by which he came. The monk said, "I beg the Master..."
He pointed out the path home. Nanquan said, "A withered tree conceals a dragon; it exists without reliance. The monk asked, "When will the Master return?
Nanquan said, "Once gone, no one knows its sound; throughout the six realms, there is no news.
The monk asked, "As for the very matter of returning home, what then? Nanquan said, "Singing alone the tune of the Hu people... (The text ends here).
The man and the people were in perfect harmony. The monk asked, "What is it like when one suddenly encounters a true知音 (zhīyīn—a person of like mind)?

Zhenyan said, "The stone figures on the mountain clap their hands together; the wild old man by the stream laughs heartily. The monk asked, "And as for the matter of returning home after having left—how is that?
Zhenyan said, "The eight kingdoms offer up court robes; the four phases undergo no change. The monk said, "Not yet..."
He carefully examined his own position and thought: "Mañjuśrī does not sit upon a golden terrace; he naturally possesses the carefree bamboo whisk.
Observe the thread coming and going of the *Lotus Sūtra*—the rhythm of striking and singing is entirely free. This is still the very flavor of Yangshan."
At that time, the World-Honored One, in the midst of the great assembly, praised Ānanda: "Excellent, excellent! It is just as you have asked:
how to establish the site of enlightenment and rescue sentient beings drowning in the final age. Listen attentively now; I shall explain it for you."
Ānanda and the great assembly responded, “So be it,” and respectfully accepted the instruction.

The Buddha told Ānanda, “You have often heard me, within the *vinaya*—which here is called the *Vinayapiṭaka*—proclaim the practice of the three definitive principles: namely, that gathering the mind constitutes the precepts; based on the precepts, concentration arises.”
Because concentration gives rise to wisdom, these are called the three untainted trainings (*trīṇy aśaikṣāṇi*).
It is further stated: "The two previously mentioned principles of certainty are: first, to examine the mind of the causal ground; second, to select the perfect faculty (*indriya*).
