By tracing back the flowing faculties to their source of non-arising and non-ceasing, one proceeds directly toward unsurpassed Bodhi, without further discussion of precepts."
The equal cultivation of concentration and wisdom is the single gateway through which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions transcend to the sublime path of *śamatha*.
This is for the purpose of guiding those of the highest faculties. As stated therein: "When the faculties and objects do not coincide, it is never that there is no precept;

it is like clarifying turbid water. It is never that there is no concentration; the inner radiance shines forth. It is never that there is no wisdom; yet one simply does not rely on [the formal categories of] precept, concentration, and wisdom."
Because one binds oneself [by transgressing], it is therefore termed the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).

Now, I shall first examine the precepts in detail and clarify the four prohibitions within the Vinaya, so as to accommodate those of middling and inferior faculties. To prevent the influence of Māra, one cannot but be strict regarding the precepts.
The Hinayana takes the formal precepts as its dharma, roughly treating only the branches; the Mahayana takes the restraint of the mind as its precept, subtly severing the root.
With the dharma-precepts, there is merely no physical transgression; with the mind-precepts, there is no mental transgression.

When the pearl of the precepts is perfectly bright, one is able to transform consciousness into wisdom, thereby emptying the five aggregates and destroying the five turbidities. What more need be said of demons?
How truly a cause for concern this matter is! The Sixth Patriarch addressed the assembly, saying: "This Dharma-gate of mine takes concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) as its foundation.

You, the great assembly, must not be deluded by the notion that concentration and wisdom are distinct. Concentration and wisdom are of one essence; they are not two. Concentration is the very substance of wisdom."
Wisdom is the function of concentration. At the very moment of wisdom, concentration resides within wisdom; at the very moment of concentration, wisdom resides within concentration.

If one understands this principle, it is precisely the equal training of concentration and wisdom. Those who practice the path should not say that concentration must first arise before wisdom is produced.

First, wisdom gives rise to concentration; these two are distinct. One who holds such a view perceives that dharmas possess two characteristics: the mouth speaks virtuous words, yet the mind is not virtuous;

though there is both concentration and wisdom, concentration and wisdom are unequal. If both mind and mouth are virtuous, then the internal and external are of one kind, and concentration and wisdom are equal.
Self-awakening and cultivation do not depend on stillness. If one disputes over priority, it is the same as [the former error].
Deluded people do not sever the struggle between victory and defeat; instead, they increase their attachment to self and dharmas, remaining unable to leave behind the four marks.

Good friends, concentration and wisdom are like a lamp and its light: where there is a lamp, there is light; without a lamp, there is darkness. The lamp is the substance of the light, and the light is the function of the lamp.
Although their names are two, their substance is fundamentally one. Thus, although the Sixth Patriarch clarified that concentration and wisdom are one—
The *Zhong* (Middle) fascicle states: "When mind and speech are both good, the internal and external are of one kind; concentration and wisdom are equal, and precepts are also included therein.
On another occasion, he said to Zhicheng: "The Dharma I preach does not depart from self-nature (*svabhāva*).

To preach the Dharma apart from its substance is called 'preaching characteristics' (*lakṣaṇa-vāda*), which leads to perpetual delusion regarding self-nature. One must know that all myriad dharmas arise entirely from self-nature."
The manifestation of the nature is the true dharma of precept, concentration, and wisdom. Listen to my verse: "When the mind-ground is free from wrongdoing, it is the self-nature precept;
When the mind-ground is free from delusion, it is self-nature wisdom; When the mind-ground is free from distraction, it is self-nature concentration.

Neither increasing nor decreasing, it is the self-existent vajra; Whether the body departs or arrives, it is fundamentally samādhi. Upon hearing this verse with sincerity, he attained realization and presented his own verse:
"The illusory body of the five aggregates—how could illusion ever reach its ultimate end? To turn back toward True Suchness (Tathatā) is for the Dharma to become impure again.

The Patriarch agreed, saying: "These are the precepts, concentration, and wisdom taught in the Most Supreme Vehicle; they are all but talk from within the house. They do not compare to the words spoken outside the gate."
The difference is as vast as that between heaven and earth.
Ānanda, what is meant by "restraining the mind"? That which I call "precepts" (śīla) is this:

if the beings of the six realms in all worlds do not harbor lustful thoughts, they will not follow the continuous cycle of birth and death. As you cultivate samādhi to fundamentally emerge from worldly toil, if the lustful mind...

It cannot be removed; the Māra cannot be cast out. Even if one possesses great wisdom and meditative concentration manifests before them, if they do not sever lust, they will inevitably fall into the paths of the Māras—either as high-ranking Māra kings, mid-level Māra subjects, or low-ranking Māra women.

These various Māras also have their own followers, each claiming for themselves that they have attained the Unsurpassed Way. After my parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Final Dharma, there will be many such as these.

The subjects of Māra flourish in this world, widely practicing greed and lust, acting as "good friends" who cause all sentient beings to fall into the pit of craving and views, thereby losing the path to Bodhi.
You must teach the people of the world to cultivate *samādhi* by first severing the mind of lust;
this is called the Tathāgata’s foremost, definitive, pure, and clear instruction from the Buddhas of the past. Therefore, Ānanda, if not...

One who abandons lust yet cultivates meditative concentration is like one who steams sand and gravel, hoping to produce cooked rice; even after hundreds of thousands of kalpas, it will only be called hot sand.

Why? Because this is not the source of rice; it is composed of sand and gravel. If you seek the wondrous fruit of Buddhahood with a body of lust, even if you attain wondrous enlightenment, it will all be rooted in lust.
With lust as its fundamental basis, you will revolve through the three miserable realms and will certainly be unable [to escape].

"Come forth! When the Tathāgata enters nirvāṇa, by what path shall you cultivate and realize [enlightenment]? You must ensure that the mechanism of desire is severed in both body and mind, such that even the nature of severance is non-existent.
Only then may you hope for the Bodhi of the Buddha. What I have spoken thus is called the Buddha’s teaching;
what is not spoken thus is the teaching of Pāpīyān."
The Master said: "The sentient beings of the six realms continue in a cycle of birth and death.
You love my mind, and I cherish your form; thus, life after life, you remain perpetually bound. Lust is the root of this, beginning with the manifestation of color through sight.
When clarity perceives form, the thought of it arises; differing perceptions breed hatred, while shared thoughts breed love. A single moment of this root of love is the very first movement."

Therefore, one must begin by prohibiting sexual desire. If one practices meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) without first prohibiting sexual desire, even if one attains subtle awakening, it will only increase the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) for lust.

Consequently, in the end, one will fail to achieve the fruit of Buddhahood and instead become a member of the demonic host. Demons also possess supernormal powers and transformations, and they too can preach the Unsurpassed Way;
yet, because their karmic habit of lust has not been eliminated, once their demonic merit is exhausted, they ultimately undergo the cycle of rebirth.
The three miserable realms are merely suffering. Lust arises through external conditions, yet the mind is its root; therefore, it is called "mental lust.
If the mind does not move, the conditions will not arise on their own. Thus, by restraining the mind and upholding the precepts, one first severs mental lust; this is termed "severing the nature."
There remains a nature of severance; as long as one has not yet abandoned its antidote, the duality of opposition remains distinct, and the latent impulse for lust still persists.
Only when even this nature of severance is absent can it be called true severance. Lust alone is the root of affliction; by severing it, Bodhi may be hoped for.
Lust alone is the source of birth and death; by severing it, Nirvana may be realized. As for what is meant by "severing," it is like...
Once hands and feet are severed, they can no longer be used. When lust is severed, one takes non-arising and non-extinction as the mind of the causal ground;
thus, one attains right concentration. Otherwise, how could one possibly obtain cooked rice by steaming sand? The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* says:
"One should not preach the Dharma to a woman while perceiving characteristics in her body that give rise to thoughts of desire. Nor...

He delights in seeing [the Dharma]. If he enters another's home, he does not converse with young girls, virgins, widows, and the like, nor does he associate with intimacy with the five kinds of impotent persons. He does not enter another's home alone;
if there is a necessary reason for entering alone, he simply keeps his mind single-pointedly on the Buddha. If he preaches the Dharma to women, he does not expose [his body].
He smiles with his teeth but does not reveal his chest. Even for the sake of the Dharma, he remains unaffectionate; how much less so for other matters.
He takes no pleasure in keeping young disciples or novice monks (śrāmaṇeras), nor does he delight in having them share the same teacher.
He always prefers sitting meditation in secluded places to cultivate and restrain his mind. This was the standard established by the former Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones. In the past...
The Second Patriarch once mingled with the crowds in brothels and taverns. When people mocked him, he said, "I am simply disciplining my own mind;
what does it have to do with you? Were one not a person of great liberation, how could one enter the mud and the water?
Chan Master Baizhang Weizheng ascended the hall and said, "Master Yantou paid three copper coins and obtained a wife. Only...
They understand how to catch shrimp, crabs, and clams, yet they do not know how to give birth to sons or raise daughters;
thus, until this very day, their family lineage has been severed. Do you wish to know Nanquan’s wife? Today, Baizhang will not spare his lips to explain it for all of you:
"Tangled hair and thorn-leaf hairpins—rare indeed in this world; her cloth skirt is still the dress she wore at her wedding. How strange!"
"I thought this was Master Huo’s wife; it turns out she looks exactly like my Master Huo. A monk asked Qingshan, "What is the house style of your Reverence?
Qingshan said, "Brocade and embroidery, a silver incense pouch; the wind blows its fragrance all along the road.
When Yantou heard of this, he sent a monk to say, "Tell Sister Eighteen that she must serve her husband, Pan, well."
Lang: Yantou was much like one who speaks of "fengliu" Chan;
yet Weizheng borrows from Yantou’s traces and makes it even more flowery—both are nothing but lotuses in midwinter (pronounced huò).
Ānanda, furthermore, among the sentient beings of the six realms in all worlds, if their minds do not kill, they will not follow along with the continuity of birth and death.
You cultivate samādhi fundamentally to emerge from worldly toil; if the mind of killing is not eliminated, you cannot emerge from the dust.

Even if you possess great wisdom and meditative concentration manifests before you, if you do not sever killing, you will inevitably fall into the realm of spirits. Those of superior grade become great... [spirits].

Those of superior power shall become *rākṣasa* ghosts; those of middling quality shall become flying *yakṣas* and various ghost generals; and those of inferior quality shall become earth-walking *rākṣasas*.
These various ghosts and spirits will also have their own followers, each claiming for themselves that they have realized the Unsurpassed Way.
After my parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Final Dharma, many such ghosts and spirits will flourish in the world, declaring that by eating meat one attains Bodhi.
"Ti-lu, Ānanda, when I permitted bhikṣus to eat the five kinds of pure meat, those meats were all produced through my supernatural power;
they originally possessed no life-force. You, O brāhmaṇa, live in a land that is mostly damp and humid, further compounded by sand and gravel, so that grasses and vegetables do not grow."
It is through the empowerment of my great compassionate spiritual power, and by virtue of my great compassion, that I provisionally designate this as "flesh" so that you may experience its flavor.
How can it be that after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, those who eat the flesh of sentient beings still call themselves disciples of the Śākya?

You should know that such meat-eaters—though their minds may appear to have opened and they may resemble those in *samādhi*—are all great *rākṣasas*; when their retribution ends, they will surely sink into the depths.

"In the ocean of suffering of birth and death, such people as these—who are not disciples of the Buddha—are still engaged in killing one another, devouring one another, and eating one another without end.
How can such people escape the three realms? You should teach the people of the world to cultivate samādhi, and next, to cease the taking of life."
This is called the second definitive, pure, and clear instruction of the Tathāgata, the World-Honored Buddha of former times.
Therefore, Ānanda, if one does not cease killing while practicing meditative concentration, it is like a person who blocks his own ears and shouts at the top of his voice.
When seeking someone, they do not hear of them; these are called those who wish to hide but reveal themselves all the more.
Pure bhikṣus and bodhisattvas, when walking on forked paths, do not tread upon living grass, much less pull it up with their hands.
How could those of great compassion take the flesh and blood of sentient beings to serve as food? If bhikṣus do not wear silk, cotton, or fine fabrics from the East, nor those of this land...

Shoes, boots, furs, and wool; milk, curd, and clarified butter (*ghṛta*): in these ways, O bhikṣu, one attains true liberation from the world and repays past debts, no longer wandering within the three realms.

Why is this? Because by consuming their bodily parts, one becomes bound to them as a condition. It is like a person who eats the various hundred grains produced from the earth; their feet do not leave the ground.
One must cause both body and mind [to remain so] toward all sentient beings—whether toward their bodies, their bodily parts, or their... [bodies].
The mind has two kinds of ointments: not wearing [robes] and not eating [food]. I declare that such a person is one who has attained true liberation.
What I have spoken thus is called the word of the Buddha; what is not spoken thus is the word of Pāpīyān.
Tong said: "Before the Buddha attained enlightenment twelve years prior, he had not yet established the Vinaya; at that time, it was permitted for bhikṣus to eat the five kinds of pure meat.
Later, because of the six groups of bhikṣus who killed animals specifically for food, the Vinaya was established from then on to prohibit this forever.

Various sutras define the five kinds of meat as those that have not been seen, heard, or suspected [to have been killed for oneself], as well as those left by birds or those that died of themselves. Now, you speak of the five..."
Pure meat is produced through supernatural transformation, much like the "wood-meat" found on Mount Tai; it is fundamentally devoid of the life-faculty (jīvitendriya), and is therefore called "pure.
That people are unable to abandon killing is because they consume it for clothing or food.

If one wears the silk, cotton, fur, or wool of sentient beings, or eats the blood and flesh of sentient beings, these all serve as conditions [for further bondage], such that one has not yet achieved true liberation. If you desire...
Can one transcend the triple world? It is like the people at the beginning of a kalpa, whose bodies possessed a golden light and whose feet seemed to ride upon the clouds;

because they consumed the "earth-fat" and ate fragrant rice, their bodies became solid and heavy, their feet no longer left the ground, and they ultimately became subject to the conditions of the earth.

Therefore, one cultivates dhyāna and practices samādhi fundamentally to avoid transgressions; yet instead, one commits acts of killing. How is this different from covering one's ears to avoid people while actually remaining exposed?
It would be more appropriate to remain silent, yet instead one shouts aloud. To wish to escape saṃsāra in such a manner is impossible.

Even if one attains dhyāna and samādhi, it is merely a demonic concentration of ghosts and spirits. This demonic concentration of ghosts and spirits resembles true samādhi; therefore, it is called "semblance."
Samādhi. Its ultimate goal is necessarily the divine path.

If the body is of the nature of flesh and blood, and its parts are of the nature of fur and hair, yet the body neither clothes nor feeds itself, it is entirely because the mind exercises restraint over it. Therefore, the gathering of the mind constitutes the precepts.
If one who has attained great liberation does not follow this code of discipline, they should possess another eye. Master Xiange was a man of unknown origins;
he received the seal of mind from Dongshan and lived among the common people in Minchuan. Throughout both winter and summer, he wore only a single robe.
Day after day, he would gather shrimp and clams along the riverbanks to fill his belly, and at night, he would stay at Baishui.

Inside the paper-money offerings at a temple dedicated to the Horse God, Chan Master Jing of Huayan wished to determine whether [the deity] was authentic or false. He first hid himself within the paper money.
Late at night, when Lianzi returned, Jing seized him and asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
Lianzi immediately replied, "The wine table and dishes before the spirit. Jing said, "It is no wonder you were born of the same root as I," but later he did not know [what happened next].
This is what is meant by one who walks among those of different kinds. Once, when the monks of the East and West Halls were disputing over a cat, Nanquan encountered them.
He addressed the assembly, saying, "If you can speak [the truth], I shall save the cat; if you cannot, I shall kill it.
The assembly was speechless. Nanquan then killed it. When Zhaozhou returned from outside, Nanquan recounted the previous conversation.
He showed it to him. Yunzhou then took off his straw sandals, placed them on his head, and walked out. Nanquan said, "If you had been there, you would have saved the cat.
Furthermore, while Xuefeng was working in the fields, he saw a snake; he lifted it up with his staff.
He summoned the assembly, saying, "Look, look! He used a knife to sever [the object] into two pieces; Xuefeng then tossed his staff behind him and did not look back.
The assembly was struck with astonishment. Feng said, "How magnificent! Xuefeng’s divine application is exactly like Nanquan’s."
Xuansha’s disregard was quite similar to Zhaozhou’s. [Zhaozhou] Quan said, "If you had been there, you would have saved the cat.
[Xuefeng] Feng said, "How clever! These two fathers and sons achieved a perfect rhythmic harmony, as if one seal had been pressed into another.
When Xuedou and Tiantong composed their verses, they were likewise drawing the gourd by following the model. Xuedou’s verse says: "Both halls are..."
Du Shanhe stirs up clouds of smoke and dust; there is nothing that can be done about it. Fortunately, Nanquan was able to issue the command:
with one stroke, he cuts it in two, regardless of bias or partiality. When the public case is resolved, one asks Zhaozhou: he wanders freely through the city of Chang’an.
"Straw sandals on the head—no one understands; once you have returned to the mountain home, you may simply rest. Tiantong’s verse says: "The monks of both halls were all in a tumultuous fray;
Old Master Wuzhuo was able to test the right from the wrong. With a sharp blade he cut them all through, so that both images vanished;
For a thousand ages, people have loved this master of the Way. This Path has not yet perished; those who can appreciate it are worthy of praise. He carved through the mountain..."
O Sea! Only the Honored Yu was great; refining stones to mend the heavens, only Nüwa was sagely. The Old Man of Zhaozhou has his livelihood:
upon the head of his straw sandals, he carries a slight comparison. Coming from amidst the extraordinary, he is yet a clear mirror; this very gold is not mixed with sand.
These two or three veteran masters take the taking of life as their Buddhist service; such are the Great Men.
This realm is therefore not something that can be fathomed by ordinary means.
Ānanda, furthermore, among the sentient beings of the six realms within this world, if their minds do not harbor theft, they will not follow along with the continuity of birth and death.
You cultivate samādhi in order to fundamentally emerge from worldly toil; yet if the thieving mind is not eliminated, you cannot escape from the dust. Even if you possess...
Though they possess much wisdom and manifest meditative concentration, if they do not sever their thieving ways, they will inevitably fall into deviant paths.

They will be possessed by various demons—superior spirits, middling ghosts and goblins, or inferior wicked persons—and these hosts of devils will each have their own followers, with every one claiming to have attained the Unsurpassed Way.
After my parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Final Dharma, such demonic and heterodox beings will flourish in great numbers.
In this world, there are those who harbor deceit and fraud while pretending to be virtuous spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).

Each claims for themselves to have attained the "Dharma of the Superior Man" (*uttaramanuṣyadharma*), deluding the ignorant and causing them to lose their right minds. Wherever they go, the households they visit suffer depletion and ruin.

Therefore, I instruct my bhikṣus to wander from place to place for alms, so that they may abandon greed and accomplish the path to Bodhi. These bhikṣus do not cook food for themselves; they rely on...
This wretched life is but a sojourning in the triple world, a single journey with its coming and going; once departed, there is no returning.

How can these thieves, wearing my robes, peddle the teachings of the Tathāgata for profit, performing all manner of deeds while claiming they are the Buddha-dharma? They instead revile those who have left the household life and possess the precepts, labeling them followers of the Lesser Vehicle.
Because of this, they mislead and delude immeasurable sentient beings, causing them to fall into the Avīci Hell. If I—
After my parinirvāṇa, if there are bhikṣus who resolve their minds with determination to cultivate *samādhi*,
and who, before an image of the Tathāgata, burn a single lamp on their body, cauterize a finger-joint, or apply a single incense stick to their flesh—

I declare that such a person shall at once settle all karmic debts from beginningless time, bid a final farewell to the world, and forever be liberated from all outflows (*āsrava*). Although they have not yet...
This clarifies the path to unsurpassed enlightenment. Such a person has already attained a mind of certainty regarding the Dharma;

even if they do not perform this minor act of relinquishing the body as a cause, should they eventually attain the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), they will inevitably be reborn as a human being to repay their past debts, just as it was with my own "horse-barley" [period], exactly so and no different.
You should teach the people of the world to cultivate *samādhi* first, and only thereafter cease from stealing; this is called the Tathāgata following the Buddhas of the past.

This is the World-Honored One’s third definitive and pure instruction. Therefore, Ānanda, if one does not abandon theft while practicing dhyāna-concentration, it is like a person pouring water into a leaking cup;
though they seek to fill it, even after passing through kalpas as numerous as dust motes, it will never be restored.
If bhikṣus do not store even a fraction of what remains from their robes and bowls, and give away any surplus from their alms-food to the hungry...
When sentient beings gather in a great assembly and join their palms in prostration to the multitude, if someone strikes or reviles them, they should regard it as identical to praise.
They must ensure that both body and mind are completely relinquished; their flesh, bones, and blood are shared with all sentient beings.

They shall not take the Tathāgata’s teachings of provisional meaning and twist them into their own interpretations to mislead beginners. The Buddha certifies such a person as having attained true samādhi, just like me.
What is thus spoken is called the Buddha’s teaching; if it is not spoken in this way, it is the teaching of Pāpīyān.
It is said in response: Greed that does not cease inevitably leads to theft. To steal another's property to provide for one's own body results in harm limited to that body alone;
therefore, even burning one's fingers as an offering to the Lamp-Lighter (Dīpaṃkara) would suffice to repay such a debt. However, if one acts as a deceitful peddler of the Tathāgata...
To misinterpret provisional teachings (neyārtha) as one's own understanding and thereby mislead beginners is what is called "stealing the Dharma.
Its harm is immeasurable. This truly arises because one secretly delights within oneself, desiring to monopolize one's own excellence and being unable to relinquish it.

It is easy to give up the body, but difficult to give up the mind. One must ensure that both body and mind are relinquished; only when the thieving mind is entirely eliminated is [the true path attained].

One may speak of attaining true samādhi. Formerly, the Brahmin Kṛṣṇa (here translated as "Pure Lineage") exercised his supernatural powers and, holding two *saṃpuṣpita* *śiṃśapā* flowers in his left and right hands, came to make an offering to the Buddha.
The Buddha called out to the ṛṣi, and the Brahmin responded. The Buddha said, "Put them down. Thereupon, the Brahmin put down the flower in his left hand. The Buddha—

The Buddha again called to the rishi, "Put it down. The Brahmin then put down a flower from his right hand. The Buddha again called to the rishi, "Put it down. The Brahmin said, "World-Honored One, both my hands are now empty; what more do you instruct me to put down? The Buddha said, "I am not instructing you to discard these flowers; you must discard [them]. By this, he meant that one must abandon all attachments. This is why it is said: "If you wish to see the Buddha, look at the mind-ground. The six external objects, the six internal faculties, and the six intermediate consciousnesses are all abandoned simultaneously;

there is no place from which they are abandoned—this is the place where you escape birth and death. Upon these words, the Brahmacārin immediately realized the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Zen Master Huanglong Weiqing, having had his mind certified by Huitang, often said to others: "The illness of those who study now is that they have not yet escaped birth and death."
Where does the illness lie? It lies in the fact that the thieving mind has not yet died. Yet this is not his fault; it is the fault of the master.
It is like Emperor Gaozu of Han, who deceived and killed Han Xin. Although Xin died, was his mind truly dead?

Among scholars of antiquity, there were those who liberated themselves from birth and death beneath a single word. Wherein lies the proof? It lies in the fact that their "thieving mind" has already died.
Yet this was not something the scholars could achieve on their own; it was truly due to the subtle and profound skill of the teacher’s hammer and tongs.
It is like Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, who sat in his great hall and beheld Hou Jing without uttering a sound or shifting his breath, yet Jing’s heart was already withered and exhausted.
The various doctrines taught elsewhere are not without their beauty; however, they are like the flowers painted by Zhao Chang—though the flowers may be lifelike, they are not real flowers.
This serves as a warning for those who would trade in a counterfeit version of the Tathāgata.

Ānanda, it is thus with the sentient beings of the six realms in this world: although their bodies and minds may be free from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, and these three practices may already be perfected, if they engage in great falsehood, their *samādhi* will not attain purity.
They will become demons of craving and views, losing their lineage as disciples of the Tathāgata.
This refers to claiming to have attained what one has not attained, or declaring to have realized what one has not realized; or seeking to be the most honored, supreme, and foremost in the world.

One says to another: "I have now attained the fruit of srotāpanna, the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of anāgāmin, the path of arhatship, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddha, and the various stages of the bodhisattvas prior to and within the ten bhūmis. One then seeks from them their prostrations and repentance.
Coveting offerings—such a person is an icchantika (one devoid of a virtuous mind). They extinguish the seeds of the Buddha, just as a person uses a sword to cut down a tāla tree.

The Buddha has prophesied that such a person will forever destroy their roots of goodness and possess no further wisdom or insight; they shall sink into the ocean of the three sufferings and never achieve samādhi.
After my parinirvāṇa, I command all bodhisattvas and arhats to manifest bodies and be born in that age of the Dharma’s decay.

Within these [realms], they manifest in various forms to deliver beings from the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*). They may appear as śramaṇas (here translated as "the diligent and tranquil"), lay devotees, kings, or government officials;
as boys or girls; and even as courtesans, widows, thieves, robbers, butchers, or merchants.
While working together with his colleagues, he praised the Buddha Vehicle, causing their bodies and minds to enter samādhi.

He never spoke of himself as being a true Bodhisattva or a true Arhat, lest he reveal the Buddha’s secret cause or speak lightly of those who had not yet studied; this was except at the time of his death.
I have entrusted this matter to you in secret. How could such a person delude sentient beings and commit a great falsehood?

You must teach the people of the world to practice *samādhi*, and thereafter eliminate all great falsehoods. This is called the fourth definitive, pure, and clear instruction of the Tathāgata and the World-Honored Buddhas of the past.

Ānanda, this secret gāthā of subtle phrases from the *Uṣṇīṣa-vijaya-sitātapatrā*, gives birth to all Buddhas of the ten directions.
By means of this mantra-heart, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions attain the state of Buddhahood.
The Supreme Perfectly Enlightened Ones of the ten directions hold this mantra-heart; they subdue all demons and restrain all heterodox teachers.
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions mount this mantra-heart and sit upon precious lotus flowers, responding to lands as numerous as motes of dust.
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions contain this mantra-heart and turn the Great Dharma Wheel in lands as numerous as motes of dust. The Tathāgatas of the ten directions maintain this mantra...

This mind can bestow the prediction of enlightenment by touching one’s crown in the ten directions. Even before one’s own fruition is accomplished, one also receives the Buddha’s prediction in the ten directions.
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions rely on this mantra-mind to rescue and deliver all beings from suffering throughout the ten directions—namely, the sufferings of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals;

the suffering of the blind, the deaf, and the mute; the suffering of encountering those one hates; the suffering of being separated from those one loves; and the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks.
Suffering! When the five aggregates are ablaze and great and small calamities arise simultaneously, one shall be liberated from them all.
Perils from bandits, perils from armies, perils from kings, perils from prisons, perils from wind, fire, and water, hunger, thirst, and poverty—these shall dissolve and vanish upon mere thought.

The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, following this mantra-heart, enable one to serve spiritual friends throughout the ten directions; within the four modes of deportment, they provide offerings as desired, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
He was invited into the assembly and honored as a Prince of the Great Dharma.

When the Tathāgatas of the ten directions attain this mantra-heart, they are able to gather and sustain their close kinsmen throughout the ten directions, causing those of the Hīnayāna to hear the Secret Treasury without giving rise to fear.
By reciting this mantra-heart, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions achieve unsurpassed enlightenment, sit beneath the Bodhi tree, and enter Great Nirvāṇa. The Tathāgatas of the ten directions...

I have come to transmit this mantra-heart. After my parinirvāṇa, entrust the affairs of the Buddha-dharma to them so that they may ultimately maintain and uphold it, strictly purifying the precepts until all are rendered completely pure.

Even if I were to speak this Buddha-peak Radiance Ghanavyūha Pañcarakṣā mantra from dawn until dusk, with its sounds linked in continuous succession and its words and phrases never overlapping, even after kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, [it could not be exhausted].
It is exhausted. Furthermore, this mantra is called the "Crown of the Tathāgata.

For you who are still in training and have not yet ended the cycle of saṃsāra, if you resolve with utmost sincerity to attain arhatship, it is impossible that you could sit in the place of practice without holding this mantra, thereby keeping your body and mind far removed from all demonic activities.
It is simply not possible.
Tong said: "The Buddha-peak Divine Mantra is inconceivable. Although it is said that one merely upholds various names and titles, their silent resonance is like a secret command within an army;
it is also like drawing upon the waters of the great ocean to extinguish a tiny spark.
Since all demonic activities are created solely by the mind, we now invoke the inconceivable realm realized by all Buddhas."
One purifies the realms with this. It is like a sovereign mind subduing the thieves of the mind; there is nothing that is not extinguished in accordance with the moment.
This is the secret cultivation and secret realization of the Supreme Vehicle (*agrayāna*), which does not rely on verbal expression, but is itself the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Therefore, it is said that all Buddhas of the ten directions are born from it. First, one attains Perfect Enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*); second, one subdues all demons and externalists.
Third, one should enter into lands as numerous as motes of dust; fourth, one turns the Great Dharma Wheel; fifth, one receives the Buddha’s prediction of enlightenment;
sixth, one delivers sentient beings from all sufferings; seventh, one becomes a prince of the Dharma; eighth, one gathers in those with whom one has a karmic affinity;
ninth, one enters Great Nirvana; and tenth, one entrusts the affairs of the Buddha-Dharma. All of these are accomplished through this mantra-heart; it is not otherwise.
Following this single path—who could possibly equal it? The purport of the named sutra does not, in its entirety, depart from this.

To say "attaining the state of Perfectly Complete Enlightenment" is precisely to enter the ocean of universal knowledge (*sarvajñatā*). To say "subduing demons and externalists" is precisely the eradication of evil incantations.
To say "responding to lands as numerous as motes of dust" is precisely the King of the Wondrous Lotus. To say "turning the Great Dharma Wheel" is precisely the Unsurpassed Jewel.
It is a seal. To say "conferring the prediction by stroking the head" refers to the mantras of consecration (*abhiṣeka*).
To say "delivering from all sufferings" refers to the salvation of Ānanda and the bhikṣuṇī Śrīmatī. To say "the great Dharma prince" refers to the myriad practices of all bodhisattvas.

To say "gathering and receiving through intimate causes" refers to protecting and rescuing those with whom one has an intimate karmic connection. To say "entering great nirvāṇa" [refers to the ultimate liberation].
This is precisely the Śūraṅgama Samādhi. To speak of "entrusting the affairs of the Buddha-dharma" refers to the definitive meaning of cultivation and realization.

This mantra-heart contains manifold meanings; all Tathāgatas of the ten directions emerge from it, and for this reason it is called the Dhāraṇī Mantra, the Mother of the Buddhas of the Ten Directions.
If one does not clarify this matter, various views will arise like swarms of bees, leading one to become a māra or a heterodox practitioner engaged in karmic activity.
Without ceasing, they undergo manifold sufferings themselves; this is common to all these lands as numerous as motes of dust.

One who can clearly understand this matter becomes a Dharma Prince, receives the Buddha’s prediction of enlightenment, and is entrusted with the affairs of the Buddha-Dharma to turn the Great Wheel of Dharma.
Not only does such a person deliver themselves, but they are also able to deliver others; this is precisely the sequence for attaining Buddhahood. Those who uphold this mantra should aspire to...
Regarding the realization of Buddhahood through seeing one's own nature, how could it ever be compared to ordinary secret mantras or scriptural passages? Baizhang said:

"If, regarding all phenomena such as existence and non-existence, you harbor even the slightest trace of a mind of attachment or defilement, then even if your feet are treading upon lotus flowers, you are still acting like a demon.
If you grasp at 'original purity' and 'original liberation,' thinking 'this is the Buddha' and 'this is myself,' [you are lost]."

Those who interpret the path of Chan as being spontaneous belong to the naturalistic non-Buddhists (*prakṛtivāda*). If one clings to the idea that it is accomplished through causes and conditions and realized through cultivation, one belongs to the causal non-Buddhists (*hetuvāda*).
To cling to existence is to belong to the eternalist non-Buddhists (*śāśvatavāda*). To cling to non-existence is to belong to the nihilist non-Buddhists (*ucchedavāda*).
To cling to both existence and non-existence is to belong to the extremist non-Buddhists (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). To cling to neither existence nor non-existence...

This belongs to the nihilistic views of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) and is also called the "deluded non-Buddhist view. Simply put, at this very moment, do not form views such as that of a Buddha or nirvana;
be entirely free from all views of existence and non-existence, and even be free from the view of non-existence—this is called right view.
Be free from all hearing, and even be free from the view of non-hearing—this is called right hearing. This is what is meant by "subduing the non-Buddhists. There is no [other way].
When the demons of ordinary beings come, this is a great divine mantra; when the demons of the two vehicles do not come, this is a great illuminating mantra;
when the demons of bodhisattvas do not come, this is the unsurpassed mantra; and even when the demons of Buddhas do not come, this is the mantra of the unequaled with the unequaled.
First, transforming the *asura* of sycophancy and crookedness among sentient beings; second, transforming the *asura* of sycophancy and crookedness among those of the Two Vehicles;
third, transforming the *asura* of sycophancy and crookedness among Bodhisattvas. These three transformations purify the land.
All phenomena—whether existent or non-existent, mundane or sagely—are like gold ore. One's own accord with the principle is like the gold itself. Gold and ore are distinct from one another.
When separated [from impurities], pure gold is revealed. Suddenly, if someone comes seeking money or seeking treasure, one transforms the gold into money and gives it to them.
It is also like the substance of flour, which is genuine and free from sand or salt; if someone begs for *tso*, one transforms the flour into *tso* and gives it to them.
It is also like a wise minister who thoroughly understands the king’s intention: when the king travels, if he asks for *sindhu-pātha*, the minister immediately presents a horse;
when it is time to eat, if he asks for *sindhu-pātha*, the minister immediately presents salt.

These serve as metaphors for those who study the profound principle (*paramārtha*), being able to master it skillfully and responding to circumstances without fail. They are also called "Lions Beyond the Six. Master Zhì said: "He acts according to the person..."
They manifest in a hundred thousand ways. A Bodhisattva of the Ten Grounds is neither hungry nor satiated; entering water, they do not drown; entering fire, they are not burned.
Even if one wished for them to be burned, it could not be done. They are constrained by numerical measures and fixed limits, whereas the Buddha is not like this.
Entering fire, one is not burned; yet if one wishes to be burned, one is burned. Entering water, one does not drown; yet if one wishes to drown, one drowns.
Such a person exercises mastery over the four elements, wind, and water. Indeed, upon reaching the stage of Buddhahood, one attains mastery over wind and water.
The nature itself is the mantra; the mantra itself is the nature. What could not be accomplished therein?
Within the inconceivable, this matter has always existed. Only through the mantra can demons be subdued. Now, Baizhang says that the absence of any demons coming forth is itself the mantra;
this, too, is profoundly significant.
Ānanda, if in any world, among the sentient beings of any given land, this dhāraṇī is written upon birch bark, palm leaves, paper, silk,
or white woolen cloth according to what is produced in that country, and kept within a fragrant pouch; and if the person’s mind is dull such that they are unable to recite or memorize it,
yet they either wear it upon their person or keep it written within their home— then you should know that for as long as that person lives, all [their obstacles] will be...

No poisons can cause them harm. Ānanda, I shall now further recite this mantra for you, to protect and deliver the world, to attain great fearlessness, and to bring about the supramundane wisdom of all beings. After my parinirvāṇa, for sentient beings in the final age...

If there are those who can recite it themselves or teach others to recite it, you should know that such beings who maintain this recitation cannot be burned by fire, cannot be drowned by water, and cannot be harmed by great or small poisons. This extends even to devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits.
Whether it be the enchantments of spirits or demons, or any malevolent incantations, none shall be able to affect them. Their minds will attain right concentration (*samādhi*).

As for all curses, sorcery, and poisonous drugs—whether from gold, silver, plants, trees, insects, snakes, or the toxic vapors of myriad things—if they enter the mouths of those people, [they shall be neutralized].

It shall become the flavor of ambrosia. All malevolent stars, as well as various ghosts and spirits, and those with cruel hearts and poisonous natures, will be unable to harbor ill intent toward such a person.
Piṇāka (the Boar-headed and Elephant-nosed ones), the various evil kings of ghosts, and their retinues, shall all acknowledge this profound kindness and constantly provide protection.
Ānanda, you should know that this mantra always possesses eighty-four thousand nayutas [of power].

He is accompanied by a multitude of Vajragarbha-rāja Bodhisattvas, numbering as many as the sands of the Ganges—each in the hundreds of millions (koṭi)—with each one having a retinue of vajra-beings who attend upon him day and night. Should there be sentient beings with distracted minds...
It is not merely through samādhi; by recollecting it in mind and upholding it with speech, this Vajra King will constantly follow those sons of good family.
How much more so for those who possess the resolute bodhicitta? This King of the Vajra Bodhisattva Treasury is subtle in essence and swift in action.

Their spiritual consciousness is awakened; at that moment, these persons are able to remember eighty-four thousand *Ganges-sand* eons with their minds, knowing them thoroughly and completely without any doubt.

From the first eon until their final body, in every successive birth, they shall never be reborn as yakṣas (*sī-cā*), rākṣasas (*chàn-rè-shí*, man-eating demons), pūtanas (*fù-dān-nà*, feverish disease demons), or kaṭapūtanas (*jiā-tā-fù-dān-nà*, foul-smelling demons).
Kumbhāṇḍas (demon-spirits who cause nightmares), Piśācas (spirits that devour vital energy), and so forth, as well as all hungry ghosts—
whether with form or without form, with perception or without perception— in such evil realms, this son of good family, if he reads, recites, copies,
transcribes, wears, or preserves [this], and makes various offerings, will not be born in states of poverty, lowliness, or unpleasantness throughout kalpa after kalpa. This...
For all sentient beings, even if they themselves do not perform meritorious deeds, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions shall bestow all their merits upon this person.
By means of this, they shall attain [the state of Buddhahood] for as many *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, which are unspeakably unspeakable.

They are always born in the same place as all Buddhas. With immeasurable merit, like evil that has accumulated for a long time (the fruit being called "one stalk with three seeds"), they cultivate together in the same place and are never separated.
Therefore, they can cause those who have broken the precepts to purify the root of their discipline;

To know that the dharma of true suchness is one is to realize that delusion fundamentally does not exist. It is like a person who becomes confused by relying on directions; the confusion has no inherent characteristic of its own.
To mistake the east for the west, the direction itself does not actually change. If one attains awakening, the "west" is found to be nothing at all.

Regarding the gateway of *tathatā* (suchness): how profound these words are! This may be taken as the true definition for the cessation of delusion.
Thus, transforming non-awakening (*abodhi*) to rely upon awakening is called unsurpassed *bodhi*; transforming birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) to rely upon non-arising is likewise so named.
It is called Great Nirvana. It is not that awakening exists separately apart from non-awakening, nor that non-arising exists separately apart from birth-and-death.
Rather, when deluded views are extinguished, true nature manifests;

Because it benefits all sentient beings in the world, it is called "unsurpassed" and "great. Furthermore, there are six types of transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).

First is the transformation that diminishes power and augments capacity: this refers to diminishing the force of defiled seeds and augmenting the functional capacity of pure seeds, thereby gradually subduing active manifestations;

it is also termed the transformation of the basis. Second is the transformation of thorough penetration: through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), one penetrates reality and, by its power, severs the two [obstructions].

The obstacle. Second is the transformation through partial realization of reality; third is the transformation through cultivation, which refers to the gradual abandonment of innate afflictions stage by stage and the realization of the transformation of the basis into reality;

fourth is the transformation of the fulfillment of the fruit, which refers to the ultimate stage where one permanently abandons all coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*) through the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*) and suddenly realizes the complete transformation of the basis into the fruit of Buddhahood; fifth is the inferior transformation.

This refers to the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha), who, weary of suffering and longing for quiescence, realize true analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) but lack superior capability.

The sixth is the "vast transformation," which refers to the stage of the Mahāyāna; therein, they are free from both longing and weariness, penetrate the two kinds of emptiness, sever the two obstacles simultaneously, and suddenly realize unsurpassed bodhi, because they possess superior capability. "What is the appearance of the seal upon your mind? Wuzu shouted, "The patterns are already manifest. Hearing this, Min attained realization and subsequently requested certification.
