"Master, stop citing these stories. Wait until I speak; let me see. Wuzu granted his request. Yunmen said, "When you ordinarily brandish the mallet and raise the whisk, is this not what is taught in the sutras:
'All phenomena in all worlds—all marks whatsoever—are precisely the wondrously luminous true mind of bodhi'?
Wuzu laughed and said, "So you have been making your living right here all along! Yunmen spoke again: "To go below..."
When Heshang struck the meditation platform, he asked, "Is this not 'returning the hearing to hear the self-nature, whereby that nature achieves the Unsurpassed Way'?
Miaoxin said, "Have you not seen it stated in the sutras: 'The wondrous nature is perfectly luminous, transcending all names and forms'?

At these words, Miaoxin was suddenly enlightened. Miaoxin left Sichuan and resided at Jia Shan; Miaoxin ceased his lectures and attended him as a follower. One night, while Miaoxin was addressing the assembly, Heshang raised a koan:
The old sail had not yet been hoisted, yet the people did not harmonize with the conditions and sought a resolution.

Wuzhuo said, "Ask me. Only after he raised the previous topic did Wuzhuo say, "The cypress tree in the courtyard. Thereupon, [the man] attained thorough penetration. He said to Wuzhuo, "The ancients said it was like a single drop falling into a vast ravine;
they did not realize that the great ocean can fall into a single drop. Wuzhuo laughed and said, "What can be done about this?"
Hanhe. Before long, he was ordered to share the master’s seat. Wuzhuo spoke a verse, saying: "Do not boast of having mastered the *Four-Part Vinaya* or completed the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*;
Cast off the clouds and investigate thoroughly from the very depths. Do not emulate Master Huilang who went personally to Mazu;
Rather, be like Deqiao who visited Longtan. For seven years I traveled back and forth at Zhaojue; For three years I soared above the Azure Cliff. Today, I trouble you to fill [this position]..."
The First Seat: Amidst a cluster of a hundred flowers appears the udumbara. The ancients truly investigated and truly realized;

they underwent countless transformations of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) before finally attaining a stable seat. Thus we know that although the extinction of delusion is called "the True," it is not easily realized.
Ānanda, if you now wish to cultivate the true samādhi and proceed directly to the Great Nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata,
you must first recognize these two causes of delusion regarding sentient beings and the world. When such delusions do not arise, this is the true samādhi of the Tathāgata.
Tong said: "True samādhi is not attained through cultivation. Whatever can be cultivated cannot be called 'true.
One must first recognize the cause of delusive conditions; once that cause is absent, inversion does not arise. Since inversion is absent,"
If one does not call this "the Real," what else could it be? The objects of perception (viṣaya) arise delusively in discrete fragments; this is the meaning of *dhātu* (realm).
These realms lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and flow on without abiding; this is the meaning of *loka* (world). The world, too, lacks intrinsic nature.
Since they lack intrinsic nature, their very substance is empty and quiescent; this is called "True Samādhi. When Chan Master Shenzan of Guling encountered Baizhang, [he said:]
Having attained awakening, he returned to his original teacher, who asked him, "While you were away from me, what work or accomplishments did you achieve?
He replied, "I have achieved nothing at all. Thereupon, the teacher sent him to perform manual labor. One day, while bathing, the teacher ordered him to remove the dirt from his body.
The Master then patted [the boy’s] back and said, "What a fine Buddha hall! Yet the Buddha is not holy. The Original Teacher turned his head and looked at him.
The Master said, "Though the Buddha is not holy, he is at least able to emit light. One day, while the Original Teacher was reading a sutra by the window, the Master [said]:
A bee was attempting to escape through a window screen. The Master saw it and said, "The world is this vast and wide, yet you refuse to come out;
you will be drilling through that old paper for donkey's years. He then spoke a verse: Refusing to leave the empty gate, You throw yourself at the window—how foolish!
Drilling through old paper for a hundred years, When will you finally emerge? The Master then set down his scriptures and asked:
"Whom have you encountered on your travels? I have observed that your speech has been extraordinary from the beginning.
The Master said, "I, this humble one, was shown a place of rest by Venerable Baizhang; I now wish to repay his compassionate virtue.

Thereupon, the Abbot informed the assembly and prepared a vegetarian feast, requesting the Master to preach the Dharma. The Master ascended the seat and proclaimed the tradition of Baizhang’s school, saying:

The numinous light shines alone, transcending the faculties and objects; its essence reveals true permanence, unbound by words and letters. The nature of mind is unstained, fundamentally and spontaneously perfected.
Simply by detaching from delusive conditions, one is the Buddha of Suchness. Upon hearing these words of his original teacher, he was awakened and said:
"Who would have expected that in my old age I would hear of the ultimate matter? This is truly what is called going directly to the Great Nirvana of the Tathāgata."
"Pan" means "not so. Rarely does it not follow the delusions of sentient beings; how could there ever be an end to this?
Ānanda, what is meant by the "delusions of sentient beings"? Ānanda, it is because the nature of the luminous mind is inherently bright and perfect.
The causal consciousness gives rise to its nature; this nature arises from deluded perception. From ultimate non-existence, it becomes ultimate existence.
This existence and that which exists have no cause for their cause, nor do they have a locus for their locus. They are fundamentally without root; based on this non-abiding, the world is established.
As for all sentient beings, they are deluded regarding their original perfect luminosity; thus, this false fabrication arises. This false nature has no substance and has nothing upon which it relies.

When one wishes to return to the truth, that which is sought as "true" is already not the true nature of Suchness. Seeking to restore what is not true results only in the complete formation of non-characteristics.

Neither arising nor abiding, neither mind nor phenomena, they arise from one another. The power of arising brings forth illumination; through perfuming, karma is formed. Like karmas attract one another;
because of this, there is the karma of sensation. Through mutual extinction and mutual arising, there thus come to be the delusions of sentient beings.
Tong said: "Previously it was stated that the continuity of sentient beings takes the clarity of awakening as its fault;

here it is stated that the inversion of sentient beings encompasses both karma and its fruit, which likewise arises from the clarity of the nature. This nature gives rise to deluded vision. Now, how can the clarity of the nature give rise to delusion?
Because there is discrimination due to this clarity, and with discrimination one falls into the realm of consciousness. This consciousness has no root."
Therefore, it is called delusion. If there is no discrimination, this is the functioning of wisdom (*jñāna*).

To be able to discriminate without defiled attachment—this is called the pure white consciousness (*viśuddha-vijñāna*), and this is called the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*). Because it does not fall into spatial location, it is called "luminous and perfect.
If it were established as a singular entity, luminosity would not be perfect; it would then become a false vision, like the example previously cited of two moons.
The shadows of the lamps are all produced by the disease of cataracts; from absolute non-existence, they become ultimate existence.
This "capacity to act" and the "object acted upon" do not have a cause that serves as their basis for being able to act. Since their cause does not exist, where could they possibly abide?
This characteristic of that which abides and that in which it abides is itself a delusive characteristic; it is understood to be utterly devoid of any root that can be found.
Abiding is fundamentally rootless; abiding is thus non-abiding. If one realizes this non-abiding, its very substance is unborn. It is not that one says it is "non-existent."
It is simply non-abiding. Based on this non-abiding, all dharmas are established; yet this does not hinder the various manifestations of the world and its sentient beings.
Within my own nature, which is perfectly luminous, there is fundamentally no obstruction. One is all, and all is one.
Since even "the real" cannot be found, how much less can there be "the delusory"? It is only through being deluded regarding this perfect luminosity that false discrimination arises.

One might suppose it arises in dependence upon the True; yet the True is not the medium for the delusive. One might suppose it arises in dependence upon objects; yet objects are not the basis of the mind.
To realize there is nothing upon which to depend is itself to be without substance. Delusion is fundamentally without substance.
Delusion is itself truth; directly beneath it is the true mind. There is no need to further eliminate delusion in order to seek truth.
If one makes false discriminations, wishing to return to truth, then this very thought of returning to truth is itself delusion. Why?
Because the nature of true suchness (*tathatā*) is fundamentally without mind; how could truth be something that can be desired? That which is desired—
"True. [I reply: It is already not true. To seek to restore what is not true is to restore what is not true, rather than restoring what is true.
Does this not clearly manifest the characteristic of being untrue? Where there is delusion, there is truth; truth and delusion are opposites. That which is "true" is itself delusion.
That which can be sought and restored belongs to the realm of conditioned activity (*saṃskāra*); such conditioned activity is not true.
Therefore it is said that "the perfect completion is without marks. Now, what are called "marks" are the mark of arising, the mark of abiding, the mark of mind, and the mark of dharmas.
To have arising where there is no arising is an error regarding arising; to have abiding where there is no abiding is an error regarding abiding.
That which dwells is not [the truth]. Where there is no mind, yet there is mind—this mind is not [the truth]. Where there is no dharma, yet there is dharma—this dharma is not [the truth].
These four non-characteristics arise one from another in succession. Relying on dharmas, the mind arises; thus, taking the objective realm as a condition, the characteristic of cognition arises.
This is the characteristic of continuity. Because the mind dwells in dharmas, based on these two preceding characteristics, it further gives rise to [subsequent states].
Grasping at signs is the conceptualization of names and words. The arising of mental dharmas is the power of birth that brings about manifestation. These four are all delusions;
when they are perfumed, they form karma, which is the phase of the arising of karma. Because there is mutual resonance through shared karma, birth and extinction continue in succession;
this is the phase of suffering bound by karma. Because these three—delusion, karma, and suffering—exist, one becomes a sentient being.
Inversion. If one is not deluded regarding the fundamental perfect clarity, then birth is non-birth, abiding is non-abiding, mind is non-mind, dharmas are non-dharmas, and delusion is non-delusion;
there is nothing that does not tend toward the Real. How, then, could there be any inversion?
Formerly, Mañjuśrī asked Vimalakīrti, "What is the root of the body? He replied, "Greed is its root. [Mañjuśrī] asked about greed:
"What is its root? He replied, "False conceptualization is its root. Question: "What is the root of false conceptualization? He replied, "Perverted perception is its root.
Question: "What is the root of perverted perception? He replied, "Non-abiding is its root. Question again: "What is the root of non-abiding?
He replied, "As for non-abiding, it has no root. Mañjuśrī, from this root of non-abiding...
"Establishing all dharmas. A monk asked Fayan, "The teachings contain the statement: 'From the root of non-abiding, all dharmas are established.
What is this root of non-abiding? Fayan said, "Form arises before substance; names emerge before naming. Tiantong’s verse says: No trace remains; all news is cut off.
White clouds have no root; what color is the clear breeze? It disperses the canopy of heaven.
It is not the mind. It possesses the power to sustain the earth; it penetrates the profound source of a thousand ages and establishes the patterns for the myriad things.
It is the convergence of the Way within every mote of dust. Everywhere is Samantabhadra; at every turn, the gates of the pavilions open.
At every point, there is Maitreya. Xuedou raised up his staff and said, "O Assembly! This staff is both form and name held up together. Form is..."
It is formless; names are themselves nameless. All the elder masters possess a segment of perfectly luminous functioning that does not fall further into intellectual understanding.
Dust mote by dust mote, world-system by world-system, one cannot find the names or characteristics of sentient beings, let alone their delusions.
Ānanda, what is meant by the inversion of the world? It is that which exists as having something; through the false arising of fragmented divisions, this realm is established.
It does not arise from a cause, nor does it abide in an abode; it flows on without staying, and thus the world is formed.
The three periods of time and the four directions intermingle and interact, transforming sentient beings into twelve categories. Therefore, the world arises from movement.
There is sound. From sound comes form; from form comes fragrance; from fragrance comes touch; from touch comes taste; from taste one perceives mental objects (*dharma*).
These six deluded false conceptions constitute the nature of karma; thus, the twelve divisions arise, and by means of them, one revolves in saṃsāra.
Therefore, the world’s sounds, fragrances, tastes, and touches exhaust the twelve transformations as a single cycle of recurrence. Riding upon this wheel of revolution, one falls into perversion.
By way of characteristics, there are worlds of beings born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, and born by transformation; those with form and those without form;
those with perception and those without perception; those who are neither with form nor without form; and those who are neither with perception nor without perception.
Tong said: "In the preceding four fascicles, the various phenomena were interpenetrating, further augmented by three layers of flux and transformation.

Therein, the *niśraya-vipāka* (the objective environment) was contrasted with the *upabhoga-vipāka* (the subjective body), thereby manifesting the merits of the six sense faculties as each being twelve hundred.

Herein, the interpenetration occurs because the objective environment follows from the subjective body; thus it is said that sentient beings undergo transformations to form the twelve categories. This is how the worlds are elucidated."
It is a matter of inversion. What was previously called "merit" is here called "inversion. Both are accomplished through the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*).
To be submerged and drowned is inversion; to transcend them is merit. It is merely a matter of turning one's hand over. As for the six faculties and the six objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*):
It is divided into twelve sections. As they are seen interwoven, they constitute twelve transformations. Sound, fragrance, flavor, and touch are produced from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
These six disordered delusions perfume and form the seeds of karmic nature; this is how the twelve categories of the perceived aspect (*viṣayabhāga*) are formed.
By means of the four great elements acting upon the twelve sections, one revolves through the twelve transformations to their ultimate limit.
This is how the twelve categories of objective parts (*nimitta-bhāga*) are formed. The sense organs and the body are direct; the objective parts of the physical world are indirect.
These objective parts, in their entirety, do not transcend the six objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*). The arising of these six objects has no inherent priority or sequence, yet here sound alone is placed first.
Why is this? When the vital energy of heaven and earth first moves, thunder resounds with sound, causing a great trembling.
The hearing of the *baili* (the long-eared dog) is the farthest-reaching of all. Thus, among the objects contacted by the six sense faculties, sound is the first to be perceived;

whereas the other five sense-objects are known only after they have gradually approached. Taste is known through the mouth, and mental phenomena (*dharma*) are known by the mind, which is the most immediate of all.
Nevertheless, one may conceive of its color because of the sound, discern its fragrance closely because of the color, and [perceive] it through touch because of the fragrance.
One knows the essence of contact (*sparśa*). Through the essence of contact, one discerns distinct flavors; through distinct flavors, one discerns the analysis of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*).

These arise in mutual dependence; they are not without a sequence of priority and posteriority. Among the twenty-five perfect penetrations (*pariṣphuṭābhijñā*), sound begins the process, while "returning the hearing" (*pratyāhāra*) concludes it.
The faculty of hearing is the most perfect; this can also be seen reciprocally therein. Nevertheless, the faculties and their objects are interwoven, each having its own [distinct nature].
"Segmentation" (duan-fen) is the meaning of "realm" (dhātu). To flow and shift without ceasing, revolving through the three realms, is the meaning of "world" (loka).

When worlds combine, the sense organs and their objects fill all space; this is the state of "existence possessing that which exists. It is not a cause for a cause; fundamentally, there is no such cause.
One falsely gives rise to conceptual discrimination; therefore, the world becomes inverted.

If the six types of deluded conceptualization are suddenly stilled all at once, one perceives no sense organs within and no sensory objects without. In this very world, there is neither a dwelling place nor anything to dwell upon;
it is fundamentally unborn from the beginning. How, then, could there be any inversion? When Chan Master Chunan first visited Fenghua Rong, Rong said, "I am not..."
"Your teacher—your teacher is Huangbo. Nan then went to visit Huangbo. Huangbo asked, "When you have not yet manifested the images of the three realms, how is it?
Nan said, "Is there anything at all right now? Huangbo said, "Setting aside for a moment whether there is or not..."

"How is it right now? Nan said, "Neither now nor ancient. Huangbo said, "The Dharma-eye of my lineage is already within your person. Later, a monk asked Nan, "What is 'easy'? Nan said, "Wearing clothes and eating food; there is no need to read sutras or study the teachings, and no need to practice the Way, prostrate, burn the body, or cauterize the crown of the head—is this not easy? The monk asked, "What is 'what is'? Nan said, "It is you yourself. The monk asked, "How can I know myself? Nan said, "If you do not recognize yourself, you will surely fall into the three realms of existence; if you do recognize yourself, you will transcend the three realms of existence. The monk asked, "How does one transcend the three realms of existence? Nan said, "If you wish to transcend the three realms of existence, you must first understand the three realms of existence. What are the three realms of existence? They are the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm. What is the realm of desire? It is the realm of the six sense organs. What is the realm of form? It is the realm of the four great elements. What is the formless realm? It is the realm of the five aggregates.

If you can understand these three realms, you will transcend them. If you cannot understand them, you will fall into them. The monk asked, "How does one understand them? Nan said, "If you can see with your own eyes, hear with your own ears, speak with your own mouth, and act with your own body, then you have understood the three realms of existence.

If you can understand the three realms of existence, you will transcend them. If you can transcend them, you will be free from birth and death. If you are free from birth and death, you will attain liberation. If you attain liberation, you will realize Buddhahood. The monk asked, "What is Buddhahood? Nan said, "It is like the empty sky; it has no form or shape, no color or scent, no sound or touch, no taste or dharma. It is neither existent nor non-existent, neither born nor extinguished, neither coming nor going. It is simply the true nature of all phenomena. This is what is called Buddhahood. The monk bowed and departed. Nan said, "Go and tell the assembly that the Dharma-eye of Huangbo is in your hands. The monk returned and related this to the assembly. Huangbo heard of it and said, "Nan has truly inherited my Dharma-eye. Nan later passed away at Mount Dongping. His remains were enshrined in a stupa on the mountain. He was seventy-three years old. He had been a monk for fifty-two years. His disciples built a memorial hall for him. The Emperor granted him the posthumous title "Great Master Zhizheng" (True Rectitude). His teachings were widely circulated throughout the world. His legacy continues to this day.

[The opponent] said, "Difficult. Nan replied: "If even a subtle thought arises, one immediately possesses the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). The three fruits and the cycle of birth and death all arise from your single thought.
Therefore, the Buddha taught the various Bodhisattvas, saying, 'They are protected by the mindfulness of the Buddha.
Master Nan has severed the boundaries of past and future, yet he remains alert to the movement of a single thought; this is truly knowing the world."
"Ānanda, as for the cause of perversion:

it arises from the delusory cycle of the world, due to the perversion of movement. Through the combination of vital energies, eighty-four thousand disordered thoughts of flying and sinking are formed.
Thus, there exist egg-born beings (aṇḍaja), such as the kalala (here translated as 'coagulated mucus'), which transmigrate through various lands."

Fish, birds, turtles, and snakes—these species abound. Due to the defiled cycle of rebirth within the world and because of inverted desires, they combine and flourish into eighty-four thousand horizontal and vertical disordered thoughts.
It is for this reason that there is the *arbuda* stage of embryonic development.
(These are called *arbuda*. They circulate through the realms of existence, filling them with humans, animals, dragons, and seers.
Because they cling to the world due to causes and revolve in saṃsāra, their inverted inclinations combine heat to form eighty-four thousand types of chaotic and agitated thoughts.
Thus, there exists the moist-phase *cariṣa* (herein called "soft flesh"), which circulates through the realms of existence, teeming with wriggling and crawling creatures that fill them.
Due to the causes of the world’s transformation and saṃsāra, and by virtue of false inversions, the conjunction of contact gives rise to eighty-four thousand new and old disordered thoughts.
Consequently, there exist *kalala* (here translated as "hard flesh") with transformative characteristics, which circulate through lands, undergo metamorphosis, and fly;
their species fill the world.
Tong said: "All phenomena within the three realms are entirely created by the mind. In sum, they are formed through the external aspect, the internal aspect, and their conjunction.
The movement of a single thought begins with false discrimination; once craving and grasping arise, it becomes defiled.
As this defilement deepens day by day, one becomes attached. In the world, there has never been one who clings to something constantly without eventually letting go."
All things ultimately follow transformation; this revolving of emotional thoughts is the natural course of things. When thought moves, the imagination is light while the emotion is heavy.

Thus, those born from eggs arise solely from imagination, while those born from wombs are caused by emotion. Eggs result merely from the mingling of vital energies; therefore, they are round and mobile.
Yet because imagination involves many fluctuations of ascent and descent, the resulting fruits of such influence differ between fish and birds. As for those born from wombs, they must...
Through the union of essence, there is growth and defilement; yet because the emotions have both biased and correct aspects, the resulting karmic fruits differ between humans and animals.

Those whose emotions are characterized by attachment cling to their objects without parting, each indulging in the intent of its particular inclination. Thus, moisture-born beings arise through the stimulus of union, waiting for the warmth of the sun before they are born.
Those whose emotions are deluded and whose vital energies are stagnant do not rely on sexual union; thus they are the wriggling and moving creatures.
Such beings respond accordingly. When their attachments change, they depart from this and entrust themselves to that; this is similar to the cycle of *pariṇāmi-śarīra* (changing death).
Yet, as this is not real, it is termed "provisional. Transformation (*nirmāṇa*) is designated by provisional names and is accomplished through the engagement of various categories.
Because it moves toward the new, it revolves; because it revolves, it is like shedding a skin with ease. Moving toward the new is like the light flight of soaring. Thus, the emotions shift.
The vital energies shift, each responding to its own seasonal conditions; therefore, this is called the cycle of transformation and rebirth.

The stage of coagulation and fluidity is the initial position upon entering the womb, the state when the embryo and egg have not yet differentiated. The stage of the bubble is the state when the embryo and egg gradually begin to differentiate.
Soft flesh is the initial sign of moisture-born beings. Since they do not enter a womb, they lack the first two stages. Hard flesh and the exoskeleton constitute the fully formed body.

There is no characteristic of softness. Furthermore, there are inherent differences in degree, from shallow to deep. All such things take the six types of chaotic deluded thoughts as the cause of inversion;
these ultimately fill and pervade everything, coalescing to form the world. Thus we know that true nature is immeasurable, and ignorance is likewise immeasurable.
Master Qingxian ascended the hall and said: "Having no other choice, I shall engage with you all."
Fotuo: "All sentient beings suffer solely because the dust of the mind has not been shed and the measures of emotion have not been eliminated.

Seeing forms and hearing sounds, they follow the waves and drift with the currents, transmigrating through the three realms and drowning in the four modes of birth. This causes right view to remain obscure and creates obstructions at every turn.
If one could cause both right and wrong to vanish together and forget both good and evil, one would sit and sever the heads of both the Reward and Transformation Buddhas."
Severing the paths of the holy and the ordinary—only upon reaching this point does one have a slight degree of resonance.
Even if it is so, within the domain of a patch-robed monk, there is as yet nothing extraordinary. Why is this? As soon as there is right and wrong, confusion arises and the mind is lost.
*Du!* A monk asked Chan Master Baoci Yu: "Sentiment gives rise to separation from wisdom; conceptualization transforms the essence into something distinct. But what about..."
"How is it when feeling has not yet arisen? The Master said, "Separated. The monk asked, "When feeling has not yet arisen, what is there to separate?

The Master said, "This young fellow has not yet met the right person. Even if one were in the realm of a patch-robed monk where feelings and thoughts do not arise, one would still require the hammer and tongs;
how much more so for those who follow the waves and drift with the current? Is there anyone among them who does not sink into the four realms of birth?"
Due to the causes of worldly obstruction and cyclic existence, and because of the hindrance of inversion, they combine and become attached, forming eighty-four thousand thoughts of turbid radiance.
Consequently, there arise the physical forms of *kalala*, the circulation through various lands, and the spiritual brilliance of portents of good and ill fortune.

These types fill the world. Due to the dissolution and circulation of the world, and because of delusion and inversion, they combine with darkness to form eighty-four thousand obscured and chaotic thoughts of the aggregates (*skandha*).
Thus, there exist formless *kalala* (embryonic stages) that circulate through various lands.

Empty, scattered, dissolving, and sinking—beings of this kind fill the world. This arises because, due to the world’s illusory cycle of rebirth and the inversion of shadows, the conjunction of conditions and recollections forms eighty-four thousand latent knots of chaotic thoughts.
Thus, there exists the *kalala* (embryonic stage) characterized by conceptual signs.
They circulate through the lands; spirits, ghosts, and numinous essences fill these realms.

Because they revolve in the cycle of delusion and dullness within the world, and due to their ignorant inversions, they combine with stubborn matter to form eighty-four thousand parched and chaotic thoughts.
For this reason, there are the "unconscious kalala" beings who circulate through the lands, their spirits transformed into earth, wood, metal, and stone, filling these realms.
Tong said: "Form belongs to the objective aspect (nimittabhāga), while perception belongs to the subjective aspect (darśanabhāga). Together they do not transcend the four propositions:
'it exists,' 'it does not exist,' 'it both exists and does not exist,' and 'it neither exists nor does not exist. These exhaust all the transformations of the world.
Those who possess form are attached to form, such as those non-Buddhists who worship external objects like the sun, moon, water, and fire; their perceptions have already become fixed."
Because it is a refined radiance, it consists merely of form. This refined radiance arises from clarity; clarity arises from awareness.
While awareness has no abiding characteristic, this refined radiance possesses beauty, and is therefore called "obstructive attachment. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

"The eighty spirits all arise from the fundamental source of obstructive attachment, thereby forming this refined radiance. Therefore, all spirits of refined brilliance are able to foreknow [the future]."
Fortune and misfortune have never been separated from the essence of awakening; they are merely obstructions that prevent its free flow. Therefore, this is called the "obstruction of perversion.
As for those without form, they are attached to emptiness—such as the non-Buddhists who, weary of existence, seek refuge in non-existence.

They are deluded, leaking, and ignorant of the teachings; thus they are called "confusion. Enveloped in darkness and obscured, they enter the realm of formlessness. This is the state of having perception but no...

Form does not constitute the substance of karma; however, because one is born into the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is likewise the dissolution of the *kalala*. Spirits, ghosts, and numinous essences have no substantial form;
they appear as if present yet are non-existent, hence they are called "phantoms" (*wangxiang*). This is like performing sacrifices and making supplications.

They rely upon reflected images and aspire to spiritual penetration; these are merely matters of recollection and imagination. They secretly construct mental forms, yet these possess no actual substance or color;
thus, there exists only the *kalala* (embryonic stage) of conceptual appearance. Earth, wood, metal, and stone possess form but lack consciousness;

because they are caused by emptiness and insentience, they are termed "delusion. Non-Buddhists reckon that even insentient things possess life-force, for metal and stone are firm and solid, or perhaps due to habitual tendencies...
The settled ash congeals; it is dull and withered. Encountering objects, it takes form, such as the "yellow-headed stone-transforming" type.
This is what is called the *asaṃjñika-kaḷala*. This is produced by the false views of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). It possesses form but lacks perception;

it is not inert like wood or stone, yet it is attached and becomes a brilliant essence. Thus, through the superior transformation of the perceived aspect (*nimittabhāga*), it becomes a material object.
There are those with perception who, lacking form, do not become ghosts or spirits, but instead disperse into the substance of space;

this is the seeing-division (darśana-bhāga) transforming through superior power into a spirit. The Śūnyatā-deva, though possessing no body, perceives touch and returns to the Formless Realm (ārūpyadhātu).
All of these are brought about by the six types of deluded false thoughts. Because the eye of the Way is not clear, one arrives at such states. A monk asked Jinfeng:
Chan Master Zhi said, "This body is without cognition, like earth, wood, tiles, or stones. What was the meaning of this?
The Master descended from his meditation seat and twisted the monk's ear. The monk cried out in pain. The Master said, "Today, for the first time, I have caught hold of this ignorant fellow.
The monk bowed and departed. The Master called out, "Acarya! The monk turned his head. The Master said, "If you go to the hall..."
[This is] the Middle [Way]. It cannot be grasped or set down. Someone asked, "For what reason? The Master said, "There are many who laugh at the 'old woman’s heart' of Jingu Peak.
Furthermore, there was once a practitioner sitting in a quiet room who shone with a brilliant light. A certain Chan master, fearing he would delude the masses, drove him away.
These are all instances of confused cultivation; they do not understand the ultimate principle of the ordinary. — Liu Jing.
I, the Subject, the Judicial Assistant, have previously composed the "Essay on Clarifying the Way and Admonishing the Confucians" to warn the world. Its text says:
"Clarifying the Way lies in seeing one's nature; that which I have awakened to is nothing other than seeing one's nature. As Mencius said: "The mouth’s desire for flavors..."
The eye’s relation to color, the ear’s to sound, the nose’s to odor, and the four limbs’ to ease and comfort—these are the nature (*xing*).
Yangzi said: "Sight, hearing, speech, appearance, and thought are what nature possesses.
If one perceives this, then one can clearly understand the Way (*dao*). One must know that the Way is not far from man; man’s relation to the Way is like... [the text continues].
Fish never for a moment depart from water; yet because they are deluded about themselves and pursue external objects, they spend their entire lives moving within it without realizing it.
What the Buddha calls "Great Awakening" (Mahābodhi) and what Confucianism calls "Prior Awakening" (Xiánjué) refers precisely to this realization. An ancient person once said:
"From antiquity to the present, there has surely been no falling away; it is clearly right before one's eyes. He further said: "The Great Way resides only in..."
For the time being, it is difficult to behold even for a moment. If you wish to recognize the true essence of the Great Way, it is not separate from sound, form, speech, and expression.
It is also said: "Night after night one embraces the Buddha in sleep; morning after morning one rises together with him. Rising and falling, they are ever相随 (mutually following);
speaking and remaining silent, they dwell together. If you wish to know where the Buddha goes, it is simply this very voice. These are the words of the Buddha.
The Way is our closest relative. When standing, one sees it present before one; when in a carriage, one sees it leaning upon the crossbar.
One looks for it as if it were in front, and suddenly it is behind. Whether one turns left or right, one encounters its source.
This is the Confucianist’s description of the Way as being most near. How is this so? Because this Way can only be transmitted through the mind.
"Not relying on words and letters. Thus, when the World-Honored One held up a flower, the wondrous mind was transmitted to Kāśyapa;
when Bodhidharma faced the wall, the fundamental principle was entrusted to Huike. Once the six petals had unfolded, the thousand blossoms vied in their splendor;

schools were divided and lineages established, each with its own tradition. Therefore, some signaled with a blink of an eye or a raised eyebrow, or by clenching a fist or pointing a finger; others administered blows or...

"Ha!"— raising the whisk, striking the mallet, holding the ritual implement, drawing the bow, rolling the ball, dancing with the tablet, dragging stones, moving earth, beating the drum, blowing the hair-whisk,
or remaining silent, speaking a word, sighing, or laughing— and even through all such various skillful means.
All of these are intimate instructions for others. Yet, because they are so intimate, many people are at a loss as to how to respond.

Those who catch a glimpse of them see nothing that separates them from the truth by even a hair’s breadth; yet those who hesitate remain worlds apart. Those who wish to clarify the Way should not treat this with indifference.
Transmitted from patriarch to patriarch, it continues unbroken to this day. It truly embodies what our Confucian tradition calls "that which there is nothing that does not encompass."

Joyful! To hear [the teaching] and not oppose it—this is where my own attainment truly lies. Reflecting back, our Confucian tradition possesses its own path. How excellent are the words of the Master:
"He silently apprehends them and unifies them with a single thread. Thus, the Way exists in what is witnessed by the eye;
the meaning is conveyed by pointing at the palm of the hand. All such instances accord with the essential gate of our school.
This wondrous principle attains the true mechanism beyond the teachings.
Yet, while the Way of Confucius was transmitted to Zisi, and Zisi transmitted it to Mencius, once Mencius had passed away, its transmission could no longer be found;
what has been handed down to the world is merely the written word. Therefore, my study must seek self-realization before it may cease. Fortunately, I have [attained this].

In the evening, one attains awakening, realizing that everything seen by the ordinary eyes, heard by the ears, conceived by the mind, spoken by the mouth, and moved by the hands and feet is none other than the wondrous.
Having attained this for a long time, it increasingly manifests before one day by day.
Whenever I attempted to impart it to others, they were unable to receive it; only then did I realize that this wondrous Way truly cannot be transmitted through written words.
Alas! This Way is transmitted when there is a person worthy of it, and it is severed when such a person is absent.
Since I have now attained it, who might be like me? Will there be such a person during the remainder of my life, or not?

That person is such that he cannot be known through ordinary means; therefore, his deeds have been recorded in chronicles, songs, and oral traditions to disseminate his story, and this treatise has further been composed to instruct my disciples.
Due to the mutual dependence of the world as a cause of saṃsāra, and because of false inversion, they combine with defilement to form eighty-four thousand disordered thoughts based on causes.
Thus, there arise non-material forms that take on material characteristics as *kalala*, circulating through the lands.
Various jellyfish and similar creatures take shrimp for their eyes; such species fill the world.

Because they are drawn into the cycle of rebirth by the characteristics of the world and because their natures are inverted, they combine through incantations to form eighty-four thousand deluded thoughts of summoning.
For this reason, there exist non-material forms and non-material *kalala* that flow through the lands, born of curses and malevolent spells; such species fill the world.

Because the world arises from the conjunction of causes with delusive saṃsāra, and due to inverted ignorance, various combinations produce eighty-four thousand types of reciprocal and chaotic conceptions.

Thus, there arise the characteristics of the *kalala* and *arbuda*, which are neither existent nor non-existent, yet constitute the perception of existence, as they circulate through the realms of existence.
Those such as the *pulu* (parasites) and others transform through the interaction of different substances; their species fill the world.

Because they revolve in a cycle of mutual enmity within the world and due to the perversity of killing, they combine to form strange beings who harbor the thought that eighty-four thousand [beings] are their parents.
Thus, there exist non-ideational and ideationless *kalala* (embryonic stages), which circulate through various lands like the earth-owl, which uses clods of earth to serve as its offspring.

And there are the *bhedana* birds, which take the fruit of poisonous trees and embrace them as their offspring; once the offspring have matured, both the parents meet their end by being eaten by them.
Such species abound. These are called the twelve types of sentient beings.
Tong said: "The presence or absence of form and perception is like the principle of yin and yang; it is sufficient to encompass all transformations.
Yet within yin there is yang, and within yang there is yin; what appears to be yin is actually yang, and what appears to be yang is actually yin. Its transformations are unfathomable."
Distracted thoughts are boundless, and sentient beings are inexhaustible; were it not for the Buddha’s Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom, who could possibly fathom them?
To depend on others and revolve in saṃsāra is to rely on external things, and thus it is called "false. The water jelly uses a shrimp as its eyes;

originally it has no color of its own, yet it acquires color by depending on another object. Though their substances are distinct, this is still called a "conjunction of defiled conditions. This is the height of perversity.
Karmic characteristics are drawn forth merely by relying on incantations and sorcery to summon them; they do not possess an inherent nature, yet those [incantations] can still draw them forth.
Therefore, it is said that their nature is inverted. These curses, spells, and bewitchments can also manifest transformations; they are not devoid of form and appearance.

However, they borrow sound to produce substance and do not proceed from the principles of natural physiology; thus, they fundamentally lack physical form. This is because the power of these incantations is produced solely through human agency.

Regarding those with different feet, such as the *pulu* (parasitic wasps) and others: they were originally silkworms and did not possess the perception of being bees, yet they come to possess the perception of being bees.
Because their substance has changed, this is not like the transmission of life within the perceptions of the womb or egg, where they eventually complete their transformation.

To curse that class [of beings] and identify with them is to transform delusion through delusion; it is to deceive and mislead others, taking what belongs to another as one's own and turning another’s property into one’s own. Therefore...
This is called "mutual inversion. Although these different species attach to one another and are said to be joined in delusion, they have not yet reached the point of being truly strange.
For instance, the earth-owl (tǔxiāo) breaks a mirror and uses other objects as its offspring; once the offspring are formed, it is instead devoured by them.

This abandonment of natural kinship and righteousness is contrary to the constant order of things; therefore, it is called "strange. All such occurrences arise from enmity and harm accumulated over many lifetimes, where beings give birth to one another only to devour one another.
Enmity turns into love; love turns into enmity. Sons repay one another in this manner, forming their own kind. The *xiāo* bird eats its mother; the *pòjìng* bird eats its father.
This is not because they lack consciousness. Yet, how could a clod of earth or a poisonous fruit possess consciousness?

As for the case of the *śrāmaṇera* who had a sore on his face, it was due to the many lifetimes of resentment and harm between Yuan Ang and Chao Cuo; though they were but a single body [in that life].

It is the poison of self-characteristics. Furthermore, it is not comparable to the separate entities of the *xiāo* (owl) species. The *àngcuò* (confusion/delusion) is not non-perception, yet the ulcer is not perception either.
These are the knots of affliction (*kleśa*), each numbering eighty-four thousand cycles of saṃsāra.

Following karma from birth to birth, they have never ceased. When the cold fills [the world] for a single moment, there is no realm that does not exist; when the cold fills [the world] for many kalpas, then—

There is no world that is not thus. Without the *sabhāga-vipāka* (direct retribution) of sentient beings, there would be nothing to evoke the *adhiṣṭhāna-vipāka* (circumstantial retribution) of the world;

without the circumstantial retribution of the world, there would be nothing to constitute the direct retribution of sentient beings. This inversion of the world is itself the inversion of sentient beings;
both originate from turning one's back on awakening and uniting with the sense-objects. There are not two causes. This is a brief demonstration of the inversions of sentient beings.
This is the source. Within the world, he has clearly demonstrated the reality of perversion. Perversion is itself the fruit of karma;
that which was previously called the "threefold continuity" is entirely subsumed within this. A monk asked Baizhang: "If one receives the precepts now..."
"Your body and speech are pure, and you have already perfected the myriad virtues; have you attained liberation?

Baizhang replied, "I have attained a small measure of liberation, but I have not yet attained liberation of mind, nor have I attained liberation in all places. [The Master] asked, "What is liberation of mind?"
And as for liberation in all places, [Baizhang] said: "Do not seek the Buddha, Dharma, or Sangha; do not even seek merit, wisdom, knowledge, or understanding.
When the sentiments of defilement and purity are exhausted, one does not cling to this state of non-seeking as being correct, nor does one dwell in the state of exhaustion.
One neither rejoices in heaven nor fears hell; bound and liberated are without obstruction. This is the very nature of body and mind, and of all things."
All such states are called liberation. Do not say that because your body, speech, and mind are pure through a mere fraction of precepts, you have thereby reached the end of the path.

You do not realize that among the gates of precept, concentration, and wisdom as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there is untainted liberation; you have not yet touched upon even a hair’s breadth of it.
Strive forward with vigor and investigate it resolutely; do not wait until your ears are deaf, your eyes are dim, your face is wrinkled, and your hair is white.
The suffering of old age afflicts the body; one is entangled in the bonds of sorrowful attachment. Tears flow from the eyes, and the heart is filled with panic and dread.
Having no foundation whatsoever, one knows not where to go. When such a time arrives, one can no longer manage one’s own hands and feet.
Even if one possesses merit, wisdom, fame, or gain, none of these can provide salvation, for the eye of the mind has not yet opened, and one thinks only of external objects.
Failing to reflect back upon oneself, one further fails to perceive the Buddha-way. All the karmic conditions of good and evil from one's entire life suddenly manifest before one.
Whether filled with joy or fear, the five aggregates of the six realms appear simultaneously;
magnificent mansions, boats, ships, carriages, and palanquins all appear with brilliant radiance, yet these are all manifested from the greed and attachment of one’s own body and mind. All of them—

Even evil realms all transform into sublime realms; yet, one is led solely by the karmic consciousness according to where craving and attachment are most intense, following that to take birth without any freedom whatsoever.
Whether as a dragon or a beast, noble or base, these states are likewise entirely undetermined.
A question was asked: "How can one obtain freedom? The Master said: "If you can obtain it now, you have obtained it. Or, when facing the five desires and the eight winds, if your mind..."
Free from grasping or rejecting, stinginess, envy, greed, or attachment, the sentiment of "mine" is exhausted; both defilement and purity have vanished.
Like the sun and moon in the sky, they illuminate without depending on external conditions. Mind after mind is like wood or stone;

every thought-moment is like extinguishing a fire on one's head, or like a fragrant elephant crossing a river—cutting through the current and passing over without further hesitation or obstruction. Such a person is beyond the reach of heaven or hell.
It is capable of encompassing all. Alas! Baizhang’s earnest instructions and admonitions were bestowed with unreserved compassion.

One must undergo a forceful awakening and constant alertness at these profound points; only then will one realize that the cause of delusion does not stem from another, and that true samādhi is inherently complete within oneself.
When both defilement and purity have vanished, one transcends that which even heaven and hell cannot encompass.
Furthermore, by what twelve kinds of things can it be overturned?
*The Great Buddha-Usnīṣa Tathāgata’s Secret Cause for Cultivation and Realization, the Ultimate Meaning of the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas, the Śūraṅgama Sūtra*,
Scroll Eight.
Ānanda, among these various classes of sentient beings, each and every one likewise possesses twelve kinds of inversion.

It is like pressing upon the eyes, causing a chaotic array of flowers to appear; thus do they invert the wondrous, perfect, truly pure, and luminous mind, becoming fully possessed of such false and deluded thoughts.
Now, as you cultivate and realize the Buddha’s samādhi, you must establish three [stages] based on these original causes of your fundamental deluded thoughts.
Only through gradual stages can it be eliminated. It is like a vessel that has held poisonous honey:
one must remove the poison, wash the vessel with various hot waters mixed with ashes and incense, and only then store ambrosia within it. What are these three gradual stages?
First, through cultivation, one eliminates its auxiliary causes. Second, through true cultivation, one hollows out its fundamental nature. Third, through advancement, one opposes its...

Regarding present karma, it is generally said that the twelve inversions all arise through transformations of the truly pure and luminous mind. They begin with a single thought of craving and grasping;
where there is craving, there is aversion, and where there is grasping, there is rejection. Thus, birth from womb, egg, moisture, or transformation all stem from emotional attachment.

Perceptions of lightness and heaviness each follow their own kind. Whether with form or without form, with perception or without perception, these are merely the two categories of existence and non-existence;

however, they are transformed through perception. As that perception gradually becomes subtle, the transformation gradually becomes pure. This would not be the case were it not for the presence of form.
If it were not formless, if it were not with perception, and if it were not without perception—internally containing both "both" and "neither"—it would truly be transformed by emotion.
As that emotion gradually stagnates, the transformation gradually becomes suffering. Emotions, perceptions, loves, and hates are presented in a chaotic jumble;
there is no category that does not exist. Therefore, within each and every category, all twelve perversions are mutually present.
Emotional perceptions are like pressing upon the eyes; inverted views are like disordered flowers. These disordered flowers exist within the great void without obstructing the great void;
these inverted views exist within the wondrous perfection without hindering the wondrous perfection.
Only when one possesses such empty and false inverted thoughts can they ultimately not obstruct the truly pure and luminous mind; only then does one perceive its wondrous perfection.
Furthermore, the wondrous, perfect true mind is the samādhi that is vast, subtle, and brilliantly clear, like a cloudless sky.
The twelve inversions have this sixfold disorderly false thinking as their fundamental cause. If the cataracts of the eyes are removed, the frantic flowers will naturally cease.
However, to eliminate these disorderly thoughts, one must establish three gradual stages. Why is this? It is like a clean vessel, originally intended to hold sweet...
A vessel that has been exposed to poison and honey—if one suddenly pours nectar into it, the nectar will instead turn into poison.
One must cleanse it with hot water, assist it with ash and incense, and allow it time through the passage of years and months;
only then will the poisonous vapors gradually dissipate and the nectar be able to enter. These three gradual stages are precisely for the purpose of purifying and eliminating discursive thoughts.
This is the hot water, ash, and incense. The previous four kinds of clear instructions—against killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying—have already established the right precepts;
now, furthermore, one eliminates the auxiliary causes of lust, anger, and delusion, and excises the primary natures of killing, stealing, and lust.

Thus, one gradually distances oneself from the active manifestation of ignorance. By advancing through this, one reverses the flow and returns to the state of oneness; the six faculties cease their outward functioning.
Ultimately, this contradicts present karma; yet the mind does not wander, emotional attachments wither away, and chaotic thoughts do not arise of their own accord.

If such perversions have no cause to arise, from what cause would they then be produced? It is simply through the single true mind that one subsequently establishes the forty-four minds of the noble stages (*ārya-bhūmi*) to enter the wondrous enlightenment of true *samādhi*.
It is like when the poison in honey has been eliminated, leaving only its sweetness.
Dew can be stored. Great Master Suixi ascended the hall and said: "This nature is fundamentally pure and replete with myriad virtues.

It is only because of the two conditions of defilement and purity that distinctions arise. Therefore, the sages awaken to it and employ it exclusively in a pure manner, thereby accomplishing the path of enlightenment.
Ordinary people are deluded by it and employ it exclusively in a defiled manner, sinking into the cycle of saṃsāra. Its...
The essence is non-dual. Thus, the *Prajñāpāramitā* says: "There is no duality, no division, no distinction, and no interruption.
If one can believe and realize that its essence is non-dual, then it is fundamentally a single pure vessel.
Whether poison or honey is stored within it, it neither diminishes nor increases; it proceeds directly toward unsurpassed bodhi, where both defilement and purity are absent.
After this discussion, it would also not be improper to eliminate the doctrine of the three gradual stages (*tri-śukla*).
What is the auxiliary cause? Ānanda, these twelve classes of beings in this world are unable to sustain themselves on their own;
they abide by means of the four kinds of nutriment, namely: edible food, contact-food, volition-food, and consciousness-food. For this reason, the Buddha said that all sentient beings—
All dwell in dependence upon food. Ānanda, all sentient beings live because they consume what is sweet and die because they consume poison.
Those sentient beings who seek *samādhi* should sever the five kinds of pungent vegetables of the world. These five pungent things, when eaten cooked, arouse lust;
when eaten raw, they increase anger. Thus, in this world, those who eat pungent things—even if they can proclaim the Twelve [Links of Dependent Origination]—[are not fit vessels].
The various classes of sūtras state that the celestial immortals (*deva-rṣi*) of the ten directions loathe their foul odor and all distance themselves from them.

As for the various hungry ghosts (*preta*), they lick the lips and mouths of those who eat such things during their meals; thus they constantly dwell with ghosts, their merit and virtue diminish daily, and they find no long-term benefit.
When those who eat pungent roots practice *samādhi*, the Bodhisattvas, celestial immortals, and benevolent deities of the ten directions will not come to protect them. Those of great power...
The Mara King, seizing an opportunity, manifested the body of a Buddha and came to preach the Dharma to them. He reviled the prohibitions and precepts, praising lust, anger, and ignorance.
At the end of their lives, they became attendants of the Mara King; when their demonic blessings were exhausted, they fell into the Avīci Hell. Ānanda!
One who cultivates bodhi must forever sever the five pungent roots; this is called the first stage of progressive cultivation.

It is generally said that "lump-food" (kavaḍīkāra-āhāra) is also called "clod-food," meaning it is eaten by being grasped with the hand. However, because there are things that cannot be so grasped, the term is translated as "segment" (piṇḍa).
A segment is like a portion cut by a blade; rice, noodles, vegetables, and the like have physical segments, and for this reason they are so named.

The food of humans. As for the food of contact (*sparśāhāra*), it is produced by the meeting of the sense faculties, objects, and consciousness; it merely contacts their subtle essence. This is the food of ghosts and spirits.

In the heavens of dhyāna, there is no substantial food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*); there is only the food of volition (*manaḥsañcetanāhāra*). Therefore, it is said that they obtain sustenance through the food of volition.

In the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), there is no food of volition; there is only the food of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*). Consciousness takes up the flavor of phenomena (*dharmarasa*), and thus one is filled with vigor.

They are also all sustained by means of self-nourishment, just as with material food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*); therefore, it is said that they all abide in dependence upon nutriment. The *Compendium* states:
"As for the nutriment of consciousness (*vijñāna-āhāra*), it is the ālayavijñāna, which abides in dependence upon the aforementioned three kinds of nutriment. How is this known?"

The five consciousnesses are the self-evident object-aspect (*nimittabhāga*) of the ālayavijñāna. The six consciousnesses and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) are the self-evident subject-aspect (*darśanabhāga*) of the ālayavijñāna.
The five consciousnesses rely on the food of physical morsels (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*); the sixth consciousness relies on the food of contact (*sparśāhāra*);

and the seventh mental consciousness relies on the food of volition (*manaḥsaṃcetanāhāra*). Thus, the consciousness-food subsists by depending upon these three types of food. All sentient beings [subsist in this manner].
One lives by consuming what is sweet and dies by consuming poison. How could the five pungent herbs and other foul, impure substances fail to incite lust and provoke anger?
Ultimately, those who distance themselves from the celestial immortals and constantly associate with ghosts are no different from those who consume poison.
Yet their lust and anger increase day by day; they will surely violate the prohibitions and precepts and fall into the Avīci Hell. This is indeed so.
Is this not a failure to be cautious regarding the subtle?

Within this, the tranquil, perfect, pure, and wondrous state of all Tathāgatas is fully manifested. This is the secret principle of perfect wisdom.
Pure conduct is perfectly integrated, leaving no trace. The Dharma-body is pure, like lapis lazuli; true wisdom is brilliant and clear, like the bright moon.
Body and mind are blissful; faculties and objects are both fused. Wondrously perfect and impartial, one attains great peace and stability.

Perfect. This is not something that human effort can bestow. The Middle Way relies upon the True; yet the Sublime is still not the True itself.

the locus of true faith is thus utterly distinct and far removed from the path of intellectual understanding.

This arises from true faith; since one's nature is not imperfect, one's penetration is not incomplete. This...

Now, when one maintains that the mind is empty and luminous, the faculties and their objects do not couple. After a long time, the True and Wondrous alone is revealed, transcending above the faculties and their objects.
Therefore, regarding the relinquishing of the body in the past and the receiving of a body in the future, all—
Bound by the latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) and the afflictions of thought, [the mind] now stands forth with brilliant clarity; thus, one attains freedom from forgetfulness.

as the true and the false are about to be fused into one, this constitutes the supernormal power of knowing past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*). This extends from the Arhats up to those in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
"Non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) can perceive eight thousand kalpas before and after; as for 'innumerable kalpas,' this refers to what is called an asaṃkhyeya-kalpa.

"This transformation cannot be contrived; is its progress not indeed refined? A monk asked Huangbo, "What is diligence?
