Now, by withdrawing its brilliance and holding it without employing it—just as Linji said, "When the 'blow-off-the-hair' blade has been used, it must be quickly polished"—one attains total mastery (*dhāraṇī*) over wondrous stillness. Total...
If one maintains immovability, then one will be eternally concentrated. Now, the nature of profound stillness is pure and original by nature;
it pervades the entire Dharma-realm and is fundamentally without agitation. It is still, yet not merely still, for it differs from the stagnant water of death-like quietude.

Therefore, it is called "wondrous stillness. When the mind abides in this concentration, wisdom is present within that concentration; this is distinct from human effort in cultivation, where one first seeks concentration.
The teachings that "wisdom comes first" and "meditative concentration comes after wisdom" are entirely unrelated [to this context].
When Zhixiang first visited the Fifth Patriarch, he lived in a hermitage as a permanent resident for twenty years. Xuance went to visit him and asked, "What are you doing here?
He replied, "I am entering meditative absorption (*samādhi*). Xuance said, "When you say you enter absorption, do you enter it with a mind or without a mind?"
"Master Ye, if one enters [samādhi] without a mind, then all insentient things—grass, trees, tiles, and stones—should likewise be able to attain samādhi.
If one enters with a mind, then all sentient beings who possess consciousness should also be able to attain samādhi.

Huáng said, "When I am truly entering samādhi, I do not perceive the existence of a mind characterized by 'existence' or 'non-existence. Cè said, "If you do not perceive the existence of a mind characterized by 'existence' or 'non-existence'..."
The mind is itself constant concentration; how could there be entering or exiting? If there were entering or exiting, it would not be the Great Concentration.
Huang asked after a long silence, "Whom does the Master follow? Xuanze said, "My master is the Sixth Patriarch. Huang asked, "What does the Sixth Patriarch take to be meditative concentration?
Xuanze said, "According to what my master taught: it is wondrously profound and perfectly tranquil; its essence and function are suchness (*tathatā*). The five..."
The aggregates (*skandhas*) are fundamentally empty; the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) do not exist. There is no exiting or entering, no fixedness and no disorder.
The nature of dhyāna has no abiding; it is the stillness of dhyāna that is free from abiding. The nature of dhyāna has no arising; it is the thought of dhyāna that is free from arising.

The mind is like space, yet even the measure of space does not exist. Upon hearing these words, Huáng ran directly to visit the Sixth Patriarch and recounted his previous conversation in full. The Sixth Patriarch said:

"It is exactly as you have said. You should simply let your mind be like empty space, without clinging to the view of emptiness. You should function with unimpeded ease; whether moving or still, remain without a deliberate mind.
Let the sentiments of ordinary and sage be forgotten, so that subject and object both vanish. When nature and characteristics are suchness (*tathatā*), there is no time when they are not so.
At this, Huáng attained great enlightenment; the mind he had cultivated for twenty years left behind no trace or influence whatsoever. That night, by the river...
The common people of the northern lands heard a voice in the air saying, "Today, Chan Master Huang has attained the Way.

Huang then returned to north of the River, where he transformed and enlightened the fourfold assembly. Furthermore, a monk asked Chan Master Xian-duan of White Deer Mountain, "What is it like when one is unmoving and profoundly tranquil?
Duān said, "This is not where you, Venerable Sir, can establish your body and life. The monk asked, "What then is it?"

Regarding the place where a student establishes their person and sustains their life, Yuanzhen said: "The clouds have the momentum to leave the mountains; the water has no sound as it plunges into the ravine.
Upon this, he attained realization. He was constantly tranquil, yet never departed from constant alertness. Thus one can fully know the Dharma-gate of the non-duality of samādhi and prajñā.
Samādhi illuminates through its radiance; when the nature of this radiance penetrates deeply, advancing alone without retreating, it is called the "Non-retrogressive Mind.
It is said in general: entering samādhi by means of wisdom ensures that the samādhi is correct; illuminating through the power of samādhi ensures that the radiance is deep.

Radiance that does not arise from the power of samādhi is superficial and rootless, unable to penetrate deeply. Now, as concentration and wisdom mutually support one another, [the practice is perfected].
The nature of illumination is profoundly penetrating; what subtlety would it not illuminate? What profundity would it not exhaust?

Thus, one is able to seek upward and advance further and further without ceasing, progressing without retreating, precisely because one perceives the depth of this illumination. Were it even slightly lacking in clarity, [the result would be different].
Consequently, there arises the intention to retreat. This stage of non-retrogression occurs because beginningless ignorance has been refined away almost entirely;
since nothing can shake or delude one, no sense of dejection or withdrawal arises. When Qianfeng ascended the hall, he said: "The Dharma-body has three kinds of illnesses and two kinds of radiance.
You must penetrate each of these individually before you can understand how to return home and sit securely. You must know that there is yet more to go beyond."
The "upper aperture" was present. Yunmen came forward and asked, "Why does the person inside the hermitage not know what is happening outside the hermitage?
Feng laughed heartily. Yunmen said, "This is still where the student has doubts. Feng said, "What kind of mental activity is yours?
Yunmen said, "I also want the Master to fully understand me. Feng said, "You must be like this before you can understand."
Sitting steadily on the ground, the Gatekeeper responds, "Yes, yes. Tiandong takes up the case and says: "To sit firmly is to have a sickness deep in the vital organs;

to employ it is for the light not to penetrate through. Even if one could move with freedom in all directions or pivot upon a single mechanism, one would still not know that there is a 'hole' above this.
Have you attained such steady sitting? In the end, the frosty night moon falls naturally before you."
Xikong: Yunmen was originally an insider; he did not concern himself with external matters. This is why he was able to sit securely.

If you have not yet reached the level of Yunmen’s realization, you must chew upon the "head-word" (hua-tou) of Qianfeng once more before you can understand the true pulse of the non-retrogressive mind.
The mind advances with serenity, maintaining its state without loss. The vital energy of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions interconnects; this is called the "mind that protects the Dharma.

It is said generally that when concentration and wisdom are fused, one enters the realm of non-arising and non-ceasing. When the mind is devoid of mind and advancement is devoid of anything to advance toward, there is a single thought-moment of resonance that is free from deliberate effort;
hence it is called "serene. As long as one has not yet reached this state of true serenity, one must still rely on conscious effort and maintenance.
Once one has reached this state of peace, it is maintained without loss. What is this "non-loss," and what is this "maintenance"?
This is the life-vein of all Buddhas, penetrating through the ten directions.
Now that I have attained the *dhāraṇī*, the life-vein of all Buddhas resides within me; our spirits can communicate, and our vital energies naturally join.

My own vital energy (*prāṇa*) interfuses with that of the Buddha; this is my protection of the Tathāgata’s Dharma. The Buddha’s vital energy interfuses with mine; this is the Buddha’s protection of my Dharma.
When one reaches this state, the thoughts of the triple world are exhausted; it is precisely the stage of the purification of the six sense faculties.
In contrast to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, it corresponds to the stage of Buddhahood; therefore, it is said that one is protected by all Buddhas.
I recall that in the past, when the Sixth Patriarch was washing his robes upon a stone, a monk suddenly appeared and prostrated himself, saying:
"Fangbian is a man from Western Sichuan. Yesterday, in the kingdom of South India, I met the Great Master Dharma, who instructed Fangbian to go quickly to the land of Tang.
He said, 'I transmit to you the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye of Mahākāśyapa, along with the *saṃghāṭī* robe; it has been passed down through six generations.'"
"Go to Caoxi in Shaoyang Prefecture and pay your respects; only then will you have fulfilled your purpose in traveling from afar.

You must wish to see the robe and bowl transmitted by my teacher. The Patriarch then displayed them; this was one verification of the meeting of their spiritual resonance. When Fengxue first arrived at Huanglong, Huanglong asked:
"When the stone horn pierces the path through the clouds, what is the meaning of the hanging branches? Fengxue replied: "Enveloped in crimson clouds..."
The Jade Image: "It obstructs the view from the plains of Zhaozhou. Longyun said, "He has come along with us. Xue said, "Monk, lower your voice. Touzi offered this verse:
"A priceless bright pearl is suspended in the dark; At night, one attempts to pierce the wooden man. Who would have known that the earthen ox saw it?
It swallows him into the abyss of crimson clouds and azure waves. When masters meet, there is no such thing as "never having seen each other before."
Do not fail to encourage one another with the earnest care of protecting and upholding [the Dharma]. This may also be seen as the mutual resolve of both parties to protect the Dharma.
Jue-ming maintains that one can, through wondrous power, turn the Buddha’s compassionate light back toward the Buddha’s state of abiding, like two mirrors facing each other.
The radiance interrelates; within it, wondrous reflections interpenetrate one another in successive layers. This is called the mind of dedication (*pariṇāmanā-citta*).
Generally speaking, "dedicating the Buddha’s compassionate light" means turning the fruit toward the cause; "turning toward the Buddha’s abiding" means turning the cause toward the fruit.
When cause and fruit are unified, the lights intersect and merge. This subtlety is difficult to express in words.
There is only this wondrous power, which does not involve effort or achievement. Its radiance is manifested through compassion and requires no expedient means.
Abiding in equality with the Buddha, there are no further gradations. Fundamental enlightenment and initial enlightenment—these two enlightenments are mutually fused.

It is like two mirrors facing each other with their light; only when this wondrous power exists can these wondrous reflections appear. Enlightened clarity maintains this state, so that deluded cognition no longer arises.
Thus, luminosity is wondrous luminosity. Wondrous luminosity is luminous wondrousness. One is all; all is one.

Wondrous reflections are layered and manifold, interpenetrating one another; they are no longer the shadows of external objects or mental objects (*dharmadhātu*). Therefore, they are called "wondrous reflections."
Here, the shadow will merge completely with the light, and the light will likewise merge completely with the shadow; it is like the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (ādarśa-jñāna).

Turning the Buddha’s wisdom into my own wisdom, and turning my own wisdom toward the Buddha’s wisdom, mind and mind illuminate one another until we are almost identical to the Buddha—how could this be merely a matter of the exchange of vital energies? —Miaoxin.
One day, Mount [Yangshan] requested his disciples to present their sayings to him. He then said, "Meet me outside of sound and form.
Yangshan presented his sayings three times, saying, "It is like two mirrors reflecting one another;
within them, there is no image. Muzhou said, "This statement is correct. But 'I am' and 'you are not'—the image has already been established. Yangshan then asked Muzhou:
"I am of dull spirit and have offered a clumsy response. I do not know how you, Reverend, presented your words before the venerable master Baizhang.
Muzhou said, "When I presented my words before the late master Baizhang, it was like hundreds of thousands of bright mirrors reflecting images;
light and shadow illuminating one another, where every atom and every world-system does not borrow from one another. Yangshan [then asked].
This was a formal expression of gratitude. These two venerable elders were skilled at explaining the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: one was like the radiance of two mirrors facing each other;
the other was like wondrous reflections entering one another in layers. Only when these are combined is the meaning of their words complete.

Xuefeng ascended the hall and said, "If you wish to understand this matter, it is like an ancient mirror set upon its stand: if a barbarian comes, a barbarian appears; if a Han person comes, a Han person appears. Xuansha...
A monk from the assembly asked, "What if one suddenly encounters a bright mirror coming toward him? Xuefeng said, "Both barbarian and Han are hidden.

Xuansha said, "The old monk's feet have not yet touched the ground. By knowing that Xuansha did not approve of Xuefeng, one knows the point where Yangshan offered his prostrations of gratitude to Muzhou.

The light of the mind illuminates secretly; one attains the Buddha’s eternal stillness, supreme, wondrous, and pure, abiding peacefully in the unconditioned. To attain this without loss is called the "abiding of the mind in ethical discipline."

The Master said: "When the light of the mind secretly turns toward the Buddha and dwells in peace, one attains the Buddha’s quiescent, wondrous, and eternally concentrated state—remaining unmoved like a mirror.
One attains the Buddha’s unsurpassed, wondrous purity—remaining unstained even when encountering the dust of the world.

This is the true unconditioned self-nature, the original Buddha of Heaven and Truth. Abiding herein, there is no action and no conditioning; there is no realization and no attainment. To have any attainment whatsoever—"
There must necessarily be loss. Where there is no gain, there is no loss. Where there is loss, one must employ precepts; where there is no loss, what need is there for precepts?
The self-nature is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); this very state is the precept. When the precept has nothing further to regulate, it is called the "True Precept.

This precept exists at the juncture of the mind’s luminosity and its subtle turning back; it is termed "mysterious" (*guhya*). It cannot be measured by the conscious intellect; how could it be sought [by such means]?
Can the precepts of permanence be discussed in the same way? The precepts are themselves concentration; the precepts are themselves wisdom. They are merely one essence with different names.
Formerly, when Shitou first arrived at Qingyuan to pay his respects, Qingyuan asked, "From where have you come?
Shitou replied, "From Caoxi. Qingyuan asked, "What have you brought with you? Shitou said, "Even before reaching Caoxi, I have not lost anything. Qingyuan said:
"If it is so," [the Master] said, "what need is there to go to Caoxi? Yuan said, "If one does not reach Caoxi, how can one know that [one's nature] is not lost?
The Master asked again, "Does the Great Master of Caoxi recognize you, Reverend? Yuan said, "Do you recognize me now?
The Master said, "Even if you recognize me, how could you truly recognize me? Yuan said, "Though there may be many horns, a single unicorn is sufficient. Later...
One day, while Yaoshan was sitting upon a rock, Shitou asked him, "What are you doing here? Yaoshan replied, "I am doing nothing.
Shitou said, "If that is so, then you are sitting idly. Yaoshan said, "If it were idle sitting, then I would be doing something.
Shitou asked, "When you say you are doing nothing, what is it that you are not doing? Yaoshan replied, "Even the thousand sages..."
[Danxia] did not recognize him. Tou then praised him with a verse, saying: "Living together from the beginning, we did not know his name;
He moves along spontaneously, just as he is. Even the sages of antiquity could not recognize him; How could ordinary people of the momentary present understand him? Danxia’s verse says:
"When the profound mystery is exhausted, it is fundamentally serene; If one were to say there are eighteen thousand [miles] between us, The moon is reflected in the clear [water]."
The river fish is no longer seen; what use is there for the fisherman to cast his trap again?
As for Yaoshan’s “non-action” (wuwei) and Shitou’s “not losing,” they are ultimately unfathomable—how profound they are! Only one who can penetrate this barrier [truly understands].
By this, one is able to attain the Buddha’s eternally concentrated, unsurpassed, wondrous purity; this may be called the "Abiding in the Mind of Precepts.
Abiding in the mastery of precepts, one is able to travel throughout the ten directions, proceeding wherever one's vows lead; this is called the "Abiding in the Mind of Vows."
The Master replied: "When one abides in the precepts with mastery, one forgets that they are precepts. When true purity is eternally concentrated, there is nowhere one cannot go.
Thus, one is able to travel through the ten directions, proceeding wherever one's vows lead. In the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) of Tiantai, even though ignorance (avidyā) has not yet been severed,"
Those born in the Land of Common Dwelling are said to be "born by vow"; this precisely accords with the present text.
Furthermore, it is taught that those in the Ten Faiths emerge into the provisional realm to benefit sentient beings; that he now travels through the ten directions likewise accords with this meaning.

On the fourth day of the twelfth month in the third year of the Chunhua era, at the hour of the horse (noon), Chan Master Nian of Shoushan ascended the hall and spoke a verse, saying: "This year I am sixty..."
7. Old and sick, I pass the days according to circumstances. This year I record the events of next year; next year I shall record the events of this very day.
When the subsequent month and day arrive, there will be no discrepancy. He ascended the hall to take leave of the assembly and spoke a verse, saying:
"The world of white silver and the body of golden hue—sentient and insentient share in one single reality. When light and darkness both cease, they are together neither..."
Zhao. In the afternoon of that day, he manifested his entire body and passed away while sitting peacefully.
His disciple Fenyang Zhao had an old friendship with Li Hou, the Governor of Longde Prefecture. The Governor offered him the Chengtian Temple, but the messenger was rebuffed three times.
Insisting that the Master must go with him, the Master laughed and said, "I, this old monk, have not stepped outside the monastery for thirty years."
"Very well. You may go ahead; we shall proceed one after the other. Why must we travel together? He then ordered that food be prepared and their provisions packed.
Having finished, he addressed the assembly, saying, "The old monk is departing. Who can follow me? One monk stepped forward and said, "I can follow you.
The Master asked, "How many li do you travel in a day? The monk replied, "Fifty li. The Master said, "You cannot follow me. Furthermore—
A monk came forward and said, "I can follow him. The Master asked, "How many li do you travel each day?
The monk replied, "Seventy li. The Master said, "Even you cannot follow me. An attendant came forward and said, "I can follow him;
wherever the Master goes, I will arrive there as well. The Master said, "You, however, can indeed follow this old monk. Having finished speaking, he addressed the messenger.

The master said, "I shall depart first," and sat away peacefully until his passing. His attendant likewise attained parinirvāṇa immediately upon standing. Is this not one who departs in accordance with their vow?
Unless one has already realized the stage of the Ten Faiths, it is not easy to reach such a state.
"Faith" (śraddhā) refers to that which is true and without delusion; it is because it accords with the ground of ultimate reality (bhūtakoṭi). Therefore, it is said: "It is simply this one matter."
This is the reality; the other two are not true. One must first cause the craving for desire to wither away and maintain a mind that is empty yet luminous;

only then can one enter the wondrous, perfect, and true nature. When this true nature unfolds and transforms, subtle habitual tendencies are all integrated and dissolved. Furthermore, one maintains this through concentration and wisdom.
One advances by means of protection and sustenance; one turns back the Buddha’s compassionate light and attains the Buddha’s pure precepts.

From this, one is born into the family of the Tathāgata, and wherever one goes, it is in accordance with one's vows. The ten levels of faith (*śraddhā*) are not the same as the ten stages of abiding (*vihāra*). Why are they both called "abidings"?

Because the Bodhisattva Asaṅga established eighteen stages to delineate the beginning and end of the ranks in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*; therefore, the first stage may also be termed an "abiding."
It is called the "Abiding" stage. Because it relies upon the wisdom of non-abiding and never regresses, it receives the name "Abiding.

Ānanda, when these good sons, through true skillful means, give rise to these ten minds, the essence of their minds radiates brilliance; the ten functions interpenetrate one another, perfectly accomplishing the One Mind.
This is called the "Abiding in the Arising of the Mind" stage.
The Master said: "From the true, wondrous, and perfect, one again gives rise to the true and wondrous; this is what is called 'true skillful means.
By means of true skillful means, these ten kinds of faith are generated. Faith is itself the truth, and truth is itself faith;

there must be no other thoughts intermingled between them. Thus the mind becomes refined. When the mind is refined and brilliant, it naturally emits radiance, whether in meditative concentration or otherwise."

Whether it be wisdom, precepts, or vows—these ten functions interpenetrate one another. Thus, while in samādhi, wisdom, precepts, and so forth are fully present; while in precepts, samādhi, wisdom, and so forth are fully present.
In sum, this reveals the original source and abides in accordance with the Buddha; therefore, it is called the "perfectly accomplished single mind.
If the ten functions are not yet perfected, the scope of the mind is not yet full. It is only when the ten functions are perfectly accomplished that [the goal] can be attained.

This is called the Stage of Arousing the Mind (*cittotpāda-vihāra*). Tiantai correlates the ten minds of the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* with the ten modes of contemplation (*daśa-yāna-dhyāna*), clearly elucidating these ten virtues in relation to the first stage of the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*). The underlying intent is likewise consistent.

Formerly, when the Sixth Patriarch entered the room after three knocks, the Fifth Patriarch surrounded him with his *kaṣāya* so that no one would see them, and preached the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* to him until reaching the passage: "One should abide nowhere."
Thus he gave rise to that mind. Under these words, the Sixth Patriarch attained great enlightenment, realizing that all phenomena do not depart from one’s own nature (*svabhāva*).

He then addressed the Fifth Patriarch, saying: "How unexpected it is that one's own nature is fundamentally pure! How unexpected it is that one's own nature is fundamentally neither arising nor ceasing!
How unexpected it is that one's own nature is fundamentally complete! How unexpected it is that one's own nature is fundamentally unmoving!"
He maintained that the inherent nature is capable of giving rise to all phenomena. The Fifth Patriarch, knowing that [Huineng] had awakened to his original nature, said to him:

"If you do not recognize your own fundamental mind, studying the Dharma is of no benefit. If you recognize your own fundamental mind and see your own original nature, you shall be called a Great Man, a Teacher of Gods and Humans, and a Buddha.
Thus, one perfectly accomplishes the One Mind. If it were as the Sixth Patriarch realized it, then one could speak of the stage of "Abiding in the Arousing of the Bodhi-mind."

The illumination within the mind is like pure lapis lazuli, with refined gold appearing within; taking that prior wondrous mind and treading upon it to form the ground is called the Dwelling of Cultivating the Ground.
It is said in general:
only when the ground of vision is clear can one truly tread upon it; if the place of vision is not clear, even if one is able to tread, it is not [true practice].
This is the melting away of one's own nature. To merely serve external pursuits is like building a house on another person’s land;
what does it have to do with oneself? Within this mind, the untaught wisdom and spontaneous wisdom are revealed, manifesting from the nature of the *dharmadhātu*.
Like pure lapis lazuli, within which refined gold appears; seeing it is ultimate truth, and awakening to it is ultimate penetration.

The place of seeing is non-dual with that of the Buddha, yet the place of practice has not yet reached full integration. From this point on, maintain and sustain this; from this point on, tread upon it.
Put each of the ten kinds of wondrous minds into personal practice and realization. Body and mind become as one, and at every step, you tread firmly upon the ground. Like...
The Grounds are analogous. Just as one who builds a house must first prepare the ground, this [stage] is merely the initial step of setting out;

therefore, it is called the Dwelling of Preparing the Ground. Chan Master Yunju Deng addressed the assembly from the hall, saying: "An ancient said, 'If you wish to take charge of and maintain this matter...'"
One must stand atop the highest mountain peak and walk upon the deepest ocean floor before one possesses even a trace of the true spirit.
If you have not yet resolved the Great Matter, you must first tread the profound path.
A monk asked, "What is the place where those who walk the upward path dwell? Ju replied, "The world is at peace. Furthermore, a monk asked Chan Master Guangfu Yuanyuan. From...
[The Master] asked, "Where do the sages above walk? Yuan said, "At the crossroads. [The Master] said, "If that is so, then they are deficient.

Yuan said, "I knew you had not yet reached this state. [The Master] asked, "What is it like after reaching it? Yuan said: *Note: This dialogue is from the *Wumen Guan* (Gateless Barrier), Case 39, concerning the monk Xuedou Chongxian and his teacher, Master Yuan.*
This is the daily meal of the household; therefore, it is called the "abiding in the ground of clarity" as practiced and realized by the various venerable masters.
Their practice is truly wondrous.
Both the mind-ground and cognitive awareness are fully clarified; they travel through the ten directions without obstruction, which is termed the "abiding in cultivation."
Tong said: "By what means does the mind know the ground? By what means does the ground know the mind?

The mind is the wondrous mind; practice is wondrous practice; and knowing is wondrous knowing. When these three virtues—principle, practice, and wisdom—are perfectly interfused, one may speak of the ground and mind engaging with knowing.
It is luminously unobscured and clearly ever-knowing; the mind itself is [the ground]."
Practice. Practice is itself the mind. As it traverses the ten directions, what further obstruction could there be? Since there is no longer any hindrance, why would one need to practice further?

Yet, this is termed "abiding through practice" for two reasons: first, because one treads upon the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) without grasping or attachment, one takes this traversing as practice;
second, because if one were to fixate on clarity and stability, that would constitute an obstruction; therefore—
To practice without obstruction is cultivation; its actual practice is non-practice, and its cultivation is non-cultivation. Master Shishuang addressed the assembly, saying:
"For those of beginner's capacity who have not yet grasped the Great Matter, one must first recognize the head, and the tail will follow of its own accord."
Shushan came forth and asked, "What is the head? Shuang replied, "You must know that it exists. Shushan said, "What is the tail?
Shuang replied, "Exhausting the present moment. Shushan said, "What is it like when there is a head but no tail? Shuang replied, "Even if you spat out gold, what could you do with it?
Shushan said, "What is it like when there is a tail but no head? Shuang replied, "It is still..."
There was one who remained dependent [on such interpretations]. Shu asked, "What is it like when the head and tail perfectly correspond?
Shuang said, "He does not form a conceptual understanding; even so, I do not yet grant him entry. Later, a monk asked Chan Master Jiufeng Qian, "What is the head?
Jiufeng said, "Opening one's eyes, one does not realize the dawn. "What is the tail? Jiufeng said, "Not sitting for ten thousand years."
"A bed. When there is a head but no tail, what then? Feng said, "In the end, it is not noble. "When there is a tail but no head, what then?
Feng said, "Though full, one has no strength. "When the head and tail are perfectly matched, what then?
Feng said, "The descendants have gained the power; those inside the room do not know. Jiufeng understood the meaning of Shishuang as if holding a single seal.
[The verse] concludes. Tiantong’s *Gāthā* says: "Ruler for the circle, carpenter’s square for the square; To act, to travel, to dwell, or to hide.

A bird that stumbles on dull wings, perching amidst the reeds; A sheep that advances or retreats, butting against the fence. Eating another’s rice, sleeping on one’s own bed. Clouds rise to bring rain; dew gathers to become frost.
Jade threads meet and pass through the eye of the needle; Cotton fibers unbroken emerge from the loom’s belly. The Stone Woman..."
The mechanism halts; the night approaches midday. The wooden man turns his path; the moon’s shadow shifts to the center. This verse is consistent from beginning to end.
One must surely cultivate in this way and practice in this way before one can correspond with the Sudden and Perfect Dharma-gate.
Their conduct becomes identical to that of the Buddha, and they receive the Buddha’s spiritual essence, much like a being in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) who seeks out its own parents.
Through the subtle and hidden communication of their latent faith, they enter the lineage of the Tathāgata; this is called the Dwelling of Noble Birth.
Tong said: "In their practice, they are equal to the Buddhas; in their partial true wisdom, they are equal to the ultimate wisdom.

They receive the Buddha’s 'breath' (qi-fen), and in their partial true principle, they are equal to the ultimate principle. What was previously called the 'meeting of breaths' still implies a duality;

having reached this point, one enters the lineage of the Tathāgata, where the two are nearly merged into one. As for the intermediate state (antarābhava) body: this [present] aggregate has already ceased, while that..."
The *gandharva* has not yet been born. Second, during the intermediate state, it remains suspended upside down in space for forty-nine days, seeking its own parents.

Through the affinity of karmic conditions, it immediately proceeds to take rebirth. This is because the *gandharva* communicates with the unseen; it is not something sought through deliberate thought.

Conventional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) is like a father; ultimate wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*) is like a mother. They unite spontaneously without requiring effort, and their resultant virtues are secretly identical.
There is nothing that can be known as to how this comes to be so. Thus, whether manifest or hidden, one may enter the lineage of the Tathāgata.
Regarding the phrase "born noble": it is like a prince dwelling in the womb; his status differs from that of commoners, and therefore he is called "noble. Noble.
This is the dharma-gate of the sudden realization of the unsurpassed, foremost Dharma. Dongshan has a diagram of the five ranks of the prince:
first is Birth; second is Court-Birth; third is Final-Birth; fourth is Transformation-Birth; and fifth is Internal-Birth.
All of these were kōans concerning the upward-pointing principle, which Shishuang expressed in verse. The first, on "Birth," says: Naturally noble offspring, fundamentally not produced by effort;
Virtue harmonizes with heaven and earth, the momentum of its nurture is magnificent. From beginning to end, throughout its single span, there is no other seed;

Its six palaces and four residences do not belong to another lineage. Superiors and subordinates live in harmony, yin and yang flow in accord; Sharing the same vital energy, their branches remain connected.
Their capacity and measure are identical. If you wish to know the father of the Prince of Birth, it is like a crane soaring through the Milky Way, emerging from its silver cage.

(II) The "Morning Birth" says: In his diligent study of the treatises on emotion, none in the world can rival him; when he emerges, his conduct in all affairs already transcends his peers. When his five-character verse is completed, it is like the snow of midwinter;
when his brush falls, even a hair’s breadth becomes clouds across the four seas. Through the accumulation of merit from ten thousand scrolls, he brings glory to the sagely age.
With single-minded loyalty, he assists the enlightened sovereign; the roles of salt and sour (minister) are not attained through innate knowledge.

What need is there to display supreme merit upon the golden scroll? The third verse concludes with: Having long dwelt among crags and ravines applying his efforts, he kept his solitary will firm by a thatched mat and a wooden door.
For ten years, his mind has been detached from what he sees and hears; for a single body, winter and summer, he has lacked even a single bolt of silk. His clarity and composure contain...

Laughing at the thoughts of three autumns past, his pure austerity and lofty reputation rank him among the sagely philosophers. Having accomplished his studies, he attains a high office to fulfill his long-held aspirations.

Recently, as the ministers and officials have not held the path of power, the Fourth Transformational Incarnation said: "Distributing the Imperial Mandate to maintain the Dharma, the majesty of governance spreads across ten thousand li of mountains and rivers.
The crimson shadow of the sun’s orb gathers upon the lower realm; the green oil-clothed banners cool the winds against the summer heat."
At that time, how could high and low neglect the service of honor and humility? Five robes warm the wayfarer; near and far alike know it. Holding the wondrous seal in hand, the borders are at peace;
when facing the sun, why would one reveal even a trace of artifice? (5) Nengsheng said: "Deep within the ninefold palace, what more need be proclaimed?
Hanging out tattered rags has long been the manifestation of the wondrous transmission. To serve the One Person alone is to be honored by heaven and earth; let others [be as they may]."

The various paths are each their own provisional means. When the purple silk curtains close, the sovereign and his ministers are separated; when the yellow gate’s drapes hang down, the prohibitions are fully maintained. Because you cling to the palaces and officials of your own region, he has thus used "yellow-leaf money" to stop your crying.

A monk asked Ruiyan, “What is the Prince at Birth? Ruiyan said, “Deep within the palace, he does not go outside. Touzi composed a verse on this: Noble and extraordinary, The purple silk curtains are drawn tight. The sovereign and his ministers are separated; The yellow gate’s drapes hang down.

Because you cling to the palaces and officials of your own region, He has thus used "yellow-leaf money" to stop your crying. Monk: How is it that the Prince at Birth does not go outside? Master: Deep within the palace, he does not go outside. Touzi’s Verse: Noble and extraordinary.
It is naturally so that there must be a time; in the spring gardens of the six palaces, few are those who accompany one. The stars cluster at midnight as the celestial wheel revolves;

when the candlelight dawns in the eastern chamber, the curtains hang in stillness. Thus, one is born into a singular path of nobility. The tradition of the Dongshan school is the most profound and subtle;
unless one enters its inner chamber, it is difficult to engage in discourse with it.

Having already entered the womb of the Way and personally received the lineage of the Awakened One, it is like a fetus that has fully formed with no deficiency in its human features; this is called the stage of "Abiding in the Fulfillment of Expedient Means.
It is further explained that once the holy embryo is fully formed, one does not merely receive its vital essence, but personally receives the lineage of the Awakened One.
He continues the life-lineage of the Buddha, responding to capacities and engaging with sentient beings, fully endowed with skillful means.

Although he has not yet reached perfection, he nevertheless possesses the essential form, albeit on a small scale—like a person in the womb whose features are complete; though the features have not yet manifested outwardly for all to see, they are nonetheless present.
Because it pertains to the application of skillful means (*upāya*), it is called "the dwelling of the perfection of skillful means.

As for the Great Master Wuzu Ren, he was a native of Huangmei in Qizhou. Previously, while serving as a "pine-planting practitioner" at Mount Poutou, he once requested of the Fourth Patriarch, saying:
"May I hear the Way of the Dharma? The Patriarch replied: "You are already old; even if you were to hear it, would you be able to transform others on a broad scale?"
"If they come again, I may still be able to delay them. He then said, "Let us go to the water's edge.
There he saw a woman washing clothes and asked, "May I stay the night? The woman replied, "I have father and brothers; you may go and ask them.
He said, "If you agree, I shall immediately venture forth. The woman nodded her head in consent, and he turned his horse and departed. This woman was the youngest daughter of the Zhou family.
Every time she returned home, she would immediately become pregnant. Her parents detested her greatly and cast her out.

Having nowhere to turn, the woman worked as a hired spinner in the village during the day and stayed beneath a public inn at night. She subsequently gave birth to a son; deeming him an ill omen, she threw him into a muddy harbor.
When she saw him the next morning, he was swimming upstream against the current, his physical form radiant and brilliant. She was greatly astonished and thus picked him up.
When he had grown to be a youth, he followed his mother to beg for food. The villagers called him "The Child Without a Surname.
One wise man encountered him and sighed, saying, "This boy lacks seven marks; he does not equal the Tathāgata. Later, he met the Fourth Patriarch, who asked, "What is your surname?
He replied, "I have a surname, but it is not a permanent surname. The Patriarch asked, "What is this surname? He replied, "It is Buddha."
The Patriarch asked, "Do you have no surname? He replied, "My surname is emptiness.

The Fourth Patriarch recognized him as a vessel for the Dharma and sent an attendant to his mother’s quarters to request that she allow him to leave the household life. Because of their past karmic connection, the mother showed no sign of reluctance.
He was subsequently ordained as a disciple and ultimately succeeded to his master’s position. A verse by Tiāntóng says: "The fruit ripens at Huangmei; the white lotus blooms.
When asked, it is only Buddha-nature, yet its substance differs from that of the ordinary fetus. The robe passed to the man of Nanling; the pines grow old on West Mountain and I return again.
Two borrowed skin-bags accomplish what task? A single jar of wind and moon, profound and free of dust."
Furthermore, a verse by Shui-an says: "The old man who went away to plant pines returns again as a joyful youth who transmits the Dharma.
He has his mother-born face but no father-given surname; this numinous sprout beyond the kalpas does not violate the spring.

Had it not been for the Way-attainer having already reached the state of the perfection of skillful means, how could he come and go with such freedom? How could he be so fully endowed with wondrous marks, abiding in suchness?
He came; his appearance was like that of a Buddha, and his mental characteristics were likewise the same. This is called the "Abiding in the Right Mind.

It is explained that his appearance is a metaphor for skillful application (*upāya*), while his mental characteristics are a metaphor for wisdom and principle (*jñāna* and *tattva*). Thus, he made his exterior identical [to a Buddha] while his interior remained slightly different.

This is not yet the rectification of the mind. Rectifying the mind is difficult to express; it must involve the simultaneous forgetting of both the ordinary and the sage, such that emotions are exhausted and the essence is revealed—only then can one speak of "rectitude.
Chan Master Guangyong of Nantapu traveled north to visit Linji, and upon returning, he served under Yangshan.
Mount said, "What have you come here for? He replied, "To pay my respects to the Master. Mount asked, "Have you seen the Master? He replied, "I have.
Mount said, "How does the Master compare to a donkey? He replied, "When I saw the Master, he did not even resemble a Buddha."
Mount [Shan] said, "If it does not resemble the Buddha, what does it resemble? He replied, "If there were anything to which it resembled, how would it differ from a donkey?

Mount Shan was greatly startled and said, "When both ordinary person and sage are forgotten, emotions are exhausted and the essence is revealed. For twenty years I have tested people with this, yet none have reached a definitive realization.
You must take responsibility for this. Every time Mount Shan pointed to him and spoke of him to others, he would say, "This man is a living Buddha in his physical body."
He is a Buddha. Observing this, his countenance is like that of a Buddha and his mental state is likewise identical.
Only when the manifestation from the Southern Pagoda draws near do body and mind merge into one, increasing day by day; this is called the Stage of Non-retrogression.
Tong said: "The previous 'non-retrogressive mind' refers to penetrating deeply into the fundamental nature, advancing without retreating; this was discussed solely in terms of the mind.
This 'non-retrogressive abiding,' however, involves the integration of body and mind, whereby they grow and increase day by day—thus progressing simultaneously in both the internal and external.
It means that one’s outward appearance and mental state remain relaxed and immersed in the practice, waiting for them to develop naturally, rather than through forced accumulation."
Merit is accumulated through successive acts of cultivation. A monk once recited the verse of Wōluán, saying:
"Wōluán has skillful means; He can sever a hundred thoughts. When facing objects, the mind does not arise; Enlightenment grows day by day. The Sixth Patriarch heard this and said:
"This verse does not clarify the ground of the mind. If you follow it in practice, it will only add further fetters. Thereupon, he showed him another verse:
"Wisdom has no skillful means; it does not sever the hundred thoughts. When the mind arises in response to objects, how can Bodhi grow?
Tiantong comments: "The sunflower turns toward the sun; the willow catkins follow the wind. Now, as for that one uppermost aperture, it neither increases nor decreases.
It is only because the habitual tendencies of consciousness have not been fully worn away that one perceives growth and decline. If...
There are those who, perceiving that which neither increases nor decreases, move toward it; they are like sunflowers turning toward the sun.
There are those who, perceiving that which neither increases nor decreases, forget it; they are like willow catkins carried by the wind.

If one is free from both [of these states] and, according to the occasion, puts on clothes and eats food, thereby nurturing the holy embryo, only then can one be said to dwell in the stage of non-retrogression.
The ten spiritual marks of the body are simultaneously perfected; this is called the Stage of Youthful Truth (*kumārabhūmi*).

Generally, these "ten bodies" refer to: the Bodhi-body, the Vow-body, the Transformation-body, the Power-body, the Adornment-body, the Majestic-body, the Mind-born-body, the Merit-body, the Dharma-body, and the Wisdom-body.
When these spiritual marks are fully perfected, one compares them to the marks of those who preceded him.
It is not lacking; it is already complete. Although its physical form is uniform, this has already become that of a youth. Therefore, it is called the "Abode of Youthful Truth" (Kumārabhūta).
Chan Master Fenyang Shao ascended the hall and said: "One who expounds the Dharma must possess the Ten Wisdoms Identical with Reality."
If one does not possess the ten knowledges that accord with reality, one cannot distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox, nor differentiate between the monastic and the lay;
thus, one cannot serve as a guide for gods and humans to adjudicate right from wrong. This is like a bird flying through the sky with broken wings, or an arrow shot at a target with a severed string.
Because the string is severed, the arrow does not hit the mark; because the wings are broken, flight through the sky is impossible. Only when the string is strong...
Wing-lao: When both emptiness and form are thoroughly penetrated, what is meant by "the ten wisdoms being identical with reality"?
I shall point them out for you, venerable elders: first, identity of substance; second, identity of the great matter; third, identity as fellow practitioners; fourth, identity of true resolve;

fifth, identity of universal pervasiveness; sixth, identity of complete possession; seventh, identity of gain and loss; eighth, identity of life and death; ninth, identity of the roar of the voice; tenth...
"Attaining entry together. It is also said: "With what kind of person does one attain entry together?
With whom does one roar with the same voice? What is it that constitutes 'together' in birth and death? What thing is it that shares gain and loss? Which one is it that is fully endowed together?

What is it that is universally pervasive together? Who is it that shares the same true resolve? Who is able to participate as a fellow student in totality? Which one is it that shares the Great [Vehicle]?"
Matter. What thing shares a single substance? Is there anyone who can point it out? If you can point it out, I shall not begrudge you my compassion.
If you cannot point it out, you have yet to possess the eye for study. You must discern this with urgency; you must know right from wrong.
The manifestation is present before us; it cannot be maintained for long. Take care. These ten wisdoms are identical with reality (*tathatā*);

they merely clarify the matters of body and environment. If the ten bodies were fully perfected, one would further enter into the subtle. Nevertheless, they are all one *bodhi*, differing only in name according to the circumstances.
If there were something separate and extraordinary, how could it be fully possessed all at once?
The formation of the womb occurs; becoming a child of the Buddha by one’s own accord is called the "Abiding as a Dharma Prince.

It is said generally that, having personally received the Buddha’s portion of vital energy and entered the lineage of the Tathāgata, one gradually forms a fetus and subsequently develops physical features.
They further increase and advance toward the stage of youth; only then do they achieve their formation and emerge from the womb as Dharma Princes.

Even for those who have already entered the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, there is still such protection and entrustment, whereby they become increasingly polished and penetrating, acting as the Buddha’s representatives to propagate the great transformation.
How truly difficult it is to achieve this! Śāriputra was born from the Buddha’s mouth and born through transformation from the Dharma.
He is the eldest son of the Buddha, and his wisdom is foremost; this has been the result of his efforts over many kalpas, not merely for a single morning or evening.
While Guishan was sleeping, Yangshan went to inquire after him. Guishan turned his face toward the wall.
Yangshan said, "Why have you become like this, Master? Guishan rose and said, "I just had a dream; try to interpret it for me."
"Look," [said Baizhang]. He looked up and took a basin of water to wash the Master's face. After a short while, Xiangyan also came to pay his respects.
Guishan said, "I just had a dream; Jizi has already interpreted it for me. You, in turn, interpret it for me."
Yan then had a bowl of tea brought forward. Guishan said, "The understanding of these two disciples surpasses that of Śāriputra.
Their wisdom is even greater than his; might they not be cases of those who have already emerged from the womb and are now emerging from it once more?"
Through these [stages], one becomes a full person. It is like a great king of a country who delegates the affairs of state to his crown prince;
when that Kṣatriya king’s eldest son has grown up, the consecration ceremony is performed for him, which is called the stage of consecration (abhiṣeka-vihāra).

Tong said: "A Dharma Prince (Dharmarāja-putra), by virtue of the characteristics of his mind of skillful means, is identical in all respects to a Buddha. He is capable of succeeding to the Buddha’s position and acting on the Buddha’s behalf;
therefore, he is illustrated through the metaphors of a crown prince of a great king or the heir-apparent of a Kṣatriya king, who undergoes the ceremony of consecration (abhiṣeka).
The son of a Son of Heaven is called a Crown Prince, while the son of a feudal lord is called an Heir-Apparent—these terms serve to signify this accomplishment."
When a person is about to be invested with the sovereignty of the state, it is similar to the rite of capping: one takes water from the great ocean and pours it over their crown.
This symbolizes that a ruler should employ the wisdom of the multitude, just as the ocean receives all streams. By using ocean water, one thereby employs all waters.
This is merely to entrust the affairs of state to them, enabling them to govern and administer; it is not yet the formal transfer of the sovereignty of the state itself.

This [stage] is indeed the true one. Because all virtues are secretly perfected within this stage, it is sufficient to enable the transformation of beings throughout the ten directions and the performance of Buddha-works;

thus it is called the "Stage of Consecration" (Abhiṣeka-vihāra). Upon reaching the tenth stage, where practice is fulfilled and one is nearly equal to Perfect Enlightenment (Samyaksaṃbodhi), one becomes fit for formal entrustment and the bestowal of the Buddha’s office.
Therefore, the stage of Dharma-cloud (Dharmameghā) is named the "Consecrated Bodhisattva. This, then, is the true [consecration].

The monk asked, "What is the lion cub? Caoshan said, "One who can swallow its parents.

When [Wuzu] let out a roar, [Dongshan] said, "Both grandfather and father are exhausted. Wuzu asked, "After they are exhausted, what then?
Dongshan said, "The whole body returns to the father. Wuzu asked, "I do not yet understand: when the grandfather is exhausted, where does the father go? Dongshan said, "That place is also exhausted.
Wuzu asked, "Why did you previously say that the whole body returns to the father? Dongshan said, "It is like a prince who is able to accomplish the affairs of an entire kingdom. Furthermore—
He said, "Ācārya, this matter must not be left isolated or stagnant; it is like scattering a few flowers upon withered wood.
This is the arising of function from essence—the so-called 'wondrously profound stillness.
The Dharma Master Sima came from Hunan and said to Baizhang, 'Recently, while in Hunan, I found a mountain named Daming (Great Miao). It can accommodate fifteen hundred [monks].'"
The Layman asked, "Is this the dwelling place of the Good Spiritual Friend?
Deshan said, "Can an old monk like me live there? The Layman asked, "Why not? Deshan said, "You, Master, are a man of bone; he is a mountain of flesh.
Even if you were to dwell there, your followers would not exceed a thousand. The Layman asked, "Is there no one among my assembly who could dwell there? Deshan said, "Wait..."
He looked through them all. At that time, Huilin Jue was serving as the First Seat (Dharma Seat Holder). Baizhang ordered his attendant to invite him there and asked, "What kind of person is this?
Jue cleared his throat once and took a few steps forward. Baizhang said, "No. Baizhang then ordered him to summon Shanzhao of Mt. Mushi.
At that time, Shanzhao was serving as the Head Cook (Director of the Kitchen). As soon as Baizhang saw him, he said, "This is truly Mt. Mushi."
He was the master. That night, Baizhang summoned Shanshan into his room and instructed him, saying, "My karmic conditions for transformation are exhausted here.
This is the superior realm of Mount Wei; you should reside there, succeed to my lineage, and extensively guide future students. Huilin asked him about this.
"I, so-and-so, am humbled to occupy the position of head monk. How can I take charge as the steward?
The Master said, "If you can utter a phrase that transcends the ordinary before the assembly, I shall grant you the position of steward.

He then pointed to a water pitcher and asked, "You must not call this a 'water pitcher. What would you call it? Lin replied, "It cannot be called a 'wooden bucket. The Master then questioned him further.
Shan kicked over the pure water jar and departed. Zhaozhou laughed and said, "The First Seat has lost to Master Shan.
Shan subsequently went to reside there; his transformation flourished throughout Hunan, and he was known as the founder of the Yangzong school.

Ānanda, these good sons, having become children of the Buddha, are endowed with the immeasurable, wondrous virtues of the Tathāgatas throughout the ten directions.
"Conformity" is called the Practice of Joy.

It is said in general that the Wondrous Virtue of the Tathāgata is such that he does not change while following conditions, and he follows conditions without changing; dwelling amidst the dust of the world, he remains unstained.

Therefore, it is called "sublime. Having already become a child of the Buddha and being fully endowed with sublime virtues, one carries the staff wherever one goes and performs the play upon whatever stage is encountered.
Thus, one can accord with all directions, delighting in the joy of dhyāna; this is the Practice of Joy, which accords with sentient beings.
These skillful means of guidance are intended precisely to manifest the wondrous virtue of the Tathāgata.

This concerns the meaning of the mind’s arising and ceasing (*citta-utpāda-nirodha*) and the meaning of the suchness of the mind (*citta-tathatā*). Regarding the suchness of the mind: it is like a bright mirror reflecting images.

The mirror is a metaphor for the mind, and the images are a metaphor for all phenomena (*dharmas*). If the mind grasps at phenomena, it immediately becomes involved with external causes and conditions; this is the meaning of arising and ceasing.
Not grasping at any phenomena is the meaning of *tathatā* (suchness). Śrāvakas hear and see the Buddha-nature; Bodhisattvas see the Buddha-nature with their eyes.
To realize them as non-dual is called the nature of equality (*samatā*). This nature has no difference, yet its functions differ:

in delusion it is consciousness (*vijñāna*), and in awakening it is wisdom (*jñāna*). To accord with principle is awakening; to accord with phenomena is delusion. Delusion is simply being deluded about oneself.
The family is one's own fundamental mind. To awaken is to awaken to the nature of one’s own house; once awakened, there is awakening forever, and one shall never again be deluded.
It is like when the sun rises: it cannot coexist with darkness. When the sun of wisdom rises, it does not coexist with the darkness of afflictions.

When the mind and its objects are thoroughly understood, false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) does not arise. Since false conceptualization no longer arises, this is precisely the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
It has existed inherently and exists now; it does not depend upon cultivating the Path or sitting in meditation. This non-cultivation and non-sitting is precisely the Tathāgata’s pure dhyāna.
If one now perceives this principle as truly authentic, one will not create various karmas and will pass the remainder of one's life according to one's lot.
With but a single robe and a single patchwork cloak, they follow one another in sitting and rising; their observance of the precepts increases in fragrance as they accumulate pure karma.

Abiding in reliance, they practice the bodhisattva path in detail as shown by the Great Master Mazu;

Remaining amidst afflictions, one should deliver sentient beings while extinguishing all marks of the perfections; turning the mind toward the unconditioned and directing it toward the path of nirvāṇa is called the dedication "Protecting All Sentient Beings While Remaining Free from the Mark of Sentient Beings."

Tong said: "When the ten practices are fully perfected, one manifests the mundane world and manifests the Buddha-lands; the one becomes the infinite, and the infinite becomes the one. This is precisely spiritual power (*abhijñā*).
That it can accomplish the rules and patterns of the Buddhas of the ten directions is precisely the work of a Buddha (*buddhakārya*). It is pure, pristine, and true."
It is the sole reality, pure and untainted, far removed from the afflictions of obstruction; it may be called that which can liberate itself.
If one were to remain solely attached to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), one would be termed a "self-enlightened man. Therefore, one ought to deliver sentient beings.

One extinguishes all marks of the perfections (*pāramitā*). One turns the mind toward non-action (*asaṃskṛta*) and directs it toward those sentient beings, so that together they may hasten upon the path to *nirvāṇa*.
While one realizes *nirvāṇa* for oneself, its nature is fundamentally non-active; thus, leading sentient beings toward *nirvāṇa* is likewise merely non-active.
Therefore, although one liberates sentient beings throughout the day, in reality, no mark of liberation can be apprehended. If one perceives that there is something to be...

To practice the *pāramitās* is to enter the realm of conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta*) and turn one’s back on the path to *nirvāṇa*; it is no longer the fundamental intent of non-arising and non-ceasing.

Therefore, to extinguish the marks of the *pāramitās* is called the "dedication that is free from the marks of sentient beings. If even the marks of the *pāramitās* do not exist, how could there be any marks of sentient beings?
A monk asked Huangbo, "Does the Buddha save sentient beings? Huangbo replied, "In reality, there are no sentient beings [to be saved]."
"Regarding those delivered by the Tathāgata, even 'I' cannot be apprehended; how then could 'non-self' be apprehended?
Both the Buddha and sentient beings are unapprehendable. Huineng said: "Presently there are the thirty-two marks and the delivering of sentient beings;
how can you say they do not exist? Baizhang said: "All that has form is entirely illusory. If one sees all forms as non-form, then one sees [the Buddha]."
The Tathāgata. A man from Shishan asked Zen Master Guifeng: "All the sutras speak of delivering sentient beings.
Yet, sentient beings are themselves not sentient beings. Why then do you trouble yourself to deliver them? Guifeng replied:

[Duan]—these may be combined to serve as a commentary on this section of the sutra. Furthermore, when Master Nanyue Huisi was prompted by Master Zhigong to send a message to him, saying:

There are sentient beings to be saved. A verse on Original Awakening says: Gazing at the misty sky while reclining upon white clouds, One does not know that beneath the mountains lies the world of heaven and earth.
From where else could there be sentient beings to save? The Tathāgatas of the three periods of time have swallowed them all in a single mouth.
The Eulogy of Nianlin Ying says: "The Buddha swallows all sentient beings in a single mouth; not even a hair's breadth remains, and only then does the Way exist.
When the sun and moon are just raised upon the tip of the staff, the three thousand worlds are stirred and the seas and mountains grow dark. Such was the Great Master.
This is truly the dedication that transcends the marks of sentient beings. How could it be merely the realization of the stage of the iron wheel?
Destroying that which is destructible and remaining far removed from all forms of detachment is called the "indestructible dedication."
Tong said: "To destroy that which can be destroyed is to depart from the mark of sentient beings. To distance oneself from all forms of distancing is to depart even from the mark of departing.

When the mark is destroyed, that which is emptied is gone; when distancing is distanced, that which empties is gone. When both subject and object are empty, original enlightenment remains undestroyed;
therefore it is called 'undestroyed. The dedication is called 'undestroyed' in order to distinguish it from the stagnation of the two vehicles."
[This refers to] emptiness and the nihilistic view of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Although all marks (*lakṣaṇa*) are destroyed, that which is indestructible remains;
this is why it is called the "indestructible dedication" (*akṣaya-pariṇāmanā*). Master Zhen asked Master Benjing:

2. Zhen said: "The Buddha delivers sentient beings because he possesses a mind; the Way does not deliver people because it is without mind.

"Name. "The Way (Dharma) is also falsely established. Both are unreal; they are all merely provisional names.

One investigates and exhausts the mind that establishes [the path], yet that mind is also non-existent. Since both are unreal, one knows them to be like dreams and illusions, and thus awakens to their fundamental emptiness.

To forcibly establish the two names "Buddha" and "Path" is the perspective of the Two Vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas). Therefore, it is said that there is neither cultivation nor action, as expressed in this verse:

What is it that is cultivated? To universally observe those who cultivate the Way is like striking out at fire to seek bubbles;

one merely watches the manipulation of puppets, which cease all at once when the strings break. While the puppets may be destroyed, the one who manipulates the puppets cannot be destroyed. Thus, when the marks of sentient beings are destroyed, space is not destroyed;
it is not that there is something called "non-destruction" existing apart from the destruction of marks.
It is destroyed; yet, being destroyed, it is not destroyed. Therefore, it is called the "Non-Destructive Dedication.
Fundamental enlightenment is serene and profound; its awakening is equal to the awakening of the Buddhas. Therefore, it is called the "Dedication Equal to All Buddhas."

Tong said: "Phenomena may be destroyed, but that which knows destruction is indestructible. Separation may be abandoned, but that which knows separation is not abandoned. This is what is called primordial enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*).
To enter the profound stillness and merge with that stillness is both consciousness and wisdom; it may also be called 'profound stillness' (*zhanran*).
What is here termed 'the profound stillness of primordial enlightenment' is not the stillness of a state where consciousness does not waver. It is only this."

Fundamental enlightenment (mūla-bodhi) is not consciousness; therefore, it can equal the enlightenment of the Buddhas. All ordinary sentiments and sagely understandings are completely melted away, leaving only a single reality.
Thus, it can be equal to all Buddhas. Although it is equal to the enlightenment of all Buddhas, it is nonetheless not yet Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi);
there is still further dedication to be made and further progress to be pursued. Therefore, it is called "equal to all."
The Buddha’s dedication. Huangbo said: "A śrāvaka (voice-hearer) attains enlightenment by means of sound; therefore, they are called 'voice-hearers.
However, they do not understand their own minds, but instead give rise to understanding based on vocal teachings.

Whether through supernatural powers or auspicious signs, through speech and movement, they hear of bodhi and nirvāṇa, and spend three asaṃkhyeya kalpas cultivating the path to Buddhahood—all of these belong to [the category of voice-hearers]."
The path of the śrāvaka is called the Buddha of the śrāvakas. [The path of the Buddha] is simply to directly and suddenly realize that one’s own mind is fundamentally the Buddha;
there is not a single dharma to be attained, nor a single practice to be cultivated. This is the unsurpassed path; this is the Buddha of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
For those who study the Way, they fear only the arising of a single thought; as soon as it exists, one is separated from the Way. Moment after moment, remain without marks. Contemplate...
To contemplate non-action (*asaṃskṛta*) is itself to be a Buddha. A practitioner of the Way who wishes to attain Buddhahood need not study all the various teachings of the Buddhas;
they need only study non-seeking and non-attachment. Non-seeking means that the mind does not arise; non-attachment means that the mind does not cease.
This non-arising and non-ceasing is itself the Buddha. The eighty-four thousand dharma-gates correspond to the eighty-four [thousand afflictions].
The thousand afflictions (*kleśa*) are merely gates for teaching and guiding others; fundamentally, there are no dharmas whatsoever. To be detached is itself the Dharma;
one who knows detachment is a Buddha. Simply by being detached from all afflictions, there is no dharma to be attained.

By savoring Huangbo’s single phrase, "One who knows detachment is a Buddha," one realizes that which the sutras call "fundamental enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*), serene and profound, an awakening equal to the awakening of the Buddhas."
In such cases, the mind leaps forth of its own accord. Furthermore, Huichao questioned Fayan: "What is the Buddha? Fayan said: "You are Huichao.
A monk asked Shushan: "What is the Buddha? Shushan said: "Why do you not ask Old Man Shushan?"
There were many who answered in this manner. In sum, they were reminded that their original enlightenment is, in this very moment, equal to that of the Buddhas.
Through the refined and true illumination, the ground becomes like the ground of the Buddhas; this is called the dedication of merit to the "reaching of all places."
Tong said: "Fundamental awakening is pure and true; it is not merely that the spiritual luminosity is self-sustained.

It can further manifest and establish its functions, treading upon them to form the ground. This ground is like the Buddha-ground, which is vastly different from the initial stage of 'cultivating the ground' (bhūmi).
Where there is this essence of True Suchness (tathatā) pervading the Dharma-realm, there is also the function of True Suchness pervading the Dharma-realm."
Because the realms [of the Buddha] are such, the Buddha’s awakening pervades all places, and the Buddha’s practice likewise pervades all places.
That which does not pervade is not the ground of the Buddha. This [practice] merely conforms to that; it is not identical with the Buddha.
Therefore, it is called the "Dedication Reaching All Places. A monk asked Linji, "What is the land of the three eyes? Linji said:

Regarding the transformation [bodies], according to the masters of the sutras and śāstras, the *dharmakāya* is taken as the fundamental essence, while the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya* are its functions.
From my own perspective, the *dharmakāya* itself does not understand how to preach the Dharma. Thus, the ancients said: "The body is established based on meaning;

the land is discussed in terms of substance. It is clearly understood that the *dharmatākāya* and *dharmatābhūmi* are dharmas established through conventional designation (*prajñapti*). This is the general principle for all lands.
Earth. Empty fists and yellow leaves used to deceive small children. What juice can be found among thorns, brambles, and withered bones?
Outside the mind there are no phenomena; within, they are likewise unattainable. What object do you seek? Chan Master Tianyi Huai ascended the hall and said:

The worlds and the Tathāgatas interpenetrate one another without obstruction; this is called the Dedication of the Treasury of Inexhaustible Merit.

It is explained that "worlds" refers to the Dharma-realm of True Suchness (tathatā), which belongs to the objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga); "Tathāgatas" refers to the essential body (svabhāva-kāya) of True Suchness.
Belonging to the aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*), the seeing and the image aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*) originally share a single source.

Therefore, although the sense organs and their objects appear distinct, they can interpenetrate one another. By raising up the aspect of seeing, the image aspect is contained within it; by raising up the image aspect, the aspect of seeing is contained within it.
Thus, what is seen is nothing other than the image, and what is the image is nothing other than what is seen. Consequently, the world and the Tathāgata mutually interpenetrate.
Fundamentally there is no obstruction; yet that one cannot avoid obstruction is because their vision has not yet been fully integrated.
Now, when the essence of reality is brilliantly manifested, it reaches every place; yet even then, one still maintains dualistic views regarding all places. Now, these places mutually interpenetrate.
The ultimate purity is present in all places, and all places are themselves that ultimate purity. Mind and environment are fused together; neither obstructs the other.

Arisen compassion in myriad ways. The *liǎo* flowers bloom upon the ancient bank; white egrets stand on the sandy shore. Dewdrops fall upon the long court *shā* grass;

This world of the Tathāgata is entirely a single whole. To awaken and enter into this from hereon is called true liberation. By means of this merit, may [all beings] be received...
They lead sentient beings; as the worlds are inexhaustible, their merits are likewise inexhaustible.

This is truly because the roots of goodness planted in former lives each accord with the inclinations of their respective natures. Although the goodness is the same...

Once the true roots have been established, all sentient beings of the ten directions are my own fundamental nature. Since this nature is perfectly accomplished, one does not lose sight of sentient beings;
this is called the dedication that accords with the equal contemplation of all sentient beings.

The Master said: "As for 'roots of goodness,' these are the roots of goodness possessed by each individual. By relying on these roots of goodness to take the path to Nirvana, the roots of goodness are transformed into true roots.
There is no specific goodness to be pointed out; there is only the single Reality.

This true nature is perfectly interfused and pervades the entire Dharma-realm. Therefore, the sentient beings of the ten directions are all my own original nature. Since this original nature is already perfect,"
Self-perfection is called "roundness" (*pariniṣpanna*). It does not prevent the convergence of sentient beings into a single essence, nor does it lose the characteristics of sentient beings.
While sentient beings may not each individually achieve perfection, my own nature is perfectly complete; there is not a single sentient being who is not Buddha-nature.
Therefore, because this nature is perfectly accomplished, not a single sentient being is ever neglected or lost. This...

To accord with and impartially contemplate all sentient beings means that regardless of whether they are humans or animals, good or evil—even down to the most minute crawling creatures—all possess Buddha-nature.
This is not merely a matter of following along with roots of goodness through equanimity;
it is as when the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging encountered people and would bow to them, saying: "I do not dare to slight you. You shall all surely [attain Buddhahood]."
"Attaining Buddhahood" perfectly accords with this intent. Master Yuyang of King Aśoka’s Monastery ascended the hall and said:

"The entire earth is the eye of the śramaṇa; throughout the ten directions is one's own light. Why is it that when the drum is beaten in Pūrvavideha in the east, it is not heard in Aparagoyānī in the west?

It is further said: "The previous statement that 'all dharmas are free from all marks' means that while within the marks, one is detached from the marks; yet there still remains..."

The characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa) remain present here; this is what is meant by "all phenomena are devoid of all characteristics. Within phenomena, one is detached from phenomena, and together with those characteristics of phenomena, they are forgotten.

When both of these are absent and every trace is utterly exhausted, there remains only the One.
The true essence is suchness, immovable; this is called the characteristic of true thusness (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa*).

One must not speak of it simultaneously in terms of characteristics, the characteristics of phenomena, or the negation of the characteristics of phenomena. When it is said to be "detached from all characteristics," the detachment from the characteristics of sentient beings is what is intended as profound.

The cognitive obstacles are purified, and true nature manifests before one. It comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; it is fundamentally suchness (*tathatā*). Therefore, it is called "True Suchness" (*bhūtatathatā*).
Master Yuyang Yu ascended the hall and said: "When walking, there are no traces of walking; when speaking, there are no footprints of speech.

Severed. Even if one says there is no leakage and one's conduct does not lose its direction, one still remains stuck within the shell of the outflows.

"Stepping beyond divisions, there is nothing; in every moment and every atom lies the essential ford. These words may be said to have captured the very marrow of True Suchness (Tathatā).
By attaining liberation herein, one immediately accords with Suchness (Tathatā).
Truly attaining that which accords with suchness (tathatā), one is unimpeded throughout the ten directions;
this is called the dedication of liberation without bondage. It is said in general: to be far removed from all marks and to be solely true suchness is what is meant by "unbound.
If there remains even the mark of suchness, one is still bound by that which is not bound; one has not yet attained non-obstruction, and thus it is not yet true liberation. True...
One who attains suchness abides in suchness; there is no further obstruction. One should then forget even the characteristic of true suchness.
Initially, one eliminates attachment to phenomena, which is called liberation from bondage. Now, one eliminates attachment to non-phenomena, which is called liberation without bondage.
Since there is no bondage and one is already liberated, what further bondage could there be? As there is nothing to bind, where could one go that would not be suchness?
This state of unimpededness throughout the ten directions cannot be discussed by anyone who has not attained that which is the most authentic within True Suchness (tathatā).
Formerly, when Luopo was first serving as Linji’s attendant, Linji often praised him before the assembly, saying:
"A single arrow from the gate of Linji—dare any man face its point? Luopo considered himself sufficient and took his leave to travel south. Linji said:
In the lineage of Linji, there was a red carp that shook its head and wagged its tail as it headed south;
one knows not in whose pickle jar it will be drowned. Having finished his travels, Pu went straight to Jia Shan and pitched a hermitage there.
For years he had not visited Jia Shan. Jia Shan then composed a letter and ordered a monk to carry it there. When the monk arrived at the ferry crossing, Pu received him and sat down immediately.
He extended his hand again to ask for the letter, but the monk had no reply. Pu struck him and said, "Go back and report this to the Master.
The monk returned and reported it to Jia Shan. Jia Shan said, "If that monk had opened the letter, he would surely have come within three days. If not..."
He opened the letter and said, "This man cannot be saved. Three days later, Pu arrived and saw Jia Shan;
he did not prostrate but stood facing him directly. Jia Shan said, "A rooster nesting in a phoenix's den—it is not its kind. Get out! Pu replied:
Having traveled from afar to seek the Way, he requested an audience with the Master. The Master said, "Before my eyes there is no *śrāmaṇera*;

Indeed, he was drowned in the pickle jar of Jia Shan. Touzi took up the case and said:
