The first two lines eulogize the severing of the tongues of all people under heaven, wherein the place of concealment leaves no trace.
This is the essential point. The latter two lines praise the "tongueless person who understands speech" and capture the meaning of "do not hide yourself where there are no traces.
Both the Great and Small Luopu attained only a single peg and were already exposed by Linji;
had they not encountered Jia Shan, they would have been nearly bound by their own lack of bondage for the rest of their lives.
The inherent virtues are perfectly accomplished, and the limits of the *dharmadhātu* are extinguished; this is called the "Infinite Dedication of the *Dharmadhātu*.
Generally speaking, from the nature of *tathatā*, the functioning of virtue is initiated; the three virtues of wisdom (*jñāna*), principle (*li*), and practice (*xing*) are all perfected.

Principle and phenomena are unimpeded; both emptiness and existence are transcended. The single nature is completely integrated, leaving no further traces. As previously stated, it reaches "all things" (*sarvatra*).

If one still harbors the view of finite quantity, then the nature of the *dharmadhātu* has not yet transcended limitation. Now, because the measure of the *dharmadhātu* has ceased, it is called "immeasurable.

[Zhang] said: "The *Avataṃsaka* is the realm of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Principle and phenomena are entirely real; there is not the slightest trace of artificiality. Therefore, within the one, there are the myriad. He realized this.
"Ten thousand become one; one returns to one; ten thousand return to ten thousand. Vast and boundless, it cannot be exhausted. Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction.
To roll up or to unroll is sovereign; there is no obstruction, all is perfectly interfused. Although this is the ultimate principle, it is still, in the end, merely ripples on a windless sea.

only when the measure of the dharma-realm ceases is it appropriate to speak of Chan. "What is the Buddha? A dried piece of dung. "What is the Buddha?"

Even such a profound discourse cannot fully exhaust its underlying meaning. Through these ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*)—dedicating the ultimate toward the conventional, and dedicating the dedication toward compassion—one brings the ultimate and the conventional into perfect fusion, such that wisdom and compassion are non-dual.
Upon reaching this point, all limited conceptual views have been completely sublimated; only then can one ascend to the stages (*bhūmi*) and realize the fruit of a Bodhisattva.
Ānanda, these sons of good family have fully perfected the forty-one pure minds. Next, they accomplish the four kinds of wondrous and perfect preparatory practices (*prayoga*).
Taking the Buddha’s awakening as their own mind, though it has not yet emerged, it is like drilling wood for fire;
desiring to ignite the wood, this is called the Stage of Heat (*uṣmagata*).

The Master said: "Regarding the forty-one stages of mind mentioned above—from the stage of Dry Wisdom up to the Ten Dedications—one gradually cultivates and refines them, gradually expanding and broadening them, and purifying mundane sentiments until they reach the utmost purity. Upon reaching this level, one must not employ supernatural powers to stimulate thought, nor can transformation assist in forced growth; one must simply move with ease and grace."
One simply waits for it to arrive of its own accord. The World-Honored One cultivated practice over many kalpas and thoroughly illuminated the profound mysteries;

yet, regarding these four kinds of wondrously perfect preparatory practices (*prayoga*), there truly exist these four stages in the interval between what is about to be accomplished and what has not yet been accomplished.

Thus far, one has not yet been able to employ it. When it is finally employed as one's own mind, it cannot be grasped or manipulated; it is like drilling wood to produce fire:

before the wood has even begun to glow, this stage is called "Warmth" (*uṣmagata*). The emergence of fire is without intentionality; once the drilling has continued long enough, the wood ignites spontaneously.

Likewise, the application of awakening is without deliberate effort; once meditative concentration (*samādhi*) has persisted for a long time, wisdom (*prajñā*) manifests naturally. This is not something that can be achieved through human exertion alone.
During that interval, Chuiyan Zhen ascended the hall and cited the verse of Longya: "Studying the Way is like drilling for fire:

Furthermore, one takes one's own mind as the path trodden by the Buddhas. Whether relying or not relying [on external conditions], it is like climbing a high mountain: the body enters into empty space.
Below this, there is a subtle obstruction, which is called the "Stage of the Summit" (mūrdhan-bhūmi).
It is said in general that one’s state of vision is no different from that of a Buddha; yet, it is still essential that one’s practice be commensurate with that vision.

Thus, one can take the awakening of a Buddha and employ it as one's own mind, and immediately, by means of one's own mind, realize what the Buddha has traversed. This is spoken of in terms of mutual interpenetration.

This is because the perception of the Buddha and the perception of oneself still persist. Therefore, whether one relies [on the Buddha] or does not rely [on him], if one perceives the Buddha, it is as if one relies on the Buddha;

One is about to enter spiritual transformation (*shenhua*), yet the slightest trace has not yet been dissolved; thus, there appears to be an obstruction.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* Sūtra regards attachment to the space-like *dharmakāya* as a "fall from the summit" (*dingduo*); this is precisely of the same category. A monk asked Zhaozhou, "What is the Wondrous Peak?"
Guḍi said, "I, an old monk, will not answer this question of yours. The monk asked, "Why do you not answer this question?
Guḍi said, "If I were to answer you, I fear it would fall into the level ground. How profound! He has answered clearly.
Later, when Baofu and Changqing were traveling through the mountains, Baofu pointed with his finger and said, "Right here..."
"This is the summit of Mount Miaofeng. Qingyun said, "That is so; it is truly a pity.

How many people know that this skull lies upon the ground? Master Sun is truly to be pitied; I fear he has fallen onto level ground.

Abiding thus, what further obstacle could there be? Even if one were to fall from the summit, there would be no affliction; how much less so on level ground?

Ānanda, these sons of good family have attained excellent penetration into great bodhi; their awakening penetrates that of the Tathāgatas and they exhaust the realm of the Buddhas—this is called the Stage of Joy (pramuditā-bhūmi).
Tong said: "What is called 'Great Bodhi' is the upward path that concerns the very life-vein of all Buddhas.
To attain penetration here is to achieve great enlightenment; to see that all marks are non-marks is to see the Tathāgata.
Having seen the Tathāgata, one is able to exhaustively realize the Buddha-realm. As for the Buddha-realm, only a Buddha and a Buddha can fully fathom it."
This is an inconceivable realm. To characterize it through the perfect fusion of the three truths (*trīṇi satyāni*) is still not exhaustive.

The preceding "Practice of Joy" is fully endowed with immeasurable sublime virtues and accords with the ten directions by means of its merit.

to awaken is for ice to form. To neither move nor awaken is to remain in stagnant water.
Setting aside for a moment the fact that the Elder of Jianfu could not show his head, how will Yuyang act today? He says: "Do not travel the path beneath the mountain. Indeed.
Yet the cry of the monkey is a sound that breaks one's heart; this is the Immovable Ground (Acalā-bhūmi). One must personally arrive there once before it can be attained.
Otherwise, how could one avoid sitting in stagnant water and making a living there?
The manifestation of the function of True Suchness is called the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*Sādhumatī-bhūmi*).

Ānanda, from this point onward, these Bodhisattvas complete their cultivation and their merit becomes perfected; therefore, this stage is also designated as the "Stage of Cultivation" (*bhāvanā-avasthā*).

Tong said: "From the mind of True Suchness, the function of True Suchness is manifested—namely, the teacherless wisdom, the spontaneous wisdom, the all-encompassing wisdom, and the four unhindered wisdoms—which expound immeasurable asankhyeya phrases and meanings without ever reaching exhaustion."

He acts as a great Dharma Master, universally delivering all classes of beings. Because he unifies wisdom and compassion, responding to the times and harmonizing with the seasons, he is called "Excellent Wisdom" (Sudhī).
Whereas the preceding stage of "Blazing Wisdom" (Arciṣmatī) refers only to one's own radiance, this present "Excellent Wisdom" refers to both wholesome dharmas and other persons.
This reveals the function of its wisdom; therefore, it is not the same [as the preceding stages].

Why is this stage, which from the Far-Reaching Ground (*dūramgamā-bhūmi*) until before the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*), has already realized the path of effortless (*anābhoga*) quiescence, still designated as the "Stage of Cultivation" (*bhāvanā-avasthā*)?
It is simply because, when measured against the perfection of the merits of the ten grounds, it is slightly deficient in its degree; thus, this stage is designated as "cultivation."

The Stage of Practice (*śikṣā-bhūmi*). This refers to the initial application of wisdom; though one has not yet forgotten wisdom, one perceives the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmamegha*) as all-pervasive, without deficiency or excess, as if there were still some interval remaining.

Furthermore, this is practicing without practice and training without training, for it is like a boat about to reach the shore where oars and paddles are no longer employed, yet it continues to move forward. One day while lying down, Yangshan dreamed that he entered...
In the inner courtyard of Maitreya’s residence, within the assembly hall, all the seats were occupied except for the second one.
Yang ascended and took his seat. A venerable elder struck the gavel and announced: "Now, the one in the second seat shall preach the Dharma. Yang rose and struck the gavel, saying:
"The Mahāyāna Dharma transcends the four propositions and cuts off the hundred negations. Listen closely, listen closely! Thereupon, the entire assembly dispersed.
Upon awakening, he recounted this to Guishan. Guishan said, "You have already entered the rank of the sages.

Yang bowed in reverence. Tiantong’s verse says: In a dream, wearing his patched robe, he visited the elders; The assembly of sages sat solemnly to his right. When it was time to act, he did not yield as the *gandi* resounded;
He preached the Dharma with fearlessness, like the lion’s roar. His mind is as calm as the ocean; His capacity is as vast as a bushel.
The shark’s eyes shed tears; the oyster’s bowels yield its pearl. Who knows that delirious speech betrays my secret? The man with the bushy eyebrows must surely laugh at the family’s ugliness.
Transcending the four propositions, cutting off the hundred negations—the Master Ma and his son have had their illness cured;

there is no need for further medicine. This was Yangshan manifesting the function of True Suchness within a dream; what need is there for cultivation? Guishan personally served as witness—truly it is so.
The stage of the person (*pudgala*) has already been revealed; it is unnecessary to speak further of the stage of faith (*śraddhā*).
The wondrous cloud of the compassionate shade covers the ocean of *nirvāṇa*; this is called the Stage of the Dharma-Cloud (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*).
It is said that the function of wisdom is perfected, such that there is no longer any self-interest, but only the benefit of others; therefore, it is the shade of great compassion.
It fills the Dharma-realm; though without mind and without conditions, it responds to those minds and conditions to perform acts of benefit.

Yet its essence is fundamentally quiescent and without action, like clouds that emerge without intention to cover all things—this is called the "Wondrous Cloud," which is the wondrous clarity of the nature-awareness.
Compassion is inherently wondrous and does not depend on cultivation; thus it is said to cover the ocean of Nirvana.

This is the self-nature of *nirvāṇa*, which is fundamentally without arising or ceasing. The ocean of enlightenment and the clouds of compassion arise in accordance with this nature, and they likewise have no arising or ceasing.
All sentient beings abide within *nirvāṇa*; yet, one causes those very sentient beings to realize the fruit of *nirvāṇa*.
Thus providing shelter and thus providing cover, without deficiency and without remainder—it is only then that it may be called "wondrous. This is the Dharma.
To use a metaphor of clouds: the Dharma is fundamentally without mind. When clouds are linked to the Dharma, then the cloud is the Dharma.
Therefore, one does not speak of the function of wisdom but speaks only of clouds; this is because they have already become indistinguishably one with the Creator, and no dualistic views are formed.

This Ground of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*) borders upon the ground of the Buddha; it is called the stage of the consecrated Bodhisattva (*abhiṣeka*). The Sixth Patriarch addressed the assembly, saying:

"Good friends, if you wish to enter the profound realm of reality (*dharmadhātu*) and the samādhi of Prajñā, you must cultivate the practice of Prajñā and recite the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
You will then immediately realize your own nature. You should know the merit of this sutra."
It is immeasurable and boundless; it is clearly praised in the sutras, though one cannot fully describe it. This Dharma-gate is the Supreme Vehicle;
it is taught for those of great wisdom and for those of superior faculties. If people of small faculties and small wisdom hear it, they will give rise to disbelief. Why is this?
It is, for example, like a great dragon sending down rain upon Jambudvīpa, over its cities and villages...
They fall and all drift away like scattered blades of grass. Yet, if it rains upon the great ocean, it neither increases nor decreases.
So it is with those of the Mahāyāna or the Supreme Vehicle: when they hear the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, their minds open and they attain awakening.

Thus they know that the nature of their own being inherently possesses the wisdom of *prajñā*; because they constantly employ this wisdom for contemplation and illumination, they do not rely on words and letters.

It is like rainwater, which does not originate from the heavens; it is originally brought forth by the dragon, causing all sentient beings, all grasses and trees, and all things animate and inanimate to receive its moisture.
The myriad rivers and streams then flow back into the great ocean, merging into a single entity.
The nature of the wisdom of *prajñā* within the fundamental nature of sentient beings is also like this. One who knows this well—
Consciousness. A person of small capacity, upon hearing this teaching of sudden enlightenment, is like grasses and trees with small root-natures;
when struck by heavy rain, they all collapse of their own accord and cannot grow. A person of small capacity is also like this:
originally possessing the wisdom of *prajñā*, they are no different from those of great wisdom. For what reason, upon hearing the Dharma, do they not [realize it for themselves]?
Awakening. Because the obstacles of false views are heavy and the roots of affliction are deep, it is like a great cloud covering the sun;
if the wind does not blow, the sunlight will not appear. The wisdom of *prajñā* has neither small nor large dimensions;

it is because the minds of all sentient beings differ in their delusion and awakening that they perceive objects externally through a deluded mind, practicing cultivation to seek a Buddha without realizing their own nature.

"Nature" refers to the small capacity. If one awakens to the Sudden Teaching, does not cling to external cultivation, but constantly gives rise to right view within one's own mind, then afflictions and worldly toil can never defile them; this is seeing one's nature.

O Good Friends, when one dwells neither in the internal nor the external, coming and going with freedom, able to eliminate the clinging mind and attain unobstructed penetration—this is the practice that can be cultivated.

It is fundamentally no different from the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras. Although the Sixth Patriarch could not recognize a single character, he preached the Dharma like clouds and rain, and was moreover able to discern the differences between the great and small capacities of those who heard the Dharma;
this alone is sufficient to supplement what was not yet fully prepared in the Ten Stages.

The Tathāgata flows against the current; the Bodhisattva likewise proceeds along it until he reaches the point where awakening and its limit intersect—this is called Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*).
Ānanda, from the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*) up to Equal Enlightenment, this awakening first attains the initial stage of Dry Wisdom within the Diamond Mind (*vajra-citta*).

Tong said: "The expedient wisdom of the Tathāgata descends according to the karmic responses of beings; thus it flows against the current and emerges. The ultimate wisdom of the Bodhisattva ascends to accord with the awakened mind;

thus it flows with the current and enters. As the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* (Yingluo jing) states: 'Equal Enlightenment is illumination within stillness; Sublime Enlightenment is stillness within illumination. This is precisely its meaning.
Because this occurs at the juncture between the two enlightenments, it is called 'entering the intersection' (*rujiao*). What is meant by 'entering the intersection' is..."

One connects with the Dharma-stream of the Tathāgata. At this stage, it is called the Stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), meaning that one’s awakening is equal to that of the Tathāgata without distinction;
it is simply that one has not yet reached the ultimate subtlety.

One must flow against the current from the great ocean of quiescent extinction (*mahā-śānti-nirvāṇa*), becoming subtly identical with all phenomena, and only then is it "Sublime Awakening" (*miao-jue*). Within the Vajra-mind, this is the initial stage of Dry Wisdom (*khan-hui*).
The Ground (*bhūmi*) is precisely the aforementioned mind of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*). Why is it that one only attains it at this point?

Previously, before connecting with the flow of the Dharma, one perceived its essence through emptiness; now, having connected with the flow of the Dharma, one finally treads upon its reality. It is like the first appearance of the moon:
its luminous, circular form is already faintly revealed, yet it was not originally deficient. Subsequently, as it reaches the crescent and then the full moon, it merely fulfills its measure.
It is merely the *maṇḍala* (perfect circle) seen at the initial stage; it is not that there are two [distinct] things.
As for what is called "Vajra," it is so named because it destroys all phenomena (*dharma*). While all phenomena are subject to destruction, this Vajra-wisdom alone is indestructible.

In the former stage, the habit-energies (*vāsanā*) have just begun to dry up, and it consists purely of wisdom. Since wisdom is non-dual, it is simply that the drying process has not yet been completed. This is already [the case] at the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*).
Previously, by destroying one stage with another stage until not a single dharma can be apprehended, it is said: "This awakening first attains the initial stage of Dry Wisdom within the Vajra Mind.
As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "The initial aspiration and the ultimate goal are not two different things."
Is this not what is meant by that? A monk asked Huangbo, "If the mind is fundamentally the Buddha, does one still cultivate the six perfections and myriad practices?
Huangbo said, "Awakening resides in the mind; it has no concern with the six perfections or the myriad practices. As for the six perfections and the myriad practices..."
All these are gates of transformation; they are merely peripheral matters for receiving beings and delivering sentient beings.

Even such things as Bodhi, True Suchness, the Ultimate Reality, Liberation, and the Dharma-body, extending all the way to the noble stages of the ten bhūmis and the four fruits—these are all gates of deliverance and have no bearing on the Buddha-mind.
The mind is itself the Buddha. Therefore, among all the gates of the various *pāramitās*, the Buddha-mind is foremost.

If one is free from the mind of birth-and-death, afflictions, and the like, then there is no need for dharmas such as *bodhi*. Thus it is said: "The Buddha preaches all dharmas to deliver my various minds;
since I have no various minds, what use have I for all dharmas? From the Buddha...
The Patriarchs did not discuss other matters, but spoke only of the one mind; this is also called the One Vehicle.

Therefore, though one searches throughout the ten directions with utmost sincerity, no other vehicle exists. This assembly has no branches or leaves, but consists only of the ultimate reality. For this reason, this meaning is difficult to believe.
Since Bodhidharma came to this land and reached the two kingdoms of Liang and Wei, there was only Master Ke as one who truly understood it.
Confidently trust your own mind. Upon hearing these words, one immediately realizes that this very mind is Buddha.
When both body and mind are non-existent, this is called the Great Way. The Great Way is fundamentally equal; therefore, one has deep faith that all living beings share the same true nature.
The nature of the mind is not different [from the true nature]; nature is itself mind, and mind is not different from nature—this is called the Patriarch. Thus it is said: "Recognize..."
At the moment of the nature of mind, it may be described as inconceivable; this very mind is not different from its nature, and is thus named the Patriarch.
One can visualize the scene where the realm of thought and awakening intersect; from the preceding stages, there is no interference whatsoever.
There is simply the one mind, which is no different from the Buddha.
In this manner, through these successive layers of single and double stages—twelve in total—one exhaustively realizes wondrous enlightenment and accomplishes the Unsurpassed Way.

It is generally said that there are seven single stages, namely: Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*), Heat (*uṣmagata*), Peak (*mūrdhan*), Patience (*kṣānti*), the Supreme Worldly Dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*), Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), and Wondrous Enlightenment (*vibuddha*).

There are five double stages, namely: Faith (*śraddhā*), Abiding (*sthiti*), Practice (*caryā*), Direction (*mukha*), and Ground (*bhūmi*). Since each stage is further layered to form ten sub-stages, [the total becomes twelve].

It is called "repetition. Thus, through these successive layers, one gradually cultivates and gradually realizes, totaling twelve stages before reaching the stage of Subtle Enlightenment (*sūkṣma-bodhi*) and accomplishing the Unsurpassed Way.
Yet, even the Stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaṅ-bodhi*) remains at the eleventh stage; therefore, it has not yet reached the ultimate within Subtle Enlightenment.

Only upon reaching the twelfth stage does one reach the ultimate. How could this Subtle [Enlightenment] possibly add anything to the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*)? It is simply that very Dry Wisdom.
Wisdom polishes and refines it until it is pure, thereby manifesting its wondrous nature. The *Compendium* states:

"The Tathāgatas of the three periods of time have transmitted to all Bodhisattvas the methods for cultivation and realization. They have weighed the depth and shallowness of their capacities and functions, and distinguished the gradations of the stages, beginning from the Ten Faiths.
However, because that which constitutes 'faith' still belongs to the realm of arising and ceasing, one must then abide in the [Ten] Minds."

The Ten Abodes (*daśa-vihāra*) are established. Furthermore, because those who abide [in the abodes] lack the function of generating the means (*upāya*) for practice, the mind of practice (*caryā-citta*) is formed, and thus the Ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*) are established.

Furthermore, because those who practice are merely seeking their own benefit and have not yet reached the level of benefiting sentient beings, there is the dedication of merit (*pariṇāmana*), and thus the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmana*) are established.
From the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) up to the Abodes, Practices, and Dedications constitutes the three stages.

This is the stage of the Three Sages (*tri-vidyā*). Furthermore, from these three sages, one immediately ascends to the First Ground (*prathamā bhūmi*). Through great compassion (*mahāmaitrī-karuṇā*), one brings about its generation, sustenance, flourishing, and fulfillment;
thus, it receives the name "Ground" (*bhūmi*). It is only at the First Ground that one is said to realize the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

This continues until the end of the Tenth Ground, where the effects of refining residual habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) become manifest, harmonizing with original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*) and true suchness (*tathatā*).
...and so forth; thus it is called "Equal Enlightenment" (*Samyaksambodhi*). This is like what the *I Ching* says regarding "exhausting the spirit and knowing transformation.
Upon reaching "Subtle Enlightenment" (*Sūkṣmasambodhi*), there is only oneness, and no characteristics of equality remain—just as one simply speaks of "the spirit" (*shen*).

This sutra is particularly distinct in that it adds the stage of "Dry Wisdom" (*Śuṣka-prajñā-bhūmi*) before the ten levels of faith, and adds the stages of "Heat," "Summit," "Patience," and "Supreme Worldly Dharma" (*Uṣmagata*, *Mūrdhan*, *Kṣānti*, *Laikāgra-dharma*) before the ten bhūmis. [The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*...]

In the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, it is said that one realizes the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) at the tenth stage (*bhūmi*). In various other sūtras, it is said that one realizes the patience of the non-arising of dharmas at the tenth stage;
yet this still remains within the count of fifty-five [stages]. Here, the World-Honored One establishes three gradual stages for the realization of the patience of the non-arising of dharmas.
These three gradual stages are established as skillful means (*upāya*) and thus do not appear within the count of fifty-five.
Beyond this, the World-Honored One’s intention was likely to demonstrate that the dharma capable of being truly realized exists even within ordinary beings.
Huangbo said to Xiu: "The Buddha and sentient beings are no different from one another. It is only because sentient beings cling to appearances and seek outwardly that they lose more as they seek.
To cause a Buddha to search for a Buddha, or to use the mind to grasp the mind—even through the exhaustion of kalpas or the end of one's life—one will ultimately [find nothing]."
One cannot attain it by seeking. When one does not know how to cultivate mindfulness of breathing and forgets all discursive thoughts, the Buddha manifests before one's very eyes.
This mind is itself the Buddha; the Buddha is itself sentient beings. When acting as a sentient being, this mind does not diminish; when manifesting as all Buddhas, this mind does not increase.
Even the six perfections and the myriad practices, as well as the merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, are inherently complete from the beginning, requiring no cultivation or addition.
When conditions arise, one acts; when conditions subside, one rests in stillness.

If one does not resolutely believe that this very mind is the Buddha, yet desires to practice by clinging to signs in order to seek some spiritual efficacy, all such efforts are mere delusions and run counter to the Way.
This mind is itself the Buddha; there is no other Buddha apart from it, nor is there any other mind apart from it. This mind is luminous and pure, just like empty space, without a single [dharma]...

To give rise to marks—whether by lifting the mind or stirring a thought—is to deviate from the essence of the Dharma; it is to be attached to marks. Since beginningless time, there has been no Buddha who was attached to marks.
To cultivate the six perfections and myriad practices with the desire to seek Buddhahood is merely a gradual process.
Since beginningless time, there has been no Buddha who followed a gradual process; one simply awakens to the One Mind, wherein not even the slightest dharma can be obtained. This is the truth.
The Buddha and sentient beings are of one mind without distinction, like empty space—unmixed and indestructible.
Like the great sun-disk illuminating the four continents, when the sun rises, its light pervades the world, yet empty space itself was never made bright.
When the sun sets, darkness pervades the world, yet empty space has never been dark.
The realms of light and darkness contend with one another, while the nature of empty space remains vast and unchanging. The minds of Buddhas and sentient beings are also like this:
if one contemplates the Buddha as having the marks of pure radiance and liberation, and contemplates sentient beings as being defiled, turbid, and obscure.

Regarding the characteristics of birth and death: one who forms such interpretations will, even after passing through kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, never attain Bodhi, because they remain attached to signs.
This single mind alone—there is not so much as a speck of dust’s worth of a dharma to be obtained—is itself the Buddha.
How wondrous, how wondrous! Were it not for Huangbo’s own realization of wondrous enlightenment, falling neither into stages nor levels, how could he have been so profoundly clear and lucid?
Having attained this teaching, one should preserve it; thus, the principles of the Perfect and Sudden [teachings] of this sutra will not obstruct one another.
These various stages all employ the ten profound metaphors for observing things as being like illusions through the diamond-like [wisdom], within the state of *śamatha*.
(What is here called "stopping") employs the *vipaśyanā* (what is here called "contemplation") of all Tathāgatas. Through pure cultivation and realization, one gradually enters deeper and deeper.
Ānanda, it is by means of these three progressive advancements that one is well able to accomplish the fifty-five stages of the true path to Bodhi.
One who practices this contemplation is said to practice right contemplation; if one contemplates otherwise, it is called wrong contemplation.
The Master said: "Regarding the ten kinds of profound metaphors: one should contemplate all karma as an illusion;
all phenomena as a mirage; all natures as the moon reflected in water; exquisite forms as space; exquisite sounds as an echo;
the buddha-fields as a city of the gandharvas; the buddha-activities as a dream; the buddha-body as a shadow; the reward body as a statue; and the dharma-body [as the nature of reality itself]."
It is like a magical illusion; it cannot be grasped or discarded because all things are empty. To penetrate deeply into this emptiness is what is called the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
This is not a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛtadharma*), for it is devoid of destruction or decay. If one views it otherwise, it is merely a phenomenon subject to arising and ceasing.

Thus, one contemplates not only conditioned phenomena as being like dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows, but even the Buddha’s *dharmakāya* is likewise viewed as being like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, and a shadow.
Therefore, it serves as a profound metaphor. Observing in this manner cannot be compared to the contemplative methods of the Lesser Vehicle;
rather, it is the wondrous discerning wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) of all Tathāgatas, endowed with adamantine insight. It illuminates through stillness and contemplates through cessation.

Like water that is utterly clear and untainted by even the slightest sediment, and like a mirror that is perfectly pure and admits not the faintest speck of dust—it is by means of this that one practices. One practices...
Yet there is no cultivation. It is by means of this that one realizes; yet in realization, there is nothing realized.

Therefore, from the stage of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*) one gradually penetrates deeper until reaching wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), never departing from this adamantine observation (*vajra-vipaśyanā*). Ground after ground is demolished, and dharma after dharma is dried up;
thus one is able to arise in union with wondrous enlightenment. Through such profound metaphors and such deep penetration, how could there be anything external?

Within the three stages of advancement, the stream of consciousness flows back entirely into oneness, thereby attaining the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

From this point, one gradually cultivates according to the practices initiated, establishing oneself in the noble stages (*ārya-bhūmi*). One is well able to accomplish the fifty-five true paths to Bodhi:
faith, abiding, practice, and direction constitute fifty; the stage of dry wisdom (*śukla-vipaśyanā*) and the four preparatory practices (*prayoga*) constitute five. Not...
Regarding the two stages of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and Wondrous Enlightenment (*vibuddha-bodhi*): these two enlightenments are true Bodhi;
they are the enlightenment itself, not the path. The fifty-five stages are the path by which one enters enlightenment.
All Tathāgatas of the ten directions who have attained Bodhi possess the wondrous *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna* as their initial expedient means. Up to the stage of Gold...
Upon close observation, the Illusion-like Samādhi (māyopama-samādhi) finds that Avalokiteśvara alone is supreme.

Thus, among the fifty-five stages of the path to Bodhi, it is through the three progressive stages of "reversing the flow and returning to the One" that one first begins the practice of "returning the hearing.
This "Illusion-like Observation" likewise culminates in the non-abiding of hearing, wherein both the perceiver and the perceived are realized as empty.

"Emptiness is that which is emptied; emptiness is extinction. This is the sequence for the cessation of arising and ceasing. One who practices this contemplation enters the single path to *nirvāṇa* of the Bhagavans of the ten directions.
If one contemplates otherwise, it does not possess the ten kinds of profound metaphors of diamond-like observation;
rather, it belongs to arising and ceasing and is therefore a false contemplation. The Tang monk Chengguan composed this while dwelling in the stage of the Earth.

The Verse on Cultivation and Realization says: "Cultivating the myriad practices as empty flowers, Sitting in meditation within a water-moon dharma-hall, Subduing the celestial Māras who are like mirror-images, One realizes the fruit of Buddhahood within a dream.
There are also briefly ten kinds of profound metaphors for this. At Mount Jia, when the Master ascended the hall, he said:
"Since the time of the Patriarchs, people have misunderstood [this teaching], and this error has been passed down to the present day. Regarding the words of the Buddhas and Patriarchs..."
This is a phrase. To act as a teacher and model for others, if one were to speak thus, one would become a madman or a person devoid of wisdom.
He merely points out to you that the non-existence of dharmas is itself the Way. The Way has not a single dharma;

there is no Buddha to be realized, no Way to be attained, no dharma to be grasped, and no dharma to be abandoned. Therefore, the old monk says: "Before one's eyes, there is no dharma. This is the meaning.
He is present before you, yet he is not a dharma of the present. If one seeks to learn from the Buddhas and Patriarchs, such a person has not yet attained the eye.
Why? Because they all belong to that which is relied upon and lack autonomy; it is fundamentally because of the vast, boundless expanse of birth and death.
The nature of consciousness has no autonomy. Whether traveling a thousand or ten thousand miles to seek a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), one must possess the correct eye;
one must seek liberation from erroneous views and definitively investigate whether the birth and death before one's eyes truly exist or truly do not exist.
If there is anyone who attains certainty, we grant you the opportunity to emerge from [delusion]. Those of superior capacity clarify the Way upon hearing a single word;
those of middling or inferior capacity wander in endless waves of confusion. Why not settle yourself within birth and death?
Where else could you seek a Buddha or an Ancestor to take over your birth and death for you? Wise people will laugh at you. If you do not understand, listen to another verse: [Verse follows]
Toiling in the maintenance of the laws of birth and death, one seeks only at the side of the Buddha. Yet, currently deluded regarding the correct principle, one beats out fire to search for a bubble.
This may serve as the definitive scale for distinguishing right contemplation from wrong contemplation.
At that time, Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What should this sutra be named? How should I and all sentient beings uphold it? The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"This sutra is named 'The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Śītavana-Bhadrā Anuttara-Ratnamudrā'."
The Pure Ocean-Eye of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions declared:
from the initial discernment of the real and the false, proclaiming the nature of the ultimate within the ultimate meaning as the section on the Path of Seeing;
from the "Royal Deva’s Flowered House" which requires entry through a gateway, to the selection of the twenty-five perfect penetrations, and so forth.
The upholding of the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa Divine Mantra constitutes the section on the cultivation of the path (mārgabhāga).

Furthermore, from the stage of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) up to the Great Parinirvāṇa, it provides a remote demonstration of the unsurpassed path of correct practice; this constitutes the section on the realization of the fruit (phalabhāga). Thus, the great purport of this single sūtra is complete.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī made this request on this account. Since he has requested the name of the sutra, it should immediately be upheld;
this constitutes the section on circulation (*parindanā*). Why would one exhaustively elaborate upon various aspects and then suddenly request the name?
It is because the fifty-five stages of the true path to Bodhi constitute the correct cause and correct fruit; it is only through failing to recognize the True Mind that confusion arises.
Because of such cultivation, there arise the revolving paths of the hells, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans, and devas.

At the moment of passing away, before warmth and sensation have been relinquished, the good and evil of one’s entire life manifest simultaneously. Death is contrary while birth is conformable; these two tendencies intersect.

When pure thought alone prevails, one immediately ascends and will certainly be born in the heavens. If within the mind of flight there is a combination of merit, wisdom, and pure vows, the mind will naturally open, and one will see the Buddhas of the ten directions and all the pure lands;
according to one's vows, one will be reborn therein. When worldly emotion is slight and thought is predominant, [one attains this state].

Rising lightly, they are not far from becoming flying immortals. As great-power ghost kings, flying yakṣas, and earth-walking rākṣasas, they roam through the four continents, moving without obstruction.
Among them, if there are those with virtuous vows and virtuous minds who protect and uphold my Dharma, [they shall attain this].

Some protect the prohibitive precepts, following those who uphold the precepts; some protect divine mantras, following those who recite mantras; some protect meditative concentration and preserve the patience of the Dharma.
These beings dwell intimately beneath the seat of the Tathāgata; their thoughts and perceptions are equanimous, neither soaring upward nor falling downward.

Those born among humans are intelligent when their thoughts are clear and dull when their emotions are deep. When emotion predominates and thought is scarce, they flow into the realm of horizontal birth;

the heavy become the fur-bearing beasts, and the light become the feathered tribes. When the seven emotions prevail over the three thoughts, they sink beneath the water-wheel and are born at the boundary of fire.

Receiving the fierce fire of their vital breath, they become hungry ghosts who are constantly burned; even water harms them, as they pass through hundreds of thousands of kalpas without food or drink.
With nine thoughts and one perception, they descend into the wheel of fire and enter the cavern of wind; at the intersection of these two, they pass through the earth.

Those who slight their lives fall into the *sāntara* hells; those who value their lives fall into the *avīci* hell. These two types of hells are for those whose emotions are purely defiled and who sink directly into the *Avīci* hell.

If they sink into the midst of the mind, it is because they have slandered the Mahāyāna, violated the Buddha’s prohibitions, spoken deceptive and false teachings, and vainly coveted offerings of faith.
Having unworthily received marks of respect, they will further be reborn in the Avīci Hell throughout the ten directions for the five heinous crimes and the ten grave offenses.
Although they have brought this upon themselves by following the commission of evil karma, within the commonality of sentient beings (nikāya-sabhāga), there is also a fundamental ground.

Tong said: "This is a general answer regarding whether these various realms of existence (gatis) are inherently present from the beginning, or whether they arise from the deluded habitual tendencies of sentient beings.
Based on the delusions of the seven realms—whether in heaven, hell, or the human world—their suffering and joy differ;
yet there is not one that does not have its own corresponding karma through which they are mutually formed. This is the original ground within the common lot (sabhāgatā), which cannot [be denied]."

That they are swept back into the state of no-root arises from the production of deluded habits. The nature of sentient beings is fundamentally true and pure, falling neither into the category of the holy nor the ordinary.
Yet, from the moment a fleeting emotional view arises, they fail to recognize it as delusion; they habituate themselves to this delusion and consequently do not abandon it.

That which arises from the physical body as a thought is a view and a habit; it resides within the constituent parts of the body. That which arises from mental formations as a thought is a view and a habit;
it resides outside the constituent parts of the body. Within the constituent parts of the body, it is caused by attachment and passion.
The mouth regarding flavors, the eyes regarding forms, and the mind regarding wealth can give rise to the water of craving. Since the nature of water is to flow downward, one falls because of this.

Beyond the physical body, through the attachment of thought and imagination—whether dwelling upon Buddha-lands, desiring birth in the heavens, or upholding wholesome dharmas—one can give rise to superior vital energy (*vāyu*).
Since the nature of this energy is to soar upward, one ascends because of this. When these thoughts are pure, then...
Those born above the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven who possess pure vows are reborn in the Pure Land. Those with the ninth visualization become flying immortals;
those with the eighth visualization become powerful ghost kings; those with the seventh visualization become flying yakṣas;

and those with the sixth visualization become earth-walking rākṣasas. Because their visualizations are superior, they encounter no obstacles wherever they go. Nevertheless, their mental states may be either deviant or correct. [The correct...]

Those who do not depart from beneath the seat of the Tathāgata—because they have maintained the precepts and recited mantras and served spiritual friends in their past lives—will ultimately become protectors of the Dharma.
If their emotional attachments are balanced, they will be born among humans. With six emotions, they become the fur-bearing beasts and winged fowl;
with seven emotions, they become hungry ghosts; with eight emotions, they are born in the *sāntara* hells; and with nine emotions, they are born in the *avīci* hell.
In the intermediate hells, those of purely emotional affliction sink directly into the Avīci Hell.
Even if this kalpa is destroyed, they are reborn in the Avīci Hells of the ten directions, with no time of escape. This is what they have invited upon themselves through their own deluded karma;
thus, there is a distinction between the pure and the turbid. If one can remain unattached to emotion, then the hells are empty. If one remains unattached to thought, then...
Heaven is empty; both emotion and thought are empty. Although one dwells among humans, the mind roams the Buddha-land.

Since the seven realms of existence have their fundamental ground, it is certain that the Pure Land also has its fundamental ground. Returning to the true, pure original nature of sentient beings—who would be born anywhere else if not in the Pure Land?
A monk asked Baizhang, "In the face of all objects, how does one attain the mind?"
It is like wood or stone moving away. [Zhao] said: "All dharmas fundamentally do not themselves say they are empty, nor do they say they are form;
they also do not speak of right or wrong, defilement or purity. Furthermore, there is no mind that binds people.

It is only that people themselves, through false and deluded conceptual attachment, produce various kinds of interpretations, give rise to various kinds of knowledge and views, and generate various kinds of craving and fear."
Simply understand that all phenomena do not arise from themselves; they exist only through one's own single thought of deluded, inverted grasping at signs.
Know that mind and objects fundamentally do not reach one another; they are liberated in their very place. Each and every phenomenon is quiescent in its own place;
each is a site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). Furthermore, this originally existing nature cannot be named or designated; it is, from the beginning, non-existent [as a substantial entity].
This is mundane, not sacred; it is neither defiled nor pure, nor is it empty or existent, nor is it good or evil.
When associated with various defiled dharmas, it is termed the realm of humans, devas, and the two vehicles. If the mind of defilement and purity is exhausted, one does not abide in bondage.

They do not abide in liberation. They are free from the mental constructs (*cittamātra*) of all conditioned and unconditioned bondage and liberation. Abiding within birth and death, their minds are sovereign;
they ultimately do not conjoin with the various delusions, false illusions, afflictions, aggregates, elements, or sense-bases of birth and death.
They are utterly detached and have no place of reliance; they are unrestrained by anything. Unimpeded in going and staying, they come and go through birth and death.
It is like the opening of a gate. Baizhang Daci, in his spontaneous and expansive exposition, darkly accords with the essential purport of this passage of the sutra.
If one can take full responsibility for this, then emotional conceptions will be instantly transcended and one will not fall into false views;
the Tathāgata will surely consider this most gratifying.
Ānanda, all of these are the results produced by the karma of those sentient beings themselves. They create ten habitual causes and undergo six types of reciprocal retribution.
What are the ten causes? Ānanda, first is the habit of sexual desire: through mutual friction it is aroused;
as this grinding continues without ceasing, a great and fierce fire is thereby ignited within. It is like a person using their own hands...
Through the act of touching and rubbing, the sign of heat manifests; as these two habits ignite one another, there arise such things as iron beds and copper pillars.

For this reason, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate sexual misconduct by the same name: the fire of desire. When Bodhisattvas perceive desire, they avoid it as they would a scorching furnace.
Second, the habit of greed involves mutual plotting that gives rise to mutual attraction; as this grasping and seizing never ceases, there is thus...
Amassed and obstructed by solid ice, one freezes within it. It is like a person drawing in cold air with the mouth, whereby a sensation of cold arises.
Because these two habits contend with one another, there occur such phenomena as the *ṭaṭa-ṭaṭa*, *pa-pa-ra-ra*, and the blue, red, and white lotus cold hells.
Therefore, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate excessive seeking with the same name: the "water of greed. When Bodhisattvas perceive greed, they avoid it as one would a miasmic sea.
Third, the habit of pride involves mutual disparagement, arising from mutual reliance; it flows on without ceasing.
Because of this, there is surging and rushing, where accumulated waves become water—just as when people use their mouths and tongues to savor flavors for one another, and because of that...

Water arises. Because these two habits strike against one another, there occur such phenomena as rivers of blood, rivers of ash, seas of hot sand and poison, and the swallowing of molten copper poured upon them.
Therefore, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions characterize pride as "drinking the water of delusion.

When Bodhisattvas encounter pride, they avoid it as they would a vast ocean. Fourth, the habit of anger clashes and conflicts; arising from mutual opposition, this resentment knots together without ceasing.

The mind’s fever gives rise to fire; it smelts the vital energy (*qi*) into metal. It is for this reason that there exist mountains of knives, iron spikes, sword-trees, wheel-blades, axes, halberds, spears, and saws.
Like a person harboring a grievance, the murderous breath flies and stirs; as these two habits strike one another, there arise all manner of punishments:
imprisonment, dismemberment, decapitation, hacking, mincing, piercing, and beating with mallets. For this reason, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate hatred as such.

Fame and profit are like swords and blades. When a bodhisattva sees anger, he avoids it as if fleeing execution. Fifth, the habit of deceitful association arises from mutual flattery and incites incessant entanglement;
thus, there exist such things as ropes, wooden stocks, shackles, and fetters. Just as water saturates a field so that grasses and trees grow, these two habits perpetuate one another;
therefore, there exist such matters as handcuffs, pillory, cangues, whips, staves, and clubs. For this reason:
All Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate deceit and falsehood as "the slanderous thief. When a Bodhisattva perceives fraud, they view it with the same dread as the appearance of a jackal.
Sixth, the habit of deception arises from mutual delusion; when such false deception does not cease, the mind becomes flighty and constructs wickedness.
Thus, there is dust, soil, excrement, urine, filth, and impurity. Just as dust follows the wind, none can see one another.
Because these two habits interact, there arise various occurrences such as drowning, being tossed about, flying, falling, drifting, and sinking.
For this reason, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions identify deception with the same name as "killing" (ghāta). When a Bodhisattva sees deception, they view it as treading upon a venomous snake.

Seventh, the habit-energy of enmity gives rise to mutual resentment, which issues from harbored hatred. Because of this, there are flying stones, thrown rocks, boxes, carriage-cages, jars, and sacks used for crushing;
it is like a person with hidden malice who nurtures evil within.

As these two habit-energies swallow one another, there arise various acts such as throwing, seizing, striking, shooting, tossing, and grasping. Therefore, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions characterize this as...
"Enemy" refers to the *vighna* (obstructing) spirits. When a Bodhisattva sees an enemy, it is like drinking poisoned wine.

Eighth, when the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) interact with clarity, it is like the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), the clinging to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and various karmas arising from false awakening. These give rise to opposition and produce contrary results.
For this reason, there are kings, messengers, officials, and legal documents for verification and execution; they are like travelers coming and going.

They meet one another; as their two habits intersect, there arise interrogations, deceptions, and cross-examinations, as well as investigations, inquiries, and thorough examinations that bring everything to light.
The children of good and evil hold registers in their hands to adjudicate all matters. Therefore, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate this evil view with the same name:
the Pit of Views. When Bodhisattvas encounter such pervasive clinging to falsehoods, it is as if they were standing on the brink [of an abyss].
The Chasm of Poison. Ninth is the habitual practice of calumny, which manifests as false accusations and slanders.
For this reason, there are mountains and stones joined together to crush, grind, plow, and rub [the offenders], just as slanderous thieves oppress and wrongfully persecute the virtuous.

Because these two habits clash with one another, there are various matters such as pressing down, hammering, squeezing, straining, and measuring. Therefore, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions characterize resentment and slander as [a source of suffering].

The same name, "Slanderous Tiger," refers to when a Bodhisattva is falsely accused; it is like encountering a thunderbolt. Tenth, the habit of litigation leads to mutual clamor, which arises from concealment and hiding.
For this reason, there is the mirror of insight that illuminates and shines forth, like being in the midst of the sun where one cannot hide one's shadow.

Because these two habits are presented together, there is the "Mirror of Karma" and the "Fire-Bead" for evil friends, which reveal past karma and provide verification through various matters. Therefore—

All Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate concealment by the same name: "the hidden thief. When a bodhisattva contemplates concealment, it is as if they were wearing a great mountain upon their head while treading upon a vast ocean.
Tong said: "The World-Honored One spoke of ten causes of habitual practice, each of which corresponds precisely to the events within the hells without the slightest discrepancy.
Habitual practice must have a cause; yet that which serves as the cause can only produce appearances such as water and fire, while lacking their actual function."
Furthermore, by combining what has been practiced, they cause the manifestation of such things as glowing hot iron and freezing ice.

However, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions clearly perceive all that is wholesome and unwholesome at the very moment it arises from its causes; thus, there is truly no need for them to practice. The Bodhisattvas clearly understand this to be harmful.
Therefore, one should remain reverently pure and refrain from transgressions, keeping far away from them. Even if hells exist, they would have no cause beforehand;
thus, it is fitting that only Buddhas and Bodhisattvas could say there are no hells. Without having attained such mental conduct, how can one empty all things?
Maitreya said: Within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are thirty-six places, namely the eight great...
Naraka (translated here as "hell"). What are the eight? First, Saṃjīva; second, Kālasūtra;
third, Saṃghāta; fourth, Raurava; fifth, Mahāraurava; sixth, Tapana; seventh, Pratāpana; eighth, Avīci.
These great narakas are each ten thousand yojanas (translated here as forty *li*) in extent. Beyond these, there are further eight cold hells.
The abodes of the hells (*naraka*). What are the eight? First, Arbuda; second, Nirarbuda; third, Aṭaṭa; fourth, Hahava; fifth, Huhuva; sixth, Utpala;
seventh, Padma; eighth, Mahāpadma. From here, thirty-two thousand *yojana*s downward, one reaches Saṃjīva.
From there, separated again by four thousand *yojana*s, there are others.
Regarding the *naraka*s: just as it is in the great *naraka* location of Saṃjīva, so it is in the first cold *naraka* location.
From this, at a distance of another two thousand *yojana*s, there are further *naraka*s.
Furthermore, it is said that within the great *naraka* of Saṃjīva, sentient beings mostly undergo such extremely punitive suffering; that is to say, those sentient beings mostly [suffer] together.
Driven by the predominance of accumulated karma, they encounter various instruments of suffering that arise in succession;
they harm one another until they faint and fall to the ground. Then, from the midst of the sky, a great voice resounds, proclaiming these words: "These sentient beings..."
They may return to the Reviving Hell; next, sentient beings suddenly rise once more. Observing this, it is clear that the hells do not lack fixed locations.
The *Jingtu Sanmei Jing* (Sutra on the Samādhi of the Pure Land) states: "In the past, King Viśāṇa fought against King Vaidarśika.
Anticipating his own defeat in battle, he made a vow to become a king of the underworld. At that time, ten of his ministers and aides..."

There are eight classes of beings who lead a multitude of one million followers, vowing to grow horns upon their heads to assist in the King’s Dharma transformation and to punish those who commit offenses;
these are the ones currently known as the Lord Yama and the Ox-Headed Attendants (Ābhangas).

Observing this, it is clear that the hells and the bodies within them do not come from the ten directions, but arise solely through the entanglements of evil karma that produce the body of a hell-being. This is lust.

The ten factors—greed, pride, anger, hypocrisy, deceit, enmity, wrong views, resentment, litigation, and vindictiveness—are largely identical to fifty-one mental concomitants (*caitta-dharma*), namely:

anger, hatred, vexation, concealment, deceit, flattery, arrogance, and harmfulness. Why are they summarized into ten? This refers specifically to the ten unwholesome courses of action (*daśākuśala-karmapatha*).
Thus, greed, hatred, pride, and wrong views belong to the category of mental action (*manas-karma*). Furthermore, "pride" is here termed *mada* (intoxication/arrogance).

The water of delusion (*moha*). Delusion resides within it. Enmity, anger, and lust belong to the category of bodily karma; yet enmity, anger, and the "killing-spirit" (and so forth) already include killing and stealing within them.
As for the four—deceit, fraud, injustice, and litigation—their verbal meanings are similar.

Why are they divided into four? They encompass the four types of vocal karma: thus, "deceit" refers to false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*); "fraud" refers to frivolous speech (*saṃbhinnapralāpa*); "injustice" refers to harsh speech (*pāruṣya*); [and "litigation" refers to slanderous speech (*paiśunya*)].
It is said: "Slander" refers to double-tongued speech; "lust" is that from which the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) originates. It is the primary source for the creation of karma;
therefore, lust is mentioned first. Lust grinds out the fire of birth, while greed sucks up the water of life, corresponding to the dream of fire when yang is in excess.

The abundance of the *āyatanas* (senses) is like dreaming of water; the iron bed and copper pillar represent their embracing one another. Lying down and sleeping is the residual habit of firm deluded thoughts.
*Papa*, *tata*, and *lala* are the sounds of enduring cold; they are synonymous with *hao-hao* and *hu-hu*.
The blue, red, and white lotuses are the colors of the ice. As for the "water of delusion," such a water exists in the Western Regions.
To drink it causes one to become deluded, much like the "Thirsty Spring" (Tan-quan) or the "Dumb Malaria" (Ya-zhang). Arrogance and indulgence likewise possess their own flavor;

thus, people collectively flatter them, remaining unaware as they sink into foul waters. The habit of lust ignites fire through the affliction of feverish passion, thereby wasting one's own essence (*bindu*).
The habit of anger ignites fire through the provocation of offensive breath, further sharpening its intensity. Fire overcomes metal.
This is the forging of spirit. Although such spirit may be fierce, it only leads to self-injury. The habit of deceit arises from reliance on villainy to produce evil;
beginning with mere mockery, it eventually spreads like creeping vines. Wisdom is like water; thus, one uses wisdom to overcome deceit.

It is like a jackal or a wolf, which, though very small, possesses the strength to devour a tiger. The habit of deception involves feigning virtue to leave others in darkness, like wind driving up dust. It causes...
People do not see it; therefore, one may rob and kill them by taking advantage of their invisibility, just as snakes and vipers also injure people because they are unseen.
This is of the same category. When anger manifests externally, the murderous energy flies and moves, which belongs to the realm of killing.
When resentment is hidden within, one harbors evil like a sack of flour, using a sack to hold a person and then striking them to death. All these are of the Yin [nature].
Secretive acts constitute theft. To contravene and harm others through ghostly poisons or poisoned wine is all a form of hidden malice. There are five types of views (*dṛṣṭi*):

first, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), which refers to clinging to the body as having a self and various forms of conceptual attachment; second, extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), which consist of clinging to either annihilationism or eternalism regarding all phenomena;

third, false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), which involve erroneous awakening and mistaken understanding that repudiates cause and effect; fourth, the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), which [clings to] what is not a fruit...

Regarding the estimation of results: this includes such cases as regarding the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) as *nirvāṇa*. Regarding the adherence to mere rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*):

this is the estimation of what is not a cause to be a cause, such as observing the precepts of cattle or dogs as a means for rebirth in heaven. These five are collectively termed "evil views" (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).

They are mutually contradictory, like travelers on a road—one going forth and one returning—whose observations conflict; therefore, they must be investigated and interrogated to expose their distortions.
It is virtuous not to bend what is not to be bent. Thus, one contorts the body and strains the blood, or measures and weighs the body and blood as if they were livestock.

When one habitually litigates with evil associates who incite one another, it serves only to oppress oneself—like carrying a mountain while treading upon the sea. Would a Bodhisattva ever willingly tread such a path?
Ah! When the five views, as well as greed, hatred, delusion, and pride, are severed, one immediately realizes the third fruit [of the path].

Because the nine grades of afflictions of the higher realms have been severed, yet these particular afflictions remain unsevered, one continues to create karma without end; where there is this cause, there is this retribution. Formerly, Li Liuhou Duanyuan asked Master Daguan:
"After a person dies, where should they go? Daguan replied: [...]* *Note: The source text provided ends abruptly after "觀" (Daguan). The translation reflects the available text.*
Wuzu said, "I do not yet know life; how can I know death? Li said, "As for life, it is upright and sincere—I already know it.
Wuzu asked, "From where does life come? Li hesitated. Wuzu struck him in the chest and said, "It is right here! What are you thinking about?"
Li said, "I understand. I was only aware of hurrying along the journey, without realizing I had lost my way. Guantokai said, "A hundred years are but a single dream.
He then asked, "Ultimately, do the hells exist or not? Guantokai replied, "The Buddhas speak of existence within non-existence—this is like seeing flowers in the sky with one's own eyes.
Your Excellency seeks non-existence within existence—this is like grasping at the moon in water with your hands. It is truly laughable!"
Previously, when seeing a prison, he did not avoid it; now, externally seeing a heavenly realm, he desires to be born there.

He does not realize that joy and fear reside within the mind, and that good and evil are accomplished therein. If you, the Grand Marshal, simply understand your own mind, naturally there will be no delusion.
Li asked: "How does one understand the mind? He replied: "Do not deliberate upon either good or evil at all. Li asked again: "After not deliberating, where does the mind go?"
Suoyuan said, "For now, please ask the Grand Marshal to return to his office. Dongshan asked a monk, "What thing in the world is most painful?
The monk replied, "The hells are most painful. Dongshan said, "Not so. To fail to clarify the Great Matter while within this 'thread of the robe'—that alone is true suffering.
Danxia’s verse says: "How many varieties of boiling cauldrons and burning coals? The hells and the three miserable realms."
This is the most bitter and painful thing. You must believe the intimate words from Xinfeng: "Do not be negligent beneath the *kāṣāya*.
If you can clarify this great matter, there will be no cause for hell; thus, hell itself is not the greatest suffering—it is failing to understand one's own mind that is the ultimate suffering.
What are the six retributions? Ānanda, all sentient beings create karma through the six consciousnesses; the evil retributions they thereby attract emerge from the six sense organs.
How do these evil retributions emerge from the six sense organs? First is the retribution of sight, which draws forth evil fruits.

When this visual karma intersects with other conditions, at the moment of death, one first sees fierce fires filling the worlds of the ten directions, and the deceased’s spirit-consciousness flies downward into them.
Riding on smoke, they enter the Avīci Hell, giving rise to two kinds of manifestations. First is clear vision:
they are able to see all manner of evil things everywhere, giving rise to immeasurable fear. Second is dark vision: in silent stillness they see nothing, giving rise to immeasurable terror.
Thus, when fire burns their hearing, it becomes boiling cauldrons and molten copper; when it burns their breath, it becomes black smoke and purple flames; when it burns their sense of taste...
It can become glowing iron balls and molten metal that burn upon contact; it can become hot ashes, furnaces, and charcoal that scorch the heart;
it can produce sparks and embers that scatter and fly, fanning and filling the void of space. Second is the retribution of hearing, which attracts and draws forth evil fruits.

When this karmic hearing intersects with such conditions, at the moment of death, one first sees waves and surges that submerge heaven and earth. The deceased’s consciousness descends and follows the current, entering the abyss.
In the intermediate hells, two characteristics are revealed: first, "open hearing," where one hears various clamors and the spirit becomes confused and disordered;
second, "closed hearing," where it is silent and nothing is heard, and the dark soul sinks into desolation. Thus, when the waves of hearing pour forth, they can become accusations and interrogations;
when poured into seeing, they can become thunder and roars, and become noxious poisonous vapors; when poured into breathing, they can become rain.
It becomes mist. It sprinkles upon various venomous insects, which completely cover the body. When it pours down flavor, it can become pus and blood, and various kinds of filth.
When it pours down touch, it can become animals or ghosts, or feces and urine. When it pours down thought, it can become lightning and hail, crushing the heart and soul.
These three—smell, karma, and their intersection—invite and draw forth evil fruits; thus, when this smelling-karma intersects, one approaches [the end].

At the time of death, one first perceives poisonous vapors filling the near and far surroundings. The deceased’s consciousness surges up from the earth and enters the Avīci Hell, manifesting two signs:
first, "open hearing," where one is permeated by various evil vapors, causing extreme mental agitation;

second, "blocked hearing," where the vapors obstruct the senses so that they do not pass through, leading to fainting on the ground. Thus, when these odors strike the breath, they can serve as the material basis [for rebirth].
If it encounters the eye, it can become fire or a torch; if it encounters the ear, it can become drowning or submersion, or boiling and seething;

if it encounters the sense of taste, it can become hunger or distaste; if it encounters the sense of touch, it can become tearing, rotting, or a great mountain of flesh with hundreds of thousands of eyes, from which immeasurable things are sucked and eaten;
if it encounters the faculty of thought, it can become ash or pestilence, or fly away.
Coarse gravel and pebbles crush their bodies. Fourth is the retribution of taste. This karmic action of taste invites evil fruits;
when this karmic influence of taste intersects, at the time of death, one first sees an iron net with fierce, blazing flames covering the entire world.
The deceased’s consciousness passes downward through the net, its head hanging upside down as it enters the Avīci Hell. Two manifestations appear: first, the inhalation of breath forms [a mass].
There is freezing ice that splits the flesh of the body; secondly, there is exhaled breath that flies up as fierce fire, scorching and rotting the marrow and bones.
Thus, when one tastes flavors, if one undergoes such tasting, one can become receptive and patient; when one undergoes such seeing, it can burn metal and stone; and when one undergoes such hearing...
Then it can become sharp weapons; passing through the breaths, it can become a great iron cage covering the entire land;
passing through contact, it can become bows and arrows, crossbows and projectiles; passing through thought, it can become flying red-hot iron raining down from the sky.
These five are the retributions of contact that summon evil fruits. When this karma of contact intersects, at the time of death, one first sees [these visions].
Great mountains close in from all four sides, leaving no way out.

The deceased’s consciousness sees a great iron city, where fire-serpents, fire-dogs, tigers, wolves, and lions, along with ox-headed jailers and horse-headed rākṣasas, brandishing spears and lances, drive them through the city gate toward the Avīci Hell.
This gives rise to two manifestations: first, the manifestation of contact, wherein the closing mountains press against the body, crushing the flesh and bones.

The blood coagulates. Second is the contact of separation: when swords and blades touch the body, the heart and liver are butchered and torn asunder. Such contact through union and such contact through succession can serve as the Way and as contemplation;
it serves as the hall and as the judgment seat. Such seeing through succession can serve as burning and scorching; such hearing through succession likewise serves as such.
Thus one can strike, hit, stab, or shoot. Through the experience of inhalation, one can form a bowstring or a quiver;
through the experience of examination, one can plow, clamp, cut, or sever. Through the experience of reflection, one can cause things to fall or fly, or roast and grill them.

A *gǔ* (a type of pestilential spirit) is formed by the gathering of various venomous insects; therefore, it ultimately becomes poison. Its resentment and toxicity are profound; therefore, it repeatedly shifts its abode yet does not forget its origin.
This decaying and baleful force entrusts misfortune and clings to disaster, entering the human body and transforming into a *huí* (roundworm).

When the form returns and takes refuge within the body, it is the legacy of hatred and resentment. As a ghost, one suffers from hunger and emptiness; as an animal, one serves to fill the bellies of others.
Through the habit of arrogance, one treats things with disdain and thus becomes the object of people’s biting indignation.

Through the practice of dark obsession, one haunts and possesses humans, thereby being born among the species of oxen, horses, silkworms, and cocoons, serving as clothing and utility for people, ultimately demonstrating nothing but the delusion of deceiving the ears and eyes. When clarity and harmony prevail within the essence, then it becomes...

Regarding *māṅlǎng* (sprites): when clarity arises within the animal realm, they become responsive manifestations (*yìnglèi*), just as the swallow of the village and the wild goose of winter respond to the four seasons without fail.
Each of these perceives according to its own nature. How could ghosts who are habituated to injustice and servitude serve as many auspicious omens?
At first, they were inverted in their understanding of right and wrong; it was not that their sense of right and wrong was unclear. Thus, [their claims] are empty fabrications.
Sentiments have been exhausted, and the mind of reality has arisen. Now, as an auspicious omen to repay this excellence, I shall bring an end to the toil of servitude.
As for the ghosts that rely on people through the habit of litigation, why do they proliferate by following their kind? They once relied upon humans.

Therefore, they always follow and comply with people; now their reward lies in being clever and wise, being docile and fit for domestication, and having their contentious hearts stilled so that they willingly accept direction.
These various false conditions arise from false views; if one awakens to Bodhi, [they cease].
Just as one whose eyes are free from cataracts cannot perceive a circular shape, it is likewise said that "originally there is nothing at all. When Xuansha ascended the hall, he said:
"Since you possess such a marvelous capacity to manifest yourself before the world, why do you not bring this forth and realize it?
Why instead do you follow others to make your living within the field of the five aggregates and the realm of ghosts? You are simply deceiving yourselves right now."
Go! Suddenly the demon of impermanence arrives; the eyes roll back, and one clings to the view of a self and the view of life.
At such a time, it is most difficult to sustain oneself—like a living tortoise shedding its shell. What great suffering!
O worthy ones, do not take your drowsy understanding and think you have already departed. You have not yet been able to cover even a hair’s breadth. Do you still understand this?
The three realms offer no peace; they are like a house on fire. Furthermore, you have not yet attained a state of true security.
You merely form large crowds and interfere in the affairs of others, flying here and there like wild deer, seeking only food and clothing.
If you act in this manner, how can you walk the royal path? Do you know that kings and great ministers do not constrain you?
You have been permitted by your parents to leave the household life; donors from the ten directions provide you with food and clothing; and the local spirits and dragon deities protect you.
You must possess a sense of shame and gratitude to repay their kindness before you can succeed. Do not fail these people.

Though you sit in rows upon long, continuous beds and spend your time consuming food until it is digested, claiming this is peace and happiness—it is not yet so; all of this is merely the matter of rice gruel and meals.
I have nurtured you until you are like a rotting winter gourd; you will be transformed and taken away, buried in the earth.
Your karmic consciousness will be vast and desolate, with no foundation to rely upon. Why has a śramaṇa come to such a state?
As for all those wriggling creatures upon the great earth, I call them dwelling in the kalpa of hell. If you do not resolve this now, tomorrow—
Entering a donkey’s womb or a horse’s belly; pulling the plow and grasping the handle; wearing iron bits and bearing saddles; being pounded by pestles and ground in mills;
being burned and boiled in water and fire—it is truly not easy to endure this. You must be deeply fearful! It is entirely your own doing. Do you understand?
If you were to realize it, from this very moment on, for eternal kalpas, I would never let you have such news again.
If you do not understand this—that the causes and conditions of afflictions and evil karma will not cease for even one or two kalpas, but shall last as long as your own adamantine life—do you know?
Great in compassion, Xuansha did not spare his bitter words; they serve as an excellent medicine for healing in the Dharma-ending age.
It is fitting that each person copy this once and place it by their seat. Master Mi [Shibi] bestowed it upon me.
While Dongshan was walking, he saw a white rabbit run past him. Yunmen said, "How magnificent! Dongshan asked, "In what way?
Yunmen said, "Like a man in white robes receiving the rank of Chancellor. Dongshan said, "Old as you are, why do you speak such words? Yunmen said, "And what about you?
Dongshan said, "A family of generations of high officials, yet for a moment fallen into obscurity. Yunmen said, "Heaven!"
The child’s verse says: Resisting the power of frost and snow, one strides level-footed through the clouds and mists.

When Xia Hui left his state and Sima Xiangru crossed the bridge, Xiao He and Cao Shen achieved the Han with their strategies, while Chao Fu and Xu You sought to evade Yao with their hearts and bodies.

Regarding honor and disgrace as causes for alarm, he possessed deep self-confidence; his true feelings mingled with the tracks of fishermen and woodcutters. For the most part, Master Mi’s insight relied upon long-accumulated cultivation.
Regarding "merit and achievement": Dongshan’s insight was singularly clear in its revelation of the original nobility.
The ancients often realized the mind through phenomena in this very manner. Furthermore, while Xuefeng and Sansheng were walking together, they saw a troop of monkeys.
