Xuefeng said, "Each of these monkeys carries an ancient mirror on its back. Sansheng asked, "How can one manifest [this] amidst the ignorance of kalpas?"
"An ancient mirror," Xuefeng said. "A flaw has arisen," he continued. Chengshan said, "As a teacher of fifteen hundred people, you do not even recognize the critical phrase.
Xuefeng replied, "The old monk’s administrative duties are too burdensome. Tiantong commented:
"If, at that moment, one had seen Xuefeng say 'A flaw has arisen,' one should have stepped forward and said, 'Yes, yes. But tell me, why was it so?"

When contention is insufficient, yielding is more than sufficient. Observing this, one knows that the functional devices of the masters are not matters of determining victory or defeat based on strength or weakness.
As you have said regarding Jewel-Lotus Fragrance and others, as well as King Vaidūrya and the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra—such evil karma originates from within themselves;
it does not descend from heaven, nor does it emerge from the earth, nor is it bestowed by humans. It is summoned by one's own delusions.
They return to receive [retribution] within the mind of Bodhi; all are but the solidification of floating, empty, and false imaginings.
Furthermore, Ānanda, when these beings from the animal realm repay their prior debts, if the debtor pays more than what was owed, such sentient beings—
When they return to being human, they must repay the surplus they received. If they possess both power and merit, they will not lose their human form among men, and shall repay that power in kind.
If they lack merit, they will return to the state of an animal to repay the remaining value.
Ānanda, you should know that if one uses money and goods, or exerts their labor, the debt is settled and the matter ends.
However, if in the interim one takes another’s life or eats their flesh, then even if they pass through as many eons as atoms of dust, they will continue to devour and slaughter one another.
It is like a revolving wheel, alternating between high and low without ceasing; it cannot be brought to rest except through *śamatha* or the appearance of a Buddha in the world.
Tong said: "King Virūḍhaka committed the offense of killing, and the World-Honored One declared that seven days later he would be extinguished by fire and enter the Avīci Hell.
He then fled onto the water, but the fire rose from within the water and ultimately extinguished him; this was the retribution for the fire of his anger.
The Bhikṣuṇī Ratnapadmagandhā committed the offense of sexual misconduct, and consequently a great, fierce fire arose from her female organ, after which..."
His body was consumed, limb by limb; this was the retribution for his lustful fire. The bhikṣu Sunakṣatra committed a great lie.

Although he could recite the twelve divisions of the scriptures and had attained the fruit of the four dhyānas, he denied cause and effect, claiming that when King Virūḍhaka slaughtered the Gautamas, there would certainly be no karmic retribution.
This was the height of unrighteousness, and thus he was born with his very body [in hell].

To fall into the Avīci Hell is not something bestowed by heaven, nor produced by earth, nor granted by others; it is merely what one has summoned through one's own delusions. Within the mind of Bodhi, there is fundamentally nothing.
It is only because of the solidification of false thoughts that suffering arises. When this solidification does not dissolve, it becomes the cause for receiving karmic retribution.
To the extent that the solidification is complete, one receives a corresponding tenfold retribution; as it gradually diminishes and lightens, one descends [to lower realms].
One becomes a beast to repay former debts; yet even after repaying them with a surplus, one is still demanded for the remainder.

If this mutual devouring does not cease, there will never be an end to it. Only if one possesses the power of *śamatha* concentration and perceives the true face of Bodhi, will these solidified karmas be transformed.
Furthermore, if one encounters a Buddha appearing in the world and has the Great Matter clarified, accumulated karma will naturally dissolve.
Were it not for this, one would continue to revolve within the three realms of existence without ever finding rest. The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:

"If a person is treated with contempt by others, their karmic offenses from previous lives—which would otherwise cause them to fall into the evil realms—are instead extinguished because they are now treated with contempt by people in the present life.
Xuedou’s verse comments: "The bright pearl is held in the palm; those who have merit are rewarded."
Neither barbarian nor Han comes; there is absolutely no skill or artifice. Since there is no skill or artifice, Pāpīyān has lost his way.
"Gautama, Gautama, do you recognize me? [The Buddha] replied, "I have seen through you. Tiandong’s verse says: "Piecing together merits and faults..."
Clinging tenaciously to cause and effect—this is like the frantic running outside the mirror by Yanruo. When the staff struck him, Baozhuo was shattered;

when Baozhuo was shattered, he came to offer congratulations, yet he said, "I have been remiss toward you all along. The preceding verse concerns being held in contempt by others; those who know me are rare.
The subsequent verse concerns the eradication of karmic offenses; the essential point lies in sudden enlightenment, for even meritorious achievements are not valued here.
This was instead brought forth through the transformative inspiration of the verses of Master Fu Dashi.
The Master’s verse says: "In a previous life there were karmic obstacles; today one upholds this sutra. Temporarily slighted by others, the heavy burden becomes light once more.

If one realizes the *paratantra-svabhāva*, one can eliminate the attachments of *parikalpita*. Constantly relying on the contemplation of *prajñā*, where would the *pariniṣpanna* not be perfected? A monk asked Yun [men].

Jū said: "There is a teaching that states: 'If this person’s karmic offenses from previous lives should have caused them to fall into the evil realms, because they are now treated with contempt by others in this life, their karmic offenses from previous lives are immediately extinguished. What is the meaning of this? Jū replied:
"When active, one should fall into the evil realms; when still, one is treated with contempt by others. Chō of Sōjū said: "To say there are dharmas external to the mind..."
One falls into the evil realms; one remains stuck in oneself; one is held in contempt by others. All the venerable elders were skilled at turning the sutras.
Since their intended meaning differs from or accords with this passage, I have recorded it here in full.
You should know now: those of the owl species, once their retribution is fulfilled and they regain their forms, are born among human beings as members of the dull-witted class.
Those of the ill-omened species, once their retribution is fulfilled and they regain their forms, are born among human beings as members of the eccentric class. Those of the fox species...
When their retribution is exhausted and they restore their physical forms, they are born among human beings, joining the ranks of the mediocre.

Those of the venomous class, when their retribution is exhausted and they restore their physical forms, are born among human beings, joining the ranks of the violent. Those of the parasitic worm class, when their retribution is exhausted and they restore their physical forms, are born among human beings.
They merge with the subtle class; those belonging to the category of food, having received their retribution and regained their form, are born among the human realm, merging with the gentle class.

Those belonging to the category of clothing, having received their retribution and regained their form, are born among the human realm, merging with the laboring class. Those belonging to the category of response...
Having fulfilled their retribution and regained their forms, they are born among the human realm and participate in the class of literary beings.

Those who possess auspicious omens, having fulfilled their retribution and regained their forms, are born among the human realm and join the class of the enlightened. Those who follow the various moral norms, having fulfilled their retribution and regained their forms, are born among the human realm.
Ānanda, these beings have all settled their karmic debts from former lives and have again taken human form.

Yet, due to the inverted calculations of karma since beginningless time, they have been born to one another and killed one another. Having failed to meet the Tathāgata and fail to hear the True Dharma, they naturally revolve within the midst of worldly toil.
Such people as these are called "those who are to be pitied."
Tong said: "Sentient beings, not having heard the True Dharma, all claim that it is natural for them to prey upon and slaughter one another.
Yet they fail to consider how Cao Meng (Cao Cao) deceived people with his fox-like cunning, viewing them as meat on a platter, only for Sima to repay him in kind."
It is like presenting a promissory note to claim its value; there is not even a hair’s breadth of discrepancy.

To borrow a cow from one person and return a horse to another—in the dark realm of the unseen, how could those who act with such audacity ever have their wills fulfilled? Ultimately, they shall receive no recompense. Therefore, when enemies meet as karmic counterparts, retribution is certain.

It must inevitably be requited; once the requital is complete, one returns to their original form. Because residual habits have not yet been transformed, those who are dark, deluded, and ignorant are many, while those who are intelligent and exceptionally gifted are few.
When they mingle with the various classes of beings, the *xiāo* (owl) will surely become obstinate;

because it covets material things, it clings to clods of earth and devours them, ultimately remaining stubborn, dull-witted, and unrighteous. The *jiù* (owl) will surely become strange, for its lustful habits are demonic.

Because [the nature of] *dāng* (dissipation) is thus, its residual habits further manifest as strange anomalies. The fox inevitably becomes base and deceitful; it is sycophantic and ignorant, showing no sign of transcendent excellence.
*Dú* (poison) inevitably becomes fierce and stubborn; resentment and hatred remain in abundance, and the flow of its venom is never exhausted. How could such anger be considered slight?
Because anger is eliminated, why would pride not become supple? Because that which is high must necessarily descend. Why would submission involve toil?

Because deception exhausts the mind and spirit, such that labor and suffering never cease. Why would vision be characterized by patterns? Because it responds to its season with clarity and brilliance, such that its variegated beauty may be observed.
When auspicious signs accord with luminosity, the crooked is eliminated and restored to straightness; thus, spiritual cognition is not obscured, following the natural order.
Yet, when one accords with the enlightened, they distinguish between calamity and fortune; thus, they attain unimpeded penetration. Regarding the phrase "participating and uniting":

it means participating and uniting with that which originally arises from the human path. Although those who originally arise from the human path are equal in their emotional dispositions and perceptions, there is nonetheless a distinction between the sharp and the dull.
Now, those coming from within the three miserable realms, eight out of ten accord with the profound depths of emotion.
Those who participate in the clarity of contemplation (*samādhi*) constitute one-tenth of that [number]. During the reign of Emperor Hui of the Jin dynasty, the Indian monk Jīvaka entered Luoyang.
When the various bhikṣus prostrated to him, Jīvaka sat upright and received their salutations.
He said to others, "Among the tens of thousands of monks in this region, I point specifically to Zhi Fayuan, saying: 'This bodhisattva has come from among sheep. He further pointed to Zhu Fahu...
Xing said, "This bodhisattva came from among the devas. Looking out at the palace, he remarked, 'In general, it resembles the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
That [palace] was produced by the power of the Path; this one, however, is merely accomplished through the power of the pure karma of sentient beings.
He then said to the śramaṇa Kṣemaka, 'The craftsman who built this palace came from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; once it was completed, he returned to that heaven.'"
Above, beneath the roof tiles of the ridge, there should be tools; let us trace them. Indeed, there were fifteen hundred vessels.
Thus, Jīvaka knew that the master craftsman had come from among the gods. He then said that Faxing had come from among the gods, while Fayuan had come from among the sheep;
this must not be in error. As for the monk Tanyi, there were pheasant feathers on his ribs, hence he was named Yi (Wings). Because he listened...

They attained liberation through the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Furthermore, the daughter of the Wang family, who was a pheasant, attained liberation after hearing only half of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*;
both had come from among the pheasants. A pheasant is a creature of refined intelligence; having been born into the human realm, she was thus able to realize the fruit of enlightenment.

Ānanda, furthermore, there are those among men who do not rely on perfect enlightenment to cultivate *samādhi*, but instead cultivate deluded thoughts and fixate their mental images to preserve the physical form.
They roam in mountain forests and remote places inaccessible to ordinary people; these are the ten kinds of immortals (*ṛṣi*). Ānanda, as for those sentient beings—
If one remains steadfast in ingesting medicinal elixirs without ceasing, and the path of the elixir is perfected, one is called a terrestrial immortal (*bhūcarā-ṛṣi*).

If one remains steadfast in consuming herbs and trees without ceasing, and the path of medicine is perfected, one is called a flying immortal (*khecarā-ṛṣi*). If one remains steadfast in refining metals and stones without ceasing...
When the transformative path is perfected, one is called a "wandering immortal" (*cāraṇa-ṛṣi*), who remains firm in movement and stillness without ceasing.

When the vital essence (*ojas*) is perfected, one is called a "sky-faring immortal" (*khe-cara-ṛṣi*), who remains firm in the flow of fluids without ceasing. When the virtue of moisture is perfected, one is called a "celestial-faring immortal" (*divya-cara-ṛṣi*).
Firmly maintaining the essence of refined color without ceasing, one achieves the perfection of absorption; this is called a Perfected Being of Penetrating Practice (*sādhaka*).

Firmly maintaining the power of incantations and prohibitions without ceasing, one achieves the perfection of ritual arts; this is called a Perfected Being of Path Practice (*mārga-gata*). Firmly maintaining contemplation without ceasing...
The perfect accomplishment of contemplation is called the Immortal of Illuminating Conduct; it is firm and interpenetrating, never ceasing.

The perfect accomplishment of resonance is called the Immortal of Refining Conduct; it is firm and transformative, never ceasing. The perfect accomplishment of awakening is called the Immortal of Transcendent Conduct.
Ānanda, these individuals all refine their minds among human beings, yet they do not cultivate true awakening.

Instead, they attain a distinct mode of existence and live for ten million years, dwelling in deep mountains or on remote islands far from the haunts of men. This, too, is saṃsāra; they are still subject to the wandering of deluded thoughts.
Failing to cultivate samādhi, when their retribution is exhausted, they return once more, scattering into the various realms of existence.
Tong said: "Those who come from the three miserable realms have not yet exhausted their residual karma; it is sufficient for them simply to cultivate the human path.

Furthermore, there are those who come from the human realm; they clearly understand the nature of evil karma and dare not practice it again, and they also know that the fundamental nature of the mind is what must be cultivated and refined.
However, they do not rely on the Tathāgata’s perfect enlightenment to enter samādhi."

Even practicing separately to cultivate deluded thoughts and preserving the form through visualization constitutes the seed of an external path (tīrthika). Within this category, there are ten kinds of immortals (*ṛṣi*).
"Immortal" (*xian*) means "to transcend"; it refers to those who can cause the body and spirit to undergo transformation so as not to die, based on the belief that a self (*ātman*) exists.

This "spiritual self" is precisely the consciousness-spirit (*vijñāna-ātman*), which is the seed of birth and death from time without beginning. Therefore, although their lifespans may reach millions of years, [they remain within the cycle].

When their lifespan ends, they return and are scattered into the various realms of existence. If a Tathāgata’s perfect enlightenment takes non-arising and non-ceasing as the fundamental ground, then the five aggregates are all empty;
he transcends the three realms instantaneously and does not even abide in the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception, let alone among the immortals.
As for the ten kinds of immortals: the first are those who ingest medicinal herbs and elixirs, such as *qiushi* (autumn stone).
First, those such as Hongyuan (Red Origin) can only prolong their lifespan but cannot achieve levitation; thus, they are terrestrial immortals (*dixingxian*).

Second, by consuming pine and cypress, *fuling* (poria), *huangjing* (daylily rhizome), *cangzhu* (atractylodes macrocephala), and the like, one’s body eventually becomes light and one is able to fly.

Third, by refining metals and stones, lead and mercury, and the nine-fold elixir (*jiuzhuan huandan*), which can be used for alchemical transformation, one may cause one's entire residence to ascend and the body to fly; thus, they are [celestial immortals].

The Wandering Immortals (Xingxian): They employ the four vehicles and the movements and stillness of yin and yang; they perform "bear-stretching" and "bird-extension" to regulate the vital breath and consolidate the essence.

After a long time, the essence transforms into breath, the breath transforms into spirit, and the spirit returns to emptiness. Leaving the physical form behind as they traverse the void, they are therefore called "Immortals Who Travel in Emptiness" (Kongxingxian).
Fifth, by swallowing the saliva [of the *khecarī-mudrā*], water ascends and fire descends; the skin becomes like ice and snow, and one is as graceful and pure as a maiden.
Not engaging with worldly desires, one is no different from a celestial being; hence, these are called "Celestial-Practice Immortals" (*tianxing xian*).

Sixth, by inhaling and absorbing refined essences—such as consuming rainbows, drinking mists, and gathering the solar essence and lunar flowers—the pure qi permeates subtly; thus, one is able to travel freely, piercing through [obstacles].
[He passed through] stone walls with no hindrance whatsoever. That frog swallows the moon’s radiance; its eyebrows possess *xiansu* (musk), which enables it to escape skillfully.
If one who merely perceives its vital energy can still attain such powers, how much more so for the refined essence of Heaven and Earth!

Seventh, by persistently maintaining the incantations and concentrating the spirit without distraction, those incantations will surely manifest their efficacy, and one may even achieve ascension. This [practice] is widely transmitted in the Western Regions.
Recite the mantra within a well for three years; it will spontaneously fly out and return to its natural state.

This is inconceivable, and is therefore called "The Practice of the Way" (Daoxing). Eighth, regarding firm contemplation: silently pay court to the Supreme Deity, or visualize [the deity] at the crown of the head.

It refers to fixing the mind upon the navel-cakra (*nābhi-cakra*) and so forth; being still yet capable of illumination, one realizes the fruit through this illuminating mind, and is thus called an "Illuminating-Practice Immortal" (*ābhāsa-carita-rṣi*).
Ninth, when *kan* (the trigram for water) and *li* (the trigram for fire) are joined in union, yin and yang intermingle, and within them there is an essence that is no ordinary essence.
It is a delusion for those who, by seeking yin to assist yang, lose their own family treasures. This response is spontaneous;
in the mere blink of an eye, one can produce the medicine and complete the elixir. What is called "difficult to encounter but easy to accomplish" refers to this.

Therefore, he was named the Immortal of Refined Practice. Tenth, while maintaining the contemplation that all things in the world are subject to transformation, he took as his sole principle that which is quiescent and immutable;
thus, he attained a state of singular, pure flavor. With his heart extinguished and his form withered, his conduct transcended the world, resembling that of the Pratyekabuddhas of the Two Vehicles.
Therefore, it is designated as "Awakening. Many in the Western Regions practice this and are reborn in the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception;
yet, taken as a whole, they fail to awaken to Right Enlightenment and merely return to delusive thought. Lü Yán, courtesy name Dōngbīn, was a native of Jīngchuān.

During the late Tang dynasty, he failed to pass the imperial examinations three times. By chance, he encountered Zhongli Quan at a wine shop in Chang’an, who bestowed upon him the art of prolonging life.
He once visited the Guizong Monastery on Mount Lu and inscribed these words on the wall of its bell tower:

“One day of pure leisure and self-mastery, The six spirits harmonize, signaling peace and well-being. Since there is a treasure within the *dantian*, there is no need to seek the Way elsewhere; When facing objects, remain without a [discursive] mind.”

"Do not ask about Chan. Not long after, he traveled by way of Huanglong Mountain. Seeing purple vapors forming a canopy, he suspected there was an extraordinary person there and entered to pay his respects.
He happened upon Long striking the drum as he ascended the hall. Recognizing that the visitor must be Master Lü, Long said in a stern voice:
Beside the seat was a person who had secretly studied the Dharma. Lü Yigan stepped forward and asked: "A single grain of millet conceals the world;
half a pint of meat in the cauldron boils mountains and rivers. Tell me, what is the meaning of this? Longzhu pointed at him and said: "This is a corpse-guarding ghost."
Lü said, "But what can be done? I have in my bag the elixir of longevity and immortality. Long said, "Even after eighty thousand kalpas, it will ultimately fall into emptiness and oblivion.
Lü was slightly surprised and flew his sword to threaten him, but the sword could not penetrate. He then prostrated himself twice and requested instruction on the ultimate goal.
Long rebuked him, saying, "I shall not ask about boiling mountains and rivers within a half-measure cauldron; how is this 'One'?"
"A single grain of millet contains a world. Upon these words, Lü attained sudden enlightenment and composed a verse, saying:
"I have cast away my gourd-bag and smashed my zither; Now I no longer yearn for gold in the water. Since first seeing Huanglong, I have finally realized that all my previous efforts were misplaced.
Huanglong instructed him to provide protection [for his practice]. Later, he visited Chan Master Jue of Zhidu in Tanzhou.

It is said: "I traveled through Shao and Chen, descending eastward along the Xiang River, where I now met Master Jue. Observing his Zen practice, I saw it was refined and lucid; his spiritual source was pure and pristine.
Sitting quietly with knees pressed together, he withdrew his radiance to illuminate within. Aside from a single robe, he had no other clothing; aside from a single bowl, he had no other food.
Having reached the shore beyond birth and death and shattered the shell of affliction, he is truly a Buddha of the present age."
The Dharma-robes lie in silent stillness, with no one to transmit them; the principles of Chan hang suspended, nearly severed.
He who shall support and revive it—must it not be our Master? I have composed this single quatrain as a record: "The enlightened push forth their hearts to save all beings;
The sages and worthies transmit the Dharma without departing from the Truth. I beg the Master to explain the meaning of the Westward Coming; Of the Seven Patriarchs, there is now no one left."
If Lü Gong had received the guidance of the Yellow Dragon, he ought to have relied upon the Perfect Enlightenment to cultivate *samādhi*,
rather than remaining among the ten classes of immortal seekers.
Ānanda, there are those among the people of the world who do not seek permanence and have not yet been able to abandon the affectionate attachments for their wives and concubines;
yet, regarding sexual misconduct, their minds do not wander or run astray, and they polish themselves until clarity arises. After the end of their lives, they dwell in proximity to the sun and moon.
This class of beings is called the Heaven of the Four Great Kings. Within the chambers of their own wives, their lustful attachment is slight, and while dwelling in purity, they—
They obtain the full flavor [of their existence]. After the end of their lives, they transcend the brilliance of the sun and moon and dwell at the summit of the human realm.

This class of beings is called the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven (here translated as the "Thirty-three Heavens"). When encountering desire, they briefly engage in union; once it has passed, they have no further thoughts of it.

In the human world, their movement is slight and their stillness is great. After the end of their lives, they abide serenely and radiantly within the void, where the light of the sun and moon shines upward upon them.
They do not fall short. These various beings possess their own radiance; such a class is called the Suyāma Heaven (this is the "Good Time" realm).
It is tranquil at all times, and though there may be contact with external stimuli, they are unable to be disturbed by them.

After their lives end, they ascend to a subtle and refined state, never descending to the lower realms or the spheres of humans and devas, until the kalpa is destroyed. Even when the three calamities arise, they remain untouched. Such is this [realm].

This class is named Tuṣita Heaven (which means "Contentment"). Having no desire for the mind, yet engaging in activities according to worldly custom, at the time of sexual union, the flavor is like chewing wax.
After death, they are born in the Heaven of Delighting in Transformations. This class is named Nirmāṇarati Heaven.
Having no worldly mind, yet performing activities identical to those of the world, they clearly transcend the engagement of such activities. At the end of life—

Afterwards, they are universally able to transcend and transform both the realms of the transformed and the untransformed. This class of beings is called the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Transformations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin).
Ānanda, these six heavens, although their forms move beyond [the lower realms], the traces of their minds still intermingle; from this point downward, it is called the Realm of Desire (Kāmadhātu).
The Master said: "The Heaven of the Four Great Kings resides halfway up Mount Sumeru, forty thousand yojanas above the ocean.
The sun and moon emerge before their palaces and circumambulate them to illuminate the four continents. From there to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven above is another forty thousand yojanas;
this is the summit of Mount Sumeru. At each of its four corners there are eight heavens, totaling thirty-two, all of which are ruled by a King."

Śakra presides over them. These two are called the gods who dwell on the earth (*bhūmi-cara*). The four above are called the gods who dwell in space (*antarīkṣa-cara*). They do not require the sun or moon and are perpetually luminous;
they distinguish day and night by the opening and closing of lotus flowers, and are therefore named the Kāmadhātu-devas (or *Kāma-bhuj*, "those who enjoy desires").

Because they are born there through the power of merit, they are called the Tuṣita (Joyful) gods. Furthermore, they are called the Saṃtuṣita (Contented), the Nirmāṇarati (Delighting in Emanations), and the Paranirmitavaśavartin (Masters of Others' Emanations); these names are not fully translated here.
For those born in this heaven, seven days later, Maitreya will emit light and rain down flowers, leading them into the small Maṇi Hall of the outer enclosure.
There he will immediately preach the Dharma for them, so as to cause them to arouse the power of diligence. Only then will he lead them into the inner enclosure.
Outside these two enclosures, there is also the Heaven of Collective Retribution, which is produced by the fruits of impure karma. [Those who] cultivate...

Those who practice the ten virtuous actions will be born in that place. While it can be destroyed by the three calamities, the phrase "where the three calamities do not reach" refers specifically to the abode of Maitreya;
this is a palace manifested through the *prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna* (subsequently attained wisdom) of the various noble ones.

When compared to the outer court in terms of their collective karmic retribution (*sāmānya-vipāka*), there is already a separation like that between a transcendent immortal and an ordinary person—how much more so for the inner court? Everything outside of this belongs to...
Regarding the realms of retribution: from the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (*Nirmāṇarati*) upward, whatever objects of enjoyment one possesses arrive according to one's thought;

because they transcend the lower heavens, they are called "Transcendent Emanations" (*vaihāyasa-nirmāṇa*). From the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin*) upward, various objects of sensual pleasure do not require one’s own effort to emanate them, as they are all enjoyed with mastery through the emanations of others.
Although these six heavens transcend the human world, they have not yet [attained...]
Detachment from desire. The *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states: "The six [senses] experience desire through embracing, holding hands, laughing, and gazing;
as these acts become increasingly subtle, their retribution becomes correspondingly higher. This is because the craving for desire is easily cast off. Whatever one is attached to constitutes desire;
therefore, regarding all matters that involve contact and activity, one clearly transcends them without the slightest lingering thought, thereby attaining mastery. It is not merely...
This refers to sexual misconduct. According to Tiantai’s teachings on the karma of the six heavens of the desire realm, all take the ten wholesome paths as their foundation.

If one additionally possesses a mind that protects the Dharma, this is the karma for the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājakāyika*). If one additionally uses compassionate means to transform others, this is the karma for the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

If one additionally refrains from harming sentient beings and is skillful and mature in practice, this is the karma for the Yāma Heaven. If one additionally cultivates meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), [the karma for the Tuṣita Heaven is attained]. Regarding the coarse...
Abiding in the subtle dwelling is the karma of the Tuṣita Heaven; the dhyāna-concentration of the desire realm is the karma of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven;

and the preparatory concentration (anāgamya) is the karma of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven. None of these seek the eternally abiding true mind, nor do they transcend the causality of conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta).
Although their karmic rewards differ, they ultimately cannot be said to equal the Great Liberation.
When the twenty-third patriarch, Venerable Harel, arrived in Central India to propagate the teachings, the king there was named Abhayasāgara; he held profound faith in the Buddha-dharma.
While the Patriarch was expounding the True Dharma, he suddenly saw two individuals dressed in vermilion and white robes who bowed to him. The King asked, "Who are these people?
The Patriarch replied, "These are the Sun and Moon Devas. Because I previously preached the Dharma for them, they have come to pay their respects.
After a long while, they vanished, and only a wondrous fragrance remained. The King said, "In the lands of the Sun and Moon, there are many..."
[The number of] kalpas is few. The Patriarch said: "In the worlds transformed by the thousand Śākyamuni Buddhas, each has ten billion Mount Merus and suns and moons.
If I were to explain this extensively, I could not exhaust it. Furthermore, when Bodhisattva Vasubandhu descended from Maitreya’s inner palace, Bodhisattva Asaṅga asked him:
"Four hundred years among humans constitute one day and night in that heaven. Maitreya..."
In a single moment, Asaṅga brought five hundred billion devaputras to the realization of the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
I do not know what dharma he preached. Vasubandhu said: "It was simply this very dharma; it was merely that the Sanskrit sounds were pure and elegant, making them a joy for all to hear.
If one can believe that it was simply this very dharma, then in the heavens and among humans, there is fundamentally no distinction between purity and defilement."
How could the eternally abiding true mind not be liberated?
*The Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata’s Enlightenment and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas*,
Fascicle Nine.

Ānanda, there are those in the world who cultivate their minds but do not rely on *dhyāna* (meditative concentration) and possess no wisdom; they are merely able to restrain their bodies and refrain from sexual desire.
Whether walking or sitting, they are free from all such thoughts, and since no defilement of craving arises, they do not remain bound to the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).

Such persons, by virtue of their mindfulness, consider themselves companions of Brahmā. This class of beings is called the Heaven of the Retinue of Brahmā (*Brahmapārṣadya*). As for their habitual tendencies toward desire...

Once these have been eliminated, the mind manifests freedom from desire; one takes delight in and accords with all forms of discipline. Such a person is able, at that time, to practice the virtue of Brahma.

This class of beings is called the Heaven of Brahma’s Ministers (*Brahmapurohita*). With body and mind wondrously perfected, their deportment flawless, and their pure prohibitions and precepts augmented by clear awakening, such a person is able, at that time, to preside over the assembly of Brahmās as the Great Brahma King (*Mahābrahmā*). Thus it is.
One class is named the Great Brahma Heaven. Ānanda, these three superior streams cannot be oppressed by any suffering or affliction.
Although they do not constitute the true, correct Samādhi, within their pure minds, the various outflows (āsravas) remain unmoved; this is called the First Dhyāna.

Ānanda, next there is the Brahmā Heaven. Those who govern the Brahmā people, perfect the Brahmā conduct, and whose minds are clarified and unmoving, from which a profound stillness gives rise to light—this class of beings is called the Heaven of Limited Light (Parīttābhā).
When their lights shine upon one another, the illumination is inexhaustible; it reflects throughout the ten directions, pervading them so that they become entirely like lapis lazuli.
This class of beings is called the Heaven of Infinite Light (Apramāṇābhā). They absorb and sustain this perfect light, forming...
Regarding the substance of the teaching, their transformative power is pure and its application is inexhaustible; such a class is called the Heaven of Light-Sound (*Ābhāsvara*).
Ānanda, these three superior streams cannot be oppressed by any anxiety or distress.

Although they have not yet attained the true Samādhi of correct cultivation, within their pure minds, gross outflows (*āsrava*) have already been subdued; this is termed the Second Dhyāna. Ānanda, such celestial beings are perfectly...
Light becomes sound; as sound is stripped away, the sublime is revealed. As this gives rise to refined practice, one penetrates the bliss of nirvāṇa.

This class of beings is called the Heaven of Limited Purity (*Parīttaśubha*). When the pure void manifests before them, it induces boundlessness; body and mind become light and tranquil, achieving the bliss of nirvāṇa.
This class of beings is called the Heaven of Immeasurable Purity (*Apramāṇaśubha*). World, body, and mind are all perfectly pure; they have accomplished the virtues of purity.
The supreme support manifests before them, and they return to the bliss of cessation. This class of beings is called the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven.
Ānanda, these three superior streams possess great conformity; their bodies and minds are at peace, and they attain immeasurable bliss.
Although they have not yet truly attained authentic samādhi, within their peaceful minds, joy is fully present; this is called the Third Dhyāna. Ānanda, furthermore, O devas and humans...
Neither body nor mind is oppressed; the causes of suffering have already been exhausted. Yet pleasure is not permanent; after a long time, it must inevitably decay and give rise to suffering.

Both the minds of suffering and pleasure are simultaneously and suddenly relinquished. The characteristics of coarseness and heaviness are extinguished, and the nature of pure merit arises. This class of beings is called the Heaven of the Birth of Merit (Puṇyaprasava-deva).
With a mind of equanimity perfectly integrated and a resolute understanding purified, they attain wondrous compliance within unobstructed merit.
Exhausting the limits of the future, this class of beings is called the Heaven of Meritorious Affection (*Puṇyapriya*). Ānanda, from this heaven there are two diverging paths.
If, regarding the previous mind of immeasurable pure light and perfected, brilliant merit, they dwell in its cultivation and realization, this class of beings is called the Vast [Heaven].

Fruitful Heaven (Bhṛhatphala). If, regarding the preceding mind, one simultaneously feels weary of both suffering and pleasure, and through diligent cultivation brings the state of equanimity (*upekṣā*) to a continuous flow, thereby fully exhausting the path of equanimity until body and mind both cease;
when the mental faculties become ashen and solidified, one passes five hundred kalpas.

Because this person takes arising and ceasing as their cause, they cannot manifest the nature that is neither-arising-nor-ceasing. For the first half-kalpa there is cessation, and for the latter half-kalpa there is birth. Thus it is.
One class is called the Heaven of No-Thought (asaṃjñisattva-deva). Ānanda, these four superior streams cannot be moved by any worldly states of suffering or pleasure.
Although they do not constitute the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) truly immovable stage, their attainment of a "something-to-be-gained" mind has reached full maturity through the application of effort.
This is called the Fourth Dhyāna.

Generally speaking, although the inhabitants of the six heavens of the Desire Realm have bodies that move about and have already departed from the two destinies of humans and devas, their mental traces still intersect with worldly concerns, and their desires have not yet reached the state of total absence;
thus, they cannot be said to be Brahmā-like. As for those who practice the Brahma-faring (brahmacarya), it is simply...
They know how to maintain the precepts and cultivate the ten paths of wholesome action, yet they do not understand *dhyāna* and lack wisdom.

Therefore, among all the prohibitive precepts, only sexual desire is difficult for them to sever; because they have the power to sever sexual desire and no longer remain within the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), they are called the Brahma-multitude (*brahmakāyika*).
Once their minds are free from desire, their precepts become true precepts, and they joyfully accord with all forms of discipline (*vinaya*); these are called the Brahma-ministers (*brahmapurohita*).

With pure precepts augmented by clear awakening—meaning that one awakens to the fact that desire is itself the nature [of reality] and that there is no longer anything to be restrained—one is called a Great Brahmā (*mahābrahman*).

When precept and meditative concentration (*samādhi*) are in union, one attains concentration through those precepts; having already departed from the eight sufferings of the desire realm, one cannot be oppressed by the coarse characteristics of suffering and affliction.
This is called the stage of "joy and bliss born of seclusion" (*vivekaja-prītisukha-bhūmi*), which collectively belongs to the first dhyāna. From this point onward...

Above this, there is no verbal expression; it is only by means of the concentrated mind that light is emitted. This light varies in its degree of excellence, thereby distinguishing between higher and lower levels.

In the Heaven of Limited Light (*Parīttābha*), the light is still inferior; when alternating emissions of abundant light occur, the radiance becomes immeasurable (*Apramāṇābha*). Yet, this has not yet reached the perfection of sound.

Upon reaching the accomplishment of the essence of teaching, one causes others to behold the light and know how to cultivate pure virtue (*brahmacarya*), so that they may receive benefits according to their individual capacities. This is as it should be.
When used inexhaustibly, the halo of light becomes sound. When this concentration arises, it emerges together with joy; thus it is called the dhyāna accompanied by joy (*prīti-sahagata-dhyāna*).
Because it cannot be assailed by subtle anxiety or longing, it is called the stage of rapture born of concentration (*samādhi-ja-prīti-sukha-bhūmi*). This belongs entirely to the second dhyāna.
From this point upward, one is free from the agitation of the preceding joy and gives rise to pure bliss (*śuddha-sukha*). This bliss is not an external object; it is transcendence.
Regarding the pure nature, it resembles taking nirvana as bliss. Initially, it is called "penetration," yet its purity is still inferior.
Subsequently, it is called "accomplishment," whereby body and mind become light and tranquil, harmonizing with the wondrous nature; yet this has not yet reached universality.
Only when the world, the body, and the mind are all perfectly pure does this supreme reliance manifest before one. This reliance upon a superior realm is not yet the ultimate reality.

This is the manifestation of quiescent extinction (*śānti*). Merely by conforming to the pure nature and returning to the bliss of extinction, the merit of this concentration arises together with a pervasive physical bliss;
thus it is called "meditation accompanied by bliss" (*sukha-sahagata-dhyāna*). Although it is free from the agitation of the preceding joy (*prīti*), it is nonetheless fully endowed with delight.

This is called the Stage of Sublime Joy Free from Rapture (*prīti-viveka-sukha-bhūmi*). It belongs generally to the third dhyāna. Rapture is an agitation that serves as the cause for the affliction of suffering;

when rapture is abandoned, the causes of suffering are exhausted, and one attains immeasurable bliss (*sukha*). This bliss is produced by conditioned factors (*saṃskṛta*) and, though pleasant, must eventually perish.

When it perishes, it becomes suffering. Therefore, by relinquishing both suffering and bliss, the coarse and heavy characteristics are extinguished, and equanimity and mindfulness become pure (*upekṣā-smṛti-pariśuddhi*).
Thus, the nature of pure merit arises; through pure virtue, one attains blessings that are beyond the reach of the three calamities. This is called "the arising of merit.

When both suffering and pleasure are forgotten, and equanimity (*upekṣā*) is maintained without anything to be relinquished, one simply delights in and accords with the unobstructed nature of merit. This is called "love for merit."
All are termed "dhyāna accompanied by equanimity" (*upekṣā-sahagata-dhyāna*). From this point, there are two divergent paths.

If one possesses the previously cultivated immeasurable light and immeasurable purity, with merit fully perfected and radiant, free from heterodox attachments and devoid of a mind of arising and ceasing, then one proceeds directly to the Vast Fruit (*bṛhatphala*), which is the fruit induced by the vastness of pure merit.
If, however, the prior mind was characterized by a dual revulsion toward both suffering and pleasure, and one has specialized in the cultivation of the mind of equanimity—
First, one abandons the coarse mind and enters the subtle mind; then, abandoning the subtle mind, one enters the extremely subtle mind.
From the extremely subtle mind, there is a continuous, uninterrupted flow until all mental conceptions are entirely relinquished and the mind becomes like cold ashes.
This is the characteristic of deluded thought; it is called the "attainment of non-conception. By this circuitous and deviant path, one is born into the Heaven of Non-conception. Such a person...

To realize that the nature of delusion is empty in essence is to see that delusion is itself truth. To loathe this birth-and-death and seek that which is non-arising and non-ceasing leads to the extinction of both body and mind;
yet this is not the true nature of non-arising and non-ceasing. It is like the "ice-fish" of the Tathāgata:

when first born in this heaven, one is not yet entirely without thought; it is only after half a kalpa that thought ceases. When the retribution is about to end, for the latter half of the kalpa, thought returns.
Yet they perceive one another through their mental states. Therefore it is said: "For the first half-kalpa there is extinction; for the latter half-kalpa there is birth.

During the intervening four hundred and ninety-nine kalpas, there is exclusively non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñika*), sustained by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). It cannot be moved by any suffering or pleasure, and is collectively termed the Four Dhyānas.
When situated in the First and Second Dhyānas, it is called "not the true cultivation of Samādhi. As for [the remaining stages]...

Regarding the third dhyāna, it is said that one has not yet correctly attained true samādhi. Upon reaching the fourth dhyāna, it is said that one has not yet reached the unconditioned stage of true immovability.
In the first dhyāna one cultivates precepts, and in the second dhyāna one cultivates concentration; these are cultivated from within pure brahmacarya.
Although one does not fall into the wrong concentrations of ghosts or spirits, this is nonetheless conditioned and does not arise from the mind of true samādhi. This is the conditioned.
The distinction between the conditioned and the unconditioned is established by this. In the third dhyāna, there is something attained; having attained it, one experiences joy.
To have attainment and to experience joy is not the true samādhi. This is the basis for distinguishing between that which has attainment and that which is without attainment.
Upon reaching the fourth dhyāna, the mind of attainment is nearly exhausted and abandoned; thus, it may be called unconditioned. Nevertheless, because of its cultivation...
This is achieved through the perfection of cultivation, yet it is not the true Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*).
If it were the true Immovable Ground, the various sufferings could not reach it; since they cannot even reach it, who could possibly move it?
Now, because one is unmoved by the worldly conditions of pleasure and pain, one takes this to be *samādhi*. This kind of *samādhi* can be cultivated and attained.
That which can be attained through cultivation is not the true samādhi. Therefore, regarding true samādhi, none can know it without possessing the wisdom of prajñā.
Now, those who cultivate the mind within the four dhyānas do so without relying on *dhyāna* (śamatha) and lack wisdom;
thus, they remain ignorant of true samādhi. As the Venerable Zhenjing said to the assembly: "This is..."
The day has already passed, and life likewise perishes accordingly; like a fish in shallow water, what joy can there be in this?

Only the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas take the tranquility of meditative concentration and cessation as their joy; this is true joy. Those who study Prajñāpāramitā take the dharma-joy and the bliss of meditation as their joy;
this is true joy. The Buddhas of the three periods of time take the four immeasurable minds—loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—as their joy.
This is true happiness. Shishuang Puhui said: "Rest! Cease! Go into a state of cold stillness!
This is the bliss of the extinction (*nirvāṇa*) of the Two Vehicles. Yunmen said: "All-encompassing wisdom penetrates without obstruction.
He raised his fan and said: "The Old Man Śākyamuni has arrived! This is the bliss of the joy of Dharma and the delight of Zen. Deshan...
The staff! Linji’s shout! This is the bliss of the compassion, mercy, joy, and equanimity of the Buddhas of the three periods.
Apart from these three kinds of bliss, nothing else constitutes bliss. Now tell me: does this entire assembly at Guizong abide within these three kinds, or outside of them?
After a long silence, he said: "Today the master of the estate has provided *khan* rice and distributed alms money. After the formal session, everyone is invited to the Sangha hall for tea.
He gave a shout. Furthermore, regarding Chan Master Dayi of鹅湖 (Ehu): Emperor Xianzong summoned him into the inner palace to debate the Dharma.
A Dharma Master asked: "In this realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), there is no dhyāna; dhyāna resides in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). Upon what does this land rely?"
Daoxian stood up. Fayi said, "The Master knows only that the realm of desire lacks dhyāna; you do not know that the realm of dhyāna lacks desire. He asked, "What is dhyāna?
Fayi pointed to the empty space with his hand. The Master had no reply.
The Emperor said, "The Master lectures on infinite sūtras and śāstras, yet even for this single point, he is at a loss. Therefore, true samādhi is truly not easy to attain."
He knows. Having known this, he transcends the three realms entirely; what need is there to speak of the four dhyānas?
Ānanda, within this state there are further five types of non-returning devas (*anāgāmin*). Within the lower realm, the nine grades of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are extinguished simultaneously;

suffering and pleasure both perish, and since there is no longer a dwelling place below, they are established within the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*) of the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā-citta*).
"Ānanda, as for their dwelling: when both suffering and pleasure have ceased and the contentious mind no longer engages, such a class of beings is called the Heaven of No Affliction (Avṛha).

When the mechanisms [of the senses] function alone and there is no ground for the friction of contact, such a class of beings is called the Heaven of No Heat (Atapa). Throughout the worlds of the ten directions..."
Their wondrous vision is perfectly clear and tranquil; being free from all traces of dust and every defilement, such a class is called the Heaven of Good Vision (Sudṛśa).

Their refined vision manifests before them, forging all things without obstruction; such a class is called the Heaven of Good Manifestation (Sudarśana). They have reached the ultimate limit of all phenomena.
Exhausting the nature of form until its very essence reaches the boundless limit—this class of beings is called the Heaven of Ultimate Form (*Akaniṣṭha*).
Ānanda, as for these Non-returners in the Heaven of Ultimate Form, even the various kings of the four levels of the fourth dhyāna can only hear of them with admiration; they cannot know or see them.
It is just as in this world, where vast wildernesses, deep mountains, and sites of the holy path are all maintained by Arhats. Thus it is in the world.
It is subtle and cannot be seen by ordinary people. Ānanda, these eighteen heavens are solitary and without companions;
as long as they have not yet exhausted the burden of form, they are called the Realm of Form (rūpadhātu).
Tong said: "Regarding the five types of non-returners (*anāgāmin*), they will no longer undergo rebirth in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Thus, while the *sakṛdāgāmin* is called 'one who does not come back' (*anāgāmin*), in reality there is no such thing as 'not coming back. The third fruit [the non-returner] is able to sever the nine grades of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*);
both the seeds and their active manifestations (*samudācāra*) are extinguished. Since there is no karma for rebirth in the desire realm, it is said that 'below, there is no place to dwell.'"

The "Five Heavens" (Pañcaśuddhāvāsāḥ) correspond to the purity of equanimity and mindfulness within the fourth dhyāna; they are merely further designations established for its increasingly subtle states.

Previously, when there was equanimity toward suffering and pleasure yet still a sense of aversion, the mind and its objects were in conflict, such that it could not be free from vexation. This intense heat is what is called "vexation" (kleśa).

Now, with both suffering and pleasure extinguished, there is no one with whom the mind contends; therefore, it is named "Free from Vexation" (Avṛha). Although the mind does not engage [with objects], it engages...

The ground still remains; the root has not yet been uprooted. Now, the mental faculties have no opposition and can extinguish the shadows of conditions, eliminating the fever of concurrent afflictions.
Therefore, it is named "Without Fever" (Anabhraka). This state of being "Without Affliction" and "Without Fever" merely removes external coarseness but has not yet revealed purity and subtlety.
Now, the wondrous vision is perfectly clear and limpid: externally, it does not depend on the arising of sensory objects; internally, it does not depend on...
Sinking defilements arise; it illuminates the worlds of the ten directions like pure lapis lazuli. This is called "Good Vision" (Sudarśana). Refined vision resides within me;
it can mold exquisite forms without obstruction. The worlds of the ten directions issue forth their transformations from me.

This is called "Good Manifestation" (Sudṛśa). "Ji" (幾) refers to the subtlest movement of vibration. Because a single atom is empty, all atoms are empty; because all atoms are empty, [the world is empty].
One minute particle is empty. When one exhaustively investigates the nature of form (*rūpa-dharmatā*) to its limit, the nature of form is empty;
this emptiness is awakening. Awakening is precisely what is called the nature of the nature of form. Emptiness arises within great awakening, like a single bubble emerging from the ocean.
This does not merely exhaust the nature of form, but also exhausts the origin of that nature. At ultimate exhaustion, form is utterly gone. As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says:
Dwelling in the Heaven of Akaniṣṭha, a place free from all faults, one attains perfect enlightenment there.
How profound are these words! That which is called "perfect enlightenment" does not abide in form, nor does it abide in emptiness;
it is only in the Heaven of Akaniṣṭha. Since the forms prior to this have already ceased and the emptiness subsequent to this has not yet arisen, it is here that one may realize the Unconditioned.
...the Unsurpassed Perfectly Complete Enlightenment. Maitreya said: "Regarding the eighteen realms of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*):
the three heavens of the First Dhyāna arise because of having cultivated the first meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) through the highest degree of intense application;

the three heavens of the Second Dhyāna arise because of having cultivated the second meditative absorption through the highest degree of intense application; the three heavens of the Third Dhyāna arise because of having cultivated the third..."

Regarding the three dhyānas: there are the four meditative absorptions (dhyāna) and the four heavens [of the form realm]. This is because one has cultivated the fourth dhyāna through the medium and superior grades of refinement.
Furthermore, there are the abodes of the noble ones where the mind does not share [with ordinary beings], which are the five Pure Abodes (śuddhāvāsa).

This is because one has cultivated the fourth dhyāna through the highest of the superior grades of refinement. Why is it that these non-returners (anāgāmin) do not abide in the levels below the fourth dhyāna?
[The former] is able to see and know; the lower heavens cultivate impure, mundane meditative concentrations, whereas this heaven cultivates the pure karma of the noble ones.
Because of this separation between the noble and the mundane, [the former] cannot see [the latter]. Yunju Ying built a hermitage on Sanfeng Peak and did not attend the hall for ten days.
Dongshan asked, "Why have you not been coming to the vegetarian feasts lately? Ying said, "Every day, a heavenly deity brings me food.
Dongshan said, "I thought you were a man of realization; it seems you still harbor such a view. Come back this evening.
When Ying arrived in the evening, Dongshan called out, "Reverend Ying! Ying responded, "Yes. Dongshan said, "Do not think of good..."
He thought, "What evil is this? [The deity] returned to Yinghuai Hermitage and sat in silent meditation. From that point on, the celestial spirit could no longer find him at all;
after three days, the sightings ceased. Furthermore, the divine monk Faben once went to a Chan temple in Xiangzhou.
He spent the summer retreat together with a monk. The Master had once said, "I reside at Zhulin Monastery in the western mountains of Xiangzhou.
Before the monastery stands a stone pillar; when you have leisure in the future, I pray that you will come to visit me.
This monk, recollecting these words, traveled there to search for him. Upon reaching a village at the foot of the mountain, he stayed overnight and inquired about his whereabouts.
The village monk asked, "How far is it from here to Zhulin Temple? The monk [Dafang] pointed toward the side of a solitary peak in the distance and said, "That place is it.
He added, "According to ancient traditions, this was the site where sages and worthies once resided;
now only its name remains. The village monk doubted this. The following morning, he went into the bamboo thicket and indeed found a stone pillar. When Dafang arrived there...
Another account says: He simply tapped on its pillar and immediately saw the man. He then struck the pillar several times with a small twig;
suddenly, wind and clouds rose up on all sides, and one could not see even a foot away. In an instant, his vision and hearing cleared, and pavilions and towers rose up before him.
Finding himself beneath the triple gate, he hesitated for a moment. Fa-ben emerged from within, and seeing him, he was greatly pleased. He asked Nan...
Regarding the former events: he led the monk through the double gates and up into the secret hall to meet the venerable elder. The venerable elder asked him the reason for his visit.
Ben said, "In my youth, we spent the summer retreat together in Xiangzhou, and I have come here at this time to pay you a visit. The venerable elder said:
"You may leave after your meal; there are no seats here. When the meal was finished, he was sent back to the three gates to bid him farewell.
Soon thereafter, heaven and earth grew dark and gloomy, and he could not discern where he was proceeding. His body remained exactly beside the stone pillar.
Thus, because the sites of the holy path are all sustained by Arhats, they are not to be spied upon by worldly people.
If this can be measured, why should there be any doubt regarding the five heavens of the Non-returners? Although they are invisible, they still possess material substance;
therefore, they are collectively termed the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Furthermore, Ānanda, within this Summit of Existence (*bhavāgra*), the ultimate limit of form, there are again two divergent paths.
If, within the mind of equanimity, one illuminates wisdom so that the light of insight becomes perfectly pervasive, one will then transcend the realm of dust and become an Arhat;
entering the Bodhisattva vehicle, such a class of beings is called a "Great Arhat who has turned the mind. If, while in the state of equanimity...

Having achieved renunciation and detachment, one perceives the body as an obstruction; by dissolving this obstruction, one enters emptiness. This class of practitioners is called the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).

When all obstructions have been dissolved, yet there remains neither obstruction nor cessation, wherein only the *ālayavijñāna* persists—along with the entirety of the *manas* and a subtle portion of it—this class of practitioners is called the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).
When both emptiness and form have vanished, the consciousness-mind is entirely extinguished.
The ten directions are tranquil and utterly devoid of any place to go; such a class [of beings] is called the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*). The nature of consciousness is unmoving;
through the exhaustive investigation of cessation, within the inexhaustible, they manifest the nature of exhaustion. It is as if existing yet not existing, as if exhausted yet not exhausted;
such a class is called the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). These have reached the limit of emptiness, yet they do not exhaust emptiness.

As for principle: those who have reached the end of the noble path from the heavens of the Non-returners (anāgāmin) constitute one class known as "Arahants of dull faculties who do not turn their minds [toward awakening].

If, however, they come from the heavens of the non-Buddhist Unconscious (asaṃjñin) gods, having exhausted their emptiness and failing to return, being deluded, leaking, and without learning, they will then enter the cycle of rebirth.
Ānanda, each of these celestial beings is but an ordinary person receiving the retribution of their own karma. As for the answer:
They all enter the wheel. That celestial king is, in fact, a bodhisattva who dwells in samādhi, gradually progressing toward the path of practice traversed by the noble assembly.
Ānanda, in these four heavens of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), body and mind are extinguished;

the nature of stability manifests, and there is no form resulting from karmic fruit. From this point until the end, it is called the formless realm. All of these fail to realize the wondrous enlightenment of clarity.
The mind accumulates delusions, giving rise to them; these delusions constitute the three realms. Within these, deluded beings follow along, sinking and drowning within the seven destinies.
As for *pudgala* (translated here as "the one who repeatedly undergoes rebirth"), each follows according to their own kind.

Tong said: "The four formless heavens (*ārūpyadhātu*) are the abodes of those śrāvakas of fixed nature. If they turn their minds back [from the Lesser Vehicle], they turn their wisdom toward compassion, saving sentient beings and benefiting all things;
not dwelling in the minor fruits, they enter the Bodhisattva vehicle and are called 'Great Arhats.

Those of dull faculties, however, are unable to manifest and develop wisdom. Furthermore, because of their concentrated mind, they take delight in the higher realms and feel aversion for the lower ones, and thus they become weary of form."
Relying on emptiness, one enters the sphere of infinite space. Once physical obstruction has dissolved, one no longer relies on form.
Even the non-obstruction of emptiness is extinguished, and thus emptiness itself has nothing further to empty. The body-faculty and the six consciousnesses have all been utterly obliterated;
only the full portion of the eighth consciousness and half of the seventh remain. The manas (seventh) consciousness originally has no fixed location, as it depends on external conditions.

When form is empty, one relies on the six consciousnesses; this is called "coarse. When internally taking the eight consciousnesses as objects, there is only internal grasping and no external objects;

this is called "subtle. This state of wearying of emptiness and relying on consciousness is named the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*). Advancing further, the consciousness-mind is entirely or partially extinguished.

This is not truly capable of extinguishing [the mind]. It merely takes the state where the conscious mind is limpid and unmoving, utterly devoid of any directionality, and considers this to be the fundamental absence of anything existing.
One thinks that the true nature has always been without a single thing, and thus this conscious mind is entirely extinguished; this is somewhat similar [to the correct method].
However, this takes a mind subject to arising and ceasing as the causal ground of the mind. As long as the mind of arising and ceasing has not been extinguished, it is like...
Rapid currents may appear as tranquil from a distance; thus, one cannot speak of the true nature in terms of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
Once the conscious mind has ceased, the nature of consciousness remains unmoving. Yet, through further investigation and refinement, even that which is unmoving must be extinguished.
This immovability is all-pervasive and perfect; it is the wondrous *tathatā*-nature of the *tathāgatagarbha*. It is fundamentally unborn and fundamentally non-existent.

Exhaustion. Within the inexhaustible, one forcefully proclaims the nature of exhaustion. That which is called "exhaustion" is merely the perception of exhaustion based on the cessation of consciousness;

yet how could the nature itself ever be exhausted? Therefore, if one regards it as existing by remaining unmoved within the nature of consciousness, it is not the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñin*);
yet if the mind and thoughts are extinguished and congealed, appearing as if it does not exist, it is not perception (*saṃjñā*).

Because one considers it to be "exhausted," it is called "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana). Yet, because subtle and minute mental flows continue without ceasing, it is as if it were not exhausted;
thus, it is also called "not non-perception. This state of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is half-dependent upon the unborn and undying, and half-dependent upon arising and ceasing.
This is precisely the realm of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). Being shrouded by consciousness, one merely speculates within the bounds of thought and recollection;
such a person is not truly able to see their nature. Those born in this heaven remain without thought for eighty thousand kalpas, after which the kalpa ends and thought returns once more.
These beings exhaust themselves in the pursuit of emptiness, yet they do not reach the wondrous principle of true emptiness, nor do they realize that emptiness arises from Great Enlightenment.

Although they may follow the holy path to the five heavens of the non-returners (anāgāmin), they do not clarify the principle that the true nature is the empty essence of awakened nature, and that the empty essence of nature is the true awakening of nature.
Failing to enter the Bodhisattva vehicle, they are ultimately termed "dull Arhats who do not turn their minds.
Though this faculty is dull, there is still hope for them to eventually turn their minds; how could they compare to those of the external paths who [seek to dwell] in the Heaven of No-Thought?

Deluded regarding conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) and outflows (*āsrava*), they claim for themselves that they are free from outflows (*anāsrava*). Yet when their retribution is exhausted, they enter the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*);

even the four heavens of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) cannot escape this cycle. Both the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are likewise the ripening of karma; once that ripening is exhausted, one enters the cycle.

Why, then, should there be any doubt? These various heavenly kings are none other than the emanations and transformations of Bodhisattvas of the various stages, who sport beyond *samādhi* and provisionally manifest gradual progression to lead sentient beings toward the ranks of the sages; they are likewise the path of practice that increases and advances step by step.
As for these four heavens of emptiness (*ākāśānantyāyatana*, etc.), body and mind are extinguished, and the nature of their fixed state manifests before them. Although...

There is no longer any form resulting from karma, yet forms resulting from meditative concentration still persist. From this point until the end, there are only these forms resulting from concentration and nothing else.

It is not possible to speak of this unless one has awakened to the wondrous, enlightened, and luminous mind and transcended the three realms. Failing to realize this, one does not transcend the three realms;
instead, one follows the seven destinies through delusion, sinking deeper and deeper in transmigration—all due to the accumulation of false imaginings.

This is how it comes about. In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there is the deluded view of desire; in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the deluded view of purity; and in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the deluded view of emptiness.

Thus, there are three realms of delusion, each of which is attached to its own destiny. The *pudgala* (individual) is that which can take up future destinies; this is precisely the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states:
"The five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) of the intermediate state are not seen by the physical eye, but are seen by the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). This is delusion.
Following its own kind, it pursues the cycle of rebirth; in short, as long as the consciousness-spirit (*vijñāna*) has not been transformed, it remains in this state.
If one can transform consciousness into wisdom (*jñāna*), one will naturally be free from these burdens. Formerly, Dizang asked Master Xiu, "Where have you come from? Xiu replied, "From the South.
Dizang asked, "How is the Buddha-dharma in the South these days? Xiu said, "Discussions are vast and extensive."
Hao Di said, "How can it compare to planting fields here where I eat my fill by farming? Xiu said, "What can be done about the three realms?
Hao Di said, "What do you call the 'three realms'? Tiantong’s Verse says: The Master established all manner of things as mere forced constructs;
Transmitted through mouth and ear, they became fragmented and confused. Planting fields and farming for one's meals are matters of daily life; It is not... [the case].
One who has fully completed their practice does not know [this]; having fully completed their practice, they clearly know there is nothing to seek.

Zhang Liang ultimately did not prize the rank of marquis. Forgetting artifice, he returned to the company of fish and birds; he washed his feet in the Canglang River amidst the autumn mists and waters.
Furthermore, Cuiyan Zhen addressed the assembly, saying: "Not seeing a single dharma is a great calamity. The mountains, rivers, and the great earth; the sun, moon, and stars; form—"
Emptiness, brightness, and darkness are not a single dharma. Holding up his staff, he said: "Ordinary people see the staff and call it a staff.
Śrāvakas see the staff and recognize it as mere empty space, thereby negating the staff.
Bodhisattvas see the staff—when has it ever hung upon their teeth? When hungry, they eat; when weary, they sleep; when cold," [they put on clothes].
Facing the fire when cold, and seeking coolness when hot—such talk fails to see that the wisdom of all-encompassing knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*) is pure.
To speak in this manner is to laugh the nostrils off the local earth-spirit; it is precisely the same flavor as farming the fields to earn one's meal.
This is the very model of transcending the three realms.
Furthermore, Ānanda, within these three realms, there are four kinds of asura classes.

Those who, belonging to the realm of hungry ghosts, ride upon supernormal powers into the air through the power of protecting the Dharma—these asuras are born from eggs and are categorized within the destiny of hungry ghosts.
If they descend from the heavens due to a loss of merit, their dwelling place is adjacent to the sun and moon.
These asuras are born from a womb and are categorized within the realm of human beings. There is an asura king who upholds the world; his power penetrates all things and he is fearless.
They are able to contend for power with the Brahma King, Śakra, Lord of Devas, and the Four Heavenly Kings.

These asuras arise through transformation and are included within the realm of devas. Ānanda, there is another class of inferior asuras who are born in the depths of the great ocean, dwelling in the mouths of underwater caverns;
they roam in the void at dawn and return to their watery abodes at dusk. These asuras arise from moisture and belong to the realm of animals.

Regarding their inclusion within the destinies (*gati*), it is generally said that *asuras* possess power equal to that of the devas, yet they lack deva-like conduct; therefore, they are called "non-devas" (*na-deva*).

The *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* states that there are five classes of *asuras*: first, those who are extremely weak and dwell among the mountains and forests of the human realm; [the second class] dwells in the west...
1. In a vast and deep mountain cavern, there is the palace of the Asuras. 2.
Twenty-one thousand yojanas beneath the great ocean to the north of Mount Sumeru, there is the palace of Rāhu, who is able to eclipse the sun and moon with his hands. 3.
Another twenty-one thousand yojanas further down, there is the palace of the Vīrūḍhaka; these are the Āgatas, who do not drink alcohol.
4. Furthermore, twenty-one thousand yojanas below, there is the palace of Mālyavat. Its women are exceedingly beautiful, while its men are ugly. 5.
Furthermore, twenty-one thousand yojanas below, there is the palace of Vemacitra—translated as "Pure Mind.
It is situated on the ocean of Kṣāroda (Salt-water) and produces sounds. He is a relative by marriage of Śakra. From the *Dīrgha Āgama*...
The *Hanyan* states: "Asuras undergo suffering three times within a single day and night; the instruments of torture come of their own accord, and they enter their palaces.

Thus it is known that this realm possesses a portion of wholesome retribution, which is why humans and devas are mentioned [separately]. However, when discussing the experience of suffering, they are actually situated below the human realm;
therefore, the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* includes them solely within the two categories of hungry ghosts and animals. This scripture...

By means of the four modes of birth—womb, egg, moisture, and transformation—as well as the four classes of beings—gods, humans, ghosts, and animals—the various emotional states and conditions of the asuras are exhaustively depicted;
in general, this accords with the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra*. When Chan Master Qinglin Qian ascended the hall, he said: "Under the gate of the Patriarchs, the 'Bird Path' is profound and subtle.
When effort reaches its limit, it turns back; if one does not reach that limit, it is difficult to clarify. You all must directly depart from the mind."
"Consciousness investigates; one must transcend the paths of both the mundane and the sagely before one can maintain [the realization]. If it is not thus, you are not my child.

A monk asked, "When one has long been burdened by [this state] yet does not meet the right time, what then? He replied, "The ruler of antiquity was one inch tall. Another asked, "I request the Master to provide a response.
He replied, "Asura holds the sun and moon in his palms. Furthermore, a monk asked Zen Master Fohai, "That which is the very mind..."

[The questioner asked: "What is it like when one is a Buddha? [The Master] said: "A topknot with two side-tufts. [The questioner asked: "What is it like when it is neither mind nor Buddha? [The Master] said: "Earrings of gold rings. [The questioner asked:

"If it is not mind, not Buddha, and not a thing, then what is it? The Master said: *Note: This dialogue is a classic example from the *Wumen Guan* (The Gateless Barrier), where the Master’s responses function as kōans to point directly to the nature of reality beyond conceptualization.*
"A bald-headed asura dances the Zhazhi; such talk as this does not emerge from the path of ordinary or sagehood.
It is a study that transcends mind, intellect, and consciousness; truly, its limits cannot be fathomed."
Ānanda, thus it is with the hells, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, seers and immortals, devas, and asuras.

When one minutely examines these seven realms, they are all merely the signs of the conditioned states of delusion; they are births resulting from false imagination and followings of karma according to false imagination.

Within the wondrous, perfect, and luminous mind that is inherently unconditioned, they are all like flowers in the sky—originally having no basis for attachment, being nothing more than a single void and falsehood. There is nothing else.
Ānanda, as for the root source: these sentient beings do not recognize their original mind and thus undergo this cycle of rebirth for immeasurable kalpas, failing to attain true purity.
This is entirely due to their compliance with killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct. By reversing these three, one gives rise to the absence of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct.
That which possesses [these] is called the realm of ghosts; that which lacks them is the celestial realm. As existence and non-existence contend with one another, the nature of samsara arises.
If one attains the wondrous arousal of samādhi, then there is wondrous, eternal stillness. Both existence and non-existence are absent; even the absence of duality is extinguished.

Since there is not even "not killing, not stealing, and not committing sexual misconduct," how could one further follow after the acts of killing, stealing, and lust? Ānanda, if the three karmas are not severed, each has its own private [delusions].
Because of these various privacies, the collective share of these privacies has a fixed location; it is not that there is no fixed place, for it arises from one's own delusion.

It arises; this arising of delusion is without cause and cannot be traced or investigated. You must exhort yourself to practice cultivation. If you wish to attain Bodhi, you must eliminate the three delusions.
If these three delusions are not exhausted, even if you should acquire supernatural powers, they will all be worldly functions of conditioned effort.
