As long as habitual tendencies are not extinguished, you will fall into the path of Māra; though you wish to eliminate delusion, your falsehoods will only increase. The Tathāgata says such people are to be pitied.
"O Compassionate One, you have falsely created this yourself; it is not the fault of Bodhi. To speak thus is called speaking correctly;
if anyone else were to say this, they would be speaking as the Māra King."

Tong said: "Previously, Ānanda asked about the wondrous mind’s pervasive perfection. Why, then, are there further realms such as those of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans, and devas?
Do these have fixed locations, or do they arise spontaneously through the karmic actions initiated by each individual?"
Each receives [their state] privately. Is this something that exists inherently from the beginning, or does it arise from the deluded habitual practices of sentient beings?
Therefore, he answers these seven realms of existence collectively: they are all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*) within the wondrous, perfect, and luminous mind of non-action.
Originally there is nothing at all, like flowers in the sky; what interference could they have with the great void? They do not exist inherently from the beginning.
Rather, they arise through deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*), and deluded thoughts follow karma—this is what is meant by "the arising of deluded habits.
Once these deluded habits exist, there are deluded fruits. Each person initiates their own karma and each receives their own private retribution.

Thus, it is not that there is no fixed locus; rather, it arises spontaneously from delusion. Delusion serves as the cause of further delusion, and this delusion acts as the cause for karmic retribution;
it is not something that occurs naturally. This arising of delusion has no external cause and cannot be traced back to its origin, for it is fundamentally and eternally quiescent.

Yet, taking the three—killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct—as its root, one follows along with the karma of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct. This is what is falsely perceived as "existence," and once existence is established, one inevitably sinks into the cycle of rebirth.
One falls into the four evil destinies; among these, the realm of hungry ghosts is the lowest. To not accord with the three [jewels] and to instead oppose them by force is false view.
If one is without [false views], one will inevitably be born into the three good destinies; among these, the heavenly realm is the highest.
Although the paths of good and evil differ, existence and non-existence mutually influence one another; thus, within the saṃsāra of the three realms, there is no end.
Resting, all is brought about by human effort; it is not the fault of Bodhi. If one attains the wondrous arousal of samādhi, one recognizes one's own fundamental mind and realizes its true purity;
this is called "wondrous. Without leaving the triple world, one suddenly transcends the triple world.
Within that quiescent, eternal, and correct concentration, there are no dualistic characteristics to be found; having already eliminated the mundane...
When the falsity of the [four] truths ceases, even the non-duality of non-existence is extinguished.

Furthermore, when the truth of *nirvāṇa* is removed and fundamental ignorance is completely melted away and purified, from where could delusion arise? From where could falsity be born? When there is not even goodness, how much less can there be evil?
This is like the fact that when the eye is originally free of cataracts, the flowers in the sky have no self-existence. Regarding the three delusions, many sutras state—

This refers to the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), the afflictions as numerous as motes of dust (*rajas-sama-kleśa*), and the afflictions of ignorance (*avidyā-kleśa*). The afflictions of views and thoughts are also called "universal afflictions" (*sāmānya-kleśa*) because they are severed in common by the practitioners of the Three Vehicles.

The afflictions as numerous as motes of dust are called "particular afflictions" (*viśeṣa-kleśa*) because they are severed by Bodhisattvas. The affliction of ignorance is the seed of karmic consciousness; it is only the Bodhisattvas of the Mahāyāna who sever this affliction.
It is like not removing the pressure of the fingers pressed against the eye: although one wishes to remove the [illusory] flowers, they only multiply.
Furthermore, if one adds hypocrisy, even if they attain supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), they will still fall into the path of Māra.

The path of Māra consists of those who do not eliminate killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct while practicing perverse meditative concentrations (*mithyā-samādhi*). Therefore, those who wish to attain unsurpassed *bodhi* should eliminate the three delusions and purify their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Once the three delusions are gone, how could the three realms exist? If one does not understand this teaching, they will merely call it *bodhi*.
"Fundamentally empty. To establish a practice for the purpose of removing delusions is the teaching of Māra. A layman once asked West Hall Master Zang, "Are there heavens and hells?
Zang replied, "There are. He asked, "Are there the Triple Gem—Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha?
Zang replied, "There are. He posed many more questions, and Zang answered them all by saying, "There are. The layman said, "Master, in speaking thus, you must not be mistaken."
"No," Zang said. "Have you ever met a venerable elder? He replied, "I once attended upon the Abbot of Mount Jing.
Zang asked, "What did Mount Jing say to you? He replied, "He said that everything is entirely non-existent.
Zang asked, "Do you have a wife? He replied, "Yes. Zang asked, "Does the Abbot of Mount Jing have a wife? He replied, "No. Zang—
It is said: "The Master of Mount Jingshan’s statement, 'Non-existence is sufficient,' is marvelous;
within ordinary speech, he points out the news of the sudden transcendence of the three realms. Furthermore, a monk asked Chan Master Dongshan Quan:
"When it is said that a pure practitioner does not ascend to heaven, and a precept-breaking bhikṣu does not enter hell, what then? Quan replied: "Having saved all beings..."
The Last Portrait: Returning him to Nirvāṇa. Danxia’s verse says: "With majestic marks and signs, a great man indeed;
throughout his life, he lacked wisdom and was just like a fool. From the beginning, even Buddhas and Patriarchs could hardly hope to match him; how could hell or heaven possibly constrain him?
This may serve as a testament for those who have wondrously given rise to samādhi.
At that moment, as the Tathāgata was about to conclude his session upon the lion throne, he took up a seven-jeweled armrest, turned toward the Purple Gold Mountain, and leaned against it once more.
He then addressed the great assembly and said to Ānanda: "You disciples in training—pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas—"
Today you have turned your mind toward great bodhi and supreme, wondrous enlightenment. I have now explained the method of true practice;
yet you still do not recognize the subtle demonic activities that arise during the cultivation of śamatha (translated as "stopping") and vipaśyanā (translated as "contemplation").
The realm of Māra has appeared before you, yet you fail to recognize it. Your mind is unpurified and not upright; you have fallen into false views.

Whether it be the *skandha-māra*, or the celestial *māra*, or you are possessed by a ghost or spirit, or beset by a *chī-mèi* (mountain-demon), your mind is clouded and ignorant, mistaking a thief for a son.
Furthermore, within that state, one may become satisfied with a mere trifle, like the unlearned bhikṣu of the fourth dhyāna who falsely claimed to have realized the noble stages.
When his celestial retribution was exhausted and the signs of decline appeared before him, he slandered the arhats and, having undergone subsequent existence, fell into the Avīci Hell.
"You should listen attentively. I shall now explain this to you in detail. Ānanda rose from his seat, as did all the other practitioners in the assembly;
with joy, they prostrated themselves and waited in reverence for the compassionate instruction. The Buddha addressed Ānanda and the great multitude.
You should know that within this world of outflows, the twelve classes of living beings possess a fundamentally enlightened and wondrous clarity.

This essence of the awakened mind is no different and no distinct from that of the Buddhas of the ten directions. It is due to your own deluded thoughts that you mistake the underlying principle, which is the fault; thus, ignorance and craving arise.
From the arising of pervasive delusion, there is the nature of space; as the transformation of delusion does not cease, worlds come into being.
Thus, these lands of the ten directions, as numerous as motes of dust, are not without outflows; they are all established through the stubborn, deluded thoughts of ignorance.
You should know that space arises within your own mind, like a fragment of cloud appearing in the vast clarity of the great void; how much more so, then, do the various worlds exist within space?
If even one among you were to give rise to true resolve and return to the source, this void of the ten directions would all dissolve and vanish.
How could the lands existing within that void fail to tremble and shatter?

When you practitioners cultivate dhyāna and adorn the samādhi, the minds of the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions and the various untainted Great Arhats will penetrate in profound harmony, remaining serene and unmoving in their respective states. All the Mara kings—

Furthermore, the ghosts, spirits, and ordinary devas saw their palaces collapse and split for no apparent reason; the great earth shook and cracked open, and all creatures—whether aquatic, terrestrial, or aerial—were struck with terror.
These ordinary beings, mired in ignorance, were unaware of this upheaval.

They had all attained the five supernormal powers, with the sole exception of the extinction of outflows (āsravakṣaya), yet they remained attached to these worldly defilements. How could I cause such a place to be shattered and torn asunder for them?
Therefore, when you are in samādhi, ghosts, spirits, celestial māras, *piśācas*, and *yakṣas* will all come to disturb you.
Yet, though those māras may be greatly enraged, within their afflictions and amidst your wondrous enlightenment, they are like wind blowing upon light.

It is like a sword cutting through water; they do not touch one another at all. You are like boiling water, while he is like solid ice. As the warmth gradually approaches, the ice will melt away before long.
To rely merely on your supernatural powers is to be but a guest; it leads only to the accomplishment of disorder and ruin.

This is because you are the master of the five aggregates within your own mind. If the master is deluded, the guest gains the advantage. Therefore, remain in *dhyāna* (meditative concentration) and awaken to the truth without confusion.

Then those demonic activities will be powerless against you. As the five aggregates dissolve and enter into clarity, all those various malevolent spirits will be constrained by the subtle, dark energy.

Since clarity can destroy darkness, they will perish from within as they draw near; how then could they dare remain to disturb your meditative concentration? This would not be the case if you were not clearly enlightened.
Deluded by the aggregates, you, Ānanda, would surely become a son of Māra and a perfected Māra-man, such as the Matanga woman;
you would be exceedingly inferior. She merely cast a spell upon you, violating the Buddha’s code of discipline; among the eighty thousand practices, she destroyed but a single precept.

Because the mind is pure, you have not yet been submerged; yet this [delusion] shall destroy your entire body of precious awakening, like a high minister’s family suddenly encountering confiscation of their property—utterly ruined and scattered, beyond all hope of rescue.
Tong said: "Māra is the Māra-śatru (the Foe). This is translated as 'The Killer' or 'The Robber,' because he can kill the life of wisdom and rob one of the wholesome dharmas.

Generally speaking, there are five kinds: the māra of the five aggregates (skandha-māra), the māra of afflictions (kleśa-māra), the māra of birth and death (mṛtyu-māra), and the celestial māra (devaputra-māra)."
Regarding demons and māras, when categorized together, there are only the *skandhamāra* (the demon of the aggregates) and the *devaputramāra* (the celestial demon).

The *skandhamāra* refers to the afflictions of birth and death that arise based upon the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). The *devaputramāra* refers to those who, having practiced perverted meditative concentrations, delight in harming the true path.
Furthermore, there are unlearned bhikṣus who, being satisfied with meager attainments, slander the Buddha by falsely claiming that Arhats do not undergo further existence.
This is the Mara of False Views; he is both the Mara of the Aggregates and the Deva-Mara. Because he slanders the Dharma, he shall immediately fall into the Avīci Hell.
When a single person awakens to the truth and returns to the source, the worlds of the ten directions collapse and vanish.

All the Mara-kings and ordinary devas see their palaces crumble and split apart, and they are struck with terror on land and in water; they then come to disturb and disrupt his meditative concentration.
The harm wrought by these celestial and demonic beings is superficial. They rely on their supernatural powers, yet they remain but guests; the host resides within me.
Therefore, one uses wondrous enlightenment to shatter worldly afflictions, like using hot water to melt ice, or using light to dispel darkness.
If the host becomes deluded, the guest seizes the opportunity to destroy my moral discipline and ruin my precious awakening, just as a butcher...
The subject is confiscated and then gradually falls into ruin; this is the profound harm wrought by the *skandha*-māra.

When the accomplishment of disorder is fully returned to its master, one must therefore cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) and attain clear awakening, so as not to be deluded by the five *skandhas*—this is the primary principle.
The *skandhas* are the covering of consciousness and emotion, like floating clouds; clarity is like the sun facing the sky.
It is revealed as being like the great void. When the aggregates (*skandhas*) dissolve and enter into clarity, one returns to the fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*).

Therefore, the wondrous luminosity of fundamental awakening is non-dual and indistinguishable from that of the Buddhas of the ten directions. It is only through delusion, craving, and false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), following along with confusion and undergoing transformation, that worlds arise.

Where there is a world, there is the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*); clinging to this dust and toil, there arise the aggregates of sensation, perception, and mental formations (*vedanā-, saṃjñā-, and saṃskāra-skandhas*).

The aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). I wish to shatter the aggregates and emerge, returning to the perfectly enlightened essence of my own mind-body, vowing to reach the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*).
Those who possess outflows, clinging and unable to let go, rely upon their supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and thus come to harass me.

If one destroys the precepts and breaks the discipline, yet associates with such as these, even if they attain the five supernormal powers, they will inevitably become children of Māra. To break through this at this very moment—this is called...
Precious Awakening. This awakening is precisely the seed for attaining Buddhahood. Relying upon this precious awakening, one enters into right concentration to realize the Dharma-body.
Thus, the mental essence of the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions and the various stainless Great Arhats merges in perfect harmony.

It constantly abides in stillness. This tranquil illumination encompasses empty space; yet even empty space is non-existent. How much more so, then, can the various contaminated lands that depend upon space for their existence?
The Master of the Avataṃsaka asked Changsha Chengyan, "Does empty space definitely exist, or does it definitely not exist?
Chengyan replied, "One may say it exists, and one may also say it does not exist. Empty...
"Empty space exists at times, but it is only a provisional existence; empty space does not exist at times, but it is only a provisional non-existence.
The Master asked, "Regarding what you have said, O Venerable One, what scriptural authority is there? The Monk replied, "Virtuous One, have you not heard what the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says:
'The empty space of the ten directions arises within your own mind, like a single fragment of cloud appearing within the vast clarity of the great void'? Is this not [the nature of] empty space?"

At the time of arising, there is merely the arising of a provisional name. It is further said: "If even one person among you awakens to the truth and returns to the source, the empty space of the ten directions will all vanish away.
Is this not the case that when empty space is extinguished, it is merely a provisional name that is extinguished?

Therefore, the Old Monk says: existence is a provisional existence; non-existence is a provisional non-existence. Because Changsha has thoroughly penetrated the wondrous luminosity of original enlightenment, he speaks thus.
Even the arising and ceasing of empty space is but an illusion; how much more so the rest? There was a venerable elder named Pengyan, who was erudite and possessed a powerful memory.
He came to visit Chan Master Baoen Ming to debate the fundamental tenets of our school.
Ming said, "Excessive words only lead further away from the Way. Now I have a question to ask you: regarding all the sages of antiquity and the former masters of our tradition, did they..."
"Is there anyone who has not attained awakening? Yan said, "If this is so, how could there be any among the sages and former worthies who have not attained awakening?
Ming said, "When one person awakens to the truth and returns to the source, the empty space of the ten directions is entirely dissolved.
Now, Mount Tiantai stands towering here; how can it be made to dissolve? Yan was at a loss for words. This is one great [matter].
If you cannot dissolve this mass of doubt, how can you speak lightly of breaking through the veils?

Ānanda, you should know that when you sit at the site of enlightenment, you must cause all thoughts to fall away. When those thoughts are exhausted, then all states free from thought will become brilliantly lucid;
movement and stillness will not shift it, and recollection and forgetfulness will be as one. Abiding in this state, you shall enter samādhi.

It is like a person with clear vision who dwells in great darkness; though their essential nature is wondrously pure, the mind has not yet emitted light. This is called the realm of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).
If the eyes become bright and clear, the ten directions open up completely, and there is no longer any gloom or obscurity—this is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of form.
Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*). Observe its origin: it takes solidified false discrimination as its root.
Ānanda, within this state, if you investigate with refined clarity until the four elements no longer interweave, then in a brief moment, your body will be able to pass through obstacles.
This is called the overflowing of refined spirit into the external realm; it is merely a temporary attainment through such effort, and is not [the ultimate state].

This is the realization of the sages. If one does not conceive of it as a state of sainthood, it is called a "wholesome realm"; however, if one interprets it as a state of sainthood, one will immediately succumb to various delusions.
Ānanda, if one further uses this mind to investigate its subtle brilliance until it penetrates the interior of the body, that person will suddenly, within their own body—
When he picks out a roundworm or a parasite, its physical form remains perfectly intact and without injury or destruction. This is called the overflowing of refined essence into the physical body;

it is merely the result of refined practice and is attained only temporarily. It is not a sign of saintly realization. If one does not conceive of it as a state of sainthood, it is called a "wholesome realm."
If one takes this to be a realization of the holy, one will immediately succumb to various demonic influences.

Furthermore, when one uses this mind to investigate thoroughly both internally and externally, at that time the *po*, *hun*, *yi*, *zhi*, and *shen* spirits—apart from the body they inhabit—will all enter into one another, acting as mutual guests and hosts.

Suddenly, one may hear the sound of the Dharma being preached in the air, or hear the secret meanings being expounded simultaneously throughout the ten directions. This is called the spirits and souls alternatingly separating and uniting.

One achieves the seeds of goodness; yet, to momentarily attain such a state does not constitute a realization of the holy. If one does not conceive of it as a holy attainment, it is called a "wholesome realm.

If, however, one interprets it as a holy realization, one will immediately fall prey to various forms of delusion. Furthermore, because this mind is clear, exposed, and brilliantly transparent, an inner radiance shines forth.
The ten directions were everywhere suffused with the color of Jambūnada gold. All species were transformed into Tathāgatas.

At that moment, Vairocana suddenly appeared—his body and environment in perfect harmony—seated upon a celestial light-terrace, surrounded by a thousand Buddhas. Ten billion lands, along with lotus flowers, all manifested simultaneously.
This is called the defilement of the awakening of the soul; the radiance of the mind, when polished and clarified, illuminates all things.
The world may temporarily appear thus, yet this is not a holy realization. If you do not conceive it as a holy attainment, it is called a "wholesome state";
if you take it for a holy realization, you will immediately be possessed by various demons.

Furthermore, if with this mind you investigate the subtle brilliance, observing without ceasing, suppressing and subduing it, or restraining and transcending it, then suddenly the empty space of the ten directions will turn into the color of the seven treasures, or perhaps into a hundred [colors].

Precious colors fill [the space] simultaneously, without obstructing one another; blue, yellow, red, and white each appear in their pure forms. This is called the power of intense concentration exceeding its limit;
such a state may be attained for a time, yet it is not a holy realization. If you do not conceive of it as a holy attainment, it is called a "wholesome state.

If you interpret it as a holy realization, you will immediately be possessed by various demons. Furthermore, if you use this mind to investigate until it becomes transparent and clear, a refined radiance [will emerge].
Without distraction, you may suddenly see various objects in a dark room at midnight as clearly as in broad daylight, yet the objects in the dark room do not vanish.
This is called the mind becoming subtle, dense, and clear, such that what is seen penetrates the profound darkness. To experience this for a time is not a sign of saintly realization.
If you do not conceive the thought of being a saint, it is called a "wholesome state"; if you take it to be a realization of sainthood, you will immediately fall under its influence.
The multitude of evils. Furthermore, when this mind enters perfectly into the void and the harmonious, the four limbs suddenly become like grass and wood;
even if burned by fire or cut by a blade, one is never aware of it. Moreover, the light of fire cannot burn or scorch them, and even if their flesh is sliced, it is as if wood were being pared away.

This is called the merging of sensory objects, where the nature of the four great elements is cast aside and one enters exclusively into purity. To attain such a state for a time does not constitute [the final realization].

This is a sign of spiritual realization. If you do not conceive the thought that you have attained sainthood, it is called a "wholesome state. If, however, you interpret it as having attained sainthood, you will immediately be possessed by various demons.

Furthermore, when this mind achieves purity and the power of the pure mind reaches its peak, you may suddenly see the great earth and the mountains and rivers of the ten directions all become Buddha-lands, replete with the seven treasures and filled with radiant light.
You may also see Buddhas and Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges filling [the space].
In the realm of space, the palaces and halls are magnificent. Looking down, one sees the hells; looking up, one observes the celestial palaces, attaining unobstructed vision.

This is called the deepening of focused contemplation through the alternation of joy and revulsion. After long practice, these visions transform into manifestations, yet they do not constitute the realization of a sage. If you do not claim them to be the state of a sage, they are known as "wholesome realms.

If you interpret them as the realization of a sage, you will immediately succumb to various demonic influences. Furthermore, if you use this mind to investigate the profound and far-reaching, suddenly—
In the middle of the night, one may see from afar the marketplaces, streets, and alleys, as well as one's kinsmen and relatives; or one may hear their voices. This is called "oppressing the mind.

When the pressure becomes extreme, the consciousness flies out, and thus many things are seen through obstructions. This is not a realization of the holy state. If you do not conceive the thought that it is a holy attainment, it is called a "wholesome realm.
If you interpret it as a holy attainment, you will immediately fall under the influence of various demons. Furthermore, by investigating this mind with extreme refinement, one may see what is good.
The forms of knowledge shift and transform; in a brief moment they become groundless, undergoing various changes.

This is called a deviant mind that harbors demons and spirits, or one who is possessed by celestial Māras entering their heart and belly. Such a person may preach the Dharma without cause, claiming to have mastered subtle meanings;

yet this is not a sign of saintly realization. If you do not regard it as a mark of sainthood, the demonic activities will subside. If you take it to be a sign of sainthood, you will immediately fall under the sway of many evils. Ānanda!

These ten kinds of meditative visions appearing before one all arise because the mind is applied in a state of mutual conflict within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). Thus, these phenomena manifest.

Sentient beings are stubborn and deluded; they do not reflect upon themselves. Encountering such conditions, they remain lost and fail to recognize them for what they are, claiming instead that they have attained the state of a sage.
This constitutes a great falsehood and results in falling into the Avīci Hell.

After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Final Dharma, you should proclaim this meaning so that no celestial Māras may find an opportunity to harm you. Maintain and protect it, and thereby achieve the Unsurpassed Way.

The Master said: "Chan-na (dhyāna) is the dharma-gate of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. To dissolve all thoughts and, by means of profound stillness, to revolve back the false and extinguish birth is *śamatha*.
When those thoughts have been exhausted, yet the state of being free from thought remains, such that everything is lucid and penetrating, this is *vipaśyanā*.
That *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are non-dual must be realized through remaining unmoved by activity or stillness, and being one in both recollection and forgetfulness—neither dull nor distracted."

Right mindfulness: entering through this, one then attains true samādhi. If there is stillness but no movement, or if memory persists while forgetting has ceased, this belongs to the realm of concentrated contemplation on appearances; it is not yet true concentration.

When first entering śamatha and vipaśyanā, if the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) has not been shattered, it is like a person with clear vision situated in great darkness, unable yet to emit light, being constrained by form.
This is called the domain of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). Once the aggregate of form is shattered, it is like the eyes becoming clear and bright;
the ten directions open wide, and the power of contemplation shines forth perfectly, unimpeded by external objects. In this way, one is able to transcend the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*).
Because form and vision are interwoven, the turbidity of the eon is formed; now that vision is no longer deluded by the phenomena of form, one is thus able to transcend it.
Furthermore, why does this aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) come into being? It takes firm delusive conceptualization as its root.

Rooted in the three—the father, the mother, and oneself—it is formed through the mutual entanglement of delusive conceptualizations. Thus, this solid physical body composed of the four great elements is produced:
solidity is earth, moisture is water, warmth is fire, and movement is wind. From these...
These four entanglements form the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*). These six are profoundly still and perfectly luminous, yet they shroud and obscure the true nature;
therefore, they are called "obscuring aggregates" (*skandha*). Now, entering *dhyāna*, one investigates the wondrous luminosity, detaching from the external objects.

When both body and environment are empty, the four great elements no longer interweave, and nature becomes separated from form. Initially, the refined spirit overflows, and the body is able to pass through obstructions, forgetting its exterior.
This was the objective realm. Subsequently, his body became transparent within; he extracted threadworms and roundworms, forgetting his own body internally.
Thereafter, his vital essence and spirit alternately separated and merged; his internal body and external body mutually acted as guest and host.
He was able to hear the essentials of the Dharma being preached in mid-air, such that he nearly forgot his physical form. Finally, an inner radiance manifested, and he beheld the realm of the Buddha.
What is colored by spiritual intuition may momentarily appear thus, yet it cannot be regarded as permanent.

If, however, one perceives the realm of the Pure Land through the *nien-fo san-mei* (Buddha-recollection samādhi), such that mind and object correspond, this is called the "correct sign" (*samyak-nimitta*) and does not fall under the preceding category.

Furthermore, if one suppresses [the mind] beyond its proper limit and sees many-colored forms, or if light arises when the suppression reaches its extreme, these are likewise accomplished through the contemplation of the ten perceptions (*daśa-saṃjñā*).
Subsequently, he secretly clarified his vision and beheld objects within the darkness. What he had previously seen was an illusory realm; what he now saw was a real realm.
This is not possible for one whose mind is not refined through intensive cultivation. Furthermore, his four limbs became ethereally integrated, as if they were mere grass and wood;
even when burned by fire or cut by a blade, he was never aware of it. This is not possible for one who has not attained pure awakening and transcended the body. Thus it was.
When the intensity of his contemplative observation reached its peak, he attained purity;
suddenly, he saw the Buddha-lands of the ten directions and both heavenly paradises and hells without any obstruction, nearly attaining the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).

Subsequently, when the intensity of his mental suppression reached its limit, he could not only see objects within a dark room, but even the markets and streets of distant lands were clearly visible to him; furthermore, he could hear sounds from the air.
He heard the sounds of the Dharma, yet he did not fail to hear the voices of his kinsmen and retinue; it was as though he had attained the supernormal power of the divine ear.

When his research reached its ultimate refinement, such that he had penetrated both the internal and external realms and they alternated as guest and host, his spirit, soul, and consciousness suddenly forgot their point of return.
Thereupon, Māra seized the opportunity to enter his innermost heart, causing his physical form to undergo transformations.
Undergoing various transformations, they preach the Dharma without cause, claiming to have attained the subtle meaning.
How could they not believe that they have been able to shatter the aggregate of form and are no longer constrained by the phenomena of form? Yet they do not realize that they are possessed by Māra.
These ten cases all arise from the diligent investigation of wondrous clarity, employing the mind of *dhyāna* while still harboring firm and solid delusions.
In this clash, form cannot immediately become emptiness, nor can emptiness immediately become form; as they contend for victory and defeat, they cannot achieve total integration.
This is the demon of the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha), which seizes the opportunity to enter. Sentient beings are stubborn and deluded;
they do not measure themselves to see how their own daily realization compares to that of the Buddha, nor how their daily practice and cultivation compare to his.
It is like this: upon casually encountering such a state, one immediately regards it as a holy realization.

Taking what is not holy to be holy, and what is not a realization to be a realization, one is internally deluded by the demon of the aggregates (*skandha-māra*) and externally influenced by the celestial demon (*deva-māra*). Having committed a great falsehood, one falls into the Avīci Hell—truly a cause for compassion.
Therefore, the World-Honored One, wishing to proclaim [this teaching] during the Age of Dharma-Decline (*mappō*), seeks to protect sentient beings and enable them to achieve the Unsurpassed Way.

Furthermore, if one’s spiritual power has reached such a point that they are able to break through the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), even when the aforementioned phenomena manifest, there are many in the Chan school who do not interpret them with a mind seeking saintliness.
For example, once Chan Master Gēhú Zhífú did not go to the hall for assembly.
When an attendant came to invite him to the hall, Zhífú said, "Today I have eaten my fill of oil-cakes at the manor."
The man said, "The Master has never entered or left. Fu said, "You simply go and ask the master of the estate.
Just as the man was about to step out the door, he suddenly saw the estate master coming to thank the Master for visiting the estate to eat oil-cakes (*youti*).
Is this not proof that the body can pass through obstructions? One day, a woman came to pay her respects to Chan Master Ruiyan. Ruiyan said, "You must leave quickly."
He returned to rescue several thousand living beings. When the old woman returned home, she saw her daughter-in-law gathering field snails; she then released them.
Furthermore, when Zen Master Zu Zhao perceived events within dozens of li while in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), no one had ever known of it.
Later, because a monk from Zhuang heard of his transgression, he went out and publicized it abroad. Zhao feared...
They delude the masses and then enter parinirvāṇa; all of these are capable [of such feats] yet do not regard them as proof of saintliness.

Ānanda, when those good men practice samādhi, within śamatha, once the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) is exhausted, they see the minds of the Buddhas appearing like reflections manifested in a clear mirror. Yet, though they perceive them, they have not yet mastered their use, just as...

When one is under the influence of a nightmare, the hands and feet appear as usual, and what is seen and heard is not confused; yet because the mind has been contacted by an external malevolent spirit, one cannot move.
This is called the domain of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). If the affliction of the nightmare ceases, the mind detaches from the body and turns back to observe its own face;

going and staying become free, and there is no longer any obstruction. This is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of sensation. Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*) and contemplate...
The cause is that false, luminous delusion serves as its root. Ānanda, when that virtuous man is within this state, he attains a great radiance;
yet because his mind’s illumination is internally excessive, he suddenly gives rise to boundless compassion at that moment.
In this way, even when observing mosquitoes and gadflies, one regards them as if they were infants; a heart of compassion arises, and one involuntarily sheds tears.

This is called the suppression and overcoming of transgressions through deliberate effort. If one awakens to this, there is no fault; it is not yet a realization of sainthood. If one maintains clear awareness and remains free from delusion, [one will progress].

After a long time, it will naturally subside and vanish. If you mistake this for a realization of the holy state (*ārya*), then the demon of sorrow (*śoka-māra*) will enter your heart and viscera. Upon seeing others, you will feel grief and weep uncontrollably;
you will lose your correct meditative absorption (*samyak-samādhi*) and shall surely fall into ruin.

Ānanda, furthermore, among those good sons in that state of concentration, when the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has dissolved and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becomes clear, a superior sign manifests before them. If they are moved to excess by this, they may suddenly—

Within this, infinite courage arises; his mind becomes fierce and sharp, and his resolve equals that of all Buddhas. He claims that the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* can be transcended in a single thought-moment.
This is called "transcending through forceful effort and haste. If he awakens to this as such, there is no fault; it is not a true realization of the holy state.

If he understands this and remains undeluded, [the affliction] will naturally subside after a long time. If, however, he takes this to be a holy attainment, then a mad demon will enter his heart and viscera. Upon seeing people...
Then they become boastful; their self-conceit is peerless. Their minds reach such a state that they see no Buddha above and no human below.

They lose right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*) and shall inevitably fall into ruin. Furthermore, among those good sons within that meditative state, when the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has dissolved and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becomes clear, they find no new realization before them and lose their former dwelling behind them.
Their power of wisdom declines, and they enter a state of collapse in the midst of their progress, leaving them utterly destitute.
Upon seeing this, a great parching thirst suddenly arises within the mind; at all times, one dwells upon it with undistracted recollection, taking this to be the mark of diligent vigor.
This is called "cultivating the mind without wisdom and thereby losing oneself. If one awakens to this as such, there is no fault;

it is not a holy realization. If one interprets it as a holy realization, then the demon of recollection will enter one's heart and viscera, seizing the mind morning and evening and suspending it [in agitation].

In one instance, having lost right concentration (*samādhi*), they shall fall into ruin. Furthermore, within that state of meditative absorption, those sons of good family perceive the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) dissolving and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becoming clear.
Their power of wisdom exceeds their concentration, yet they lose its sharp intensity;

harboring various superior qualities within their minds, they themselves suspect their own minds to be Vairocana (translated here as "Pure Fulfillment"). Believing this meager attainment to be sufficient, this is called "misapplying the mind."
They forget constant discernment and sink into mere intellectual views; though there is no fault in awakening from this state, it does not constitute a realization of the holy.

If they mistake this for a holy attainment, then the demon of inferiority and easy contentment will enter their hearts and bellies. Seeing others, they will claim for themselves, "I have attained the unsurpassed ultimate truth.
Having lost right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*), they shall surely fall into ruin. Furthermore, among those good men within that meditative absorption:

Seeing that the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has dissolved and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) has become clear, one has not yet attained a new realization, yet the former mind has already perished.
Surveying these two boundaries, one naturally encounters hardship and peril; suddenly, within the mind, an inexhaustible anxiety arises, like sitting upon an iron bed or drinking a lethal poison.
The mind has no desire to live; it constantly seeks out others to end its life so as to attain liberation early.

This is called practicing while failing in skillful means. If one awakens to this, there is no fault; it is not a sign of saintly realization. If one takes this to be a sign of saintly realization, then a demon of constant sorrow will enter one’s heart and viscera to a certain extent.
Grasping a sword or blade in hand, one will cut off one’s own flesh, taking pleasure in relinquishing one’s life.

Or they may be constantly filled with sorrow and flee into the mountains and forests, unable to bear the sight of others; having lost their right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*), they shall fall into ruin.

Furthermore, within that state of meditative absorption, those sons of good family see the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) dissolve and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanāskandha*) become clear and manifest, abiding in purity.
After the mind has become settled and secure, suddenly an infinite joy arises spontaneously within it; the heart is filled with such rapture that one cannot restrain it.

This is called "pliancy" (praśrabdhi) without wisdom acting as its own restraint. To realize this is not a fault, but it is not a realization of the Holy Path. If you mistake it for such a realization, [you will fall into error].
Then, a portion of the Māra of Delightful Pleasure will enter their heart and core; upon seeing people, they will laugh.
Beside the roads, they will sing and dance by themselves, claiming to have already attained unimpeded liberation, yet they have lost right concentration and are destined for downfall.

Furthermore, within that state of meditative concentration, those good sons perceive the dissolution of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and the clarity of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).

Believing themselves to have reached sufficiency, they suddenly experience groundless great conceit (*māna*), extending even to pride (*māna*), excessive pride (*atimāna*), and pride beyond pride (*mānātimāna*).

Whether it be overweening pride or inferiority complex, they may arise simultaneously; such that one’s mind still holds even the Tathāgatas of the ten directions in contempt, let alone those of lower rank, the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
This is called "seeing oneself as superior while lacking the wisdom to save oneself. If one awakens to this, there shall be no fault.
This is not a sign of attaining the state of a sage. If one mistakes this for such an attainment, then a portion of the great demon of self-conceit will enter their heart and inner being.
They will cease to pay homage to stupas and temples and will destroy scriptures and images, saying to their donors: "These are merely gold and copper, or perhaps clay and wood."
The sutras are made of tree leaves or woven flowers; the physical body is true and eternal. To fail to show reverence to it, while instead venerating earth and wood, is truly a perversion.
Those with deep faith should destroy such objects and bury them in the ground, lest they mislead sentient beings.
They will enter the Avīci Hell and lose their right concentration, destined for a downward fall.

Furthermore, within that state of meditative absorption, those sons of good family see the aggregate of form dissolve and the aggregate of sensation become clear; within this clarity and vigor, they perfectly realize the subtle principle and attain great accordance.
Suddenly, an immeasurable sense of lightness and ease arises in their minds; they then claim to have attained the state of a sage and achieved great mastery.
This is called attaining various states of lightness and purity through wisdom. If one awakens to this as such, there is no fault; it is not yet the realization of a sage.

If, however, one takes this to be the realization of a sage, then a portion of the "demon of attachment to lightness and purity" will enter their heart and innermost being. They will then consider themselves fulfilled and no longer seek further progress. Many such cases occur.
The unlearned bhikṣu misleads sentient beings with his doubts and errors; he falls into the Avīci Hell and loses right concentration, destined for further descent.

Furthermore, within that samādhi, those sons of good family see the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) dissolve and the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) become clear. Within this clarity and awakening, they...
One attains a nature of empty luminosity. Within this state, one suddenly turns toward eternal extinction, repudiating cause and effect and entering exclusively into emptiness.

When the mind of emptiness manifests before one, even if a long-standing understanding of annihilation arises within the mind, there is no fault in such awakening; yet it does not constitute a holy realization.
If one forms a holy understanding [of this], then the demon of emptiness will enter their heart and viscera;

they will then slander those who uphold the precepts, calling them followers of the Small Vehicle, claiming that since Bodhisattvas have realized emptiness, what is there to be upheld or transgressed? Such a person will constantly drink wine and eat meat before faithful donors.
They engage extensively in lewd and impure acts. By means of the power of Māra, they captivate those before them so that no suspicion or slander arises.

Once the ghost’s mind has long since entered them, they may consume excrement and urine, as well as wine and meat; all such things are equally empty. Thus they violate the Buddha’s disciplinary code and lead others into sin by error.

They will lose their right concentration and fall into ruin. Furthermore, among those sons of good family within that state of meditative absorption, when the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has dissolved and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becomes clear, they relish its empty luminosity, which penetrates deep into the marrow of their bones. Suddenly, an infinite craving arises within their minds.

When attachment reaches its extreme, it gives rise to madness, which is then termed greed and desire. This is called a state of meditative concentration that appears peaceful and harmonious as it enters the mind;
lacking wisdom to sustain oneself, one mistakenly enters into various desires. If one awakens to this, there is no fault, for it is not a realization of the holy.

If one takes it to be a holy realization, then the demon of desire will enter one's heart and viscera, leading one to constantly claim that desire is the path to Bodhi, converting laypeople and practicing desire with them indiscriminately.
Those who engage in sexual misconduct are called "sons who uphold the Dharma. By the power of spirits and ghosts, they gather ordinary and ignorant people during the final age;
their number reaches one hundred, and thus even up to one hundred or two hundred, or five, six, or seven hundred, until it fills many thousands or tens of millions.
The Mara’s mind felt revulsion and departed from his body. Deprived of his majestic power, he fell into royal peril, misled sentient beings, and entered the Avīci Hell.
He lost his right concentration and was destined for a downward fall, Ānanda.

These ten kinds of visionary states appearing during dhyāna are all caused by the interaction between the mind and the skandha of sensation; therefore, these phenomena manifest. Sentient beings are stubborn and deluded, failing to recognize this themselves.
Reflecting upon this, when encountering such causes and conditions, they become deluded and fail to recognize themselves, claiming instead that they have attained the state of a sage.

Having committed a great falsehood, they fall into the Avīci Hell. You all should likewise take the words of the Tathāgata and, after my parinirvāṇa, transmit them during the Final Dharma age, causing all sentient beings everywhere to awaken to this meaning.
Do not allow celestial Māras to find an opportunity; maintain and protect [this teaching] so that it may be perfected.
The Master said:
"If the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has not yet dissolved, the mind remains attached to form; thus one perceives various extraordinary realms, yet the demons have not yet entered the mind.
When the aggregate of form ceases but the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) remains, 'sensation' refers to the empty capacity of the first five consciousnesses."
The capacity to receive illumination can apprehend objects, appearing like reflections manifested within a bright mirror. This empty and luminous essence ought to be the Buddha-mind;
why then is it considered a deluded thought? It is merely that one gives rise to a single attachment, desiring to realize it as a truly attained reality.
This is what it means to be shrouded by the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*); thus, it cannot be called "right reception" (*samyag-vedanā*).

Therefore, as long as the aggregate of sensation has not been shattered, one does not depart from the five faculties (*pañcendriya*). It is like the mind being contacted by an external malevolence and bound by a nightmare;

although there is a sense of empty clarity, it cannot be employed. Once the aggregate of sensation is shattered, clarity no longer depends on the faculties. It is like when the affliction of the nightmare has ceased; the mind—

Moving and staying are free and easy, yet one is able to turn back and observe one's own face. When emptiness and luminosity function freely, one immediately transcends the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*).
When the faculty of sight grasps various objects, they interweave to form turbidity; now that emptiness and luminosity are no longer obstructed, this is the prior uprooting of that view.
Once the root of the faculty of sight has been uprooted, who is there for the view to grasp as its object, such that it would act upon them?
"Turbid" means that the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) has not yet been dissolved and the mind has not yet emitted light. Once the aggregate of form is exhausted, one attains great radiance;
this, however, is merely the delusion of empty luminosity. One who possesses true awakening regards even this empty luminosity as belonging to the realm of objects.

Only by refining the wondrous clarity and suppressing [the mind] excessively within does one reach the ultimate state of forgetting the self, such that all things are seen as oneself. Thus, when looking at a mosquito...
When one views a gadfly as an infant, compassion arises; when the void-clarity manifests before one, the emotion of gratitude becomes excessive.

Thus, one thinks that the Buddhas may be equaled, and a spirit of valor is born. If meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is strong while wisdom (*prajñā*) is slight, then between the new and the old, there is a profound lack of reliance.
Consequently, memories sink in without dispersing, and the mind hangs upon a single point, which one mistakenly considers to be diligence. If the power of wisdom exceeds [that of concentration]...
In a state of meditative concentration, one may then doubt whether one is a Buddha oneself; easily giving rise to complacency, one becomes mired in intellectual views.

One claims for oneself that one has already attained the light of universal illumination, thinking not only that one can equal all Buddhas, but even surpassing them. Losing one's footing in both advancement and retreat, one creates hardship for oneself, saying:
"I have a great affliction because I possess this body; I shall constantly seek to end my life so as to attain liberation early. Thus it is not so.
Once the mind has settled in recollection without distraction, and having attained peace and stability within purity, the anxieties of hardship and peril no longer arise;
thus, infinite joy is born. Having attained this joy and unimpeded liberation, one loses all restraint in song and dance.
This is because one lacks wisdom to restrain oneself. When one is excessively joyful and self-satisfied, great *asmimāna* (conceit) arises.
There are seven types of conceit: namely, *māna*, *atimāna*, *mānātimāna*, *abhimāna*, *ūnamāna*, *asmimāna*, and *mithyāmāna*.

*Mana* (pride) is a lack of respect. *Adhimāna* (excessive pride) refers to being proud because one considers oneself superior to others. *Mānātimāna* (pride beyond pride) combines both types of pride;

it is not only a lack of respect but also the deliberate act of treating others with contempt. *Abhimāna* (conceit) refers to considering oneself superior. *Ūnamāna* (inferiority pride) [refers to considering oneself inferior when one is actually equal].

Because one is arrogant toward those who are superior and venerable, it is *asmimāna* (the conceit "I am"). Because one reckons that there is a self within the aggregates (*skandha*), and because of this *asmimāna*, it is *mithyāmāna* (false conceit).

Because it takes what is correct as being correct, and because one takes the True Dharma as an object of focus during meditative concentration, it is not called *mithyāmāna*. To claim superiority over what has not yet been attained is [conceit];

to boast of one's own inferiority while being lowly is [conceit]. Thus, one is arrogant toward those who are superior and venerable. If one possesses the power of wisdom, one will achieve perfect realization.

The subtle principle is that when form dissolves, luminosity becomes perfect and one attains great pliancy (*praśrabdhi*). Pliancy is among the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*), and its essential nature belongs to meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
If concentration is conjoined with wisdom (*prajñā*), the Noble Path can be traversed; yet, if one is satisfied with this alone and seeks no further progress, [the path remains obstructed].
Sitting within a light and pure cave, he is thus called an unlearned bhikṣu.

If, through the purity of equanimity and mindfulness, he enters exclusively into emptiness and gives rise to the understanding of annihilationism, thereby repudiating cause and effect and slandering the observance of precepts as the fruit of the Hīnayāna.
When a Bodhisattva realizes emptiness, there is neither observance nor violation; thus, they may break the monastic precepts (*vinaya*).

Although such a person considers themselves to have attained transcendence, they do not realize they are being driven by Māra. When the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is empty and luminous, if one does not crave its flavor, then desire will not arise.
Only when craving reaches its extreme does madness erupt, leading one mistakenly into various desires; thus, affliction and desire become two.
The object and the [affliction] arise simultaneously. Tiantai said: "Desires and forms have arisen since birth; these may be suppressed and halted.
But what arises now is an affliction of such blazing intensity that, upon encountering external objects, the mind goes mad and the eyes grow dark, like a sleeping lion that roars when touched."
If one does not recognize them, they can lead a person to commit great and heavy sins. A single thought of attachment brings such poisonous influence as this;
because it clings to the state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), its manifestation is most fierce and its harm is greatest.
These ten types all arise from attaining a nature of empty luminosity, whereby the mind of *dhyāna* and the deluded thoughts of empty luminosity interact with one another.
Because of victory and defeat, each has their own attachments. If one acts with madness, recollection, pride, or sorrow, or engages in sexual misconduct, know that this is an attachment to Māra.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Māra can enter the minds of all sentient beings, causing them to take refuge in his faction."

Like glue and lacquer, even if one’s hands were severed or one’s arms cut off, one would not consider it difficult. When one is firmly grasped by the power of Māra, the situation is exactly like this;
yet when security and pliancy are attained and the empty mind manifests before one, one gains self-confidence that one is a Buddha—how could one then fail to lose oneself in right concentration?

In truth, one who is in right samādhi is never without emptiness, and is never without clarity; yet, in the end, they do not form a conceptual understanding of "emptiness-clarity. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* says:
"Deeply attached to false and illusory dharmas, they stubbornly cling to them and refuse to let go; thus they slander those who uphold the precepts and the like.
Therefore, to harbor merely the view of a Buddha within one's breast is itself Māra. This is seen in the case of Xiu of the Northern School, whom Jiangmochang encountered. Xiu—
[The Master] asked, "Your name is 'Subduer of Māras. Here there are no mountain spirits or forest monsters; have you yourself become a Māra?
He replied, "Where there is a Buddha, there is a Māra. Xiu said, "If you are a Māra, you must dwell in the inconceivable realm.
He replied, "Even this Buddha is empty; what realm could there be? Furthermore, Master Zhilin would frequently scold Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra, calling them "spirits."
There was a sorcerer who held a wooden sword and claimed he could subdue demons. As soon as he saw a monk come to visit him for instruction, he would cry out, "A demon has come!
A demon has come! and brandish his sword wildly. He returned to his quarters in this manner for ten years; thereafter, he set aside his sword and remained silent.
A monk asked, "Before twelve years had passed, why did you subdue the māras? He replied, "Thieves do not strike the homes of the poor.

The monk asked, "After twelve years had passed, why did you no longer subdue the māras? He replied, "Thieves do not strike the homes of the poor; therefore, it was only by means of non-subduing that I subdued the māras.
Since I subdued the māras through non-subduing, if there were two ways of subduing the māras, one would truly not be acting as a sage."
This is one who understands through the mind. It is precisely because he does not produce a "sage-mind" that this is not the work of Māra.

When Linji arrived at the stupa of the First Patriarch, the temple attendant said, "Should you first pay homage to the Buddha or first pay homage to the Patriarch? Linji replied, "I pay homage to neither the Buddha nor the Patriarch.
The attendant asked, "What grievance do you have with the Buddha and the Patriarch? Linji shook his sleeves and departed. This was not a failure to pay homage to the stupa.
Regarding the term "temple" (miào): once, while at Huilin Monastery, Danxia encountered a great cold. He took a wooden Buddha and burned it for fire.
The head monk of the monastery rebuked him, saying, "How can you burn my wooden Buddha? Danxia prodded the ashes with his staff and said, "I am burning it to retrieve the *śarīra*.
The head monk said, "A wooden Buddha—how could it have *śarīra*? Danxia replied, "Since there are no *śarīra*, take another one."
The two venerable ones were cremated. Subsequently, the Master’s own beard and eyebrows fell out. Tizi took up the case, saying, "Not knowing how to be a guest, you trouble the host.
He then offered this verse: "Upon the ancient crag, moss seals the door; cold seeps through the panels. Those who fly are struck with alarm; those who run are lost."
Deep in the night, the fires of Tingzhou burn with cold intensity; at dawn, the fisherman suddenly falls into doubt: "Is this not someone destroying scriptures and images?

It is precisely because the masters of the two monasteries harbor demons of Buddhas and patriarchs, and demons of scriptures and images within their chests that Linji and Danxia employ extraordinary means to uproot them—yet they ultimately fail to awaken. This is the realm of the great man.
This realm is not known by ordinary people; how true it is!

Ānanda, when that son of good family practices samādhi and the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) is exhausted, although his outflows (āsrava) are not yet ended, his mind detaches from its physical form like a bird escaping from a cage.
He is already able to achieve this, ascending from this ordinary body through the sixty stages of the Bodhisattvas.
The stage of the Sage. Attaining the mind-born body (*manomayakāya*), one proceeds everywhere without obstruction. It is like a person who, while in deep sleep, utters words in a dream;
although that person has no distinct awareness, the words they speak possess rhythmic cadence and sequential order, causing those who are not asleep to fully understand their meaning.
This is called the domain of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). If all stirring thoughts cease and floating perceptions are eliminated, then within awakening—

The mind is clarified, like dust and grime being removed. When one cycle of birth and death is fully illuminated from beginning to end, it is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*). Observe its origin: deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*) serves as its root. Ānanda,
When that good man’s aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) has become empty and subtle, and he is not beset by perverse thoughts, his perfect concentration gives rise to illumination.

Within this *samādhi*, his mind comes to cherish perfect clarity; he sharpens his refined contemplation and greedily seeks out skillful methods. At that time, the celestial Māra watches for an opportunity to exploit him.

A flying spirit may possess a person, who then speaks of the sutras and the Dharma. The person, unaware that they are possessed by a demon, claims for themselves that they have attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*.
They come to the place of a seeker of skillful means—a son of good family—and arrange a seat to preach the Dharma;
their form may momentarily appear as a bhikṣu so that the person may see them, or they may become Śakra, or a woman, or a bhikṣuṇī.
Or while sleeping in a dark room, their bodies emit a brilliant light. Such people are deluded and confused, mistaking themselves for Bodhisattvas;

they believe in their teachings, which agitate their minds, causing them to violate the Buddha’s precepts and secretly indulge in lustful desires. They are fond of speaking of calamities, auspicious signs, and supernatural transformations.
Some claim that the Tathāgata has appeared in such-and-such a place; others speak of the kalpa-ending fire or of weapons.
They terrify people, causing their family wealth to dissipate without cause. These are called "strange ghosts" who have grown old and become demons, vexing and disturbing these people.
A sense of satiety arises in the mind, and it departs from the person’s body. Both the disciple and the teacher fall into royal peril.
You should be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth; if you are deluded and unaware, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.

Ānanda, furthermore, when a good man’s aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becomes empty and subtle, he is no longer beset by perverse thoughts. Within the samādhi that illuminates through perfect concentration, his mind comes to love wandering and flight. His...

They contemplate with intense focus and greedily seek out experiences. At that time, a celestial Māra watches for an opportunity and sends his essence to possess a person, who then speaks the Dharma and the scriptures with their own mouth.
The person does not realize they are possessed by a Māra, and claims to have personally attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*.

He comes to the place of those good sons seeking spiritual travel, spreads out a seat, and preaches the Dharma; his own physical form undergoes no change. Those listening to the Dharma suddenly find themselves...
They see their own bodies seated upon jeweled lotus flowers, their entire forms transformed into a mass of purple-gold light;

every member of the assembly perceives themselves thus, attaining what they have never experienced before. These people are deluded and confused, mistaking themselves for Bodhisattvas. Their minds are licentious and dissolute, and they violate the Buddha’s precepts, secretly indulging in greed and desire.
They delight in saying that various Buddhas have appeared in the world, claiming that such-and-such a person at such-and-such a place must be [an emanation of a Buddha].
"A certain Buddha has manifested an emanation here; such-and-such a person is actually a certain Bodhisattva and others who have come to transform the human realm.

Because that person sees them, a longing arises in their heart, yet false views secretly emerge and the wisdom of all-knowledge is extinguished. This is called a *pūtana* ghost; having grown old, it becomes a demon.
It harasses and disturbs this person until its desires are satisfied, at which point it leaves the person's body. Both the disciple and the teacher fall into ruin."
This is the peril of kings. You should perceive it beforehand; do not enter into the cycle of rebirth. If you are deluded and unaware, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.

Furthermore, O virtuous man, when the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) becomes empty and subtle, and you are not beset by perverse thoughts, such that through the manifestation of perfect concentration you enter the samādhi, your mind may come to cherish a lingering attachment.
As you clarify your refined contemplation and greedily seek a point of accord, the celestial Māra will watch for his opportunity and dispatch a refined spirit—

He attaches himself to a person and speaks of the Dharma with his mouth. That person is actually unaware that they are possessed by a māra, and they also claim to have personally attained unsurpassed nirvāṇa.
He comes to the place where the seeker of the Way, the son of good family, resides, spreads out a seat, and preaches the Dharma.
His form and those listening to the Dharma appear externally unchanged; yet he causes those listeners, even before hearing the Dharma, to experience spontaneous awakening in every thought-moment.
They undergo transformations. Some attain the knowledge of past lives; some attain the knowledge of others' minds; some see the hells;
or they know all manner of good and evil affairs among humans. Some speak verses aloud; some recite sutras themselves. Each finds joy and delight, attaining what they have never experienced before.

Such people are deluded and confused, mistaking themselves for Bodhisattvas. They harbor deep attachment in their hearts, violating the Buddha’s rules of discipline, and secretly practice lust. From their mouths...

They delight in saying that there are great and small Buddhas, that such-and-such a Buddha was a former Buddha and such-and-such a Buddha was a later Buddha, and that among them there are true Buddhas and false Buddhas, male Buddhas and female Buddhas;
the same applies to Bodhisattvas. Because such people hold these views, they wash away their original mind and easily fall into deviant enlightenment.
These are called "possessing ghosts" (*mèiguǐ*); having grown old, they become demons (*mó*). They harass and disturb this person until they feel satisfied, at which point they depart from him.
Regarding the human body: if both disciple and teacher fall into royal peril, you must be the first to awaken so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*).

If you are deluded and ignorant, you will fall into the Avīci Hell. Furthermore, O good man, when the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becomes empty and subtle, and you are not beset by demonic influences, the perfect concentration (*samādhi*) will manifest.

Within this *samādhi*, if your mind loves the fundamental source and exhaustively investigates the transformation of things—the beginning and end of their nature—your spirit will become refined and clear.

When their minds greedily seek analytical discernment, the celestial Māra seizes the opportunity to manifest. He hovers over a person, causing his essence to possess them; the possessed one speaks the teachings of the Sūtras with their own mouth.
That person was previously unaware they were possessed by a demon, and they also claim to have personally attained unsurpassed Nirvāṇa.

They come to the place of that seeker of the fundamental source, a good man, where they arrange seats and preach the Dharma. Their body possesses majestic spiritual power, which subdues and overcomes the seekers, causing them—

Though they had not yet heard the Dharma while seated there, their minds were naturally subdued. These people regarded the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa* and *bodhi-dharmakāya* as being none other than the physical bodies of flesh present before them;
that fathers and sons, generation after generation, mutually giving birth to one another, was itself the eternally abiding *dharmakāya* without interruption.
They pointed to the present moment as the very Land of Buddhas, seeing no separate Pure Abodes or Golden [World].

Regarding their physical appearance, such people believe and accept [their claims], losing their former resolve; they surrender their bodies and lives in devotion, attaining what they have never experienced before.
These deluded and confused individuals mistake them for Bodhisattvas. Upon investigating their hearts, one finds they violate the Buddha’s precepts and secretly practice lustful desires.
They are fond of saying that the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue are all pure lands, and that the male and female organs are themselves Bodhi and Nirvana.
In truth, there is no such thing; those who believe this are merely speaking defiled words. This is called a malevolent spirit of pestilence or a haunting demon;
having grown old, it becomes a mara that torments and disturbs the person. Once its desires are satisfied, it leaves the person’s body, and both the disciple and the master fall into royal peril.
You must be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth; if you are deluded and unaware, you will fall into the Avīci Hell. Furthermore, O virtuous one...

When a man’s faculties are refined and subtle, yet his inner essence remains hollow, he escapes from perverse thoughts and attains a brilliant illumination within perfect concentration (*samādhi*). Within this state of *samādhi*, his mind longs for a responsive resonance;

he circulates through his studies with intense scrutiny, greedily seeking a hidden spiritual response. At that time, a celestial demon (*devaputra-māra*) watches for such an opportunity and hovers over a person, causing its essence to possess them.
This demon speaks the teachings of the sutras, while the man, unaware that he is possessed by a demon, likewise claims to have attained the Unsurpassed Way himself.
Nirvāṇa. He comes to the place where those seeking the response—good sons—reside, spreads his seat, and preaches the Dharma.
He is able to cause the listeners to behold his body for as long as a hundred thousand years; their hearts give rise to affection and attachment, such that they cannot bear to part from him.
They become his servants, providing the four types of offerings without feeling weary. Each person among those in his assembly comes to know that this former teacher was originally virtuous.
Knowledge. They give rise to a distinct craving for dharmas that is as sticky as glue or lacquer; they experience what they have never had before.
These people are deluded and confused, mistaking themselves for Bodhisattvas. They draw near to their minds, violating the Buddha's precepts and secretly practicing lust. They are fond of saying:
"In a previous life, during such-and-such a birth, I first delivered such-and-such a person; at that time, he was my wife, concubine, or brother. Now he has come..."
He will falsely claim, "I shall accompany you back to such-and-such a world to make offerings to such-and-such a Buddha," or say, "There is another realm of Great Radiance where a Buddha dwells;
it is the place where all Tathāgatas rest. Those who do not know the truth will believe these deceptive words, lose their original resolve, and fall under his influence.
This is called a *rākṣasa* ghost who has become a demon in old age; he will harass and disturb this person until he is satiated.
A thought arises that causes the spirit to leave the person’s body; both the disciple and the teacher will then fall into royal peril.
You should be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth; if you are deluded and unaware, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.

Furthermore, O virtuous man, when the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) becomes empty and subtle, and you are not beset by deviant thoughts, you will manifest clarity within the samādhi of perfect concentration. Your mind will then desire to penetrate further, and through diligent self-discipline, you will delight in dwelling therein.

The aggregates are quiescent; he seeks stillness and silence. At that time, a celestial Māra seizes the opportunity and sends his essence to possess a person, who speaks the teachings of the sūtras with their own mouth.
That person was originally unaware they were possessed by a Māra, and they likewise claim to have personally attained unsurpassed nirvāṇa.
They come to the place of the good son who seeks the aggregates, arrange seats, and preach the Dharma, causing those who listen to each recognize their own past karma. Or, at times...
There, he spoke to one man, saying, "Though you have not yet died, you have already become an animal.

He commanded another man to step on his tail from behind, causing the first man to be instantly unable to rise. At this, the entire assembly bowed their hearts in humble submission. Some people gave rise to [doubtful] thoughts;
having already discerned the source of this, they acted outside the Buddha’s Vinaya, intensifying their ascetic hardships and slandering and reviling the bhikṣus.

The followers will expose private matters, not avoiding public censure or suspicion. They will delight in speaking of future calamities and blessings, which, when the time comes, will be accurate down to the finest detail.
This is a powerful ghost who has grown old and become a demon; he will harass and disturb these people until he becomes satiated, at which point he will leave their bodies.
Both the disciples and the teacher will then fall into royal punishment. You must be aware of this beforehand so that you do not enter [into such a state].
They wander in saṃsāra, deluded and ignorant, falling into the Avīci Hell.

Furthermore, when a good man’s aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becomes empty and subtle, and he is not beset by perverse thoughts, yet within this samādhi of perfect concentration and luminous clarity, his mind comes to cherish knowledge and vision; he applies himself with diligent effort to investigate and seek after past lives.
At that time, a celestial Māra seizes the opportunity, dispatching a refined spirit to possess a person, who then speaks of sūtras and the Dharma. This person—
He was entirely unaware that he was possessed by a māra, yet he claimed to have attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*.

He went to the place where that seeker of the Dharma, the son of good family, resided, spread out his seat, and preached the Dharma. Without cause, that man obtained a great precious jewel at the site of the preaching.
At times, that māra would transform into an animal, with its mouth holding the jewel, as well as various rare treasures, books, scrolls, and talismans. All these were marvelous.
He gives strange objects to people first, and later they are worn upon their bodies;
or he entices listeners by hiding bright moon-jewels underground that illuminate the spot, so that these listeners experience what they have never known before.

He eats many medicinal herbs but does not consume fine delicacies, or at times eats only one sesame seed and one grain of barley per day, yet his body remains plump and full because Māra’s power sustains him. Thus he slanders [the Buddha].
Bhikṣu, you revile the assembly and do not avoid reproach and suspicion.

You are fond of speaking in your mouth of hidden treasures in other regions and the secret lairs of sages and worthies from the ten directions. Those who follow after you often encounter strange and extraordinary people;
these are spirits of mountains, forests, lands, city walls, rivers, and peaks who have grown old and become demons. Some of them propagate lust and destroy the Buddha-dharma.

Regarding the precepts: if one secretly indulges in the five desires with those who serve them, or if there are those who practice asceticism, subsisting solely on grasses and trees, and through erratic conduct cause distress to such people, they will become weary and satisfied, depart from the person's body, and cause both the disciple and the teacher to fall into royal peril.
You should perceive this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth; if you are deluded and unaware, you will fall into the Avīci Hell. Furthermore, O virtuous one—

When a man’s faculties are refined and subtle, yet his mind is not free from perverse thoughts, and he has attained a clarity through perfect concentration (*samādhi*), he may then come to cherish supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and various transformations within that state.
He investigates the source of these transformations and greedily seeks divine power. At that time, a celestial demon (*deva-māra*) watches for such an opportunity;
it flies its essence into a person, who then speaks the sutras and the Dharma. The man is truly unaware that he is possessed by a demon, and he likewise says:
