Having attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa* himself, he comes to the place where that son of good family who seeks supernatural powers resides, spreads his seat, and preaches the Dharma.
This person may then take fire in his hand and, grasping that light with his hand, distribute it over the heads of the fourfold assembly who are listening.
On the heads of all these listeners, the fire-light reaches several feet in length; yet it lacks the quality of heat and never burns them. Or [he may use] water...
He walked upward as if treading on level ground; sometimes he sat motionless in mid-air, or entered into a jar, or stayed within a sack.
He passed through windows and pierced through walls without ever encountering any obstruction. Only regarding weapons did he lack mastery.
Claiming for himself to be a Buddha, he wore white robes and accepted the prostrations of bhikṣus. He slandered dhyāna and the Vinaya, reviled his followers, and exposed their secrets.

Regarding human affairs, they do not avoid scandal or suspicion. They constantly speak of supernatural powers and mastery while in their mouths; or again, they cause people to see Buddha-lands by the side.
These are the delusions of ghosts' powers and possess no reality. They praise sexual misconduct and do not condemn coarse behavior, taking various vulgarities as the transmission of the Dharma.
These are called the great-power mountain spirits, sea spirits, wind spirits, and river spirits of heaven and earth.

The essence of the earth; the accumulated essences and malevolent spirits of all grasses and trees over many kalpas; or again, dragon-spirits; or immortals whose lives have ended but who return to life as spirits;

or those whose period of immortality has expired and, according to their reckoning, should die, yet whose forms do not dissolve and become possessed by other monsters, aging into demons that harass and disturb these people;
once they have become satiated and the thought of leaving arises, they depart from the person’s body, causing both the disciples and the teacher to fall into ruin.
"O King, you must be forewarned. If you do not enter into the cycle of rebirth, yet remain deluded and ignorant, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.

Furthermore, O virtuous man, when the aggregate of perception (*vedanā-skandha*) becomes empty and subtle, and you are no longer beset by perverse thoughts, your perfect concentration (*samādhi*) will manifest clarity.

Within this *samādhi*, if your mind comes to love the entry into cessation (*nirodha*) and you investigate the nature of transformation, greedily seeking the profound emptiness, at that time the celestial Māra will wait for his opportunity and dispatch his refined essence."

He attaches himself to a person and speaks the Dharma of the sutras with their mouth; yet that person never realizes they are possessed by a māra, and they even claim to have personally attained unsurpassed nirvāṇa.
He comes to the place of a son of good family who seeks emptiness, spreads out a seat, and preaches the Dharma.
In the midst of the great assembly, his form suddenly becomes empty, and the multitude sees nothing. Then he suddenly emerges from the void, appearing and disappearing at will. Or he manifests...
Their bodies were translucent like lapis lazuli. Sometimes their hands and feet emitted the fragrance of sandalwood; sometimes their excrement and urine were like thick rock honey.

They slandered the precepts and held those who have left the household life in contempt. Constantly they spoke of the non-existence of cause and effect, asserting that upon one death there is eternal extinction and no further rebirths, nor any distinction between ordinary beings and sages.
Though they attained a state of empty stillness, they secretly indulged in lustful desires and received [their karmic retribution].
Those who harbor desire may also attain a state of empty mind, thereby repudiating cause and effect. This is known as the vital energy of solar and lunar eclipses;
it is like gold, jade, *zhicao* fungi, qilin, phoenixes, tortoises, and cranes that, after passing through thousands of myriads of years, do not die but become spirits.

These emerge in the land and, when old, become demons to harass and disturb such people. Once they have become satiated and their minds are fulfilled, they depart from the person's body. Both disciples and masters often fall into [this trap].
This is the peril of kingship. You should perceive it beforehand; do not enter into saṃsāra. If you are deluded and unaware, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.
Furthermore, O son of good family, when the skandha of sensation is empty and subtle, and you are not beset by deviant thoughts, the perfect concentration (samādhi) becomes manifest.

Within this samādhi, if your mind longs for longevity and you laboriously investigate the subtlest points, greedily seeking eternal years and abandoning the coarse process of birth and death to suddenly hope for the subtle signs of the transformation-death (pariṇāma-maraṇa), [you shall fall].
While it remains thus, at that time the celestial Māra seizes his opportunity. He dispatches an essence to possess a person, who then speaks the teachings of the sūtras with their own mouth.
The person, however, does not realize they have been possessed by a demon; they also claim to have attained unsurpassed nirvāṇa themselves.

They come to the place of that son of good family who seeks the Way, arrange their seat, and preach the Dharma. They speak fondly of traveling to other lands without hindrance, even traversing ten thousand *li* in the blink of an eye.

Furthermore, having obtained those objects from that direction, or at one place within a single residence, let it be said that over the span of several paces, a person is made to travel from the eastern wall to the western wall.
Though this person runs with great haste for many years, they do not arrive.

Because of this, their mind gains conviction and they suspect that the Buddha has appeared before them; they constantly say with their own mouths: "The sentient beings of the ten directions are all my children; I have given birth to them."
"O Buddhas! I have appeared in this world; I am the Primordial Buddha. My appearance in the world is spontaneous and not attained through cultivation.

This is called the Sovereign Heavenly Mara who dwells in the world. He causes his retinue—such as the Cāmuṇḍas (demons that devour vital essence), the Four Heavenly Kings, and the Piśāca youths (the Piśācas who serve the Four Heavenly Kings)—who have not yet resolved for enlightenment, to exploit their empty clarity and consume their vital essence."
Or, without relying on a teacher, the practitioner may personally see Vajrapāṇi, who proclaims, "I grant you long life.

He then manifests in the form of a beautiful woman and indulges extensively in lustful desires. Before even a year has passed, his liver and brain will wither away, and he will begin to speak to himself alone.

Their voices sound like those of malevolent spirits; those who do not discern them beforehand will mostly fall into royal calamities. Before they even encounter formal execution, they have already withered and died, causing distress and confusion to others until their own demise.
You should recognize this in advance so as not to enter the cycle of saṃsāra; if you are deluded and ignorant, you will not understand.

They shall fall into the Avīci Hell. Ānanda, you should know that these ten kinds of Māras, during the time of the final age, will appear within my Dharma, having left the household life to practice the Way;
they may either possess a human body or manifest their own forms, all claiming to have already attained the realization of Perfectly Complete Enlightenment.
They praise lust and violate the Buddha’s discipline. These were originally evil demonic teachers who, together with their demonic disciples, transmitted lust from one to another.
Thus, such perverse spirits bewitch their hearts and entrails; for as few as nine lifetimes, or for many more than a hundred generations, they cause those who practice true cultivation [to fall].
They will all become the retinue of Māra; after their lives end, they will inevitably become subjects of Māra, lose the Perfectly All-Knowing One, and fall into the Avīci Hell.
You must not yet seek extinction first; even if you attain the stage of No-More-Learning (aśaikṣa), remain with your vows to enter that age of the Final Dharma.
Arouse great compassion to rescue and deliver those sentient beings who possess a correct mind and deep faith, so that they do not become attached to demons and may attain right knowledge and vision.
I have now delivered you from birth and death; if you follow the Buddha’s words, this is called repaying the Buddha’s kindness.

Ānanda, these ten kinds of manifestations during the practice of dhyāna are all the result of the interaction between the mind and the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of mental formations); therefore, these phenomena appear. Sentient beings...
Stubborn and deluded, they fail to measure themselves. Encountering these causes and conditions, they remain lost and do not recognize their own state;
claiming instead to have attained sainthood, they commit a great falsehood and fall into the Avīci Hell.

You must take the words of the Tathāgata and, after my parinirvāṇa, transmit them during the Age of Dharma-Decline, causing all sentient beings everywhere to awaken to this meaning. Do not allow celestial Māras to find an opportunity; preserve [this teaching].
"Protecting and sustaining [the practitioner] until they achieve the Unsurpassed Way.

Tong said: "If the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) has already been exhausted while the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has not yet been eliminated, how can one achieve the sixty stages of the sages?

This means that once the five faculties have been uprooted and the mind has already detached from the physical form, one proceeds from this ordinary body upward through the stages of Bodhi, beginning with—"
The three stages of advancement are followed by the fifty-five positions on the true path of Bodhi, culminating in the two awakenings of Equality and Subtlety;
together these constitute the sixty sagely positions. They are called "sagely" (*ārya*) to distinguish them from the ordinary.

As long as one has not yet shed the sense organs and their objects, being obstructed by them, one is like a bird in a cage. Once the sense organs and their objects have dissolved, clarity dwells within the faculties.
He emerges like a bird leaving its cage, attaining the *manomaya-kāya* (mind-made body). From the first stage (*bhūmi*) through the tenth, there are three types of *manomaya-kāya*:
First, the *manomaya-kāya* that enters the bliss of *samādhi*. This refers to the mind being tranquil and unmoving;

it corresponds to the stage of entering emptiness from the first faith up to the seventh faith. Second, the *manomaya-kāya* that awakens to the self-nature of phenomena (*dharmasvabhāva*). This refers to universally entering...
The Buddha-field has the Dharma as its intrinsic nature; this corresponds to the stage of emerging from the provisional [world] through the eight levels of faith.

The third type is the spontaneously born, effortless body of mind-made form (*manomaya-kāya*). This refers to comprehending the Dharma realized by the Buddha, which corresponds to the middle stage of cultivation during the nine and ten levels of faith.
This mind-made body is precisely the initial entry into the mind-made body of the bliss of samādhi. However, regarding conceptualization...
The skandhas have not yet been destroyed. This is just as previously seen in the dark chamber, like a person speaking in their sleep;

although it already possesses the rhythms and sequence of speech, it is said that by means of this, one ascends through the sixty stages of the sages and achieves definitive accomplishment, causing the thought-constructions to cease and no longer sleep.
They all understood his words. This is called the realm of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). If floating thoughts are eliminated, it is like awakening from a dream;
one is no longer obscured by perceptions, and within the fundamental substance of awakened clarity, there is not even a speck of dust.

Thus, the entire cycle of birth and death is perfectly illumined from beginning to end. Birth and death and nirvāṇa have no different characteristics; therefore, it is said that the entire cycle of birth and death is so.

Its arising constitutes the head; its ceasing constitutes the tail. Since the characteristic of arising is not seen and the characteristic of ceasing is not seen, it is said that "the head and tail are illuminated all around.
It is like a bright mirror from which impurities have been removed; its radiance is no longer disturbed. This is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
All afflictions exist because of perception and thought; only when thought is exhausted does perception perish. The mind of arising and ceasing is extinguished, and thus afflictions [are eliminated].

From what does it arise? It is thus able to transcend the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kāṣāya*). As for how perception (*saṃjñā*) arises, it takes pervasive deluded conceptualization (*yuanxiang*) as its basis.

Perception is capable of fusing and transforming, causing the mind to follow objects and objects to follow the mind. If all movement of thought is exhausted, then both mind and object vanish together;
thus, one is able to shatter pervasive deluded conceptualization. [This occurs when] one becomes attached to the essence of empty luminosity.

Then Māra enters their minds. Now, because you do not become attached to this empty clarity—which seems to possess a subtle quality of pervasive integration—it is said that the "aggregate of sensation" (vedanā-skandha) is empty and wondrous, and you do not encounter perverse thoughts.
Nevertheless, within this samādhi, the sense of pervasive integration has not yet been fully transformed.
Then Māra will take advantage of that state of integration to delude them.

Thus, if the mind loves luminous perfection and greedily seeks skillful means, then a *graha* spirit with a habit of greed—having grown old and become a Māra—will attach itself to a person and speak of self-transformed skillful means and other such teachings to delude them.
If the mind loves wandering and greedily seeks experience, then a *pūtana* spirit with a habit of lust—having grown old...

When those who have become demons possess a person, they speak of heterodox views such as the "Other-Transformation" (paranirmita) and other such teachings to delude them; the person’s mind then cherishes these entanglements, greedily seeking points of accord.

When those who falsely practice as shape-shifting ghosts or old demons possess a person, they speak of teachings regarding the awakening of others' minds and the recollection of past lives to delude them;
the person’s mind then cherishes these roots, greedily seeking analytical discernment. Thus, it is through resentment...

Those who have practiced the poison of *gū* (sorcery) and the habit of deception, or who were malevolent ghosts that became demons in old age, will possess people and speak of teachings such as "the Buddha is present before you" to delude them;
their minds will crave immediate responses, and they will greedily seek mysterious manifestations.

Then, those who have practiced the habit of anger and were pestilence ghosts that became demons in old age will possess people and speak of teachings such as "mysterious manifestations save people" to delude them.

When the mind’s affection penetrates deeply and it delights in dwelling in the obscure and silent, then a ghost with powerful habitual tendencies of pride who has aged into a demon will attach itself to a person,

confusing them by preaching such things as the laws of future causes and effects. When the mind’s affection seeks knowledge and views, greedily craving past lives, then a ghost with habitual tendencies toward vision—
such as a ghost of a mountain forest, a local deity, a city guardian, a river, or a peak— who has aged into a demon [will likewise attach].
They possess people and speak of marvelous jewels and extraordinary phenomena to delude them.

Those whose hearts cherish supernatural powers and who study the source of transformations will be possessed by ghosts that rely on human hosts—beings that have been mountain spirits, river sprites, grasses, or trees for many kalpas, or immortals who died and became monsters, or those who grew into demons through old age.
These possess people and speak of grasping light and walking upon water.
They delude others with such supernatural powers as passing through walls or entering jars; their hearts crave entry into extinction and they greedily seek the profound emptiness.
Thus, they vainly practice the pursuit of auspicious omens—such as the vital essence of the sun and moon, gold, jade, and *zhicao* fungi, as well as the qilin, phoenix, tortoise, and crane.

The immortal is a spirit. When those who have grown old and become demonic possess a person, they preach that there is no cause and effect, using such doctrines as entering and exiting empty space to delude them.
Their hearts crave longevity, greedily seeking eternal years; they wish to cast off the stage of segmented birth (*vipāka*) in order to seek the stage of transformation (*nairmāṇika*).

Believing that subtle marks are eternally abiding, they sever the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*) and claim to be born in the land of the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā-bhūmi*). This is not the worldly [truth].

At such times, demons may succeed in deluding them. Thereupon, the Lord of the Māras, who dwells in the sixth heaven of the Desire Realm, shall cause his retinue, including the piśācas, to harass and disturb these people.

Among the piśācas, those who have already resolved for enlightenment will protect and uphold the True Dharma; those who have not yet resolved for enlightenment will devour the vital essence of humans.
When the vital energy (*prāṇa*) arrives, it manifests in the form of a beautiful woman, causing one's liver and brain to wither away; this is indeed too cruel.
This is what is meant by "the higher the Way, the more prevalent the demons. One must not fail to be strict in one's precautions. Now, perfect clarity and skillful means—

To travel through Buddha-lands, to achieve profound and continuous realization, to discern the fundamental source, to respond to subtle influences with distant resonance, to enter deeply into stillness, to know past lives, to possess unimpeded supernormal powers, and to enter the samādhi of cessation for eternal kalpas without decay—all these are matters within the scope of authentic practice.
To investigate these matters with diligence is not an error; however, it must begin with the cultivation of loving-kindness.
This is followed by greed, whereby the mind becomes attached; where there is attachment, there is desire.
Thus, Māra seizes upon this craving and fulfills this greed, leading them with lustful desires until they disregard the breaking of their moral discipline (*śīla*).

Māra has also thoroughly investigated *nirvāṇa*, yet he alone was unable to sever sexual desire; therefore, he enters into the perverse concentration (*mithyā-samādhi*) of ghosts and spirits, using it to harm what is correct.
This is their business. They seek to harm those who would return to the Right Path and do not wish for the Right Path to succeed.

If the Right Path were to succeed, both conceptual thought and mental imagery would be extinguished, and their demonic palaces would all be utterly shattered. How could they not employ a hundred stratagems to harass and disturb it?
After Ānanda had selected the perfect method of penetration (*pratyavekṣā-vaipulya*), he vowed to deliver all sentient beings of the final age.

Deeply concerned that false teachers would preach the Dharma as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he requested instructions on how to establish a *bodhimaṇḍa* (place of practice) to remain far from demonic activities and ensure that his mind of Bodhi never regresses.
At this, the World-Honored One enumerated all such demonic matters in full and instructed him.

He made a vow to remain within that period of the Final Dharma, giving rise to great compassion to rescue and deliver sentient beings, ensuring they do not fall under the influence of demons and attain right awakening.
He earnestly transmitted the precept against sexual desire from one to another, truly fearing the difficulty of severing the impulse toward lust.
Even though Mātaṅga was exceptionally lowly and inferior, and even though the divine spells of Brahmā were not yet sufficient—
How strange! He was still able to violate the Buddha’s disciplinary code by destroying even a single precept;

how much more so when he sends his essence to possess others and manifests various supernatural transformations—who could possibly not be deluded by him? Generally speaking, such demons possess only the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*) and no further.
He dazzles them with the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*), yet ultimately reduces them to praising lust; such is the extent of his artifice.

If one shatters the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) and realizes the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*), there will be no internal resonance and nothing external that can act upon one.

Even Māra would not dare to look directly at such a person with his own eyes, so how could he dare to cause disturbance? Tianyi Huai addressed the assembly, saying: "Two thousand years ago, the Great Awakened One..."
“World-Honored One, you wish to lead the assembly of noble ones to the sixth heaven to preach the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra.

You have issued a decree that all fierce and malevolent ghosts and spirits from other lands and this world, from the human realm and the heavens, must assemble together to receive the Buddha’s entrustment and protect the True Dharma.
Should there be any who do not attend, the Gate-Keeper Kings of the Four Quarters shall fly fiery iron wheels to pursue them.”
He issued the command for them to assemble. Once they had gathered, there was not one who did not comply with the Buddha’s decree;
each made a grand vow to protect and uphold the True Dharma. Only one Māra King said to the World-Honored One:

"Gautama, I shall wait until all sentient beings have attained Buddhahood, until the realm of sentient beings is emptied and the very name 'sentient being' no longer exists; only then will I resolve upon Bodhi."
The mind remains unchanging even when facing peril; such a one is a true great man.

O virtuous ones, how can you utter a single turning word to give vent to the indignation of the Yellow-Faced Gautama? Ordinary spiritual powers, wondrous functions, wisdom, and eloquence—all these are utterly useless here.
Throughout the entire land of Jambudvīpa, there is no one who does not love the Buddha; yet, when it comes to this point, what [can be done]?
"What is this Buddha? What is this Māra? Is there anyone who can distinguish between them? After a long silence, he said:
"If you wish to recognize Māra, it is when you open your eyes and see light. If you wish to recognize the Buddha, it is when you close your eyes and see darkness.
With his staff, he pierced through the nostrils of both Māra and Buddha at once. Miaoxi offered a substitute phrase on their behalf, saying: "I almost called them by the wrong names!"
"You are the Demon King. This statement contains two points of defeat (*parājaya*). If anyone can point these out, I grant that they possess the eyes of a Zen monk (*samgha-bhikṣu*).
Master Bimozhan of Mount Wutai constantly carried a wooden staff.
Whenever he saw a monk come to prostrate, he would immediately thrust the staff across the monk's neck and say: "Which demon enticed you to leave the household life? Which demon..."
Mei instructed him, saying: "I will send you on a pilgrimage. If you can speak, you shall die beneath the execution post; if you cannot speak, you shall also die beneath the execution post.
Speak quickly! Speak quickly! Among his disciples, few were able to respond. Fayan spoke on his behalf, saying: "Beg for my life. Fadeng spoke on his behalf, saying: [He remained silent].
He merely extended his neck to show it to him. Xuánjué spoke on his behalf, saying, "Old man, you could have put down your pitchfork.
When Wǎngshān Tōng visited him, as soon as he saw him, he did not prostrate but instead leaped into [Yán’s] embrace.
Yán patted Tōng’s back three times. Tōng rose, clapped his hands, and said, "Brother, from three thousand *li* away, you have deceived me into coming here! Three thousand.
"To lure me out from within my village," he thought, and he immediately turned back. These venerable masters manipulate their spiritual powers (*ṛddhi*) so that even demons cannot perceive them.
One day, Guishan asked Yangshan, "Of the forty fascicles of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, how much was spoken by the Buddha and how much was spoken by Māra?
Yangshan replied, "It is all spoken by Māra. Guishan said, "In the future, there will be no one [to understand this]."
Nanyue asked, "What about Yangshan? Nanquan replied, "Huiji is merely a matter of one lifetime's conduct;
where does his practice reside? Yangshan said, "I value only that your eyes are correct; I do not speak of your practice. Thus, he was able to possess Yangshan’s eye for discerning the Dharma.
Then there will be no further apprehension of demonic activities.
*The Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause and Realization of the Tathāgata’s Great Uṣṇīṣa and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas*,
Fascicle Ten.
Ānanda, when that son of good family practices samādhi and the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is exhausted, his ordinary dreams and fantasies will vanish.
Whether awake or asleep, he remains constant and unified. His awakened clarity is empty and still, like a cloudless sky; there are no longer any coarse or heavy shadows of external objects.
When he contemplates the worlds, the great earth, mountains, and rivers, they appear as reflections in a clear mirror: they come without adhering to it, and pass away without...

Traces are received in response to emptiness; all habitual patterns are utterly extinguished, leaving only the singular, pure reality. From this, the fundamental source of birth and death is revealed.
One perceives the twelve classes of sentient beings throughout the ten directions, exhausting every variety.

Although one has not yet fully understood the individual origins of their respective destinies, one sees their common basis of birth, which is like a shimmering mirage—vibrant, clear, and turbulent—serving as the ultimate ground for the floating sense organs and their objects.
This pivotal point is called the domain of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations).

If this clear yet flickering fundamental nature enters into its original clarity, and once clarified, the habitual tendencies of the fundamental nature vanish like waves subsiding and transforming into still water, it is called the exhaustion of the *saṃskāra-skandha*.
Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of sentient beings. If one examines its origin, one finds that subtle and hidden delusive thoughts constitute its root. Ānanda!

It should be known that those sons of good family who have attained right awareness within *śamatha*—with their minds stilled, luminous, and upright—cannot be taken advantage of by the ten classes of celestial Māras.
Only then are they able to investigate with refinement and exhaust the root of all living beings.

When the source of the elements (*dhātu*) within the root of beings is revealed, they observe its profound purity and its perfectly turbulent, moving source. Those who give rise to conceptual calculations regarding this perfectly complete source are such persons.
They fall into two kinds of causeless theories. First, such a person perceives that there is no fundamental cause. Why is this?
Because once this person’s vital faculty has been completely shattered, they ride upon the eight hundred merits of the eye-organ and see all sentient beings throughout eighty thousand kalpas.
They witness the winding currents of karma as beings die here and are born there; they see only sentient beings revolving in those very places for eighty thousand kalpas.

Externally, they perceive no objective basis and thus form this interpretation: "These sentient beings of the world throughout the ten directions have existed spontaneously for eighty thousand kalpas without cause.
By such conceptualization, they lose the correct universal knowledge and fall into the ranks of the heterodox, deluding themselves regarding the nature of Bodhi.
Second, these people see that the end has no cause. Why is this? Because these people, having already perceived the root of birth, [see its beginning].
Know that humans are born as humans; realize that birds are born as birds. Crows have been black from the beginning; cranes have been white from the beginning.

Humans and devas are fundamentally upright; animals are fundamentally horizontal. White is not produced by washing; black is not created by dyeing. From eighty thousand kalpas ago, there has been no further change or alteration.
Now, even as this physical form comes to its end, it is likewise so. Since I have not seen bodhi from the very beginning, how could there be any further matter of attaining bodhi?
One should know that today all phenomena are fundamentally without cause; by means of this discernment, [one realizes this].

Losing the knowledge of right universal wisdom, they fall into the ranks of external paths and become deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi. This is called the first type of external path that establishes the doctrine of causelessness.
It is further explained:

as long as the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has not been exhausted, one grasps at forms when awake and forms dreams when asleep; thus, one pursues the coarse objects of the external environment.
Regarding the matter of double images: once the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has been exhausted, one maintains internal stillness within the profound seclusion;

whether waking or sleeping, there is constant unity. This awakened clarity is empty and tranquil, like a mirror reflecting brightness. Although it leaves no trace of coming or going, there nevertheless remains a luminous shadow-image;

yet this is still merely a peripheral matter of mental objects (*dharma-rajas*). Previously, when the external objects were turbid and distracting, one merely followed the flow of arising and ceasing, failing to perceive the fundamental source.

Now, receiving illumination and response within emptiness, there is only the single, refined, and true reality. Since birth and extinction have ceased, its fundamental source is revealed from this point on.
What is seen is the same as the basis of life—continuous, dense, and subtly shifting; this is what is called the "whirling waves without wind.
"Wild horses" refers to drifting dust motes; "twinkling" refers to the light of fireflies. Such is the subtle movement of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
It is like the mote-dust illuminated by sunlight, shimmering and utterly devoid of any abiding characteristic; arising and ceasing momentarily, it possesses no coarse shadow.
Hence it is called "clear agitation. The four great elements of clear agitation constitute the four dusts of the floating roots;
their substance is fundamentally empty. This ultimate pivot and aperture truly resides herein. Through the arousal of adhesion within the profound stillness, the six faculties come into being.
From humans and devas down to ants, there are none who do not possess the four great elements and the six sense faculties;
thus, these constitute the common foundation for the birth of the twelve classes of sentient beings. This is called the realm of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

Whether considering their general or specific characteristics, one can perceive that the life-continuums of individual sentient beings differ, and that their wisdom and merit are unequal, due to the manifestation of seeds accumulated through habitual practice over many lifetimes.

This pertains to the limits of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*); therefore, it cannot be fathomed by the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). However, the nature of this aggregate of formations—its clarity and turbulence—is fundamentally without turbulence;
hence it is called the "original nature. That it cannot help but be turbulent is due to the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) accumulated over many lifetimes.
Therefore, it is called "original habituation. Habituation cannot clarify itself through further habituation; only when the nature returns to its source can it become clarified and still.

When one uses this clarified and still nature to clarify that original habituation, then the signs of shifting and flowing are exhausted. Just as waves cease when the wind dies down, they transform into clear water.
Having transformed into clear water, reaching the state of profound stillness where there is no movement, this is called the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
When these are exhausted, such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*). As for the turbidity of sentient beings:

birth and death ceaselessly continue, and the movement of karma constantly shifts. Now, one comes to rest within that which was incessant; one does not shift within that which was constantly shifting. One is on the verge of entering cessation (*nirodha*).
Thus, one is able to transcend it. However, the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) shifts secretly, and one is never aware of it; it takes subtle, hidden delusions as its basis.
To break through and eliminate it within its profound stillness and secrecy requires one who has attained a thorough realization of the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).

Such a person remains constant whether waking or sleeping, thereby attaining right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*), just as described previously regarding being unmoved by motion or stillness, and remaining the same in memory or forgetfulness.
First: You should abide in this state and enter *samādhi*. It is permissible to take this as a stage of awakening, but it is not permissible to grasp it as an actual realization.
Therefore, for one whose aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has been exhausted, the mind is concentrated and luminous;
perverse thoughts do not arise of their own accord. Thus, even the ten classes of celestial Māras have no opportunity to enter. Heaven...

Previously, while Māra had not yet abandoned his perverse thoughts, he manifested supernatural transformations. Now that the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has been exhausted, he contemplates and perceives the profound, pure source of movement;
he has indeed entered the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñi-sattva-deva*), which the celestial Māras of the six desire realms cannot even glimpse.
Profound stillness is fundamentally unmoving. Circular agitation is movement that has never truly moved; therefore, it is called the "source of movement.

Although this source of movement is circular, it does not transcend birth and death. Those who engage in conceptual calculations regarding this are, in essence, calculating within the realm of birth and death that there is no cause.
First, they perceive that there is fundamentally no cause, yet fail to realize the causal conditions of wholesome and unwholesome karma; they merely—
This is produced by consciousness; it relies solely on the appearance of arising, which is momentarily absent. Yet, the flow of formations (saṃskāra) continues without ceasing.

Within that state of meditative concentration, one develops the supernormal power of knowing past lives (pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna) and perceives the saṃsāric wandering of sentient beings for eighty thousand kalpas, like a ring without end.

Thereupon, one concludes that sentient beings exist spontaneously without cause; beyond those eighty thousand kalpas, there is nothing observed in the darkness, and thus one certainly does not know of the Bodhi [of the Buddhas].

This constitutes the primary cause. Second, there are those who see only the superficial results and deny their causes; they fail to realize that good and evil karmic fruits are summoned solely by the mind.
Relying merely on their supernormal powers, they claim to perceive the long-term karmic fruits beyond eighty thousand kalpas as being in a state of fixed, unchanging form.

They thus assert that the distinctions between humans and animals, or black and white, have always existed horizontally and vertically in this manner, and are not attained through cultivation. This is certainly not the case.
To know that Bodhi is the ultimate fruit is correct; to be deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi is not called "correct knowledge.

To know only the eighty thousand kalpas preceding and following [the present] is not called "universal knowledge. The non-Buddhist Makkhali Gosāla claimed that the suffering and pleasure of sentient beings are not obtained through karma, but are all spontaneous.
It is precisely because of this view that he held these two [extremes] to be causeless. He perceived only the seven consciousnesses as being without [a cause].

When the roots of perception temporarily cease their transmission, this speculative calculation arises. Internally, because the seven consciousnesses rely solely upon the eighth consciousness, and since their arising has no fundamental source, one concludes that the root is causeless.
Externally, because the seven consciousnesses rely solely upon the six consciousnesses, and since their investigation yields no utility, one concludes that the branches are causeless.
Seeing only that their flow continues without ceasing, one then asserts they are spontaneous.
It was thus. Jingqing asked Lingyun, "What is it like before chaos has been divided?
Yun said, "The pillar conceives. Jingqing asked, "What is it like after division? Yun said, "Like a fragment of cloud appearing within the great clarity (*tàiqīng*).
Jingqing asked, "Does that great clarity itself receive this mark? Yun did not answer. Jingqing said, "If so, then sentient beings..."
Dongqing arrived. Yunmen did not respond. Dongqing asked, "What is it like when one has attained pure clarity, free from even a single speck?
Yunmen said, "This is still the flow of the eternal and constant. Dongqing asked, "What is the flow of the eternal and constant?
Yunmen said, "It is like a mirror that is always bright. Dongqing asked, "Is there anything further beyond this? Yunmen said, "There is. Dongqing asked, "What is this 'further'?"
Regarding the preceding matter, Yun said: "Bring me the mirror and shatter it, and I shall see you. Tiantong comments:
Whether divided or undivided, the jade mechanism moves at night; whether pointed or unpointed, the golden shuttle is cast in the dark. It is simply a state of uniform, pure clarity.
Before attaining the tenfold perfection of peace and stability, tell me: once the mirror has been shattered, where do you meet?
Do you understand? "When the old hare of the clear autumn swallows the light, the azure dragon sheds its bones in the limpid waters.

This is the true, eternal flow that precisely accords with the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations); yet, like a mirror that is ever-luminous, it also accords with the clarity reflected by a mirror.

There is no difference. If one can shatter the mirror and see its true face—like a blue dragon emerging from the clear water after shedding its bones—then one is close to transforming consciousness into wisdom.
How could it be merely a matter of breaking through the skandha of formations?
Ānanda, when these good sons within this *samādhi* concentrate their clarity and align their minds, Māra finds no opportunity.

They exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings and contemplate that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source. Those who give rise to speculative calculations regarding this perfect and eternal reality fall into the four theories of universal permanence.
The first is when a person exhaustively investigates the nature of both mind and objects and finds them to be without cause; having practiced this...

They are able to know the births and deaths of all sentient beings throughout the ten directions within twenty thousand kalpas; they see that these cycles revolve without ever being lost, and thus reckon them to be permanent.
Second, these people exhaustively investigate the origin of the four great elements and perceive their four natures as eternally abiding;
through cultivation, they are able to know the births and deaths of all sentient beings throughout the ten directions within forty thousand kalpas, seeing that their essence is constant and never...
Third, this person exhausts the six sense faculties and the *manas* that grasps them;

because the fundamental source within the *citta*, *manas*, and *vijñāna* is eternally constant by nature, they cultivate the ability to know all sentient beings throughout eighty thousand kalpas as circulating without loss, originally abiding permanently, and exhausting their existence without losing their nature—thus reckoning it to be permanent. Fourth...
Once this person has exhausted the source of perception, the principle of their nature no longer flows, ceases, or revolves. The mind of birth and extinction has now been eternally extinguished;
within this principle, it naturally becomes non-arising and non-extinguishing. Yet, because they are measured by the mind, they reckon this state to be permanent.

Due to this reckoning of permanence, they lose correct universal knowledge and fall into the ranks of external paths, deluding themselves regarding the nature of Bodhi. This is called the second [delusion].
The non-Buddhists establish theories of circularity and permanence.
It is said in response: those who establish the theory of causelessness perceive it as annihilation; those who establish the theory of circularity and permanence perceive it as permanence.

Even if one infers it to be both annihilation and permanence, or neither annihilation nor permanence, it does not, in total, transcend the false views of annihilationism and eternalism. This exhausts the possibilities of birth.

The Fundamental Source of Cyclic Nature (*Lìběn*). Reaching the ultimate, it is the primordial source of agitation. Seeing that it is empty yet ever-emergent, and moving without end, one reckons it as permanent.
From the broad to the narrow, from the coarse to the subtle, there is a general sequence.

First, it pervades the five aggregates (*skandha*), the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), and the two spheres of mind and objects; all exist spontaneously without cause, circulating without loss. Second, it merely points to...
The nature of the four great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—is pure and capable of forming the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) for sentient beings; its essence is eternally unchanging.
The third refers to the manas, the seventh consciousness, which is the mind that clings to and appropriates [the body] as the basis for the six sense faculties and mental cognition.
The intention that grasps and the consciousness that grasps, as to their original source and location, are precisely the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
Although sentient beings undergo cyclic existence, this aggregate of formations is never lost; thus these seven consciousnesses constitute a permanent nature.
It is like seeing a thin stream and calling it still water. Since beginningless time, this has been the root of birth and death, yet deluded people call it the "original person."
This is what is meant by that. Fourth, they falsely recognize the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) as the principle of spontaneity.

They claim that once the mind of arising and ceasing has been extinguished, the state of its permanent cessation spontaneously becomes non-arising and non-ceasing; yet this occurs within the midst of arising and ceasing.
They calculate that there is neither birth nor extinction, like seeing empty space and claiming it is eternally abiding, yet not knowing that even empty space can perish.
Furthermore, they take this as eternal through mental calculation; this is not comparable to truly seeing its eternity.
These four [stages] have not yet beheld the true, eternal flow of the eight consciousnesses, let alone perceive the nature of Bodhi within the evolving consciousnesses. — Ruyi (Rui)
Yan asked Yantou, "What is the fundamental eternal principle? Yantou said, "Movement. Yan asked, "What is it like when there is movement?
Yantou said, "One does not see the fundamental eternal principle. Yan paused in thought. Yantou said, "If you consent to this, you have not yet escaped the roots and dust."
"Unwilling to consent, he would sink forever into birth and death. Yanguan then prostrated. A Celestial Child (Tiantong) offered this verse:

"The perfect pearl has no hole; the great uncut jade is not carved. What the man of the Way prizes is the absence of sharp edges. Cast away the path of 'consent,' and the root-dust of the senses becomes empty.
Liberated from all dependence, one lives with vivid clarity. This is seeing the original, ever-abiding state with ultimate truth. "Consent"—one...

One must still discard even the [concept of] "words," let alone calculatingly grasping at a divine self (ātman) that falls into the den of "perfect permanence"—in the end, such a one will surely sink into ruin; how could they ever be permanent?
Furthermore, among those good sons within samādhi who have stabilized their minds in right concentration, the Māras find no opportunity.

They exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings and contemplate that profound, pure, and eternally quiescent source of movement. Yet, if they give rise to conceptual calculations regarding self and others, such persons fall into four inverted views:
the theory that one part is impermanent and one part is permanent. The first of these is when such a person contemplates the wondrously luminous mind.
Pervading the worlds of the ten directions, they take this profound stillness to be their ultimate divine self (*paramātman*).

From this, they reckon that their self pervades the ten directions, fixed and immovable in its luminous clarity; thus, all sentient beings are born and die within the center of their own mind, and this nature of their own mind—
This is called "permanence. That which undergoes arising and ceasing is truly of an impermanent nature.

Second, if a person does not contemplate their own mind, but instead contemplates throughout the lands of the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, seeing the places where kalpas are destroyed, they call this the "ultimate nature of impermanence."

That which is indestructible throughout the kalpas is called ultimate permanence. Third, this person separately contemplates their own mind as being subtle, refined, and extremely dense, like a minute particle;
it transmigrates through the ten directions, its nature never changing or shifting, yet it can cause this body to arise and perish in an instant.
That which is indestructible in nature is called the self-nature of permanence. That from which all death and birth flow forth is called the nature of impermanence.

Fourth, this person knows that the aggregate of perception has been exhausted, yet they perceive the flow of the aggregate of formations; because the aggregate of formations flows constantly, they reckon it to be the nature of permanence.
Form, sensation, perception, and so forth have now been extinguished; this is called impermanence.

Because of this calculation that one part is impermanent and one part is permanent, they fall into the ranks of the non-Buddhists and become confused regarding the nature of Bodhi. This is called the third non-Buddhist doctrine:
the theory of partial permanence.
Tong said: "This is both the view of permanence and the view of impermanence. The fundamentally wondrous and luminous mind pervades the ten directions; it has never not been so.
However, to grasp at it as a divine self (ātman) is incorrect. To insist that it is the 'self' is precisely the manas-clinging to the consciousness (vijñāna).
Although it is said to be concentrated, luminous, and unmoving, its subtle and minute shifting within is itself arising and ceasing."

It is merely that [the seeds] do not recognize themselves. Since you designate the temporary immobility of the mind-nature as "permanence," and further designate the arising and ceasing of all sentient beings as "impermanence," there would then be two "selves" pervading the ten directions;
how could this not be inverted? Setting aside the mind-nature for a moment and considering only the land, even in the third dhyāna...
Below this [level], that which is subject to the three calamities is called impermanent. From the fourth dhyāna upward, the calamities cannot reach;

this is called ultimate permanence. Regardless of the physical realm, when speaking solely of the nature of the mind, because its nature does not undergo change or displacement, it is called the permanence of the self-nature (*ātman*).
"Dying here and being born there" is called the nature of impermanence. Initially, one synthesizes self and others to collectively calculate permanence and impermanence;

subsequently, having distinguished self and others, one individually calculates permanence and impermanence. Furthermore, one takes the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) as self and form, sensation, and perception as others.

The continuity of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is called the nature of permanence; the cessation of perception (*saṃjñā*) and the other aggregates is called the nature of impermanence.
To divide permanence and impermanence within a single mind is to have a dualistic mind—is this not a perversion?

Compared to the previous theory of "perfect permanence," this view is slightly less dogmatic; nevertheless, its fundamental source is impure and remains entirely a fallacious calculation. —Zhongguoshi.
The Master asked the monk, "From where have you come? He replied, "I have come from the South. The Master said, "How do the teachers (knowledgeable ones) of the South instruct people?
He replied, "The teachers of that region directly point out to students that 'this very mind is Buddha. Buddha has the meaning of awakening.
You now fully possess the nature of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing. This nature is well able to raise the eyebrows, blink the eyes, and come and go."
Its application pervades the entire body; when the head is touched, the head knows it; when the feet are touched, the feet know it. Therefore, it is called "Perfectly All-Knowing" (Samyak-saṃbuddha).
Apart from this, there is no other Buddha. This body is subject to birth and death, but the nature of the mind has never undergone birth or death since beginningless time.
As for the birth and death of the body, it is like a dragon shedding its bones, a snake sloughing its skin, or a person casting off old clothes.
"Zhai, the body itself is impermanent, yet its nature is eternal. This is roughly what is taught in the South.
The Master said, "If that were so, there would be no distinction between you and the non-Buddhist outsider Śreṇika.
He claimed: 'Within this body of mine, there is a divine spirit (ātman). This spirit is capable of knowing pain and pleasure; when the body perishes, the spirit departs.'"
It is like a house that has caught fire; when the owner of the house goes out, the house is impermanent, yet the owner is eternal.

If one examines this closely, there is no way to distinguish the heterodox from the orthodox—what could possibly be correct? In my recent travels, I have frequently encountered such figures, and lately they have become even more numerous.
They gather several hundred followers at a time, looking up at the heavens with their eyes and claiming to represent the fundamental tenets of the Southern School. They...
He has altered the *Platform Sūtra*, interpolating miscellaneous discourses and excising the Sage’s intent, thereby deluding later disciples; how can this constitute the verbal teaching?

Alas! Our school is lost. If seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing were themselves the Buddha-nature, then Vimalakīrti should not have said that "dharmas are apart from seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.
If one acts within seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, then this is [merely] seeing...
"To hear, perceive, and know is not the seeking of the Dharma. The assembly further asked, "The *Lotus Sūtra*, a sūtra of definitive meaning, speaks of 'opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
How is this to be understood? The Master said, "It says 'opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision,' but it does not say 'the knowledge and vision of bodhisattvas or those of the two vehicles.
How could the deluded and inverted views of sentient beings be the same as the Buddha’s knowledge and vision? Xingchang then asked the Sixth Patriarch:
A disciple said, "I have often read the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, yet I do not understand the meaning of 'permanence' and 'impermanence. I beg you to explain this for me.
The Patriarch replied, "'Impermanence' refers to the Buddha-nature. 'Permanence' refers to the discriminating mind that distinguishes between all good and evil dharmas.
The disciple said, "What the Master has explained greatly contradicts the text of the Sūtra. The Patriarch replied, "I transmit the Buddha’s Mind-Seal; how could I..."
[The student] dared to contradict the Buddhist scriptures, saying: "The sutras state that Buddha-nature is eternal, yet you, Master, say it is impermanent.
All dharmas, both good and evil, up to and including the bodhicitta, are all impermanent, yet you, Master, say they are eternal.
This is a contradiction that causes students to become increasingly confused. The Patriarch said: "In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, I heard from the nun Anupama..."
After reading it through once from memory, he then expounded upon it. Not a single word or a single meaning failed to accord with the scriptural text;
even unto you, he never made two different explanations. [The student] said, "My capacity for learning is shallow and my understanding dim.

I pray that the Master will grant me a detailed and thorough instruction. The Patriarch said, "Do you know? If Buddha-nature were permanent, what further need would there be to speak of the various dharmas of good and evil?"
Even until the exhaustion of kalpas, not a single person would have given rise to the bodhicitta.
Therefore, when I speak of impermanence, it is precisely the Buddha’s teaching on the Way of True Permanence.

Furthermore, if all dharmas were merely impermanent, then every individual thing would possess its own self-nature that undergoes birth and death, and there would be places where the nature of true permanence does not pervade. Therefore—
When I speak of "permanence," it is precisely the Buddha’s teaching on the true meaning of impermanence.
This is because ordinary people and non-Buddhists cling to false permanence, while those of the two vehicles conceive of the permanent as impermanent; thus, together they form the eight inversions.
Therefore, within the definitive teachings on Nirvana, I refute those biased views and explicitly proclaim true permanence, true bliss, and true self.

"Zhenjing, you have now turned your back on the true meaning. By taking the impermanence of cessation and the permanence of certain death as your standard, you have misinterpreted the Buddha’s final, subtle, and perfect words.
Even if you were to read them a thousand times, what benefit would there be?
At this, Xingchang suddenly attained great enlightenment and spoke a verse, saying: "Because of clinging to the mind of impermanence, the Buddha taught the nature of permanence. Not knowing..."
Regarding "expedient means": it is like picking up pebbles from a spring pond; now that I no longer exert effort, the Buddha-nature manifests before me.
It was not bestowed by a teacher, nor is there anything for me to acquire. The Patriarch said, "You have now attained thorough penetration; you should be named Zhiche (Thorough Penetration)."
Having offered their thanks with ritual prostrations, they withdrew. As for this profound meaning of the eternal and the impermanent, those non-Buddhists have not even dreamed of it.

Furthermore, within samādhi, these good sons of noble family maintain a firm and concentrated right mind; thus Māra finds no opportunity, and they exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings.

Contemplating that profound stillness, one perceives the source of constant agitation. Those who engage in conceptual calculations regarding its various states fall into the four theories of finitude.
First, such a person calculates the origin of birth; as the flow of mental activity never ceases, they calculate the past and the future.

That which is called "finite" refers to calculating the successive moments of the mind. That which is called "infinite" refers to when this person contemplates eighty thousand kalpas and perceives sentient beings;
yet prior to those eighty thousand kalpas, there is silence, with nothing heard or seen. This state of being without hearing or seeing is called "infinite."
There are sentient beings who dwell in what is called "having limits. Third, there are those who reckon that their own self possesses the nature of boundlessness through universal knowledge;

yet all such people appear within the scope of my knowledge, while I have never known the nature of their knowing—thus they are said not to have attained a mind of boundlessness, but to possess only a limited nature.
Fourth, there are those who exhaustively investigate the emptiness of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), based on what they perceive.
The Path of the Mind: To deliberate upon all sentient beings within a single body, calculating that they are all half-born and half-extinguished;
to clarify that everything existing in the world is such that one half has limits and one half is limitless;

and thereby, through such deliberations on the finite and the infinite, to fall into the ways of external paths and become deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi—this is called the fourth external path.
Establishing the thesis that existence has limits, he replied:

"This [distinction] arises by analogy from permanence and impermanence. Permanence and impermanence are spoken of in terms of *svabhāva* (intrinsic nature) and belong to the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving aspect);

limits and lack of limits are spoken of in terms of temporal states (*avasthā*) and belong to the *nimitta-bhāga* (perceived aspect). [There are two types: first, the temporal states of the three periods; second..."
These are the states of seeing and hearing; third, the state of self and other; and fourth, the state of arising and ceasing.
These collectively pertain to the states of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations), wherein one falsely gives rise to conceptual constructions.

First, because the functioning of the *saṃskāra-skandha* flows without ceasing, and by virtue of this flowing function, it constitutes the three time periods of past, future, and present; therefore, it is called "having limits. By virtue of its non-ceasing nature...

Because the continuity [of existence] is without limit, it is called "boundless. Second, because one calculates only within eighty thousand kalpas—the extent of what is seen and heard regarding sentient beings—it is called "bounded";
because beyond eighty thousand kalpas there is no place where they are seen or heard, it is called "boundless."
Third, one calculates that the self universally knows all sentient beings; this is called "boundless nature.

Whether that cognitive nature is pervasive or non-pervasive, the self merely knows for itself that it once did not know [them]. Thus, it is restricted to its own self-knowledge and cannot extend it to the self [of others];
it possesses only "finite nature. Fourth, one exhaustively investigates the emptiness of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*): what existed before is now absent. This is due to...
If one calculates the primary retribution of sentient beings, they are half-born and half-extinguished; the secondary retribution of the world-system is likewise half-born and half-extinguished.
This half-birth constitutes "having limits," while this half-extinction constitutes "being limitless.

These four types of having limits do not, in total, transcend the aforementioned views of the cyclic birth and extinction of sentient beings, as well as the destruction and non-destruction of kalpas; they are merely discussed in terms of spatial boundaries. A monk asked:
National Teacher Zhong said: "When a person of knowledge instructs a student, they simply tell them to recognize their own nature.
When the time of impermanence arrives, cast this shell-and-leakage body aside; when the conscious intelligence of the numinous platform departs with sudden clarity, it is called liberation."
The Master said: "What more is there to say? This is still merely the measure of the Two Vehicles and the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

Those of the Two Vehicles loathe and seek to escape birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), while delighting in *nirvāṇa*. The non-Buddhists likewise say, 'I have a great affliction because I possess a body,' and thus they proceed toward the obscure principle (*avidyā-tattva*).
The *srotāpanna* enters for eighty thousand kalpas, and the remaining three fruits [of the path] enter for sixty..."

[The Pratyekabuddhas remain] for forty-two thousand kalpas; the Pratyekabuddhas dwell in the concentration of emptiness for ten thousand kalpas; the non-Buddhists dwell in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception for eighty thousand kalpas.
When the kalpas of these two vehicles are fulfilled, they are still able to turn their minds toward the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna), whereas the non-Buddhists return immediately to saṃsāra.

[A questioner] asked: "Is it that the Buddha-nature is of one kind, yet distinct [in its manifestations]? The Master said: "It is not of one kind. [The questioner] asked: "Why? The Master said: *Note: The text provided appears to be a fragment from a dialogue concerning the capacities and destinies of different spiritual practitioners—Pratyekabuddhas, non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), and those of the Two Vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas)—and their relationship to the Buddha-nature.*
[The student] asked, "Is there that which is entirely without arising and ceasing? Or that which is half-arising and half-ceasing, and half-non-arising and non-ceasing?

The Master said, "In this place of mine, the Buddha-nature is entirely without arising and ceasing. Your Buddha-nature from the South is half-arising and half-ceasing, and half-non-arising and non-ceasing.
[The student] asked, "How are these distinguished? The Master said, "This [Buddha-nature of mine] is such that body and mind are one."

"Just as the body has nothing external to it, it is entirely without birth or extinction. Your body in the south is impermanent, while the nature of the spirit is permanent; thus the mind is half-born-and-extinguished and half-not-born-and-not-extinguished. [The monk] asked: "How can the Master’s physical body be the same as the Dharma-body, which is without birth or extinction? The Master said: "Why have you fallen into a heterodox path? [The monk] replied: The Master said: "Why have you fallen into a heterodox path? [The monk] replied: "Because the physical body is subject to change, whereas the Dharma-body is eternal. How could they be the same? The Master said: "If you say this, you are like a person who, seeing the moon reflected in the water, thinks the moon itself has fallen into the water. You do not realize that the moon in the sky is originally undivided; how then could it fall into the water? You are merely clinging to the physical form and failing to perceive the true essence. Therefore, you are confused about the distinction between the provisional and the real, and thus you speak of 'half-born-and-extinguished' and 'half-not-born-and-not-extinguished. This is why I say you have entered a heterodox path. The monk was silent and did not respond. The Master said: "I have already explained it for you; why do you remain silent? The monk said: "I am not silent; I am simply reflecting on what you have said. The Master said: "If you are reflecting, you are still attached to the words. If you are not reflecting, you are still attached to the silence. Both are heterodox paths. The monk was speechless. The Master said: "I have exhausted my explanations for you; you must now reflect for yourself. The monk bowed and withdrew. The Master said: "This is called 'the gate of non-duality. The monk departed. The Master said: "He has finally understood. The monk returned later and said: "I have realized it. The Master said: "What have you realized? The monk said: "I have realized that the physical body and the Dharma-body are originally one and the same; there is no longer any distinction between them. The Master said: "You have indeed entered the correct path. The monk bowed and withdrew. The Master said: "This is called 'the gate of the identity of the provisional and the real. The monk departed. The Master said: "He has truly attained liberation. The monk returned once more and said: "I have realized that all phenomena are ultimately empty and quiescent; there is neither birth nor extinction. The Master said: "You have indeed entered the ultimate truth. The monk bowed and withdrew. The Master said: "This is called 'the gate of the great emptiness. The monk departed. The Master said: "He has finally reached the source. The monk returned yet again and said: "I have realized that the mind is originally pure and luminous; it is neither subject to birth nor extinction. The Master said: "You have indeed entered the treasury of the Tathāgata. The monk bowed and withdrew. The Master said: "This is called 'the gate of the original purity of the mind. The monk departed. The Master said: "He has truly attained the fruit of enlightenment. The monk returned for the final time and said: "I have realized that there is no self and no other; all is but the manifestation of the One Mind. The Master said: "You have indeed entered the realm of the Buddhas. The monk bowed and withdrew. The Master said: "This is called 'the gate of the non-arising of the One Mind. The monk departed. The Master said: "He has finally reached the ultimate destination. The monk returned once more and said: "I have realized that there is no practice and no attainment; all is but the functioning of the Great Mirror Wisdom. The Master said: "You have indeed entered the state of the Great Bodhisattva. The monk bowed and withdrew. The Master said: "This is called 'the gate of the Great Mirror Wisdom. The monk departed. In those places, there are also passages stating that while this aggregate ceases, another aggregate arises; that although the body undergoes transformation, the nature of the spirit is not extinguished.

Have you not seen Master Sengzhao say: "To discuss the Truth is to contradict the conventional; to follow the conventional is to contradict the Truth.

[The monk] said, "Master, you also say that 'the mind itself is Buddha. The masters of the South say the same. How can there be any difference between them?

You, Master, should not consider yourself right and others wrong. The Master said, "In some cases, the names differ but the substance is the same; in other cases, the names are the same but the substance differs.
It is because of this that confusion arises. Take, for example, bodhi, nirvāṇa, tathatā, and buddha-nature: these have different names but the same substance."
The true mind and the deluded mind; Buddha-wisdom and worldly wisdom—these names are identical, yet their essences differ.

Those in the South have mistakenly taken the deluded mind to be the true mind, identifying a thief as their own son. Some take worldly wisdom and claim it to be Buddha-wisdom, like confusing fish eyes for bright pearls.
They must not be treated as the same; matters require careful discernment. [The questioner] asked: "How can one become free from these?"

[The student] said, “I have. The Master said, “Simply observe the aggregates, sense bases, elements, and spheres in detail; investigate each one thoroughly—is there even a hair’s breadth that can be found?

He replied, “Body and mind are by nature detached; what is there to destroy? The Master said, “Is there anything further outside the body?”

[The student] said, "There are no external objects. [The Master] asked, "Since body and mind have no exterior, how could there be further objects? The Master said, "Are you destroying the characteristics of the world?

He replied, "The characteristics of the world are themselves without characteristics; why use anything further to destroy them? The Master said, "If that is so, then you have departed from error. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:

Furthermore, among those good sons within *samādhi*, whose minds are firm, concentrated, and upright, the Māras find no opportunity.
They exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings and contemplate that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source.

If such a person gives rise to speculative calculations within their cognition and views, they will fall into four kinds of inverted, "undying" equivocation and pervasive false theorizing. The first is when this person contemplates the source of transformation.
To perceive the locus of flux is called "change. To perceive the locus of continuity is called "permanence. To perceive the locus of the seen is called "arising.
Not perceiving the locus of seeing is called "cessation. This is the cause of continuity; it is the state where the nature is uninterrupted.

That which is called "increase" refers to the state within the primary continuity. That which is called "decrease" refers to the points of separation therein. That which is called "existence" refers to each respective place of arising.
That which is called "non-existence" refers to each mutual point of cessation. When observing through principle as a whole, one perceives distinct aspects through the application of the mind.
There were seekers of the Dharma who came to inquire about its meaning, but he replied, "I am now both arising and ceasing; both existent and non-existent;
both increasing and decreasing. At all times, he confused their speech, causing those before him to lose the essential passages.
Second, this person contemplates the mind with keen observation and finds that it has no mutual location; because there is nothing [to grasp], they attain realization.
When someone comes to question them, they respond with only a single word, saying merely "non-existence. Apart from this non-existence, there is nothing further to be said.

Third, this person contemplates the mind with keen observation and finds that each has its own location; because there is existence, they attain realization. When someone comes to question them, they respond with only a single word.
They merely assert that it "is," and beyond this, they have nothing further to say. Fourth, there are those who hold the view that both existence and non-existence apply;
because their object is bifurcated, their minds are likewise distracted. When someone comes to question them, they reply: "It is both existent and non-existent."
Furthermore, within the state of non-existence, it is not the case that there is also existence. All such equivocation and confusion cannot withstand rigorous inquiry.

By means of such speculative reckoning, one engages in deceptive sophistry and nihilism, falling into the ranks of the external paths and deluding the nature of Bodhi. This is what is called the fifth type of externalist.
The four perversions, the immortality of evasive equivocation, and the pervasive false discourses are collectively termed "the view that things both exist and do not exist.
This refers to what was previously mentioned as the views of permanence and impermanence, and the finite and the infinite.

There is still a distinction; they have not yet become confused. This [view] asserts that [things] are both permanent and impermanent, and both finite and infinite—a total muddle that allows for no rigorous inquiry.
It is truly a frivolous and absurd doctrine, the height of perversity.
Based on the upper migratory realm of the "finite" sphere, it designates this as "change," while the continuity of the "infinite" sphere—
That which is called "permanence" refers to the state perceived within eighty thousand kalpas; that which is called "arising" refers to the state perceived beyond eighty thousand kalpas;

and that which is called "cessation" refers to the state where nothing is seen. Furthermore, within the continuity [of existence], that which is uninterrupted is reckoned as "increase," like the gradual waxing of the bright fortnight;
that which is separated in the interim is reckoned as "decrease," like the waning of both the dark and bright fortnights at the end of the month.
Furthermore, regarding each respective place of birth, they collectively designate it as "existence"; regarding each respective place of extinction, they collectively designate it as "non-existence.

Within the arising and ceasing of the single aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), they divide it into eight meanings; yet when observing them through principle as a whole, both possibilities are equally valid, and they cannot determine a definitive conclusion.
At all times, they confuse their discourse and remain submerged within the aggregate of formations.
One cannot transcend the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Therefore, one is merely driven by arising and ceasing. Furthermore, when distinguishing between existence and non-existence:
for those who realize the characteristic of momentary cessation, they speak only of its non-existence;
for those who realize the characteristic of momentary arising, they speak only of its existence. Moreover, when synthesizing existence and non-existence, it is said:
"Existence is also non-existence; non-existence is also existence. Within existence there is not non-existence; within non-existence there is not existence.
Although these terms appear reciprocally, they differ slightly from what preceded. In the former case, both ends were presented together, which could not lead to a definitive resolution.
Here, however, only one end is raised, yet both ends are fully contained therein. Thus it is said: 'also'."
Existence is itself non-existence; one does not speak exclusively of non-existence. Within non-existence, there is no "is-ness"; one does not speak exclusively of "is-ness.
When knowledge and vision are confused and disordered, there is no fixed standard. One becomes muddled and bewildered, falling into error and falsehood.

It is called "pervasive conceptualization" (parikalpa) because one conceptualizes existence and conceptualizes non-existence, birth and cessation, increase and decrease, and constant change—conceptualizing everything. In reality, this is of no benefit for attaining [liberation]. In brief:
This is mere conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). Nevertheless, for a master who has attained thorough mastery of all directions, one may say "it exists" and one may also say "it does not exist";
there is a way of emergence in every situation. A monk asked Zhaozhou, "Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not? Zhaozhou said, "It has.

Furthermore, within samādhi, those sons of good family who maintain a firm, concentrated, and upright mind leave no opening for Māra to gain advantage; they exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings.

Observing that profound clarity, one constantly disturbs the fundamental source. Those who give rise to conceptual calculations regarding this inexhaustible flow fall into the error of perceiving signs after death;
their resolve becomes inverted. Either they cling to their own bodies, claiming "form is the self," or they perceive the self as being pervasive.
Pervading the entire realm, one thinks, "I have form," or, following that prior condition, as it turns back toward oneself, one thinks, "Form belongs to me," or "I depend upon it.
Within the continuity of formations, one thinks, "I am in form"—all such conceptualizations are assertions that there is a mark [of self] after death.

Thus, in this cycle, there are sixteen aspects. From these, one may calculate that affliction and enlightenment are ultimately two distinct natures that proceed side by side without ever touching one another.
Because of such speculative reckoning regarding existence after death, one falls into the ranks of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).

This deludes the nature of Bodhi. This is called the sixth heterodox school established within the five aggregates, which is the inverted view of a mind that maintains there is a mark of existence after death.
It is said in general that the calculations of the preceding five schools—whether asserting existence, non-existence, or both existence and non-existence—do not go beyond these three propositions.
Not yet having seen that which transcends both [existence and non-existence], they still remain stuck within the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations).

Therefore, they now speculate regarding whether there is a mark after death or no mark, or whether it is both existent and nonexistent or neither; furthermore, regarding subsequent existences, they give rise to the two views of annihilationism and the view of nirvāṇa.
