Having exhausted the root of all living beings and contemplated that profound, pure, and eternally quiescent source of movement, they eliminate the prior [delusions] of form, sensation, and perception, yet still give rise to conceptual calculations.
This person falls into the signless state after death; their resolve becomes inverted. They perceive that form has ceased and the physical body has no basis;

they observe that perception has ceased and the mind has no attachments; they know that sensation has ceased and there is no further continuity; the nature of the aggregates has dissolved and dispersed.
Even if there were the faculty of life-force, in the absence of sensation and perception, one would be identical to grass and trees.

Since this physical substance cannot be apprehended even while present before us, how could various characteristics possibly exist after death? Examining it through this logic, the characteristics are absent after death; thus it is a continuous cycle.
There are eight kinds of signlessness. From these, some may speculate that the causes and effects of nirvana are all empty, existing merely as names, and ultimately subject to total cessation.
Because they calculate that there is nothing after death, they fall into the ways of external paths and become deluded regarding the nature of bodhi.
This is called the seventh heterodox school, which establishes the theory of the post-mortem absence of signs (*animitta*) within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), based on a perverted mind.
It is generally said that this is the view of annihilationism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*). However, it examines the cessation of form, sensation, and perception;

specifically, it concerns the physiological principle of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), which will ultimately be annihilated. When the aggregate of formations ceases, one returns to the ocean of the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*). As for that [school]—
Such a reckoning is not yet free from the view of non-existence. However, the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is not something that can be extinguished;

yet they merely perceive its cessation and consequently reckon that the causes and effects of nirvāṇa are entirely empty and ultimately annihilated. They do not realize that this [cessation] is specifically characterized by the absence of marks (animitta).
It is not that there is no道理 (principle) here. Thus, by taking the four *skandhas* as present, the cause perishes and the future fruit is extinguished;

combining these constitutes the eight aspects of signlessness (*animitta*). This establishes the "theory of the inversion of mind regarding signlessness after death" within the context of the five *skandhas*.
This theory was also first formulated based on the mutual absence [of dharmas], attaining realization through the absence of causes. — From the *Chángshā Cén Yīn*.
When the monk passed away, [the Master] rubbed him with his hand and said, "Great assembly, this monk has truly upheld the essential principles for all of you and deliberated upon them.
Do you understand? He then spoke a verse: "Not a single dharma before the eyes, Nor a person present in that very place.
The vast and boundless diamond body— Neither false, nor yet real. He further said: "Not recognizing the diamond body, one instead calls it..."
Dependent origination: throughout the ten directions, all is true quiescence. Who is there, and who is practicing?
When Dongshan was about to pass away, he said to the assembly, "I have an idle name remaining in the world; who can rid me of it? No one in the assembly could respond.
At that time, a novice monk stepped forward and said, "Please grant me your Dharma-name. Dongshan replied, "My idle name has already been extinguished. Shishuang remarked, "None."
When someone gained his approval, Yunju said, "If there were such a thing as a 'leisurely name,' it would not belong to my late master.
Caoshan said, "From antiquity to the present, no one has been able to discern it. Shushan said, "The dragon possesses the mechanism for emerging from the water; no one can discern it.
Dayang Ming'an asked Liangshan, "What is the formless site of enlightenment? Liangshan pointed to Guanyin.
Yangshan said, "This is a painting by the Recluse of Wu. Yangping was about to offer a word of response when Yangshan hurriedly asked, "This has form;
what is that which is formless? At these words, Yangping attained realization. He prostrated himself and then returned to his original position to stand.
Yangshan said, "Why do you not utter a single phrase? Yangping replied, "I would not decline to speak, but I fear it would only fill the paper."

Mozhao laughed heartily and said, "These words shall be inscribed upon stone. Later, they were indeed carved onto a stele. Touzi took up the case and remarked: "The Way is vast, spanning past and present;
those who travel it find it difficult to cross. The mountain is perilous and steep; those who would climb it have no means of access.
If one does not illuminate the traces of the predecessors, there will be no time to tread the path and enter. Therefore, awakening arises from oneself; the seal is thus..."

Relying on the masters, they provide proof through successive generations to continue the Buddha’s life-force of wisdom. This is like asking for directions at a remote precipice when one's strength is exhausted;
it is like a cliff face with no door when one's efforts to advance or retreat have reached their limit. Once the golden dragon has lost its water, the garuḍa swiftly seizes it;
having separately penetrated the waves and surges, one returns once more to the fundamental station. O worthy ones, at such a time as this, do you still know the ancients?
Does he descend from his station? If you can perceive this, it may be said that ten-thousand-fathom peaks are shattered and a thousand waves are exhausted.

The Dragon Palace and the celestial realms share their eaves; the Phoenix Pavilion and the stars merge in their radiance. The pine trees on the crags enshroud auspiciousness; the mists and grasses of the valley are fragrant.
Without violating the gate of transformation, the myriad mountains emerge far beyond. If you do not know where he has descended, then the cliffs are vast and no one asks.

The dragon grieves that the blue sea is deep. The verse says: When the path is exhausted at the precipitous cliff, one asks the mountain elder; he points elsewhere, saying the ridge to the west of the crag is closer than the east.
As one prepares to advance, mist hangs down and the mountain vapors grow heavy; turning the head for a moment, the sun is seen glowing red.
If you can obtain some news regarding this formlessness, then even though it is called "formless," it does not hinder anything.

Furthermore, among those sons of good family within samādhi who have stabilized and concentrated their correct minds, such that Māra finds no opportunity, they exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings and contemplate that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source.
While abiding in the midst of mental formations (*saṃskāra*), they simultaneously suppress feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*), dualistically calculating both existence and non-existence.
Their own essential nature is undermined. Such people fall into the nihilistic and non-nihilistic views that arise after death, giving rise to inverted theories.

Within form, sensation, and perception, they see both existence and non-existence; within the flux of mental formations, they observe both non-existence and not-non-existence. Thus they cycle through these states, exhausting the aggregates and the realms.
Eighth is the characteristic of neither [existence nor non-existence]. Upon encountering any one of these conditions, they all claim that after death there is neither existence nor non-existence.

Furthermore, because they reckon that the nature of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is subject to change and transformation, their minds give rise to a penetrating realization that both existence and non-existence are neither [the case], and that both the void and the real cannot be determined. It is through such deliberation that they arrive at this conclusion.

"Neither existing nor non-existing after death; the subsequent limit is dark and obscure, as there is nothing that can be spoken of. Thus they fall into the ranks of the heterodox, deluding themselves regarding the nature of Bodhi.
This is called the eighth heterodox school. Abiding within the five aggregates, they maintain the inverted doctrine that one neither exists nor does not exist after death.

Tong said: "This is neither the view of existence nor the view of non-existence. It arises from the simultaneous reckoning of both existence and non-existence, whereby their own essences mutually negate one another.

Not only do form, sensation, perception, and mental formations cease, but existence is itself non-existence; as the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) undergoes transition and change, non-existence is itself not non-existence.
By contemplating this cycle and its reversals, one sees that what previously ceased once existed; thus, although it is non-existent, it is not non-existent. As for the present..."
That which exists must ultimately perish; though it exists, it is not truly existent. Because one employs these four aggregates in pairs for calculation, eight "non-existences" (asat) are formed.

Whichever single condition is cited, each possesses both the characterized (sanimitta) and the uncharacterized (animitta). This merely involves observing the presence or absence of characteristics within those conditions.

This is not yet refined. Furthermore, within the arising and ceasing, the flux and transformation of the nature of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), one sees that within arising there is already cessation;
therefore, it is not existent. One sees that within cessation there is already arising; therefore, it is not non-existent.

This state where both existence and non-existence are negated can only be perceived by observing the nature of conditioned phenomena; it cannot be achieved by those who have not attained penetrating awakening through the mind. That which exists yet is not existent—this is...

This refers to "wondrous existence. It is non-existent yet not non-existent; this is called true non-existence. It is the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*), the primary ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) within the Way.

Those [who hold such views] merely perceive both negation and affirmation within the nature of conditioned activity. Consequently, regarding the final limit of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), they remain muddled and blind.
Thus, they lose their bearings between the void and the real, knowing not where to turn. Having no place of refuge, there is nothing further to be done.
Even if one wished to manifest the realm of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which is neither arising nor ceasing, it could not be attained;

how much less so the True Suchness (*tathatā*) and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), the supreme principle of non-arising and non-ceasing? That which they call "thorough awakening" [is merely this].
This is merely the awakening of a pratyekabuddha; it cannot be called true awakening. This state of being neither existent nor non-existent is likewise derived from previous sophistry.

To say that existence is itself non-existence, or that within non-existence there is not existence—pushing this logic to its extreme regarding what happens after death—one first formulates such a theory, which is uniformly termed "inversion. When a non-Buddhist asks the Buddha, he does not answer.
There was one who said: "When there is speech, there is no silence. After a long while, the World-Honored One remained silent. The non-Buddhist practitioner praised him, saying:
"The World-Honored One, with great kindness and great compassion, has cleared away my clouds of delusion and enabled me to enter. After the non-Buddhist had departed, Ānanda asked the Buddha:
"What realization did that non-Buddhist have that he claimed to have 'entered'? The Buddha replied: "It is like a fine horse that, upon seeing the shadow of a whip, [responds immediately]."
[The Buddha] went. The World-Honored One granted this non-Buddhist the status of a fine horse; he was one whose mind had given rise to supernatural penetration and awakening.

Xuedou’s verse says: "The mechanism of the wheel has never yet turned; once it turns, it must run in both directions. When the clear mirror suddenly confronts its stand, it distinguishes beauty from ugliness in an instant.
Once the treacherous and the ugly are distinguished, the clouds of delusion disperse. Where could dust arise at the gate of compassion? Reflecting on this...
A fine horse catches the shadow of the whip; chasing the wind for a thousand *li*, it can be called back. "Called back!"—he snaps his fingers three times.
A monk asked Fayan, "What is the Bodhi that meets the eye before a deceased monk? Fayan said, "It is right before you.
The monk asked again, "When a deceased monk passes away, where does he go? Fayan said, "How many [deceased monks]..."
The deceased had already passed away. The monk said, "What can be done about it now? Yanguan said, "You do not recognize the deceased monk.
Fayen called out with all his might, yet [the monk] still did not turn his head. If you can gain insight into this, you may be said to have transcended all four propositions.

The numinous root alone is revealed. Furthermore, among the sons of good family within *samādhi*, those who stabilize and concentrate their upright minds so that demons find no opportunity, and who exhaustively investigate the origin of all living beings,
observing that profound clarity which is yet the source of constant agitation— yet subsequently harbor conceptual calculations regarding non-arising— such persons fall into [the error of]...
The seven theories of annihilation: some reckon that it is the destruction of the body; some that it is the destruction of desire; some that it is the destruction of suffering;

some that it is the destruction of extreme bliss; and some that it is the destruction of extreme equanimity. Thus they cycle through these until the seven limits are exhausted, wherein [existence] is extinguished before one's eyes; once extinguished, there is nothing more.
Based on this speculative reckoning that there is annihilation after death, one falls among the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) and becomes deluded regarding the nature of bodhi.
This is called the ninth non-Buddhist school: the perverse doctrine of the mind that establishes the annihilation of the five aggregates after death.

Tong said: "Previously, one observed the existence of the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) while feeling, perception, and consciousness were absent; now, this aggregate of formations is also absent. Therefore it is said that 'the subsequent is non-existent.
That which preceded death and that which follows are without characteristics, belonging merely to the single limit of the cessation of the body. This exhausts the seven limits."

Cessation occurs such that they do not arise again. Their bodies belong to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), encompassing both humans and devas. When desire is exhausted, they belong to the first dhyāna; when suffering is exhausted, they belong to the second dhyāna;
when extreme bliss is reached, they belong to the third dhyāna; and when extreme equanimity is reached, they encompass the fourth dhyāna and the two formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Although it is said that five matters are extinguished, this actually includes all seven stages. This refers to those non-Buddhists who enter the state of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*); in general, they are similar to those who have not heard the Dharma.
The bhikṣus share the same view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*), claiming that having already realized the fruit, they will not undergo further existence;
thus they establish the doctrine of annihilation after death. Master Kaixian Zhaoshan ascended the hall and said:

"The regulations of the monastic groves and the ancestral style of the Buddhas consist of one session of inquiry and one request, one gruel and one meal. But tell me, what do these clarify? It is simply that the minds of you all are not..."
Stop. If you can stop where there is no stopping, then in the station of mindfulness there is no thought;
you naturally accord with the principle of non-arising. To speak in such a way is to laugh until others’ mouths fall apart. *Chan*.
A monk asked Yunmen, “If one does not give rise to a single thought, is there still transgression? Yunmen said, “Mount Sumeru. Baiyun ended with a verse: *Mount Sumeru*.

Ah! It fills the universe. The Great Compassion of the Thousand Eyes cannot see through it. Unless one can personally master the art of riding a cow backward, one will spend a lifetime following after others.
Tiantong’s Verse says: Without giving rise to a single thought, there is Mount Sumeru.
Shaoyang’s Dharma-giving is not stingy in intent. If you are willing to come, he hands it over with both hands; If you try to grasp it, ten thousand fathoms deep, it is unclimbable.
The vast blue sea is wide; white clouds are idle. Do not allow even a hair’s breadth to enter between them. The mimicked crowing of a rooster cannot deceive me;
I refuse to let you pass the barrier in a state of confusion. These two verses make a great distinction.

If you rely on them and fail to give rise to a single thought, and do not understand the message of riding a cow backward, this is merely the mimicked crowing of a rooster; you will inevitably follow along with it.
Such a person is already late; how could they possibly penetrate the pivotal mechanism of the ultimate state?

Furthermore, among those sons of good family within *samādhi*, their minds are firm, concentrated, and upright, so that demons find no opportunity; they exhaustively investigate the fundamental nature of all living beings.

Observing that profound stillness, they constantly disturb the fundamental source. Subsequently, regarding future existence, those who give rise to speculative calculations fall into the doctrine of the five nirvāṇas.
Alternatively, taking the desire realm as the true basis for transformation, they observe its perfect luminosity and, because they give rise to attachment and longing for it, [they fall into error].
Either because the nature of the first dhyāna is free from sorrow; or because the nature of the second dhyāna is free from suffering;

or because the third dhyāna is accompanied by supreme bliss; or because in the fourth dhyāna both suffering and pleasure have vanished, and one no longer undergoes the nature of saṃsāric birth and death.

Deluded regarding the heavens of outflows (*sāsrava*), they conceive them as unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Regarding these five abodes as secure and as a supreme, pure refuge, they thus cycle through them until reaching their ultimate limit in these five places.

By such conceptualization, they calculate that nirvana is manifest within these five states; consequently, they fall into the ranks of external paths (*tīrthika*) and become confused about the nature of bodhi.
This is called the tenth heterodox school, which establishes the inverted doctrine of attaining nirvana within the five aggregates through the five present states.

Ānanda, these ten kinds of deluded understandings regarding *dhyāna* all arise because the mind is applied to the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) in a state of mutual conflict; thus, these realizations appear.

Sentient beings are stubbornly deluded and fail to reflect upon themselves; when they encounter these present manifestations, they mistake delusion for understanding and say of themselves: [“I have attained it.”]
To claim sainthood is a great falsehood; one shall fall into the Avīci Hell.

You must take these words of the Tathāgata and, after my parinirvāṇa, transmit them throughout the Dharma-ending age, so that all sentient beings may universally awaken to this meaning. Do not allow the demons of the mind to give rise to deep calamities within themselves.
Maintain and protect [this teaching] to extinguish false views, and instruct their bodies and minds to open to the realization of the true meaning. In the state of non-...
The supreme path does not encounter byways or forks. Do not let the mind pray for attainment and be satisfied with little; rather, act as the pure pointing finger of the Great Awakened King.
It is said in general:
"Since it is stated that there is no end to what follows and follows, why is there yet again 'what follows and follows'? This is because this realm is profound and pure.
The fundamental source is constantly disturbed; this "extinction that cannot be attained" means one has not reached the site of true quiescent extinction.
One falsely perceives within the state of extinction something that can be realized, and thus speaks of "successive existences.

This is because the activity-aggregate (saṃskāra-skandha) momentarily pauses, and when the perfect luminosity briefly manifests, one immediately claims that this absence of arising and ceasing is itself nirvana. Thus, one calculates nirvana based on these five states.

If Nirvana were to possess these five [aspects], could it truly be called "true Nirvana"? That is to say, having already extinguished the seven previous limits, one establishes the five types of Nirvana.
Craving for perfect luminosity is shared by both humans and devas; when both suffering and medicine have vanished, one does not undergo birth or extinction.
This is the same as the four dhyānas and the formless heavens. These five states are secure, yet they do not transcend the three realms.
The outflows of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), existence (*bhava-āsrava*), and ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*) remain latent as before.

Merely through the mastery and perfection of conditioned effort (*saṃskṛta-vyāpāra*), they attain only the meditative absorption of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), yet claim to have attained the fruit of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-phala*).
Deluded within the midst of the outflows, they fail to realize this for themselves; when their kalpa is exhausted, they return to the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*). How could this be true *nirvāṇa*?

Yes. Sengzhidao requested further instruction from the Sixth Patriarch, saying, "Since I left the household life, I have studied the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* for more than ten years, yet I have not clarified its great meaning.
I pray that the Master will deign to instruct me. The Patriarch asked, "What is it that you have not clarified?"
[The monk] said, "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are dharmas of arising and ceasing. When arising and ceasing have ceased, extinction is bliss.
He then expressed doubt regarding this. The Patriarch asked, "How do you doubt it? [The monk] replied, "All sentient beings possess two bodies, namely the physical body and the Dharma-body.
The physical body is impermanent, subject to arising and ceasing; the Dharma-body is permanent and lacks cognition."

There is no discernment. As the Sūtra says, "When birth-and-death has ceased, quiescent extinction is bliss. I do not yet understand: which body undergoes this quiescent extinction, and which body experiences this bliss?
If it is the physical body (*rūpakāya*), then at the time of its death, the four great elements disperse;

this is entirely suffering. That which is suffering cannot be called bliss. If it is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) that is quiescently extinguished, then it would be identical to grass, trees, tiles, and stones—who then would experience bliss?
They experience pleasure. Furthermore, the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) is the substance of arising and ceasing, while the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are the function of arising and ceasing.

One substance and five functions; arising and ceasing are constant. When there is arising, the function emerges from the substance; when there is cessation, the function is withdrawn back into the substance.
If one allows for further rebirth, then the class of sentient beings is neither interrupted nor extinguished. If one does not allow for further rebirth, then [they] would forever...
"Returning to quiescent extinction, one becomes identical to insentient things. If this were so, then all dharmas would be suppressed and subdued by nirvana;
they would not even be able to arise—what joy could there be in that? The Patriarch said, "You are a son of the Śākyas;
why do you practice the heterodox views of annihilationism and eternalism to discuss the Dharma of the Supreme Vehicle? According to what you have said, form itself..."
To claim that there is a separate Dharma-body apart from the physical body, and to seek quiescence by departing from birth and death;

or to infer the permanence and bliss of Nirvana while asserting that it possesses physical bodies and enjoyments—this is nothing other than clinging to birth and death and being addicted to worldly pleasures. You should now understand this.
The Buddha [taught] for the sake of all deluded people who, regarding the combination of the five aggregates as their own self-nature, discriminate all phenomena as external objects;
who love life and hate death, drifting through every thought-moment, unaware that these are like dreams and illusions, false and empty.
They undergo saṃsāra in vain, perceiving the eternal bliss of nirvāṇa as a state of suffering, and thus spend their days in restless pursuit.
Out of compassion for them, the Buddha reveals the true bliss of nirvāṇa: in each moment there is no characteristic of arising, and in each moment there is no characteristic of ceasing;

since there is further nothing to be extinguished through cessation, this is the manifestation of śamatha-vimokṣa (quiescent extinction). At the time of its manifestation, there is likewise nothing [to be attained].
That which can be apprehended through direct perception is called "eternal bliss. This bliss has no experiencer, nor is there anyone who does not experience it.

How could there even be such a thing as the designation of "one substance with five functions"? How much more so when you speak of the dharma of *nirvāṇa* that suppresses and restrains, causing things never to arise again!
This is to slander the Buddha and destroy the Dharma. Listen to my verse: "The Unsurpassed Great *Nirvāṇa*..."
The *pāṇa* (the bowl) is perfectly luminous and eternally quiescently radiant. The ignorant call it death; non-Buddhists cling to it as annihilation;
those seeking the two vehicles regard it as non-action. All these belong to the calculations of the emotional mind, the very root of the sixty-two views.
They falsely establish empty and provisional names—what could they be called the true meaning? Only those of transcendent capacity penetrate this without grasping or rejecting. By means of...

One knows the phenomena of the five aggregates and the "self" within those aggregates; all externally manifested forms and each individual characteristic of sound are equal, like dreams and illusions.
One does not give rise to views of ordinary beings or sages, nor does one form a conceptual understanding of nirvana.

Having severed the two extremes and the three periods of time, one constantly employs the functions of the sense faculties without giving rise to the thought of "functioning. One discerns all phenomena without giving rise to the notion of "discernment."

Do not harbor other thoughts. When the kalpa-fire burns the ocean floor and the winds blow the mountains until they collide, the bliss of true permanence and quiescent extinction—such is the mark of Nirvana.
I now speak these words by force, so that you may abandon your heterodox views; do not follow the literal meaning of my words, for I permit you to know but a small portion.
Chizhi, upon hearing this verse, attained great enlightenment, prostrated himself, and withdrew. This is as the Sixth Patriarch discussed.
Directly pointing to the true meaning, one becomes a Great Awakened King. This pure pointer truly accords with its words:

when fragmented views do not arise, the demons of the mind naturally subside. It is hoped that the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) may thus be shattered, and one may transcend the turbidity of sentient beings.

Ānanda, when those sons of good family who cultivate *samādhi* have exhausted the *saṃskāra-skandha*, the natures of all worlds—the subtle, pure, and restless movements, the commonality of the life-force—suddenly shatter and dissolve.
The deep channels through which the *pudgala* repays its karma and the suspended resonance between cause and effect are severed.
Regarding the heaven of *nirvāṇa*, they are on the verge of great awakening, like a rooster looking back as it crows at dawn.

In the east, there was already a refined radiance. The six sense faculties were empty and pure, no longer wandering or dissipated. Internally and externally (or, internally within), all was profoundly clear and bright.

Entering that which cannot be entered, he deeply penetrated the fundamental origins of the twelve classes of beings who receive life throughout the ten directions. He contemplated these origins as they are grasped by their very source.

All categories are not summoned; throughout the realms of the ten directions, they have already attained their commonality. Their refined essence does not sink, but manifests what is obscure and secret.

This is called the domain of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). If, within this state where all categories have attained their commonality, one grinds away the six gates, [the aggregate of consciousness will dissolve].
The union and separation are accomplished; seeing and hearing penetrate one another; their mutual functions are pure.

The worlds of the ten directions, as well as body and mind, are like vaidūrya (this blue precious stone), transparent and clear inside and out. This is called the exhaustion of the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate).
Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of life. Observing its origin, one sees that the mountain elephants of emptiness and inverted false thoughts constitute its root.
Tong said: "The natures of all worlds do not transcend the nature of the twelve classes of beings subject to birth and death.

Within the subtle, pure, and restless movement of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations), although there is no coarse appearance of birth and death, its fundamental state is constantly in motion, renewing itself without ceasing.
This is precisely the mechanism for the manifestation of the *sabhāgatā* (commonality). When the *saṃskāra-skandha* is exhausted, this mechanism collapses; it is what is called 'the mechanism.'"
Profound and invisible; subtle and beyond pointing out. It is like the main cord of a net, like the toggle of a garment.
Because these cords and toggles exist, they constitute the root-source of birth and extinction, the *pudgala*, and the body that takes rebirth through the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
In responding to causes and receiving fruits, there is a continuous resonance that is not mistaken by even a hair’s breadth. Now, the mechanism of life has been shattered.
If the causal karma has thus perished, what is there to draw forth the fruit and retribution? If the body no longer exists, who is there to recompense the cause?
When both cause and effect have vanished, the resonance between stimulus and response is severed. This is because the profound channels that transmit the subtle and fine [energies] have been cut off.

The movement of these channels is extremely minute; as long as the channels do not break, the life-root does not break. Only when the channels are severed and the mechanism is extinguished can [the process of rebirth be halted].

One enters the realm of non-arising. When the preceding three *skandhas* (aggregates) are exhausted, it is like the first crowing of a cock: the distinct colors have not yet differentiated, and one still remains in a state of dim obscurity.
When this *saṃskāra-skandha* (aggregate of formations) is exhausted, it is like the cock’s subsequent crowing: looking toward the east, the distinct colors are already present.

Upon entering this *vijñāna-skandha* (aggregate of consciousness), the six sense faculties become empty and still; they no longer exhibit signs of wandering, fleeing, agitation, or disturbance, but are profoundly luminous.

It is transparent and pure; it is within and yet further within, deep and yet deeper, until one reaches the point where there is nowhere to enter, directly arriving at the ground of the original source.
Therefore, previously I did not clarify the individual origins of their respective mandates, seeing only the mechanism of shared birth.
Now that I have reached the fundamental causes by which the twelve classes receive their mandates, I see that they are identical and no longer see them as born.
Thus it is. Observe their source and grasp their origin; do not allow them to drift, do not allow them to gallop away.
Since this has no beginning, that will naturally not be summoned. Throughout the entirety of the ten directions, there is only mind and only consciousness.
How could there be any difference? Having attained this sameness, heaven and earth share the same root as I, and the myriad things are one body with me—perfectly integrated.
It is the single ocean of the *ālayavijñāna*. If one gazes upon its refined essence without falling into dullness or torpor, then that which is neither seen nor heard is called the ultimate profound;
that which is neither sound nor smell is called the ultimate secret. Gradually, within this, they manifest and become revealed.

Although one has been able to discover this, it has not yet reached a state of crystalline clarity; it still remains shrouded by the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). Therefore, it is called the "domain of the aggregate of consciousness.

If, regarding the source from which the twelve classes of beings receive their life-force, one has already attained identity within the midst [of that source], one can, through the power of meditative concentration and wisdom, grind away and refine the six sense-gates, such that what is divided may be joined and what is obstructed may be opened. Once opened—
This is the union of freedom. It clarifies that one does not follow the sense organs; thus, what is seen and what is heard are adjacent to perfect penetration (*pariśuddha*).
Then the six faculties become pure and can be used interchangeably. This is what was previously called "returning the flow to restore the One" and "the six functions no longer operating.
Thereupon, the lands of the ten directions are brilliantly pure, like a crystal ball with a bright moon suspended within it. This is also described as follows:
The worlds of the ten directions, as well as one’s own body and mind, are like vaidūrya—the egg of the garuḍa.
They are pure, brilliant, and transparent, like a diamond; they cannot be destroyed.

Since both internally, the body and mind, and externally, the world, are luminously clear and penetrating, it is not merely that their refined colors manifest. All Tathāgatas are secretly perfect and...

Pure and wondrous things all appear within it. This person immediately attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), which is what is called the stage of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi*).
Those who have not exhausted the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) cannot reach this state. The aggregate of consciousness is subtle and difficult to sever;

it is the very root of the life-force (*jīvitendriya*) and the primary source from which one receives life. All things begin here. Now that the aggregate of consciousness is exhausted, both the faculties and their roots are exhausted. All...
One does not summon categories; to do so is to falsely conceptualize those that are not summoned. The ten directions are all the same; to do so is to obliterate that which is identical.
Thus, one is able to transcend the turbidity of life. Ancient masters held that life is a composite of the three—vitality, warmth, and consciousness.
At the moment of taking birth, the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) comes first. If the fundamental consciousness has already departed, then vitality...
As warmth ceases to follow, this consciousness departs and life ends; such is the case for all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). How, then, could this be called "transcending the turbidity of life"?
That which is called the "exhaustion of the aggregate of consciousness" refers to a consciousness that is neither coming first nor departing last.

That which is called "transcending the turbidity of life" refers to one who has already realized the path of an Arhat and will not undergo further existence. How can this be spoken of lightly? Furthermore, previously...
The bodies of sentient beings each follow their own kind. For those whose aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) has been exhausted, these channels have already been severed.

If this life-channel of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) becomes even more subtle, it is therefore called "insubstantial and void" (*wangxiang xuwu*). "Insubstantial" (*wang*) means as if non-existent; "substantial" (*xiang*) means as if existent.
Being both existent and non-existent, it is ultimately void and non-existent. That which is void and non-existent is neither born nor extinguished.
Suchness (*tathatā*) is the essence. That which is "formless" (*wangxiang*) is the shadow of arising and ceasing within the eight consciousnesses.

Therefore, relying on Suchness is called Right Enlightenment (*samyag-bodhi*); relying on the eight consciousnesses constitutes deluded awakening. Because it turns its back on enlightenment and unites with sensory objects, it is termed inverted false conceptualization.
When the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is exhausted, one transforms consciousness into wisdom (*jñāna*), transforming arising and ceasing to rely upon the non-arising.
It is extinguished. Apart from eliminating this delusive, non-substantial, vacuous, subtle, and inverted false conceptualization, how could it be easy to exert such power?
A monk asked Xiangyan, "What is the Way? Yan said, "A dragon’s cry within a withered tree.
The monk asked, "What is one who is on the Way? Yan said, "The eyes within a skull. The monk then raised this question for Shishuang. "What is..."
"The dragon roars within the withered tree. Shuangyun said, "It still carries a trace of joy. The monk asked, "What is the eye within the skull?
Shuangyun said, "It still carries a trace of consciousness. He then asked Caoshan, "What is the dragon roaring within the withered tree?
Caoshan replied, "The life-blood is unbroken. The monk asked, "What is the eye within the skull? Caoshan replied, "..."
[The Master] did not finish speaking. The monk asked, "I wonder if there is anyone who can hear it? Shanshan said, "Throughout the entire world, there is not a single person who does not hear it.
The monk asked, "I wonder what verses the dragon's roar consists of? Shanshan said, "If you do not know what verses they consist of, those who hear them will all perish.
Shanshan then showed him [the meaning] with a verse: "The dragon roars from the withered tree."

The True Path of Seeing (*tattva-darśana-mārga*). When the skull is devoid of consciousness, the eyes first attain clarity. When the joyful consciousness (*nandī-vijñāna*) is exhausted, all news and traces are extinguished.
How can a person discern the purity within the turbidity? Tiantong (Tian-tong Jue) comments: "The King dwells within the gate; the minister does not go out the gate.

Therefore, when both joy and consciousness are exhausted, the son returns to the father. This is called "the attainment of dryness" (*gāndha-prāpti*), which refers to what is known as the exhaustion of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
There are no such passages; yet evil ones are able to clarify these passages.

Ānanda, you should know that this good man has exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) and returned to the source within consciousness (*vijñāna*); he has already extinguished birth and death.

Yet, while their subtle and wondrous state of quiescence is not yet perfected, they are able to cause their own physical sense organs to merge and open, and to communicate with all classes of beings throughout the ten directions.

Their awareness penetrates universally, enabling them to enter the perfect source. If, regarding that which they take as their refuge, they establish it as a truly permanent cause, [they fall into the error of permanence].
Those who give rise to such resolute conviction fall into the attachment to causes and their underlying reasons.

They become companions of the *tattva* (Principle of Darkness) to which the Śābikara (the Yellow-haired Heretic) resorts, thereby becoming deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and losing their true knowledge and vision. This is called the first instance of establishing a mind that seeks to acquire something;
it results in a fruit toward which one turns for refuge. It is far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvana, giving rise to the seeds of external paths.

Tong said: "The consciousness-aggregate (vijñāna-skandha) is profoundly luminous, yet it flows due to activity. Since the activity-aggregate (saṃskāra-skandha) has been emptied, the appearance of the flowing stream of birth-and-death has already been extinguished.

Nevertheless, it still relies upon the source of consciousness, that place of profound stillness where there is no flow; therefore, its subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction is not yet perfected.
As for 'quiescent extinction,' it means that once birth-and-death has ceased, one no longer further employs cessation to extinguish that birth-and-death. Now...

The cessation of birth and death still belongs to the realm of deliberate effort; therefore, it is not yet supreme. Because the fundamental source of consciousness remains present, it is not yet perfected.

Nevertheless, having returned to the source of consciousness and worn away the six gates until they converge in a single location, one is able to cause the six faculties within one’s own body to interpenetrate.

Reaching this state, their functions are mutually interchangeable, and their union and separation are without obstruction. Through the faculties as a medium, clarity is manifested, and mastery over them is exercised with complete ease.
Not only is one’s own inner clarity awakened, but it also penetrates the awakening of all classes of beings throughout the ten directions.
The awakening of all classes of beings is my own awakening; my own awakening is the awakening of all classes of beings. Our cognitions are mutually interpenetrating, merging as one without duality.
One is able to enter the source of awakening (*bodhi*), which is perfectly interfused and unobstructed. This source is the ultimate perfection;

it is the very source from which all classes of beings receive their life-force, and it is also the source from which all classes of beings give rise to awakening. Life is established by this source, and awakening arises from this source.
Since it is that from which awakening itself emerges, one does not perceive any characteristic of knowing or perceiving. Thus, while the awakened state is not permanent, there is no one who awakens.
Because it is permanent, awakening returns to impermanence; this is precisely true permanence. Returning to the source within consciousness is the cause of true permanence.
This specifically refers to that state prior to the manifestation of the eight consciousnesses, which is dark and beyond perception, yet is taken as the place of ultimate rest.
This is what non-Buddhists call the "Dark Principle" (Tattva). Since there is both a destination and a cause, it is capable of—

The cause and the causal basis are both merely delusions. To establish a mind that seeks attainment and to achieve a fruit that is attained—both cause and effect thus fall into what is conceptually constructed.
Where there is "having" (objectification), there is no perfection; where there is "having," there is no truth.
