The Daoist said, "My Way is correct. The Master said, "It is not. If your Way were truly correct, you would have been able to match me.

You are merely a solitary soul without a master. Because of this, the Daoist ceased his further disputations. Even if one were to respond with perfect clarity, it would still not transcend the ultimate truth (*tattva*);
it remains vastly distant from the Unsurpassed, Perfectly Equal, and Right Enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Ānanda, furthermore, there may be a son of good family who has exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and has already extinguished birth and death;

yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of cessation (*śamatha*), he has not yet perfected it. If, with respect to that which is his refuge, he regards it as his own self-body, and develops a resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) that all sentient beings within the twelve categories throughout the entirety of the realm of empty space are but a single class flowing forth from within his own body—this person then falls into the error of "the subject and its object."

The subject—the Lord Maheśvara (the Māra-king at the summit of the realm of form)—manifests boundless bodies to become his companion. Thus they delude the Buddha’s Bodhi and lose their true knowledge and vision.
This is called the second [stage]: establishing the subject as the mind and accomplishing the fruit of subjective activity. It is far removed from perfect penetration.
Turning their backs on the city of Nirvana, they give rise to the seeds of great pride and the celestial arrogance that "I am omnipresent and perfect.

It is explained: in the aforementioned theories of permanence and impermanence, they contemplate the wondrously luminous mind as pervading the ten directions of space, taking its profound stillness to be the ultimate divine self (*ātman*).
From this, they calculate that the self pervades the ten directions, remaining fixed in clarity and unmoving; thus, all sentient beings...
"Birth. Within my own mind, there is the notion that birth and death occur spontaneously; this is precisely what is called the view that everything flows forth from within one's own body.
Because that [view] observes the phenomena (*dharma*), it calculates birth and extinction; because this [view] observes the source (*mūla*), it calculates the capacity for agency.
Although it clings to the "self" as being able to produce those [phenomena], in reality it cannot do so; therefore, it is called the "clinging to the capacity and the lack of capacity. (10)
The two classes of beings receive their life-force from its source; if they grasp it as residing within themselves, they say, "Life issues forth from me," and there is nothing wrong with this.
Why, then, do you say that [the mind] is not the agent? It is because the three realms are but mind and the myriad dharmas are but consciousness (*vijñapti*).
Since no mark of a self (*ātman*) can be found, the mind is able to give rise to the myriad phenomena. Now, if one regards the source of consciousness as one's own essence, one then says:

"The universe rests in his hand; the myriad transformations arise from his body. This is like peering into the ocean and seeing it capable of producing bubbles, yet one's own person has not yet escaped being a bubble.
How could a bubble produce another bubble? To have even a trace of "ability" to grasp [this state], though one manifests vast supernatural powers, all ultimately reduces to arrogance;
for it is to claim ability where there is actually an inability to do so. Maheśvara...
Śūla has three eyes and eight arms; he rides a white ox and holds a white fly-whisk.

He is able to manifest the bodies of infinite sentient beings and thus claims that sentient beings flow forth from his own self. The realm where he dwells is the Akaniṣṭha Heaven (the Peak of Form), which has not yet transcended the triple world.
To claim that one can produce the triple world while not having emerged from it—is this not self-conceit? To establish "I" as the source...
The mind of "arising" conceives that "I" can accomplish "that" matter; as long as one maintains this single notion of being able to see, one cannot be self-perfected.
Therefore, it is said that this is to be at odds with and far removed from perfect penetration, turning one's back on the city of Nirvana. Xuefeng addressed the assembly, saying:
"The entire earth is gathered up and made the size of a grain of millet; it is tossed before you. You lacquer buckets do not understand—beat the drum and let us all go see! Xuefeng.
Dousong said: "The ox-head is submerged; the horse-head turns back. Within the mirror of Caoxi, there is no dust. Though the drum is beaten, you do not see it.
When the hundred flowers bloom in spring, for whom do they open? On another day he said: "The entire earth is a single eye of the śramaṇa.
Where, all of you, will you void your excrement? When Zhaozhou heard this being cited, he said:
"If the Acharya returns, send a spade with him. The verse by Haiyin says: "The single eye of the śramaṇa admits nothing;
the myriad phenomena emerge from it. Who among men recognizes Zhaozhou’s spade?
This matter of letting go must be handled with subtle care. The verse by Biefeng Yin says: "Where did Xuefeng defecate? Zhaozhou sent a spade."
A śramaṇa with but one eye—how utterly chaotic he is! Hehehe! Within the land of the Great Tang, the drum rolls;
in the land of Silla, the dance sways. Behold this manner of proclamation by Xuefeng: he seeks only that one may recognize the original single type of outflow.
In the ground of ultimate reality, there is not the slightest trace or sign. If one speaks of "ability" [to attain it]...
To claim that understanding can lead to awakening and that it serves as the source of all phenomena is merely the empty prattle of a charlatan;
you must employ Zhaozhou’s spade before you can succeed.

Furthermore, good son, though you may exhaustively investigate the emptiness of all conditioned formations and thereby extinguish birth and death, you have not yet perfected the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction.

If, regarding that to which one has returned and that upon which one relies, one suspects that one’s own body and mind flow forth from it, and that the voids of the ten directions all arise from it— then,
with respect to that ground from which everything arises and flows forth, one should form the understanding that it is the true, eternal body, free from arising and ceasing.
Amidst arising and ceasing, they prematurely reckon it to be eternally abiding; thus they are deluded regarding non-arising and likewise confused about arising and ceasing.
Dwelling securely in this delusion, those who conceive such a resolute conviction fall into the attachment to permanence and non-permanence, taking the Lord God (Īśvara) as their companion.

They are deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and have lost their true knowledge and vision. This is called the third: establishing causes based on the mind, thereby producing false conceptualized effects.
It is far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvana, giving rise to the seeds of inverted perfection.

Tong said: "Previously it was said that if one establishes the cause of true permanence based on what is returned to, then since there is something to which one returns, this 'I' has something to which it returns.

That to which my 'I' returns is truly able to produce me; thus, I myself began to doubt that my body and mind flow forth from that source-consciousness, and that the empty space of the ten directions all arise from it, rather than arising from myself. Therefore, it is said: 'All...'"
It arises. It does not flow from a self; therefore, it is called "proclaiming and flowing. Before there was a self, this consciousness already existed.

Not only does it give rise to the self, it can give rise to all things. Thus, one gradually begins to perceive that the *puruṣa* (spiritual self) is eternal, and that the source of consciousness is likewise eternal.
While the spiritual self still pertains to the seven consciousnesses, the source of consciousness is purely the state of the eighth consciousness before any movement has occurred. This is...

Taking this to be non-arising and non-ceasing, they conceive of it as a truly permanent body. Within this state of profound stillness and lack of movement, amidst subtle arising and ceasing, they prematurely calculate it to be eternally abiding.
Not only do they fail to see the true nature of non-arising and non-ceasing, but they are also deluded regarding the present phenomena of arising and ceasing.
Dwelling securely in their delusion, they mistake it for a superior understanding; thus, they take what is impermanent to be permanent.
It is eternal. Therefore, one falls into the attachment of permanence and non-eternality.

For example, those who reckon that Maheśvara can produce the self consider him to be eternal, yet they do not realize that Maheśvara is likewise not an eternally abiding deity. A Daoist scripture states: "As for the Taiyi..."
The primal qi first arose above the Great Void. There is the Heaven of the Jade Capital (*Yujing*), with eight heavens in each of the four directions, wherein thirty-two emperors reside.
Above the Jade Capital are the Three Clarities (*Sanchong*)—the Heavens of Jade Clarity (*Yuqing*), Supreme Clarity (*Shangqing*), and Great Clarity (*Taiqing*).
Above the Three Clarities are the Ten Heavens of the Sovereign of Emptiness (*Xuhuang*). Therein dwell the Primordial Elder and the Primordial Honored One.
The Nine Sovereigns (Jiuhuang) resided therein; these are the Heaven of Form-Peak (Rūpadhātu) and the Heaven of Space-Abiding (Ākāśānantyāyatana).

These matters are not detailed by the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), who consequently regard them as the fundamental source for the generation of heaven and earth. It is even claimed that the Celestial Sovereign (Tianhuang) descended with the nine qi to form the primordial chaos (hundun).
Furthermore, the Western Regions likewise regard the Great Brahmā Heaven (Mahābrahmā) as the Lord of the World; both views originate from this perspective. This, then, is...

The establishment of causes depends on the mind; the dependence of causes on the source of consciousness is able to give rise to a self. Thus, the fruit of false discrimination is established, whereby one falsely discriminates permanence. This is not due to a real self;
rather, the previous calculation held that the self was complete and gave rise to things, while this calculation holds that those [things] are complete and give rise to the self.

Therefore, it is called "inverted completeness. This is because one wishes to forget the self and forget the capacity [to create], yet cannot completely eliminate the characteristic of arising. Hence it is said:
This violates and distances one from perfect penetration and turns one’s back on the city of Nirvana. Daning Kuan addressed the assembly, holding up his staff and saying:
"The life-force of the Buddhas of the past and the administrative principles of the Buddhas of the future are both contained right here. Now they are put to use, becoming clouds and rain."
It is an auspicious omen and a blessing; it benefits both humanity and the heavens.

Whether entering birth or facing death, whether appearing or disappearing, unfolding or rolling up, throughout other worlds—if one were to have a mouth all over one’s body, one could not finish describing it; if one were to have eyes all over one’s body, one could not exhaustively perceive it.

"A single thought-moment corresponds [to all time]; in an instant, ten thousand kalpas. Furthermore, Ciming addressed the assembly, saying: "When Daowu beats the drum, the four quarters of the world participate together.
When the staff is held crosswise, it encompasses the heavens and the great earth; when the alms bowl is turned, it turns the world."
It covers and overturns worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Now I ask you all: where do you establish yourselves and sustain your lives?

If you know the place where one establishes oneself and sustains one's life, then whether eating gruel or rice in Uttarakuru, or eating gruel or rice on the long benches of the monastery—it is the same.
These venerable masters point directly to that which is truly unborn.
Cessation is the eternally true body. Now tell me: does it have a place of rest, or does it not? You may well harbor doubts about this.

Furthermore, good son, you have exhausted all conditioned phenomena to the point of emptiness, and have already extinguished birth and death; yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction, it is not yet perfected.

If, regarding all that is knowable, one’s knowledge is pervasive and complete, then based on that knowledge one establishes an understanding such that the grasses and trees of the ten directions are all called sentient beings and are no different from humans;
when grasses and trees become humans, and humans die and return to becoming the grasses and trees of the ten directions, there is no discrimination—this is universal knowledge.

Those who give rise to such resolute conviction fall into the attachment of "knowing non-knowing. They become companions to the two heterodox teachers, Bāṭa and Śākani, who cling to the notion that all is consciousness.
Thus they lose sight of the Buddha’s Bodhi and forfeit true knowledge and vision. This is called the fourth calculation: regarding the mind that perceives all as perfect.
It results in false and erroneous fruits, strays far from perfect penetration, turns its back on the city of Nirvana, and gives rise to the seeds of inverted cognition.

Tong said: "Previously, you returned to the principle of *amūrta-tattva* (the obscure ultimate), which is dark and devoid of cognition, yet you maintained that cognition can ultimately never be extinguished.

Consequently, you established a doctrine based on this cognition, asserting that consciousness fundamentally possesses awareness and that all phenomena arise through the transformation of this cognition.
Based on this, you reckoned that the essence of cognition pervades all dharmas, even claiming that insentient things everywhere possess cognition without any discrimination."
Therefore, to consider ignorance as knowledge is called inverted knowledge. The *Tanzi Huashu* says: "An old lacquer tree transforms into a feathered immortal;
withered wheat transforms into a butterfly. These are instances of moving from the insentient to the sentient.
A virtuous woman transforms into a stone of integrity; a mountain earthworm transforms into a lily. These are instances of moving from the sentient to the insentient. Which of these is...?
He asked: "Who is 'I'? Who possesses consciousness? Who lacks consciousness? All things are but one thing; all spirits are but one spirit.
This is the realization that these grasses and trees are people, and people are grasses and trees. A monk asked National Teacher Huizhong:
"An ancient worthy said, 'The verdant green bamboo is entirely the Dharma-body; the lush yellow flowers are nothing other than the Buddha-mind.'"
If there are those who do not accept it, calling it a heterodox teaching, and yet there are also those who believe in it, calling it inconceivable, one does not know how to respond.
The Master said: "This is essentially the realm of Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī; it is not something that ordinary beings can believe or accept.
It accords with the intent of the definitive Mahāyāna sūtras. Thus, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says: 'The Buddha-body is all-pervading.'"

Within the *dharmadhātu*, he universally manifests before all sentient beings; responding to conditions and meeting with those who call upon him, there is nowhere he does not reach, yet he always remains upon this seat of Bodhi.
Since the verdant bamboo does not emerge outside the *dharmadhātu*, is it not, indeed, the *dharmakāya*?
Furthermore, the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "Because form is boundless, *prajñā* is also boundless. Since the yellow chrysanthemum does not transcend...
"Form—is this not Prajñā? These are profound and far-reaching words; it is difficult for those who do not understand them to direct their attention toward them.
Thereupon, the Zen guest paid his respects and departed. Furthermore, the Master of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra asked Master Dazhu:
"Why did the Zen guest not permit that 'the verdant green bamboo is entirely the Dharmakāya,' and that 'the luxuriant yellow flowers are none other than Prajñā'?"
The Master Zhu said: "The Dharma-body has no form; it takes shape in response to the green bamboo. Prajñā has no cognition;

it manifests its characteristics in relation to the yellow chrysanthemums. It is not that the yellow chrysanthemums and green bamboo possess the Prajñā and the Dharma-body; therefore, the Sūtra says:"
"The Buddha's true Dharma-body is like empty space; it manifests forms in response to things, like the moon reflected in water.
If the yellow flowers were prajñā, then prajñā would be identical to insentient matter. If the green bamboo were the Dharmakāya, then the Dharmakāya could still exercise functional application.
Master, do you understand? The master replied, "I do not understand this meaning. Zhuhong said, "If one has realized their nature, they would say 'yes'."
It is also acceptable; it is also acceptable that the Way is not so. One speaks according to function, without being obstructed by right or wrong.

For one who has not seen their nature, speaking of green bamboos is to become attached to the green bamboos; speaking of yellow flowers is to become attached to the yellow flowers; speaking of the Dharma-body is to be obstructed by the Dharma-body.
When they speak of Prajñā, they do not recognize Prajñā; thus, all have fallen into contentious debate.
The presiding master (Zezhu) bowed in thanks and departed. Miaoxi said, "The assembly discussed it, saying: 'These two venerable elders have thus refined one another.

One has attained its essence (ti), and the other has attained its function (yong). He who attained the function established himself within phenomena (shi); he who attained the essence [established himself within] principle (li)..."

Above, one sweeps away all traces; this is what is called the ground of ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), where not a single speck of dust is admitted. Within the gateway of Buddha-activity, not a single dharma is abandoned.
I am the Dharma King, sovereign over the Dharma; whether suppressing or exalting, there is neither gain nor loss.
Such a view as this is called "a dwarf watching a play. My own perspective, Wondrous Joy, must also be known by all of you.
"It is not seeing the road; it is merely enough to drive away the flies on the back of a donkey. Furthermore, a monk asked Yunmen, "What is the pure Dharma-body?
Yunmen said, "A flowered medicinal fence. The monk asked, "What is it like when one goes forth in this very way? Yunmen said:
The Golden-Maned Lion. Xuedou’s verse says: "Flowers and medicinal herbs in the railing; do not be negligent. The star is on the scale, not on the pan.
To act thus is most reckless. Behold, everyone, the golden-maned lion! Tiantong comments:
When a thief comes, one must strike; when a guest comes, one must wait. Yunmen and Xuedou—both were masters of their craft.
Is there anyone here who can go directly like this? One must by all means avoid bumping one's head or knocking one's forehead [against the wall].
Consider the realization of these two venerable elders: how perfectly wondrous it is! Yet even going directly like this is not permissible, let alone calculating "perfection" within that state.
The mind produces false and erroneous results.

Furthermore, son of good family, one may exhaustively investigate the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) until birth and death have been extinguished; yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction, it has not yet reached full perfection.
If one has already attained conformity within the interfused mutual functioning of the sense organs, then all things will arise through universal transformation:

one seeks the light of fire, delights in the purity of water, loves the circulation of wind, and contemplates the perfection of matter, each venerating and serving these according to their respective inclinations.
Taking these various sensory objects as the fundamental cause for their manifestation, they establish a doctrine of eternal permanence. Such people fall into the attachment to birth and non-birth.

They become companions to the Kāśyapas (the three descendants of the tortoise clan) and the Brahmins who, with diligent hearts and arduous labor, serve fire and revere water in their quest to transcend birth and death.
Thus they lose sight of the Buddha’s Bodhi and forfeit true knowledge and vision. This is called the fifth form of clinging.
They venerate [these objects] with deluded minds that follow after external things, establishing false causes for seeking and falsely hoping for results.
Thus they distance themselves from perfect penetration and turn their backs on the city of Nirvana, giving rise to the seeds of perverted transformation.
Tong said: "Once the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) is empty, the six sense faculties function interchangeably;

each faculty is perfectly interfused, providing the impetus for transformations that proceed without obstruction. Thus, through this perfect interfusion and transformation, everything is able to arise.
These six faculties exist by virtue of the pure four great elements (*mahābhūta*), and the nature of these pure four great elements abides eternally in the world, never having ceased."
It ceases and subsides. Since the six sense organs can be manifested and all sensory objects are thereby aroused, these pure four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are their fundamental cause.
Although the present earth, water, fire, and wind are subject to change, cessation, and impermanence, the ground that serves as their fundamental cause remains eternally abiding and indestructible;
therefore, when one seeks the radiance of fire, the nature of that radiance is eternally abiding.
Furthermore, they delight in the purity of water because the nature of purity is eternally abiding; they love the circulation of wind because the nature of circulation is eternally abiding;
they observe the formation of dust because the nature of formation is eternally abiding.

In each of these cases, they revere and serve them in order to seek liberation from birth and death; it is not merely that they revere their external appearances, for they wish to rely upon those appearances [to attain their goal].
It is the attainment of their true nature. For example, when the youth Candraprabha first practiced the contemplation of water, it took many kalpas before he could become one with water.
The intent behind the veneration of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) is somewhat similar to this:

they wish to merge with the nature of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) to become one, remaining eternally in the world and termed "neither arising nor ceasing. This is to seek that which is not worth seeking.

To seek that which is not there is called false seeking; to hope for that which is not to be hoped for is called false hoping. The four great elements can give rise to that which is conditioned and subject to arising;

the four great elements can transform that which is conditioned and subject to transformation. Yet, while the four great elements serve as the basis for what is produced, they do not actually produce it;
while the four great elements serve as the basis for what is transformed, they do not actually transform it. To cling to this non-arising and yet...

It is for the sake of giving rise [to awakening]. Because it transforms through inverted principles, it is called "inverted transformation" (*diànhuà*). Furthermore, the mind is the source of all transformations; all myriad things emerge from the mind.
Now, being deluded, one follows after objects and abandons the fundamental to attend to the derivative; yet one wishes to transcend birth and death.

Returning once more to the cycle of birth and death, they lose their wisdom and insight, falling into such ignorance. Is this not to be far removed from perfect penetration and to turn one's back on the city of Nirvana?
To regard this as the forgetting of knowledge and the extinguishing of views, hoping thereby to reach the state beyond birth and death—this is difficult indeed.
Formerly, whenever Master Luzu saw a monk approach, he would simply face the wall. When Nanquan heard of this, he said: "I usually tell people..."
To take responsibility before the empty eon, or to grasp the meaning when the Buddha had not yet appeared in the world—even then, one could not find even a single person or half a person who did so.
When he acts like that, it will be "donkey-year" (an eternity) before he gets anywhere. Baofu asked Changqing, "As for Luzu, where does his essential point lie?
Having been told this by Nanquan, Changqing said, "To withdraw oneself and yield to others—there is not one in ten thousand who can do so."
Tiantong’s verse says: Within the plain there is flavor; its subtlety transcends conceptual thought. It is as if something persists, ever-present before the manifestation of forms;

It is as if one is dazed and like a fool—this is the nobility of the Way. When jade is carved with patterns, its primal purity is lost; When pearls dwell in the abyss, they shine with their own natural beauty.
How refreshing! The clear autumn air grinds away the summer heat. A single fleck of idle cloud separates the heavens from the waters below.
Could this be something with which the Wall-Gazing Brahmin might converse? Furthermore, Xuefeng asked a monk, "Where have you come from?"
The monk said, "It is the Divine Light (Śrīghoṣa) coming. Feng said, "By day it is called sunlight; by night it is called firelight.
What is the Divine Light? The monk had no reply. Feng spoke on his behalf, saying, "Sunlight, firelight. But tell me:
does sunlight and firelight suffice as the Divine Light? One must see that all marks are not marks before one can accord with the non-arising.

Furthermore, good son, you have exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena and have already extinguished birth and death; yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction, it is not yet perfected.
If, within this perfect luminosity, you reckon that the clarity itself is a void and thus negate the myriad transformations, you will take this eternal cessation as your ultimate refuge.
Those who give rise to such superior resolve fall into the attachment of taking refuge in that which is no refuge. Among the Śūnyatas in the Heaven of No-Thought, they become their companions;
they are deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and have lost their true knowledge and vision. This is called the sixth: the "perfectly empty mind of non-existence."

This results in the fruit of emptiness and non-existence; it violates and distances one from perfect penetration, turns one’s back on the city of Nirvana, and gives rise to the seeds of annihilationism.
[The Master] explained: "Previously, you falsely reckoned the four great elements as being neither born nor extinguished; this was falling into the view of eternalism.

Now, by destroying the manifold transformations and relying upon perpetual extinction, this is falling into the view of nihilism. Within clarity there is emptiness, and within emptiness there is clarity; they appear as if manifesting a perfect luminosity."

They cling exclusively to the notion that within meditative clarity there is only voidness and nothingness; taking non-existence as their refuge, they dwell seated in emptiness and thereby fall into the fruit of the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*).
Like the *śūnyatā* (Śunyata) who is bodiless yet perceives touch, they are made to see for a moment by being reflected in the light of the Tathāgata.
Because they take emptiness as their cause, they achieve emptiness as their result. This is the severing of the lineage of the Tathāgata. So it is said.
This refers to the rotten seed of the plantain sprout. The non-Buddhists take this to be nirvana, yet they are thousands of miles away from true nirvana.
A monk asked Yunmen, "What is it like when the tree withers and the leaves fall? Yunmen said, "The golden wind reveals its essence. Xuedou’s verse comments:
"Since the Master has his own school, his answer likewise accords with it. The three phrases can be distinguished; they form a single cluster."
Vast is the sky; across the great plains, the cool breezes rustle. High above the heavens, the sparse rain falls in mist.
Do you not see the guest who has sat long at Shaolin and has not yet returned? He rests in stillness amidst the dense thickets of Xiong’er Mountain.

How could those who have no place of their own to return to ever fathom even a ten-thousandth part of this? Xuansha ascended the hall and said: "The Way of the Buddha is leisurely and expansive; there is nothing..."

The Path: It is the gate of liberation that has no gate; it is the intent of the Way-man that has no intent. It does not abide within the three periods of time, and therefore it cannot be subject to rising or sinking.
To establish it is to deviate from the Truth; it does not belong to the realm of conditioned fabrication. To move within it is to give rise to the root of birth and death.

If you remain still, you will become intoxicated and mired in dullness; if both movement and stillness are extinguished, you fall into a state of empty nothingness. If both movement and stillness are grasped together, you merely encounter a vague and superficial buddha-nature.
You must face the sensory objects and look into the mirror, like a withered tree or cold ashes, applying yourself as the occasion demands.
It does not lose its appropriateness; it is like a mirror reflecting all images without its radiance being disturbed, or like a bird flying through the air without mixing with the color of space.
Therefore, throughout the ten directions there are no reflected images, and within the three realms there are no traces of movement. It does not fall into the mechanism of coming and going.
The mind does not abide in the middle. There is no sound of a drum within a bell, nor is there the sound of a bell within a drum; the bell and the drum do not intersect.
In every phrase there is no before or after; it is like a strong man extending his arm—relying on no external power—as a lion strides forth.
How could one seek a companion? In the nine heavens, all obscurations are severed; where is there any need for penetration? This single segment of radiance has never been dimmed.
If you reach this state, the essence is tranquil and eternally lucid; like the blazing brilliance of the sun, it is without limit or surface.
Within the void of Perfect Enlightenment, it remains unmoving; swallowing and eclipsing heaven and earth, it shines forth in total clarity. Xuan Sha and Yun Men have seen through Nirvana.
The essence of *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* is fundamentally without arising or ceasing. To manifest such subtle and wondrous excellence is sufficient to cause the hair of non-Buddhists to stand on end.

Furthermore, good son, although you have exhausted all conditioned phenomena into emptiness and thereby extinguished arising and ceasing, your realization of the subtle and wondrous within quiescent extinction is not yet perfected.

If one regards the perfect and eternal as being such that the body is solidly constant, identical to the essence which is perfect and circular, and never decays or passes away, and thus gives rise to a resolute conviction, this person falls into the attachment of grasping at both desire and non-desire.
They become companions to those *asita* (here translated as "the Peerless") who seek long life;
they are deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and lose their true knowledge and vision. This is called the seventh attachment, clinging to the source of life, establishing it as a cause.

These are false causes that lead to the fruit of long-term toil; they are far removed from perfect penetration and turn one’s back on the city of Nirvana, giving rise to the seeds of prolonged delusion.

The Master said: "Upon glimpsing the perfect luminosity, one immediately calculates it to have a characteristic of emptiness within the light; upon glimpsing the perfect permanence, one immediately calculates it to have a characteristic of indestructibility within the constant.
Even the wise cannot avoid this. Yet, while the perfect luminosity has never ceased to be empty, that emptiness cannot [be grasped as a fixed characteristic]."

Grasping. To grasp at emptiness is to fall into nihilism; yet the essence of perfect fullness is never not constant, and this constancy cannot be grasped. To grasp at constancy is to head toward weariness.
As Zhuangzi said: "The Great Mass of Earth exhausts me with life. Furthermore, it is like the stretching of a bird’s wings in the *Tàishàng jīng* (Scripture on the Great Emptiness).
Exhaling the old and inhaling the new is also a laborious task; hence it is called "prolonged toil" (*cháng láo*).

An alternative version reads "prolonged confinement" (*cháng láo*), which refers to the fruit of abiding permanence (*zhǒng zhù guǒ*). Furthermore, this physical body composed of the four great elements is constrained by fixed karma;
its *fen-duàn* (segmented) nature cannot become *biàn-yì* (transformative), just as the *biàn-yì* nature cannot become *fen-duàn*. The body is fundamentally impermanent; in truth, it is not...
It may be craved; yet now one craves it with attachment, desiring that it endure for a long time. This is called craving that is not the grasping of craving.
Although there are long-lived seers who have attained the arts and realized this state, they do nothing more than solidify their delusory bodies.

Regarding the nature of true permanence which cannot be destroyed, this [state] is vastly remote from it; therefore, it is called "contrary and distant perfect penetration" (*viyukta-pariśuddha-samāpatti*), as it turns its back on the city of Nirvāṇa.

By clinging to the source of life and fixing the consciousness in a state of profound stillness where it does not waver, one is able to transcend the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*) and be born in the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
This is the first type of non-Buddhist practitioner in the Western Regions.
As for those who regard the body as eternally abiding, even the most eminent among them, after eighty thousand kalpas have passed, return to the cycle of saṃsāra.
How can it be said that they are able to abide eternally? Once Master Xuansha mistakenly took some medicine, and his entire body became red and festering.

A monk asked him, "What is the solid, enduring Dharma-body? Xuansha replied, "Drops of pus dripping everywhere. Master Huai composed a verse on this which says: "Drop by drop, throughout the whole body."
This is festering pus. On a fishing boat, one’s true lineage is revealed; people look only at the fishing line, failing to see the red smartweed standing opposite the white lotus.
Master Duan said: "Once someone asked Fahu, 'What is the pure dharma-body? He simply answered him:
'The stench of excrement perfumes the heavens. He also said: 'One is born by transformation upon the petals of a lotus.'"
"Child, tell me: are you the same as the ancients, or are you different? The *Lotus Sūtra* also has a verse that says:
'When the stench of excrement perfumes the heavens, it is but a coincidence; How could the *Lotus Sūtra* dare to proclaim it for your sake?
If there were a nostril in your nose that pierced through to the heavens, You might roam at will without being pierced. These venerable masters spoke even of the solid, adamantine Dharma-body."
One would feel like vomiting at the mere thought of it; how much more so for this wretched and inferior physical body—how could one wish to falsely prolong its existence?

Nevertheless, there are those who come by virtue of the power of their vows, not through the attainment of cultivation. Such was Baozhang (Precious Palm), a native of Central India who lived for a thousand years.

He was born in the twelfth year of the reign of Emperor Weile of the Zhou dynasty. At birth, his left hand was clenched into a fist; he received the tonsure at the age of seven, whereupon the fist opened, and for this reason he was named Baozhang. During the Wei dynasty...

During the Jin dynasty, he traveled through this land and entered Shu to pay homage to Samantabhadra. He never ate food and daily recited over a thousand scrolls of the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other sutras.
One who praised him said: "His weary jade teeth are cold, like a rushing mountain spring;
sometimes sitting at midnight, the gods and ghosts weep before his steps. One day, he said to the assembly: "I have a vow to remain in this world."
He was a thousand years old; this year he was six hundred and twenty-six, which is why he was called "The Thousand-Year-Old One.
He subsequently traveled to Mount Wutai, then moved his residence to Huayan on Mount Zhurong, Shuangfeng at Huangmei, and Donglin on Mount Lu.
He soon arrived at Jianye, where he encountered Master Bodhidharma entering the Liang court. He went there to inquire into the essential meaning [of the Dharma] and attained awakening.
Emperor Wu, holding him in high esteem for his seniority in the monastic order (*dharma-lakṣa*), invited him into the inner palace. Not long after, he traveled to Wuzhou, where he composed a verse:

"In the city of Liang I met the Teacher; Through Zen practice, I realized the mind-ground. Drifting through the two provinces of Zhejiang, I have fully enjoyed the finest mountains and waters. He then followed the current downstream.
He traveled southward to India, stayed at Mount Mao, ascended Mount Taibai, and passed through Yandang.

He lingered for a long time among the seventy-two hermitages of Mount Cuifeng, returned to Mount Chicheng, and rested at Yunmen, Fahua, and other locations. Finally, he returned to the stone caverns where he had first arrived.
There is a verse that says: "Having traveled to the end of the four hundred prefectures of China, it is here that the wayfarer most delights to roam."
This was the fifteenth year of the Zhenguan era. Later, he resided at Baoyan Monastery in Pujiang, where he maintained a close friendship with Meditation Master Lang.
Whenever they exchanged messages, he would dispatch a white dog to deliver them; Lang likewise employed a green monkey as his messenger.

Thus, he inscribed upon Lang’s wall: "The white dog arrives carrying a letter; the green monkey returns with the bowl washed. This was on the first day of the New Year in the second year of the Xianqing era.
He fashioned a statue by hand, which was completed on the ninth day. He asked his disciple Huiyun, "To whom does this resemble? Huiyun replied, "It is no different from the Master himself.
Thereupon, he bathed, changed his robes, and sat in the lotus posture. Addressing Yun, he said, "I have remained in this world for one thousand one hundred and seventy-two years;
I am now about to depart from this life. Listen to my verse: "Originally there is neither birth nor death; now..."
He also manifested birth and death, saying, "I have attained a mind that comes and goes; in years to come, I shall return here. He then entrusted them with these words:
"Sixty years after my passing, there will be a monk who comes to take my bones; do not refuse him. Having spoken, he passed away.
Forty-six years later, the Elder Dafu arrived at the site of the stupa from Yunmen and paid his respects, saying, "I hope the stupa will open."

He opened it. After a short while, the door of the stupa indeed opened. His bones were linked together like rings, appearing the color of gold. Sengfu immediately took them to Qinwang Hill, where he erected a stupa to enshrine them.

From the Dingmao year of the reign of Emperor Weilie of the Zhou dynasty until the Dingyi year of the Xianqing era of Emperor Gaozong of the Tang dynasty, exactly one thousand seven hundred and twenty-two years had passed.
Having reached this land, more than four hundred years had elapsed. [At that time], those of the external Daoist sect sought [to take them].
"Long-lived one, how many people are there who can be like Baozhang?

Furthermore, good son, though they have exhausted all conditioned activities into emptiness and already extinguished birth and death, they have not yet perfected the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction."
Observing that life is interpenetrating, they nevertheless remain within the dust and toil of worldly existence, fearing its total exhaustion.
At this juncture, they sit within a lotus palace, extensively transforming the seven treasures and greatly increasing their precious warmth.

Indulging their own minds, those who give rise to such superior understanding fall into the attachment to "the real as unreal" and become companions of the *Tāṭakīkāra* (a name for a heaven of others' transformations). They lose sight of the Buddha’s Bodhi and forfeit it.

This cognitive view is called the eighth cause for giving rise to perverse thoughts, which establishes the fruit of blazing afflictions. It is far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvana, producing the seeds of celestial demons.

Tong said: "The consciousness aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*) constitutes the life-source for the twelve classes of sentient beings. My life connects with theirs, and their life connects with mine; therefore, it is called 'mutual interpenetration.
If the consciousness aggregate were to be exhausted, the lives of all sentient beings throughout the ten directions would be exhausted simultaneously, and my own life would likewise be exhausted.
Who then would realize the principle of true permanence? Who would be the sentient beings to be transformed? There would be true permanence in name only, but no substance."

Those who have realized the true and eternal fear that [their merit] will be exhausted; wishing to remain amidst the dust and toil of the world to deliver sentient beings, they first sit within a lotus palace and extensively manifest the seven treasures.
Their intention is indeed not unwholesome. However, as they subsequently increase their retinue of precious ladies and indulge their desires, depraved thoughts enter them.
Relying on these depraved thoughts while seeking to realize the true and eternal and to give rise to transformative activity, they fail to achieve their goal.
Regarding objects, they do not realize they are false; therefore, this is called "clinging to true non-existence.
Takkirāja is the lord of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven at the summit of the desire realm, one who can transform objects of desire to entertain himself.

While not all inhabitants of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven are Māras, the divine transformations of the Māra King are similar to theirs, and thus he dwells together with them. It is only the objects of desire that are as [described].
Fire; therefore, it is called "blazing dust. The ten preceding types of celestial māras each take the secret practice of lust as their business.
These are triggered by perverse thoughts and cannot be restrained. One who is without attachment is called a deva;
one who has attachment is called a māra. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* says: "You all must not delight in dwelling within the burning house of the triple world. Be without greed."
These are coarse and inferior forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles. If one gives rise to craving through attachment to them, one will be consumed by them.

Formerly, Udraka Rāmaputra, by means of mundane wisdom, suppressed the afflictions of the lower stages, attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and possessed the five supernormal powers.
At that time, the ruler honored him and welcomed him into the palace. The women of the palace prostrated themselves at his feet in salutation.

When Udraka Rāmaputra touched the hands of the women, desire was born within him, and he consequently lost his supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). Having finished his meal, he walked slowly back to the mountains. Thus, the verse says:
"As soon as a single thought of desire arose, he lost the five supernormal powers. This is the Heaven of Delighting in Transformations (*Nirmāṇarati*).

Māra subdues them by means of the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha) and thereby gains mastery over them; yet there has never been a case where he does not lose them through the arousal of perverse thoughts.
Once the karmic retribution is exhausted, one immediately falls into ruin. How could such pleasure be permanent? Therefore, it is said that even the "true" is truly non-true.
As for the supernatural powers manifested by the Great Being Vimalakīrti, at that very moment, the Buddha Sumerudīpa-rāja dispatched three...
Twelve thousand lion thrones—lofty, vast, magnificent, and pure—entered the room of Vimalakīrti.
These had never been seen before by the bodhisattvas, the great disciples, Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings;
yet his room was so expansive that it accommodated all thirty-two thousand lion thrones without any obstruction. Master Baojue said: "By means of the master..."
The height and breadth of the seats for the sons of the Buddha, and the narrowness of the Vimalakīrti chamber—when one contemplates this, it immediately presents an obstacle.
This is truly the power of supernatural penetration (*ṛddhi-bala*); therefore, it is inconceivable.

Furthermore, son of good family, you have exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena and have already extinguished birth and death; yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction, it is not yet perfected.

Within the clarity of life, you distinguish between the refined and the coarse, and resolve the true from the false. You regard cause and effect as a mutual recompense, seeking only for a response through resonance.

They turn their backs on the path of purity—namely, seeing suffering and abandoning its origin, realizing cessation and cultivating the path—and having come to rest within cessation, they no longer advance.
Those who give rise to such resolute conviction fall into the category of the śrāvakas of fixed nature; they become companions to those arrogant monks who lack learning.
They are deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and have lost their true knowledge and vision. This is called the ninth stage of perfecting the essence.

This corresponds to the mind. It results in the fruit of quiescent wandering, being far removed from perfect penetration and turning one's back on the city of Nirvana, thereby giving rise to the seeds of entanglement within emptiness.

"O World-Honored One, we have hitherto remained ordinary and have not received the subtle and detailed instructions of the Tathāgata. Furthermore, regarding these five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*):
are they to be eliminated simultaneously, or are they exhausted sequentially? Within these five layers, what constitutes their ultimate realm?
We only pray that the Tathāgata will manifest great compassion, clarify the minds and eyes of this great assembly, and serve as a guide for all sentient beings of the future age."
"Come, Ānanda. This essence of the eye is fundamentally true, wondrously luminous, and primordially awakened, perfectly pure.
It does not harbor birth and death, nor any defilements, even unto empty space; all these arise solely from the production of false conceptualization.

This is originally the wondrously luminous, true essence of primordial awakening, yet through delusion it gives rise to the various vessel-worlds, just as Yajñadatta, in his confusion, mistook his own head for a reflection. Falsehood is fundamentally..."
There is no cause. Within the midst of false conceptualization, one establishes the nature of causes and conditions; those who are deluded regarding causes and conditions call it "spontaneity.
That nature of space is likewise truly born from illusion. Both causes and conditions and spontaneity are merely the conceptual constructions of the deluded minds of sentient beings. Ānanda!

One knows that which arises from delusion and explains the causes and conditions of delusion; yet if delusion is fundamentally non-existent, then even explaining the causes and conditions of delusion is fundamentally nothing at all—how much more so for those who, failing to understand this, speculate that it is produced by spontaneity?
Tong said: "The question posed by Ānanda concerns whether [defilements] are eliminated all at once or exhausted sequentially.

To resolve the two approaches of sudden and gradual, and to serve as a 'heavenly eye for humanity' for future generations, the World-Honored One first demonstrated the supreme path of 'simultaneous elimination through awakening.
This depends solely on entering into the subtle, true, wondrously luminous, and fundamentally enlightened perfect purity. This essence is not..."

Regarding the deluded karma of birth and death, as well as the various defilements and deluded conditions—even down to empty space, which is neither karma nor a condition—it is like the great ocean that does not harbor a corpse.
Thus, the marks of the five aggregates, birth and death, defilements, and even empty space have no place to adhere.
Seeing this, one realizes that the wondrous clarity is originally pure and true; how could there be [any further delusion]?
Because it is the original enlightenment (mūla-bodhi) within delusion, it is inherently perfect and pure. How could there be any defilement?

That which undergoes the flux of worldly birth and death belongs to sensation, perception, and mental formations; that which is turbid with dust and grime belongs to form; and that which depends upon space to exist belongs to the eight consciousnesses—all these arise from false conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
Since this is the wondrously luminous, true essence of original enlightenment, by what cause does it arise?
Delusion gives rise to the various perceptions of the receptacle world and its dual aspects of appearance and form. This delusion is fundamentally without cause.
As previously stated regarding the case of Yan-rda-da (Śaśaviṣāṇa) who, in his confusion, mistook his own head for a reflection—everyone knows this is a delusion.
From what does this delusion arise? If one considers it to have causes and conditions, it is not caused by conditions; if one considers it to be spontaneous, it is not spontaneous. It is not...
Causes and conditions do not arise spontaneously; is this not the nature of empty space? Yet it is not even the nature of empty space itself.
That nature of empty space is like a single bubble rising from the ocean; when viewed by Great Awakening, it is still but an illusion.
How much more so for the dust and defilements of birth and death that rely upon empty space—could these not be the illusion within an illusion? Therefore, it is said that there are causes.
The nature of conditions and the so-called nature of spontaneity are both conceptual constructions of the deluded mind; fundamentally, they do not truly exist.

Since they are neither caused by conditions nor spontaneous, the delusion of the five aggregates is originally devoid of self-nature. Being devoid of self-nature, they are fundamentally unarisen from the beginning.
Delusion is fundamentally non-arising; where, then, can one seek delusion? Therefore, one must know the place where delusion arises before one can speak of the causes and conditions of delusion.
How does this delusion arise? How should it be extinguished? Only then can the sequence for the dissolution of the five aggregates be discussed.
If delusion is originally non-existent, then delusion is itself reality. Since the very place of its arising is unknown, from what could it proceed?
Yet you name it "causes and conditions" (hetu-pratyaya). From where, then, do you derive the notion that it is "spontaneous" (svabhāva)?

If one’s eyes are free from cataracts and one sees but a single moon—since there has never been a second moon in the first place—where could one seek a second moon with which to debate causes and conditions or spontaneity?
This vehicle dissolves all at once through awakening; it is the most supreme, perfect, and sudden Dharma-gate.
It goes without saying how they are eliminated, yet they have never failed to be eliminated simultaneously;
it is simply a matter of awakening to and entering the subtle, true, wondrously luminous, fundamentally enlightened, and perfectly pure state, with nothing else remaining.
A monk asked Changsha Chengyan, "Does the person of original nature still attain Buddhahood? Chengyan said, "Do you think the Son of Heaven of the Great Tang still cuts thatch or mows grass?"
Touzi’s verse says: "Layer upon layer of mossed halls, the purple vapor deep; The stars divide their positions, rectifying heaven and earth.
The Golden Wheel does not govern the realm of Jambudvīpa— How could it compare to the precious seals of the feudal lords?
Furthermore, a monk asked Chan Master Jiufeng Man: "Everyone says they come to seek instruction; I wonder, does the Master still provide salvation? Man said: "You..."
"Does the Great Mountain lack even an inch of soil? Wumen said, "I have traveled across the four seas in search—what was the purpose of this?
Faman said, "Yanjiao lost his head and his mind went mad. Wumen said, "Is there anyone who is not mad? Faman said, "There is. Wumen said, "Who is this one who is not mad?
Faman said, "Suddenly awakening on the road, yet with eyes still closed. This refers to the clarity of awakening.
This constitutes a fault. Since the root of delusion has already been severed, Yanruo’s madness arose without cause.
Those who have not yet perceived their original face will find it difficult to reach this realization.

Therefore, the Tathāgata has revealed to you that the fundamental cause of the five aggregates is likewise nothing but deluded thought. Your body was originally produced through the thoughts of your parents;
had your mind not been characterized by such thought, it could not have entered into these thoughts to transmit life.

As I previously said, when one thinks of the taste of vinegar, saliva flows from the mouth; when one thinks of ascending a high peak, a tingling sensation arises in the soles of the feet—even though the precipice does not yet exist.
Since the sour object has not yet arrived, your substance cannot possibly belong to the same category as false illusions. How could saliva be produced by merely speaking of the sour?
Therefore, you should know that this manifest physical body of yours is called the first solid delusion.
Tong said: "I wonder why thought arises? It arises from consciousness (*vijñāna*). The initial point at which consciousness moves is called the source of thought.
Consciousness is the life-root (*jīvamūla*); it is transmitted by depending on thought. When consciousness moves, thought arises; when thought arises, life is established."

When life is established, the four great elements are complete; that is to say, it is the union of these three—life-force (*jīva*), warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—that constitutes a human being.
Therefore, when one's own conception merges with the conception of the parents, the superiority or inferiority of their merit follows whatever they have wished for.
The physical body manifests as something solid and firm. Prior to its manifestation, there was only thought (*saṃjñā*);
prior to thought, there was only consciousness (*vijñāna*). This conscious spirit does not die; it is called the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).

Desiring this life-faculty to be firm and long-lasting, once the physical body has manifested, one fears only its decay and destruction. This is precisely the solidification of deluded thought (*vikalpa*).

This is a clear verification. If one were to say that this body truly exists as it upholds the qi of heaven, earth, yin, and yang, rather than being established through delusion, then speaking of vinegar would not necessarily cause saliva to flow, and speaking of a precipice would not necessarily cause a sensation of numbness in the feet; it would certainly not be a matter of transmigrating through delusion.
Yet now, water issues from the mouth and numbness arises in the feet; these are not necessarily real objects, but arise solely due to mental conception. Thus...
This body is entirely of the same category as deluded thoughts; therefore, it corresponds with what is produced by delusion.
How, then, can one be surprised that this body does not arise from the thoughts of its parents? It is simply thought following upon thought, like sourness arising from water.
That a physical body manifests is clear evidence that this physical body is a solidified deluded thought; hence, it is called the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha).

Stubborn deluded conceptualization serves as its root. If one realizes that this conceptualization is neither born of causes and conditions nor born spontaneously, but is entirely illusory, then it is extinguished in this very moment.
Fundamentally, it has never possessed form; who then could interweave with it to create the turbidity of the kalpa?
Thus, one is able to empty the turbidity of the kalpa. National Teacher Zhong ascended the hall and said: "The green creeper entwines..."
Ascending directly to the summit of the cold pine, the white clouds are limpid and vast, appearing and disappearing within the great void.

All phenomena are fundamentally at rest, yet it is people who create their own clamor. Yunmen entered the hall and said: "All you venerable sons of the Buddha, do not engage in false imaginings. Heaven is heaven."
