"Do not falsely discard it. The Master said, "Bring me back my *huatou* (critical phrase).

Now, practitioners clearly know that the myriad dharmas are fundamentally at rest and that the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) does not exist; they clearly know that deluded thoughts are delusions and have nothing to do with them.
Why, then, is the aggregate of form not empty? It is simply because one has not yet clarified Yunmen’s *huatou*. Investigate!

This very "mind of imagining height" which has been described is able to cause your physical form to truly experience astringency and bitterness. Because it arises from sensation, it can move the material body.
As you now experience both the favorable and the adverse before you, these two manifest states drive you about;
this is called the second false imagination, "empty clarity."
The Master said: "When thoughts arise in the mind, the body becomes aching and constricted. There must first be one who experiences [feeling] before its expression manifests in the physical form.
Where there is thought, there is experience; where there is experience, there is manifestation. Thus, pleasant feeling is favorable and beneficial, while painful feeling is adverse and detrimental.
These two manifestations alternate and shift, driving one on without rest. Who is it that undergoes this experience?"

Only through emptiness can one receive; only through clarity can one apprehend. This empty clarity is false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) belonging to the first five consciousnesses; it is the "seeing-division" (*darśana-bhāga*).

Because the seeing and the perceived (*nimitta*) are intermingled, it is called the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*). If one realizes that this apprehension does not arise from causes and conditions, [one transcends it].
It does not arise spontaneously; therefore, it belongs to the realm of delusion. Although it possesses a hollow clarity, it fundamentally lacks an intrinsic nature.
Since it lacks an intrinsic nature, it is originally unborn. Since it is originally unborn, who is there to receive?
Who is there to see? Thus, it can shatter the turbidity of views. Zhaozhou, ascending the hall, said: "Bodhi, Nirvana, True Suchness, and Buddha-nature—all are merely labels."
The physical body and clothing are also called afflictions. Upon the ground of the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), where would they be placed?
When the single mind does not arise, the myriad dharmas are without fault. You need only investigate the principle and sit and observe for twenty or thirty years.
If you do not understand, cut off this old monk’s head and take it with you! Dream-like illusions and empty flowers are but a vain grasping. If the mind does not differ, the myriad dharmas are one.
Since suchness cannot be obtained from without, why do you still cling to it so tenaciously? You are like a sheep, randomly picking up things and putting them into your mouth.

When I saw Master Yaoshan say, "If someone asks you something, simply tell them to shut their dog-like mouths," I too told them to shut their dog-like mouths. To grasp at "I" is defilement; not grasping at "I" is purity.
It is just like a hunting dog that desires nothing but to catch and eat its prey. Where, then, is the Buddha-dharma?
Among thousands and tens of thousands of people, all of whom are seekers of the Buddha, can one find a single true practitioner?
If you are a disciple of the Empty King, do not let the sickness of the mind become the most difficult to cure. Furthermore, a monk asked Dongshan: "Constantly and diligently wipe it clean."
"Why do you not receive the bowl-cloth? Shishuang said, "Even if one were to say, 'From the very beginning there is not a single thing,' one still would not receive his bowl-cloth.
The monk asked, "I wonder what kind of person deserves to receive it? Shishuang said, "One who does not enter the gate.
The monk asked, "As for one who does not enter the gate, would they still receive it? Shishuang said, "Even so, they would not receive it."
He did not give it to anyone else. Again he asked, "Even if one were to say, 'From the very beginning there is not a single thing,' one still would not be worthy of receiving his bowl and satchel.
Tell me, who is worthy? If you can provide a turning word here that fits, tell me, what word will you provide?
A certain senior monk offered ninety-six turning words, none of which were accepted. Finally, he said:
"Suppose he brings it forward, yet the other does not accept it. Shanshan approved of this. Xuedou said, "Since he does not accept it, that is an eye;
if he had brought it forward, he would surely be blind. Tiantong took up the case and said, "Changlu does not think so. You must bring it forward;
if you do not bring it forward, how can you know he does not accept it? You must not accept it; if you do not not accept it, how [can you know]?"
"Exempting the future. That which is "coming" must surely be the eye; not receiving it is truly being blind. Do you understand?

"Illuminating the entire substance until there is no dependence; the whole body merges with the Great Way. This was brought forth from the transformation of the bhikṣu Dīrghanakha, who fell into two-sided error.
One must directly neither accept nor reject; only then can one transcend the turbidity of views.
It is due to your thoughts that your physical body is moved; yet the body is not of the same category as thought. For what reason does your body follow the dictates of thought?
Through various grasping at images, the mind gives rise to formal perceptions that correspond to thought. When awake, this is the conceptualizing mind; when asleep, it becomes various dreams.
Thus, your shifting thoughts and restless deluded sentiments are called the third false imagination, that of "interfusion.
It is said in response: "Thoughts and considerations have no form, while the physical body has substance. When thought moves, the body follows; for what reason is it driven by them?
It is because they are fused through conceptualization. The mind gives rise to empty imaginings, which take on the appearance of substantial objects. Various mental responses..."

It corresponds with mindfulness; it is through perception (*saṃjñā*) that this is made pervasive. It causes the mind to follow objects and causes objects to follow the mind, stirring up deluded emotions without ceasing, whether awake or asleep.
This belongs to the fundamental limit of discursive thought (*vikalpa*); its power is able to penetrate and harmonize things without obstruction.

This is the functioning of the sixth consciousness (*ṣaṣṭhavijñāna*). This constitutes the nesting place of afflictions (*kleśa*). If one recognizes this perception, it is not produced by causes and conditions.
They do not arise spontaneously; they are illusory in their very essence, and thus empty and quiescent in their very essence.

Since thought is fundamentally unarisen, what afflictions could possibly act as demons? Formerly, while Yangshan was in samādhi within the monks' hall, at midnight, he no longer perceived mountains, rivers, or the great earth, nor temples, buildings, or people—even his own body was entirely identical to the void. At dawn, he...
It resembles the case of Guishan. Guishan said, "When I was at Baizhang, I attained this state; it is the merit of the dissolution of pervasive delusion and the clarification of the mind.

If you preach the Dharma in the future and someone surpasses you, there is no such possibility. Tiantong cites the *Niyatāniyatagati-parivarta* (The Chapter on the Determinate and Indeterminate) of the *Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna*, saying:
"Abiding at all times, do not give rise to deluded thoughts; nor, regarding the various deluded minds..."
Does it not cease and extinguish? It dwells within the realm of delusive thoughts. Does it not apply further discernment? Within this lack of discernment, does it not distinguish the reality?
The verse says: Majestic and dignified, vast and unimpeded; thrusting the head into the fray, planting the feet where it is secure.
When the thread beneath the feet snaps, I am free; when the clay at the tip of the nose is exhausted, you must stop chiseling. Do not move!
Amidst the old papers of a thousand years, one compiles the medicine. Layue Jue once asked a monk who was lecturing on the scriptures:
"How does one dwell at all times without giving rise to deluded thoughts? The monk replied, "To give rise to them is itself an illness.

He asked again, "What is meant by 'not suppressing or extinguishing the various deluded minds'? The monk replied, "To suppress them is itself an illness. He asked yet again, "What is meant by 'abiding in delusion'?"
When asked, "Do you not apply further cognition to the object of thought? he replied, "Cognition itself is the sickness.
Again, he was asked, "How is it that in the absence of cognition, one does not discern reality? He replied, "Discernment itself is the sickness.

Master Jue laughed and said, "You recognize the medicine, but you do not yet recognize the taboos within the medicine. Baojue then composed a verse for him, which begins: "The yellow flowers bloom profusely..."
Emerald bamboos rustle; the Jiangnan region is warm with its mild climate, while the northern frontier is cold with its spring chill. After the traveler has departed, there is no further news;
all that remains are the clouds and mountains to be gazed upon until old age. These venerable masters may truly be said to have the thread beneath their feet severed, moving freely in all directions.
They serve as the perfect model for those who would shatter the *skandha* of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
The principle of transformation does not abide; it shifts and moves in secret with every passing moment. Nails grow and hair sprouts; vital energy wanes and the face wrinkles.
Day and night they alternate, yet one never awakens to this. Ānanda, if this were not you, how could its substance undergo change? If it must be truly you, why do you have no awareness of it?
Thus, your various formations (saṃskāras) ceaselessly flow from moment to moment; this is called the fourth deluded thought, subtle and hidden.
The Master said: "The delusion of solidity is not separate from the dust of form; the delusion of empty clarity still stands in opposition to form;
the delusion of pervasive integration belongs to the internal dust, wherein there are images to be grasped and objects to be attained.
As for the delusion of profound concealment, no image can be discerned and no object can be seized. It is ever-new and does not abide, shifting and migrating in secret toward—"
When one is born, the nails grow and the hair lengthens; when one approaches extinction, the vital breath dissipates and the face wrinkles.
Day and night they alternate before us, yet I am not aware of it. If I consider it not to be myself, my body is changing daily;
if I consider it to be myself, yet I have no awareness of it. This is a most profound and hidden delusion, shifting and flowing from moment to moment. It is impossible—

This may be compared to an object; those who do not understand it simply attribute it to the principle of transformation. The aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) belongs to the seventh consciousness.
Since it has already departed from all conceptualizations, it cannot be perceived; yet its flow of arising and ceasing is most subtle.
It does not, in total, transcend the cycle of rebirth within the three realms; therefore, it is termed the "turbidity of sentient beings" (*sattva-kaṣāya*). If, in every thought-moment, one does not—
Rest. There is a place of rest; therein one does not undergo the cyclic existence of sentient beings.
A monk asked Chan Master Longya Dun: "When the two mice gnaw at the vine, what then? Longya said: "One must have a place to hide oneself before it can be so.
The monk asked: "What is this place of hiding? Longya said: "Do you see me? Danxia’s verse says: "The cold moon relies..."
Resting upon the distant peaks above, ten thousand acres of calm lake are sealed with the light of a silken scroll. A fisherman’s song startles the herons from the marshes;
they fly out among the reeds, their tracks unseen. Thus one knows this place of concealment, where even gods and ghosts cannot gaze, and the *skandha* of action (*karmabhava*) can no longer delude.
For these subtle births and deaths are tied to the two realms of light and darkness, day and night.
They replace one another, and their physical forms undergo transformation like two rats gnawing at a vine, gradually dissolving away.
This belongs to the category of obscure and hidden delusions; yet, that which dwells within the body leaves no trace—this is sufficient to refute them.
Furthermore, that which you call "constant"—the place where your essence is bright and lucid, and remains unmoving—does not manifest as seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing within the body.
If it were truly pure and real, it could not admit the cultivation of delusion; for what reason, then, did you all once in years past behold a strange object?
As years passed, there was neither recollection nor forgetfulness. Later, when suddenly looking back upon those former wonders, the memory was as vivid as ever, without the slightest loss.
Thus, within this state of refined clarity and profound stillness, it is perfumed by every thought-moment; how could one possibly calculate its extent?

Ānanda, you should know that this stillness is not real. It is like a rapid torrent of water that appears tranquil at first glance; because the current is so swift, it is not perceived, yet it is not that there is no flow.
If this were not the source of thought, how could it receive the habitual tendencies of delusion? It is not due to the mutual functioning, opening, or closing of your six sense faculties.

This deluded thought can never be extinguished. Therefore, within what you currently see, hear, perceive, and know, through repeated habituation, there arises a profound clarity that is internally insubstantial and void;
this is the fifth inverted, subtle, and refined thought. Ānanda, these five aggregates of clinging are formed by these five types of deluded thoughts.
Tong said: "The arising and ceasing of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) does not stop for even a single thought-moment; it is merely subtle and hidden, and thus invisible.

When one reaches the state of profound stillness where there is no movement, birth and death have already been extinguished. Why then is it called deluded thought? It is because the essence of consciousness remains lucid and brilliant.
Within this very essence of lucidity, good and evil do not sprout, and both the conscious mind and its objects have subsided, remaining in a state of profound stillness."

It is still and concentrated, appearing somewhat similar to the essential reality of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya-jñāna*), yet it is not in fact the essential reality of original enlightenment.

The essential reality of original enlightenment does not fall within the realm of seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing; therefore, it is not subject to perfuming (*vāsanā*). Now, in this state of profound stillness where there is no movement, consciousness has nowhere to abide and falls into the state of non-defined neutrality (*avyākṛta*).
The nature of this non-defined neutrality is pervasive throughout direct perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*), yet it does not transcend the first five [consciousnesses].

Consciousness perceives the realms of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing. Although this seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing lacks deliberation or conceptual calculation, it is nonetheless capable of receiving and being perfumed by objects.
Thus, when one encounters a wondrous thing, there is neither recollection nor forgetting; yet if one happens to look upon it again, the memory remains vividly present.
It is like a fish trapped between ice: as soon as it encounters an object, its consciousness awakens, and though it is subject to arising and ceasing, these processes have never been extinguished.

Furthermore, you should know that this stillness is not the true reality. Within the state where every thought-moment is permeated by conditioning, various habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are repeatedly cultivated;
these subtle, constant habits have not yet ceased, much like a string of beads. Because of this lucid clarity, there arise seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.

Since these faculties of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing do not exist apart from the sense organs and their objects, they are able to stir the environment and receive permeation, thereby allowing for the containment of habitual tendencies.

Because of deluded karma, one knows that it is not truly profound stillness. One must reverse the flow to restore the oneness, dissolve and polish the six gates, and completely detach from the faculties and their objects.
When the six faculties function interchangeably, there is only a single, pure reality; this reality manifests through the faculties as clarity, and its opening and closing are free and spontaneous.
Delusive habits have no place to lodge; thus, the mouth is like the nostrils, and the eyes resemble the eyebrows. One observes forms with the ears, yet forms cannot shake one;
one hears sounds with the eyes, yet sounds cannot draw one away. This is what is meant by "wondrously profound total retention" (miao-zhan zongchi), wherein delusive thoughts have no way to enter.
This is because the first five consciousnesses have not yet entered into discursive thought and remain intimately joined to the eighth consciousness.

Because they are proximate, the sixth and seventh consciousnesses transform based on the preceding [consciousnesses], while the fifth and eighth are perfected based on the fruits. Without the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), one cannot transform the first five consciousnesses.
Upon the transformation of consciousness into wisdom (*vijñāna-parāvṛtti*), one attains its true stillness;

only then does one believe that the seeds of the eight consciousnesses undergo subtle arising and ceasing, which are not perceived due to the rapidity of their flow, yet are not without flow. Although they appear tranquil, they are not truly so.

This is not called true stillness. That stillness, though it perceives internally, is like a phantom or a void; it consists of subtle and refined conceptualizations that seem to exist yet are as if non-existent, for they have never been without thought.

Therefore, it is also termed "deluded thought" (*vikalpa*). This is because the eighth consciousness, by depending on the non-arising and non-ceasing [nature] and merging with the arising and ceasing, constitutes consciousness.
If one turns away from the dust [of objects] and unites with awakening, one relies upon the non-arising and non-ceasing.
This is called right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*). If one turns one's back on awakening and joins with the sensory objects, relying upon birth and extinction, this is called perversion (*viparyāsa*).

The source of perception (*saṃjñā*) is the initial movement of consciousness; the five kinds of false conceptualization all arise from this. Due to a single moment of delusion, one accepts and grasps these [objects], thereby obscuring oneself;
hence they are called the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*), also known as the five aggregates of grasping. All are false.
Perception (*saṃjñā*) is the root of this. Yongjia said: "To clearly recognize within a single thought-moment: that which is vividly distinct is the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*);
that which is experienced and retained in the mind is the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*); and the mind taking this principle as its object..."
This is precisely the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). To function according to this principle is the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

To defile the true nature is the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). These five aggregates, in their entirety, are a single thought-moment; and this single thought-moment, in its entirety, is completely the five aggregates.
To clearly perceive them within a single thought-moment, without any sovereign master, is the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-jñāna*). Thus one sees.
"It is like an illusion or a transformation"—this is the wisdom of the emptiness of dharmas (*dharmasūnyatā*). It must be as Yongjia said:
"When both person and dharmas are empty, the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) is exhausted, and only then can one transcend the turbidity of life.
Zhaozhou asked Touzi, "What is it like when a person who has undergone 'great death' returns to life? Touzi said, "Night travel is not permitted; you must arrive by dawn. Xuedou’s verse on this:
The verse says: "To have eyes while alive is no different from being dead; why need one examine the 'medicine taboos' of a master? Even the ancient Buddhas said they had never reached it;
who knows who can scatter the dust and sand? Tiantong’s eulogy says: "The mustard-seed city and kalpa-stone exhaustively reach the primordial source.
The living eye shines through the vast emptiness of space. Not permitted to travel by night, one arrives at dawn; the sound of the home has not yet reached..."
Willingly entrusting the great fish [to the net]—this is the wondrous transcendence of conceptual thought. In the primordial source, there is no room for the cultivation of delusion.
On the ground of ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), one arrives without moving a single step; this is clearly the standard for transforming consciousness into wisdom (*vijñāna* → *jñāna*).
If you now wish to know the depth of the causal realms: only form and emptiness constitute the limit of form; only contact and separation constitute the limit of sensation;
only recollection and forgetfulness constitute the limit of perception; only cessation and arising constitute the limit of mental formations.
The profound stillness merges with profound stillness, returning to the limit of consciousness.

Ānanda asked previously about these five successive stages: "To what do they converge as their boundaries? This detailed response explains that there are causes and boundaries, proceeding from the shallow to the deep.
Form is not form by itself; it is manifested through emptiness. This is the boundary between form and emptiness.
This is the realm of form (*rūpa-dhātu*). Feeling does not feel itself; feeling exists because of contact (*sparśa*). This contact is free from extremes;

this is the realm of feeling (*vedanā-dhātu*). Perception does not perceive itself; perception exists because of the recording of names. This recording is free from forgetfulness; this is the realm of perception (*saṃjñā-dhātu*).

"Formations do not form themselves; they are called 'formations' because their arising and ceasing are incessant. This limit of arising and ceasing is the realm of formations (*saṃskāra-dhātu*). Consciousness is termed 'lucid clarity.
Having already extinguished arising and ceasing, its nature enters primordial clarity and merges with that lucidity.

To have an entry and a merging is to have a limit; this is the realm of consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*). Thus, the entry into lucidity constitutes the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*); true lucidity is [the state beyond it]."
The nature-consciousness is clear and knowing; this clear knowing is itself wisdom (*jñāna*). Between wisdom and consciousness, there exists a boundary.

True nature is not called "penetrating stillness" (*zhanru*) because it pervades the entire *dharmadhātu* and thus has no coming or going. To emerge from stillness is activity; to penetrate into stillness is consciousness.
When one is profoundly and internally clear within stillness, such that there is nowhere to enter, one immediately reaches the stage of non-arising and non-extinction. This is the gradual [approach].

It penetrates the subtlest realms. Proceeding from the five objects and the five consciousnesses, through the sixth and seventh consciousnesses, it reaches the eighth consciousness; this is the boundary of the shallow and deep levels of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Once one merges with the profound stillness and attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), how could there be any boundaries to be perceived?
Since there are no boundaries, one realizes the emptiness of the five aggregates. When the five aggregates are all empty, one transcends the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*).

What is called "dividing your profoundly still, perfect, wondrous, enlightened, and luminous mind" into seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing—from beginning to end—undergoes five layers of turbidity.
Only when this occurs does it finally return to its profound stillness. The *Huan yuan guan* (Contemplation of Returning to the Source) states:

"Because of the appearances of sensory objects, every thought-moment undergoes transition and change; this is precisely birth and death. By contemplating these sensory appearances, the characteristics of arising and ceasing are exhausted."
Emptiness is without substantiality; this is itself *nirvāṇa*. The *Zhizhèngchuán* states: "To conceptually differentiate dharmas such as form and sound moment by moment is called 'transformation.
When one contemplates these dharmas of form, sound, and so forth, they are found to have no source for their arising or ceasing;
they are liberated in their very place. First, contemplating one's own eye, it says: "This eye cannot see its own substance. Even its own substance..."
It is not seen. How then can other things be seen? Next, observe the object before you: if you see this as a tree, how can it be a tree?
If you see it as not a tree, how can you see it as a tree? Next, observe the three periods of time:
if what is seen exists in the present, then the past and future should also exist. If the past and future do not exist, then...
"Even that which is presently appearing should be non-existent. This is the essential principle for returning to the source. Master Miaoyan ascended the hall and said:
"The mind of a man of the Way is fundamentally straightforward and without artifice; it has no back and no front, and is free from deceitful or false thoughts at all times."
Seeing and hearing are ordinary; there is nothing more to be added or hidden. Nor does one close the eyes or stop up the ears. It is simply that the mind does not cling to objects—this is it.
The sages of old spoke only of the faults and afflictions on the side of turbidity.

If there are no such things as these numerous evil thoughts, emotional views, perceptions, and habitual tendencies, then it is like the autumn waters, clear and still, pure and unconditioned, limpid and unimpeded.
He is called a man of the Way, and is also named a man of no affairs. These few words from Mount Wei directly reveal the message of the stillness entering into union with stillness;
once the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) has been entirely dissolved, what further matter could there be?
These five aggregates originally arise in successive layers; their cause of arising lies in consciousness, and consciousness is eliminated by means of form.

In principle, they are suddenly realized through awakening, and upon awakening, they are simultaneously dissolved. Yet in practice, they are not suddenly removed, but are exhausted through a gradual process. I have already shown you this knot in the *kalpavṛkṣa* cloth.
What is it that you do not understand? I ask this of you once more. You should thoroughly investigate the root of these deluded thoughts so that your mind may attain clarity.

Transmit this teaching to all practitioners of future ages during the period of the Final Dharma, enabling them to recognize the nature of their delusions and to develop a profound weariness with their own self-arising [delusions].
Knowing that there is *nirvāṇa*, one does not cling to the triple world.
Tong said: "When Ānanda previously asked whether [defilements] are eliminated all at once or exhausted sequentially, my initial answer directly pointed to the supreme state:
it lies solely in awakening to and entering into the subtle, true, wondrously luminous, fundamentally enlightened, and perfectly pure nature, wherein no further deluded thoughts exist."
They may be eliminated; there is no further sequence to be pointed out, which is what is meant by "riding upon awakening to eliminate them all at once.
This answers that while phenomena are not suddenly eliminated, they are exhausted through a gradual process. Out of compassion, I have spoken somewhat diffusely;
this is what is meant by "sudden yet leaving nothing out of the perfect [teaching]. These five aggregates, as the root-source of the faculties, arise in overlapping layers. Their arising...

The cause: the eight consciousnesses, which are the fundamental source of ideation, give rise to the two divisions of subjectivity (seeing) and objectivity (appearance). From the internal, the external is constructed; from the subtle, the coarse arises.
Now, one wishes to extinguish these five aggregates (*skandhas*). This extinction proceeds gradually; first, one begins with the elimination of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).

From the external to the internal, and from the coarse to the subtle, there is no lack of sequential order. However, if one discusses the principle of *tathatā* (suchness), once awakened, one immediately reaches the stage of Buddhahood;
what gradations could there be? Realizing that the aggregates (*skandhas*) have no substance, they are entirely empty in their very essence;

thus, through awakening, they are simultaneously dissolved, and one is immediately free from all affairs. Yet, as for the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) from beginningless time, having been perfumed for a long duration, they manifest as active conduct (*samudācāra*).
Ignorance binds one in five layers; how could it be uprooted all at once? Therefore, one must gradually refine and eliminate it until it is exhausted through successive stages.

It is like a knot in a *kalpa*-cloth: the cloth itself has no inherent difference, yet the knots must necessarily be removed step by step. First, one attains the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*);

next, the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*); and next, the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*). Only then does one attain the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and quiescent extinction manifests before one.
Therefore, failing to recognize the illusory root of the faculties, the mind follows the transformations of consciousness and fails to attain liberation.

Now, clearly knowing this to be illusory—and that illusion has no fundamental cause—the mind opens up in this very moment, realizing the bliss of Nirvana. Having realized Nirvana, one reaches the state of non-arising and non-extinction.
One then perceives those five aggregates as illusory, arising spontaneously without cause and originally devoid of self-nature; this is truly profound and worthy of deep reflection.
One should cultivate revulsion. If the five aggregates are not extinguished, one will transmigrate through the three realms and cycle through birth and death;

what joy could there be in this that one would cling to it and refuse to let go? This awakening to the false root of the mind is the foremost skillful means for the Buddhas and World-Honored Ones in their wondrous *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna*, and it is that which should be practiced in successive stages. Furthermore, it distances one from fifty kinds of demonic activities.
These practices are all sufficient to serve as clear instructions for the Dharma-ending age. Therefore, he entrusted them to be circulated, saying:
"The Ten Questions of Master Shishan Answered by Chan Master Guifeng. Question One: What is the Way? How does one cultivate it?
Must it necessarily be accomplished through cultivation, or is it without the need for effort? Answer: Non-obstruction is the Way; awakening to delusion is cultivation. As for the Way...
Although the fundamental nature is perfect and complete, delusion arises as a burden. When deluded thoughts are entirely exhausted, this is precisely what constitutes cultivation and realization.

Question: If [enlightenment] is achieved through cultivation, it would be a product of effort (*abhisamskāra*). It would then be identical to worldly phenomena—false, unreal, and subject to destruction after its formation.

How, then, can it be called "transcending the world" (*lokottara*)? Answer: Productive effort is karmic bondage; it is termed "false" and "worldly. True non-action (*anabhisamskāra*)—[is transcendence].
This is the practice. It is indeed the true transcendence of the world. [The interlocutor] asks three times whether that which is practiced is sudden or gradual.
If it is gradual, one forgets what precedes and loses what follows; how then can these be assembled to form a whole? If it is sudden, the myriad practices are manifold in method;
how could they be perfected all at once? The answer is: True Principle is suddenly perfected through awakening, while deluded sentiments are gradually exhausted through their cessation.
Sudden perfection is like a newborn infant, whose limbs are already fully formed in a single day;
gradual cultivation is like the growth of an adult, whose character and spirit are only established after many years. These three responses may serve as a commentary on this section of the scripture.
Furthermore, Guifeng answered the inquiry of Minister Wen Cao, saying: "Although the True Principle is suddenly realized, this emotion..."

It is difficult to eliminate this all at once. It is like when the wind momentarily ceases and the waves temporarily pause; how could the practice cultivated throughout a single lifetime immediately become identical to the functioning of a Buddha?
One should simply take emptiness and stillness as one's own essence and not identify with the physical body;
one should take True Suchness as one's own mind and not identify with deluded thoughts. If deluded thoughts arise, do not follow them at all. Then, at the time of death—
"Natural karma cannot bind. Huanglong Huitang answered Vice Minister Han Zonggu’s question, saying:
"If there are no superfluous dharmas outside the mind, one does not know what these afflictions and habitual tendencies are that one wishes to exhaust.
If you give rise to such a thought, it turns into recognizing a thief as one's own son. Since the time of the ancient patriarchs, there has only been verbal expression;..."

This is administering medicine according to the specific illness. Even if there were habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of afflictions, they would simply be treated with the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision.
All such [teachings] are expedient means (*upāya-kauśalya*) intended to guide and attract beings.

If it were truly the case that there were habitual tendencies to be cured, it would imply that there are phenomena existing outside the mind that could be exhausted—like a sacred tortoise dragging its tail along the road, which only serves to leave more tracks behind. To sweep away these traces...
This is the arising of a trace. One might say that by using the mind to employ the mind, one’s perception of illness becomes increasingly deep.

If one can clearly realize that there is no dharma outside the mind and no mind outside dharmas, then since both mind and dharmas are non-existent, whom would one wish to further instruct in order to suddenly bring them all to an end?
According to Huìtáng’s perspective, there has been "not even a single thing" from the very beginning; where, then, could dust and grime ever settle? According to Guīfēng’s response:
One must immediately and constantly wipe it clean; do not allow it to be defiled by dust and grime.

Master Huìtáng maintains that this is sudden, using the analogy of a person dreaming of being bound in shackles and chains: upon waking, would they still need to remove those shackles and chains? Certainly not.
Master Guīfēng maintains that this is gradual, using the analogy of water freezing into ice and losing its function for irrigation: one must wait for the fire and sun to gradually approach.

This is the beginning of its circulation. The *Zongjing lu* states: "Those who enter our school must first know that there is [something fundamental], and only then may they take it up and maintain it.
Furthermore, the beginning and the end must correspond; one must not have deficiencies in principle or practice, nor allow for a discrepancy between mind and speech.
If one enters the Mirror of the School, both principle and practice will be perfected. Judging by the Mirror of the School, Dajian [Huineng] possessed only a single eye."
The two eyes penetrate with perfect clarity. Why is this? The Great Mirror possesses principle but lacks practice;

it is said to be primordially and eternally pure, requiring no wiping away of dust. The Great Penetration has already attained awakening yet must still cultivate; by wiping away the dust, the mirror becomes bright.

Therefore it is said: "The correct, though correct, is actually biased; the biased, though biased, is actually round. Unless one has long studied the school of Dongshan, one should not treat this lightly.
...discussing this.

Ānanda, suppose there were another person who filled all the empty space throughout the ten directions with the seven treasures, and offered them to as many Buddhas as there are motes of dust, serving and making offerings to them with a mind that never wasted a single thought. What do you think? Would such a person...
"By virtue of this cause and condition of giving to the Buddha, would one not obtain much merit? Ānanda replied, "The void is inexhaustible; precious jewels are boundless.
In the past, there was a sentient being who gave the Buddha seven coins; by relinquishing his body, he still attained the rank of a Wheel-Turning King.

How much more so when, before our very eyes, the void is exhausted and the Buddha-lands are filled everywhere with such precious jewels? Even if one were to contemplate this for an entire kalpa, it would still not suffice."
"It is possible. How could there be any limit to this merit? The Buddha told Ānanda, "The words of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas are never false.

If there were another person who had committed the four grave offenses and the ten pārājika offenses (translated here as 'abandonments'), they would pass through the Avīci hells of this world and other worlds in a mere instant, continuing until they have exhausted the entirety of the ten directions of the Uninterrupted Hells, experiencing them all without exception."
If one can, with a single thought, take up this Dharma-door and reveal it to those of later learning during the final age, that person's karmic obstacles will be extinguished at that very moment.
The causes for the suffering of the hells they were to undergo will be transformed into a land of peace and bliss.
The merit they obtain shall surpass that of the previous donor by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, ten million billionfold, and even beyond all calculation or analogy.
[The opponent] could not reach [this conclusion].
Tong said: "If space were filled to overflowing with the seven treasures, would there be such a thing in the world?
Yet, when viewed with the Buddha-eye, churning the long rivers into cream and curd, or transforming the great earth into gold, are but ordinary matters; how much more so [the case at hand]!"
The wondrous nature of True Suchness is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm; this is the family treasure.
By being able to realize the pure Dharmakāya, one arrives at the place of the supreme jewel. How could this jewel not fill all of empty space?
Thus, even when offering the seven worldly treasures—gold, silver, pearls, shells, coral, agate, and mother-of-pearl—to the Buddha, it is still [merely a worldly practice].
One shall obtain immeasurable merit. To offer this profound resolve to every dust mote and land is what is called repaying the Buddha’s kindness.
It enables every person to reach the place of treasure; for this is the supramundane treasure that can distinguish between mundane treasures.

Therefore, it cannot be equaled by any worldly treasure. The meritorious retribution obtained from it is likewise beyond calculation. Not only does one obtain merit, but one can also eliminate transgressions.
Merit brings its own retribution, and transgression brings its own retribution; merit and transgression do not offset one another.
Thus, even if one attains celestial blessings, one cannot escape the suffering of hell. Among all sins, none are more grave than the five heinous acts (*pañcānantarya*).
Killing one’s father, harming one’s mother, shedding the blood of a Buddha, and causing a schism in the Saṃgha—these are merely cited as the four grave offenses (catvāraḥ pārājikāḥ).
Parents are of one essence; the Three Jewels (triratna) are not to be treated lightly. What was previously called the "four abandonments" refers to killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying;
what was called the "eight abandonments," and here the "ten abandonments," do not in total go beyond the ten unwholesome karmas (daśākuśalakarmapatha), which are as stated before.

The ten habitual causes result in the sixfold mutual retributions. For those whose karmic offenses are heavy, when this current Avīci Hell is destroyed, they are transferred to other regions, eventually reaching the Avīci Hells of the ten directions, where they must experience each one in turn; how bitter it is!

Yet, with a single thought of turning the mind, one may take this Dharma-treasure and reveal it to those of later learning, transforming delusion into awakening and transforming afflictions into Bodhi.

Ti. Although one remains within the ocean of birth and death, there is inherently the bliss of nirvana. This is a matter of self-repentance for one’s own transgressions and self-liberation from one’s own karma;
even a Buddha cannot bestow this power upon another. To be without transgression is itself to obtain merit;
to be without suffering is itself to experience bliss. Therefore, those who reveal the Dharma-treasure to others not only exempt themselves from sin, but also cause [others] to...
Everyone shall be exempt from their transgressions. Not only will they obtain blessings for themselves, but they shall also cause everyone else to obtain those blessings.
Not only will they acquire treasures for themselves, but they shall also cause everyone to acquire the supreme treasure. When treasures fill the world, how could they have a fixed location?
How, then, can one compare the amount of merit obtained by offering the seven treasures to the Buddha with [other merits]? Although the Buddha—
Speaking truthful words exempts one from transgression and brings merit; such are its immeasurable virtues.
This sutra is clearly praised as being pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm, inexhaustible and peerless in its majesty.
A monk asked Zen Master Daling, "What is meant by 'pure in all places'? Daling replied, "When cutting the branches of jade, every inch is [jade]."
Jewel. When sandalwood is split, every fragment is fragrant. Danxia’s verse says: "Heaven and earth are entirely golden bones; all phenomena fully manifest the pure and wondrous body.
The jade maiden turns her back to the wind, neither clever nor clumsy; the numinous sprout blooms with elegance, unaware of spring.
If this is so, then would there not be no further appearances of hell and the like? Why, then, was Devadatta born directly into hell?
This refers to the Avīci Hell. Devadatta slandered the Buddha and was cast alive into hell.
The Buddha commanded Ānanda to convey his message: "How are you faring within the hell? Devadatta replied, "Though I am in hell, it is as pleasant as the third dhyāna heaven.
The Buddha again commanded Ānanda to ask, "Do you intend to seek release? Devadatta replied, "I shall emerge as soon as the World-Honored One arrives."
Ānanda said, "The World-Honored One is the Great Teacher of the Three Realms; how could he have any portion [of karma] that leads to the hells?
Dadao said, "How could I have any portion [of karma] that leads me out of hell? Cuiyan Zhen said, "These words were spoken by the person himself from his own mouth.
Tishya (Devadatta) was the Buddha’s cousin and Ānanda’s elder brother; having already attained supernatural powers, he pushed a mountain to crush the Buddha. At that time, there was a Vajra...
He attempted to protect [the Buddha], yet he wounded his own feet and hands until they bled. Desiring to harm the Buddha, he gathered all his followers;

however, while traveling halfway there, he fell alive into hell. This was because even when he was the king of deer, he had already practiced together with the Buddha, and now their feelings were as equal as those of siblings;
thus this transformation occurred. Furthermore, it was because his deluded mind was too heavy. It was not yet...
It is easy to turn back [from the path], but one must wait until the karmic fires of hell have burned everything dry before awakening can arise.
The Buddha prophesied that Devadatta would also become a Buddha after many kalpas; yet, while in hell, he had no perception of entering or leaving it.
Who knows that he might not transform that very hell into a Land of Bliss?
Ānanda, if there are sentient beings who can recite this sutra and uphold this mantra as I have extensively explained— though one could not exhaust them even at the end of an eon—
and who follow my instructions and practice the Way according to the teaching, they will directly attain Bodhi, and no further demonic activities shall arise.
The Master said: "A single thought can transform [one's state], thereby eliminating karmic offenses and attaining immeasurable merit.

If one can constantly recite this sutra and constantly maintain this dharani, the blessings obtained will not be exhausted even throughout kalpas as numerous as dust motes. If one can practice the Way according to the teachings,"
One will certainly attain perfect enlightenment, and no further demonic activities will arise.

This sutra and this mantra are most thorough and complete in elucidating the wondrous awakening, and most comprehensive and exhaustive in guarding against the demons of the five skandhas; thus, demons cannot cause delusion.
Thus, the Way of Awakening is accomplished. However, if one maintains the recitation of mantras and sutras without clarifying one's own nature, one will again be bound by demons.

A monk asked Baizhang: "When it is said that 'to rely on the sutras to explain their meaning is to be at enmity with the Buddhas of the three ages, and to deviate from a single word of the sutras is to speak like a demon,' what does this mean?
Baizhang replied: "To cling to stillness and movement is to be at enmity with the Buddhas of the three ages; apart from this, there is nothing else."
"Seeking [the truth] while speaking like a demon. Later, a monk asked Tong’an, "To interpret the meaning according to the sutras is to be at enmity with the Buddhas of the three periods;
to deviate from a single word of the sutras is to speak like a demon. What is the principle behind this? Tong’an said, "A solitary peak rises loftily, unattached to mists and clouds;
a sliver of moon spans the sky, while white clouds drift apart on their own. Danxia’s verse says: "Clouds fly high on their own, the water..."
Self-flowing. Sea and sky vast and open, a hollow boat floats upon them. At night, one does not stay to lodge in a reed cove;
one stands far beyond both the middle and the two ends. This is neither identical to nor separate from the meaning of the scriptures;
it possesses its own point of emergence. If one can awaken to this, demons cannot delude them. Chan Master Daoshu of Shouzhou understood the subtle under the words of Shenxiu.

He then divined a site at Mount Sanfeng in Shouzhou and settled there, dwelling in a thatched hut. There was often a rustic man who wore simple, plain clothing and whose speech and demeanor were strange and unconventional.
Beyond his ordinary laughter and conversation, he would manifest the form of a Buddha, or the forms of bodhisattvas, arhats, celestial immortals, and so forth.
At times he emitted divine light, and at other times produced resonant sounds. When the disciples witnessed these phenomena, none could fathom their origin. As it was said:
This lasted for ten years. Afterwards, [the spirit] became silent, leaving no trace or form. The Master addressed the assembly, saying:

"The wild man employs many-colored arts and wiles to dazzle and delude people; it requires only that this old monk neither see nor hear him. His arts and wiles are finite, while my non-seeing and non-hearing are inexhaustible.
If you understand the principle of the inexhaustibility of non-seeing and non-hearing, you will reach right up to Bodhi."
He has never lacked anything. Since the Māra of the aggregates (*skandha-māra*) has been utterly extinguished, what need is there to fear any other celestial Māras?

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, all the worldlings, devas, humans, asuras, as well as the bodhisattvas, followers of the two vehicles, holy seers, youths, and those who have first resolved [to attain enlightenment] from other directions...
The powerful spirits and deities were all greatly delighted; they paid their respects and departed.
Tong said: "The Buddha’s preaching of this sutra is the most supreme, perfect, and sudden Dharma-gate. The Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice."
Each understood according to their own kind; thus, according to the measure of what they had realized, they all attained the joy of the Dharma and departed with leaping exultation. Why was this?
Because the nature that has existed from the beginning is fully possessed by each and every one. Thus, Zhaozhou addressed the assembly, saying: "Studying the scriptures is within birth and death;
not studying the scriptures is also within birth and death. How, then, do you all intend to escape?"
He departed. The monk then asked, "What about when neither is retained? Zhizhou said, "If it is real, then one attains it;
if it is not real, how can one escape birth and death? Tiantong’s verse says: Even while reading sutras, one is still within birth and death; sitting amidst a basket of food, there is nothing to eat.
Even while not reading sutras, one is still within birth and death; amidst a heap of brocade robes, there is nothing [to wear].
He was about to step onto it when, suddenly, a crow cawed once. He turned his body and leaped for joy, the whole family delighted.
Do not hesitate! Now he is cast before the multitude; even the Great Compassionate One with a thousand hands cannot lift him up.

When the Master of the Seat from Western Sichuan arrived at Huayan, he asked whether the meaning of the Patriarchs and the meaning of the Teachings were the same or different. Huayan said: "They are like the two wheels of a cart, like the two wings of a bird."
The two attendants said, "We thought there was something extraordinary and unique about the Zen school; it turns out it does not transcend the meaning of the teachings.
Later, hearing that Jia Shan’s transformation was flourishing, they sent a junior disciple to inquire about their previous remarks. Jia Shan replied, "'Carving sand' is no talk of engraving jade;
'tying grass' contradicts the intent of a man of the Way. When the junior disciple returned and reported this to the Master, the Master praised him.
He paid homage from afar, saying: "I thought that the meaning of the Chan school was no different from that of the Teachings; it turns out there is something truly extraordinary here.

He did not see that a monk once asked Muzhou, "Are the intent of the Patriarchs and the intent of the Teachings the same or different? Muzhou replied, "The green mountains are themselves green mountains;
the white clouds are themselves white clouds. Tiantong took up this case and said: "If you can recognize Muzhou at this point, you will understand."
From the appearance of the Buddha in the world to the coming of the Dharma from the West, these have all been men who did not abide within their proper bounds.

Do you recognize them? "The arms are long, but the sleeves of the robe are short; the legs are thin, but the straw sandals are wide. A monk asked Luopu, "Are the meaning of the Patriarchs and the meaning of the Teachings the same or different?
Luopu said, "The sun and moon revolve together in their brilliance; who says there is another path? The monk said, "If that is so..."
Manifestation and concealment follow divergent paths; right and wrong are not of one measure. Pufu said: "If you have simply not lost your sheep yourself, why must you weep at the fork in the road?
Danxia’s verse says: "The moon filters shadows through pine trees high and low; the sun shines upon the heart of the pond, heaven above and earth below."
The blazing sky is magnificent, yet not at its zenith; the full moon in the autumn night is round, yet one does not perceive it as such.
If one realizes this, then where the sun and moon do not reach, there is another heaven and earth. How could those who make a living out of the petty concerns of religious sects ever fathom this?

After writing this "Preface to the Zongtong of the Śūraṅgama," I, Zeng Jinjian—whose courtesy name is Fengyi and whose style name is Shunzheng—a native of Laiyang in Chu, am one whose nature is devoted to the inner scriptures and whose innate faculties are sharp and keen.
Previously, I had gained the recognition of Mr. Wang Fengzhou through my literary achievements; before long, we subsequently formed a bond of spiritual friendship.

Subsequently, he again took Master Luo Jinxī as his teacher, whereby his learning progressed further. He continued to investigate with meticulous refinement and profound reflection, exerting himself to explore the ultimate matter.
In the *wuchen* year of the Wanli era (1583), he served as a Lang in the Ministry of Sacrifices after passing the jinshi examinations;

while bedridden at Shaolin Temple, he suddenly attained awakening upon hearing the sound of a bell and clearly perceived the source of the Dharma. From then on, he was adept in all circumstances, transcending conventional norms and rising above worldly customs. When...

He was esteemed by great elders such as Wang Longxi, Luo Nian’an, and Li Zhuowu, as well as by those with whom he associated, including the renowned worthies Qu Yuanli, Guan Dongming, Yuan Liaofan, and Wang Kengtang;
all praised him, and contemporary opinion accorded with this. Throughout his life, he took it as his personal responsibility to widely protect the holy teachings.
When Jingshan Monastery sought to commission the carving of the Fangce Dazang (the portable edition of the Tripitaka), he...
His power in promoting [the Dharma] was preeminent. He once composed a vow-text together with Yuanli and others, which was carved and included within the Tripitaka.
His writings were extensive; they were all words of definitive meaning realized through his own mind, devoid of the conventional literary habits of worldly discourse.

This treatise consists of ten fascicles. It elucidates the principles of the Truths with clarity and coherence, further extensively incorporating the public cases (*gong'an*) and sayings of past masters to mutually illuminate each section alongside the scriptural texts.
This constitutes an unprecedented innovation and is truly an essential compendium that integrates both the Chan school and the doctrinal teachings (*zong-shuo*).
As stated in the author’s preface, such a work as this ought to exist within the world.
This is the Discourse Master. It is to be regretted that the original woodblocks have long been submerged and extant copies are few and far between.

Therefore, together with two or three others who are dedicated to this school, I have re-carved them in Zhongzhe, so that we may collectively establish a firm and ultimate karmic connection and ensure that the intent of his Dharma-giving remains inexhaustible.
Furthermore, I have gathered old accounts and arranged them in a brief sequence, using this to record a small portion of his life and conduct.
